info.t: Recurrent seizures + anion-gap acidosis + altered consciousness suggest INH toxicity. The complete triad is not required.
Support oxygenation and ventilation; obtain bedside glucose, IV/IO access and cardiac monitoring. Correct hypoglycemia.
Give a benzodiazepine and obtain IV pyridoxine immediately. Open Seizures for doses; do not wait for an INH level.
Call pharmacy and Poison Control now: 1-800-222-1222. Confirm grams available, concentration and delivery time.
Trend pH, lactate, electrolytes, renal function and CK. Persistent coma requires consideration of ongoing nonconvulsive seizures. Severe toxicity needs critical care.
Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, maximum 4 mg, at no more than 2 mg/min. May repeat once after 5 minutes if still seizing; prepare airway support.

Known ingestion: adult initial dose matches INH mass, mg for mg, maximum 5 g. Child initial dose is the lowest of ingested INH mass, 70 mg/kg, or 5 g. These are initial limits, not a total-course ceiling; further dosing requires toxicology guidance. Unknown ingestion: adult 5 g IV; child 70 mg/kg IV, maximum 5 g. Give at 500 mg/min in D5W (5 g takes 10 minutes). If seizures stop early, infuse the remainder over 1–2 hours.

Escalate promptly to ICU/toxicology for anesthetic seizure suppression with airway control and EEG. Additional pyridoxine is toxicologist-directed; Queensland advises reassessing repeat dosing at 30 minutes. Avoid automatic repeat-dose orders.
Urgently arrange IV supply/transfer. Enteral pyridoxine is a toxicologist-directed contingency with aspiration precautions, not a reason to delay resuscitation.

EXTRIP suggests against adding dialysis to standard care. Consider it only in the unusual setting of unavailable standard-dose pyridoxine AND seizures refractory to GABA-A modulators. Evidence is very low quality.

Vitamin B6 → pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP) Glutamate → GABA requires glutamate decarboxylase and its PLP cofactor. INH/metabolites disrupt B6 availability and activation, reducing inhibitory GABA synthesis.

Pyridoxine restores substrate for GABA synthesis. Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor activity. Their actions are complementary; experimental synergy was demonstrated in animals, not a human randomized trial.

Sustained convulsions increase lactate production and oxygen demand. Acidosis and depressed consciousness may be profound; persistent abnormalities require reassessment for continued seizures, hypoperfusion and coingestants.
Sodium-channel blockade does not correct the GABA deficit. Phenytoin/fosphenytoin should not replace pyridoxine and benzodiazepines for INH seizures.

info.h: Do not await the full triad
info.t: Treat the suspected syndrome; seizures may precede the complete presentation.

info.h: Do not wait for an INH level
info.t: Treatment is clinical; confirmation must not delay antidote.

info.h: Do not confuse mg with g
info.t: 1 g = 1,000 mg. Verify formulation and total administered dose.

info.h: Do not substitute prophylactic B6 dosing
info.t: Routine supplementation is not an overdose antidote regimen.
Use the INH-specific seizure rescue pathway.

info.h: Do not equate paralysis with seizure control
info.t: Neuromuscular blockade hides motor activity; use EEG when indicated.

info.h: Do not give enteral antidote into an unprotected airway
info.t: Discuss route and aspiration risk with toxicology.
Follow the narrow EXTRIP exception, not acidosis alone.
- Severe BP with acute organ injury? - Which organ is injured? - Exception present? - Urgency: no organ injury

- First-hour target: SBP no more than 25%, then gradual further reduction within 24 to 48 hours - General case only. Compelling conditions (dissection, pregnancy, pheochromocytoma) use their own goals. Do not dose to a MAP percentage.
- Pick the agent by organ at risk - Pregnancy severe-range pathway - Pitfalls and agents to avoid
- ICU, admit, or discharge decision - Discharge only for urgency
- Use Pediatric hypertensive emergency. Adult numbers do not apply to children.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT drop BP faster than the first-hour limit
info.t: Overly rapid drops can worsen renal, cerebral, or coronary perfusion. In the general case the guideline limit is SBP no more than 25% in the first hour. See first-hour target.
Absorption is unpredictable and hypotension can be abrupt. In pregnancy, use the immediate-release oral protocol only. See pitfalls.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start IV drugs for severe BP without organ injury
info.t: Severe BP without acute organ injury is urgency. It is managed with an oral regimen and reassessment. See urgency node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give hydralazine alone for rate control, or labetalol in reactive airway disease or heart block
info.t: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia. Labetalol is contraindicated in reactive airway disease and should not be given with second- or third-degree heart block or bradycardia. See beta-blocker branch.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the dissection screen
info.t: Tearing pain, a pulse or BP deficit, or a widened mediastinum changes the agent. Beta-blocker is first-line for dissection. See dissection branch.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the general MAP rule for intracerebral hemorrhage
info.t: The ICH target and timing are set in the ICH consult. See ICH branch.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade in pheochromocytoma
info.t: Unopposed alpha stimulation can worsen the crisis. Give phentolamine first. See pheochromocytoma branch.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat cocaine toxicity without toxicology input
info.t: Phentolamine is the listed agent for catecholamine excess, including cocaine toxicity. Toxicology and the chest pain hub govern. See cocaine branch.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give nitroprusside in acute cerebrovascular disease
info.t: Avoid it in acute cerebrovascular disease unless other agents are not available. See nitroprusside.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge severe BP with any organ injury
info.t: Discharge is for urgency only, with no organ injury, reliable oral therapy, follow-up, and clear return precautions. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT size tidal volume on actual body weight
info.t: Tidal volume is set on predicted body weight. Actual weight in an obese or edematous patient gives a large VT and high plateau pressure. Ventilation start

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start at the old high tidal volume
info.t: The 12 mL/kg PBW comparator in the ARDSNet trial had higher mortality than 6 mL/kg PBW. Ventilation start

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT keep plateau above 30 cmH2O
info.t: Reduce VT in 1 mL/kg PBW steps to the 4 mL/kg floor. Plateau above 30 is the protocol trigger to act. Plateau check | Reduce VT

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT chase a normal PaCO2 with high tidal volume
info.t: Permissive hypercapnia is the protocol. Raise rate first. Raise VT only for pH below 7.15, and only then accept plateau above 30. Acidosis

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT label ARDS on a ratio without checking mimics
info.t: The Berlin definition needs PEEP or CPAP of at least 5 cmH2O, bilateral opacities, and no full cardiac or fluid explanation. Start | Berlin check | Mimics

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give liberal fluids once perfusing
info.t: After shock is corrected, the conservative strategy improved ventilator-free and ICU-free days. Do not withhold fluid in shock. Fluids

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start continuous paralysis as routine
info.t: ESICM 2023 strongly recommends against routine continuous neuromuscular blockade in moderate to severe non-COVID ARDS. ATS 2024 conditionally suggests it in early severe ARDS. ROSE showed no mortality benefit from early continuous blockade. Treat the dyssynchrony cause first. Blockade check | Blockade

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay prone when the entry ratio is met
info.t: Prone ventilation reduced 28-day mortality in severe ARDS (P/F <150, FiO2 ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5) on invasive ventilation when sessions were long enough. Check screening, then turn. Prone criteria | Prone schedule

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat ECMO as a proven survival step
info.t: EOLIA did not significantly reduce 60-day mortality and stopped for futility. Refer for assessment when gates are met. ECMO gate | ECMO referral
- Confirm Berlin criteria with an ABG on PEEP of at least 5 - Exclude cardiac and volume mimics - Grade severity

- Size VT on predicted body weight; start 6 mL/kg PBW (2008 protocol summary starts at 8) - Keep plateau at or below 30 cmH2O - Reduce VT in 1 mL/kg steps to a 4 mL/kg floor - Permissive hypercapnia: rate first, VT only below pH 7.15 - Set PEEP and FiO2 pairs, minimum PEEP 5 - Conservative fluids once perfusing

- Prone for severe ARDS (P/F <150, FiO2 ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5), invasive ventilation - Prone session length per ESICM and ATS - No routine continuous neuromuscular blockade for non-COVID ARDS (ATS 2024 conditional in early severe ARDS); treat dyssynchrony cause first
- Check EOLIA-type gates despite optimal ventilation - Refer for ECMO evaluation when gates are met
- ICU admission with the ventilation plan in the handoff

info.h: 🛑 Contusion without shock: avoid reflex large-volume fluid
info.t: With hemorrhagic shock or bleeding, hemorrhage resuscitation still governs. In non-shocked contusion, avoid reflex large-volume fluid (expert opinion). The restrictive-fluid data are observational. Volume overload can worsen oxygenation (consensus). Contusion management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clear a patient on a low RibScore or a normal first film
info.t: RibScore predicts pulmonary complications; it does not rule them out. A normal first film does not exclude occult pneumothorax, hemothorax or contusion. RibScore | Occult injury.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat rib fractures with opioids alone
info.t: Opioid-only plans leave splinting pain in place and limit deep breathing and coughing. Regional block and a multimodal plan are the goal. Analgesia route.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give an NSAID before bleeding and renal review
info.t: Anticoagulation, bleeding risk and reduced renal function change the risk. Check all three before any NSAID. The ketorolac label lists advanced renal impairment, renal-failure risk from volume depletion, and suspected or confirmed bleeding as contraindications. Systemic ladder.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT promise a pneumonia benefit from non-flail fixation
info.t: The pooled signal is mixed-design and mostly non-flail Asian cohorts; the single non-flail controlled trial (partly randomized, 23 of 110) does not report pneumonia in its abstract. Refer to thoracic or trauma surgery; the ED does not decide fixation. Surgical evidence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT change ventilator support without reassessing oxygenation
info.t: Reassess oxygenation after every ventilator change, and reassess work of breathing with it. Flail chest.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge with an unresolved anticoagulation or bleeding question
info.t: Discharge needs oxygenation normal, pain controlled orally and bleeding concerns resolved, with written return precautions. Disposition.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume a flail or bilateral injury is "just ribs"
info.t: A flail or bilateral pattern changes ventilation, analgesia and surgical referral. Fracture pattern.

info.h: 6. Closed loop, cecal, large bowel, hernia
info.t: - Closed loop: surgical consult now - Cecal volvulus: surgical pathway - Malignant large bowel obstruction: stent - Incarcerated hernia with obstruction
- Resus / ICU versus admission

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trial non-operative care with strangulation signs
info.t: Fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, or continuous pain excludes a non-operative trial. Strangulation needs surgery now. Strangulation node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT read a normal exam or a single normal lab as clearance
info.t: Strangulation can be present with a benign exam. Lactate, D-dimer and immature granulocyte counts are observational and conflicting. Use them as context, never to rule out. Strangulation node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip CT with IV contrast for ischemia
info.t: Wall enhancement, ascites, mesenteric haziness and closed-loop pattern decide the route more than the transition point. CT read

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT continue a non-operative trial past its checkpoints
info.t: Strangulation signs go to surgery. At 72 hours without resolution, reassess for surgery; WSES 2017 calls 72 hours a safe trial length and longer is debated. WBC above 10,000/mm3 is a peritonitis marker with low sensitivity and specificity, not a stop rule. Checkpoints

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT read contrast in the colon as cure
info.t: Contrast reaching the colon within 24 hours predicts resolution. It does not establish recurrence risk. Resolving SBO

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt sigmoid endoscopy with ischemia or peritonitis
info.t: Advanced mucosal ischemia, perforation, impending perforation, peritonitis or septic shock means emergency colectomy. Sigmoid entry

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop at sigmoid detorsion, or use detorsion alone, sigmoidopexy or mesosigmoidoplasty for a fit patient
info.t: Detorsion alone recurs. Offer sigmoid colectomy, ideally during the index admission. Endoscopic fixation is for prohibitive operative risk only. Colectomy plan | Prohibitive risk

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stent malignant large bowel obstruction prophylactically or with perforation
info.t: Reserve stent for symptomatic, radiologically confirmed malignant obstruction without perforation. Large bowel node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give water-soluble contrast without safety checks
info.t: Confirm NG position and aspiration precautions, check allergy, and watch for anaphylactoid reaction. Lethal aspiration is reported. The NG route is off-label (label: oral or rectal only). Do NOT give if strangulation, peritonitis or perforation is suspected. Trial node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge from the ED on the basis of this pathway
info.t: No discharge pathway for obstruction is sourced here. Admit and reassess. Disposition

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give fibrinolytics for suspected SCAD
info.t: Fibrinolysis is contraindicated in suspected SCAD per ESC-ACCA 2018. The AHA 2018 statement does not address fibrinolysis. Antithrombotic plan.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anticoagulate SCAD by default
info.t: If anticoagulation was started at presentation with no other indication, consider stopping it once SCAD is diagnosed (AHA 2018). Chronic indications are not sourced in this draft. Antithrombotic plan.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stent a SCAD lesion without intracoronary imaging
info.t: Intracoronary imaging confirms an intramural hematoma or multiple lumens (AHA 2018). Requiring it before every stent, and the wire-position rule, are expert opinion pending sign-off. PCI node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rush a stable SCAD patient to PCI
info.t: Conservative care is generally preferred when the patient is stable with no ongoing ischemia, no hemodynamic instability, and no high-risk anatomy (AHA 2018). Angiographic healing is reported in most restudied patients (observational). Revascularize or conserve.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge conservatively managed SCAD from the ED without cardiology review
info.t: Monitored admission for conservatively managed SCAD; duration and discharge criteria with cardiology. Monitored admission.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give a nitrate before checking for a PDE-5 inhibitor
info.t: Nitrates are contraindicated with sildenafil, vardenafil, and tadalafil. The sildenafil label gives no safe interval after a dose. The tadalafil label contraindicates nitrates. The post-dose interval is not confirmed in this review; do not give a nitrate without a documented PDE-5 washout set by pharmacy or cardiology. Nitrates can cause profound hypotension. Nitroglycerin is a named acute-pain drug in this consult. Vasospasm treatment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume non-selective beta-blockers are safe in vasospasm
info.t: Caution is expert opinion based on a theoretical unopposed alpha effect (AHA 2018 notes concern about worsening vasospasm). Separately, the SCAD beta-blocker question is discussed with cardiology on its own page. Vasospasm treatment. SCAD beta-blocker evidence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the stimulant history in young rest-pain patients
info.t: Ask about cocaine, methamphetamine, and other stimulants. Substance history changes the vasospasm pathway. Stabilise.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT confuse ergonovine with methylergonovine
info.t: Ergonovine is an intracoronary test agent for provocation. Methylergonovine is a postpartum hemorrhage drug. Provocation testing.
• Triage: STEMI pattern, ACS, MINOCA, or mimic • Stabilise: treat as ACS, ask about stimulants and pregnancy • Route by mechanism
• Spasm criteria: nitrate response plus captured ECG or spasm • Cath-lab provocation for spasm • SCAD: dissection on angiography • MINOCA sorting

• SCAD stable, no ongoing ischemia: conservative • SCAD ongoing ischemia: PCI with intracoronary imaging • SCAD antithrombotic limits: no fibrinolytics, antiplatelet conflict • SCAD beta-blocker: evidence • Vasospasm: CCB first, nitrate add-on, PDE-5 check
• Recurrence, follow-up, pregnancy • Disposition by final diagnosis • Monitored admission: SCAD • Discharge: vasospasm with a plan • Escalate: ongoing ischemia or unclear diagnosis

1. Press SIZE. 2. While its menu is open, press SIZE again or rotate SPEED DIAL to a larger size. The manual displays options 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0. Increase from 1.0 to 2.0 or 4.0 as needed to inspect a low-amplitude tracing. 3. Confirm the displayed size and avoid clipping. This changes display gain, NOT shock energy. Alternative: SPEED DIAL → CHANNEL 1 → SIZE → desired size, then press the dial. Prepare controls during CPR and assess the underlying rhythm during the scheduled brief check. Increased gain cannot distinguish noise from VF by itself.

info.pt: MAP Goals in Acute Spinal Cord Injury
info.t: | Parameter | 2013 AANS/CNS | 2024 AO Spine / Praxis | |-----------|---------------|------------------------| | MAP lower bound | 85–90 mmHg | 75–80 mmHg | | MAP upper bound | (none stated) | 90–95 mmHg | | Duration | 7 days | 3–7 days | | Strength | Level III | Suggested — treatment option | The 2024 guideline widened the window deliberately: a 5-mmHg band (85–90) is not practically maintainable at the bedside, and chasing it drives vasopressor escalation without demonstrated benefit.

info.pt: MAP Goals in Acute Spinal Cord Injury
info.t: Weak. This is one of the softest standard-of-care numbers in neurotrauma. • The 85–90 mmHg figure traces to small observational cohorts and a single prospective series — no randomized trial has ever compared MAP targets in acute SCI. • The 2024 guideline graded its own recommendation as a suggestion, not a standard. • Evidence was judged insufficient to recommend any spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) target, despite SCPP being mechanistically more sensible than MAP. • Observational data associate both MAP <75 and MAP >95 mmHg with worse neurologic outcomes and more adverse events — this is why an upper bound now exists. Over-augmentation is not benign. Bottom line: aim 75–95 mmHg. Do not

info.pt: MAP Goals in Acute Spinal Cord Injury
info.t: No vasopressor has been shown superior in acute SCI. The 2024 guideline found no included study evaluating norepinephrine for safety or effectiveness in this population. | Agent | Comment | |-------|---------| | Norepinephrine | Common first choice on expert consensus — α + β activity supports both MAP and chronotropy in neurogenic shock. Not guideline-validated. | | Dopamine | Associated with increased complications, particularly in patients >55 years. Avoid. | | Phenylephrine | Pure α — may worsen reflex bradycardia in high cervical injury. | Neurogenic shock is a diagnosis of exclusion in trauma. Rule out hemorrhage before attributing hypotension to cord injury.

info.pt: MAP Goals in Acute Spinal Cord Injury
info.t: • Arterial line — cuff pressures are inadequate for titrating a narrow window. • Start the clock at injury, not at ICU arrival. • 3 days is an acceptable duration. The 2024 range is 3–7 days; 7 days is not mandatory and each additional pressor-day carries risk. • Bradycardia from unopposed vagal tone in cervical cord injury may need atropine or chronotropic support independent of MAP. • Treat the correctable causes of low MAP first (hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, tamponade) before crediting the cord.

A fractured or disrupted larynx is a structurally unstable conduit. Every standard airway manoeuvre assumes the airway is a tube that holds its shape. Here it does not. Two failure modes drive everything below: 1. False passage — a blindly advanced tube or bougie dissects through disrupted mucosa into the paratracheal soft tissue. The airway is now lost and the neck is filling with air and blood. 2. Completing a partial separation — a partially transected larynx or cricotracheal junction is held in continuity by remaining soft tissue. Instrumentation, or the distal end retracting into the mediastinum, converts it to complete separation.

info.h: Why Blind / Unguided Intubation Is Hazardous
info.t: • The tube follows the path of least resistance, which in a fractured larynx is through the fracture, not through the glottis. • Mucosal disruption, submucosal haematoma and oedema obliterate the normal landmarks — a cords-visible impression can be a mucosal flap. • Passing a tube can displace fracture fragments distally. • Paralysis abolishes the patient's own compensation. A patient maintaining a marginal airway with tone and positioning may lose it entirely at induction, with no reliable rescue below.

info.h: Why Cricothyrotomy Is Not the Rescue Here
info.t: This is the counterintuitive point. • Cricothyrotomy enters at the cricothyroid membrane — inside the zone of injury. In laryngeal fracture you are cutting into the fractured structure itself. • In complete laryngotracheal separation, cricothyrotomy serves little purpose and can convert a partial separation into a complete one. The distal trachea has already retracted; the cricothyroid membrane no longer leads anywhere useful. • Laryngeal fracture and laryngotracheal disruption are relative contraindications to cricothyrotomy — one of the few settings where the surgical-airway-always-works heuristic is false. • Cricotracheal separation carries reported mortality ~27–40%, much of it airway-re

| Approach | Role | |----------|------| | Awake tracheostomy under local, distal to the injury | First choice in significant laryngeal trauma. Enters below the injured segment, preserves spontaneous ventilation, no paralysis. Use a cuffed, non-fenestrated tube. | | Awake flexible fiberoptic intubation | Reasonable when the airway is stable and you need to visualise before committing. Blood and secretions frequently defeat it — have the trach set open. | | Endotracheal intubation | Acceptable only if Schaefer's criteria are met (below). | | RSI / direct laryngoscopy | Avoid. | | Cricothyrotomy | Last-ditch CICO only, accepting it may fail or worsen the injury. | Never leave the bedside. These

info.h: Schaefer's Criteria — When Intubation Is Acceptable
info.t: Intubation may be considered in laryngeal trauma only when all three hold: 1. The larynx and trachea are clearly intact and in continuity 2. The airway is visualised by direct endoscopic inspection 3. The operator is highly experienced If any one is uncertain, the answer is a tracheostomy distal to the injury.

• Subcutaneous emphysema (especially expanding) • Hoarseness, voice change, aphonia • Stridor • Haemoptysis • Loss of palpable thyroid cartilage prominence / palpable step-off • Odynophagia, dysphagia • Anterior neck tenderness or ecchymosis over the larynx Any of these mandates airway planning before imaging. A CT is only for patients you are confident will keep breathing while inside the scanner.

HI-MAP — the original five windows: Heart, IVC, Morison's (FAST), Aorta, Pneumothorax. Memory aid: the patient has a low MAP, you want a HI-MAP. Pump / Tank / Pipes — Perera's expanded framing, which adds pleural effusion, interstitial (B-line) assessment, and lower-extremity DVT. Same protocol, different scaffolding. This app's hypotension consult uses HI-MAP at the bedside; the physiologic grouping below is how to *think* about the findings. Target time: 2–5 minutes.

Four windows: parasternal long, parasternal short, apical 4-chamber, subxiphoid. | Finding | Points to | |---------|-----------| | Pericardial effusion + RA/RV diastolic collapse | Tamponade — obstructive | | Hyperdynamic, small, kissing LV | Hypovolaemic or distributive | | Poor LV contractility, dilated LV | Cardiogenic | | RV ≥ LV, septal flattening (D-sign), McConnell's | Massive PE — obstructive | Global contractility by eyeball is enough. Do not chase EF numbers in a crashing patient.

Fullness — IVC (subxiphoid long axis, 2 cm from RA junction) | IVC | Suggests | |-----|----------| | Small (<2 cm), >50% respiratory collapse | Low CVP — volume responsive | | Plump (>2 cm), minimal collapse | High CVP — volume is not the answer | Leakiness — FAST + thoracic windows Free fluid in Morison's, splenorenal, pelvis → haemorrhage or third-spacing. In RUSH, slide the RUQ/LUQ probe superiorly to look above the diaphragm for pleural effusion / haemothorax. Compromise — lungs • Absent lung sliding + lung point → pneumothorax (obstructive) • Diffuse B-lines → interstitial oedema — the tank is overfilled or leaking

Arterial: abdominal aorta from epigastrium to bifurcation. • Outer-wall-to-outer-wall >3 cm = aneurysm. In a hypotensive patient with a AAA, assume rupture and stop scanning. • Intimal flap → dissection. Also check the proximal aorta on parasternal long. Venous: two-point compression of femoral and popliteal veins. • Non-compressible vein + RV strain = PE with a confirmed source.

| Shock type | Pump | Tank | Pipes | |-----------|------|------|-------| | Hypovolaemic | Hyperdynamic, small LV | Flat IVC ± free fluid | AAA / aortic rupture | | Cardiogenic | Poor contractility, dilated LV | Plump IVC, B-lines, effusions | Normal | | Obstructive | Effusion + collapse, or RV strain | Plump IVC; PTX if no sliding | DVT if PE | | Distributive | Hyperdynamic early, depressed late | Normal/flat IVC, peritoneal fluid if source | Normal |

• RUSH classifies shock; it does not exclude a diagnosis. A normal RUSH does not rule out PE, sepsis, or adrenal crisis. • Operator-dependent. Meta-analytic accuracy is good for obstructive and hypovolaemic shock, weakest for distributive. • Mixed shock is common and defeats a single-category read. Treat the finding in front of you and rescan after intervention. • IVC assessment is unreliable in mechanical ventilation, raised intra-abdominal pressure, and isolated RV failure.

info.h: The Number That Matters in Trauma
info.t: Hypotension thresholds — systolic BP below which a child is hypotensive: | Age | Hypotension if SBP < | |-----|----------------------| | Term neonate (0–28 d) | 60 mmHg | | Infant (1–12 mo) | 70 mmHg | | Child (1–10 y) | 70 + (2 × age in years) | | >10 y | 90 mmHg | Worked: a 4-year-old is hypotensive below 78 mmHg (70 + 8). ⚠️ This is the 5th-percentile floor, not a goal. It is the number below which a child is unambiguously abnormal — not a resuscitation target. A child sitting one point above it is not reassuring. ⚠️ Hypotension in a child is a LATE finding. Children compensate by tachycardia and vasoconstriction and can lose 30–45% of blood volume before SBP falls. By the time the number

| Age | Awake | Sleeping | |-----|-------|----------| | Neonate (0–28 d) | 100–205 | 90–160 | | Infant (1–12 mo) | 100–180 | 90–160 | | Toddler (1–3 y) | 98–140 | 80–120 | | Preschool (3–5 y) | 80–120 | 65–100 | | School age (6–12 y) | 75–118 | 58–90 | | Adolescent (12–21 y) | 60–100 | 50–90 | Bradycardia in a child is a peri-arrest sign until proven otherwise — usually hypoxia. Oxygenate and ventilate before you reach for atropine. Compressions at HR <60 with poor perfusion.

| Age | Breaths/min | |-----|-------------| | Infant (<1 y) | 30–60 | | Toddler (1–3 y) | 24–40 | | Preschool (3–5 y) | 22–34 | | School age (6–12 y) | 18–30 | | Adolescent (≥12 y) | 12–18 | A normalising respiratory rate in a previously tachypneic distressed child is an ominous sign, not an improving one — it usually means fatigue.

info.h: Systolic BP — Lower Limits of Normal
info.t: | Age | SBP lower limit | |-----|-----------------| | Term neonate (0–28 d) | 60 | | Infant (1–12 mo) | 70 | | 1–10 y | 70 + (2 × age) | | >10 y | 90 | Use an appropriately sized cuff — a cuff that is too small reads falsely high and will mask shock.

• These bands come from healthy resting children; they are consensus values, not strongly evidence-based, and they overlap widely with illness. • Fever, pain, fear, crying and a strange room all raise HR and RR. Interpret a single set of numbers with the child, not instead of the child. • Trends beat snapshots. A serially rising HR at rest is more meaningful than one out-of-range value. • Use a length-based resuscitation tape for weight-based dosing rather than age estimates. • Chronic conditions, congenital heart disease and beta-blockade invalidate the bands entirely.

| Type | Mnemonic | Fracture line | |------|----------|---------------| | I | S — Slipped | Through the physis only | | II | A — Above | Physis + metaphysis (Thurston-Holland fragment). Most common (~75%) | | III | L — Lower | Physis + epiphysis, into the joint | | IV | T — Through | Metaphysis + physis + epiphysis | | V | R — Rammed | Crush of the physis | Physeal fractures are 15–30% of all paediatric bony injuries. The physis is weaker than the surrounding ligament, so the mechanism that sprains an adult ankle fractures a child's physis.

| Type | Arrest risk | Why | |------|-------------|-----| | I | Low | Line runs through the hypertrophic zone; germinal and proliferative layers spared | | II | Low | Same plane as I; metaphyseal fragment does not involve germinal layer | | III | Higher | Crosses the germinal layer and the articular surface | | IV | Higher | Crosses the germinal layer, articular surface, and risks a bony bridge across the physis | | V | Highest / worst prognosis | Germinal layer crushed. Usually diagnosed retrospectively — initial films are often normal | Overall physeal complication rate is roughly 2–14%. ⚠️ Important caveat — do not counsel families off the type alone. Salter-Harris type has poor predictiv

Types I and II — usually closed reduction and immobilisation. • Accept some residual displacement; remodelling potential is high in the young. • Avoid repeated forceful reduction attempts — each attempt is another insult to the physis. One good reduction beats three mediocre ones. Types III and IV — these are intra-articular. • ≥2 mm displacement or articular step-off → surgical fixation. • <2 mm may be managed non-operatively with close radiographic follow-up. • Fixation principle: screws placed transversely within the epiphysis, parallel to and not crossing the physis. If the physis must be crossed, use smooth pins or wires and remove them early. Type V — often unrecognised acutely. Immobi

• Tillaux fracture — SH III of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis, in adolescents whose medial physis has already closed. • Triplane fracture — SH IV of the distal tibia; appears as SH III on AP and SH II on lateral. CT is usually required to define it. Both are transitional fractures of late adolescence and both are intra-articular — the ≥2 mm rule applies.

Every physeal fracture, including type I, needs orthopaedic follow-up until skeletal maturity or until documented normal growth. • Growth arrest is not apparent at the time of injury. It presents months to years later as angular deformity or limb length discrepancy. • Serial radiographs assess for physeal bar formation. • Counsel the family at discharge that a simple growth plate fracture requires long-term monitoring — this is the single most commonly missed step. • A normal radiograph does not exclude a SH I or SH V. Point tenderness over a physis after an appropriate mechanism is treated as a fracture.

info.h: Why It Matters in the ED
info.t: Your consultant will ask which tooth, and will not accept the front one on the top left. Getting the number right the first time is the difference between a five-minute call and a photograph exchange. The Universal Tooth Designation System is the ADA standard in the United States (adopted 1968), also called the American system. Two systems you may encounter but should not use in a US chart: • FDI (ISO 3950) — two-digit; permanent 11–18/21–28/31–38/41–48, primary 51–55/61–65/71–75/81–85. Standard internationally. • Palmer — quadrant bracket + number 1–8. UK, Australia.

The path: start at the patient's upper right third molar (#1), run across the upper arch to the upper left third molar (#16), drop straight down to the lower left third molar (#17), and run back across the lower arch to the lower right third molar (#32). A single continuous loop. Upper (maxillary) — patient's right to left | # | Tooth | # | Tooth | |---|-------|---|-------| | 1 | R 3rd molar (wisdom) | 9 | L central incisor | | 2 | R 2nd molar | 10 | L lateral incisor | | 3 | R 1st molar | 11 | L canine | | 4 | R 2nd premolar | 12 | L 1st premolar | | 5 | R 1st premolar | 13 | L 2nd premolar | | 6 | R canine | 14 | L 1st molar | | 7 | R lateral incisor | 15 | L 2nd molar | | 8 | R central in

Primary (deciduous) teeth are lettered, always uppercase. Same loop, 20 teeth. Upper: A = upper right 2nd molar → J = upper left 2nd molar Lower: K = lower left 2nd molar → T = lower right 2nd molar | Upper | Tooth | Lower | Tooth | |-------|-------|-------|-------| | A | R 2nd molar | K | L 2nd molar | | B | R 1st molar | L | L 1st molar | | C | R canine | M | L canine | | D | R lateral incisor | N | L lateral incisor | | E | R central incisor | O | L central incisor | | F | L central incisor | P | R central incisor | | G | L lateral incisor | Q | R lateral incisor | | H | L canine | R | R canine | | I | L 1st molar | S | R 1st molar | | J | L 2nd molar | T | R 2nd molar | Letters versus nu

• Chart orientation is from the dentist's view, facing the patient — the patient's right appears on the left of the chart. When you say #8, say the patient's right upper central incisor as well. Redundancy costs nothing. • Missing, unerupted and extracted teeth still hold their number. The count never shifts. • Supernumerary permanent teeth are numbered 51–82, following the same loop (#51 sits beside #1; #82 beside #32). • A mixed dentition (roughly ages 6–12) will have both numbers and letters in the same mouth. Chart what you actually see. • Count, don't guess. Start from the midline and work outward: central incisor, lateral incisor, canine, 1st premolar, 2nd premolar, 1st molar, 2nd mola

Record all four: 1. Number or letter (e.g. #8, or E) 2. Plain-language name (upper right central incisor) 3. Permanent vs primary 4. Injury and extraoral dry time (e.g. avulsed, 25 min dry, transported in milk) Example: #8 — permanent upper right central incisor — avulsed, 25 min extraoral dry time, transported in milk, replanted at 32 min, flexible splint applied.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call it a benign hydrocele until torsion is excluded
info.t: "Painless" is a trap. Intermittent torsion/detorsion presents as recurrent, waxing-waning swelling, and malignancy is classically painless — labeling the mass benign on first look is how testes and diagnoses are lost. Run the Sick Check first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay the OR for imaging when the torsion exam is convincing
info.t: A high TWIST score, an abnormal lie, or an absent cremasteric reflex is a straight-to-OR situation. Salvage falls off sharply after ~6 hours of ischemia, and a Doppler that delays exploration costs the testis. Emergent urology + manual detorsion.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on Prehn sign to rule out torsion
info.t: Epididymo-orchitis is the main torsion mimic, and a positive Prehn sign or a preserved cremasteric reflex does NOT exclude torsion. When you cannot confidently exclude it, get a Doppler and urology — a missed torsion loses the testis. When in doubt, image.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for imaging in suspected Fournier gangrene
info.t: Pain out of proportion plus systemic toxicity, crepitus, or dusky skin is a surgical emergency — mortality rises with every hour to debridement. Resuscitate and get surgery to the bedside; CT only if it will not delay the OR. Emergent debridement.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt taxis on a hernia with strangulation signs
info.t: A single gentle reduction is reasonable only when there are NO signs of strangulation. Severe tenderness, skin change, or toxicity means reducing dead bowel back into the abdomen — that is dangerous; go to emergent surgery, not manual pressure. Reduce / surgery gate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT biopsy a solid intratesticular mass transscrotally
info.t: A firm, non-transilluminating intratesticular mass is a tumor until proven otherwise. Transscrotal biopsy violates lymphatic planes and seeds tumor — the standard is scrotal US + AFP/beta-hCG/LDH and urgent urology for radical inguinal orchiectomy. Tumor pathway.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss a persistent erection as mere swelling
info.t: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is time-critical for erectile function — a rigid, painful erection >4 h needs corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine, not observation. The same urgency applies to any constricting object or paraphimosis. Time-critical detumescence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a new adult hydrocele or right-sided varicocele without ultrasound
info.t: A new or tense adult hydrocele can hide an underlying tumor, and a new right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele can signal a retroperitoneal/renal mass. Reassure only after imaging excludes these. Outpatient ultrasound.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT lay a massively bleeding patient flat/supine
info.t: Patients with massive hemoptysis die of asphyxiation, not exsanguination — supine positioning soils both lungs and drowns the good one. Position bleeding-lung-DOWN and secure the airway early with a large ETT. Massive hemoptysis airway priorities.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay IR embolization or bronchoscopy chasing a perfect diagnosis
info.t: In massive bleeding, definitive control comes from bronchial artery embolization and rigid bronchoscopy — waiting for a tidy diagnosis lets the patient bleed into the airway. Call IR and thoracics NOW; CTA localizes once stable. But do not oversell the embolization: technical success is 81-100% and immediate clinical success 70-99%, yet 10-58% rebleed, and spinal cord infarction from non-target embolization occurs in 0.2-6.5%. It buys time; it does not cure the cause. Control the airway and the vessel first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT leave a suspected-TB patient in an open ED bay
info.t: Hemoptysis with fever, weight loss, or night sweats is active pulmonary TB until excluded, and an unmasked patient in an open bay exposes every staff member and patient nearby. Airborne-isolate first (N95, negative pressure, mask the patient), diagnose second. Isolate before you work it up.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anticoagulate a confirmed PE into a massive pulmonary bleed
info.t: Minor infarct-related hemoptysis does not preclude anticoagulation, but massive/brisk hemoptysis flips the calculus — full anticoagulation into a life-threatening lung bleed can be fatal. Treat the bleeding first, weigh clot burden, and consider an IVC filter. When massive bleeding contraindicates anticoagulation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reverse anticoagulation for blood-tinged sputum
info.t: Reversal is for life-threatening bleeding only — reflexively reversing minor streaking exposes a mechanical valve, recent VTE, or fresh stent to catastrophic thrombosis. Weigh thrombotic risk, and never stop at the blood thinner: the amplifier is not the diagnosis, so still work the source. Reserve reversal for the life-threat.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call it "just bronchitis" in a smoker ≥40 or with weight loss
info.t: Bronchitis is the commonest cause of mild hemoptysis, but a smoker ≥40, weight loss, or recurrent bleeding demands imaging and follow-up to exclude malignancy — anchoring on bronchitis misses lung cancer. Image and arrange follow-up before you reassure.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT work up a GI bleed as hemoptysis
info.t: Misattributed hematemesis (dark, coffee-ground, acidic, preceded by nausea) sent down the pulmonary pathway delays endoscopy and transfusion. Confirm the blood is truly pulmonary — bright, frothy, alkaline, coughed — before committing; always ask "vomited or coughed?" Exclude pseudohemoptysis first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge on a normal chest X-ray alone
info.t: Malignancy can present with a single small bleed and a normal CXR — a benign film does not exclude a serious cause. Discharge only trivial, stopped, low-risk bleeding with reliable follow-up, and complete the outpatient CT if any risk feature is present. Safe-discharge criteria and return precautions.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on "it's probably a DVT"
info.t: A swollen leg hides limb- and life-threats that share the presentation: acute ischemia, phlegmasia, necrotizing infection, compartment syndrome, and DVT with PE. A cold pulseless limb, a dusky tense limb, or pain out of proportion overrides the DVT reflex — work the limb-threat first. Sick Check first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for imaging before calling surgery in a necrotizing infection
info.t: "Cellulitis" that hurts far more than it looks, with toxicity, crepitus, or dusky/bullous skin, is a necrotizing soft-tissue infection and a surgical emergency. Mortality rises with every hour of delay — a convincing exam goes straight to the OR for debridement, not to the CT scanner. Emergent debridement, do not wait for imaging.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for a pulseless limb to diagnose compartment syndrome
info.t: Pulselessness is a LATE finding — rising compartment pressure strangles muscle and nerve within hours while pulses are still present. Act on a tense compartment with pain on passive stretch and paresthesia; fasciotomy is time-critical. Do not wait for pulselessness.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT elevate or apply cold to an ischemic limb
info.t: In acute limb ischemia, elevation and cold both drop perfusion pressure and worsen the ischemia. Keep the limb dependent and warm, anticoagulate with heparin, and get emergent vascular surgery — salvage is time-dependent. Keep the limb warm and dependent.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for the leg ultrasound when chest symptoms suggest PE
info.t: A swollen leg with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, or hypoxia is a pulmonary embolism until excluded. Start anticoagulation and work up the PE (CTPA, assess stability) now — do not delay treatment waiting on the leg ultrasound. Work up the PE now.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT blame asymmetric edema on the heart and miss a superimposed DVT
info.t: Heart failure can present asymmetrically, but a failing, immobile patient is prothrombotic — cardiac edema and DVT coexist. Do not anchor on "cardiac edema" and skip the DVT workup in the asymmetric leg. Still exclude a superimposed DVT.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust a single negative ultrasound when DVT suspicion is high
info.t: A negative initial compression ultrasound can miss a propagating calf-vein thrombus. If clinical suspicion remains high, arrange a repeat ultrasound in about one week rather than clearing the patient outright. Repeat US in ~1 week if suspicion is high.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat "cellulitis" with pain out of proportion as benign
info.t: Cellulitis can be early necrotizing infection and can hide a coexisting DVT. Mark the border and reassess — pain out of proportion, toxicity, crepitus, or rapid spread sends you back to surgery, and prominent swelling warrants excluding a DVT. Keep the necrotizing and DVT safety nets up.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clear a hip on a normal X-ray when the patient cannot bear weight
info.t: A normal or subtle plain film does NOT rule out an occult or insufficiency fracture in the elderly/osteoporotic patient with groin pain who cannot walk. Missed fractures displace with continued weight-bearing and lead to AVN and immobility — get MRI (detects within hours) or CT before calling it safe. Occult fracture — advanced imaging.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss an adolescent's knee or thigh pain
info.t: Up to a quarter of SCFE cases present with knee/thigh pain and NO hip complaint — the classic trap. An obese teen 8-15 with out-toeing and obligate external rotation on passive flexion needs a frog-leg lateral of both hips, not a knee workup. SCFE — adolescent gate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT let a suspected SCFE keep bearing weight
info.t: Continued weight-bearing can convert a stable slip into an unstable one, which carries a far higher risk of avascular necrosis. Make the patient strictly non-weight-bearing immediately (wheelchair, not crutches) and get urgent ortho for in-situ pinning; do not attempt reduction in the ED. SCFE — non-weight-bearing + ortho.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics in a septic-looking hip
info.t: Arthrocentesis before antibiotics is ideal, but a hip usually needs image-guided aspiration — do NOT let that delay abx in a toxic/septic-appearing patient. The joint is destroyed within ~24-48 h; give empiric vancomycin + gram-negative coverage and get emergent ortho for washout. Septic hip — aspirate + treat.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for imaging to call surgery in necrotizing infection
info.t: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity is the alarm for nec-fasc. If the exam is convincing, do NOT wait for imaging to consult surgery — start broad-spectrum abx (vanc + pip-tazo + clinda), resuscitate aggressively, and get to emergent operative debridement. Deep infection — source control.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT label it transient synovitis without excluding septic arthritis
info.t: Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion. If the child cannot bear weight, is febrile, or has any inflammatory-marker bump, do not clear the hip — Kocher-stratify, image, and aspirate before reassuring. Discharge only with strict return precautions for fever, worsening pain, or non-weight-bearing. Transient synovitis — exclusion diagnosis.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT exclude AVN on a normal early X-ray
info.t: In a patient with steroids, alcohol, sickle cell, or SLE, plain films are often normal before subchondral collapse — a normal X-ray does NOT exclude osteonecrosis. MRI is the most sensitive test; outcome is stage-dependent, so early diagnosis and referral matter. AVN — risk gate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a patient who cannot bear weight without advanced imaging
info.t: Do NOT send home anyone who cannot bear weight with a normal plain film and no MRI/CT, any fever or systemic sign, an unexcluded septic joint, or an un-imaged possible SCFE. Counsel that a normal X-ray does not rule out a hip fracture or early AVN — they need an MRI first. Discharge — universal checklist.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on "psych" before a glucose and a focal exam
info.t: "He's not acting right" is a medical complaint until proven psychiatric — anchoring on psych is how patients die of hypoglycemia, meningitis, or sepsis in the waiting room. Check a point-of-care glucose on everyone, first, and treat abnormal vitals, a focal deficit, age >40 with new symptoms, or visual hallucinations as pointing AWAY from a primary psychiatric cause. Sick Check first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for the LP or CT to give antibiotics
info.t: Fever plus new behavior change is meningitis/encephalitis until excluded, and every hour of delayed antibiotics costs lives. Give empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+ ampicillin if >50/immunocompromised) with dexamethasone, and add acyclovir for possible HSV encephalitis, the moment you suspect it. Treat empirically now.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clear for psychiatry with any organic red flag remaining
info.t: Abnormal vitals, a focal deficit, new symptoms after age 40, visual hallucinations, disorientation, or an acute fluctuating course all mean the patient is NOT medically cleared. Do not transfer to a psychiatric facility or anchor on "psych" until the medical workup is complete. Not cleared — keep working it up.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give benzodiazepines for delirium
info.t: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium and prolong confusion in the elderly — reserve them for alcohol/sedative withdrawal only. Use non-pharmacologic measures first and reserve low-dose antipsychotics for agitation that threatens safety. Delirium management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give glucose before thiamine in the malnourished or alcoholic patient
info.t: Administering dextrose first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in the thiamine-depleted patient. Give thiamine before (or with) glucose whenever malnutrition or alcohol use is suspected. Give thiamine first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start insulin before replacing potassium in DKA
info.t: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can trigger fatal hypokalemia — do NOT start the insulin infusion if K+ is <3.3 mEq/L until it is replaced. Resuscitate with fluids first, then insulin with careful potassium repletion. DKA sequence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay steroids for confirmatory testing in adrenal crisis
info.t: Adrenal crisis is rapidly fatal and steroids are the only lifesaving intervention — give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately and do not wait on cortisol results. Draw a cortisol first only if it will not delay treatment. Steroids now.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge an unexplained acute behavior change
info.t: An acute behavior change without an identified cause is an undiagnosed emergency, not a disposition — observe or admit for serial exams and completion of the workup. Treat the driver before any discharge. Observe / admit for workup.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give dextrose before thiamine
info.t: In any patient with prolonged poor intake, glucose in a thiamine-deficient state precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy. Give thiamine 100 mg IV first, then dextrose-containing fluids. Thiamine before dextrose.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call it a functional syndrome when there are red flags
info.t: Bilious or bloody vomiting means obstruction or GI bleed; headache + focal deficit means raised ICP; shock + hyponatremia/hyperkalemia means adrenal crisis until proven otherwise. CVS/CHS/functional vomiting are diagnoses of exclusion — screen and resuscitate first. Red-flag screen.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on a GI cause
info.t: Vomiting can be the sole presenting sign of DKA, raised ICP, or adrenal crisis — miss these and the patient decompensates while you treat nausea. Check ketones/VBG, image the head when neuro signs are present, and consider empiric hydrocortisone. Target the organic cause.
Every reproductive-age woman needs a βhCG before imaging or teratogen exposure — it changes the workup, the antiemetic choices, and prevents fetal harm. βhCG in every reproductive-age woman.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give opioids for gastroparesis or CHS
info.t: Opioids slow gastric emptying and perpetuate the vomiting cycle in both gastroparesis and cannabinoid hyperemesis. Use prokinetics, antiemetics, and cause-directed therapy instead. Avoid opioids.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT expect standard antiemetics to work in CHS
info.t: In cannabinoid hyperemesis, ondansetron and opioids typically fail — the effective agents are topical capsaicin, haloperidol/droperidol, and cannabis cessation. Recognize the triad plus hot-water bathing and route to the dedicated pathway. Standard antiemetics fail in CHS.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give steroids or ondansetron before 10 weeks gestation
info.t: Methylprednisolone for refractory HG and early ondansetron both carry an association with orofacial clefts if used before 10 weeks — reserve steroids as last-resort and counsel on the ondansetron signal via shared decision-making. Avoid steroids before 10 weeks.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stack QT-prolongers without checking the QTc
info.t: Ondansetron, haloperidol, droperidol, and promethazine all prolong the QT — layering them without a baseline ECG risks torsades. Check QTc before stacking, and cap metoclopramide duration to avoid tardive dyskinesia. QTc before stacking antiemetics.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on "just a UTI"
info.t: Dysuria is undifferentiated, and the lethal misses hide behind the same symptom: obstructive urosepsis, an untreated STI, acute bacterial prostatitis, retention, and priapism. Run the Sick Check and screen every one before you reach for an antibiotic script. Sick Check first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat an obstructed, infected kidney with antibiotics alone
info.t: Infection plus obstruction is pus under pressure — a urologic emergency that decompensates fast. Antibiotics will not save it; the patient needs emergent source control (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) alongside the sepsis bundle. Resuscitate + decompress.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT let a normal urinalysis rule out an STI
info.t: A clean UA does not reassure — sterile pyuria with discharge in a young, sexually active patient is gonorrhea/chlamydia until NAAT says otherwise. Miss it and you seed PID and epididymo-orchitis; keep a low threshold to send NAAT. Normal UA is not enough.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT vigorously massage a tender prostate
info.t: In suspected acute bacterial prostatitis, aggressive prostate massage can precipitate bacteremia. Do a gentle DRE only, and remember the UA can be normal — the exam, not the dipstick, makes this diagnosis. Gentle exam only.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss cauda equina behind urinary retention
info.t: Retention can be the presenting sign of a neurologic catastrophe. Screen for saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, and fecal incontinence — red flags mean emergent MRI and spine consult, not just a catheter. Screen cauda equina.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT sit on a painful erection lasting over 4 hours
info.t: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is time-critical and threatens erectile function the longer it persists. This is not a next-day urology problem — confirm the type, then aspirate and give intracavernosal phenylephrine with urology on the phone. Time-critical detumescence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget post-obstructive diuresis after decompression
info.t: Draining a large-volume retention can trigger brisk diuresis and dangerous electrolyte shifts. Monitor urine output, check a BMP for post-renal AKI and hyperkalemia, and replace fluids/electrolytes when the output runs high. Watch after draining.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call it uncomplicated cystitis when a red flag is present
info.t: Fever, flank pain, pregnancy, a male patient, discharge, or obstruction risk means this is no longer simple cystitis. Do not hand out a short antibiotic course — re-triage to the upper-tract, STI, prostatitis, or retention branch. Re-triage the complicated patient.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT let a normal ear exam end the visit
info.t: Ear pain with a normal ear is referred pain until proven otherwise — and jaw/ear pain can be an anginal equivalent. Do not let a clean canal falsely reassure you; get an ECG and troponin in the at-risk patient.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss severe pain out of proportion as swimmer's ear
info.t: In a diabetic or immunocompromised host, deep unrelenting pain (worse at night) with canal granulation ± a facial-nerve palsy is necrotizing otitis externa — skull-base osteomyelitis, not routine external otitis, and it will not respond to topical drops. Image, start systemic anti-pseudomonal therapy, and call ENT via the necrotizing OE gate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT just re-dose drops when a high-risk host fails to improve
info.t: Pain out of proportion, granulation tissue, or a diabetic/immunocompromised host means this is not simple otitis externa — re-dosing topical antibiotics only delays a skull-base infection. Loop back to the necrotizing gate, image, and consult ENT.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT overlook post-auricular swelling or a protruding auricle
info.t: Post-auricular swelling/erythema with a protruding auricle and fever is mastoiditis — a suppurative complication of otitis media that can extend to a subperiosteal abscess or intracranial spread (meningitis, sinus thrombosis, brain abscess). Get a contrast CT, start IV antibiotics, and consult ENT via the post-auricular gate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT irrigate or delay a button battery or insect in the canal
info.t: A button battery in the canal is an emergency — liquefactive/alkaline injury demands emergent removal, and irrigation is contraindicated for a battery, a live insect, or organic material that swells. Immobilize an insect first and act now on the time-sensitive trauma pathway.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for vesicles before treating Ramsay Hunt
info.t: Zoster oticus has worse facial-nerve recovery than Bell palsy, and the vesicles can lag the pain while the palsy may follow — waiting to confirm the rash costs the nerve. Reassess and treat early with antivirals + steroids when vesicles or a facial droop appear.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT put ototoxic drops in a possibly perforated TM
info.t: With an open or possibly perforated tympanic membrane, ototoxic drops can damage the inner ear — choose TM-safe agents. Verify TM integrity before prescribing on the otitis externa treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without complication return precautions
info.t: Benign-looking otitis can evolve into a dangerous complication, so every discharge needs explicit red-flag counseling — severe worsening pain (esp. diabetic), post-auricular swelling, facial droop, high fever, or neck stiffness/headache. Give the necrotizing/mastoiditis return precautions and named follow-up.

Hemorrhoids and a colorectal cancer can coexist — a visible benign source does not clear the bleed. New rectal bleeding at age >=50, or any alarm feature (weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, altered bowel habits, a mass), still needs a documented colonoscopy plan. Benign is a diagnosis of exclusion.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume bright-red blood per rectum is a lower source
info.t: A brisk upper-GI bleed can present as maroon stool or even BRBPR, and ~10-15% of severe "lower" bleeds are actually upper. Melena, hematemesis, a BUN:creatinine ratio >30, or varices/ulcer risk means treat as UGIB until excluded — IV PPI, endoscopy, and hemodynamics drive it, not the color of the blood. Chase the upper source.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send an unstable, actively bleeding patient to a prolonged prep
info.t: A brisk bleeder cannot tolerate hours of bowel prep before colonoscopy — you lose the window to control hemorrhage. Resuscitate first; if too brisk or unstable for scope, go to CT angiography and IR embolization. Match the study to the phenotype.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give empiric antibiotics when EHEC is suspected
info.t: Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli plus antibiotics raises the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Hold empiric abx in suspected EHEC, and check CBC/smear/renal function for HUS while you work the infectious-colitis pathway. Stool studies and rehydration first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reflexively transfuse platelets or reach for FFP
info.t: Platelet transfusion is generally NOT beneficial for antiplatelet-associated GI bleeding, and FFP is second-line for warfarin. Match reversal to the agent: 4-factor PCC + vitamin K for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, 4-factor PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors (andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US). Agent-specific reversal.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reduce-and-forget a rectal prolapse
info.t: Reduce the prolapse early to prevent incarceration, but a non-reducible, dusky, or strangulated prolapse is a surgical emergency — not a bedside discharge. Assess viability and get colorectal surgery involved. Reduce, assess, refer.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a patient who is not truly stable and low-risk
info.t: Ongoing or high-volume bleeding, orthostasis, a dropping or low Hb, a high Oakland score (>10), an undocumented source in a high-risk patient, or anticoagulation with a significant bleed all forbid discharge. Only send home the self-limited, non-orthostatic, Oakland <=10 patient with reliable follow-up, written return precautions, and a colonoscopy plan for age >=50 or alarm features. Meet every discharge criterion.

Unilateral facial pain alone does not diagnose bacterial rhinosinusitis — dental disease, migraine, trigeminal neuralgia, cluster/TAC, HZO, and eye emergencies all masquerade as "sinus" pain. Bacterial sinusitis requires >10 days without improvement, double-worsening, or severe purulence with fever before you label it. Screen the dangerous lanes first in the sinus/ear pattern.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for biopsy or ultrasound before steroids in suspected GCA
info.t: In age >50 with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms, delaying glucocorticoids risks permanent, irreversible vision loss. Normal ESR/CRP lowers but does not exclude giant cell arteritis when the story is high-risk. Start steroids when suspicion is meaningful in the GCA lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT let a normal facial or dental exam close a dissection story
info.t: Unilateral face/head/neck pain with partial Horner syndrome, transient monocular vision loss, TIA/stroke symptoms, or recent neck trauma/manipulation is a carotid/vertebral dissection until CTA head/neck says otherwise. A clean mouth exam does not rule out a vascular catastrophe. Work it through the neurovascular lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge an eye red flag without visual acuity and an ophthalmology plan
info.t: Red painful eye, halos, vision loss, proptosis, or painful/restricted EOM signals AACG, orbital cellulitis, or HZO — all time-sensitive and sight-threatening. Never send these home on assumption. Document acuity and secure ophthalmology in the eye/orbit lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send an airway-risk deep-space infection supine to CT without an airway plan
info.t: Trismus, muffled voice, drooling, dysphagia, or floor-of-mouth elevation means Ludwig angina or deep neck infection — laying the patient flat can lose the airway. Prioritize airway before imaging. See the deep-space infection lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold antivirals in zoster just because it is beyond 72 hours
info.t: Ocular involvement, immunocompromise, new lesions, or severe disease still warrant antiviral therapy past the 72-hour window. Pre-eruptive zoster mimics trigeminal neuralgia or dental pain — recheck skin and eye and give return precautions if no rash yet. Details in the zoster lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antibiotics for uncomplicated pulpitis
info.t: Uncomplicated pulpitis or localized apical periodontitis without systemic involvement needs dental source control and analgesia, not empiric antibiotics. Reserve antibiotics for spreading cellulitis, deep-space concern, or systemic illness. Rules in the dental/odontogenic lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a first severe facial pain with a vague benign label
info.t: Without a confident benign phenotype, a documented negative danger screen, pain control, and specific follow-up, discharge is unsafe — use observation or targeted imaging instead. "Return if worse" is not a plan. Meet every criterion in the discharge lane.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT diagnose dementia during an acute or fluctuating change
info.t: Acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, or sudden loss of baseline function is delirium or medical illness until proven otherwise — dementia is a risk factor, but delirium is the actionable emergency. Check glucose, oxygenation, meds/toxins, retention, and focal deficits before ever labeling this cognitive decline. Delirium first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on a UTI to explain confusion
info.t: Confusion alone is not a UTI diagnosis — IDSA recommends assessment for other causes, not antibiotics, for bacteriuria without urinary symptoms or systemic infection signs. The reflex UA → positive culture → antibiotics loop lets the real cause go untreated. Infection edge case.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give haloperidol or risperidone in suspected Lewy body dementia
info.t: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, or parkinsonism signal marked neuroleptic sensitivity — high-potency dopamine blockers can cause severe, even life-threatening reactions. Favor nonpharmacologic de-escalation and the lowest-risk option. Lewy body / Parkinson pattern.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reach for antipsychotics or restraint before screening triggers
info.t: Agitation is a symptom, not the diagnosis — pain, retention, constipation, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, infection, withdrawal, or head injury may be driving it, and antipsychotics carry a boxed-warning mortality risk in elderly dementia. Screen medical triggers and de-escalate first, unless immediate danger blocks essential care. Agitation trigger screen.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge the diagnosis instead of the safety situation
info.t: A cognitive label is not a disposition — recurrent falls, unsafe gait, no reliable caregiver, medication mismanagement, poor intake, wandering, or suspected neglect all mandate protected disposition, not a routine discharge. Discharge the actual safety situation, not the chart problem. Disposition decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume a dementia diagnosis removes capacity
info.t: Capacity is decision-specific, and a dementia diagnosis alone does not strip it — assess whether the patient can understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a stable choice for the exact decision at hand. Overriding a capable refusal, or honoring an incapable one, both cause harm. Capacity and safety.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT diagnose dementia from a single ED screen without collateral
info.t: An abnormal Mini-Cog or MoCA during delirium, pain, hearing loss, or a language mismatch does not diagnose dementia, and a normal brief screen does not rule out early disease. Collateral history and objective loss of ADL/IADL independence are required. Collateral and function.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the time-sensitive mimics before calling it progression
info.t: Stroke, ICH/subdural, CNS infection, nonconvulsive seizure, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, B12/thyroid disease, and rapidly progressive dementia can masquerade as decline — a new gait disorder with urinary symptoms may be treatable NPH. Escalate imaging and neurology for red flags. Time-sensitive mimics.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call stridor or a strained voice "anxiety"
info.t: Laryngeal dystonia is rare but obstructs the airway, and a terrified, hyperventilating patient invites the wrong label. Do not dismiss it as panic until it improves after anticholinergic and the airway is clearly safe — treat now and set up for RSI. Airway screen: laryngeal dystonia.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT keep anchoring on dystonia when the anticholinergic fails
info.t: Adequate diphenhydramine or benztropine should improve true dystonia in 5-30 min; no response means the diagnosis is wrong. Reset the differential and hunt for seizure, NMS/serotonin syndrome, tetanus, hypocalcemia, CNS infection, or stroke. No response: reset the differential.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give more dopamine blocker for the nausea or agitation
info.t: Piling on another antiemetic or antipsychotic to settle the patient feeds the exact drug that caused the reaction and can worsen it. Stop the offending agent instead of redosing it. First-line ED treatment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT redose an antipsychotic when NMS is on the table
info.t: Fever, altered mental status, or generalized lead-pipe rigidity point to NMS, not focal dystonia, and more D2 blockade is dangerous. Stop the dopamine blocker, cool, and escalate. Dystonia vs NMS vs serotonin syndrome.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat true angioedema as buccolingual dystonia
info.t: A tongue that feels swollen may be dystonia, but visible progressive lip/tongue/uvula swelling, urticaria, wheeze, or hypotension is anaphylaxis — give epinephrine first. Diphenhydramine does not treat shock or bronchospasm. Allergy / angioedema mimic.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send them home without an oral anticholinergic course
info.t: The culprit dopamine blocker outlasts a single dose of IV/IM diphenhydramine or benztropine, so symptoms recur after the antidote wears off. Continue oral anticholinergic 24-72 h to prevent relapse. Prevent recurrence.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge with any lingering airway symptom
info.t: Voice change, dysphagia, or laryngeal involvement — even if improved — carries recurrence and aspiration risk and needs 12-24 h of monitoring. Discharge only after full airway-safe resolution. Observe / admit.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rechallenge without documenting the exact drug and phenotype
info.t: A vague "allergy" note lets the same dopamine blocker get reordered, and prior reaction plus re-exposure is the highest-risk setup. Record drug, dose, route, and phenotype, and avoid close D2-blocking relatives. Avoid rechallenge.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start a leisurely LFT workup before screening for acute liver failure
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: ALF is time-critical and easy to miss when you anchor on the R-factor pattern. INR >=1.5 + any altered mentation, without known cirrhosis, is ALF until proven otherwise — check coags, ammonia, glucose, and mental status up front. Screen ALF first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for King's College Criteria before transferring to a transplant center
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: The criteria are highly specific (~90%) but only modestly sensitive, so a patient who does not yet meet them can still be dying. Transfer early — do not wait for criteria to be fully met. Transfer thresholds and timing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reflexively correct the INR in acute liver failure
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: The INR is a key prognostic trend and a King's College input; blindly reversing it with FFP/vitamin K masks the trajectory clinicians and the transplant team need. Correct coagulopathy only for active bleeding or a procedure. ALF supportive care.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold N-acetylcysteine or miss an acetaminophen ingestion
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: APAP toxicity can hide in a med/supplement list and drive massive transaminitis; Hy's law (hepatocellular injury + bilirubin >2x ULN, no other cause) flags ~10% mortality. Stop the offending agent and give NAC — it also helps early non-APAP ALF. DILI and NAC.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give corticosteroids for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis before excluding sepsis and GI bleed
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: Steroids in an infected or bleeding patient worsen outcomes. Reserve them for Maddrey >=32 only after sepsis and GI bleed are excluded. Alcohol-hepatitis management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT launch a full liver workup for an isolated high ALP without checking GGT
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: A high ALP with a normal GGT is not hepatobiliary — it points to bone, growth, or placenta, and a liver workup is a wasted, misdirecting chase. Confirm the source before treating it as liver disease. Isolated ALP, normal GGT.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge obstructive cholestasis without imaging the ducts
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: A cholestatic pattern with high GGT can be stones, stricture, or malignancy — and ascending cholangitis (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain +/- shock/AMS) is an emergency. Get an RUQ ultrasound first, escalate to MRCP/ERCP. Image the ducts.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge rapidly rising LFTs or any ALF feature
info.pt: Hepatitis / Acute Liver Failure — Do NOT
info.t: Mild stable transaminitis can go home with a timed recheck, but ALF features, severe symptoms, obstruction, or uncertain rapidly climbing LFTs require admission. Premature discharge here misses a decompensating liver. Disposition criteria.

• Isotonic crystalloid; correct dehydration. • Replace K and Mg; recheck after repletion. • Give thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose in prolonged poor intake — glucose first can precipitate Wernicke.

info.h: Step 2 — Screen the can’t-miss organic causes
info.t: • βhCG in every reproductive-age woman before imaging or teratogen exposure. • Bilious/bloody vomiting → obstruction / GI bleed. • Headache + focal deficit / papilledema → raised ICP. • Shock + hyponatremia/hyperkalemia → adrenal crisis. • Polyuria, Kussmaul, fruity breath → DKA.
CBC, CMP (glucose, Na, K, Ca, BUN/Cr), lipase, LFTs, VBG + serum ketones + lactate, urine βhCG, UA. ECG for a baseline QTc before QT-prolonging antiemetics.

• Pregnant → Hyperemesis gravidarum ladder. • Chronic heavy cannabis ± hot-water bathing → CHS (dedicated consult). • Delayed emptying / diabetic / post-surgical → Gastroparesis. • Stereotypical episodes, well between → Cyclic vomiting syndrome.
QTc before stacking QT-prolongers; limit metoclopramide duration (tardive dyskinesia); avoid opioids in CHS/gastroparesis; discharge on PO tolerance with follow-up.

• Exclude surgical, infectious, metabolic, neurologic, and molar-pregnancy mimics before labeling symptoms hyperemesis. • Give thiamine before dextrose when prolonged vomiting or poor intake creates deficiency risk. • Reassess volume status, electrolytes, renal function, QTc risk, oral tolerance, and disposition after each treatment step.

The chart shows medication options and escalation branches from its original publication. Formulations, pregnancy-safety evidence, dosing conventions, and local protocols evolve. Do not stack QT-prolonging or sedating agents without reassessing risk, and do not let the image replace the consult’s current exclusion and disposition pathway.
• Pyloric botulinum toxin is NOT recommended (ACG 2022). • Refractory: gastric electrical stimulation, G-POEM — GI referral.

Confirm the tooth/region and the target block (use the Block Selector tool). Remember: maxillary teeth respond to infiltration / superior-alveolar blocks (porous bone); mandibular teeth need the inferior alveolar block (dense bone). Obtain verbal consent: transient lip/tongue numbness, self-inflicted bite injury while numb, failed/partial block, hematoma, and (for the IANB) transient facial palsy. Document allergies and anticoagulation.

Before drawing up, compute the maximum weight-based dose and the cartridge count (Max Dose tool). Dental cartridges are 1.8 mL each; most intraoral blocks use only 0.3–1.8 mL. Track cartridge count, especially in children.

• 3 mL or dental aspirating syringe; 25–27 ga needle (use a 1.5-inch “long” needle for the IANB) • Dry the mucosa with gauze, apply topical benzocaine 20% for 1–2 min • Choose agent: lidocaine 2% with epi 1:100,000 (standard) or bupivacaine 0.5% with epi (long duration) • Good light + suction.

• Maxillary infiltration: mucobuccal fold at the root apex of the target tooth • Infraorbital / mental / greater-palatine / nasopalatine: the named foramen (keep a finger over it) • IANB: palpate the coronoid notch; position the barrel over the contralateral premolars, entry ~1 cm above the occlusal plane lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe.

• Keep the bevel toward bone; advance to target depth • ASPIRATE before injecting — double-aspirate (rotate 90°) for the IANB • For the IANB, contact bone first, then withdraw ~1 mm (no bone contact risks parotid injection → facial palsy) • Inject SLOWLY (≥1 min per cartridge) • Deposit ADJACENT to, never INTO, the foramen; stop if the patient reports an electric shock.

Wait 3–5 min (infiltration/maxillary) or 5–10 min (IANB). Test pinprick/cold versus the contralateral side — lower-lip numbness signals a successful IANB. Partial/none → re-confirm landmark/depth, supplement, and recheck the running total. Warn the patient (especially children) not to bite or burn the numb lip, cheek, or tongue.

info.h: Do NOT inject the IANB without bone contact
info.t: Advancing too deep/posterior WITHOUT contacting the medial ramus risks injecting into the parotid gland → transient facial nerve (CN VII) palsy (facial droop, can’t close the eye). Always contact bone, withdraw ~1 mm, then inject. The palsy is self-limited — protect the eye and reassure.

The inferior alveolar and posterior superior alveolar blocks are the highest-risk for intravascular injection (IA vessels; pterygoid venous plexus). Aspirate before EVERY injection; double-aspirate (rotate 90°) for the IANB. Positive aspiration → withdraw and redirect.

info.h: Do NOT inject into a foramen
info.t: Depositing anesthetic INSIDE the foramen or intraneurally causes persistent paresthesia. Inject adjacent to the greater-palatine, infraorbital, or mental foramen. Stop immediately if the patient reports an electric-shock sensation.

info.h: Do NOT inject through infected tissue
info.t: Active infection/cellulitis at the injection site is a contraindication — it risks spreading infection and the block often fails in acidic infected tissue. Choose an alternative landmark or coordinate drainage.

info.h: Do NOT forget the bite warning
info.t: A numb lip, cheek, or tongue is easily bitten or burned — this is the most common complication, especially in children. Explicitly warn every patient and caregiver, and document it.

info.h: Do NOT exceed the max dose
info.t: Multiple blocks stack up fast. Track cartridge count (Volume Tracker tool) and stay under the calculated maximum. Watch for LAST: perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste → seizures/cardiac collapse. If suspected → stop, 100% O2, treat seizures, and give 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion (LAST Rescue tool); ACLS with reduced epinephrine (≤1 mcg/kg).

Confirm the wound region and the target block (use the Block Selector tool). Obtain verbal informed consent: transient numbness, failed/partial block, hematoma, intravascular injection, nerve irritation. Document allergies and anticoagulation status.

Before drawing up, compute the maximum weight-based local-anesthetic dose (Max Dose tool). Facial blocks need only 1–3 mL each (ear ring ~6–8 mL), but verify whenever combining a block with wound infiltration.

• 3 mL syringe, 25–27 ga needle • Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or alcohol); let dry • Choose agent: lidocaine 1–2% (onset 2–5 min, 1–2 h) or bupivacaine 0.25–0.5% (onset 5–10 min, 4–8 h) • Buffer lidocaine 9:1 with sodium bicarbonate to reduce injection pain.

The supraorbital, infraorbital, and mental foramina all align vertically at the mid-pupillary line. Palpate the foramen (or the coronoid notch / superficial temporal pulse / ear base, depending on block) and keep a fingertip over it to direct flow.

• Warn the patient of a brief sting • Advance toward the target and ASPIRATE (the face is densely vascular) • Inject SLOWLY — slow injection = less pain • Deposit anesthetic ADJACENT to, never INTO, the foramen (intraneural injection causes persistent paresthesia) • Stop immediately if the patient reports an electric shock.

Wait 5–10 minutes, then test pinprick across the territory versus the contralateral side. Full anesthesia → proceed. Partial/none → re-confirm the landmark, re-block, or add small-volume local infiltration at the deficient edge (recheck the running total against the max dose).

info.h: Do NOT inject into a foramen
info.t: Depositing anesthetic INSIDE the foramen (or intraneurally) causes persistent paresthesia / nerve injury. Inject adjacent to the foramen. Stop immediately if the patient reports an electric-shock sensation.

The face is densely vascular — angular, infraorbital, superficial temporal, and inferior alveolar vessels all run with the target nerves. Aspirate before EVERY injection. Positive aspiration → withdraw and redirect.

info.h: Do NOT inject through infected skin
info.t: Overlying cellulitis/infection at the planned injection site is an absolute contraindication — it can seed deeper tissue. Choose an alternative approach or infiltrate after irrigation.

info.h: Do NOT aim toward the globe
info.t: For periorbital blocks (supraorbital, infratrochlear), keep the needle on the orbital rim and direct away from the globe to avoid globe injury.

info.h: Do NOT exceed the max dose
