info.t: Multiple sites or block-plus-infiltration can stack up. Track the running total (Volume Tracker tool) and stay under the calculated maximum. Watch for LAST: perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste → seizures/cardiac collapse.

Stop injecting, call for help, 100% O2, manage the airway, treat seizures with a benzodiazepine, and give 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion (LAST Rescue tool). Run ACLS with reduced epinephrine boluses (≤1 mcg/kg); avoid propofol if unstable.

info.pt: TEG Basics — When to Use & Limits
info.t: • Major trauma hemorrhage / massive transfusion — to target the specific deficit (factors vs fibrinogen vs platelets vs lysis) instead of fixed-ratio product. • Rapid point-of-care differentiation of the mechanism of coagulopathy. • Detection of hyperfibrinolysis (LY30) to direct TXA. • Strongest non-trauma evidence: cardiac surgery and liver transplantation (product reduction). • PlateletMapping (separate assay) for elective/peri-procedural antiplatelet assessment — not the acute bleed.

info.pt: TEG Basics — When to Use & Limits
info.t: TEG 6s (cartridge), rapid-TEG (rTEG), and citrated-kaolin TEG 5000 report the same parameter names (R, MA, LY30) with materially different cutoffs. Always know which analyzer produced the result. This consult uses TEG 6s trauma-cartridge thresholds.

info.h: Blind Spots — What TEG Cannot See
info.pt: TEG Basics — When to Use & Limits
info.t: • Aspirin / P2Y12 platelet inhibition — standard TEG is thrombin-driven and overrides drug-induced platelet inhibition (needs PlateletMapping). • Von Willebrand disease — high-shear vWF-mediated adhesion is not captured. • Hypothermia — the sample is warmed to 37 °C, masking the patient's true cold coagulopathy. • Vessel-wall/endothelial contribution, mild factor deficiencies, and LMWH/DOAC effects are poorly captured.

info.pt: TEG Basics — When to Use & Limits
info.t: Viscoelastic-guided transfusion in trauma is a conditional recommendation on VERY LOW quality evidence (EAST 2020). A single-center RCT (Gonzalez 2016) showed a mortality benefit, but the multicenter ITACTIC trial (2021) was negative for its primary outcome. TEG supports clinical judgment; it does not replace it.

Reaction time: how long until the clot starts to form (the tracing splits from one line into two). Prolonged (>10 min) = factor deficiency or anticoagulant. The CKH channel (kaolin + heparinase) isolates a heparin effect: if CK-R is prolonged but CKH-R is normal, heparin is the cause.

Functional fibrinogen MA: clot strength with platelets chemically blocked, so it reflects fibrinogen alone. Low (<14 mm) = inadequate fibrinogen → cryoprecipitate / fibrinogen concentrate. Correct this BEFORE platelets — fibrinogen also contributes to overall clot strength.

Maximum amplitude of the rapid-TEG channel: the strength of the fully formed clot (~80% platelets, ~20% fibrinogen). Low (<52 mm, especially <45 mm) with adequate fibrinogen = platelet deficit/dysfunction → platelets.

Percent clot breakdown 30 min after maximum strength. Elevated (>2.6% on TEG 6s) = hyperfibrinolysis → TXA. A pinching/narrowing of the tracing tail is visible well before the LY30 number officially posts.
• CK-R ↑ → factors → plasma / PCC • CFF-MA ↓ → fibrinogen → cryoprecipitate (first) • CRT-MA ↓ → platelets (after fibrinogen corrected) • CK-LY30 ↑ → fibrinolysis → TXA
Only after CFF-MA is adequate (≥15 mm).

• Keep the patient WARM (sample runs at 37 °C — TEG masks hypothermia). • Correct ionized calcium (citrate chelates Ca²⁺). • Correct pH / acidosis. • Pursue surgical source control — TEG cannot detect anatomic bleeding.

• Anticoagulant: heparin (check CKH-R), warfarin, DOAC • Clotting factor deficiency (II, V, VII, IX, X), liver disease • Severe hypofibrinogenemia (early) • Dilutional coagulopathy from crystalloid/large-volume resuscitation

• Trauma-induced/dilutional hypofibrinogenemia • DIC (consumption) — a flat CFF tracing with low CRT-MA • Obstetric hemorrhage (fibrinogen falls early and fast) • Hyperfibrinolytic consumption of fibrinogen
• Thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction (uremia, hypothermia, drugs) • Low fibrinogen contributing to a low MA (check CFF-MA — fix first) • Severe combined coagulopathy in massive hemorrhage
• Hyperfibrinolysis of trauma-induced coagulopathy • Hyperfibrinolytic DIC, obstetric hemorrhage • Note: very low LY30 (<0.8%) = fibrinolysis shutdown — a distinct high-mortality phenotype

info.h: Normal TEG in a bleeding patient
info.t: • Surgical/structural (anatomic) bleeding — TEG cannot see it • Aspirin/P2Y12 platelet inhibition (TEG is thrombin-driven; needs PlateletMapping) • Von Willebrand disease • Hypothermia (sample warmed to 37 °C masks it), acidosis, hypocalcemia

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply one analyzer's cutoffs to another
info.t: TEG 6s, rTEG, and CK-TEG 5000 report R/MA/LY30 with different normal ranges. Using rTEG thresholds on a TEG 6s result (or vice versa) can trigger the wrong transfusion. Confirm the assay. Assay note.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give platelets for a low CRT-MA before checking fibrinogen
info.t: A low overall MA is frequently driven by low fibrinogen. Correct CFF-MA with cryo first and recheck — cryo also raises the CRT-MA. Fibrinogen first.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust a normal TEG to exclude antiplatelet effect
info.t: Standard TEG is thrombin-driven and overrides aspirin/P2Y12 inhibition — the CRT-MA can look normal on a fully inhibited platelet. Use PlateletMapping and clinical context. PlateletMapping.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume a normal TEG means no hypothermic coagulopathy
info.t: The sample is warmed to 37 °C, so the TEG cannot reflect the patient's actual (cold) temperature. Rewarm aggressively regardless of the tracing. Normal-but-bleeding.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start TXA late without weighing harm
info.t: CRASH-2 showed TXA given >3 h after injury may INCREASE death from bleeding. Within 3 h it reduces mortality. TXA decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT chase TEG numbers in an obvious surgical bleed
info.t: A normal TEG in a bleeding patient points to an anatomic/surgical source. Definitive source control and even 1:1:1 replacement take priority over tweaking products. Normal-but-bleeding.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT extrapolate the protamine logic into trauma uncritically
info.t: The CK-R vs CKH-R → protamine approach is derived from cardiac surgery/ICU and is not validated in trauma. Use judgment. Heparin effect.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a single TEG to drive an entire resuscitation
info.t: TEG-guided therapy is iterative. Re-test every 30–60 min / per MTP round, and forget neither calcium nor pH. Reassess.
Compute the R-factor = (ALT ÷ ALT-ULN) ÷ (ALP ÷ ALP-ULN). • R >5 → hepatocellular • R 2–5 → mixed • R <2 → cholestatic This single number routes the rest of the workup.

Hepatocellular: viral (A/B/C/D/E), alcohol (AST:ALT >2:1), ischemic/shock liver (ALT in thousands, rapid rise/fall), drug/toxin incl. acetaminophen, MASLD/MASH, autoimmune, Wilson, hemochromatosis. Cholestatic: confirm hepatic source with GGT, then extrahepatic/obstructive (image the ducts) vs intrahepatic (PBC, PSC, drug, infiltrative). Mixed: usually DILI or evolving viral — trend the labs.

info.h: Step 3 — Never miss acute liver failure
info.t: ALF = INR ≥1.5 + hepatic encephalopathy + illness <26 weeks without prior cirrhosis. Apply King's College Criteria, start supportive care (NAC, watch cerebral edema), and transfer early to a transplant center.

• Ischemic / shock liver — rapid rise then ~50%/day fall after a hemodynamic insult; LDH high. • Acute viral hepatitis — A, B, E (E severe in pregnancy). • Drug / toxin — acetaminophen (give NAC), mushroom (Amanita), idiosyncratic DILI. • Autoimmune hepatitis flare — ↑IgG, ANA/ASMA. • Acute biliary obstruction — transient transaminase spike from a passing stone (then cholestatic pattern follows). • Wilson disease (young) and Budd-Chiari / venous outflow obstruction — don't forget vascular.
Any massive transaminitis with rising INR and encephalopathy is acute liver failure until proven otherwise — apply King's College Criteria and transfer early.
Readable bedside grid. Choose by the clinical target first, then use onset and risk profile to choose the safest sedative.

Seconds: - Propofol, etomidate, IV ketamine. Early minutes: - Fentanyl IV, midazolam IV, droperidol IV, ketamine IM. Later minutes: - Droperidol IM, haloperidol IM, olanzapine IM, ziprasidone IM, nitrous mask setup, dexmedetomidine if no load. Long tail: - Lorazepam/diazepam, phenobarbital, olanzapine, ziprasidone, repeated benzodiazepines, stacked sedatives.

Apnea/obstruction: - Propofol, benzo/opioid stacking, intoxication, OSA/COPD. Hypotension: - Propofol, dex loading, high total sedative burden, shock physiology. QT/EPS: - Droperidol, haloperidol, and ziprasidone, especially QTc >500 ms, electrolyte depletion, QT polypharmacy, Parkinson/Lewy body. Bradycardia: - Dexmedetomidine, beta-blockers, high vagal tone, conduction disease. Myoclonus: - Etomidate. Saliva/emesis/laryngospasm: - Ketamine. Long-tail oversedation: - Phenobarbital, lorazepam, diazepam, olanzapine, repeated benzodiazepines.

Brief deep sedation: - Propofol when BP and airway setup are ready. - Etomidate when hypotension from propofol is a major concern. Painful procedure needing dissociation: - Ketamine, especially pediatric, severe pain, bronchospasm, or preserved respiratory-tone priority. Lower-depth anxiety plus analgesia: - Midazolam plus fentanyl in small separated aliquots. Brief cooperative procedure: - Nitrous oxide if no closed-space contraindication and patient can cooperate.

Immediate violent danger: - Ketamine IM/IV when prolonged physical struggle is more dangerous than dissociation. Stimulant, hyperthermia, withdrawal, seizure physiology: - Benzodiazepines are physiology-first treatment. Cool, check glucose, monitor ventilation, and treat complications. Undifferentiated severe agitation: - Droperidol plus midazolam is evidence-supported when QT/stimulant hyperthermia are not dominant. Primary psychosis, not crashing: - Antipsychotic-focused pathway. Use lower dosing in older/frail patients. QT or Parkinson/Lewy risk: - Avoid reflex butyrophenone stacking. Use ECG/electrolytes when safe and choose alternatives when clinically appropriate.

Post-intubation: - Treat pain first. - Set a RASS target. - Propofol for deep titratable sedation if BP tolerates. - Dexmedetomidine for cooperative light sedation, NIV, or extubation bridge. - Ketamine as analgesic/sedative adjunct when bronchospasm, pain, or propofol hypotension matters. Withdrawal or seizure-risk state: - Benzodiazepine or phenobarbital effect is required. - Dexmedetomidine is adjunct only and does not prevent withdrawal seizures.

Older/frail: - Start 25-50% lower, redose slowly, avoid stacking. Severe acidosis or shock: - Pair sedation with airway, ventilator, pressor, and immediate post-intubation minute ventilation plan. Propofol and apnea can crash the patient. QT risk: - Do not delay lifesaving control. Get ECG first when practical for known long QT, QTc >500 ms, torsades history, QT polypharmacy, electrolyte depletion, syncope, chest pain, stimulant tox, older/frail, renal failure, or repeated antipsychotic dosing. OSA/COPD/intoxication: - Use ETCO2 when available, lower depth, separated aliquots, and airway rescue setup before dosing.
Do NOT give deep sedation without suction, oxygen, BVM, airway adjuncts, monitor, BP cycling, and a person assigned to monitor the patient.
Do NOT choose a drug by habit. Analgesia, anxiolysis, amnesia, dissociation, deep hypnosis, cooperative sedation, withdrawal control, and chemical control are different targets.
Do NOT rapidly stack benzodiazepines, opioids, phenobarbital, alcohol co-ingestion, sleep meds, or propofol without reassessing ventilation and airway obstruction.
Do NOT use routine propofol dosing in shock, hypovolemia, severe RV failure, or frailty. Dose-reduce heavily or choose a different strategy.
Do NOT assume ketamine eliminates airway risk. Reassess after control for hypoventilation, emesis, saliva, laryngospasm, acidosis, hyperthermia, and occult trauma.

Do NOT repeatedly dose droperidol or haloperidol in QTc >500 ms, torsades history, severe low K/Mg/Ca, or heavy QT polypharmacy when safer alternatives fit. Do not delay emergency control for ECG in an immediate threat.
Do NOT use dexmedetomidine alone for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. It may calm autonomic signs but does not prevent seizures or delirium tremens.
Do NOT forget phenobarbital has a long tail and no rapid reversal. Track cumulative dose and co-sedative load before redosing.
Do NOT discharge or leave unmonitored until airway, ventilation, perfusion, mentation, pain/nausea, gait when relevant, and sedation trajectory are safe.

info.pt: State of Extreme Agitation with Aggression
info.t: - Treat as hyperactive delirium with severe agitation, not a final diagnosis. - Call team, assign roles, minimize stimulation, and avoid prone/compressive restraint. - Immediate threat: chemical control now. Do not delay lifesaving sedation for ECG or labs. - Stimulant/hyperthermic phenotype: benzodiazepines, rapid cooling, fluids, and complication surveillance. - Immediate violent threat: ketamine 4-5 mg/kg IM when prolonged struggle is more dangerous than dissociation. - Undifferentiated severe agitation without high QT/stimulant hyperthermia: droperidol 5-10 mg plus midazolam 5 mg is evidence-supported. - Older/frail: start 25-50% lower, avoid routine benzodiazepines unless withdrawal/sti

info.pt: State of Extreme Agitation with Aggression
info.t: - Core temperature. - Glucose, oxygenation, ventilation/ETCO2. - VBG/ABG with lactate when severe. - ECG, K, Mg, Ca, renal function. - CK now and repeat if rising, UA/urine output. - Troponin if stimulant, chest pain, dysrhythmia, shock, older patient, or concerning ECG. - Coags/fibrinogen/LFTs/platelets if hyperthermia or severe illness. - Search for heat stroke, serotonin syndrome, NMS, sepsis, CNS emergency, seizure, withdrawal, toxic ingestion, pain, urinary retention, and trauma.
• Lidocaine 1-2% PLAIN, ~2-4 mL total for a digital block. • Max lidocaine plain ≈ 4.5 mg/kg. • Bupivacaine 0.25-0.5% plain gives longer post-procedure analgesia if desired.

Traditional teaching avoids epinephrine in digits. Modern evidence supports low-concentration commercial lidocaine-with-epinephrine in healthy digits, but for a brief toe procedure PLAIN anesthetic is the simplest safe default, especially with any vascular concern.
Two-point block at the dorsolateral base of the proximal phalanx bilaterally; aspirate before injecting; wait 5-10 min; test before cutting.
• Field must be DRY and bloodless (tourniquet on) — phenol is neutralized by blood/fluid. • Protect the surrounding skin (perionychium) with petrolatum.

• Use a tightly-wound cotton-tipped applicator. • Apply ~88% phenol to the exposed lateral matrix, especially the lateral horn. • Three 30-second applications (≈90 s total) is a common protocol; 30-60-90 s ranges are described. • Roll the applicator firmly into the matrix groove.

• Flush copiously with isopropyl alcohol (or sterile saline) after the final application to stop ongoing chemical burn. • Over-application or inadequate neutralization burns surrounding tissue and delays healing.

• Palpable dorsalis pedis / posterior tibial pulses? • Brisk capillary refill in the toe? • Diabetes — glycemic control, neuropathy, prior foot ulcers? • Known peripheral arterial disease / claudication?
Avulse for symptom relief if needed, but DO NOT apply phenol. Refer to podiatry / foot-and-ankle surgery for definitive matrixectomy under controlled conditions. Document pedal pulses / consider ABI.

• Keep the dressing clean and dry for the first 24 hours. • After 24 h, soak the toe in warm soapy water 1-2× daily, then apply petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment and a clean non-stick dressing. • Some clear or blood-tinged drainage for 1-2 weeks is normal after phenol — the area weeps as it heals.
• Wear open-toe or wide, soft footwear until comfortable. • Elevate the foot and limit standing/walking for the first day or two. • Over-the-counter pain relievers as directed.
• Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, or pus (infection) • Fever • Increasing pain after the first few days • Bleeding that will not stop with pressure • Numbness, blue color, or cold toe
Healing usually takes 2-6 weeks. See your primary care doctor or podiatrist if it has not healed by then, or if the nail grows back ingrown.

1. Antibiotic ointment — bacitracin or Neosporin: available in any ED; apply thickly, reapply q1-2h. 2. Surfactant emulsifiers — polysorbate (Tween-80), De-Solv-It, Tarsol: purpose-made, dissolve tar fastest where stocked. 3. Mineral oil / petrolatum / butter: household petroleum sources (case-reported effective). 4. Vitamin E ointment: reported effective and skin-friendly.
Acetone, gasoline, or other organic solvents — they cause chemical injury to already-burned skin.
Tar is petroleum-based, so a petroleum/surfactant emulsifier dissolves it without harming skin. Apply generously, cover, dwell, reapply, and let the tar lift off on its own.

• Rule of Nines (adults) or the patient’s palm (incl. fingers) ≈ 1% TBSA for small/patchy burns. • Count partial- and full-thickness burn only; exclude superficial (erythema-only). • Depth cannot be judged while tar covers the skin — estimate after clearance.

• Partial-thickness > 10% TBSA • Any full-thickness burn • Burns to face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, or major joints • Inhalation injury, electrical/chemical burns, or significant comorbidity • Burns in patients who will need special social/rehab support

• A standard 14-16 Fr 2-way Foley has no irrigation channel and clogs with clots. • Use a 3-way (triple-lumen) catheter: balloon, drainage, and irrigation lumens. • Typical size for clot retention: 22-24 Fr (larger lumen drains clots and allows irrigation).
Confirm intravesical placement (urine/blood return) BEFORE inflating the balloon. Larger catheters are stiffer — gentle technique; lubricate well.
Keep the effluent light pink to clear and prevent NEW clots from forming. CBI does not break existing clots — those are removed manually first.

• Brisk/bright-red bleeding → run inflow fast (wide open initially) to keep effluent dilute. • As effluent lightens → slow the inflow stepwise. • Clear/light-pink and stable → maintain a low maintenance rate. • Re-darkening effluent → increase inflow and reassess for a re-bleed/clot.
Track net fluid: true urine output = total drainage − irrigant instilled. Maintain a closed sterile system.

1. STOP the irrigation inflow immediately. 2. Manually aspirate the catheter with a Toomey syringe to clear an obstructing clot. 3. Check for kinking and verify the balloon has not slipped into the urethra. 4. If outflow does not promptly recover, or there is severe pain / peritoneal signs → urology now (cystoscopy ± imaging). 5. Do not restart CBI until free drainage is re-established.

• Cannot clear clots manually or bladder will not drain (needs cystoscopic evacuation) • Outflow obstruction not resolving / suspected bladder injury • Brisk ongoing bleeding, dropping hemoglobin, or hemodynamic change • Suspected tumor source or recent urologic surgery complication

• CBC, coagulation panel, type-and-screen if significant bleeding • Review and correct anticoagulation • All gross hematuria with clot retention needs outpatient urologic evaluation (cystoscopy ± upper-tract imaging) to exclude malignancy, regardless of resolution.

• Corticosteroid: triamcinolone 10-20 mg, OR methylprednisolone 20-40 mg, OR dexamethasone 4 mg. • Mixed with lidocaine 1% ~0.5-1 mL for volume + immediate comfort. • Small total volume — the sheath is a small space.

• Dexamethasone is non-particulate (some prefer it to reduce subcutaneous atrophy risk). • Use the smallest effective steroid dose. • Avoid repeated injections at short intervals — diminishing returns and cumulative tissue effects.

• Injectate flows with LOW resistance. • Passive tendon-excursion test: have the patient gently move the digit/thumb — if the needle moves with the tendon, you are IN the tendon; withdraw 1-2 mm until the needle stays still and flow is free. • Ultrasound guidance, if available, confirms intra-sheath placement and helps with a de Quervain EPB septum.
STOP. Do not force. Withdraw slightly until free flow is achieved, then inject slowly.

info.pt: Eye vs Eyelid vs Skin Triage Card
info.t: Lids/lashes stuck together; eye likely intact underneath. Most common. → topical anesthetic + ointment dwell or gentle hook; never force.

info.pt: Eye vs Eyelid vs Skin Triage Card
info.t: Glue instilled mistaking it for eyedrops; foreign-body sensation; fragments on cornea/conjunctiva. → rule out globe injury, fluorescein, remove only loose fragments, ophthalmology if symptomatic.

info.pt: Eye vs Eyelid vs Skin Triage Card
info.t: Fingers, lips, other skin, no eye involvement. → warm soapy soak + petroleum; gentle roll-apart.

info.h: Large-Bore ETT as a Suction Catheter (DIY DuCanto)
info.t: Accomplishes: Clears massive airway soiling (vomit, blood, food chunks) far better than a Yankauer — a 10.0 ETT gives a ~10 mm bore vs the Yankauer’s ~3.6 mm — when a large-bore suction catheter isn’t available. How to: 1. Grab a size 10.0 ETT (or the largest available). 2. Attach rubber suction tubing to the ETT 15 mm adaptor. 3. Connect the tubing to the wall suction canister. 4. Activate suction and insert the ETT into the airway to clear debris. Equipment: Size 10.0 endotracheal tube, suction tubing, wall suction canister. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: NPA as a Conduit for NG Tube Placement
info.t: Accomplishes: Boosts first-attempt nasogastric tube success in sedated/intubated patients (first-pass ~83% vs ~47%). How to: 1. Lubricate and insert an appropriately sized NPA into a nostril (usually the right). 2. Thread a lubricated NG tube through the NPA lumen. 3. Once the NG tip exits the NPA into the oropharynx, advance into the esophagus with head flexion / chin tuck. 4. Leave the NPA in place or remove it as clinically indicated. Equipment: NPA, lubricated NG tube, lubricant, syringe for placement check. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

Accomplishes: Exchanges a supraglottic (King) airway for an endotracheal tube while maintaining tracheal access, using a cut disposable bronchoscope as a bougie. How to: 1. Pass a disposable bronchoscope through the King airway port and side port into the trachea toward the carina. 2. Cut the disposable scope at the level of the handle, leaving a “fiberbougie” in the trachea. 3. Withdraw the King device over the cut scope (modified Seldinger) while suctioning. 4. Advance the ETT over the fiberbougie. 5. Confirm passage through the cords with video/direct laryngoscopy, then capnography and CXR. Equipment: Disposable bronchoscope, ETT, 50 mL syringe, video/direct laryngoscope, trauma shears, s

Accomplishes: Non-invasively breaks laryngospasm (often peri-sedation or pediatric) before resorting to a paralytic. How to: 1. Find the “laryngospasm notch” just behind each earlobe — bounded by the mandibular ramus in front, the mastoid behind, and the skull base above. 2. Place a fingertip in each notch as superiorly as possible (do not slide down the mandible). 3. Push both sides firmly inward toward the skull base while simultaneously pushing anteriorly, like a jaw thrust. 4. Maintain firm pressure — spasm typically breaks within 1–2 breaths. 5. If it fails, proceed to positive-pressure ventilation, deepen sedation, or give a paralytic. Equipment: None (examiner’s fingers). _Source: ALi

info.h: SALAD — Suction-Assisted Laryngoscopy for the Soiled Airway
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps profuse vomit or blood out of your view during intubation of a massively soiled airway, so you can pass the tube on the first attempt instead of drowning the camera. How to: 1. Hold a rigid (DuCanto or Yankauer) suction catheter in an overhand grip so it mimics the curve of the laryngoscope blade. 2. Suction the mouth and oropharynx first, then insert the laryngoscope blade hugging the tongue so the camera/optics do not submerge in vomit. 3. Use the rigid suction itself as a tongue depressor/lifter to seat the blade and expose the cords. 4. Decontaminate the hypopharynx, then park the suction tip in the proximal esophagus to drain ongoing emesis; the blade pins the cathet

info.h: Bimanual Laryngoscopy to Improve a Bad Glottic View
info.t: Accomplishes: Instantly upgrades a poor laryngoscopy view by letting the intubator optimize external laryngeal manipulation with their own hand before an assistant locks it in — outperforms cricoid pressure and BURP. How to: 1. During direct or video (Macintosh-geometry) laryngoscopy, reach around with your free RIGHT hand and press on the patient’s thyroid cartilage while watching the screen. 2. Move the larynx (back, up, and toward the patient’s right) until the glottic view is best — the force opposes your laryngoscope lift. 3. Once optimized, have an assistant place their hand exactly where yours is and say “keep this pressure and direction.” 4. Release your right hand — now free to pass

Accomplishes: Intubates the anticipated difficult or non-cooperative airway (angioedema, obstruction, can’t lie flat) while the patient keeps breathing, using dissociative-dose ketamine instead of a paralytic-first RSI. How to: 1. Pre-oxygenate and FULLY set up for RSI and a failed airway FIRST — a paralytic must be drawn up and immediately available to convert at any moment. 2. Give ketamine in small aliquots (about 25 mg, or ~0.5 mg/kg) IV every ~15 seconds, titrating to dissociation (average effective total ~1–2 mg/kg). 3. Optionally topicalize the airway with atomized lidocaine for extra tolerance. 4. Perform gentle laryngoscopy and pass the tube while the patient breathes; this demands

info.h: Nasopharyngeal Oxygenation via a Repurposed NPA
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers high-flow positive-pressure oxygen straight into the pharynx of a crashing upper-airway patient (angioedema, anaphylaxis, end-stage COPD) when you cannot get a mask seal. How to: 1. Lubricate and place a standard nasopharyngeal airway through either nostril. 2. Connect standard wall-suction tubing (via its included adapter) to the external end of the NPA. 3. Connect the other end of that tubing directly to a wall oxygen flowmeter. 4. Turn the oxygen flow up well beyond the marked 0–15 L/min range to deliver >25 L/min of positive-pressure oxygen into the posterior pharynx. 5. Watch for gastric insufflation and use it as a bridge while you prepare a definitive airway. Eq

info.h: ETT as a Guide for Rapid Orogastric Tube Placement
info.t: Accomplishes: Places an orogastric tube in seconds in an intubated patient when blind OG insertion keeps coiling in the mouth, using a spare endotracheal tube as a rigid conduit to the esophagus. How to: 1. Use ONLY on an already-intubated patient with a protected airway (this risks vomiting otherwise). 2. Grip a lubricated 8.0 ETT like a dart in your dominant hand; stand at the patient’s side and gently advance it down the oropharynx into the esophagus without forcing. 3. Cover the ETT hub with a glove to stop gastric contents from spraying out. 4. Thread a lubricated 16–18 French NG/OG tube through the ETT into the stomach and connect it to suction. 5. After imaging confirms position, remo

info.h: Duoderm Seal to Temporize a Leaking Tracheostomy
info.t: Accomplishes: Restores the seal and PEEP around a leaking trach cannula in a vent-dependent patient, buying time until a longer cannula or surgical fix is available. How to: 1. Puncture the center of a Duoderm dressing with suture scissors — use a small puncture, not a linear cut, so the hole does not run. 2. Push the tracheostomy tube through the punctured Duoderm so the dressing hugs the cannula tightly. 3. Insert the cannula into the stoma using standard technique. 4. Press the Duoderm firmly onto the surrounding neck skin to create an occlusive seal, then recheck the vent for resolution of the leak. Equipment: Duoderm (hydrocolloid) dressing, suture scissors, tracheostomy tube. _Source:

info.h: Walk-Up Ketamine Dosing for Delayed Sequence Intubation
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you sedate the agitated, hypoxic patient enough to actually pre-oxygenate (mask, NIV, or high-flow) before paralyzing, while titrating slowly to dodge the sharp blood-pressure drop and apnea a single big ketamine bolus can cause. How to: 1. Use for the patient who needs intubation but is too agitated or air-hungry to tolerate pre-oxygenation — DSI is really a procedural sedation where the “procedure” is denitrogenation. 2. Set up fully for RSI and a failed airway FIRST; have a paralytic drawn up and ready to convert. 3. Instead of a full 1–2 mg/kg push, give ketamine in 25–50 mg IV aliquots every ~30–60 seconds, watching the patient with each step. 4. Stop adding ketamine

info.h: Tourniquet Infusion to Upsize an IV
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Converts a small existing IV (e.g., 22G) into access for a larger-bore catheter in volume-depleted / difficult-access patients, often avoiding a central line (~68% success). How to: 1. Confirm the patient can tolerate a small fluid bolus. 2. Place a tourniquet proximal to the existing small IV (for AC placement, just above the elbow). 3. Rapidly infuse 50–100 mL through the small IV to distend the veins between it and the tourniquet. 4. Cannulate the now-dilated vein with the larger catheter. Equipment: Tourniquet, existing IV, IV fluids, larger-bore catheter. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Cut IV Tubing for a 2-Person Ultrasound Nerve Block
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets a second operator inject while the sonographer keeps the probe and needle motionless during an US-guided nerve block. How to: 1. Connect a length of IV extension tubing between the block needle and the syringe. 2. Operator 1 holds the probe and needle and watches the screen. 3. Operator 2 aspirates and injects via the tubing on command, keeping the needle tip still. Equipment: IV extension tubing, block needle, local anesthetic syringe, ultrasound. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Easier EJ vein cannulation in difficult peripheral access by improving vein engorgement and stabilization. How to: 1. Place the patient in Trendelenburg to engorge the EJ. 2. “Wing” the position to tense and anchor the vein. 3. Cannulate the EJ along its course toward the clavicle. Equipment: IV catheter, standard IV supplies. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Performs US-guided PIV access without slippery gel contaminating the site / sterile field. How to: 1. Use saline (or a sterile transparent film over the probe) as the coupling medium instead of gel. 2. Maintain probe contact and visualize the vein. 3. Cannulate without gel fouling the site. Equipment: Ultrasound, saline or sterile film, IV catheter. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Ergonomic fix so the probe cord doesn’t twist your wrist during US-guided PIV. How to: 1. Drape the probe cord over your forearm or shoulder before scanning. 2. Orient the probe marker so the cord falls away from your working hand. 3. Scan and cannulate without cable tension. Equipment: Ultrasound probe. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Ultrarapid Adenosine Push via Pressure Bag
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers undiluted adenosine to the heart at high flow to terminate SVT, exploiting its very short half-life — combines single-syringe speed with a large flush. How to: 1. Prime a pressure bag with saline tubing; close the roller clamp. 2. Connect the line to the patient’s angiocatheter. 3. Attach the undiluted adenosine syringe to the Y-site nearest the patient. 4. Open the roller clamp for high-pressure flow. 5. Rapidly inject the adenosine into the tubing. Equipment: Pressure bag with primed saline line, IV angiocatheter, undiluted adenosine syringe, Y-site connector. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Chest-Tube Rewarming With a Foley Bag Connector
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Connects warmed IV fluids to chest tubes for thoracic lavage in severe hypothermia, using the Foley bag’s built-in connector as an adapter. How to: 1. Connect warmed IV fluids to the Luer-lock port on the Foley bag tubing. 2. Insert the tapered nozzle of the Foley tubing into the chest tube. 3. Clamp proximal to the Luer lock to limit backflow. 4. Run warm fluid into one tube and drain from the adjacent tube. 5. Continue standard rewarming. Equipment: Foley catheter bag/tubing, warmed IV fluids, chest tubes, clamp. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Inflate a Blakemore/Minnesota Balloon Without a Manometer
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Measures and titrates esophageal balloon pressure for variceal tamponade using a manual BP cuff gauge when no manometer is available. How to: 1. Detach the manual BP cuff so only the tubing to the gauge remains. 2. Connect that tubing to the male Luer of a 3-way stopcock; attach the balloon to one female port and a 50 cc syringe to the other. 3. Turn the stopcock away from the gauge and inject 10 cc of air. 4. Rotate the stopcock to isolate the syringe and read the gauge. 5. Repeat in 10 cc increments to reach 30 mmHg (max 45 mmHg if still bleeding). 6. Watch units — manometers often read cmH2O; balloons use mmHg (1 cmH2O = 0.74 mmHg). Equipment: Manual sphygmomanometer, 3-way

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Stops persistent ascitic fluid leak from a paracentesis site using a tight gauze ball plus stretched film for sustained pressure. How to: 1. Apply benzoin tincture around the leak to improve adhesion. 2. Roll gauze into a tight ball and press firmly over the leak. 3. Stretch a transparent film dressing over the gauze center while keeping pressure. 4. Add 2–3 more stretched film layers. 5. Leave in place 24–48 hours; optionally combine with tissue adhesive. Equipment: Benzoin tincture, 2x2 gauze, transparent film dressing x3–4. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Tamponades bleeding from a penetrating wound (e.g., neck / junctional) by inflating a Foley balloon in the wound tract. How to: 1. Insert a Foley catheter into the bleeding wound tract. 2. Inflate the balloon to tamponade the vessel. 3. Clamp the catheter and secure; arrange definitive surgical management. Equipment: Foley catheter, syringe/saline, clamp. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Alternative to a Pressure Bag for IV Fluids
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers rapid fluid boluses when a pressure bag is unavailable. How to: 1. Wrap a BP cuff around the fluid bag and inflate, OR use a 3-way stopcock + syringe for a push-pull setup. 2. Squeeze/inflate to accelerate flow while monitoring the bag. Equipment: IV fluid bag, BP cuff or 3-way stopcock + syringe. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Punch Biopsy to Extract a Small Retained Foreign Body
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Atraumatic removal of a small, deeply embedded soft-tissue foreign body (e.g., glass, splinter, metal) that resists forceps. How to: 1. Localize the foreign body to its single most-tender point (ultrasound helps). 2. Anesthetize locally; pick a site that is not cosmetically sensitive and is neurovascularly low-risk. 3. Center a 1–2 mm dermal punch biopsy tool directly over the maximal tender point. 4. Punch down to core out a small cylinder of tissue containing the foreign body. 5. Remove the core with the foreign body inside; irrigate, and leave the small punch defect to heal by secondary intention. Equipment: 1–2 mm punch biopsy tool, local anesthetic, forceps, irrigation, ul

info.h: Rubber Tourniquet Wrap for Stuck Ring Removal
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Milks edema out of a swollen finger so a stuck ring slides off without cutting it. How to: 1. Tightly wrap the finger with a flat phlebotomy tourniquet in a distal-to-proximal direction, wrapping over the ring itself. 2. Have the cooperative patient hold the proximal end taut for ~15 minutes to drive out edema. 3. Lubricate, then unwrap and slide the ring over the now-decompressed tissue. 4. If still stuck, consider a cold-water soak first or move to a ring cutter. Equipment: Flat rubber phlebotomy tourniquet, lubricant. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Ring removal (Chavez)._

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Drains a large abscess (>5 cm) without painful packing changes; noninferior to standard I&D in adults and superior/less painful in children. How to: 1. Anesthetize and make a small (~5 mm) stab incision at one edge of the abscess; break up loculations. 2. Make a second small incision at the opposite edge of the cavity. 3. Irrigate the cavity through both incisions. 4. Pass a vessel loop (or a sterile glove/tourniquet strip) through one incision, out the other, and tie the ends loosely — leave slack, do not tension. 5. Tell the patient to shower and gently jiggle the loop daily; they cut and remove it at home once drainage stops (usually 7–10 days). Equipment: Scalpel, vessel lo

info.h: Topical TXA-Soaked Gauze for Oral & Socket Bleeding
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Stops oozing dental-socket or oral-mucosal bleeding at the bedside, even in anticoagulated patients, with a cheap readily-stocked agent. How to: 1. Suction clot and identify the bleeding socket or mucosal site. 2. Soak a 4x4 gauze with about 500 mg (5 mL) of the 100 mg/mL IV tranexamic acid solution. 3. Place the soaked gauze directly over the site and have the patient bite down (or hold firm pressure) for 15–20 minutes. 4. Re-inspect; repeat once if still oozing. Escalate to FloSeal, sutures, or ENT/IR if bleeding is brisk or airway is threatened. 5. Discharge with TXA mouthwash instructions when appropriate. Equipment: 100 mg/mL IV tranexamic acid, 4x4 gauze, suction, syringe

info.h: Apply EMLA Early for Lumbar Punctures
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives a near-painless skin wheal and improves first-pass LP success in adults and children by starting the slow-onset topical anesthetic at the front of the workup. How to: 1. The moment an LP is anticipated, apply a thick layer of EMLA (2.5% lidocaine / 2.5% prilocaine) over the target interspaces. 2. Cover with an occlusive transparent film dressing to drive penetration. 3. Let it sit at least 60 minutes (use the labs/imaging wait) — onset is the rate-limiting step, so start it first, not last. 4. Wipe off, prep, and still infiltrate deeper lidocaine for the track; EMLA only numbs skin. 5. Safe in neonates ≥37 weeks gestation; avoid with local-anesthetic allergy or methemoglo

info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives a sonographically visible, real-time approach to the subclavian vein when the clavicle blocks the usual infraclavicular view — useful when IJ and femoral sites are unavailable. How to: 1. Place the patient supine, head slightly turned away; the target site sits just lateral to the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid. 2. Use a small-footprint endocavitary (curved) probe — it nests into the supraclavicular fossa better than a flat linear probe. 3. Angle the probe to get a long-axis view of the subclavian vein where it joins the internal jugular. 4. Advance the needle in-plane under continuous ultrasound, watching the tip enter the vein, then thread the wire by Seldin

info.h: Needle-to-Needle Ultrasound Alignment for a Retained Needle
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Locates and extracts a broken-off or deeply embedded metallic needle by lining up an introducer needle exactly parallel to it under ultrasound, so you dig in the right plane instead of blindly. How to: 1. Find the retained needle on ultrasound and rotate the probe until you see its full length in long axis (a bright linear echo). 2. Anesthetize, then introduce a large-gauge (14–16G) needle in-plane alongside the probe. 3. Adjust your needle’s angle until both needles appear as parallel bright lines in the same long-axis view — that confirms you are tracking the same depth and plane. 4. Advance your needle to the tip of the foreign body and use it as a guide to grasp and withdra

info.h: Water-Bath Ultrasound for a Soft-Tissue Foreign Body
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Sharper imaging of a superficial foreign body or distal-extremity structure by submerging the part — the water standoff removes near-field artifact and lets you scan a tender area without pressing on it. How to: 1. Fill a basin with room-temperature water and submerge the affected hand or foot. 2. Hold the linear transducer perpendicular to the skin, about 1 cm OFF the surface, fully under the water. 3. The water column acts as a built-in standoff pad, so you image the foreign body in the optimized focal zone with no probe pressure or pain. 4. Fan through the area; wood, glass, and plastic show as bright echoes, often with posterior shadowing or reverberation. Equipment: Basin

info.h: Cutting Needle to Release a Refractory Hair Tourniquet
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Cleanly severs a hair/thread tourniquet strangling an infant’s toe or finger when edema hides the strand and forceps unwrapping has failed — averting ischemia and digit loss. How to: 1. Examine the deep crease circumferentially; the constricting hair is often invisible against skin once the digit is swollen. 2. Apply a digital block / topical anesthetic and immobilize the digit. 3. Pick the dorsal midline (extensor surface), where the neurovascular bundles are NOT, as your cut site. 4. Lay a small cutting (e.g., PC-1) needle flat into the depth of the groove and lever/cut outward across the band until the strand divides and the constriction releases. 5. Confirm the full strand

info.h: String-Yank to Remove an Embedded Fishhook
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Fast, low-resource removal of a barbed fishhook, often with no anesthetic and no incision, when the barb sits near the surface. How to: 1. Lay the affected part flat against a firm surface and stabilize it. 2. Loop a strong string (monofilament line, 0-silk, or umbilical tape) around the bend (midpoint) of the hook. 3. With your other hand, press down on the shank/eye of the hook to disengage the barb from the tissue, keeping the shank parallel to the skin. 4. While maintaining that downward pressure, give a single firm, quick yank on the string parallel to the shank, 180° along the entry path. 5. Cover the field with gauze before yanking so the freed hook does not fly. If it f

info.h: Glove-Finger Tourniquet for a Bleeding Digit
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Creates a controlled digital tourniquet from a single exam glove so a profusely bleeding finger laceration can be examined and repaired in a bloodless field. How to: 1. Cut the finger off an exam glove and snip a small hole in its tip. 2. Roll that glove finger onto the patient’s injured digit, then roll it proximally so it self-rolls into a tight “ring” tourniquet at the base. 3. Keep the hole small for maximum tension; if too loose, use the pinky finger of the glove or start with a smaller glove. 4. Examine and repair, then ALWAYS remove the ring at the end — a rolled glove ring is easy to forget and can cause digital ischemia. Equipment: Single exam glove, scissors. _Source:

info.h: M-Mode Line to Aim a US-Guided Peripheral IV
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Shows exactly where the probe’s centerline projects, so you advance the IV needle along the right trajectory instead of guessing where mid-screen sits on the probe. How to: 1. Center the target vein in the middle of the ultrasound screen in short axis. 2. Press the M-mode button ONCE — a vertical reference line appears down the middle of the image, marking the probe’s centerline. 3. Line up your IV catheter with the corresponding center notch on the probe face. 4. Insert the needle in that plane and advance — the M-mode line predicts the needle’s path to the vein. 5. This is a free stand-in for a “biopsy guide” feature that not every machine has. Equipment: Ultrasound with M-mo

info.h: Arm-Board Finger Immobilization for a Pediatric Hand Procedure
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Isolates one finger and pins a squirming child’s hand still for a nailbed repair, laceration, or foreign-body removal — and hides the procedure from the child’s view to cut anxiety. How to: 1. Lay the child’s forearm on an adult-size rigid IV arm board, leaving extra board sticking out past the fingertips to use as a handle. 2. Tape the wrist and forearm to the board snugly but NOT circumferentially tight — leave room to check perfusion. 3. Tape down every finger joint EXCEPT the digit you are working on, securing each to the board so the child cannot pull or twist away. 4. The single freed finger is now isolated in your field; the taped-down neighbors and the board handle stop

info.h: Bougie-Guided (Seldinger) Chest Tube in the Obese Patient
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Guarantees a chest tube actually reaches the pleural space instead of getting lost in subcutaneous fat, by railroading it over a bougie left in the chest after finger thoracostomy. How to: 1. Make your incision and bluntly dissect over the rib into the pleural space; perform a finger sweep to confirm you are inside the thorax (feel lung or empty cavity, not fat). 2. Keeping your finger in the tract, slide a standard airway bougie alongside it into the pleural cavity, coude tip leading. 3. Confirm the bougie sits intrathoracic (it advances freely and easily past your fingertip into the cavity). 4. Load the chest tube over the bougie like a guidewire and advance the tube along th

info.h: Bubble Study to Confirm Central Line Placement at the Bedside
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Confirms a central venous catheter is in the vein (not an artery) and excludes pneumothorax in minutes with ultrasound, ~24 minutes faster than waiting on a chest x-ray. How to: 1. First scan the lung apices for pleural sliding to rule out a pneumothorax from the stick. 2. Look at both internal jugular veins to make sure the catheter did not get misdirected up the neck. 3. Put the ultrasound on the heart in a subcostal or apical four-chamber view so you can see the right atrium. 4. Have a partner inject 10 mL of saline (agitated for more bubbles) into the CVC’s distal port while you watch the right atrium. 5. A prompt shower of microbubbles in the right heart confirms venous pl

info.h: Angiocatheter Instead of a Needle for Knee Arthrocentesis
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you tap or inject a knee without a rigid metal needle sitting in the joint — a soft catheter stays put through syringe swaps, lets you milk out every fluid pocket, and spares cartilage from needle movement. How to: 1. Prep and anesthetize for arthrocentesis in the usual way (anteromedial or anterolateral approach). 2. Put an 18-gauge angiocatheter (instead of a plain needle) on the syringe. 3. Insert while aspirating; the instant synovial fluid returns, advance the plastic catheter into the joint and withdraw the inner needle. 4. Aspirate through the indwelling catheter; gently milk/manipulate the knee to herd fluid toward the tip, and aspirate as you slowly withdraw to ca

info.h: IV Tubing as an LP Opening-Pressure Manometer
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Measures CSF opening pressure during a lumbar puncture when no dedicated spinal manometer is on the tray, using the giving set every ED already stocks. How to: 1. Keep the patient in the LATERAL DECUBITUS position with legs relaxed — a sitting position or a straining/Valsalva patient falsely raises the reading. 2. Once you have free CSF flow, attach a three-way stopcock to the spinal needle hub. 3. Connect a length of standard IV giving-set tubing to the stopcock, held vertically against a tape measure or ruler. 4. Open the stopcock to the tubing and let CSF rise; read the height of the fluid column above the needle in cm. 5. Interpret cautiously — a giving set tends to UNDERES

info.h: Lateral Insulin-Needle Drainage of a Subungual Hematoma
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Evacuates a painful subungual hematoma without drilling through the nail plate — you enter alongside the nail with a fine needle, avoiding the cracking and nail-bed contact of the drill or cautery methods. How to: 1. Confirm an intact nail with a simple hematoma (no large nail-edge laceration or displaced distal phalanx fracture needing repair); clean the digit. 2. Take a 29-gauge extra-fine (insulin) needle and orient it PARALLEL to the nail at the hyponychium (the free distal edge). 3. Aim toward the most distal portion of the hematoma, keeping the needle closer to the underside of the nail than to the nail bed. 4. Advance just until you penetrate the blood pocket, then withd

info.h: Blood-Pressure Cuff as a Wide, Adjustable IV Tourniquet
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Distends veins for difficult IV access more comfortably and controllably than a rubber band tourniquet — the wide cuff compresses evenly and lets you dial in the exact pressure that fills the veins without occluding arterial inflow. How to: 1. Wrap a standard BP cuff around the arm proximal to your target vein. 2. Inflate to roughly the patient’s diastolic pressure (or start low and creep up) so venous outflow is blocked but the radial pulse stays palpable. 3. Let the veins fill for a minute, then cannulate as usual. 4. Deflate the cuff once the catheter is in and flushing. Equipment: Blood-pressure cuff with manometer/bulb, IV catheter. _Source: Approach to Difficult Vascular

info.h: Stethoscope as a Neck Tourniquet for External Jugular Cannulation
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Plumps up a flat external jugular vein for IV access when you have no good way to tourniquet the neck — a stethoscope looped around the neck increased EJ cross-sectional area about 4-fold in one minute, without compressing the trachea or needing Trendelenburg. How to: 1. Position the patient supine with the head turned slightly away from the target side. 2. Loop the tubing of your stethoscope around the patient’s neck (binaurals/chestpiece acting like the tourniquet ends), snug but comfortable, occluding the superficial EJ without restricting the airway. 3. Wait ~1 minute for the EJ to distend and become visible/palpable. 4. Cannulate the EJ as usual; have the patient hum if yo

info.h: Glass Cleaner (Windex) as a Slick Lubricant for Ring Removal
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Slides a stuck ring off a swollen finger when soap and water fail, using the surfactant in ammonia-based glass cleaner as a super-slick lubricant — a fast, atraumatic alternative before resorting to a ring cutter. How to: 1. First milk the edema distally: elevate the hand and compress the finger from tip to base for a minute to push swelling proximally. 2. Spray or apply a generous amount of ammonia-based glass cleaner (e.g., Windex) around the ring and finger — the surfactant is far more slippery than soap. 3. Twist and rock the ring while applying steady distal traction, working it over the knuckle. 4. Reapply cleaner as needed; combine with the string/elastic-wrap or oxygen-

info.h: Zigzag Posterolateral Tract for Olecranon Bursa Aspiration
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Aspirates an olecranon (or prepatellar) bursa while preventing the dreaded chronic draining fistula — a long, angled skin tract self-seals once the needle is out, unlike a straight perpendicular stick. How to: 1. Position the elbow flexed ~90 degrees resting on a table; prep the skin and avoid the MEDIAL approach (the ulnar nerve runs there). 2. Enter from a posterolateral point a centimeter or two AWAY from the most fluctuant peak, not directly over it. 3. Angle the needle obliquely (a “zigzag” / Z-track), advancing through skin and subcutaneous tissue before entering the bursa, so the skin and bursal puncture sites do not line up. 4. Aspirate to dryness, keeping the needle pa

info.h: Ultrasound to Find the Pedal Pulse for an ABI
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Pinpoints the dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial artery when you cannot palpate it, so you can get a true ankle-brachial index instead of wasting minutes whisking the Doppler over the wrong spot. How to: 1. Place a linear (high-frequency) ultrasound probe over the expected location of the dorsalis pedis (lateral to the EHL tendon on the dorsum) or posterior tibial (behind the medial malleolus) artery. 2. Find the pulsatile vessel on the screen and mark the skin directly over it with a pen. 3. Put the continuous-wave Doppler probe exactly on that mark to lock onto the arterial waveform. 4. Inflate the ankle cuff and record the pressure at which flow returns; divide by the higher

info.h: IV Catheter to Deflate a Stuck Gastrostomy Tube Balloon
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Frees a G-tube whose balloon cuff will not deflate so you can replace it at the bedside instead of calling surgery or IR. How to: 1. Trace the tube near the skin and identify the balloon-cuff lumen by its different coloration. 2. Bend the G-tube so a catheter can enter the cuff lumen parallel to the skin, and slip a barrier between tube and patient to avoid a needlestick. 3. Insert a 22G IV catheter into the cuff lumen, then withdraw the inner needle. 4. Attach a 10 cc syringe to the catheter and aspirate the balloon fluid until the cuff collapses. 5. Remove and replace the gastrostomy tube using standard technique. Equipment: 22G IV catheter, 10 cc syringe, skin barrier, repla

info.h: AC Vein Plus Lidocaine Pretreatment to Kill Propofol Burn
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Eliminates the searing pain of a propofol push so an awake patient stays calm during induction of procedural sedation. How to: 1. Whenever you can, start the IV in the antecubital fossa rather than the hand — a larger proximal vein dilutes the propofol fast and hurts far less. 2. For a hand or wrist IV that you cannot move, pretreat first: place a tourniquet proximal to the site. 3. Inject 0.5 mg/kg of lidocaine IV (about 35 mg = 3.5 mL of 1% for a 70 kg adult) and leave the tourniquet up for 30–120 seconds so the anesthetic dwells in the vein wall. 4. Release the tourniquet, then push the propofol through the now-numbed vein. 5. Warn the patient that some pressure is normal; t

info.h: Gravity Large-Volume Paracentesis With an Angiocatheter
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Drains a tense ascites with only an angiocatheter and IV tubing when no paracentesis kit or vacuum bottle is available. How to: 1. Ultrasound-mark a pocket of fluid (classically the left lower quadrant, lateral to the rectus and inferior epigastric vessels); prep and drape sterilely. 2. Anesthetize the skin and track, then advance a large-bore (14–16G) angiocatheter using a Z-track until you aspirate fluid; thread the cannula in and withdraw the needle. 3. Connect IV extension tubing to the catheter hub and run the far end into a basin or empty container set BELOW the patient on the floor. 4. Let gravity siphon the ascites out; raise the head of the bed and reposition the patie

info.h: Hyaluronidase Perimeter Injection for IV Extravasation
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Rescues tissue after a non-vesicant IV infiltrates by enzymatically spreading and speeding reabsorption of the trapped fluid, often shrinking the swelling within 15–30 minutes and heading off necrosis. How to: 1. Stop the infusion immediately and, before removing the IV, gently aspirate back through it to pull off any residual extravasated drug; elevate the limb. 2. Dilute hyaluronidase to 15 units/mL (the vial is usually 150 units/mL — draw it into a tuberculin syringe with a 25G or smaller needle). 3. Give 15 units through the existing catheter, then remove the catheter. 4. Inject five 0.2 mL aliquots (1 mL total) subcutaneously in a ring around the LEADING EDGE of the infilt

info.h: Small Syringe to Unblock a Clotted IV or PICC Line
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Reopens an obstructed peripheral IV or PICC that won’t flush with a standard 10 mL syringe, sparing a heparin or thrombolytic flush and often a re-stick. How to: 1. Confirm the line is clotted, not just kinked or clamped — check for kinks, a closed clamp, and correct positioning first. 2. Swap your 10 mL syringe for a saline-filled 3 mL syringe; the smaller barrel generates far higher pressure per unit of force on the plunger (Pascal’s principle). 3. Attach the 3 mL syringe and apply gentle, steady pressure — it usually takes very little force to dislodge the clot. 4. Once it flushes, aspirate to confirm blood return, then flush normally and resume use. 5. Do NOT force it: if t

info.h: Saline Float to Advance a Catheter Past a Valve
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Salvages a peripheral IV that gets flashback but won’t thread because the catheter tip is hung up on a venous valve, floating it through instead of abandoning the stick. How to: 1. Get flashback, then lower the needle/catheter nearly parallel to the skin and advance the catheter a few more millimeters off the needle first — this alone fixes many failures. 2. If it still won’t advance, leave the catheter in the vein and remove the needle. 3. Attach a saline-filled syringe to the catheter hub. 4. Simultaneously push a slow, gentle flush while advancing the catheter — the fluid opens the valve and “floats” the catheter through it. 5. Stop and reassess if you see a bleb or feel res

info.h: Nasal Speculum to See Into an Umbilical Foreign Body
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Turns a deep, blind umbilical pit into a directly visualized cavity so a retained foreign body (lint ball, jewelry, “omphalolith”) can be grasped under sight after skin retractors and blind probing fail. How to: 1. Clean the umbilicus and give topical or local anesthetic if the tract is tender. 2. Insert a long ENT nasal speculum into the umbilical tract, closed. 3. Open the speculum blades to retract the walls and light up the cavity (add a headlamp). 4. Identify the foreign body under direct visualization. 5. Remove it with bayonet or fine forceps; irrigate and re-inspect for retained material. Equipment: Long nasal speculum, forceps (bayonet/fine), headlamp, irrigation, loca

info.h: Angiocatheter-First Central Line to Skip a Seldinger Step
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes the fiddly step of feeding a bare angiocatheter over the wire during a central line by cannulating the vein with the kit’s angiocatheter from the start, so the guidewire threads straight through it. How to: 1. Prep and drape as usual; note the central line kit ships with BOTH a long introducer needle and a long angiocatheter. 2. Cannulate the target central vein using the ANGIOCATHETER (not the bare needle) while applying negative pressure on the syringe. 3. On venous return, advance the angiocatheter off its needle into the vessel WITHOUT a guidewire. 4. Remove the needle/syringe and feed the guidewire directly through the seated angiocatheter, then continue the Seldin

info.h: Bend the Angiocatheter for a Shallow External Jugular Stick
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Clears the mandible so you can approach the external jugular vein at a shallow enough angle to thread it — the fix for the short, chubby, or immobile neck (kids, obese patients) where a straight needle keeps hitting bone. How to: 1. Place the patient in Trendelenburg and turn the head away to engorge and expose the EJ. 2. Bend the proximal one-third of the angiocatheter needle up about 10–15 degrees (do NOT bend right at the hub — that blocks catheter feeding). 3. Enter the skin over the EJ at a shallow angle; the bend lets the tip ride under the mandible instead of into it. 4. On flashback, drop the angle further and feed the catheter off the needle as usual. 5. Secure the lin

info.h: Straighten a J-Tip Guidewire to Reload It Into the Needle Hub
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you re-feed a curved J-tip guidewire back into the needle hub one-handed when the plastic introducer sleeve is missing or unusable, so you don’t lose the wire or the venous access. How to: 1. Keep one hand stabilizing the needle in the vein; the J-tip has a flexible inner ribbon wire inside an outer coil spring. 2. With the other hand, grip the guidewire just proximal to the J and STRETCH it — increasing the outer coil density there pulls the J-tip straight. 3. Feed the now-straightened tip into the needle hub while maintaining the stretch. 4. Release the stretch once the tip is inside the hub — the J-shape springs back and you advance the wire normally. 5. Never force a w

info.h: Reversed-Glove Wrap for Safe Guidewire Disposal
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Prevents the blood-flick needlestick/splash exposure that happens when you try to stuff a long, springy guidewire into a rectangular sharps bin. How to: 1. After the line is placed, do NOT jab the straight wire at the sharps slot — that whips a drop of blood off the tip. 2. Coil the guidewire loosely around two or three of your gloved knuckles. 3. Peel that glove off inside-out over the coiled wire so the wire ends up wrapped inside the reversed glove. 4. Drop the whole contained bundle into the sharps bin. 5. Doff and replace the glove and continue. Equipment: The used guidewire, an exam glove, sharps container. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Safer guidewire disposal (Bry

info.h: Removable Arterial-Line Guidewire as a Spare
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives you a backup guidewire to salvage a tricky ultrasound-guided deep IV (e.g., basilic vein) when the vein is cannulated but the catheter won’t thread and no dedicated wire is stocked. How to: 1. Grab an Arrow Seldinger-based arterial-line kit — its guidewire is removable. 2. Look along the clear guidewire sheath for a narrow lengthwise slit and slide the guidewire out through it. 3. Note the black plastic handle on one end — keep hold of it so the wire is never lost into the catheter. 4. Feed the freed wire through your in-place IV catheter to stabilize access, then advance a longer catheter over it Seldinger-style. 5. Keep the wire under control at all times and never let

info.h: Yankauer Suction to Contain the Foul Abscess Smell
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps the room (and staff) from being overwhelmed by a putrid abscess during I&D by moving the odorous pus straight into a closed suction canister instead of letting it drain into open air. How to: 1. Set up wall suction with a Yankauer tip and a closed canister as usual. 2. Make only a small initial stab incision — just big enough to admit the Yankauer tip. 3. Insert the Yankauer tip into the opening and suction out as much pus as possible directly into the canister. 4. The principle: you are transferring the smell from one closed system (the abscess) into another closed system (the wall canister) rather than releasing it into the room. 5. Then extend the incision and complete

info.h: Thin LP Needle + 60 mL Syringe for Atraumatic Paracentesis
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you tap ascites (e.g., to rule out SBP) with far less catheter/needle trauma, less pain, and less post-procedure ascitic leak than a large-bore needle or angiocatheter. How to: 1. Prep and drape the LLQ (or POCUS-marked) pocket sterilely and anesthetize the tract. 2. Take a thin 22– or 24-gauge lumbar-puncture needle and discard the stylet. 3. Attach it directly to a 60 mL syringe. 4. Advance while gently aspirating until ascitic fluid returns; withdraw a diagnostic 30–60 mL. 5. For culture yield, inoculate blood-culture bottles at the bedside — this raises sensitivity to >90%. Equipment: 22– or 24-gauge spinal (LP) needle, 60 mL syringe, sterile prep, local anesthetic, bl

info.h: Squeeze Test to Confirm Intraosseous Placement
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Detects an IO needle that has passed through bone into soft tissue — a failure mode standard signs (marrow aspirate, firm needle, easy flush) can miss — preventing undetected extravasation of resuscitation drugs and fluids. How to: 1. Place the IO and confirm the usual signs (marrow return, firm seating, ability to flush). 2. Begin flushing or infusing fluid through the line. 3. With both hands, firmly compress the soft tissue circumferentially around the insertion site. 4. Watch the flow: continued flow means the needle is intramedullary (good); flow that stalls or drops sharply means the needle is in soft tissue (misplaced), because your squeeze back-pressures the extravasate

info.h: DIY Capnography Nasal Cannula for Procedural Sedation
info.pt: Procedures & Access — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives you continuous end-tidal CO2 monitoring during procedural sedation so you catch apnea/hypoventilation seconds before the pulse-ox drops, without a dedicated (often unstocked) sampling cannula. How to: 1. Take a standard oxygen nasal cannula and cut one prong near its base with scissors. 2. Connect the cut-open prong lumen to the ETCO2 sampling line from the monitor. 3. Leave the other prong intact and running low-flow O2 as usual. 4. Place on the patient: one prong now delivers oxygen, the other samples exhaled CO2. 5. Watch the waveform — a present waveform means the patient is breathing, a flat line means apnea. This lets you safely give supplemental O2 (which masks des

Accomplishes: Anterior nasal packing for epistaxis using oxidized cellulose — an alternative to commercial tampons that dissolves and doesn’t require removal. How to: 1. Take a strip of Surgicel (oxidized regenerated cellulose). 2. Roll it into a compact “burrito.” 3. Pack it into the bleeding anterior nasal cavity for tamponade and hemostasis. Equipment: Surgicel, nasal speculum, bayonet forceps. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Dual Foley Catheter for Massive Epistaxis
info.t: Accomplishes: Improvised posterior + anterior tamponade for severe / posterior epistaxis when a commercial dual-balloon device isn’t available. How to: 1. With the mouth open, insert a 14-Fr Foley into the nostril until the tip is visible in the posterior oropharynx. 2. Inflate the first balloon with 15–20 cc air. 3. Pull the catheter forward until it seats against the posterior choana. 4. If bleeding persists, insert a second Foley to resistance and inflate ~15 cc for added surface tamponade. Equipment: Two 14-Fr Foley catheters, syringe/air, lubricant. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

Accomplishes: Improves placement and hydration of a Merocel nasal tampon, easing insertion and expansion. How to: 1. Pass an angiocatheter alongside/through the Merocel to direct saline. 2. Insert the Merocel into the nasal cavity. 3. Inject saline through the angiocatheter to rapidly expand the tampon in place. Equipment: Merocel nasal tampon, angiocatheter, saline syringe. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

Accomplishes: Clears nasal secretions in a congested infant (e.g., bronchiolitis) when a commercial aspirator isn’t available. How to: 1. Assemble a low-pressure aspirator from suction tubing and a small suction catheter. 2. Apply gentle suction to each nostril to evacuate secretions (keep pressure low to protect mucosa). Equipment: Suction tubing, small suction catheter, wall suction on a low setting. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: DIY Ear Irrigation Catheter for Cerumen
info.t: Accomplishes: Builds a safe, low-cost ear-irrigation rig to flush impacted cerumen or a foreign body when a commercial bulb/irrigator isn’t stocked. How to: 1. First confirm the tympanic membrane is intact — do not irrigate a perforated or post-surgical (tube) ear. 2. Remove the needle from an 18G angiocatheter and trim the plastic cannula short so it cannot reach the TM. 3. Fill a 20–60 mL syringe with body-temperature water/saline (cool fluid triggers vertigo and vomiting) and attach the cannula. 4. Straighten the canal (pull pinna up and back in adults), aim along the canal wall, and irrigate in pulses. 5. Catch runoff in an emesis basin held under the ear; repeat, softening first with a

info.h: Acetone to Dissolve a Glued or Foam Ear Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Chemically softens or dissolves certain ear-canal foreign bodies (Styrofoam beads, a glue/cyanoacrylate plug) so they can be removed atraumatically instead of being grasped and fragmented. How to: 1. First confirm the tympanic membrane is intact — acetone is contraindicated with any TM perforation or tympanostomy tube. 2. Confirm the object is acetone-susceptible (Styrofoam, cyanoacrylate); do NOT use it on organic matter, button batteries, or vegetable foreign bodies that may swell. 3. Instill a few drops of acetone (nail-polish remover) into the canal with the affected ear up. 4. Wait about 30 minutes for the object to dissolve or loosen. 5. Gently suction or irrigate out the

info.h: Needle-Cap Bumper Guard for Peritonsillar Abscess Drainage
info.t: Accomplishes: Prevents over-advancing the spinal needle into the carotid (which sits 2–2.5 cm posterolateral to the tonsil) during PTA aspiration by capping insertion depth. How to: 1. Choose a 3.5-inch 18G spinal needle for the deep narrow oropharynx. 2. Trim the distal ~1 cm off the plastic needle sheath, then slide it back over the needle so only about 1–1.5 cm of tip protrudes. 3. Tape the cut sheath to the syringe so it cannot slide back during the procedure. 4. Use POCUS first when available to map carotid depth, then aspirate at the point of maximal fluctuance no deeper than the exposed tip. 5. For I&D, similarly tape the scalpel guard so the blade only exposes ~1 cm. Equipment: 3.5-i

info.h: Magnetized Hemostat to Retrieve a Metallic Ear/Nose Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Extracts a small ferromagnetic object (a BB, button-cell fragment, metal bead) from the ear canal or nose without grasping and pushing it deeper, using gear every ED already stocks. How to: 1. Confirm the object is metallic and likely ferromagnetic on history/exam (and on x-ray if a button battery must be excluded — batteries need urgent removal, not delay). 2. Grab the donut-shaped cardiac/pacemaker magnet kept for defibrillator troubleshooting. 3. Touch the tip of a metal hemostat or alligator forceps to the magnet for several seconds — this temporarily magnetizes the instrument tip. 4. Advance the now-magnetized tip up to (not past) the object under direct visualization; the

info.h: Tongue-Blade Bite Test to Screen for Mandible Fracture
info.t: Accomplishes: A fast, no-cost bedside screen for mandibular fracture — roughly 95–96% sensitive, so a clearly normal test makes fracture unlikely and helps prioritize imaging. How to: 1. Place a wooden tongue blade between the patient’s molars on one side and ask them to bite down hard. 2. Grasp the protruding end and twist/torque it, trying to snap the blade against their clenched bite. 3. A patient with an intact mandible bites hard enough that you can rotate and crack the blade. 4. A patient who releases the bite or cannot tolerate the torque from pain is a POSITIVE test — image the mandible. 5. Test both sides; pair with exam for malocclusion, step-off, and sublingual hematoma. It is a s

Accomplishes: Anesthetizes a finger with ONE volar injection instead of the traditional two- or three-stick ring block, with comparable success and less needle-stick pain. How to: 1. Prep the volar finger base; identify the proximal digital (palmar) crease where the finger meets the palm. 2. Insert the needle subcutaneously at the midpoint of that crease, just under the skin on the volar side (you are depositing on top of the flexor tendon sheath, not into it). 3. Inject 2–3 mL of plain lidocaine as a subcutaneous wheal; the anesthetic spreads laterally to bathe both digital nerves. 4. Wait about 5 minutes; ~75% are fully anesthetized by 5 min and nearly all by 10 min. 5. Use PLAIN local ane

info.h: 18G Introducer Trick for a Flimsy Atraumatic LP Needle
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you drive a thin, flexible small-gauge atraumatic (pencil-point) spinal needle — which lowers post-LP headache rates — without it bending or buckling on the skin. How to: 1. Choose an atraumatic 22–25G pencil-point needle to minimize the dural defect (post-LP headache ~4% with 22G atraumatic vs ~40% with a 20G cutting needle). 2. After local anesthesia, puncture only the skin and superficial soft tissue with a standard 18G needle to create a track — it acts as an introducer/trocar. 3. Leave the 18G hub seated, then thread the flexible atraumatic needle THROUGH the 18G introducer so the rigid sheath keeps it from flexing. 4. Advance the atraumatic needle in the usual midlin

info.h: Nasal Trumpet Guide for Less-Traumatic Nasopharyngoscopy
info.t: Accomplishes: Cuts the pain and mucosal trauma of flexible nasopharyngoscopy by padding the scope through the sharpest turn in the nasal passage. How to: 1. Anesthetize first: viscous lidocaine into the nares plus nebulized lidocaine to numb the nasopharynx. 2. Insert a soft, malleable nasal trumpet (nasopharyngeal airway) into the nostril as a protective conduit. 3. Thread the fiberoptic scope through the lumen of the trumpet so the cable rides inside the soft tube, not against raw mucosa, through the painful inferior turn past the conchae. 4. Advance to the posterior pharynx/larynx to inspect for foreign body or laryngeal edema. 5. If the trumpet rim blocks your view, pull it back slightly

info.h: Tongue-Blade “Nose Pincher” for Constant Epistaxis Pressure
info.t: Accomplishes: Forces uninterrupted nasal compression for anterior epistaxis, fixing the real reason nosebleeds persist — patients keep releasing pressure every few seconds to check. How to: 1. First have the patient blow out clots and apply a topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline) if available. 2. Tape the ends of two wooden tongue blades together to form a hinged “clothespin.” 3. Wedge the soft cartilaginous part of the nose (not the bony bridge) between the open ends so the blades squeeze both nostrils shut. 4. Leave the pincher clamped in place for a full 15–20 minutes — the constant, hands-free pressure the patient cannot fidget with is what stops the bleed. 5. Release and re-inspect; i

info.h: Drain a Nasal Septal Hematoma Before It Eats the Cartilage
info.t: Accomplishes: Evacuates a septal hematoma so the avascular septal cartilage keeps its blood supply, heading off septal necrosis, abscess, and a permanent saddle-nose deformity. How to: 1. Suspect it after ANY nasal trauma: examine both nares and gently press the septum with a cotton swab — a normal septum is thin and firm, a hematoma is a soft, boggy, bluish bulge that compresses. 2. Anesthetize topically/locally, then incise the mucosa over the most fluctuant point with an 11-blade. 3. Express and suction the clot; a small Penrose drain or a corner of glove can keep the pocket open. 4. Place bilateral anterior packing or a quilting/mattress suture to compress the leaves of mucosa back again

info.h: Mother’s Kiss for a Pediatric Nasal Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Expels an anterior nasal foreign body in a young child with a parent-delivered puff of positive pressure — no instruments, no sedation, and it often avoids a trip to the OR. How to: 1. Best for a cooperative caregiver and a smooth, anteriorly located object; warn against button batteries or magnets, which need urgent instrument removal instead. 2. Have the parent explain it as a “big kiss” so the child is not frightened. 3. The parent occludes the UNAFFECTED nostril with a finger, pressing it closed. 4. The parent places their mouth over the child’s open mouth to form a seal and gives a short, sharp puff — first gently until they feel the glottis close (resistance), then one mo

info.h: Pelvic Speculum as a Lit Tongue Depressor for PTA Drainage
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives you both bright light and tongue depression for peritonsillar abscess aspiration when no laryngoscope is free, and frees one of your hands by letting the patient hold the device. How to: 1. Take a disposable fiberoptic-lit plastic vaginal speculum and remove the top blade, leaving the single bottom blade with its attached light. 2. Hand the lit half-speculum to the seated, anesthetized patient and have them depress their own tongue base with it. 3. Put a Yankauer suction in the patient’s other hand for self-suction, which frees BOTH of your hands for the needle and syringe. 4. Aspirate the point of maximal fluctuance under the bright direct light; keep the needle shallow

info.h: Pediatric Video Laryngoscope to See and Grab an Ear Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Turns a frustrating, poorly-lit ear-canal foreign-body removal into a hands-free, magnified, two-handed procedure — the screen shows the object while both your hands work, beating the cramped otoscope view. How to: 1. Position the child (papoose or parent-held) and straighten the canal by pulling the pinna up and back. 2. Insert a Miller 0 (pediatric) video-laryngoscope blade, such as a C-MAC, into the ear canal aperture to light and magnify the canal on the screen. 3. With the canal and object displayed, pass alligator forceps, a cerumen loop, or a right-angle hook alongside the blade under direct video. 4. Grasp or hook the object and withdraw; the video view confirms you hav

info.h: Frazier Suction to Extract a Live Insect From the Ear
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes a live or dead insect from the ear canal in one intact piece, avoiding the shredding and retained debris that forceps cause on a friable insect body. How to: 1. First immobilize the insect: instill viscous (or plain) lidocaine to drown it and stop the distressing movement. 2. Connect a Frazier suction tip to low continuous wall suction. 3. Consider light sedation — the buzzing sensation is very distressing and a still patient protects the canal. 4.
