Once the insect is confirmed dead, advance the Frazier tip slowly into the canal under direct visualization. 5. Suction the insect out whole rather than grasping and fragmenting it; re-examine the canal and TM. Equipment: Fra

info.h: Walk Anesthesia Up the Nose With Viscous-Lidocaine Q-Tips
info.t: Accomplishes: Numbs the most sensitive spot — where an NG tube or scope turns the corner into the nasopharynx — AND tests for adequate anesthesia before instrumentation, making NG placement and nasopharyngoscopy far less painful than blind atomization. How to: 1. Load the cotton end of a long Q-tip with copious viscous lidocaine. 2. Slide it into the nostril along the intended NG/scope path. 3. Stop advancing when you meet resistance or the patient feels discomfort; twirl the Q-tip to coat the mucosa. 4. Wait until the patient can no longer feel the swab at that depth. 5. Reload, advance a bit further, and repeat until you reach the nasopharynx, then proceed with the NG tube or scope. Equipm

info.h: DIY Lidocaine-Oxymetazoline Atomizer for Painless NG/Nasal Tubes
info.t: Accomplishes: Anesthetizes AND vasoconstricts the nose in one atomized spray so NG-tube placement and nasopharyngoscopy stop on the first try — patients typically only give you one or two attempts before they refuse. How to: 1. Grab a stock nasal oxymetazoline (Afrin) spray bottle — the small pump atomizer is what you want. 2. Using a 25G needle through the bottle stopper, draw OUT a few mL of the oxymetazoline and inject IN 5–10 mL of 1–2% lidocaine, mixing the vasoconstrictor and anesthetic in the same atomizer. 3. Have the patient sniff while you actuate 2–3 sprays into each nostril; the pump finely atomizes the mix so it coats the whole nasal mucosa. 4. Wait a few minutes — anesthesia an

info.h: Wet the Merocel Tip for a Painless Tampon Insertion
info.t: Accomplishes: Eases the most painful part of placing a Merocel nasal tampon — the dry, rigid, sharp leading edge scraping the naris — so the sponge slides in deeper and more comfortably for anterior epistaxis. How to: 1. Pretreat the nostril: have the patient blow out clots and apply topical oxymetazoline plus a little lidocaine if available. 2. Take the compressed, dehydrated Merocel tampon — note its leading tip is a hard, sharp edge that catches on mucosa. 3. Dip or wet ONLY the tip of the tampon with a few drops of water or saline so that leading edge softens into a rounded cushion. 4. Keep the rest of the sponge dry and compressed, then slide it straight back along the FLOOR of the nose

info.h: Improvised Condom-and-Angiocath Suction Device for a Nasal Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Builds a gentle, sealed suction-extraction tool to pull a smooth anterior nasal foreign body (a bead, popcorn kernel) out of a child’s nose when commercial suction tips and balloon catheters are not handy. How to: 1. Confirm an anterior, smooth, non-organic object; button batteries and magnets need urgent instrument removal instead, not a suction trick. 2. Cut the closed tip off a condom and tape the open end over the hub of a large-bore (e.g., 18G) angiocatheter to make a soft, atraumatic suction cup. 3. Apply plenty of lubricant around the foreign body and the device tip. 4. Connect the angiocatheter to low wall suction, seat the soft condom cup against the object under direc

info.h: Oxymetazoline Straight Onto the Nasal Packing
info.t: Accomplishes: Adds local vasoconstriction at the bleeding site by soaking the nasal tampon itself with oxymetazoline, so the packing both tamponades AND shrinks the vessels — even useful for posterior bleeds. How to: 1. After controlling clots, insert the compressed Merocel/cotton tampon along the floor of the nose as usual. 2. Instead of expanding it with plain saline, drip oxymetazoline (Afrin) directly onto the inserted tampon. 3. The packing expands to tamponade while the alpha-agonist is delivered right onto the mucosa for vasoconstriction. 4. Top up with a few more drops if bleeding persists; reassess in 15–20 minutes. 5. Pair with topical TXA on the same packing when available for an

info.h: Tissue-Adhesive on a Swab to Pull Out a Hard Ear Foreign Body
info.t: Accomplishes: Extracts a smooth, hard, non-organic ear foreign body (a bead or plastic pellet) that forceps and cerumen loops just skid off of — without shoving it deeper toward the eardrum. How to: 1. Visualize the object under direct otoscopy or a video laryngoscope for magnification, and confirm it is smooth/hard and non-organic. 2. Put a SMALL amount of tissue adhesive (Dermabond) on the wooden end of a cotton-tipped applicator (or a plastic ear pick with the tip cut flat for more surface contact). 3. Under direct vision advance the glued end to just touch the surface of the object — do NOT overload the glue or it will drip and cement the object to the canal wall. 4. Hold it in gentle co

info.h: Cervical Collar to Hold the Jaw After a TMJ Reduction
info.t: Accomplishes: Prevents the frustrating early re-dislocation of a reduced anterior TMJ (temporomandibular joint) by holding the mouth closed, replacing the bulky, slip-prone Kerlix/ACE chin wrap. How to: 1. Reduce the anterior TMJ dislocation with your usual technique and confirm normal occlusion. 2. Apply a semi-rigid cervical collar (Aspen or similar) instead of a chin-lift head bandage. 3. Seat the collar so its chin piece pushes the chin gently upward, keeping the teeth together. 4. Counsel the patient to avoid wide mouth opening and to eat a soft diet. 5. Leave the collar on for support and arrange follow-up; especially useful for recurrent/lax-ligament dislocators. Equipment: Semi-rigid

info.h: Two-Person IV-Tubing Aspiration for Peritonsillar Abscess
info.t: Accomplishes: Splits peritonsillar abscess drainage into two easy jobs so you focus entirely on aiming the needle while an assistant does the awkward one-handed aspiration, improving control and yield in a tight, gagging airway. How to: 1. Prep as usual: topical then injected local anesthetic, good light, and a needle guard (trim the spinal-needle sheath so only ~1 cm of tip is exposed to stay clear of the deep carotid). 2. Attach IV extension tubing to the hub of the spinal needle, and connect the far end of the tubing to a syringe. 3. You hold and direct ONLY the needle; puncture the mucosa over the point of maximal fluctuance (superior pole first). 4. Once through the mucosa, have the ass

info.h: DIY Soft Ear Curette From a Polyester Applicator
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you clear impacted cerumen and see a pediatric tympanic membrane without the canal bleeding and trauma a rigid metal curette causes — the softer, shapeable tool is better tolerated and lowers parental anxiety. How to: 1. Take a polyester-tipped applicator (a malleable-handle swab, NOT a wooden cotton swab). 2. Fold the applicator in half. 3. Twist the two apposing edges together into a single stiffer curette shaft. 4. Bend the tip to match the child’s ear-canal angle and the location of the wax plug. 5. Under direct otoscopic vision, gently scoop the cerumen out. Equipment: Polyester-tipped applicator (e.g., Puritan-style flexible swab). _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade —

Accomplishes: Turns gauze from a mouth sponge into a true pressure plug directly over the bleeding socket. How to: Fold damp gauze or a dental roll into a compact plug, seat it directly over the extraction socket, and have the patient bite continuously for 30-60 minutes. Do not let the patient peek every few minutes.

Accomplishes: Concentrates antifibrinolytic medication exactly where saliva keeps breaking down clot. How to: Soak a dental roll or gauze plug with TXA, place it directly over the socket, and have the patient bite continuously for 20-30 minutes. Repeat or combine with Surgicel/Gelfoam and suture if needed.

Accomplishes: Gives a low-tech pressure/tannin adjunct when dental supplies are limited. How to: Moisten a black tea bag, wrap it in gauze if needed, place it over the socket, and have the patient bite for 20-30 minutes. Use as backup only, not as definitive care for brisk bleeding.

info.h: Dry Socket: Irrigate, Do Not Curette
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes debris without stripping fragile socket tissue or worsening pain. How to: Use gentle saline irrigation, dental block/analgesia, and dental dressing/follow-up when available. Avoid aggressive scraping of the socket.

info.h: Sinus Communication: Do Not Prove It
info.t: Accomplishes: Avoids enlarging a suspected oroantral communication. How to: If posterior maxillary extraction symptoms suggest sinus communication, avoid probing and forceful irrigation. Give sinus precautions and arrange dental/OMFS follow-up.

info.h: N95 Nose-Bridge Splint for an Avulsed Tooth
info.t: Accomplishes: Stabilizes a reimplanted avulsed or subluxed permanent tooth in the ED when no dental splint kit is on hand — a temporizing bridge to the dentist. How to: 1. Time matters — reimplant a permanent tooth as fast as possible (viability drops sharply after ~30–60 min). 2. Lightly rinse the tooth and socket with saline; pat dry. 3. Reimplant the tooth into correct anatomic position. 4. Bend the pliable metal nose-bridge wire from an N95 mask (or a non-rebreather) to span the target tooth plus one adjacent tooth on each side; cut and round the edges. 5. Apply 2-octyl cyanoacrylate (tissue adhesive) to the inner splint and the buccal surfaces, bonding the splint across the teeth. 6. Wa

Accomplishes: Rapid bedside screen for markedly elevated intraocular pressure when a tonometer isn’t at hand. It can rule IN a hard eye but cannot rule out elevated pressure — it does not replace tonometry. How to: 1. Have the patient gently close both eyes. 2. Gently press both globes through the closed lids with fingertips. 3. Compare firmness of the affected eye to the normal eye. 4. A “rock hard” globe suggests acutely elevated IOP / angle closure. Equipment: None (examiner’s fingers). _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Bacitracin to Remove Nail Glue From Eyelids
info.t: Accomplishes: Frees eyelids/lashes glued shut by accidental cyanoacrylate (super/nail glue) without acetone or forceps that can scratch the cornea. How to: 1. Liberally coat the affected lid margins with bacitracin (petroleum-based) ointment. 2. Wait 15–20 minutes undisturbed. 3. Gently tease the lids and lashes apart with cotton-tipped applicators — avoid vigorous massage (residual hard glue can abrade cornea). 4. Irrigate copiously with saline. 5. Perform an ocular exam; consider ophthalmology referral. Equipment: Bacitracin ointment (1–2 tubes), cotton-tipped applicators, irrigation saline. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Trickle-In Eyedrops via the Medial Canthus
info.t: Accomplishes: Anesthetizes or medicates the eye of a patient who reflexively squeezes shut and cannot tolerate a drop placed directly on the cornea. How to: 1. Lay the patient supine with the nose pointing at the ceiling. 2. Have the patient keep the eye gently closed — do not force the lids open. 3. Drip several drops of the anesthetic/medication into the medial canthal well (the inner-corner pocket). 4. Ask the patient to blink or briefly crack the eye; the pooled solution trickles under the lids and coats the surface. 5. Once the topical anesthetic takes effect, the now-comfortable eye usually opens for exam. Equipment: Topical ophthalmic anesthetic/medication, supine positioning. _Source

info.h: Nasal Cannula for High-Volume Eye Irrigation
info.t: Accomplishes: Hands-light, well-tolerated continuous eye irrigation for chemical exposures — a cheaper, more comfortable alternative to the Morgan lens that every ED already stocks. How to: 1. Anesthetize the eye with a topical drop first (e.g., proparacaine) and check/adjust pH after irrigating. 2. Attach a standard nasal cannula to IV tubing spiked into a 1 L crystalloid bag (the tubing fits snugly into the cannula). 3. Rest the nasal prongs across the bridge of the nose so each prong directs flow into one eye. 4. Open the IV tubing wide and let the saline flood both eyes; have the patient look in all directions to irrigate the fornices. 5. Catch runoff in a basin or with towels; continue

info.h: Photograph Slit-Lamp Findings With a Smartphone
info.t: Accomplishes: Captures a sharable image of a dendritic ulcer, abrasion pattern, or corneal edema to send to ophthalmology — no expensive camera adapter required. How to: 1. Position the patient comfortably at the slit lamp and focus the finding through the eyepiece as usual. 2. Without moving the slit lamp or the patient, step back from the eyepiece. 3. Hold the smartphone camera lens flush against the eyepiece where your eye just was. 4. Let the camera autofocus on the illuminated image, then capture; a small adapter steadies it but is optional. Equipment: Slit lamp, smartphone camera. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Photograph slit lamp findings (Silver/Lin)._

info.h: Fluorescein to Find a Wandering Contact Lens
info.t: Accomplishes: Reveals a clear, hard-to-see soft contact lens (or a torn fragment) that a patient swears is still in the eye but you cannot visualize. How to: 1. Confirm the patient has NOT already removed the lens — fluorescein permanently stains a soft lens, so you only do this when you actually intend to find and remove it. 2. Instill a drop of fluorescein into the affected eye. 3. The soft-lens gel matrix soaks up the dye and turns yellow-green; sweep the fornices and under the upper lid with a cobalt-blue light. 4. The now-stained lens (or fragment) stands out clearly — grasp and remove it. 5. Irrigate afterward and re-examine the cornea for an abrasion. Equipment: Fluorescein strip or d

info.h: Saline-Rinsed Strip as a Gentle Fluorescein Dropper
info.t: Accomplishes: Makes an improvised liquid fluorescein dropper so you can dose the dye onto a squirmy patient’s eye (e.g., an infant) without the discomfort of touching a paper strip to the cornea. How to: 1. Remove contact lenses first (fluorescein permanently stains them). 2. Open only ONE end of the fluorescein strip package. 3. Flush a saline vial in and out of the open packet several times until the fluid turns yellow. 4. Use that yellow-tinted saline vial as an eyedropper, trickling it onto the eye; corneal epithelial defects glow green under blue light. 5. Mucus also stains — have the patient blink to tell them apart (mucus moves, a true defect stays put). Never reuse or share dye (Pseu

info.h: Bevel-Flick Technique for Corneal Foreign Body Removal
info.t: Accomplishes: Lifts an embedded corneal foreign body off the eye at the slit lamp while minimizing extra epithelial/conjunctival damage — you scoop under it with the flat of the bevel instead of scraping. How to: 1. Anesthetize BOTH eyes with topical proparacaine (numbing the other eye reduces reflex blinking); try irrigating the cornea first — a truly superficial foreign body may simply float off. 2. Mount a small needle (a 25-27G or even a 29G insulin/TB needle looks less threatening) on a syringe used as a handle, bevel UP and facing away from the eye. 3. Stabilize your dominant hand on the patient’s zygoma, bring the needle into the slit-lamp field, and approach the foreign body nearly t

Accomplishes: Makes a vision-saving lateral canthotomy/cantholysis for orbital compartment syndrome faster and far less bloody by pre-crushing the lateral canthus to mark the cut. How to: 1. Confirm orbital compartment syndrome (proptosis, “rock hard” eye, vision loss, afferent pupil defect, IOP often >40); the ONLY absolute contraindication is suspected globe rupture, so rule out laceration, hyphema, irregular pupil, IOP <5, or positive Seidel. 2. Inject ~2 mL of 1–2% lidocaine WITH epinephrine into the lateral canthus with a 25G needle, pointing away from the globe. 3. Clamp a needle driver (or hemostat) horizontally from the lateral canthus to the bony orbital rim — feel the lower jaw hit

info.h: Benzoin for Traction on Bloody, Swollen Eyelids
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you retract markedly swollen, blood-slicked eyelids for a trauma ocular exam when fingers and a cotton swab keep slipping — without putting pressure on a potentially ruptured globe. How to: 1. First rule out obvious globe rupture (irregular pupil, extruded contents, positive Seidel); if present, shield the eye and do NOT manipulate the lids. 2. Clean and DRY the upper and lower eyelid skin so they are no longer bloody — benzoin will not grip wet skin. 3. Apply a thin layer of tincture of benzoin to the eyelid skin only, carefully avoiding the eye, lash line, and conjunctiva. 4. Let it dry to a tacky finish (~1–2 minutes). 5. Now use your fingers or cotton-tipped applicator

info.h: Bend the Needle Tip Into a “Spoon” for Corneal Foreign Body Removal
info.t: Accomplishes: Turns the scary sharp needle into a tiny blunt scoop so you lift a corneal foreign body OFF the eye rather than risking a deeper jab — reassuring for the patient and safer if they flinch. How to: 1. Anesthetize with topical proparacaine and seat the patient firmly at the slit lamp; try irrigation first — a loose foreign body may just float off. 2. Grasp a 25G needle (hub on a syringe used as a handle) with a hemostat near the tip. 3. Bend the very tip of the needle ~45–60 degrees AWAY from the bevel, creating a small hook/spoon shape. 4. Stabilize your hand on the patient’s cheek and approach tangentially; slide the concave bent tip UNDER the foreign body and lift it out like a

info.h: Urine Dipstick to Check Eye pH in Chemical Burns
info.t: Accomplishes: Measures ocular surface pH during a chemical-burn irrigation when dedicated pH paper is missing, repurposing a ubiquitous urine reagent strip to guide your irrigation endpoint. How to: 1. Cut a urine dipstick so the pH reagent pad is the last pad on the end of the strip. 2. After topical anesthesia, gently touch that pad to the lower conjunctival sac (fornix), watching the trimmed sharp edge away from the cornea. 3. Read the color against the bottle chart; the urine-strip pH range (about 5–8.5) is reliable for this purpose. 4. Keep irrigating and rechecking every few minutes until the pH normalizes to ~7.0–7.4 and stays there. 5. If the reading sits outside the 5–8.5 window, sw

info.h: Paracanthal “One-Snip” Decompression for Orbital Compartment Syndrome
info.t: Accomplishes: Decompresses a sight-threatening retrobulbar hemorrhage with a single scissor cut, skipping the harder-to-strum cantholysis step of a full lateral canthotomy. How to: 1. Confirm orbital compartment syndrome (proptosis, “rock hard” eye, vision loss, afferent pupil defect, IOP often >40); rule out globe rupture first — that is the one absolute contraindication. 2. Inject a little 1–2% lidocaine with epinephrine just lateral to the lateral canthus, needle pointed away from the globe. 3. Pinch the full thickness of the lower eyelid about 1 cm directly below the lateral canthus with a hemostat for ~30 seconds to crush a bloodless line. 4. Make ONE full-thickness vertical snip throug

info.h: Ocular Ultrasound for the Shut, Swollen Traumatic Eye
info.t: Accomplishes: Checks pupil reactivity and extraocular-muscle entrapment when the lids are too swollen to open — without prying them apart and pressing on a possibly ruptured globe. How to: 1. Lay a GENEROUS layer of sterile lubricating jelly over the closed, swollen lid so the probe never touches or presses the globe (the gel is your standoff). 2. Rest a high-frequency linear probe gently on the lid with minimal pressure. 3. Entrapment check: in the axial plane ask the patient to look left and right, then sagittal plane look up and down — asymmetric globe excursion suggests an entrapped extraocular muscle. 4. Pupil check: angle the probe to bring the iris and lens into view, shine a light in

info.h: Paperclip Retractor for Double Lid Eversion
info.t: Accomplishes: Exposes the superior fornix under the upper eyelid — the classic hiding spot for a retained subtarsal foreign body causing repeated vertical corneal abrasions — when no commercial Desmarres retractor is on hand. How to: 1. Anesthetize the eye thoroughly with a topical anesthetic to reduce reflex blink. 2. Unbend a paperclip and re-bend the wide distal end into a small smooth curve; wipe it with an alcohol swab. 3. Evert the upper lid once over a cotton-tipped applicator while the patient looks down. 4. Slide the smooth curved paperclip end under the everted lid margin and lift to achieve full double eversion, exposing the fornix. 5. Inspect and sweep out any foreign body, then

info.h: Roll a Cotton-Tipped Applicator to Retract a Swollen Eyelid
info.t: Accomplishes: Retracts an edematous, traumatized eyelid to inspect the globe without a formal retractor and without pressing on a possibly ruptured eye — the rolling motion, not lifting, is the key. How to: 1. First rule out obvious globe rupture (irregular pupil, extruded contents, positive Seidel); if present, shield the eye and do not manipulate the lids. 2. Anesthetize with a topical drop if the patient is squeezing shut, and lay the patient supine. 3. Rest a cotton-tipped applicator horizontally on the surface of the swollen upper (or lower) lid. 4. Slowly rotate/twirl the applicator so the lid margin “rolls” up onto it — do NOT push down into the orbit; the lid climbs onto the shaft wi

info.h: Active Voiding Trial (AVT) for Foley Removal
info.t: Accomplishes: Tests whether a patient can void adequately right after catheter removal, reducing repeat catheterization, retention, and CAUTI risk. How to: 1. Instill 250–400 cc sterile saline through the Foley by gravity or slow push; stop early if discomfort/fullness. 2. Clamp the catheter to prevent drainage. 3. Deflate the balloon and remove the catheter; document the instilled volume. 4. Assist the patient to void immediately (males standing, females sitting). 5. Compare instilled vs voided volume and report within one hour; notify if the trial fails. Equipment: Sterile saline, in-place Foley, catheter clamp, syringe. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

Accomplishes: Non-invasive first attempt to abort low-flow (ischemic) priapism before aspiration/phenylephrine (~40% success in studied patients). How to: 1. Have the patient perform vigorous exercise immediately (stair climbing, squats). 2. Do not delay invasive management more than a few minutes if exercise fails. Equipment: None. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Release of an Entrapped Metal Zipper
info.t: Accomplishes: Frees skin caught in a metal zipper without procedural sedation, minimizing pain. How to: 1. Pull the garment away from the zipper to reduce stretch on trapped skin. 2. Apply lidocaine gel to the site for 2–3 minutes. 3. Identify the exposed teeth closest to the slider and carefully cut the zipper there, avoiding skin. 4. Gently advance the slider body forward to disengage it from the teeth. 5. Add more gel/lubricant to ease sliding; the zipper halves then release. Equipment: Lidocaine gel, blade or scissors (wire/trauma cutters). _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: IV Lidocaine Rescue for Renal Colic
info.t: Accomplishes: Opioid-sparing rescue analgesia for severe renal colic when NSAIDs and standard analgesia are inadequate or contraindicated. Evidence is mixed, so use this as a monitored rescue option, not first-line renal colic therapy. How to: 1. Confirm a renal-colic phenotype and screen for infection, solitary kidney/AKI risk, uncontrolled vomiting, AAA mimic, testicular/ovarian mimic, and other high-risk alternate diagnoses. 2. Use NSAID therapy first when safe; add acetaminophen/opioid rescue per usual pathway. 3. If pain remains severe and no lidocaine contraindication is present, give lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg IV slowly over about 10 minutes, max 200 mg. 4. Put the patient on a monitor durin

Accomplishes: Shrinks a swollen, trapped foreskin with osmosis so it can be reduced without procedural sedation or a dorsal slit — useful when manual compression alone fails. How to: 1. Confirm paraphimosis (retracted foreskin stuck proximal to the glans with a constricting band and distal edema) — this is time-sensitive; do not delay reduction in a dusky/compromised glans. 2. Mix ~50 mL of 50% dextrose with 2% lidocaine jelly (a Urojet works) to make an osmotic, analgesic slurry. 3. Soak gauze in the slurry and wrap it over the glans and edematous foreskin; cover with a condom or condom-Foley to hold it in contact. 4. Wait up to ~1 hour: the high sugar concentration draws fluid out of the s

info.h: Guidewire Railroad for a Difficult Urethral Catheterization
info.t: Accomplishes: Gets a Foley into a bladder you cannot blindly cannulate (stricture, false passage, big prostate) at the bedside, sparing the patient a suprapubic tube or after-hours urology call. How to: 1. After failing standard and coudé-tip attempts, instill lidocaine jelly and pass a soft hydrophilic (Terumo/Glidewire) guidewire gently down the urethra. 2. Advance until at least two-thirds of the wire is in — that length guarantees the soft J-tip is coiled in the bladder, not a false passage. Never force against resistance. 3. Perforate the very tip of a Foley catheter with a 16G IV cannula to create an over-the-wire channel. 4. Railroad (thread) the Foley over the guidewire into the blad

info.h: “Foley Balloon Be Gone” — Free a Retained Catheter With a Stuck Balloon
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes a Foley whose balloon will not deflate (failed inflation valve or a channel plugged by crystals) without cutting blindly or yanking, which can injure the urethra. How to: 1. First try the simplest step: cut the catheter across the inflation (balloon) port arm distal to the bifurcation — this removes the one-way valve and the balloon water often drains on its own. 2. If it still will not drain, gently pass a thin lubricated guidewire down the now-open inflation channel to push past obstructing exudate/crystals; the balloon then empties. 3. Do NOT overinflate to “burst” the balloon blindly and never cut the catheter flush at the meatus (you lose your handle and balloon fr

Accomplishes: Restores blood flow to a torsed testis at the bedside, buying time and relieving pain while the patient goes to the OR — it is a temporizing bridge, never a substitute for surgical exploration. How to: 1. Stand facing the supine or standing patient; give analgesia (a spermatic-cord block or IV opioid) since manipulation is painful. 2. Detorse like opening a book: rotate the affected testis from MEDIAL to LATERAL — patient’s right testis turns counterclockwise, left testis turns clockwise (as you face them). 3. Lift the testis slightly cephalad as you rotate; most torsions are 180-720°, so repeat the same direction 1-3 times until pain eases and the testis drops and lies vertica

info.h: Jacobi Ring Catheter for a Bartholin Abscess
info.t: Accomplishes: Drains a Bartholin abscess when the Word catheter will not fit or keeps falling out, using a looped catheter that stays put and forms a durable epithelialized tract. How to: 1. Anesthetize and make a stab incision into the abscess cavity on the medial mucosal surface. 2. Thread suture material through the lumen of an 8-French rubber tube (butterfly tubing works for the loop variant). 3. Pass one end of the tube into the incision, then bring the other end out through a second small incision a short distance away (loop-drainage style). 4. Tie the suture ends together so the catheter forms a ring/loop bridging the cavity. 5. Leave it in place to maintain drainage and let the tract

info.h: DIY High-Volume Irrigation From a Saline Bottle Cap
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers fast, high-pressure, high-volume irrigation of an open fracture or grossly contaminated wound when a 30 mL syringe and angiocatheter are too slow. How to: 1. Grab a sterile bottle of normal saline (the rigid pour-bottle, not an IV bag). 2. Punch several evenly spaced holes through the plastic screw cap with an 18-gauge needle, creating a multi-stream “shower head.” 3. Screw the cap back on and squeeze the bottle firmly to drive a strong pressurized spray into the wound. 4. Refill or open new bottles as needed; multiple people can irrigate at once while the patient is mobilized to the OR. 5. Ensure a large open exit so you are not pressurizing a closed space, and wear a

info.h: Crack a Stuck Tungsten Ring With a Vise Grip
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes a tungsten-carbide ring from a swollen or injured finger — standard ring cutters cannot scratch tungsten, but it is brittle and shatters under compression. How to: 1. Confirm the ring is tungsten (very hard, heavy, scratch-resistant) — ring cutters and even bolt cutters fail on it, so do not waste time. 2. Borrow an adjustable locking vise grip / locking pliers (hospital engineering or your own toolkit). 3. Position the jaws across the band and apply firm, steady compression. 4. The brittle tungsten fractures and cracks apart rather than bending. 5. Carefully collect every fragment — broken edges are sharp — and re-examine the finger for cuts and residual constriction.

info.h: Depilatory Cream to Dissolve a Hair Tourniquet
info.t: Accomplishes: Releases a hair or thread tourniquet strangling a digit, toe, or genitalia by chemically dissolving the hair — no cutting near tender, edematous tissue. How to: 1. Confirm the constricting band is HAIR or a synthetic thread that depilatory cream can break down (it dissolves keratin/some synthetics; it will NOT touch elastic or rubber bands). 2. Confirm intact skin with no open wound at the site — do not apply depilatory cream to broken skin or mucosa. 3. Apply a generous layer of depilatory cream (e.g., Nair) over the constricting hair and the surrounding groove. 4. Wait about 3–8 minutes for the cream to chemically dissolve the hair; the band loosens and releases. 5. Wipe and

How to: 1. Confirm paraphimosis (foreskin stuck proximal to the glans with a constricting band and distal edema); this is time-sensitive — do not delay if the glans is dusky/compromised. 2. Give analgesia first (topical EMLA, a dorsal penile nerve block, or IV opioid); a numb patient lets you compress effectively. 3. Fill an exam glove with ice and a little water, then invaginate (push in) the thumb of the glove to make a pocket. 4. Slide the edematous glans and foreskin into the ic

info.h: Point the Coude Balloon Port Up to Clear an Enlarged Prostate
info.t: Accomplishes: Gets a Foley past an obstructing prostate (BPH) or a posterior false passage on the first try by guaranteeing the curved coude tip rides over the obstruction instead of digging into it. How to: 1. Choose a coude (curved-tip) catheter for the anticipated difficult male — the bend hugs the natural upward curve of the bulbar/prostatic urethra and is less likely to create a false passage than a straight tip. 2. Before insertion, find the balloon-inflation port (the small side knob at the drainage end): the curved tip points the SAME direction as that port. 3. Hold the catheter so the balloon port — and therefore the tip — points UP toward the ceiling (anterior/cephalad) the entire

info.h: Plaster Ear Splint to Stop an Auricular Hematoma Reaccumulating
info.t: Accomplishes: After draining an auricular hematoma (cauliflower ear), a molded plaster splint presses the skin back onto the cartilage so blood cannot refill the perichondrial space — the real failure point of these injuries. How to: 1. Drain the hematoma first (incision or needle aspiration) and clean the ear. 2. Cut a short plaster roll to the shape of the ear and soak it in water. 3. Lay ONE thin layer of padding against the ear so the wet plaster will not stick to the skin. 4. Press the plaster firmly into the natural contours of the auricle so it conforms and applies even compression; tuck gauze behind the ear for counter-pressure. 5. Pile several layers of gauze over the top and hold t

info.h: Three-Way Stopcock for Priapism Aspiration and Irrigation
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you aspirate and irrigate the corpus cavernosum through ONE needle in ischemic priapism, avoiding repeated sticks and the anxiety of leaving a bare 18G needle parked in the penis. How to: 1. Consent, place the patient on cardiac and BP monitoring (you will be injecting phenylephrine), then sterile prep and do a dorsal penile nerve block with 1% plain lidocaine at the 10 and 2 o’clock positions; wait ~10 minutes. 2. Build the circuit: attach a ≥19G butterfly to a 3-way stopcock, with a saline-filled syringe on one port and an empty syringe on the other. 3. info.h: Ultrasound-Guided Posterior Tibial Nerve Block for the Sole of the Foot
info.t: Accomplishes: Anesthetizes most of the plantar foot for a heel/sole laceration or plantar foreign body without the exquisite pain of injecting local directly into the tight, nerve-dense sole. How to: 1. Position the patient with the leg externally rotated and the medial ankle facing up; palpate the posterior tibial pulse just behind the medial malleolus. 2. Place a high-frequency linear probe transversely just proximal to the medial malleolus and find the posterior tibial artery; the nerve sits right beside it as a hyperechoic “honeycomb” bundle (use color Doppler to locate the artery first). 3. info.h: Hyaluronidase Injection to Melt Paraphimosis Edema
info.t: Accomplishes: Rapidly softens a tensely swollen, irreducible paraphimotic foreskin — especially in children and infants — so it can be reduced by hand, without the 30–60 minute wait that osmotic sugar or iced-glove methods require. How to: 1. Confirm true paraphimosis (foreskin trapped behind the corona forming a constricting ring) and give adequate analgesia (topical then, if needed, a dorsal penile block); rule out arterial compromise, which needs emergent urology. 2. Reconstitute hyaluronidase to 150 units/mL. 3. With a fine (25–27G) needle, inject small aliquots (about 0.1–0.3 mL each) subcutaneously into one or more sites of the edematous foreskin. 4. info.h: Multiple Needle Puncture to Decompress Paraphimosis Edema
info.t: Accomplishes: Drains the trapped interstitial fluid out of a swollen paraphimotic foreskin through tiny needle holes so you can squeeze the edema flat and reduce it, when osmotic methods are too slow and hyaluronidase is not stocked. How to: 1. Confirm paraphimosis and provide analgesia (topical anesthetic, or a dorsal penile nerve block with plain lidocaine); rule out arterial compromise. 2. Clean the edematous prepuce with antiseptic. 3. Puncture the swollen foreskin superficially with a fine hypodermic needle (25G) in multiple spots — several to a dozen small punctures over the most edematous tissue. 4. info.h: Terbutaline + Nitroglycerin for Vasopressor Extravasation When Phentolamine Is Missing
info.t: Accomplishes: Reverses the blanched, ischemic skin of a peripheral vasopressor (or accidental epinephrine auto-injector) extravasation when phentolamine — the standard antidote — is not stocked, restoring perfusion and preventing tissue necrosis. How to: 1. Stop the infusion, but leave the IV catheter in and aspirate back whatever vasopressor you can before pulling it; get reliable alternate access. 2. If phentolamine is available, use it (5–10 mg diluted in 10 mL saline, injected subcutaneously around the site); the steps below are the phentolamine-unavailable backup. 3. info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Repairs/secures a nailbed laceration without sutures — faster and less painful than suturing the bed. How to: 1. Achieve hemostasis (digital block + finger tourniquet) and clean the nailbed. 2. Approximate the nailbed laceration. 3. Apply cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive to hold the bed (and replaced nail plate) in position. Equipment: Tissue adhesive (cyanoacrylate), digital block supplies, the avulsed nail plate if available. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Fingertip Shave Laceration — LET + Tourniquet + Glue
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Manages a bleeding shallow shave/mandoline fingertip laceration without suturing. How to: 1. Soak the wound in LET (lidocaine-epinephrine-tetracaine) for anesthesia and vasoconstriction. 2. Apply a digit tourniquet proximal to the injury for a bloodless field. 3. Apply tissue glue liberally to approximate the flap/edges. Equipment: LET solution, finger tourniquet, tissue adhesive. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Sterile Gel for Bloody Scalp Lacerations
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Clears matted blood/clot/hair from a scalp wound for visualization and closure — without shaving the scalp. How to: 1. Do preliminary irrigation if needed. 2. Apply a generous amount of sterile water-soluble lubricating gel to the clotted area and matted hair. 3. Wait 3–5 minutes for the gel to penetrate fibrin and soften clot. 4. Massage gently in circles with gloved fingers to separate hair and loosen clot. 5. Irrigate with saline (water-soluble gel rinses away easily). 6. Proceed with standard cleaning and closure. Equipment: Sterile water-soluble lubricating gel, gloves, irrigation saline. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Warm the Local Anesthetic Before Injecting
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Cuts injection pain at no cost or risk — a meta-analysis of 18 studies shows warmed local anesthetic hurts significantly less than room-temperature. How to: 1. While gathering and prepping the rest of your laceration supplies, set the lidocaine or bupivacaine vial in a small tub of warm water. 2. Let it sit a few minutes to reach roughly body temperature (about 37–40°C); a warm IV-fluid cabinet or running warm tap water over the vial also works. 3. Draw up and inject as usual, slowly, with a small-gauge needle. 4. Note that warming (and buffering) shortens lidocaine shelf life, so warm only what you will use. Equipment: Local anesthetic vial, warm water bath or fluid warmer, sy

info.h: Silk-Suture Retraction for a Squirmy Tongue Laceration
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Holds a slippery, jumpy tongue protruded and still for repair without fingers or clamps in the bite zone, giving a clear two-handed field. How to: 1. Anesthetize the tongue (topical, then a lingual/local block). 2. Pass a single 0-silk suture straight through the central body of the tongue, staying midline and as anterior as possible to avoid the lingual artery. 3. Use that suture as a handle to gently pull the tongue forward and hold it out while you work. 4. Repair the laceration with 4-0 or 5-0 chromic gut (absorbable); a dry field helps — an assistant can blow air through a Yankauer to keep saliva off. 5. Remove the silk retraction suture at the end; the chromic repair sutu

info.h: Electrocautery Trephination of a Subungual Hematoma
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Painlessly decompresses a painful subungual hematoma (>25% of the nail or severe pain) through the nail plate, with minimal nailbed-injury risk and no anesthesia. How to: 1. Confirm there is no displaced distal phalanx fracture needing other care and that the nail folds are intact (if disrupted, consider nail removal/repair instead). 2. CONTRAINDICATION CHECK: do NOT use electrocautery on acrylic/gel artificial nails — ignition risk; use a needle or another method. 3. Rest the fingertip on a firm surface and center the heated cautery tip over the hematoma. 4. Apply the tip to melt a hole straight through the nail; once it reaches the blood the tip cools and self-limits, protect

info.h: Tegaderm Dam to Stop Tissue-Adhesive Seepage Near the Eye
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps runny cyanoacrylate (Dermabond) from tracking into the eye, eyebrow, or hairline when gluing a wound near the eyelid or scalp. How to: 1. Cut an oval or circular window out of the center of a transparent Tegaderm (the clear dressing in any IV/central-line kit). 2. Peel and adhere the Tegaderm to dry skin so the cut-out window frames just the laceration; press the window edges down to seal against seepage. 3. You do NOT need to stick the whole dressing down — sealing the inner rim is enough, and leaving it loose avoids pulling out eyebrow or lash hairs on removal. 4. Approximate the wound and apply the tissue adhesive within the window; the Tegaderm rim dams any “run.” 5.

info.h: Head Basin to Wash Out a Bloody Scalp Laceration
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Builds a “hairdresser sink” from a plastic basin so you can flush clotted blood out of the hair and irrigate a scalp wound without soaking the patient or the gurney — and it works on a C-collared patient who cannot reach a sink. How to: 1. Take an emesis/wash basin and cut a semicircular or rectangular opening in its rim, leaving a 2–4 inch lip at the bottom so fluid still pools and does not pour out. 2. Pad the cut edges (tape or gauze) for comfort, then cradle the back of the head in the basin so the neck rests in the cut-out notch — the collar can stay on. 3. Put the patient in slight Trendelenburg so runoff flows toward the basin, not down the back. 4. Irrigate with a pullo

info.h: Hair Apposition Technique (HAT Trick) for Scalp Lacerations
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Closes a linear scalp laceration by braiding and gluing the patient’s own hair — no anesthetic, no staples, no return visit, and it unravels on its own in about a week. How to: 1. Irrigate and inspect the wound; the technique needs hair at least ~3 cm long on both sides (use the modified clamp version for shorter hair). 2. Dry the surrounding hair thoroughly — tissue adhesive will not stick to wet hair. 3. Grab 3–7 strands on one side of the wound and the same on the other side. 4. Cross the two bundles and twist them through a single 360° revolution to appose the wound edges; do NOT tie a knot. 5. info.h: V-to-Y Flap for a Laceration Under Tension
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Closes a gaping or V-shaped wound whose edges will not meet without ischemic tension, redistributing the pull so the flap tip keeps its blood supply instead of necrosing. How to: 1. Identify a V-shaped flap laceration where simple interrupted sutures would blanch and strangle the tip. 2. Anesthetize and irrigate; gently debride only clearly devitalized edges. 3. Anchor the point of the V FIRST with a half-buried horizontal mattress (corner) suture — the needle passes through the dermis of the flap tip, not the epidermis, so you do not crush its tenuous blood supply. 4. This pulls the V forward into a Y configuration, advancing the flap and spreading tension across the limbs of

info.h: 18G Needle Spin-Trephination of a Subungual Hematoma (No Block)
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Painlessly drains a tense subungual hematoma using just an 18-gauge needle and no anesthesia — the safe alternative to electrocautery in patients with acrylic/gel nails, where cautery is a fire hazard. How to: 1. Confirm no displaced distal-phalanx fracture or disrupted nail folds (those may need nail removal / bed repair instead). 2. Clean the nail with iodine, NOT flammable alcohol, and let it dry; identify the central darkest point of the hematoma under bright light. 3. Hold an 18-gauge needle perpendicular (90°) over that central point. 4. Spin the needle between your fingers like a drill, letting the bevel bore its own hole through the nail plate — do NOT push down hard; t

info.h: Topical Lidocaine Jelly for Skin Tears and Road Rash
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Anesthetizes large, fragile wounds too big or too thin to inject around, while the jelly base rehydrates skin flaps and loosens embedded debris for easier cleaning. How to: 1. Apply 2% lidocaine jelly liberally over the skin tear or abrasion and cover loosely with gauze. 2. Wait 10–15 minutes of contact time. 3. Irrigate gently, then reapply a thin layer of jelly. 4. Unfold and reposition skin flaps over the wound bed; for road rash, debride debris with soft surgical sponges during irrigation. 5. Wipe off remaining jelly before closing with steri-strips or sutures. Respect the 4.5 mg/kg lidocaine max (about 15 mL of 2% jelly in a 70 kg adult). Equipment: 2% lidocaine jelly, loo

info.h: Dissolve Adherent Tar Off a Burn With Petrolatum Ointment
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes hot-tar (bitumen) stuck to a burn without the further tissue destruction and pain of harsh solvents or peeling — the petrolatum base plus emulsifier lifts the tar gradually while protecting the wound. How to: 1. Cool the tar immediately with water; do NOT peel adherent cooled tar (it strips skin). 2. Do NOT use gasoline or caustic solvents. 3. Smear the tarred area generously with a petrolatum-based ointment (e.g., bacitracin, or a polysorbate/Tween-80 emulsifier ointment). 4. Cover with an absorbent dressing. 5. info.h: Split-Tourniquet + Glue Hemostasis for a Fingertip Dermal Avulsion
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Stops the brisk ooze of a fingertip skin-avulsion (“de-gloving” of the pulp) and seals it with tissue adhesive in one shot, often sparing the patient sutures. How to: 1. Have the patient soak the injured fingertip in 1% lidocaine WITH epinephrine for ~5 minutes in a small cup — this numbs it and the epinephrine vasoconstricts to cut bleeding. 2. Slice a standard IV tourniquet lengthwise (trauma shears) so it is thin, encircle the proximal digit, and clamp the two ends with a needle driver. 3. info.h: Use the Native Fingernail to Reapproximate a Nailbed Laceration
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Repairs a clean nailbed laceration WITHOUT suturing the fragile bed — the patient’s own fingernail is used as the splint that aligns the lacerated edges and protects the eponychial fold so a normal nail regrows. How to: 1. Use this for a relatively CLEAN nailbed laceration (a stellate crush that already shattered/required removing the nail is better sutured or glued). 2. Get a bloodless field: digital block, then a finger tourniquet (a cut glove finger works). 3. Gently lift the proximal nail fold and ease the existing nail plate up just enough to expose the laceration, but DO NOT avulse it. 4. Irrigate and reapproximate the nailbed edges underneath; the overlying nail naturall

info.h: modHAT: Kelly Clamps to Close a Short-Hair Scalp Laceration
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Extends the glue-and-hair (HAT) scalp closure down to hair as short as 1 cm — below the ~3 cm the bare-fingers technique needs — by twisting the bundles with instruments instead of fingertips. How to: 1. Irrigate and inspect the wound; reach for this version when the hair is too short to twist by hand but still at least ~1 cm long. 2. Dry the surrounding hair well — tissue adhesive will not grip wet hair. 3. Grasp a small bundle of hair on each side of the wound with its own Kelly (curved hemostat) clamp. 4. Use the clamps to cross and twist the two bundles a single 360° turn so the wound edges appose; do NOT tie a knot. 5. Place just ONE drop of tissue adhesive on the twist (m

info.h: Double Staple Gun for the Squirming Child’s Scalp Laceration
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Closes a tiny 2-staple scalp laceration in one move on an awake, frightened child, avoiding the painful chase for the second staple after the first one makes the child bolt. How to: 1. Reserve this for a SHORT scalp laceration that needs only about two staples (longer wounds are better suited to the HAT trick or sedation). 2. Anesthetize the wound as best you can and have the child held/positioned still by a caregiver or staff. 3. Recruit a second provider so each of you holds a skin stapler. 4. Position both staplers along the wound edges, each held perpendicular to the scalp, over its intended staple site. 5. Count down out loud (“3-2-1-go”) and fire both staplers at the same

info.h: Part the Hair With Petroleum Ointment So It Stays Out of Your Stitches
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Holds hair off a scalp laceration so strands do not get caught in your sutures or staples, which would otherwise risk wound dehiscence, foreign-body reaction, or infection. How to: 1. Irrigate and inspect the scalp wound as usual. 2. Scoop a generous amount of a thick petroleum-based ointment (bacitracin, plain petroleum jelly, or similar) onto a gloved finger or applicator. 3. Smear it along both wound edges, slicking the surrounding hair flat and away from the laceration to each side. 4. info.h: IV Catheter Sheath as a DIY Wound-Irrigation Splash Shield
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers ideal-pressure (5–8 PSI) wound irrigation AND shields you from the infectious splash-back when no commercial splash guard is stocked. How to: 1. Draw irrigation saline into a 20–35 mL syringe — the large barrel plus a small orifice is what generates the 5–8 PSI that actually lowers bacterial load (a bulb syringe makes only 0.5–1 PSI and is too weak). 2. Pull the plastic sheath (cannula) off an 18- or 19-gauge IV catheter and twist it onto the syringe tip in place of a needle. 3. info.h: Steri-Strip + Suture Combo for Fragile, Thin Skin
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Closes lacerations in elderly or chronic-steroid patients whose paper-thin skin cheese-wires through under a bare suture. How to: 1. Clean and irrigate the wound as usual and dry the surrounding skin so the strips will adhere. 2. Lay Steri-Strips LONGITUDINALLY along each wound edge (parallel to the laceration), a few millimeters back from the edge, to build an artificial “skin layer.” 3. Place your sutures THROUGH the Steri-Strips rather than bare skin, so the strip spreads the tension and the suture cannot pull through. 4. Tie down gently — the strip-reinforced edges hold without tearing. 5. Dress as usual; longitudinal placement gives more even tensile strength along the edg

info.h: Tie-Over Bolster Dressing Using the Suture Tails
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Builds a self-contained pressure dressing over a sutured wound from the suture tails themselves — no tape or wrap needed, and the patient can remove it for a wound check. How to: 1. Close the laceration, but leave the suture tails long (about 6–8 cm) instead of trimming them short. 2. Roll a piece of gauze into a bolster and lay it directly over the sutured wound. 3. Tie the long tails across the top of the gauze bolster so it presses evenly onto the wound — giving hemostasis and apposition without tape. 4. After 1–2 days the patient cuts the over-tied knots to lift off the gauze, inspect, and clean; the underlying wound sutures stay intact. 5. Especially useful on hairy or con

info.h: Vessel-Loop “Shoelace” + Staples for a Wound That Won’t Close
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gradually pulls together the gaping, retracted edges of a fasciotomy or other tense soft-tissue wound over days using the elastic stretch of skin, avoiding (or shrinking) a skin graft. How to: 1. Along each wound edge, place skin staples a couple centimeters apart, staggered so a staple on one side sits between two on the other. 2. Anchor one end of a Silastic vessel loop to the staple at one end of the wound. 3. Thread the vessel loop back and forth through the staples like lacing a shoe, running it from side to side down the length of the wound. 4. Tension the loop just until the skin edges begin to draw together (do not force pale, blanched edges together — skin viscoelastic

info.h: Tattoo the Vermillion Border Before You Numb the Lip
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Preserves the exact lip-margin landmark on a through-the-vermillion laceration, because local anesthetic and swelling erase it — even a 1–2 mm step-off at the vermillion border is a visible cosmetic defect. How to: 1. BEFORE injecting anesthetic or irrigating, take a fine-tip surgical marker. 2. Place a precise ink dot on the vermillion-cutaneous border on each side of the wound. 3. Now anesthetize (a mental or infraorbital block distorts the lip far less than local infiltration) and irrigate. 4. Place your FIRST suture to align the two marked dots exactly, re-approximating the border. 5. Close the rest of the wound in layers as needed. Equipment: Fine-tip surgical marking pen,

info.h: Bicarbonate-Buffered Lidocaine for a Painless Injection
info.pt: Wound Care — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Neutralizes the acidic pH of commercial lidocaine so infiltration burns far less and takes effect faster, without reducing anesthetic efficacy — directly improving tolerance of laceration repair and abscess I&D. How to: 1. Draw up the lidocaine (with or without epinephrine) you plan to inject. 2. Add 8.4% sodium bicarbonate in a 9:1 or 10:1 ratio (e.g., 9 mL lidocaine + 1 mL bicarb). 3. Gently mix and use promptly — buffered lidocaine has a short shelf life, so mix it at the point of use. 4. Inject slowly through a small-gauge needle as usual. Equipment: Lidocaine (+/- epinephrine), 8.4% sodium bicarbonate, syringe, small-gauge needle. _Source: Cepeda MS, et al. Adjusting the p

info.h: Ultrarapid Adenosine Push via Pressure Bag (SVT)
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers undiluted adenosine to the heart at high flow to terminate SVT, exploiting its very short half-life — combines single-syringe speed with a large flush. How to: 1. Prime a pressure bag with saline tubing; close the roller clamp. 2. Connect the line to the patient’s angiocatheter. 3. Attach the undiluted adenosine syringe to the Y-site nearest the patient. 4. Open the roller clamp for high-pressure flow. 5. Rapidly inject the adenosine into the tubing. Equipment: Pressure bag with primed saline line, IV angiocatheter, undiluted adenosine syringe, Y-site connector. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade._

info.h: Modified Valsalva (REVERT) to Convert Stable SVT
info.t: Accomplishes: Roughly doubles cardioversion of stable SVT versus the standard strain (43% vs 17% in the REVERT trial) and often spares the patient adenosine. How to: 1. Confirm the patient is hemodynamically stable and sit them semi-upright (Fowler’s) on a gurney. 2. Strain phase: have them blow into a 10 mL syringe just hard enough to move the plunger (~40 mmHg) for 15 seconds (a 10 mL syringe reliably generates this pressure). 3. Immediately at the end of the strain, lay them flat and have an assistant passively raise both legs to ~45° for 15 seconds. 4. Return the patient to semi-upright and re-check the rhythm/monitor after about a minute. 5. Repeat once if needed before escalating to ad

Accomplishes: Delivers a fast adenosine bolus solo, diluting the drug with saline in one syringe so it reaches the AV node before the short half-life expires — no stopcock, extension tubing, or second nurse needed. How to: 1. Draw 6 mg (2 mL) of adenosine into a 20 mL syringe, then draw saline up to a total of 20 mL (a 10 mL syringe with 5–18 mL of saline also works if 20 mL is unavailable). 2. Connect directly to the IV hub closest to the patient (an antecubital or more proximal vein is ideal). 3. Push the entire 20 mL as fast as you physically can, in 1–2 seconds. 4. Watch the monitor; if SVT persists, repeat with 12 mg (4 mL) of adenosine topped to 20 mL with saline. Equipment: 20 mL (or

info.h: Lewis (S5) Lead to Unmask Hidden P-Waves
info.t: Accomplishes: Amplifies invisible atrial activity to confirm atrial flutter or distinguish VT from SVT at the bedside in seconds, using only the leads already on the patient. How to: 1. Start with the patient on the standard limb leads. 2. Move the Right Arm electrode to the manubrium (just right of the sternum, 2nd intercostal space). 3. Move the Left Arm electrode to the 5th intercostal space at the right sternal border (4th ICS right sternal border for the rapid variant). 4. Move the Left Leg electrode to the right lower costal margin. 5. Record and read Lead I — flutter waves and AV dissociation that were invisible on the 12-lead now stand out. Equipment: Standard ECG machine with limb l

info.h: Water-Soaked Gauze to Get an ECG on a Hairy Chest
info.t: Accomplishes: Gets clean ECG tracings on a very hairy chest without stopping to shave, when adhesive electrodes will not stick and you are getting artifact or flatline leads. How to: 1. Recognize the problem: loose leads on hairy skin give wandering-baseline artifact or no signal at all. 2. Generously soak a few gauze squares with plain water (saline also works). 3. Lay a wet gauze square over each electrode position where the lead will contact hairy skin. 4. Press the electrode down onto the wet gauze so the water bridges the gap — water conducts the cardiac signal and maximizes contact area. 5. Record immediately; if you still get artifact at a site, shave a small patch there as backup. Eq

info.h: Double the ECG Paper Speed to Unmask a Tachycardia
info.t: Accomplishes: Spreads out a fast, cramped rhythm so hidden P-waves, flutter waves, and QRS morphology become readable when you cannot tell SVT from flutter from VT at 25 mm/sec. How to: 1. Acquire the standard 12-lead at the usual 25 mm/sec first. 2. On the ECG machine, change the paper/recording speed setting to 50 mm/sec (double speed). 3. Re-record — every complex and interval is now stretched to twice its width, like pulling a string taut, so buried atrial activity separates out. 4. Remember the calibration changed: at 50 mm/sec each small box is 0.02 s and rates appear halved, so interpret intervals against the new scale (or simply use it to SEE the waves, then measure on the standard s

info.h: Posterior Leads (V7–V9) to Catch a Posterior STEMI
info.t: Accomplishes: Confirms an isolated posterior MI — a STEMI-equivalent that looks like benign anterior ST depression on a standard 12-lead — by recording directly over the back of the heart, so the patient gets the cath lab instead of a missed occlusion. How to: 1. Suspect posterior MI when V1–V3 show horizontal ST DEPRESSION with tall, broad R waves and upright T waves (the mirror image of an anterior STEMI), especially alongside an inferior or lateral MI. 2. Keep the limb leads on; peel leads V4, V5, V6 off the front of the chest. 3. Place them around the LEFT side onto the back, all in the SAME horizontal line as V6: V7 at the posterior axillary line, V8 at the tip of the scapula (mid-scapu

info.h: Sit the Patient on Their Hands to Quiet a Tremor-Artifact ECG
info.t: Accomplishes: Eliminates upper-extremity movement artifact (Parkinson’s, essential tremor, shivering) that buries the ECG tracing, so you get a readable 12-lead without sedation or repeated attempts. How to: 1. Place the ECG limb and precordial leads as usual. 2. Have the patient sit on both hands, palms down, tucked under the buttocks and thighs. 3. This braces the arms and dampens the tremor at its source so the limb-lead baseline settles. 4. Acquire the tracing immediately. 5. If it is still noisy, drape a warm blanket over the shoulders and have the patient consciously relax before re-recording. Equipment: ECG machine, exam table or chair, warm blanket (optional). _Source: ALiEM Trick of

info.h: Ice-Water Slurry to the Face to Break Infant SVT (Diving Reflex)
info.t: Accomplishes: Terminates stable supraventricular tachycardia in neonates and young infants via the mammalian diving reflex — a vagal maneuver you can do while IV access and adenosine are being prepared. How to: 1. Keep the infant on continuous ECG monitoring with defibrillator pads already in place. 2. Wrap the arms snugly in a towel to keep them out of the way. 3. Fill a bag (or soak a washcloth) with an ice-and-water slurry (~5 °C / ice plus a little water). 4. Apply it firmly over the WHOLE face — forehead, eyes, and bridge of the nose — for ~15–30 seconds; do not occlude breathing longer than tolerated. 5. Watch the monitor for abrupt conversion. Do NOT use carotid massage or eyeball pre

info.h: Abdominal-Pressure “Push Me Away” Valsalva for SVT
info.t: Accomplishes: Generates an effective vagal strain in a patient who cannot follow blow-into-a-syringe instructions — the patient pushes against your hands on their belly, which is intuitive and easy to coach. How to: 1. Confirm the patient is hemodynamically stable and on a cardiac monitor; lay them supine. 2. Have the patient relax the abdomen, then place both of your hands flat near the umbilicus. 3. Apply firm downward pressure and tell the patient to “push my hands away” using their belly — bearing down against your resistance creates the Valsalva strain. 4. Hold the strain for ~15 seconds, then release; if combining with the modified Valsalva, lay them flat and raise the legs at this poi

info.h: Pre-Charge the Defibrillator Before the Rhythm Check
info.t: Accomplishes: Cuts peri-shock hands-off time by charging the defibrillator during ongoing compressions, eliminating the second CPR pause in ACLS and preserving coronary perfusion pressure. How to: 1. Assign a timekeeper to warn the team 15–30 seconds before each scheduled rhythm check. 2. With chest compressions continuing UNINTERRUPTED, the defib operator charges the device in anticipation. 3. At the 2-minute mark, pause compressions briefly and check the rhythm. 4. If VF/pulseless VT, immediately deliver the already-charged shock and resume CPR — the hands-off interval is just the rhythm glance. 5. If the rhythm is asystole/PEA, safely DISARM/dump the stored charge and resume compressions.

info.h: Flip the Leads to Read a Dextrocardia ECG
info.t: Accomplishes: Unmasks an anterior MI that a standard left-sided ECG hides in true dextrocardia, by re-recording with mirror-image lead placement so the tracing reads normally. How to: 1. Spot the dextrocardia clues: negative QRS with an inverted P in lead I, an upright (positive) aVR, poor R-wave progression across the precordium, and right-axis deviation. 2. First exclude simple left-arm/right-arm reversal, which mimics this but KEEPS normal precordial R-wave progression — only the limb leads look flipped in LA/RA reversal. 3. If true dextrocardia is likely, swap the right-arm and left-arm electrodes. 4. Move the precordial leads to the MIRROR positions on the right chest (V1R–V6R): V1–V2 s

info.h: Confirm TRUE Capture During Transcutaneous Pacing (Don’t Trust the Monitor)
info.t: Accomplishes: Stops you from being fooled by “false capture” during transcutaneous pacing of unstable bradycardia — the pacing spike creates electrical artifact that mimics a QRS, so a patient with zero real capture can look paced while still in arrest. How to: 1. Do NOT judge capture off the pacer’s distorted ECG alone. 2. Read morphology: FALSE capture shows a near-vertical spike into a phantom complex with a slightly curved return to baseline and tiny, unimpressive T waves. TRUE electrical capture shows a genuine wide QRS each followed by a broad, discordant T wave. 3. Confirm MECHANICAL capture independently: palpate a femoral (not carotid — muscle twitch fools you) pulse timed to the sp

info.h: Sugar Test for Bell’s Palsy (CN VII Taste)
info.t: Accomplishes: Bedside check of anterior-tongue taste (chorda tympani / CN VII) to support facial-palsy assessment. How to: 1. Gently hold the tongue out with gauze. 2. Sprinkle a little sugar on one anterior side of the tongue; rinse with water between sides. OR 3. Mix 2 tsp sugar in 1 tbsp water, draw into a syringe, and drip onto the target side. 4. Have the patient report any difference in taste between sides. Equipment: Sugar (powder or dissolved), gauze, syringe/dropper (optional). _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

Accomplishes: Alternative BPPV diagnostic and treatment maneuvers for patients who can’t tolerate standard Dix-Hallpike/Epley (kyphosis, obesity, back pain, orthopnea). How to: 1. Loaded Dix-Hallpike: flex the head forward 30° in the plane of the affected posterior canal for 30 sec before going supine; use pillows under the thoracic spine for kyphotic/elderly patients. 2. Sidelying test: rotate the head 45° contralateral to the tested canal, then descend to the ipsilateral side (good when the patient can’t lie flat). 3. BBQ/Lempert roll (horizontal canal): from supine, roll the head in 90° steps through a full 360°, holding 30 sec at each step (>90% success). 4. Semont maneuver: rapidly tran

info.h: Dix-Hallpike Without Hanging the Head Off the Bed
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets you do a Dix-Hallpike on a narrow ED gurney where you can’t safely extend the patient’s neck off the end of the bed. How to: 1. Stack 2–3 folded blankets on the gurney where the patient’s shoulders will lie. 2. Rotate the head 45° toward the tested ear and sit the patient so the shoulders will land on the blankets. 3. Lay the patient back so the shoulders rest on the blanket stack and the head drops into ~20–30° of neck extension over the blanket edge — no overhang needed. 4. Hold 30–60 sec and watch for nystagmus/vertigo. Equipment: 2–3 folded blankets, a standard gurney. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Dix-Hallpike maneuver variation._

info.h: Low-Dose Propofol Rescue for Refractory Migraine
info.t: Accomplishes: May abort severe migraine after standard ED therapy has failed, while avoiding opioids. This is an off-label rescue technique with limited and conflicting evidence. Standard migraine therapy remains dopamine antagonist/NSAID/acetaminophen/magnesium/dexamethasone or nerve-block strategy per local pathway. How to: 1. First rule out red flags: thunderclap onset, meningismus, focal deficit, pregnancy/postpartum concern, immunocompromise, anticoagulation, trauma, cancer, fever, papilledema, altered mental status, or new headache age >50. 2. Try standard ED migraine therapy first unless contraindicated. 3. If migraine remains severe and the patient is monitored in an airway-capable a

info.h: Transnasal Sphenopalatine Ganglion Block for Headache
info.t: Accomplishes: Aborts refractory migraine, cluster, or post-dural-puncture headache noninvasively with only a cotton swab and lidocaine — no needles, no opioids. How to: 1. Put the patient supine in the sniffing position and place them on a monitor (nasal mucosa is highly vascular). 2. Soak a long 10 cm cotton-tipped applicator in 1–4% lidocaine (or 0.5% bupivacaine). 3. Insert it into the naris on the headache side, advancing along the superior border of the middle turbinate. 4. Apply firm, steady pressure (like seating nasal packing) until you meet the posterior nasopharyngeal wall. 5. Leave it in place 5–10 minutes; relief is often dramatic. Repeat on the other side for bilateral pain. Equ

info.h: Smartphone Selfie Mode for Gaze Testing in Aphasic Patients
info.t: Accomplishes: Tests voluntary horizontal gaze (NIHSS “best gaze”) in a patient who can’t follow verbal commands, by exploiting their reflex to track their own familiar face on the screen. How to: 1. Open the phone’s camera app and switch to “selfie” (front-facing) mode. 2. Hold the screen ~30–40 cm in front of the patient so they see their own face. 3. Slowly move the phone side to side and watch whether the eyes track horizontally in both directions. 4. Note any conjugate gaze deviation or failure to cross midline as you would on the formal NIHSS. Equipment: Smartphone with a front-facing camera. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Gaze testing using selfie mode (Bortolon 2017)._

Accomplishes: Tests the corneal (blink) reflex (CN V afferent, CN VII efferent) in an obtunded patient without dragging a cotton wisp across the cornea and risking an abrasion. How to: 1. Grab a pre-filled sterile saline flush syringe (the kind used to flush IVs). 2. From a few centimeters away, squirt a few drops of sterile saline directly onto the cornea. 3. Watch for a reflexive blink; test each eye and compare. 4. An intact blink confirms the CN V–VII reflex arc without touching the eye. Equipment: Pre-filled sterile saline flush syringe. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — Corneal reflex test (saline-drop method)._

info.h: Landmark Greater Occipital Nerve Block for Refractory Headache
info.t: Accomplishes: Aborts migraine, occipital neuralgia, and cluster headache at the bedside without opioids or ultrasound. A single landmark-based injection often gives relief that outlasts the anesthetic. How to: 1. Seat the patient with the head flexed forward (palms supporting the face) or prone over a chest pillow. 2. Palpate the external occipital protuberance (OP) and the mastoid process (MP); mark the point one-third of the way from the OP toward the MP. 3. Confirm there is no palpable occipital-artery pulse at your target. 4. Prep with chlorhexidine or alcohol; draw up 2–4 mL of 0.25–0.5% bupivacaine or 1–2% lidocaine into a 25–27g 1.5-inch needle. 5. Insert from an inferior angle; if yo

info.h: Directed Saline Irrigation for Nasal Suctioning in Infants
info.t: Accomplishes: Clears a congested infant’s nose with saline irrigation while keeping the baby much less wet, distressed, and squirmy — and reassures anxious parents that home suctioning is safe. How to: 1. Connect an angiocath tip to a J-loop and attach that directly to a saline flush syringe. 2. Rest the base of your non-dominant hand against the infant’s cheek for control. 3. Use two fingers of that hand to direct the angiocath tip into one nostril. 4. Hold the flush syringe in your other hand and irrigate in short bursts, suctioning between. 5. Use your forearms to gently pin the infant’s arms so they can’t bat the equipment away. Equipment: Angiocath tip, J-loop (IV extension loop), salin

Accomplishes: Treats refractory nausea/vomiting from chronic cannabis use — IV haloperidol outperformed ondansetron in the HaVOC trial. How to: 1. For CHS-pattern intractable vomiting, give IV haloperidol as an antiemetic (per HaVOC dosing). 2. Topical capsaicin and hot showers are adjuncts. Equipment: IV haloperidol (alternative: ondansetron). _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Dilute Naloxone for a Titrated Opioid Reversal
info.t: Accomplishes: Reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression in an opioid-dependent patient while avoiding the abrupt, miserable (and vomiting/agitation-prone) precipitated withdrawal a full 0.4 mg push causes. How to: 1. Confirm this is for ventilatory depression, NOT frank apnea/respiratory arrest — if the patient is apneic, give standard full-dose naloxone and ventilate instead. 2. Draw 1 mL of naloxone 0.4 mg/mL into a 10 mL syringe. 3. Add 9 mL of normal saline to make 10 mL of a 0.04 mg/mL solution; clearly label the syringe with drug and concentration (do not use an unlabeled flush). 4. Give 1-2 mL (0.04-0.08 mg) IV every 60 seconds, titrating to adequate spontaneous breathing — not f

info.h: Calcium Gluconate Gel in a Glove for a Hydrofluoric Acid Hand Burn
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers continuous topical calcium to bind fluoride ions and relieve the severe, out-of-proportion pain of a hydrofluoric acid burn to the fingers or hand when commercial 2.5% calcium gluconate gel is not stocked. How to: 1. Irrigate the burn thoroughly with water first. 2. Make the gel: mix ~75 mL of water-soluble lubricant (K-Y jelly) with ~25 mL of 10% calcium gluconate solution (or stir 2.5 g calcium gluconate powder into ~100 mL of lubricant) to roughly a 2.5% gel. 3. Squeeze a generous amount of the gel into a surgical or exam glove. 4. Have the patient slide the affected hand into the glove and wear it for at least 30 minutes of continuous contact. 5. Reassess: pain oft

info.h: Isopropyl Alcohol Inhalation for Acute Nausea
info.t: Accomplishes: Rapid, cheap, non-invasive relief of acute nausea — sniffing an alcohol prep pad cut nausea scores more than placebo within 10 minutes, often before you can even draw up an antiemetic. How to: 1. Use for undifferentiated acute nausea/vomiting where a fast, low-risk option is wanted (great at triage while IV access and antiemetics are pending). 2. Open a standard 70% isopropyl alcohol prep pad (the same wipe used to clean skin). 3. Hold it about 1–2 cm under the patient’s nose. 4. Have them take slow, deep nasal breaths from the pad. 5. Repeat with a fresh pad as needed; benefit is short-lived (~10–20 minutes), so pair it with a conventional antiemetic for sustained control. Avo

info.h: Nebulized Naloxone for a Gentle, IV-Free Opioid Reversal
info.t: Accomplishes: Reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression through a face mask in a patient you cannot get an IV on (common in injection drug users), giving a steady, self-titrating dose instead of an abrupt push. How to: 1. Use for a spontaneously breathing patient with depressed but present respirations — NOT for frank apnea/arrest, which needs full-dose naloxone and bag-mask ventilation. 2. Draw up 1–2 mg of naloxone. 3. Add normal saline to reach a total volume of 3–5 mL in a standard nebulizer cup. 4. Run it on a simple face mask at 6–8 L/min of oxygen and let the patient breathe the mist. 5. It self-titrates — as the patient wakes they pull the mask off, limiting overshoot; watch for

info.h: Sodium Bicarb Ampule as a Stand-In for 3% Saline in Crashing Hyponatremia
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers immediate hypertonic sodium from the crash cart when 3% saline is not at the bedside. A bicarb ampule can reverse acute hyponatremic seizures/coma in seconds while pharmacy sends the 3% NaCl. How to: 1. Use ONLY for a seizing or obtunded patient with confirmed/strongly suspected ACUTE symptomatic hyponatremia — not chronic asymptomatic hyponatremia (rapid correction there risks osmotic demyelination). 2. Grab a 50 mL ampule of sodium bicarbonate 8.4% off the crash cart (50 mL = 50 mEq Na, comparable to ~100 mL of 3% saline at 51 mEq). 3. Push 1 ampule slowly IV over 5–10 minutes. 4. Recheck serum sodium. 5. If Na has risen <4–6 mEq/L and symptoms persist, repeat with a

info.h: Topical Capsaicin Cream on the Belly for Cannabinoid Hyperemesis
info.t: Accomplishes: Aborts the intractable vomiting of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) by chemically recreating the relief patients get from compulsive hot showers — capsaicin activates skin TRPV1 receptors and dampens substance-P signaling. How to: 1. Confirm a CHS pattern (chronic cannabis use, cyclic vomiting, learned hot-shower/hot-bath relief). 2. Apply a thin layer of 0.075% capsaicin cream (0.025% also reported effective) to the abdomen over a hand-sized area. 3. Wear gloves to apply and keep it well clear of the eyes, mucous membranes, and genitals. 4. Give it 30–45 minutes; reapply or widen the area if partial. Combine with an antiemetic (e.g., haloperidol) for refractory cases. 5.

info.h: Oral Oil to Encapsulate Aluminum/Zinc Phosphide Pellets
info.t: Accomplishes: In aluminum or zinc phosphide (rodenticide/fumigant) ingestion — an antidote-less poison with 30–70% mortality — early oral oil coats the pellets and suppresses ongoing phosphine gas generation in the gut, with signal toward reduced mortality and intubation. How to: 1. Recognize the ingestion early: garlic/fishy breath, “black vomit,” refractory shock, and a severe metabolic acidosis. 2. Protect staff FIRST — exhaled and vomited phosphine gas is toxic; ventilate the room and treat vomitus/lavage waste as hazardous. 3. Give oral or NG paraffin (mineral) oil early to encapsulate the pellets and blunt phosphine release. 4. Resuscitate aggressively in parallel: airway, vasopressors

info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Fast non-invasive screen to rule in/out DKA in a hyperglycemic patient (AUC ~0.95–0.96; correlates with bicarbonate/anion gap). How to: 1. Place a nasal capnography cannula and obtain the ETCO2 reading. 2. Interpret: ETCO2 ≥35–36 mmHg ≈ ~100% sensitivity to exclude DKA (rule out); ETCO2 ≤21 mmHg = 100% specificity for DKA (rule in). Equipment: Capnography monitor with nasal cannula. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Whole Blood on a Urine Pregnancy Cassette
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Rapid hCG result when urine is unavailable (95.8% sensitivity, 100% specificity, ~97.9% NPV; saves ~21 min). How to: 1. Place 2–3 drops of whole blood (from a routine draw) onto a standard urine hCG cassette well. 2. Process per the kit’s normal instructions and interpret as usual. Equipment: Standard POC urine hCG kit, whole blood from a routine draw. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: The “Jedi Mind Trick” for Obstruction of Care
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: De-escalation phrase to get a patient/family/consultant to cooperate when they’re blocking necessary care. How to: 1. Calmly say: “I am sure you can understand the implications of both of us missing this diagnosis.” 2. This shares accountability and reframes the decision around the shared risk of a missed diagnosis. Equipment: None (verbal technique). _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Simplifies outpatient cephalexin to twice-daily dosing for better adherence in susceptible skin/soft-tissue infections. How to: 1. Prescribe cephalexin 1 g PO twice daily. OR 2. Use cefadroxil for once-daily dosing where available. Equipment: None. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Rapid abortive treatment of a severe acute trigeminal neuralgia flare in the ED. How to: 1. Give IV/IM phenytoin or fosphenytoin for the acute flare (carbamazepine remains the chronic mainstay). Equipment: Phenytoin or fosphenytoin (IV/IM). _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Treats an acute gout flare with a low-dose regimen that’s far better tolerated (less GI toxicity) than older high-dose protocols. How to: 1. Give colchicine 1.2 mg loading dose. 2. Follow with 0.6 mg one hour later. Equipment: Colchicine tablets. _Source: EMCrit 426 — Dr. David Carr._

info.h: Oxygen-Mask Strap to Remove a Stuck Ring
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Slides a stuck ring off a swollen finger using the stretchy elastic strap from an O2 face mask — thinner and stretchier than string, so it slips under the ring better and milks edema distally. How to: 1. Cut the elastic strap off a standard oxygen face mask. 2. Thread one end UNDER the ring (a hemostat tip helps feed it through). 3. Wrap the strap snugly around the finger distal-to-proximal, coil by coil, past the knuckle, compressing the swelling out toward the fingertip. 4. Grab the end that was fed under the ring and unwind it from the proximal side; as it unwinds it walks the ring distally over the compressed tissue and off. 5. Lubricate and repeat if needed; if the ring is

info.h: Digital Rectal Massage for Intractable Hiccups
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Aborts refractory (intractable) hiccups by triggering a vagal reflex, an option to try before reaching for chlorpromazine or other drugs. How to: 1. Reserve this for hiccups that have failed simpler vagal/respiratory maneuvers (breath-hold, Valsalva, swallowing granulated sugar) and are distressing or persistent. 2. Explain the maneuver, get verbal consent, and have a chaperone present; document both. 3. Don a glove, lubricate, and perform a slow, rhythmic digital rectal massage — the same technique as a vagal maneuver reported to break the hiccup reflex arc. 4.
