Hiccups often stop abruptly; if they recur, the maneuver can be repeated. 5. If still intractable, move on to pharmac

info.h: Honey for a Witnessed Esophageal Button-Battery Ingestion
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Buys time and reduces caustic esophageal injury while a child with a recently swallowed button battery awaits urgent endoscopic removal — honey coats the battery and its alkaline current path, slowing tissue burn. How to: 1. Use ONLY for a witnessed/known button-battery ingestion in a child ≥1 year, within 12 hours, who can swallow and protect their airway. 2. Do NOT delay imaging, GI/ENT consult, or transfer — this is a bridge to emergent endoscopic removal, not a substitute. 3. Give 10 mL (2 teaspoons) of honey by mouth every 10 minutes, up to ~6 doses, while arranging removal. 4. Hard stops: do NOT give if age <1 year (botulism risk), suspected perforation/sepsis/mediastinit

info.h: Serial Venous Lactate Clearance Instead of a Central Line in Sepsis
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Tracks resuscitation in severe sepsis with cheap peripheral venous lactates instead of placing a central line for ScvO2 — a ≥10% drop over 2 hours is as good a target as ScvO2 ≥70%. How to: 1. Draw a venous lactate at time zero (a venous gas works; you do not need an arterial stick or a central line). 2. Resuscitate with fluids through peripheral access; gauge volume status with a quick IVC ultrasound 1–2 cm from the right atrium (small/collapsing = give more; plump/static = euvolemic). 3. Repeat the venous lactate at 2 hours. 4. Calculate clearance: (initial − repeat) ÷ initial × 100. A drop of ≥10% signals adequate resuscitation, on par with hitting an ScvO2 of ≥70%. 5. If la

info.h: Angiocatheter-as-Caulk-Gun for Clean Dental Cement Application
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Delivers fast-drying temporary dental cement precisely onto the exposed dentin of a fractured tooth (Ellis class II/III) without the usual messy, clumsy finger application, protecting the pulp until dental follow-up. How to: 1. Gather everything FIRST — dental cement sets fast, so have your delivery system ready before you mix. 2. Remove the plastic catheter from an 18-gauge angiocatheter and seat the catheter hub onto a 3 mL syringe. 3. Mix a slightly larger-than-usual quantity of the dental cement. 4. Pull the syringe plunger out, load the cement into the back of the barrel, reinsert the plunger, and advance until cement reaches the fine catheter tip. 5. Dry the tooth, then u

info.h: MidaKet (Midazolam + Ketamine) to Cut Procedural Sedation Side Effects
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Combines midazolam with ketamine for procedural sedation so you can use a lower total ketamine dose — which reduces hypersalivation and emergence agitation — often without needing a separate antisialagogue. How to: 1. Use for a monitored painful procedure (e.g., fracture/joint reduction, abscess I&D) in an airway-capable setting with full monitoring. 2. Give a small dose of midazolam first (e.g., 1–2 mg IV in a typical adult, per local protocol) to blunt emergence phenomena. 3. Titrate ketamine to dissociation; the co-administered midazolam lets you reach effect with less total ketamine. 4. Because lower ketamine doses produce less salivation, a routine antisialagogue (atropine

info.h: Topical Lidocaine Cream on a Child’s Abscess Before You Cut
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Putting 4% lidocaine (LMX-4) cream on a pediatric skin abscess under occlusion either drains it spontaneously (no cutting at all) or pre-numbs the skin — either way it cuts the need for procedural sedation. How to: 1. For a child with an uncomplicated cutaneous abscess (skip the face, genitalia, perianal, and pilonidal areas), apply a thick layer of 4% lidocaine (LMX-4) cream over the abscess and a small margin. 2. Cover with an occlusive dressing (e.g., Tegaderm) and leave it on for 30–40 minutes. 3. Re-examine: in the original series ~24% of treated abscesses drained spontaneously under the dressing, and the cream group needed procedural sedation less often (24% vs 41%). 4. I

info.h: Low-Dose Opioids for Air Hunger on Noninvasive Ventilation
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Eases the subjective breathlessness (“air hunger”) that makes a dyspneic patient fight a tight BiPAP/CPAP mask, improving tolerance and success of noninvasive ventilation without suppressing the drive to breathe. How to: 1. Optimize the ventilator and mask fit first — treat the underlying cause and coach the patient before reaching for medication. 2. For persistent air hunger despite good NIV settings, give a small IV opioid dose (e.g., morphine 1–2 mg or fentanyl 12.5–25 mcg in a typical adult), titrated to comfort. 3. Watch that you are relieving the sensation of breathlessness, NOT snowing the patient — the goal is a calmer, better-synchronized patient who keeps the mask on.

info.h: Cotton Wisp Splint for an Ingrown Toenail
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Lifts the offending edge of an early ingrown toenail off the inflamed nail fold so new nail grows over the skin instead of into it — a nail-sparing alternative to partial nail avulsion for mild cases. How to: 1. Reserve for mild/early ingrown nails without frank abscess; anesthetize with a digital block or topical anesthetic if needed (often unnecessary for gentle cases). 2. Use the tip of a curved hemostat to gently free the lateral nail edge from the sulcus. 3. Roll a small (2–3 cm) wisp of cotton into a compact cylinder and saturate it with alcohol. 4. Tuck the cotton wisp under the freed lateral edge of the nail so it cushions the nail off the soft-tissue fold. 5. Have the

info.h: Angiocatheter Splint for Toe Paronychia / Nail-Fold Pain
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps the lateral nail fold open after draining a toe paronychia or excising an ingrown nail edge, so the regrowing nail glides over a plastic “rail” rather than burrowing back into the skin. How to: 1. Anesthetize the toe with a digital block; often simply elevating the nail out of the lateral fold releases pus and relieves the paronychia. 2. If the lateral nail edge must be excised, do so and clean the sulcus. 3. Take the plastic sheath from an 18-gauge angiocatheter (discard the needle) and cut a short length. 4. Slide the plastic sheath into the potential space between the nail edge and the lateral nail fold as a splint. 5. The new nail grows out over this plastic rail; giv

info.h: Syringe-Barrel or IV-Bag Funnel to Push Charcoal Down an NG Tube
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Gets thick, gritty activated charcoal (or lavage fluid) down an NG tube fast and gravity-fed, instead of fighting to force the slurry through a small syringe over and over. How to: 1. Confirm NG placement and keep the patient upright to reduce aspiration risk. 2. Funnel method: pull the plunger out of a 60 mL catheter-tip syringe, attach the empty barrel to the NG port, and pour the charcoal/fluid into the open barrel — gravity carries it down. 3. IV-bag method: cut the corner off (or empty) a 1 L IV bag, fill it with the charcoal slurry, then connect standard IV tubing snugly to the NG port and let it infuse. 4. Tape the tubing-to-NG junction — gritty charcoal tends to leak an

info.h: Pure Rotation to Remove an Embedded Tick Intact
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Extracts an attached tick with its mouthparts intact — rotating rather than yanking is more reliable at pulling the whole tick out, reducing retained mouthparts and later granuloma or infection. How to: 1. Grip the tick as close to the skin as possible, at its head/thorax, with fine-tipped forceps or a hemostat — do NOT squeeze the swollen abdomen (that can make it regurgitate). 2. Do not pull upward or apply traction to the skin. 3. Rotate the tick about two full revolutions around the long axis of its body; the backward-pointing “denticles” on its mouthparts release better to twisting (shear) than to pulling (tension). 4. Lift the tick straight off once it disengages; inspect

info.h: Chin-Tuck Double-Swallow for an Esophageal Food Bolus
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Clears an impacted esophageal food bolus at the bedside and may avert transfer for endoscopy. A borrowed dysphagia-rehab swallowing maneuver reopens the esophagus with no drugs and no scope. How to: 1. First confirm the patient is protecting the airway and handling secretions — a complete obstruction with drooling/inability to swallow saliva needs urgent ENT/GI, NOT this maneuver. 2. Hand the patient a glass of water. 3. Have them stand fully upright. 4. Instruct them to flex the neck and tuck the chin firmly to the chest. 5. Have them take a swallow of water, and the instant it starts down, immediately initiate a SECOND swallowing effort (the “double swallow”). 6. If the bolus

info.h: Glucagon + Fizzy Drink + Water to Flush an Esophageal Food Bolus
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Medically clears a distal esophageal food-bolus impaction so you may avoid or defer endoscopy — glucagon relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, an effervescent agent distends the esophagus with gas, and a water chaser adds a hydrostatic push to move the bolus into the stomach. How to: 1. First confirm the patient is protecting the airway and can handle secretions — complete obstruction with drooling/inability to swallow saliva needs urgent ENT/GI, NOT this maneuver. Rule out a sharp object, bone, or suspected perforation before giving anything by mouth. 2. Give glucagon 1 mg IV slowly over ~1 minute (rapid push provokes vomiting); warn the patient that nausea is common. 3. Wai

info.h: Pour Sugar on an Incarcerated Rectal Prolapse to Shrink It
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Osmotically pulls edema out of a swollen, irreducible rectal prolapse so it can be manually reduced at the bedside, avoiding the OR. Ordinary table sugar draws water out of the boggy mucosa in about 15 minutes. How to: 1. Confirm an incarcerated/edematous rectal prolapse that resists gentle direct reduction; give analgesia and position the patient lateral decubitus or knee-chest. 2. Liberally pack and coat the entire exposed prolapsed mucosa with granulated table sugar. 3. Wait ~15 minutes — the hyperosmolar sugar draws fluid out and visibly shrinks the mucosa. 4. Apply steady, gentle circumferential pressure to reduce the prolapse back through the anus. 5. If it will not reduc

info.h: Pre-Calibrated Hand as an Instant Wound Ruler
info.pt: General & Diagnostics — Tricks of the Trade
info.t: Accomplishes: Measures a laceration, abscess, or cellulitis border on the spot without hunting for a ruler — size drives repair coding and lets you trend cellulitis — by using your own hand pre-measured against known landmarks. How to: 1. Once, up front: measure your own hand with a ruler and memorize a few landmarks — full finger-spread span (e.g., 20 cm), palm width (e.g., 8 cm), and the width of your little-finger DIP (about 1 cm). 2. At the bedside, lay the relevant part of your hand alongside the wound or lesion. 3. Add the landmarks to estimate the size (e.g., “one palm plus three pinky-widths ≈ 11 cm”). 4. Document the measurement for the chart and billing. 5. Re-mark and re-measure a

info.h: Cunningham Maneuver for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Analgesia-sparing, often medication-free reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation by relaxing the spasmed biceps. How to: 1. Seat the patient upright; sit facing them with their forearm resting on yours. 2. First fix the scapula: have the patient sit up straight, puff out the chest, pull both shoulders back, and relax. 3. Rest the patient’s hand on your shoulder; place your hand in their antecubital fossa. 4. Massage the biceps, deltoid, and trapezius while gently encouraging the elbow downward. 5. Let the relaxed humeral head slide spontaneously back over the glenoid rim — no traction-countertraction force. Equipment: A chair and a calm, cooperative patient (no sedation r

Accomplishes: Higher first-attempt success and less pain than supination-flexion for radial-head subluxation (94% vs 69% first-pass). How to: 1. Hold the child’s elbow at 90° flexion with one hand, thumb resting over the radial head. 2. Grasp the wrist with the other hand. 3. Firmly hyperpronate the forearm (turn the palm fully downward/outward). 4. Feel for a click over the radial head — it usually signals successful reduction. 5. If it fails, repeat or try supination-flexion as the alternate. Equipment: None. _Source: ALiEM Tricks of the Trade — Nursemaid elbow reduction (Bek 2009)._

info.h: DIY Finger Traps from a Gauze Roll
info.t: Accomplishes: Improvises finger-trap traction for a distal radius reduction when commercial finger traps aren’t stocked. How to: 1. Tie a gauze roll around the patient’s fingers in a loop that grips without strangling. 2. Suspend the looped fingers from an IV pole with the elbow near 90° and off the bed. 3. Loop stockinette around the biceps and hang light weight for counter-traction. 4. Let gravity/traction overcome spasm for several minutes before applying dorsal reduction pressure. 5. Pad thin/elderly skin with Coban or foam tape to prevent injury. Equipment: Gauze roll, IV pole, stockinette, light weight, Coban/foam tape. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trade — DIY finger traps._

Accomplishes: Keeps a reduced fracture from drifting back out of alignment — “crooked splints make straight bones.” How to: 1. After reduction, apply the splint material along the fracture. 2. While it sets, press with three points of force: one over the apex of the deformity and two on the opposite side, proximal and distal to the fracture. 3. This creates a fulcrum that bends the splint and holds the reduction. 4. Use broad, flat pressure (palm/thenar) — never fingertips, which leave focal pressure points. 5. Re-check neurovascular status before and after; keep the splint snug but not constrictive. Equipment: Plaster or fiberglass splint material, padding, stockinette. _Source: NUEM Blog —

info.h: Knee Extension to Reduce a Lateral Patellar Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Quick, usually sedation-free reduction of the common lateral patellar dislocation by relaxing the extensor mechanism. How to: 1. First confirm this is a PATELLAR dislocation, not a true tibiofemoral knee dislocation (the latter carries popliteal-artery risk and needs vascular assessment). 2. Have the patient lie supine; support and gently flex the hip to relax the quadriceps and rectus femoris. 3. Slowly extend the knee while applying steady, gentle medial pressure to the lateral edge of the displaced patella. 4. The patella usually “pops” back into the trochlear groove as the knee reaches full extension. 5. Obtain post-reduction AP, lateral, and sunrise views to check for oste

Accomplishes: Uses gravity and leg internal rotation to reduce most unstable ankle fracture-dislocations with minimal hands-on force before splinting. How to: 1. Provide analgesia first — an ankle hematoma block (plus oral ibuprofen/acetaminophen/oxycodone) often avoids the need for procedural sedation. 2. With the patient supine, flex the hip and knee to ~90°. 3. Grasp the great toe / forefoot and lift the leg so it dangles, letting gravity distract the ankle. 4. Apply gentle internal rotation and inversion of the foot; the talus and mortise usually realign as the leg hangs. 5. Hold the reduced position and apply a posterior + stirrup (sugar-tong) splint, then re-check neurovascular status

info.h: Radial Gutter Splint for 2nd/3rd Metacarpal Fractures
info.t: Accomplishes: Immobilizes index/middle metacarpal fractures from both sides while leaving the other fingers free — the radial-side equivalent of the ulnar gutter. How to: 1. Cut a 3–4 inch wide splint long enough to span the wrist to the fingertips. 2. Bisect the splint lengthwise from the fingertip end back to the wrist, creating two tails. 3. Place dry gauze or cotton between the 2nd and 3rd fingers to pad them. 4. Fold the two tails so they sandwich the volar AND dorsal aspects of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals. 5. Wrap and mold with the wrist slightly extended and MCPs flexed; leave the 4th/5th fingers and thumb free. Equipment: Plaster or fiberglass splint roll, padding/stockinette, gauze,

info.h: Captain Morgan Technique for Posterior Hip Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a dislocated (often prosthetic) hip using the operator’s own propped leg as the lever, sparing your back and avoiding standing on the gurney — 92% success in the original series. How to: 1. Lay the patient supine and fix the pelvis to the bed with a strap, or have an assistant press down on the bony pelvis. 2. Flex the patient’s hip and knee to 90°. 3. Plant one foot on the gurney and tuck your knee under the patient’s flexed knee (the “Captain Morgan” pose). 4. Hold the patient’s ankle down with one hand while plantar-flexing your own ankle so your propped knee lifts the femur upward (anterior force). 5. Add gentle internal/external rotation of the leg until the head r

info.h: Legg Maneuver for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: A single-operator, leverage-based anterior shoulder reduction that needs no assistant and little or no sedation. How to: 1. Seat or recline the patient and gently abduct the affected arm to about 90°, supporting it at the wrist. 2. Place your forearm into the patient’s axilla to act as a fulcrum against the humeral neck. 3. Apply slow, steady axial traction down the abducted arm while letting the muscles fatigue and relax. 4. Use your axillary forearm to ease the humeral head laterally and over the glenoid rim. 5. Adduct and internally rotate the arm once reduced; confirm neurovascular status and post-reduction film. Equipment: A chair/gurney; optional intra-articular lidocaine

info.h: Reverse Sugar-Tong Splint for Distal Radius Fractures
info.t: Accomplishes: Volar-and-dorsal distal-radius immobilization that avoids the painful buckling a standard sugar-tong creates at the elbow fold — more comfortable and faster to wrap. How to: 1. Size a 3-inch fiberglass splint roll to span the forearm. 2. Cut transversely through the fiberglass at the midpoint, leaving the cast padding intact as a “bridge.” 3. Seat the padding bridge in the patient’s first webspace (between thumb and index). 4. Fold the two halves so they sandwich the volar and dorsal forearm up toward the elbow. 5. Let the ends overlap and curl snugly at the elbow; wrap with elastic bandage and mold the reduction. Equipment: 3-inch fiberglass splint roll, cast padding, elastic

Accomplishes: Reduces a stubborn metacarpal-neck (boxer’s) fracture when axial traction and simple push-back fail, using the flexed proximal phalanx as a lever against the metacarpal head. How to: 1. Anesthetize with a hematoma block or ulnar nerve block. 2. Flex the MCP joint to 90° — this tightens the collateral ligaments and locks the proximal phalanx to the metacarpal head. 3. Flex the PIP joint to 90°. 4. Push the proximal phalanx dorsally to drive the metacarpal head back up while stabilizing the metacarpal shaft. 5. Apply counter-pressure on the dorsal shaft to seat the reduction; immobilize in an ulnar gutter splint. Equipment: Local anesthetic (hematoma or ulnar block), ulnar gutter

info.h: Saline Joint Insufflation for a Stuck Patellar Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a subacute or difficult lateral patellar dislocation that resists the standard knee-extension maneuver, floating the patella up over the femoral condyle and sparing sedation or the OR. How to: 1. Sterile-prep the lateral knee; consider intra-articular lidocaine. 2. Insert a large-bore needle into the knee joint. 3. Insufflate sterile normal saline to distend the joint and lift the patella clear of the condyles. 4. Slowly extend the knee while applying gentle medial pressure on the lateral edge of the patella. 5. Confirm reduction and obtain AP, lateral, and sunrise films. Equipment: Sterile normal saline, large-bore needle and syringe, intra-articular lidocaine, sterile

info.h: Stimson Hands-Free Traction with Wrist Restraints (Shoulder)
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets an anterior shoulder dislocation self-reduce hands-free while you tend to other patients, using a soft wrist restraint to suspend a constant axial load instead of holding weights. How to: 1. Place the patient prone with the affected arm hanging off the bed toward the floor. 2. Pad the bed edge under the axilla to protect the neurovascular bundle. 3. Secure a soft wrist restraint with ~10 lb of weight to the wrist for steady axial traction. 4. Leave the arm to hang and let the rotator cuff and deltoid fatigue over 15-30 minutes. 5. Return and check — the joint has often self-reduced; confirm with post-reduction films and a neurovascular exam. Equipment: Soft wrist restraint

info.h: Park Method (Axillary Fist Fulcrum) for Shoulder Reduction
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces an anterior shoulder dislocation single-handed without traction-countertraction, using your fist in the axilla as a fulcrum to lever the humeral head back over the glenoid rim. How to: 1. Seat or recline the patient; provide analgesia or intra-articular lidocaine. 2. Place your fist in the patient’s axilla against the displaced humeral head. 3. Adduct the patient’s elbow against your fist while applying gentle axial distraction. 4. Use your fist as a fulcrum to slide the humeral head over the anteroinferior glenoid lip. 5. Confirm reduction and neurovascular status; sling the arm. Equipment: Analgesia or intra-articular lidocaine, sling. _Source: ALiEM Trick of the Trad

info.h: Dextrose + Lidocaine Prolotherapy for Chronic Joint Pain
info.t: Accomplishes: Offers an outpatient/sports-medicine option for chronic osteoarthritis-type joint pain when standard conservative therapy is limited or ineffective. Evidence is best for knee OA, with potential pain/function benefit but variable study quality. This is not an ED hot-joint injection trick. How to: 1. Use only after diagnosis is clear: chronic OA or ligament/tendon-related pain, not undifferentiated acute monoarthritis. 2. Do NOT inject a joint with fever, erythema, severe warmth, rapidly worsening effusion, immunocompromise concern, bacteremia risk, fracture, overlying cellulitis, or possible septic arthritis/crystal arthritis needing arthrocentesis. 3. Discuss as a planned outpa

info.h: Stacked Tongue Blades to Reduce a TMJ Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Relocates an acute jaw (temporomandibular) dislocation without putting your thumbs at bite-risk inside the mouth, by fatiguing the spasmed masseters with a sustained over-stretch. How to: 1. Confirm a true anterior TMJ dislocation (open-locked jaw, often bilateral after a wide yawn); consider procedural analgesia or a masseter/auriculotemporal block for spasm. 2. Build a stack of several wooden tongue blades and place it between the molars on the dislocated side. 3. Have the patient bite gently on the stack, which OVER-exaggerates the open position and stretches the chewing muscles even further. 4. Hold that sustained stretch for a few minutes until the masseter/temporalis fati

Accomplishes: Reduces an anterior TMJ (jaw) dislocation from OUTSIDE the mouth — no thumbs between the molars, no bite risk, and it avoids triggering the gag reflex. How to: 1. Confirm an anterior mandibular dislocation (open-locked jaw, often after a wide yawn); provide analgesia or a masseter/auriculotemporal block to relax spasm. 2. Stand at the side of the seated patient. Locate the displaced coronoid process: feel the bony bump that has slid forward in the cheek, just below and in front of the zygomatic arch. 3. Place your thumb on that coronoid process on one side and your other thumb on the same landmark on the opposite cheek. 4. Push the coronoid process(es) steadily DOWNWARD and BAC

info.h: Whistler Forearm-Fulcrum Reduction for a Dislocated Hip
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a posterior hip dislocation using your forearm as the lever, so you never have to climb onto the gurney like the Captain Morgan technique — same physics, easier on your back. How to: 1. Lay the patient supine; have an assistant flex the UNAFFECTED knee and stabilize the pelvis on the bed. 2. Slide your forearm under the affected leg into the popliteal fossa, and let that same hand grasp the assistant-held unaffected knee for an anchor. 3. With your other hand, grasp the affected lower leg near the ankle. 4. Flex the dislocated hip to 90°; your forearm is the fulcrum and the affected lower leg is the lever. 5. Pull down on the lower leg — this flexes the knee over your f

info.h: Buddy-Tape a Toe Fracture — Pad the Web and Leave the Nail Showing
info.t: Accomplishes: Functionally splints a non-displaced lesser-toe fracture using the adjacent toe as a stabilizer, while two small habits prevent the classic complications — maceration and a missed rotational deformity. How to: 1. First reduce any angulated/displaced toe under a digital block; most lesser-toe fractures are minimally displaced and need only taping. 2. Place a strip of gauze or cotton in the web space BETWEEN the injured toe and its neighbor — skin-on-skin taping macerates and breaks down. 3. Tape the injured toe to the adjacent (usually larger) toe at the proximal and distal phalanx, snug but not circumferentially tight. 4. Leave the NAIL BEDS exposed and visible — lining the nai

info.h: Davos (Boss-Holzach-Matter) Self-Reduction for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets the patient reduce their own anterior shoulder dislocation with self-applied traction, usually with no sedation and minimal pain — ideal first-line, especially for recurrent dislocators. How to: 1. Confirm an anterior dislocation in a calm, cooperative patient and attempt EARLY (within ~30 minutes); avoid if the dislocation is old (>7–10 days) or a fracture is suspected. 2. Seat the patient on the gurney and have them flex the knee on the SAME side as the dislocated shoulder to 90°, foot flat. 3. Have the patient lace the fingers of both hands together around the front of that flexed knee. 4. Ask them to lean slowly BACKWARD with the neck slightly extended until the arms p

info.h: Pencil Fulcrum Reduction for a Pediatric Extra-Octave Fracture
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a displaced little-finger proximal phalanx “extra-octave” fracture in a child using a simple pencil as a fulcrum — gentler and lower-resource than the forceful Jahss maneuver, often without sedation. How to: 1. Confirm an extra-octave fracture: a base-of-proximal-phalanx fracture of the little finger with ulnar deviation and dorsal/volar angulation, classically from a ball striking the abducted finger. 2. Provide analgesia (digital block or intranasal analgesia in a child as needed). 3. Lay an ordinary pencil at the base of the FOURTH web space, snug against the metacarpophalangeal joint of the little finger — this is your fulcrum. 4. With the pencil held as the pivot,

info.h: Syringe Roll for Patient Self-Reduction of a TMJ Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Lets the patient self-reduce an anterior TMJ dislocation by biting and rolling a syringe — no sedation and no provider hands in the bite zone (97% success, 77% under one minute). How to: 1. Confirm an anterior (not lateral or posterior) TMJ dislocation. 2. Place a 5 or 10 mL syringe horizontally between the posterior molars on the dislocated side, like a bit. 3. Instruct the patient to gently bite and roll the syringe back and forth between the upper and lower teeth. 4. The rolling motion walks the condyle back over the articular eminence and self-reduces the joint. 5. Confirm reduction and normal occlusion; advise a soft diet and to avoid wide opening. (Will not work in edentu

info.h: Finger-Trap Gravity Disimpaction for Distal Radius Fractures
info.t: Accomplishes: Pre-disimpacts a displaced distal radius fracture passively with traction and gravity so the final manipulation is far easier — you set it up and walk away to see other patients. How to: 1. Anesthetize with a hematoma block: insert a 25-gauge needle dorsally into the fracture hematoma at ~30°, aspirate to confirm blood return, then instill 8–12 mL of lidocaine. 2. Suspend the hand vertically in finger traps (index and middle fingers), arm pointing to the ceiling. 3. Hang 2–5 kg of weight from the upper arm with the elbow flexed at 90° for countertraction. 4. Give light anxiolysis and tell the patient to fully relax the arm. 5. Leave it for about 10 minutes (go see another patie

info.h: Single-Operator Posterior Elbow Reduction by Coronoid Disengagement
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a posterior elbow dislocation solo — no assistant, no forceful hyperextension traction, less neurovascular risk. How to: 1. Place the patient supine with the elbow gently flexed; provide analgesia or intra-articular lidocaine. 2. With one hand grasp the wrist/forearm and apply GENTLE in-line distraction — not the forceful traction of traction-countertraction methods. 3. With the thumb of your other hand, push the displaced olecranon/coronoid distally and forward to disengage the coronoid process from the olecranon fossa. 4. As the coronoid clears, gently flex the elbow and feel for the confirmatory clunk of reduction. 5. Recheck and document neurovascular status, then i

info.h: Hematoma Block Instead of Sedation for Ankle Fracture-Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Gives analgesia comparable to procedural sedation for closed reduction of an ankle fracture-dislocation, without the respiratory/cardiovascular risk, extra staffing, or delay — letting you reduce a time-sensitive injury faster. How to: 1. Identify the fracture site and prep the skin with antiseptic. 2. Insert the needle into the fracture hematoma / ankle joint and aspirate to confirm a flash of blood (intra-articular/intra-hematoma placement). 3. Infiltrate local anesthetic into the hematoma and joint space; wait 5–10 minutes for onset. 4. Reduce by reversing the deforming force: flex the knee to relax the gastroc-soleus, plantarflex the ankle, and apply traction with anterior

info.h: Mallet Finger — Splint the DIP in Extension, Leave the PIP Free
info.t: Accomplishes: Treats a mallet finger (extensor tendon avulsion at the DIP, dropped fingertip) non-operatively while avoiding the single most common cause of failure — letting the DIP flex even once and resetting the healing clock. How to: 1. Confirm a mallet finger: the patient cannot actively straighten the fingertip; x-ray to check for an avulsion fragment (most are still managed non-operatively unless the fragment involves >1/3 of the joint or there is volar subluxation). 2. Apply a stack/foam or aluminum splint holding ONLY the DIP joint in full extension (slight hyperextension is acceptable; do NOT force marked hyperextension, which blanches the skin). 3. Leave the PIP joint completely

info.h: The Fulcrum Technique for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Single-operator anterior shoulder reduction that uses your own forearm as a fulcrum in the axilla, succeeding where traction-countertraction fails and requiring no assistant. How to: 1. Seat the patient upright on the gurney; provide analgesia or intra-articular lidocaine as needed. 2. Stand on the affected side and pass your forearm across the front of the patient, tucking it deep into the axilla so your forearm sits against the displaced humeral head as a fulcrum. 3. With your other hand, grasp the patient’s wrist or distal forearm on the affected side. 4. Apply slow, steady downward traction on the arm while levering the humeral head over your forearm fulcrum — the fulcrum c

info.h: Ultrasound-Guided Intra-Articular Lidocaine for Shoulder Reduction
info.t: Accomplishes: Provides pre-reduction analgesia for an anterior shoulder dislocation with equal success to procedural sedation but fewer adverse events and shorter ED stay — essentially a hematoma block of the glenohumeral joint. How to: 1. Prep the posterolateral shoulder sterile: chlorhexidine, sterile gloves, sterile gel, and a probe cover. 2. Place the probe to visualize the glenohumeral joint and the gap left by the dislocated humeral head. 3. Use a SPINAL needle — a standard needle often will not reach the deep joint. 4. Advance under direct ultrasound guidance into the joint; you almost always get a flash of blood (hemarthrosis) confirming intra-articular position. 5. Inject 15–20 mL o

info.h: Ultrasound-Guided Ulnar Nerve Block for Boxer’s Fracture Reduction
info.t: Accomplishes: Provides clean analgesia for reduction and splinting of a 5th-metacarpal (boxer’s) fracture when severe swelling makes a hematoma block fail — a forearm ulnar nerve block anesthetizes the little finger and ulnar hand without procedural sedation. How to: 1. Position the forearm supinated; scan the volar mid-forearm with a high-frequency linear probe. 2. Find the ulnar artery, then identify the round, honeycomb ulnar nerve sitting just ULNAR (medial) to the artery. 3. Trace proximally a few centimeters to where the nerve separates from the artery — block there to avoid the vessel. 4. Under real-time ultrasound, advance an in-plane needle and deposit 5–10 mL of local anesthetic to

info.h: Stockinette DIY Skyhook for Hand/Arm Elevation
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps a swollen or injured upper extremity continuously elevated from an IV pole, reducing edema in hand infections and post-reduction swelling without tying up staff or stacking pillows. How to: 1. Stretch stockinette fingertip-to-fingertip across the patient’s body and cut to that length (size 2 for peds, 3 for an average adult, 4 for larger arms). 2. Cut the stockinette lengthwise for about one arm’s length (roughly the first third to half of the tube). 3. Slip the injured arm into the uncut portion so the two cut tails hang front and back across the torso. 4. Tie the cut tails under the opposite armpit like a “Miss America” sash to anchor it. 5. Use the remaining uncut end

info.h: Parvin Gravity Hang for a Posterior Elbow Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a posterior elbow dislocation single-handed with minimal force, letting gravity plus a hanging wrist weight fatigue the muscles — often with little or no procedural sedation. How to: 1. Place the patient PRONE on the gurney with the injured arm hanging straight off the edge, elbow flexed toward the floor; provide analgesia or an intra-articular block. 2. Tuck a rolled towel or pillow under the distal humerus, just proximal to the elbow, as a fulcrum. 3. Hang a 5–10 lb weight from the wrist (or apply gentle downward wrist traction) and wait several minutes for the muscles to relax. 4. As the olecranon slides distally, gently guide it forward and feel for the reduction cl

info.h: Gravity-Assisted Reduction of an Ankle Fracture-Dislocation (GARA)
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a displaced ankle fracture-dislocation using the leg’s own weight, no procedural sedation. It cuts the team from ~4 people to 2 and lets gravity do the reduction while you get the plaster ready. How to: 1. Give adequate analgesia (an ankle hematoma block often suffices; IV sedation is not required). 2. Position by direction of displacement: for the common externally-rotated LATERAL displacement, lay the patient on their side with the injured ankle facing UP; for POSTERIOR displacement, place the patient prone. 3. Let the lower leg hang off the end of the bed (or rest the thigh on a firm support) so gravity applies sustained axial traction to the ankle. 4. Wait ~5–10 min

info.h: Towel-Clip Reduction of a Posterior Sternoclavicular Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Pulls a posteriorly displaced medial clavicle off the mediastinal structures (trachea, esophagus, great vessels) it may be compressing, when abduction-traction alone fails. How to: 1. First get a CT chest (with angiography) BEFORE manipulating — a posterior dislocation is a potential vascular/airway emergency; have surgical backup available. 2. Reduce only within ~10 days of injury (older injuries go to the OR). 3. Under procedural sedation, place the patient supine with a bolster between the scapulae. 4. Try abduction-traction first: abduct the ipsilateral arm to ~90° and apply steady traction to translate the medial clavicle anteriorly. 5. If that fails, prep the skin sterile

info.h: Soft-Wrap / Buddy Tape a Boxer’s Fracture Instead of Reducing and Casting
info.t: Accomplishes: Spares many 5th-metacarpal-neck (boxer’s) fractures the pain of a hematoma-block reduction and a bulky ulnar-gutter cast — a simple soft wrap gives equivalent hand function and healing with better comfort and earlier motion. How to: 1. Confirm an isolated 5th metacarpal NECK fracture with acceptable angulation (up to ~70° is well tolerated at the neck) and NO rotational deformity or scissoring of the flexed fingers — rotation still needs reduction/referral. 2. Skip formal reduction and rigid casting for these acceptable fractures. 3. Buddy-tape the ring and little fingers together and apply a soft supportive wrap (e.g., a compressive elastic bandage) for comfort. 4. Encourage e

info.h: Prone Scapular Manipulation for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces an anterior shoulder dislocation by repositioning the glenoid to the humeral head (rather than muscling the head into the glenoid), frequently without procedural sedation. Prospective ED series report roughly 90% first-attempt and near-100% overall success with no complications. How to: 1. Place the patient PRONE on the gurney with the dislocated arm hanging straight down over the edge. 2. Allow several minutes of relaxation — the weight of the arm alone sometimes reduces it. An optional 5–10 lb hanging weight on the wrist fatigues the spasming muscles. 3. Identify the inferior tip of the scapula. 4. Stabilize the superior-medial border of the scapula with the fingers o

info.h: Double Sugar-Tong Splint to Hold an Unstable Distal Radius Reduction
info.t: Accomplishes: Locks out elbow motion so a reduced, unstable distal radius fracture does not re-displace overnight. A single sugar-tong loosens as the patient extends the elbow in their sleep; a second limb blocks that motion and holds the reduction. How to: 1. After reduction, apply the standard forearm sugar-tong (volar-to-dorsal, folded at the elbow) with the forearm in the alignment that maintains reduction. 2. Add a SECOND sugar-tong limb oriented across the elbow to block elbow flexion/extension. 3. Three-point mold the splint over the fracture while the plaster/fiberglass sets — broad palmar pressure, never fingertips. 4. Wrap snugly (not constrictively) and recheck neurovascular statu

info.h: Buddy-Splint the Legs When a Traction Splint Is Contraindicated (Femur)
info.t: Accomplishes: Immobilizes a mid/distal femur fracture when a traction splint cannot be used — an ipsilateral tib-fib or ankle fracture, or an open ankle, where the distal traction hitch would pull directly on a second fracture. The uninjured leg becomes the splint. How to: 1. Confirm a contraindication to traction (ipsilateral lower-leg/ankle fracture, open ankle, or a fracture/dislocation near the ankle hitch site). 2. Pad generously between the legs over all bony prominences (knees, malleoli). 3. Bind the injured leg to the uninjured leg at several levels — thigh, above and below the knee, and at the ankles — with cravats or wide straps. 4. Keep the binding snug enough to limit motion but

info.h: FARES Oscillation Method for Anterior Shoulder Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Single-operator anterior shoulder reduction using gentle vertical oscillation to defeat muscle spasm, often with no assistant and little or no sedation. How to: 1. Lay the patient supine with the affected arm at the side, elbow fully extended, forearm in neutral (thumb up). 2. Grasp the patient’s hand/wrist with both of your hands and apply gentle in-line longitudinal traction — no countertraction. 3. Add small vertical oscillations (~5 cm up-and-down excursion, about 2–3 per second) and keep them going continuously. 4. While maintaining traction and oscillation, slowly abduct the arm past 90°. 5. Near 120° add gentle external rotation; the humeral head slips back with a clunk

info.h: Bed-Rail Hanging-Arm Reduction for a Posterior Elbow Dislocation
info.t: Accomplishes: Reduces a posterior elbow dislocation without turning the patient prone and without heavy traction, using a padded raised bed rail as the fulcrum — easier on your back and safer under light sedation. How to: 1. Provide analgesia or light sedation (elbow reduction is a leverage problem, not a spasm problem). 2. Raise the head of the bed to 30–45° and pad the ipsilateral bed rail, then raise it. 3. Hang the affected arm over the padded rail so the rail sits at the mid-humerus as a fulcrum, with the forearm dangling. 4. Supinate the forearm and flex the elbow to about 90° to disengage the coronoid from the olecranon fossa. 5. Place both thumbs on the olecranon and apply steady dow

info.h: Thumb-to-the-Floor Traction to Hold a Distal Radius Reduction While Splinting
info.t: Accomplishes: Keeps a reduced distal radius fracture in position — and stops the sugar-tong from sliding off the elbow — by having the assistant pull the thumb straight up while pointing it toward the ground, relaxing the brachioradialis so the reduction holds during plaster application. How to: 1. After reduction (finger-trap traction plus a hematoma or nerve block), have an assistant take over traction on the thumb. 2. Instruct them to point the patient’s thumb toward the FLOOR while pulling straight up and slightly volar. 3. This position relaxes the brachioradialis so it will not re-displace the fracture while you work. 4. Apply the sugar-tong from the distal palmar crease, around the el
• Painful skin + URI-like prodrome — "the rash that hurts" • Nikolsky / Asboe-Hansen signs, ≥2 mucosal sites
• EM vs SJS vs overlap vs TEN by % BSA detachment • EM is a distinct entity; MIRM/RIME in kids
• Stop the drug now — review last 4–8 weeks • High-risk: allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfa, NSAIDs
• SCORTEN — day 1 AND day 3
• ⅔-Parkland fluid, titrate to UOP 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr • Urgent ophthalmology, mucosal/wound care, NO prophylactic abx
• Adjuvant therapy is derm-guided (weak evidence) • >10% BSA → ICU; TEN → burn center
Typical target lesions — three concentric zones, <3 cm, well-defined, acral. Nikolsky-negative. EM is infection-driven (HSV) and is not on the SJS/TEN spectrum.
Hemorrhagic crusting of the lips and mucosal desquamation. Mucosal involvement at ≥2 sites is characteristic of SJS/TEN.
Confluent dusky skin with full-thickness epidermal detachment — Nikolsky-positive. >30% BSA defines TEN.
Extensive epidermal loss on the back during the subacute phase.

• Trigger: infection — HSV (dominant), Mycoplasma • Lesions: *typical* targets — 3 concentric zones, <3 cm, well-defined • Distribution: acral (dorsal hands/feet) → proximal • Nikolsky: negative • Course: self-limiting over 1–2 weeks • EM minor = no/minimal mucosa; EM major = mucosa + systemic symptoms (still EM)

• Trigger: drugs (4–28 day latency) • Lesions: dusky/purpuric macules + *flat atypical* targets → detachment • Distribution: truncal/central, spreading • Nikolsky: positive • Mucosa: ≥2 sites in most • Classification: SJS <10% · overlap 10–30% · TEN >30% BSA detachment

Acral typical targets + HSV history + Nikolsky-negative → EM (manage as EM). Truncal dusky macules + flat atypical targets + Nikolsky-positive + recent drug → SJS/TEN (stop the drug, burn-style supportive care).

• Allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01) • Anticonvulsants — carbamazepine (HLA-B*15:02 in Han Chinese/SE Asian), lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital • Sulfonamide antibiotics — TMP-SMX (cotrimoxazole), sulfasalazine • Nevirapine, abacavir (HLA-B*57:01) • Oxicam NSAIDs (e.g., piroxicam, meloxicam)
Cephalosporins, macrolides, quinolones, tetracyclines, acetic-acid NSAIDs.
Use the ALDEN algorithm (latency, drug present at index day, dechallenge/rechallenge, notoriety, alternative causes) when multiple drugs are plausible. Score ≥6 = very probable culprit.

info.pt: The 6 P's of Acute Limb Ischemia
info.t: • Pain — early and severe • Pallor — pale / marble-white skin • Pulselessness — absent distal pulses (confirm with handheld Doppler) • Paresthesia — sensory loss; an EARLY and ominous sign • Paralysis — motor deficit; a LATE, limb-threatening sign • Poikilothermia — perishingly cold limb

info.pt: The 6 P's of Acute Limb Ischemia
info.t: Pain, pallor, pulselessness and coldness come first. Paresthesia then paralysis mark progression toward irreversible injury — once motor function is lost, the salvage window is closing. Skeletal muscle tolerates roughly 6 hours of ischemia before irreversible necrosis.

info.pt: The 6 P's of Acute Limb Ischemia
info.t: • Two large-bore IVs, IV analgesia, NPO (likely OR) • Keep the limb dependent and warm-not-hot — never apply direct heat to insensate skin • Handheld Doppler of pedal arterial + venous signals • Start IV heparin and call vascular EARLY — do not wait for imaging

info.pt: Ischemic Limb — Things That Kill / Do NOT
info.t: 🛑 Do NOT delay anticoagulation or the vascular consult to chase advanced imaging in an obviously threatened limb. 🛑 Do NOT reperfuse a nonviable (Rutherford III) limb — releases potassium, myoglobin and acid load and can be lethal. That limb goes down the primary amputation pathway. 🛑 Do NOT apply direct heat to an insensate ischemic limb — burn risk. Keep it dependent and warm-not-hot. 🛑 Do NOT use CK/lactate/myoglobin to decide whether to revascularize — they are reperfusion/rhabdo baselines, not gatekeepers.

info.pt: Ischemic Limb — Things That Kill / Do NOT
info.t: • Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — a warm, swollen, cyanotic limb from massive DVT is the mimic that looks opposite to arterial ischemia. • Aortic dissection extending to the iliacs presenting as a unilateral cold pulseless leg. • Compartment syndrome after revascularization — fasciotomy if pressure >30 mmHg. • Reperfusion hyperkalemia / rhabdo / AKI — monitor and treat aggressively; dialysis if refractory.

• Relative proptosis — globe bulges forward vs the other side • Tense, tight eyelids — hard to open, "rock-hard" globe, resistance to retropulsion • RAPD — relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) in the injured eye Proptosis + tense orbit + RAPD = orbital compartment syndrome until proven otherwise. Decompress.

info.h: Vision loss is a LATE sign
info.t: ⚠️ Decreased acuity is present in fewer than half of OCS cases. Do NOT wait for blindness to act. Supporting signs: severe eye pain, ophthalmoplegia, markedly elevated IOP, chemosis, cherry-red macula.

• Normal IOP 10–21 mmHg • >30 mmHg with symptoms → call ophthalmology, prepare to decompress • >40 mmHg → decompress now • Retinal ischemia becomes irreversible at ~90–120 min from onset — the clock started at symptom onset.

info.h: The two rules that save the eye
info.t: 1. OCS is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT delay for CT, tonometry, or ophthalmology when the picture is obvious. 2. The cantholysis decompresses (~30 mmHg drop), not the canthotomy (~14 mmHg). Never stop at the skin cut.
• Topical ophthalmic anesthetic drops to the globe • Inject ~1–2 mL lidocaine with epinephrine into the lateral canthus, needle tip directed away from the globe.
Lay a straight hemostat across the lateral canthus from the canthal angle to the orbital rim and crush ~1 minute — devascularizes tissue (less bleeding) and marks the incision line.

With toothed forceps lifting skin away from the globe, cut horizontally through the crushed canthus toward the orbital rim, ~1–2 cm (max 2 cm — facial nerve temporal branch). This exposes the tendon but does NOT decompress.

• Grasp the lower lid at the lateral last-lash, pull up and out to tension the inferior crus • Point scissors toward the nose, inferior-posterior, away from the globe • Strum the taut tendon (guitar-string twang), then cut the inferior crus until the lower lid is completely free.

Success = swinging eyelid, IOP <40 (ideally <30), softening globe, improving acuity/RAPD. If still tense AND the inferior crus is confirmed fully released → divide the superior crus (higher bleed/ptosis risk — lacrimal artery/gland, levator). Refractory → OR.
Ophthalmology consult parallel to, never before, the procedure. CT orbit after decompression. Lid repair deferred. Admit for serial exams.

The lateral canthal (palpebral) tendon anchors the lateral eyelids to the orbit and prevents forward globe movement. It has a superior crus and an inferior crus. Releasing it from the rim lets the globe move anteriorly, expanding orbital volume and dropping pressure.

The tendon inserts on the lateral orbital (Whitnall) tubercle — a bony prominence on the inner surface of the lateral orbital wall, ~5 mm posterior to the rim (range 1.5–5 mm), ~10 mm below the frontozygomatic suture. It is behind the rim margin, not at it.

The inferior crus reliably decompresses, and working inferiorly avoids the superiorly located lacrimal gland, lacrimal artery, and levator aponeurosis — the structures whose injury causes bleeding and ptosis. A bloodless cut means you are in the correct (avascular) tendon plane.

🛑 Do NOT delay decompression for CT, tonometry, or ophthalmology when OCS is clinically obvious. Image after, not before. 🛑 Do NOT stop at the canthotomy (skin cut). It drops IOP only ~14 mmHg. The cantholysis is what decompresses (~30 mmHg). Incomplete cantholysis is the #1 failure mode. 🛑 Do NOT wait for vision loss — it is present in <50% of OCS. Act on proptosis + tense orbit + RAPD. 🛑 Do NOT point scissors toward the globe and do NOT push on the globe — direct everything outward/posterior, toward the nose. 🛑 Do NOT routinely cut the superior crus first — start inferior; the superior region holds the lacrimal artery/gland and levator (bleeding, ptosis).

• Globe rupture — enophthalmos, teardrop/peaked pupil, hyphema, IOP <5, Seidel+. If the orbit is soft and rupture is likely → shield, no pressure, no cut, emergent ophthalmology. If the orbit is tense and vision-threatened, decompress gently while avoiding all globe pressure. • Incomplete release — if IOP stays high, re-explore and finish dividing the inferior crus before adding the superior crus. • Refractory OCS after both crura → OR for orbital/septal decompression. The procedure can be repeated/extended. • Adjuncts (mannitol, acetazolamide, IOP drops, HOB up) do NOT replace decompression.

• Acute cluster headache attack not responding to high-flow O₂ + SQ sumatriptan, OR triptan contraindicated. • Status migrainosus refractory to IV cocktail when DHE is contraindicated. • Rescue analgesia for breakthrough cluster while bridging to verapamil. • Generally outpatient or short-stay friendly; can be repeated.

The sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) sits in the pterygopalatine fossa, just deep to the posterior end of the middle nasal turbinate. The mucosa over the SPG is thin (1-1.5 mm), allowing topical anesthetic to diffuse to the ganglion without an injection. No needle is required for the simple ED-friendly version. The fascia overlying the SPG is the only barrier between the topical anesthetic and the ganglion.

• 4% lidocaine solution (preservative-free if possible), 1-2 mL per side. Avoid 10% solution (overdose risk). • A delivery device — options: • SphenoCath (FDA-cleared catheter, $30-50/unit) — preferred when available. • Cotton-tip applicator (long, 4-6 inch) — soak tip in lidocaine, advance to posterior nasopharynx along the floor of the nose. • Atomizer / MAD (mucosal atomization device) mounted on a 3-mL syringe. • Topical decongestant (oxymetazoline 0.05%) optional — improves penetration in congested patients. • Tilt-back position or recumbent with head extended 45°.

Step 1. Position patient supine with neck extended OR seated head-tilted-back at 45°. Step 2. Apply oxymetazoline 2 sprays per nostril 2-3 min before procedure (optional, improves diffusion). Step 3. Soak the tip of a long cotton-tipped applicator in 4% lidocaine. Step 4. Advance the cotton tip along the FLOOR of the affected nostril (parallel to the hard palate). Goal: tip rests at the posterior nasopharynx, just behind the middle turbinate. Estimated depth = distance from nostril to tragus (~7-8 cm in adults). Step 5. Leave in place 5-10 minutes. Reposition gently if patient gags (advanced too far). Step 6. Remove. May repeat on contralateral side if bilateral headache. Step 7. Observe for

• Local lidocaine allergy. • Facial fracture or nasal trauma on the target side. • Severe nasal anatomic deformity that prevents safe applicator advance. • Active epistaxis. • Caution: pregnancy (lidocaine Category B; small dose generally acceptable but document risk discussion).

• Bitter taste / temporary numbness of soft palate and posterior pharynx — common, self-limited. • Lightheadedness. • Epistaxis (rare; minimize trauma during advance). • Lidocaine toxicity (overdose) — DO NOT exceed 4 mg/kg total dose; 1-2 mL of 4% solution per side = 40-80 mg total, well below toxicity threshold in adults. • Vasovagal reaction (rare).

The Cady RCT (Headache 2015) showed statistically significant decrease in cluster attack severity at 15 min vs sham (saline). Effect modest but reproducible. SphenoCath device-based RCTs have similar profile. Most peer-reviewed evidence is for cluster headache; status migrainosus use is supported by smaller series. Routine in many academic headache centers as rescue therapy.

• Acetaminophen 1 g PO/IV q6h (max 3 g/day in pregnancy; FDA Category B). First-line analgesic across all trimesters. • Metoclopramide 10 mg IV (Category B). Anti-emetic + central anti-migraine effect; pre-treat with diphenhydramine 25 mg IV to prevent EPS. • Diphenhydramine 25 mg IV (Category B). Adjunct for nausea + EPS prevention; mild sedation. • IV hydration with normal saline 1-2 L.

• Magnesium sulfate 1-2 g IV over 30 min — Category D in pre-eclampsia but acceptable short-term for migraine; monitor reflexes. • Greater occipital nerve block (bupivacaine 0.5% plain, 2-3 mL per side; NO epinephrine in pregnancy due to vasoconstriction). First-line procedural option, repeatable. • Sphenopalatine ganglion block (intranasal 4% lidocaine via cotton-tip or SphenoCath). Document risk discussion — lidocaine Category B, small dose, generally acceptable.

• Prednisone 60 mg PO × 5 days (low cumulative dose; Category C). May be used short-term for status migrainosus. • Methylprednisolone IV for status migrainosus refractory to above. • Consider admission for hydration + observation; obstetric co-management.

First trimester (0-13 wk): • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac) — relative risk of miscarriage; avoid if alternative exists. • Triptans — limited data; case reports suggest no major teratogenicity (sumatriptan registry data ~10 yr); reserve for severe cases after risk discussion. Second trimester (14-27 wk): • NSAIDs acceptable short-term (avoid third-trimester window). • Triptans — same as above. Third trimester (28-40 wk): • NSAIDs CONTRAINDICATED after 30 weeks — premature ductus arteriosus closure, oligohydramnios. • Triptans CONTRAINDICATED in third trimester per ACOG (vasoconstriction concern). ALL TRIMESTERS — absolute contraindications: • Ergots (ergotamine, methylergonovine) —

info.h: Bridge / Prophylaxis if Cluster or Frequent Migraine
info.t: • Propranolol — Category C; widely used in pregnancy for migraine prophylaxis. Start 40 mg PO BID. • Amitriptyline — Category C; start 10-25 mg qHS. • Memantine and CGRP antagonists — limited pregnancy data; avoid. • OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) for chronic migraine — limited data; consult headache specialist.

• Postpartum eclampsia / PRES / CVST can present as severe headache up to 6 weeks postpartum — always include in differential. • Breastfeeding-safe acute meds: acetaminophen, ibuprofen, sumatriptan (low milk transfer), metoclopramide. Avoid prolonged metoclopramide (>2 weeks) due to maternal depression risk. • Reinstate prophylaxis if held during pregnancy; verapamil acceptable for cluster (compatible with breastfeeding).

• MRI without gadolinium is preferred over CT — no ionizing radiation, no fetal risk in any trimester (ACOG 723). • CT head when MRI unavailable or unstable patient — fetal dose <0.005 mGy (negligible). • MRV/MRA for posterior fossa headache, postpartum severe headache (CVST risk), or persistent thunderclap with negative non-contrast. • Gadolinium contrast generally avoided in pregnancy (Category C-D) but may be used if benefit clearly outweighs.
• Cloudy effluent ± abdominal pain • Exit-site / tunnel signs • Drain or fill problem, abdominal bulge • Volume / hyper-K / hyperglycemia • Bloody effluent or refractory pain
• Apply ISPD diagnostic criteria — 2 of 3 • Start empiric IP antibiotics within 6 h • Reassess at day 3 • Refractory / fungal = pull catheter
• Exit-site vs tunnel • Exit-site treatment • Tunnel infection — high peritonitis risk
• Outflow failure — start with constipation • Dialysate leak • Abdominal wall hernia • PD-related hydrothorax
• Hyperkalemia in a PD patient • Volume overload / UF failure • Hyperglycemia from dialysate
• Hemoperitoneum • Encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis • PD failure → HD bridge
• Admit — medicine • Admit — ICU • Home with PD nurse follow-up

• Bacterial peritonitis — WBC >100/µL, >50% PMN, positive culture • Fungal peritonitis — chronic abx exposure, immunocompromised, refractory bacterial peritonitis • Mycobacterial peritonitis — endemic regions, prior TB, sterile pyuria of the effluent

• Eosinophilic peritonitis — eos >10% on differential, recent dialysate change, self-limited • Chemical peritonitis — disinfectant, hypertonic dialysate, drug additive • Sclerosing / encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis — long PD duration, bowel obstruction

• Hemoperitoneum — menstrual reflux, ovarian cyst, viscus rupture, anticoagulation • Chylous effluent — triglycerides >100 mg/dL, milky white, lymphatic injury or malignancy • Fibrin / debris — high in 1st bag after dwell, clears with heparin 500 U/L

• Polymicrobial enteric organisms → ruptured viscus / diverticulitis • Bloody effluent in postmenopausal patient → malignancy / cyst rupture / trauma • Persistent cloudy effluent + obstipation → encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis
• Cefazolin 15–20 mg/kg IP once daily (single bag, ≥6 h dwell) • Vancomycin 15–30 mg/kg IP every 5–7 days (re-dose by trough <15 µg/mL)
• Ceftazidime 1000–1500 mg IP once daily • Gentamicin 0.6 mg/kg IP once daily (preferred in high ESBL areas per PDOPPS) • Tobramycin 0.6 mg/kg IP once daily — equivalent to gentamicin
• Cefepime 1 g IP once daily — non-inferior to dual therapy in 2 RCTs • Increase load + maintenance by 25% if residual urine >100 mL/day

• APD has shorter dwells than CAPD — use a daytime full-fill dwell to deliver the antibiotic dose • Vancomycin needs ≥4 h dwell (target ≥6 h) to exceed MIC for 50% of the cycle • Cefazolin and ceftazidime have been validated for short-dwell cycling

• Vancomycin + ceftazidime are compatible in the same 1 L bag — NEVER mix in the same syringe (precipitates) • Use separate syringes for each antibiotic when injecting into the bag • Add heparin 500 U/L to dialysate while effluent is cloudy — prevents catheter fibrin obstruction • Avoid IV ceftriaxone when IP option exists — better tissue levels with IP
• Coag-negative Staph, culture-negative, streptococcus: 2 weeks • S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, polymicrobial: 3 weeks • Fungal: ≥2 weeks after catheter removal

info.h: Acute Indications to Pull the Catheter
info.t: • Refractory peritonitis (still cloudy at day 5 of appropriate IP abx) • Fungal peritonitis — within 24–48 h of diagnosis • Tunnel infection with deep-cuff involvement on ultrasound • Hemodynamic instability from peritoneal sepsis • Catheter perforation / extrusion

• Relapsing peritonitis (≥2 episodes within 4 weeks) • Encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis • Refractory ultrafiltration failure with hypertensive heart failure • Hydrothorax not amenable to pleurodesis • Patient choice / inability to perform exchanges safely

1. Temporary HD access — internal jugular tunneled catheter. AVOID subclavian (preserves future fistula sites). 2. Remove PD catheter within 24–48 h for fungal/refractory peritonitis; can defer for stable patients. 3. Permanent HD access — AV fistula preferred. Refer to vascular surgery from the ED. 4. Transplant referral if not already listed.

• Bacterial peritonitis with catheter removal: PD return possible after 2–3 weeks if peritoneal membrane recovers • Fungal peritonitis: PD return possible after ≥6 weeks with negative effluent cultures • EPS, hydrothorax with failed pleurodesis: PD usually NOT resumable

info.h: When to Drain in the ED
info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: • Suspected peritonitis — need effluent for cell count + culture (ISPD 2-of-3 criteria). • Volume overload / dyspnea — therapeutic decompression while arranging HD bridge. • Suspected hemoperitoneum — diagnostic drain (note color). • Suspected dialysate leak / hydrothorax — drain dry before imaging. • Pre-imaging — most radiologists prefer dry abdomen for CT. Do NOT drain emergently if the patient is actively exchanging at home with no symptoms and you do not need the fluid for diagnosis. Talk to nephrology first.

info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: • PD transfer set already attached to patient (or sterile new transfer set if disconnected) • Empty drain bag (5 L preferred) — gravity drainage • Two pairs sterile gloves + surgical mask + cap (for you and the patient) • Chlorhexidine 2% swabs • Sterile drape • 4×4 gauze • 3 sterile specimen containers (cell count + Gram stain + culture) • 2 blood culture bottles (aerobic + anaerobic) for the direct inoculation technique • 10 mL syringe + 18 g needle for sampling • Heparinized green-top tube if hemoperitoneum suspected (rules out clotting bias) Sterile-to-sterile rule: any time the transfer set is opened, double-mask + sterile gloves. PD peritonitis is overwhelmingly touch contamination.

info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: 1. Position — patient supine or semi-recumbent. Bag below the level of the abdomen (gravity drainage). 2. Mask + cap on patient and operator. Wash hands. Open sterile field. 3. Inspect transfer set for cracks, soiling. Wipe the connection port with chlorhexidine ×30 s, allow to dry. 4. Connect the empty drain bag to the patient outflow port using the existing twist-clamp / spike per the patient's system (Baxter HomeChoice, Fresenius Liberty, etc.). 5. Open the drain clamp. Effluent should flow 200–300 mL/min. Total drain volume is typically 1.5–2.5 L over 10–20 min. 6. Sample effluent at mid-stream — not first 10 mL (catheter contaminants) and not last 50 mL (sediment). • 3 mL into purple-to

info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: • Clear / straw yellow → normal effluent. Cell count <100/µL. Look elsewhere. • Cloudy / hazy → peritonitis until proven otherwise. WBC >100/µL with >50% PMN confirms. • Frankly bloody → hemoperitoneum. Send hematocrit, type/screen. Most causes benign (menses, ovarian cyst, exercise) but assess for visceral rupture if hemodynamic change. • Brown / fecaloid → bowel perforation. Surgical emergency. CT abd/pelvis + broad-spectrum IV abx (NOT just IP) + general surgery now. • Chylous / milky → triglyceride-rich. Consider lymphatic leak, EPS, calcium channel blocker effect. • Bilious → cholecystitis with rupture or biliary-peritoneal fistula. Surgical consult.

info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: • Never re-use a drain bag. Single-use only. • Never disconnect the transfer set without masking. ~30% of peritonitis is touch contamination. • Cell count requires ≥2 h dwell — if patient is on rapid APD cycles (1 h dwells), the WBC will be falsely low. Note dwell time on the lab requisition. • Direct inoculation into blood culture bottles is mandatory for adequate yield — do NOT just send effluent in a urine cup. • If the patient came in mid-exchange: drain what is in, do not abort an instill in progress (risk of overfill leak + pain). • Hypotension on drain: rare but possible in volume-depleted patients. Slow the drain by partially clamping; check BP. • Catheter dysfunction during the drai

info.pt: ED Procedure: Drain PD Fluid Safely
info.t: "PD effluent drained at [time]. Volume [mL]. Appearance [color/clarity]. Effluent cell count + diff sent, ≥5 mL inoculated into aerobic + anaerobic blood culture bottles, Gram stain pending. Empiric IP [cefazolin/vancomycin + ceftazidime/gentamicin OR cefepime monotherapy] [dose] administered at [time] via [bag/syringe technique]. Heparin 500 U/L added. Next dwell ≥6 h. Nephrology aware."

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT inject without aspirating first
info.t: The occipital artery runs near the GON and feeds vertebral collaterals. Intra-arterial injection can cause seizure, transient neurologic deficit, or stroke. Aspirate before EVERY injection. If blood returns, withdraw and redirect 1-2 mm medially before re-aspirating.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use epinephrine-containing local anesthetic
info.t: Vasoconstriction near the vertebral system risks ischemia. Use PLAIN bupivacaine 0.5% or PLAIN lidocaine 1-2% only.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT inject through infected skin
info.t: Cellulitis or active scalp pathology at the injection site is an absolute contraindication. Find an alternative therapy (pharmacologic, sphenopalatine block).

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use steroid adjunct in pregnancy
info.t: Local anesthetic alone is safe in pregnancy and one of the few non-pharmacologic options for refractory pregnancy headache. Avoid corticosteroid adjunct due to fetal exposure concerns.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT exceed 4 steroid blocks per year
info.t: Repeated triamcinolone or methylprednisolone injections cause patchy alopecia at the injection site and Cushingoid features. Counsel patients; use LA-only between steroid blocks.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT block bilaterally for cluster headache
info.t: Cluster is unilateral. Block only the symptomatic side. Bilateral blocks are reserved for migraine variants per AHS guidance.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the red-flag screen
info.t: ONB does not treat secondary headache. Confirm SAH, dissection, CVST, AACG, meningitis, and hypertensive emergency are ruled out before any procedural therapy. Send the patient back through Headache Hub if uncertain.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without documenting the GON sensory exam
info.t: Baseline + post-procedure exam protects against missing a true neurologic complication (intra-arterial, hematoma) by ascribing it to "expected numbness."

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use nasal cannula instead of NRB for O₂
info.t: Cluster requires 100% O₂ via non-rebreather at 12-15 L/min. Nasal cannula peaks at ~40% FiO₂ — inadequate. Pure cluster patients failing "O₂" who were on NC have not actually had an O₂ trial. Link: O₂ first-line node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the red-flag screen
info.t: Cluster autonomic features overlap with carotid dissection (Horner), AACG (red eye, mid-dilated pupil), CVST (postpartum / hypercoag), and SAH. Always exclude these before initiating cluster-specific Rx. Red-flag exclusion module

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start verapamil without baseline ECG + plan for serial ECGs
info.t: Cluster doses (480-960 mg/d) cause PR prolongation in 19% and AV block in 4% per Cohen Neurology 2007. 12-lead ECG BEFORE every dose escalation + 10 days after. Halt for PR >0.22 s, any 2nd/3rd-degree AVB, brady <50, sx hypotension. Verapamil ECG protocol

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give a triptan within 24 h of an ergot (or vice versa)
info.t: Additive vasoconstriction. Specifically: no sumatriptan/zolmitriptan within 24 h before/after DHE or ergotamine. Document interval explicitly before dosing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT exceed 2 SQ sumatriptan doses in 24 h
info.t: Max 2 × 6 mg SQ per 24 h with ≥1 h between. Use ONB or IN lidocaine if still attacking after the 24-h cap. Sumatriptan node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give triptan with uncontrolled HTN, known CAD, prior MI/stroke, basilar/hemiplegic variant, or pregnancy
info.t: Coronary vasospasm risk. Use DHE only if non-pregnant + no CAD. In pregnancy: O₂ + GON block (LA-only or LA + low-dose steroid per OB) are the safer abortive options.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT switch CBZ-associated hyponatremia to oxcarbazepine
info.t: Oxcarbazepine causes MORE hyponatremia than CBZ (~15-30% vs ~10%). If a cluster patient on CBZ-class drug develops low Na, stop the offending med, correct Na, switch to a non-Na-lowering alternative (gabapentin, baclofen, lamotrigine) with neurology input. [Dong J Headache Pain 2005; Berghuis Epilepsia 2017]

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start lithium without thyroid/renal/electrolyte baseline + interaction screen
info.t: Narrow therapeutic window (target 0.6-0.8 mEq/L for cluster). NSAIDs (incl. indomethacin), thiazides, ACE-I/ARB, metronidazole, and dehydration RAISE lithium level — toxicity at >1.2, severe at >2.5. Best reserved for chronic cluster with reliable outpatient monitoring. Lithium node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a prednisone bridge more than 2-3 times per year
info.t: Cumulative steroid toxicity: AVN, cataract, osteoporosis, glucose dysregulation, mood. After 2-3 bridges in a year, switch to ONB bridge or CGRP mAb (galcanezumab) for the next bout.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a cluster patient without screening for suicidal ideation
info.t: "Suicide headache" carries the highest SI rate of any primary headache disorder. Document a safety screen, provide 988 / crisis resources, and arrange neurology follow-up within 1 week.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT counsel "alcohol only during bouts" — they must AVOID alcohol entirely during the bout
info.t: Even a single drink during an active bout reliably triggers an attack within ~30-60 min. Outside the bout, alcohol does not trigger. Same for nitrates and nitroglycerin during active bout.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start CBZ or oxcarbazepine without HLA-B*1502 screening in at-risk ancestry
info.t: Han Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese, Filipino, Malay, and Indonesian ancestry carry HLA-B*1502 at ≥10% population frequency. The allele confers a several hundred-fold elevated risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis on CBZ or oxcarbazepine (FDA boxed warning 2007). Order the test before the first dose; bridge with gabapentin or baclofen while results pending. HLA screen node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT switch CBZ-associated hyponatremia to oxcarbazepine
info.t: Oxcarbazepine causes MORE frequent and MORE severe hyponatremia than CBZ — incidence ~15-30% vs ~10% (Dong J Headache Pain 2005; Berghuis Epilepsia 2017). Stop the offending Na-lowering anticonvulsant, correct sodium with fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic, then switch to a non-Na-lowering alternative (gabapentin, baclofen, lamotrigine) with neurology input. Ladder node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give CBZ or valproate to a pregnant patient unless benefit clearly outweighs risk
info.t: CBZ (Category D) causes neural tube defects and craniofacial anomalies. Valproate is the most teratogenic anticonvulsant in clinical use. Plan the switch to baclofen / gabapentin / lamotrigine BEFORE conception with neurology input. If a pregnant patient presents on CBZ, do not abruptly discontinue (withdrawal risk) — taper under neuro guidance. Patient ed node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT escalate lamotrigine faster than the FDA-mandated schedule
info.t: Stevens-Johnson risk on lamotrigine is dose-related AND titration-rate-related. Start 25 mg daily; increase by 25 mg every 2 weeks; target 200-400 mg/d for TN. Any rash → STOP immediately. Faster titration nearly always increases the rash incidence to the point of being contraindicated. Ladder node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume primary TN in patients <40 yo, with bilateral symptoms, or with sensory deficit
info.t: Atypical features require MRI brain with contrast + dedicated FIESTA/CISS trigeminal sequences BEFORE starting CBZ — secondary TN (multiple sclerosis, tumor at cerebellopontine angle, vascular loop) requires different management. Pure V1 distribution is also uncommon for primary TN. Differential node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgical referral once AAN/EFNS refractoriness criteria are met
info.t: Refractory = failure of ≥2 first-line agents at adequate dose AND duration with disabling pain. At that point, additional medication trials cost months of severe pain, weight loss, and suicide risk. Refer to neurosurgery; let the surgical team decide between MVD, percutaneous rhizotomy, and gamma knife — do not pre-select the procedure in the ED. Surgical node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge an acute TN crisis without addressing fluid + nutrition
info.t: Severe TN reliably causes dehydration and weight loss because patients fear chewing and swallowing. Treat ED fluid + electrolyte deficits, encourage liquid nutritional supplements, and document weight if able. Patients in nutritional crisis need admission for IV bridge therapy. Patient ed node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge any new TN patient without a suicide screen
info.t: TN carries one of the highest SI rates among chronic pain syndromes. Screen explicitly, provide 988, document, and ensure neurology follow-up within 2 weeks. The Facial Pain Association (fpa-support.org) is a patient-led, well-vetted resource worth recommending.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge any thunderclap HA without imaging
info.t: Mortality from missed SAH is ~50% over 30 days. Even atypical migraineurs can present with first-thunderclap SAH. Non-contrast CT is ~98% sensitive within 6 h of onset but sensitivity drops sharply after. After 6 h or negative CT with persistent suspicion, LP for xanthochromia is the rescue test. SAH consult carries the Ottawa SAH Rule. Thunderclap node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay empiric antibiotics for imaging in suspected meningitis
info.t: Target antibiotic within 1 hour of suspicion. CT before LP is indicated when AMS, focal deficit, papilledema, immunocompromise, recent seizure, or age >60 — but that does NOT delay the empiric dose. Give antibiotics, then image, then LP. Meningitis consult. Fever node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT turn lights off or give mydriatic drops in suspected AACG
info.t: Dim light → pupillary dilation → worsened angle closure. Mydriatic drops do the same. Painful red eye + mid-dilated pupil + IOP >40 = emergent ophthalmology. Treat IOP medically while ophthalmology mobilizes. AACG consult. Eye node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust standard pulse oximetry in suspected CO toxicity
info.t: Carboxyhemoglobin reads as oxyhemoglobin on standard SpO₂. Use co-oximetry — arterial or venous blood gas with co-ox, OR a specialized SpCO finger probe. Place patient on 100% O₂ via NRB while disposition decided. CO Toxicity consult. Tox node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order routine "headache panel" labs
info.t: No defined panel. Targeted labs only — ESR/CRP for suspected GCA (age ≥50 + new HA + jaw claudication / visual / scalp tenderness / polymyalgia), CO-Hgb for exposure, β-hCG for reproductive-age females (broadens differential), tox for ingestion. Shotgun panels distract from the imaging decision. Imaging node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip fundoscopy when raised ICP is on the differential
info.t: Papilledema changes the differential immediately — IIH, CVST, mass. Document present-or-absent explicitly. Even a "fundi non-visualized — dilated eye exam deferred" note is better than silence. Sick check node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip diphenhydramine when giving Compazine
info.t: Akathisia rate with Compazine is high — diphenhydramine 25 mg IV concurrent dramatically reduces it. Skipping it leaves the patient miserable and looking for the exit. Reglan + Benadryl pairing is also standard; the akathisia rate is slightly lower with Reglan but still real. Rescue cocktail

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give opioids or butalbital combos for benign-pattern HA
info.t: Acute opioids in the ED for migraine worsen recurrence rates and accelerate medication-overuse HA. Butalbital combinations (Fioricet) carry barbiturate dependence risk. The standard parenteral cocktail (Compazine + Benadryl + Toradol + Mag + NS) outperforms opioid rescue in pain control AND prevents the downstream chronification. Rescue cocktail

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge if a new neurologic finding appeared after the cocktail
info.t: Pain that escalates differently after rescue, or any new focal deficit on the post-cocktail recheck, means the original triage missed something. Stop the discharge plan, image now, and return to time-critical exclusions. Reassess node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume primary headache in pregnancy / postpartum without targeted workup
info.t: Pregnancy and the postpartum period dramatically broaden the differential. Pre-eclampsia, CVST, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy, and cervical artery dissection are all more common. BP trend + neuro exam + low threshold for imaging (MRI without gadolinium preferred when available). HTN in Pregnancy consult. Pregnancy node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without written return precautions
info.t: The hub triage is a snapshot — patients can develop red flags hours later. Written return precautions covering first-or-worst severity, new neurologic symptom, fever or stiff neck, persistent vomiting, severe pain unresponsive to home Rx, vision change, or seizure are part of every discharge bundle. Discharge node

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the hub as a treatment playbook
info.t: The hub is a triage map. Once you commit to a phenotype, leave the hub and work the deep-dive consult — that consult holds the dosing, monitoring, and disposition criteria specific to the diagnosis. Duplicating clinical content here would silently desynchronize from the deep-dives.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT defer the pregnancy test on any female of reproductive age
info.t: Ectopic, ruptured corpus luteum, heterotopic pregnancy, and pre-eclampsia all change the workup. β-hCG is faster than the differential. Quantitative β-hCG + bedside or formal TVUS if positive. First-Trimester consult

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay AAA imaging in the older patient with back/flank pain
info.t: AAA classically presents as renal colic mimicker in age ≥50. Bedside US is ~99% sensitive for AAA presence (not for rupture, but presence + the right clinical story is enough). If unstable: OR not CT. AAA consult

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust a soft abdomen in suspected mesenteric ischemia
info.t: Pain out of proportion to exam is the classic teaching for a reason — early mesenteric ischemia has a benign abdomen with elevated lactate and risk factors (AFib, CHF, vasculopath, hypercoagulable). CTA mesenteric NOW. Delay is the lethal step. Mesenteric Ischemia consult

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold analgesia waiting for the surgeon
info.t: Multiple RCTs and SAEM/ACEP policy: appropriate analgesia does NOT obscure surgical exam findings. Patients with adequate pain control have BETTER exam reliability. Withholding opioids is a quality-of-care failure.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the ECG for epigastric pain in age ≥50
info.t: Inferior MI presents as epigastric pain ~25% of the time in older adults, diabetics, and women. ECG + troponin in the bundle for any epigastric pain or atypical risk profile. STEMI consult

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge for "constipation" without ruling out obstruction or AAA
