info.t: No-stool + abdominal pain + age ≥50 is a triple-threat that gets discharged as constipation and bounces back ruptured. Plain film or CT, vascular exam, rectal exam, and an honest reassessment of pretest probability.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgery for additional imaging in clear peritonitis
info.t: Rigid abdomen + free air on upright CXR or bedside US = OR. CT confirms a diagnosis the surgeon already needs to operate on. Image only if it changes the surgical plan, not to make the call.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the hub as a treatment playbook
info.t: The hub is a triage map. Once you commit to a phenotype, leave the hub and work the deep-dive consult — that consult holds the dosing, monitoring, and disposition criteria specific to the diagnosis.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without written return precautions
info.t: Abdominal pain dispositions miss appendicitis, ectopic, AAA, and dissection at non-trivial rates even after a reassuring ED workup. Written return precautions covering worsening pain, fever, vomiting, syncope, GI bleeding, and inability to tolerate PO are mandatory.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip β-hCG in any female of reproductive age
info.t: Ectopic pregnancy presents identically to appendicitis (RLQ pain, peritoneal signs, low-grade fever). Quantitative β-hCG before imaging strategy decisions, before antibiotics, before consenting for surgery.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgical consult for the imaging result
info.t: High-risk AAS/Alvarado + classic exam can proceed to surgical consult in parallel with imaging. Imaging waiting time is operating-room waiting time.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT default to CT in young/lean/pregnant patients
info.t: US-first protocol saves radiation in pediatric and pregnant populations. Graded-compression US has ~85% sens in trained hands. If non-diagnostic, escalate (MRI in pregnancy, CT in young adults). Anchoring on CT in everyone is a quality-of-care miss.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge equivocal imaging + ongoing pain without observation
info.t: Indeterminate CT/US ("dilated appendix, no clear inflammation") + persistent RLQ pain has a non-trivial false-negative rate. Serial exam, serial labs, admit or short-stay obs.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume antibiotic-only therapy is safe for everyone
info.t: CODA trial showed non-inferiority for uncomplicated appendicitis without appendicolith. Exclusions: perforation, abscess, appendicolith on imaging, signs of complicated appendicitis, suspected malignancy. ~30% recurrence at 1 year. Shared decision; default remains appendectomy.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT under-cover anaerobes in suspected perforation
info.t: Piperacillin-tazobactam OR ceftriaxone + metronidazole. Bowel flora coverage is non-negotiable for perforation/abscess. Single-agent ceftriaxone alone is inadequate.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the suspicion of malignancy in older patients
info.t: Adults >40 with appendicitis carry elevated risk of underlying cecal/appendiceal malignancy. Mandates interval colonoscopy follow-up after recovery. Discharge plan must include the GI/surgery referral.

Document visual acuity, pupil size/reactivity/shape, EOMs, ptosis, IOP if open globe is not suspected, red eye, trauma signs, headache/neck pain, and focused neuro exam. Emergencies: pupil-involving CN III palsy, acute painful Horner syndrome, acute angle closure, open globe, orbital compartment syndrome, and brainstem stroke.

info.h: 2. Measure in Bright and Dim Light
info.t: Measure both pupils in bright room light, then dim the room and remeasure after several seconds. Anisocoria greater in bright light means the larger pupil is abnormal. Anisocoria greater in the dark means the smaller pupil is abnormal. Same difference in light and dark, usually <1 mm, supports physiologic anisocoria if the exam is otherwise normal.

Think CN III palsy, acute angle closure, traumatic mydriasis/iris injury, pharmacologic mydriasis, or Adie tonic pupil. CN III signs, headache, pain, ptosis, diplopia, or EOM abnormality trigger emergent aneurysm imaging.
Think Horner syndrome, physiologic anisocoria, uveitis/iritis, or miotic exposure. Acute painful Horner syndrome needs same-day head and neck vascular imaging for carotid dissection.

Emergent consult/imaging for CN III palsy, painful Horner, stroke signs, acute angle closure, open globe, or serious trauma. Urgent ophtho/neuro-ophtho for new unexplained anisocoria. Discharge only when physiologic or clear pharmacologic pattern is supported by a normal eye/neuro exam and reliable return precautions.

The larger pupil is abnormal because it is not constricting normally. ED differential: CN III palsy, pharmacologic mydriasis, Adie tonic pupil, traumatic iris sphincter injury, acute angle closure, or prior ocular surgery.
The smaller pupil is abnormal because it is not dilating normally. ED differential: Horner syndrome, uveitis/iritis, miotic medication exposure, or less commonly brainstem/cavernous sinus disease.

Physiologic anisocoria is common and usually <1 mm. It should be chronic, similar on old photos if available, and paired with normal VA, EOMs, neuro exam, no ptosis, no red eye, no trauma, and no headache/neck pain.
A light/dark pattern localizes the abnormal pupil, but it does not by itself prove the cause is benign. Red flags override the pattern.

Unilateral anisocoria usually requires one-eye exposure: wrong-eye drops, diagnostic dilation, hand-to-eye transfer, leaking nebulizer mask, aerosol/spray exposure, plant toxin, cosmetic/skin product, or chemical splash. Systemic drugs usually affect both pupils; if only one pupil is abnormal, look for asymmetric topical exposure or another diagnosis.

Common causes: atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate, tropicamide, scopolamine patch transfer, ipratropium or tiotropium nebulizer/inhaler exposure, glycopyrrolate, anticholinergic hyperhidrosis wipes, Datura/jimson weed, Brugmansia/angel trumpet, belladonna/atropa, and botulinum toxin near the orbit. Pattern: isolated large poorly reactive pupil, glare/blurred near vision, normal EOMs, no ptosis, no red painful eye, and compatible exposure. An anticholinergic-blocked pupil usually will not constrict to 1% pilocarpine.

Common causes: phenylephrine or epinephrine ophthalmic drops, ocular/nasal decongestants such as oxymetazoline, naphazoline, or tetrahydrozoline, cocaine, amphetamines, ephedrine-like products, and adrenergic aerosol exposure. Pattern: mydriasis may preserve some light response because the sphincter is not fully blocked. Conjunctival blanching supports topical adrenergic exposure. CN III red flags still override the exposure story.

Common causes: pilocarpine or carbachol glaucoma drops, older cholinesterase-inhibitor miotics such as echothiophate/demecarium/physostigmine, brimonidine or apraclonidine glaucoma drops, organophosphate/carbamate pesticide or animal flea product exposure, and nerve-agent/cholinergic chemical exposure. Systemic opioids or clonidine usually cause bilateral miosis. Unilateral miosis should still trigger Horner/uveitis screening unless there is a clear one-eye exposure.

Ask specifically: eye exam or dilation today? Glaucoma drops in the patient or household? Motion-sickness patch? Nebulized bronchodilator or anticholinergic mask leak? Nasal or eye decongestant spray? Contact with plants, gardening, herbal products, or tea leaves? Pesticide/flea product splash? Cosmetics, wipes, skin medication, or occupational/veterinary medication? Was only one eye rubbed after handling the product?

Do not diagnose pharmacologic anisocoria if ptosis, diplopia, EOM abnormality, severe headache, neck/face pain, eye pain, red eye, trauma, vision loss, focal neuro findings, or acute painful Horner pattern is present. Drop testing must not delay imaging when CN III palsy or carotid dissection remains possible.

Larger pupil plus ptosis, diplopia, abnormal EOM, headache, eye pain, progressive or incomplete CN III findings: image emergently for aneurysm/compressive lesion and involve neurology/neurosurgery plus ophthalmology.

Smaller pupil plus mild ptosis/dilation lag with acute headache, neck/face pain, trauma, or neurologic symptoms: same-day CTA/MRA head and neck for carotid dissection and brainstem/cavernous sinus causes.

Halos, vomiting, cloudy cornea, fixed or mid-dilated pupil, or high IOP: treat as acute angle closure until proven otherwise. If trauma/open globe is possible, shield the eye and avoid pressure/tonometry.
If onset is unclear, exam is limited, old photos are unavailable, or drug exposure is uncertain, disposition follows the highest-risk remaining feature. Do not force a physiologic label.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT routinely give TXA for GI bleed
info.t: HALT-IT trial (n=12,009, Lancet 2020) showed TXA did NOT reduce death from bleeding (4.0% vs 4.0%; RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.82-1.18) and INCREASED venous thromboembolism (0.8% vs 0.4%; RR 1.85, 95% CI 1.15-2.98) and seizures (0.6% vs 0.4%; RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.03-2.93). The ACG 2023 lower GI bleeding guideline now makes a STRONG recommendation AGAINST antifibrinolytics in GI bleeding. Reverses prior CRASH-2 thinking. Do NOT extrapolate trauma TXA practice to GI bleed.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the rectal exam
info.t: Melena vs hematochezia vs bright red blood vs occult blood changes the source map and the urgency. The rectal exam happens in the first 5 minutes alongside vitals. A "GI bleed" without a rectal exam is a story with no data.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transfuse to Hgb 10 in stable variceal bleeding
info.t: Villanueva 2013 NEJM RCT: restrictive transfusion (Hgb trigger 7) had lower mortality and rebleeding than liberal (Hgb 9) in upper GI bleeding, especially cirrhotics. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens variceal bleeding.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT chase a normotensive BP in active bleeding
info.t: Permissive hypotension (SBP 90-100 mmHg) until source control is current EAST guidance for hemorrhagic shock — pushing BP to 120 with crystalloid blows clots off, dilutes coagulation factors, and worsens outcomes. Blood, not crystalloid; lower BP target until endoscopy/IR.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget ceftriaxone in cirrhotic UGIB
info.t: AASLD Class I rec: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily in any cirrhotic with UGIB reduces mortality (NNT ~22 for mortality benefit). Bacterial infection precipitates rebleeding. Antibiotic prophylaxis is non-negotiable in this population. Duration: the 2017 AASLD guidance and ESGE allow up to 7 days; AASLD 2024 caps it at up to 5 days and stops it once bleeding is controlled and there is no active infection. Ceftriaxone is preferred over oral norfloxacin in advanced cirrhosis and in settings with high quinolone resistance.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discount the AEF herald bleed
info.t: Prior aortic graft + GI bleed = aortoenteric fistula until proven otherwise, even if the bleed seems small ("herald bleed"). 30-50% mortality. CTA emergent, vascular surgery STAT. Do NOT scope first — bleeding into the duodenum from a graft erosion is not a GI problem.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT hold anti-motility / opiate agents in IBD flare with bloody diarrhea
info.t: Loperamide / opioids in severe UC can precipitate toxic megacolon. Anti-motility agents are CONTRAINDICATED in suspected IBD flare with bloody diarrhea. Use Truelove-Witts criteria, hospitalize severe disease, IV steroids early.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume hematochezia is lower in the shocked patient
info.t: 10-15% of hematochezia presentations are brisk UPPER GI bleeds (rapid transit). In a shocked patient with hematochezia, the upper source must be ruled out (NG lavage is no longer recommended; EGD before colonoscopy is the safer pathway).

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay anticoagulation reversal for "confirming" the bleed
info.t: In any actively bleeding anticoagulated patient with hemodynamic compromise, reversal happens in parallel with resus — not after confirming source. 4F-PCC for VKA and for FXa inhibitors (andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US), idarucizumab for dabigatran. Time to reversal = time saved.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the hub as the treatment playbook
info.t: The hub triages. Dosing, monitoring, and disposition for each phenotype live in the deep-dive consults (UGIB, LGIB, anticoag-reversal, massive-transfusion, AAA, IBD-flare, mesenteric). Once you commit to a phenotype, leave the hub and work the consult.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give ceftriaxone empirically for Pakistan/Iraq travelers
info.t: XDR Typhi (Klemm 2018; Yousafzai 2019) is endemic in Pakistan since 2016 and confirmed in Iraq. It carries plasmid-mediated resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolones, AND third-generation cephalosporins. Ceftriaxone will fail. Default to azithromycin (uncomplicated) or meropenem (complicated). Use the XDR Risk calculator to stratify.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on Widal serology
info.t: Widal has poor sensitivity and specificity (cross-reacts with malaria, dengue, other Salmonella; false negatives in early disease and with prior vaccination). Blood culture is the diagnostic standard. Do not start or withhold antibiotics based on Widal alone.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the malaria smear
info.t: Any febrile returned traveler from a malaria-endemic region needs malaria thick-and-thin smears (or RDT) regardless of typhoid suspicion. Co-infection is common; missed P. falciparum kills faster than missed typhoid. Send 3 negative smears over 24 h before excluding malaria clinically.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ciprofloxacin as empiric monotherapy
info.t: >85% of global Typhi isolates carry gyrA mutations conferring fluoroquinolone resistance (decreased susceptibility or full resistance). Even "susceptible" isolates by old breakpoints have clinical failure rates >30%. Fluoroquinolones are no longer first-line. Reserve only when susceptibility is confirmed and no alternatives.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay dexamethasone in severe disease
info.t: Hoffman 1984 NEJM RCT: high-dose dexamethasone (3 mg/kg load, then 1 mg/kg q6h ×8 doses) cut mortality from 55.6% to 9.5% in severe typhoid with shock, stupor, or coma. The benefit is well-replicated. Give in parallel with antibiotics, not after.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss intestinal perforation in weeks 3-4
info.t: Perforation peaks at weeks 3-4 of illness and carries 10-30% mortality. Sudden worsening abdominal pain, peritonism, free air on imaging, or unexplained shock in a known typhoid case = surgical emergency. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast, broad-spectrum antibiotics (add anaerobic coverage), urgent OR. Do NOT manage non-operatively.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without confirmed follow-up
info.t: Outpatient azithromycin is reasonable for uncomplicated typhoid but only with reliable <48 h reassessment. Defervescence takes 3-5 days even with appropriate antibiotics — slow response is normal. Premature switch to a different antibiotic for "not responding" is a common error. Counsel patients on expected timeline + return precautions (worsening pain, bleeding, AMS, intolerance of PO).

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget the chronic carrier state
info.t: 1-5% of patients become chronic biliary carriers, shedding Typhi for >1 year. Stool cultures at 1, 2, and 3 months post-treatment confirm clearance. Persistent carriers need ciprofloxacin ×4 weeks or cholecystectomy (Typhoid Mary). This is a public health issue, not just an individual one — high-risk occupations (food handler, healthcare) require clearance before return to work.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip notifiable disease reporting
info.t: Typhoid is reportable in all 50 states. Report to county/state health department promptly. Failure to report delays contact tracing and source identification — most US cases are travel-acquired but secondary household transmission occurs.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on typhoid without ruling out parallel diagnoses
info.t: The Endemic Regions calculator surfaces the parallel febrile-traveler differential — malaria, dengue, rickettsial disease, leptospirosis, viral hepatitis, amebic liver abscess, HIV seroconversion, TB. Workup is broad: malaria smear, blood cultures, hepatitis serologies, HIV, RUQ US if hepatomegaly. Do not narrow until data support narrowing.

info.h: Do NOT skip the universal labs
info.t: APAP and salicylate levels are mandatory on every unknown ingestion, even when the patient denies them. They are common, treatable, and silent. Missing them is the most common preventable bad outcome in tox.

info.h: Do NOT trust the urine drug screen
info.t: UDS misses fentanyl analogs, designer benzos, synthetic opioids, GHB, and ketamine. It false-positives on poppy seeds, certain antibiotics, and many psych meds. It rarely changes management in the first 6 hours. Do not let it drive treatment.

info.h: Do NOT invert the order: resus, decon, antidote
info.t: Stabilize physiology before charcoal. Charcoal without an airway plan is aspiration pneumonia and a worse trajectory. Antidotes come third - except when they are the resus itself (atropine, glucagon, calcium, bicarb).

Titrate to respiratory effort, not consciousness. Rapid full reversal triggers precipitated opioid withdrawal, pulmonary edema, and agitation. >70% of street fentanyl carries xylazine - naloxone will not fix the sedation, ventilate the patient.

info.h: Do NOT intubate salicylate unless absolutely required
info.t: Salicylate patients are breathing off acid. Apnea + paralysis = catastrophic acidemia. If you must intubate, match minute ventilation, induce with ketamine, and consider rocuronium short-burst with rapid sedation depth.

info.h: Do NOT give physostigmine with QRS prolongation
info.t: Anticholinergic toxicity reverses with physostigmine, but TCA and many other agents have mixed anticholinergic + sodium-channel blockade. Physostigmine in a wide-QRS patient can cause asystole. Confirm narrow QRS and pure toxidrome.

info.h: Do NOT medically clear for psych without trajectory
info.t: Staggered APAP, sustained-release CCB, lithium, and salicylate look benign early and decompensate late. Repeat labs at the observation window for the agent and document a clear trajectory before psych transfer.

Regional Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) has live access to outbreak data, antidote stock locations, dosing for rare agents, and tox consult. They will call you back faster than the patient deteriorates.

info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Vitals: tachy, HTN, hyperthermic, tachypneic. Pupils: mydriasis (reactive). Skin: diaphoretic. Mental status: agitated, paranoid, hyperalert. Bowel sounds: normal or increased. Agents: cocaine, methamphetamine, MDMA, bath salts, PCP, theophylline, caffeine overdose, decongestants. Treatment: benzos + cooling. Avoid pure beta-blockers (unopposed alpha).

info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Vitals: tachy, mildly hypertensive, hyperthermic. Pupils: mydriasis (often poorly reactive). Skin: dry, red, flushed. Mental status: delirium, "mad as a hatter", picking at the air, mumbling. Bowel sounds: absent, urinary retention. Agents: diphenhydramine, atropine, scopolamine, TCAs (mixed picture), antipsychotics, jimson weed, antiparkinson agents. Treatment: benzos + cooling + Foley. Physostigmine only with narrow QRS and pure toxidrome. Mnemonic: hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask.

info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Vitals: brady (early), then tachy late. Pupils: miosis. Skin: diaphoretic. Mental status: confused, seizures, coma. Bowel sounds: hyperactive, defecation/urination/emesis. Agents: organophosphates, carbamates, nerve agents, pilocarpine, certain mushrooms, nicotine. Treatment: decontaminate (PPE!), atropine to dry secretions (DOUBLE q5 min), pralidoxime infusion for OP. Mnemonic: SLUDGE-BBB (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramping, Emesis, Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia) and DUMBELS.

info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Vitals: tachy, HTN, hyperthermic, hyperreflexic. Pupils: mydriasis. Skin: diaphoretic, flushed. Mental status: agitated, restless, anxious. Bowel sounds: hyperactive. Distinguishing finding: clonus, especially lower extremities, and inducible/sustained clonus. Tremor, hyperreflexia. Agents: SSRIs + MAOIs, SSRIs + tramadol/linezolid/methylene blue, fentanyl + serotonergic, MDMA, dextromethorphan in serotonergic patient. Treatment: stop agents, benzos, cooling, cyproheptadine 12 mg PO then 2 mg q2h for moderate-severe.

info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Vitals: brady, hypotensive, hypoventilating, hypothermic. Pupils: miosis (PINPOINT). Skin: normal or cool. Mental status: stuporous, coma. Bowel sounds: decreased. Agents: heroin, fentanyl + xylazine, morphine, oxycodone, methadone, tramadol, diphenoxylate (peds). Treatment: ventilate, titrate naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV to respirations, watch for renarcotization and concurrent xylazine sedation (will not reverse with naloxone).

info.h: Toxidrome look-alikes worth a separate mention
info.pt: Unknown Ingestion - Toxidromes at a Glance
info.t: Sedative-hypnotic: somnolence, slurred speech, ataxia, near-normal vitals. Agents: benzos, barbs, GHB, zolpidem. Sodium-channel blocker: wide QRS, hypotension, seizures, AMS. Agents: TCA, bupropion, diphenhydramine in massive dose, cocaine. Treat with bicarb regardless of substance. Methylxanthine: tachy, GI distress, agitation, severe hypokalemia, seizures. Agents: theophylline, caffeine. Withdrawal: mirror of the chronic toxidrome - opioid withdrawal looks like cholinergic-light; benzo/ETOH withdrawal looks like sympathomimetic.
Any acute chest pain needs an ECG acquired and reviewed within 10 minutes. Repeat ECGs matter when pain changes or the story remains concerning.

info.h: Do NOT anticoagulate or lyse a possible dissection
info.t: Tearing pain, pulse/BP deficit, neuro deficit, severe HTN, or back pain should trigger dissection posture before routine ACS antithrombotics.

info.h: Do NOT call a resolved-pain Wellens patient low risk
info.t: Pain resolution is typical in Wellens. Stress testing can precipitate infarction. Use the Wellens consult and urgent cardiology pathway.

info.h: Do NOT wait for imaging in tension pneumothorax
info.t: Hypotension or peri-arrest physiology with unilateral absent breath sounds is a clinical decompression diagnosis.

info.h: Do NOT discharge after severe post-emesis chest pain without considering rupture
info.t: Boerhaave syndrome is uncommon but high mortality when missed. Toxic appearance, subcutaneous air, pleural effusion, or severe pain after retching should move to NPO, antibiotics, CT contrast strategy, and surgery.

info.h: Do NOT let a negative first troponin override a concerning story
info.t: High-sensitivity troponin pathways are serial risk tools. Dynamic ECG, recurrent pain, unstable physiology, or high-risk story still needs observation or admission.

info.h: Do NOT trust pulse ox alone
info.pt: Shortness of Breath Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Work of breathing, mental status, ventilation, waveform quality, and co-oximetry context matter. CO and methemoglobinemia can fool standard pulse oximetry.

info.h: Do NOT delay NIV in the right phenotype
info.pt: Shortness of Breath Hub - Do NOT
info.t: COPD hypercapnic failure and hypertensive pulmonary edema often improve rapidly with NIV. Waiting until exhaustion makes intubation more dangerous.

info.h: Do NOT flood undifferentiated dyspnea reflexively
info.pt: Shortness of Breath Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Shock needs perfusion, but pulmonary edema, RV failure, and renal failure can worsen with blind fluids. Reassess lungs, heart, IVC, and perfusion repeatedly.

info.h: Do NOT send unstable dyspnea to CT unprepared
info.pt: Shortness of Breath Hub - Do NOT
info.t: If the patient may crash on the scanner table, stabilize airway, oxygenation, pressors, and procedure plan first.

info.h: Do NOT treat anaphylaxis with antihistamines first
info.pt: Shortness of Breath Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Airway, bronchospasm, or shock from anaphylaxis is epinephrine-first disease. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

info.pt: Altered Mental Status Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Glucose is immediate, reversible, and can mimic stroke or psychiatric disease. Check it early and recheck after treatment.

info.h: Do NOT call it psychiatric before delirium/mimics are addressed
info.pt: Altered Mental Status Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Abnormal vitals, altered cognition, new onset, intoxication, withdrawal, infection, trauma, metabolic disease, or neurologic findings all require medical workup.

info.h: Do NOT use urine drug screen as the resuscitation test
info.pt: Altered Mental Status Hub - Do NOT
info.t: ECG, glucose, ventilation, acid-base status, temperature, and targeted tox labs change immediate care more reliably.

info.h: Do NOT delay CNS infection treatment for CT or LP
info.pt: Altered Mental Status Hub - Do NOT
info.t: When meningitis/encephalitis is plausible, give empiric therapy after blood cultures if possible. Imaging and LP follow without delaying treatment.

info.h: Do NOT discharge persistent unexplained AMS
info.pt: Altered Mental Status Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Persistent AMS is not a discharge diagnosis. Admit, observe, image, or obtain EEG/LP based on the remaining differential.

info.h: Do NOT skip glucose, ECG, or potassium thinking
info.t: Hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia/hypokalemia, ischemia, dysrhythmia, and tox ECG patterns can all present as weakness and can change management immediately.

info.h: Do NOT discharge inability to walk
info.t: Inability to stand or ambulate at baseline after treatment is a high-risk functional finding, even when the complaint sounds nonspecific.

info.h: Do NOT let normal SpO2 clear neuromuscular respiratory risk
info.t: GBS and myasthenia can fail by ventilation, cough, secretion handling, and bulbar weakness before oxygen saturation falls.

info.h: Do NOT call it deconditioning until localization is addressed
info.t: Repeat the neuro exam after fluids, glucose correction, analgesia, or rest. Look for focality, reflex changes, bulbar findings, and gait failure.

info.h: Do NOT overtrust urine drug screen
info.t: Medication list, ECG, acid-base status, glucose, and tox levels drive immediate care more reliably than UDS.

info.h: Do NOT sort dizziness by word choice alone
info.t: Patients use vertigo, dizziness, lightheadedness, imbalance, and weakness inconsistently. Timing, triggers, objective gait, ocular motor findings, neuro exam, ECG, glucose, and vitals are safer.

info.h: Do NOT use HINTS outside acute vestibular syndrome
info.t: HINTS is for continuous AVS with spontaneous nystagmus and a trained examiner. It is not a screening test for vague dizziness, resolved spells, BPPV, presyncope, or patients without nystagmus.

info.h: Do NOT clear posterior stroke with a normal CT
info.t: Non-contrast CT can miss early posterior fossa ischemia. Central ocular signs, severe truncal ataxia, focal neurologic findings, dissection features, or inability to walk need stroke imaging/neurology thinking even after CT.

info.h: Do NOT discharge inability to walk
info.t: Unsafe gait or inability to ambulate at baseline is an objective high-risk finding. Reassess after treatment and document the walking exam before discharge.
Hypoglycemia, dysrhythmia, ACS, bleeding/anemia, sepsis, CO toxicity, overdose, and medication effects can present as dizziness. Glucose and ECG are low-cost, high-yield tests in unclear cases.

info.h: Do NOT rely on antipyretics in true hyperthermia
info.t: Acetaminophen and NSAIDs target a raised set point. In heat illness, toxidromes, NMS, and thyroid storm the set point is normal - they do not work, and NSAIDs add renal/GI/coagulopathy risk. Active cooling is the treatment.

info.h: Do NOT trust a peripheral temperature
info.t: Oral and axillary temps underestimate core. A normal peripheral reading does not exclude life-threatening core hyperthermia. Measure rectal/esophageal/bladder temp.

info.h: Do NOT wait for the diagnosis to start cooling
info.t: Core >40C with AMS is a cooling emergency. Begin active cooling within minutes while the cause-specific workup runs.

info.h: Do NOT give succinylcholine when rhabdomyolysis is likely
info.t: If paralysis is needed for intractable hyperthermia with rigidity, use rocuronium/vecuronium. Succinylcholine risks lethal hyperkalemia in rhabdo.

Cyproheptadine (serotonin syndrome), dantrolene/bromocriptine (NMS), and thionamide+beta-blocker+iodine (thyroid storm) are not interchangeable. Bromocriptine is contraindicated in serotonin syndrome. Confirm the diagnosis first.

info.h: Do NOT send an airway-risk neck infection to CT without a plan
info.t: Drooling, stridor, muffled voice, trismus, floor-of-mouth elevation, or severe swelling should trigger ENT/anesthesia/airway planning before supine CT.

info.h: Do NOT miss dissection in posterior neck pain
info.t: Posterior headache/neck pain plus Horner, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, manipulation, minor trauma, or strangulation needs CTA consideration.
Gait change, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, bilateral symptoms, or bowel/bladder symptoms are cord-level warnings.

info.h: Do NOT delay meningitis therapy for CT/LP logistics
info.t: Blood cultures are useful when they do not delay therapy. Antibiotics and acyclovir are time-sensitive when CNS infection is plausible.

info.h: Do NOT recommend neck manipulation when dangerous causes remain possible
info.t: Avoid manipulation advice when dissection, fracture/instability, myelopathy, or spine infection is still on the table.

info.h: Do NOT miss early cauda equina
info.t: Ask specifically about urinary retention/hesitancy, saddle sensation, bilateral sciatica, progressive leg weakness, and bowel dysfunction. Pain response does not clear cauda.

info.h: Do NOT require fever for spinal epidural abscess
info.t: SEA can present without fever. IVDU, bacteremia, immunosuppression, diabetes, recent spine procedure, or focal tenderness should raise suspicion.

info.h: Do NOT call abrupt vascular back pain musculoskeletal
info.t: Older vascular-risk patient plus abrupt severe pain, syncope, hypotension, abdominal pain, or pulse deficit should trigger AAA/dissection posture.

info.h: Do NOT image uncomplicated mechanical back pain reflexively
info.t: Absent red flags, advanced imaging rarely helps acute low back pain and can mislead. Image when results change management.

info.h: Do NOT discharge inability to ambulate safely
info.t: A patient who cannot walk at baseline after ED treatment needs observation, admission, imaging, or a safer mobility plan.

info.h: Use This For Radicular Back Pain
info.t: Use this card when the patient has radiating leg pain, numbness, paresthesias, positive straight-leg raise, or focal distal weakness after cauda equina, infection, fracture/cancer, and vascular causes have been screened.
Pain/sensory: anterior thigh, medial knee, and medial leg. Motor: knee extension / quadriceps weakness. Bedside screen: squat and rise. Reflex: patellar reflex diminished.

Pain/sensory: lateral leg, dorsum of foot, and great toe region. Motor: great toe extension and ankle/foot dorsiflexion weakness. Bedside screen: heel walking. Reflex: no consistently reliable bedside deep tendon reflex; medial hamstring may help when available.
Pain/sensory: posterior leg, lateral foot, and plantar foot. Motor: plantar flexion of foot/great toe weakness. Bedside screen: toe walking. Reflex: Achilles reflex diminished.

Document side, pain distribution, sensory loss, motor strength, gait screen, reflexes, straight-leg raise/crossed straight-leg raise, and whether bowel/bladder/saddle/progressive bilateral symptoms were absent or present.

- L4, L5, and S1 patterns overlap; localize by clustering pain, sensory, motor, reflex, and provocative-test findings. - L5 is commonly tested by great toe extension and heel walking because a reliable reflex is often absent. - New or progressive motor deficit, inability to ambulate, bilateral symptoms, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, fever/infection risk, cancer risk, or trauma should move back to the red-flag pathway. - Imaging decisions should follow red flags and management impact, not the dermatome map alone.

info.h: Do NOT delay steroids for GCA waiting on ESR/CRP or biopsy
info.t: In age >50 with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, or PMR, give high-dose IV methylprednisolone immediately. Untreated GCA has a ~30% rate of contralateral blindness. Biopsy remains valid within a short window after starting steroids.

info.h: Do NOT image pituitary apoplexy before giving stress-dose steroids
info.t: Apoplexy is adrenal crisis until proven otherwise. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before MRI; patients crash hemodynamically during imaging delays.

info.h: Do NOT anchor on the eye when the pattern is cortical
info.t: Bilateral loss with altered mental status, severe hypertension, or no RAPD points to PRES, occipital stroke, or methanol, not an isolated optic nerve. Methanol needs gap workup and antidote, not ophthalmology alone.

info.h: Do NOT order thick-cut CT for traumatic optic neuropathy
info.t: Thick cuts miss canal fractures. Request thin-cut (1 mm) bone-algorithm CT of the face and orbits, and get neurosurgery/oculoplastics involved early.

info.h: Do NOT discharge unexplained persistent optic-nerve vision loss
info.t: A new RAPD with central scotoma and color desaturation is optic nerve until proven otherwise and needs a diagnosis or an urgent neuro-ophthalmology/stroke plan before discharge.

Concentric (circular) mucosal rings protrude through the anus, with a palpable sulcus (groove) between the prolapse and the anal verge because the full bowel wall has telescoped out. This is the lesion this consult is built for.
Radial folds (spokes of a wheel), no sulcus, often with visibly engorged hemorrhoidal columns. Usually reducible with gentle pressure and rarely strangulates. Same edema-reduction principles apply.

Children most often have mucosal prolapse, usually benign and self-limited. A finger that passes into a sulcus alongside the mass suggests intussusception presenting at the anus rather than simple prolapse.

Type guides aggressiveness of follow-up: full-thickness prolapse needs colorectal referral and (for new-onset/age >50) colonoscopy to exclude a lead point or malignancy; isolated hemorrhoidal prolapse is managed with constipation control and hemorrhoid care.

info.h: Do NOT reduce nonviable or ruptured prolapse
info.t: Necrosis, gangrene, strangulation, peritonitis, instability, or a ruptured prolapse with eviscerated bowel is a surgical emergency. Reducing dead bowel or a perforation into the abdomen is harmful. Keep eviscerated bowel moist and call surgery.

info.h: Do NOT force an edematous prolapse
info.t: Edema, not anatomy, usually blocks reduction. Relieve it first with the granulated-sugar technique (10-15 min dwell) and good sphincter relaxation. Forceful pushing risks mucosal injury and rupture.

info.h: Do NOT skip analgesia / sphincter relaxation
info.t: A tense sphincter and pain defeat reduction. A perianal block plus light sedation frequently allows reduction that pressure alone could not.

info.h: Do NOT discharge new-onset prolapse without a plan
info.t: New full-thickness prolapse, age >50, bleeding, weight loss, or change in bowel habits warrants colonoscopy to exclude a lead point or malignancy, plus colorectal referral - reduction is only temporizing.

info.h: Do NOT forget the pediatric cause
info.t: In children, look for the driver: constipation/straining (most common) and cystic fibrosis (prolapse can be the presenting sign - low threshold for sweat chloride).

Complete obstruction: the patient cannot manage secretions (drooling, cannot swallow saliva). Aspiration risk. Also emergent: any esophageal button battery or sharp/pointed object (use the GI Foreign Body pathway).
Food bolus without complete obstruction (partial - can still swallow saliva). Endoscopy within 24 hours; do not let it drift past the 24-hour mark.
A food bolus should NOT remain impacted beyond 24 hours regardless of symptoms. Prolonged mucosal contact causes pressure necrosis, ulceration, and rising perforation risk.
Pharmacologic agents (glucagon) are low-yield adjuncts. In complete obstruction, arrange endoscopy immediately rather than waiting to see if a drug works.

info.h: Do NOT use papain / meat tenderizer
info.t: Proteolytic enzymes (papain) are contraindicated - associated with esophageal perforation and severe mucosal injury. This is a historical practice that causes harm.

info.h: Do NOT push or give pharmacology when perforation is suspected
info.t: Crepitus, severe chest/back pain, fever, or sepsis = suspected perforation. NPO, water-soluble (not barium) contrast CT/esophagram, antibiotics, and emergent surgery/GI. Glucagon, effervescent agents, and forceful push are all contraindicated.

info.h: Do NOT use effervescent agents in complete obstruction
info.t: Gas-forming agents trapped above a complete block raise intraluminal pressure and perforation risk.

info.h: Do NOT leave a bolus impacted beyond 24 hours
info.t: Prolonged contact causes pressure necrosis, ulceration, and perforation. Complete obstruction needs endoscopy within ~6 hours; any bolus within 24 hours.

info.h: Do NOT skip the EoE biopsy
info.t: Eosinophilic esophagitis is the leading cause of food impaction in young men and recurrent impactions. Obtain >=6 esophageal biopsies at the index endoscopy even if the mucosa looks normal, and start a PPI.

info.h: Do NOT miss a button battery hiding behind food
info.t: A button battery in the esophagus causes liquefactive necrosis within hours and is a same-hour emergency. Confirm the impaction is truly soft food; route dangerous objects to the GI Foreign Body pathway.

info.h: Do NOT accept "I lost vision in my left eye" without covering the good eye
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Patients routinely lateralize a homonymous hemifield defect to one eye. Cover each eye separately. If the deficit is still present when the unaffected eye is covered, this is a retrochiasmal/occipital process and belongs on the brain-stroke pathway, not the eye pathway.

info.h: Do NOT wait for perfect fundoscopy to activate a vascular pathway
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Early CRAO/TMVL can be subtle and ED fundoscopy is imperfect. Sudden painless monocular loss needs ophthalmology/stroke thinking based on history and exam.

info.h: Do NOT treat CRAO with ocular massage or anterior chamber paracentesis
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: The 2021 AHA/ASA scientific statement found no evidence that conservative maneuvers (ocular massage, paracentesis, IOP-lowering agents, hemodilution) improve outcomes and noted they may be harmful; pooled recovery with these measures (7.4%) was lower than untreated natural history (17.7%). CRAO is an acute ischemic stroke: activate the stroke pathway. Two randomized trials of IV thrombolysis (THEIA 2025, TenCRAOS 2026) were negative, so thrombolysis is a shared-decision consideration at a stroke center, not a default.

info.h: Do NOT treat suspected endophthalmitis with IV antibiotics alone
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Definitive therapy is emergent vitreous tap plus INTRAVITREAL antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime) by ophthalmology. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study found systemic antibiotics conferred no benefit. Ordering IV antibiotics and waiting for a morning consult is a vision-losing delay.

info.h: Do NOT miss GCA in age >=50
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Vision symptoms plus headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR, diplopia, or elevated ESR/CRP should prompt empiric steroids when suspicion is high.

info.h: Do NOT put pressure on a possible open globe
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: No tonometry, no ocular ultrasound, no patch pressure. Use a rigid shield, antiemetic, analgesia, NPO, CT orbit, and ophthalmology.

info.h: Do NOT call a painful red eye conjunctivitis until IOP and cornea/anterior chamber fit
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: AACG, keratitis, uveitis, endophthalmitis, and orbital processes can threaten sight.

info.h: Do NOT discharge unexplained persistent vision loss
info.pt: Monocular Vision Loss Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Persistent monocular loss needs an actionable diagnosis or an urgent specialist/stroke plan.

info.h: Do NOT treat airway-risk dental infection as a simple toothache
info.t: Drooling, voice change, trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth firmness, tongue elevation, or neck swelling can become an airway emergency.

info.h: Do NOT prescribe antibiotics for uncomplicated pulpitis by reflex
info.t: ADA guidance recommends analgesia and definitive dental treatment for most uncomplicated toothache/pulpitis without systemic involvement.

info.h: Do NOT use opioids as the default dental pain plan
info.t: NSAIDs with acetaminophen are first-line for most acute dental pain when safe. Dental blocks are often high-yield.
Abscess and odontogenic infection need drainage, extraction, root canal, or dental procedure when indicated. Medication alone is often temporary.

info.h: Do NOT ignore missing tooth fragments
info.t: If a tooth or fragment is unaccounted for after trauma, consider aspiration or embedded soft-tissue fragment.

1. Airway/deep infection first: voice change, drooling, stridor, floor-of-mouth elevation, severe trismus, dysphagia, neck swelling, toxicity, immunocompromise, or rapidly progressive swelling -> airway-capable room, OMFS/ENT, antibiotics, and CT only after airway safety. 2. Active bleeding: identify the socket, suction, remove loose clot only if needed for visualization, direct socket pressure, local hemostatic packing, suture if needed, and topical TXA for persistent mucosal/socket bleeding. 3. Day 2-5 severe empty-socket pain: dry socket / alveolar osteitis. Treat pain, gentle irrigation, dental dressing/follow-up. No routine antibiotics unless cellulitis, fever, purulence, or systemic ri

• Put light, suction, gauze, topical anesthetic/local block, and dental box supplies at bedside. • Ask: extraction date, tooth/site, surgeon/dentist, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, liver disease, renal disease, platelet/coagulation history, antibiotics already started, smoking, vigorous rinsing/spitting/straw use. • Examine: socket clot, active bleeding point, exposed bone, purulence, vestibular swelling, floor of mouth, tongue elevation, trismus, dysphagia, voice, facial/neck swelling, maxillary sinus symptoms. • Choose the lane: bleeding, dry socket, infection, sinus communication, medication issue, or routine post-op course. • Disposition requires a concrete dental/OMFS plan, pain control,

• PPE, good light/headlamp, Yankauer suction, emesis basin. • Dental mirror, cotton pliers/forceps, irrigation syringe, saline. • 2x2 gauze, dental rolls, cotton rolls. Black tea bag backup if supplies are limited. • Topical anesthetic plus local anesthetic with epinephrine when safe. • Needle/syringe for block or local infiltration.

• Oxidized cellulose/Surgicel. • Absorbable gelatin sponge/Gelfoam. • Collagen plug if stocked. • Topical thrombin if stocked. • Tranexamic acid for soaked gauze/dental roll. • 3-0 or 4-0 chromic gut or silk, needle driver, pickups, scissors. • Hemostat and suture scissors.

• Saline irrigation syringe. • Dental block supplies. • Eugenol-containing or medicated dry-socket dressing if stocked. • Analgesia plan: NSAID plus acetaminophen first line when safe. • Dental follow-up instructions. ED dressing is a bridge, not definitive care.

info.h: Do Not Do With the Dental Box
info.t: • Do not pack so much material that the patient cannot bite pressure directly over the socket. • Do not keep checking every few minutes. Direct pressure only works if uninterrupted. • Do not aggressively curette a dry socket. • Do not probe or forcefully irrigate a suspected oroantral communication. • Do not reverse anticoagulation reflexively for controlled dental bleeding.

info.pt: Topical TXA for Dental Socket Bleeding
info.t: • Use tranexamic acid oral solution 500 mg/5 mL, or injectable TXA 100 mg/mL placed on gauze/dental roll when oral solution is unavailable. • Fold gauze or dental roll into a small firm plug that sits directly over the socket. • Soak the plug with TXA, place it over the bleeding socket, and have the patient bite continuously for 20-30 minutes. • Repeat once if bleeding improves but persists. • If still bleeding, combine with socket packing such as Surgicel/Gelfoam/collagen plug and suture/figure-of-eight when appropriate.

info.pt: Topical TXA for Dental Socket Bleeding
info.t: • Persistent oozing after direct pressure. • Anticoagulant or antiplatelet patients when local control is preferred. • Mucosal/socket bleeding where clot keeps lysing in saliva. • Bridge while arranging dental/OMFS help for refractory bleeding.

info.pt: Topical TXA for Dental Socket Bleeding
info.t: • TXA is an adjunct. It does not replace identifying the socket, direct pressure, packing, or suture when needed. • Avoid swallowing large amounts of TXA solution. • Escalate if brisk bleeding, hemodynamic instability, airway contamination, expanding hematoma, or inability to maintain pressure. • Check local policy/formulary for available concentration and route.

• NSAID plus acetaminophen is first-line for most acute dental pain when safe. • Consider dental block for severe pain or dry socket bridge. • Avoid routine opioid-first plans. Use brief rescue only when first-line therapy is unsafe or inadequate and follow-up is concrete.

• Do not use antibiotics for dry socket alone or uncomplicated post-extraction pain. • Use antibiotics when cellulitis/spreading infection, fever/systemic signs, purulence with surrounding cellulitis, immunocompromise, or deep space concern is present. • Antibiotics are adjuncts. Dental/OMFS source control is still required for abscess or infected extraction site.

• Local hemostasis first for most dental bleeding. • Do not reflexively stop or reverse anticoagulants for controlled socket bleeding. • Check INR for warfarin patients with significant bleeding or if status is unknown. • Escalate reversal decisions only for major bleeding, hemodynamic compromise, airway risk, or bleeding not controlled with local measures.

• Recent maxillary molar or premolar extraction. • Air, fluid, or bubbling through the socket. • Unilateral maxillary sinus pressure, foul drainage, or fluid entering nose/mouth. • Visible socket communication or large bony defect. • Recurrent bleeding or pain after posterior maxillary extraction.

• Do not aggressively probe the socket to prove the communication. • Avoid forceful irrigation if the communication is suspected. • Look for infection, retained root fragment, facial swelling, and systemic illness. • Discuss with OMFS/dentist for closure timing and follow-up urgency. • Consider imaging when retained fragment, facial fracture, deep infection, or uncertain anatomy changes management.

• No nose blowing. • Sneeze with mouth open. • No straws, smoking, forceful spitting, or vigorous rinsing. • Soft diet and head elevation. • Return for fever, worsening facial swelling, purulent drainage, uncontrolled bleeding, or inability to swallow/handle secretions.

Accomplishes: Turns gauze from a mouth sponge into a true pressure plug directly over the bleeding socket. How to: Fold damp gauze or a dental roll into a compact plug, seat it directly over the extraction socket, and have the patient bite continuously for 30-60 minutes. Do not let the patient peek every few minutes.

Accomplishes: Concentrates antifibrinolytic medication exactly where saliva keeps breaking down clot. How to: Soak a dental roll or gauze plug with TXA, place it directly over the socket, and have the patient bite continuously for 20-30 minutes. Repeat or combine with Surgicel/Gelfoam and suture if needed.

Accomplishes: Gives a low-tech pressure/tannin adjunct when dental supplies are limited. How to: Moisten a black tea bag, wrap it in gauze if needed, place it over the socket, and have the patient bite for 20-30 minutes. Use as backup only, not as definitive care for brisk bleeding.

info.h: Dry Socket: Irrigate, Do Not Curette
info.t: Accomplishes: Removes debris without stripping fragile socket tissue or worsening pain. How to: Use gentle saline irrigation, dental block/analgesia, and dental dressing/follow-up when available. Avoid aggressive scraping of the socket.

info.h: Sinus Communication: Do Not Prove It
info.t: Accomplishes: Avoids enlarging a suspected oroantral communication. How to: If posterior maxillary extraction symptoms suggest sinus communication, avoid probing and forceful irrigation. Give sinus precautions and arrange dental/OMFS follow-up.

info.h: N95 Nose-Bridge Splint for an Avulsed Tooth
info.t: Accomplishes: Stabilizes a reimplanted avulsed or subluxed permanent tooth in the ED when no dental splint kit is on hand — a temporizing bridge to the dentist. How to: 1. Time matters — reimplant a permanent tooth as fast as possible (viability drops sharply after ~30–60 min). 2. Lightly rinse the tooth and socket with saline; pat dry. 3. Reimplant the tooth into correct anatomic position. 4. Bend the pliable metal nose-bridge wire from an N95 mask (or a non-rebreather) to span the target tooth plus one adjacent tooth on each side; cut and round the edges. 5. Apply 2-octyl cyanoacrylate (tissue adhesive) to the inner splint and the buccal surfaces, bonding the splint across the teeth. 6. Wa

info.h: Use Photos as Context, Not Diagnosis
info.t: The photo is included as a general extraction reference. Post-extraction ED diagnosis still comes from timing and exam: active socket bleeding, severe day 2-5 empty-socket pain suggesting dry socket, cellulitis/purulence suggesting infection, or posterior maxillary symptoms suggesting oroantral communication.

info.h: Do NOT call it psychiatric before glucose, vitals, attention, tox, and neuro red flags
info.pt: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Do NOT
info.t: New psychosis is a symptom. Delirium, tox, withdrawal, infection, seizure, endocrine disease, trauma, and neurologic disease can all present psychiatrically.

info.h: Do NOT use blanket labs as a substitute for examination
info.pt: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Do NOT
info.t: ACEP supports targeted medical assessment guided by history, exam, vitals, and risk factors. Red flags still deserve expanded workup.

info.h: Do NOT miss autoimmune encephalitis red flags
info.pt: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Rapid progression, seizure, movement disorder, catatonia, autonomic instability, decreased consciousness, speech dysfunction, or hyponatremia should trigger neurology thinking.

info.h: Do NOT escalate antipsychotics blindly in possible catatonia
info.pt: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Catatonia and malignant catatonia require a different pathway. Consider lorazepam challenge and medical evaluation.

info.h: Do NOT discharge first-episode psychosis without a real safety and follow-up plan
info.pt: New Onset Psychosis Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Collateral, weapons access, SI/HI, command hallucinations, grave disability, support, and rapid first-episode follow-up must be explicit.

info.pt: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Ectopic pregnancy can present with pain, bleeding, syncope, shoulder pain, or minimal symptoms. History and contraception do not safely exclude pregnancy.

info.h: Do NOT rule out torsion with normal Doppler flow
info.pt: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Intermittent torsion and dual ovarian blood supply can preserve flow. High-suspicion torsion still needs OB/GYN consultation.

info.h: Do NOT wait for STI results to treat PID
info.pt: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Do NOT
info.t: CDC minimum clinical criteria support empiric treatment when PID is plausible and no better cause explains pain.

info.h: Do NOT anchor on gynecology when the abdomen is surgical
info.pt: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Appendicitis, diverticulitis, bowel pathology, urinary obstruction, and vascular disease can present as pelvic pain.

info.h: Do NOT discharge unresolved high-risk pelvic pain
info.pt: Pelvic Pain, Female Hub - Do NOT
info.t: Persistent severe pain, peritoneal signs, unstable vitals, pregnancy risk, vomiting, fever, or diagnostic uncertainty needs observation, imaging, or consultation.
Ectopic pregnancy can present as bleeding with little pain. Reproductive-age bleeding is pregnancy-related until tested.

info.h: Do NOT do a digital exam in late pregnancy bleeding before previa is excluded
info.t: Bleeding at 20 weeks or later needs OB involvement and placental-location awareness.

info.h: Do NOT treat unstable bleeding as routine AUB
info.t: Shock physiology, syncope, heavy ongoing bleeding, or symptomatic anemia needs hemorrhage support and specialty involvement.
Even if bleeding stops in the ED, postmenopausal bleeding requires gynecology follow-up for malignancy-risk evaluation.

info.h: Do NOT discharge pregnancy of unknown location without a plan
info.t: Repeat beta-hCG, repeat ultrasound timing, ectopic precautions, and reachable follow-up must be explicit.

info.h: Do NOT diagnose colic before a complete undressed exam
info.t: Remove socks and diaper. Check hair tourniquets, cornea, mouth, ears, groin, genitalia, skin, extremities, bruising, and burns.

info.h: Do NOT ignore abnormal vitals or high-risk age
info.t: Young infants with fever, hypothermia, toxic appearance, poor feeding, or abnormal perfusion need age-based infectious workup.
Bilious vomiting, distension, episodic severe crying, bloody stool, or lethargy between episodes needs intussusception/obstruction thinking.
Always examine scrotum/groin/genitalia. Torsion, incarcerated hernia, urinary retention, and genital hair tourniquet can present as crying.

info.h: Do NOT discharge unsafe caregiver situations
info.t: Persistent caregiver distress, unsafe dynamics, injury concerns, inability to feed, or inability to return should change disposition.

1. Announce traumatic arrest and assign airway, chest, blood, ultrasound, and procedure leads. 2. Activate trauma surgery, MTP, OR/IR, and massive hemorrhage resources. 3. Treat HOTT causes in parallel: hypovolemia, oxygenation, tension pneumothorax, tamponade. 4. Perform bilateral finger thoracostomies/chest tubes when chest trauma or obstructive physiology is possible. 5. Decide early if resuscitative thoracotomy is indicated. 6. Move to definitive source control after ROSC or transient response.
Chest compressions and epinephrine should not delay hemorrhage control, oxygenation, bilateral decompression, thoracotomy, or operative source control in a true traumatic arrest.

Control external bleeding, apply tourniquets/packing, place pelvic binder when indicated, activate MTP, minimize crystalloid, replace calcium during high-volume transfusion, and move toward OR/IR/REBOA-capable source control when appropriate.

BVM with high-flow oxygen immediately. Intubate when it can be done without delaying hemorrhage control or chest decompression. Confirm with waveform capnography and reassess ventilation after thoracostomy.
Use bilateral finger thoracostomies or chest tubes early in traumatic arrest with chest trauma, positive pressure ventilation, or suspected obstructive physiology.

Use cardiac ultrasound only if it does not delay intervention. In selected penetrating arrest or selected blunt arrest with signs of life, resuscitative thoracotomy is the definitive tamponade intervention.
Penetrating thoracic trauma with signs of life, witnessed arrest, or very short CPR interval. This is the scenario with the strongest evidence for neurologically intact survival benefit.

Penetrating extrathoracic trauma with signs of life or short CPR; selected blunt traumatic arrest with witnessed arrest, signs of life/cardiac motion, short CPR interval, and a potentially correctable thoracic cause.
Blunt traumatic arrest without signs of life, prolonged downtime, devastating nonsurvivable injury, or no cardiac activity after HOTT interventions.
Open Thoracotomy Procedure

- Activate MTP early - Tourniquet compressible extremity hemorrhage - Pack junctional wounds and apply direct pressure - Place pelvic binder at greater trochanters when pelvic injury is possible - Use balanced blood products per local protocol - Replace calcium during high-volume transfusion - Use TXA when indicated by local protocol and timing - Move early to OR/IR/REBOA-capable source control

- Crystalloid-heavy resuscitation - Waiting for CT before source control in an unstable or arresting patient - Repeated low-yield peripheral IV attempts when IO/central access is faster - Delaying blood to complete noncritical diagnostics

- Injuries are incompatible with life - No signs of life and prolonged downtime - Asystole with no cardiac motion after reversible causes are addressed - Blunt traumatic arrest without signs of life - No response after hemorrhage control, oxygenation, bilateral decompression, and tamponade assessment/intervention

Mechanism, arrest timing, CPR duration, signs of life, rhythm, cardiac ultrasound findings, airway/oxygenation, bilateral thoracostomy/chest decompression, hemorrhage interventions, blood products, thoracotomy decision, and final response.

1. Confirm indication and call trauma surgery/OR. 2. Supine, left arm up if feasible, wide prep. 3. Large left anterolateral incision at 4th/5th intercostal space from sternum toward posterior axillary line. 4. Enter pleura over superior rib; finger sweep; spread ribs. 5. Evacuate hemothorax and suction. 6. Open pericardium anterior to phrenic nerve from apex toward aortic root. 7. Relieve tamponade, control cardiac wound, perform open massage. 8. Cross-clamp descending thoracic aorta above diaphragm if exsanguinating below diaphragm or empty heart. 9. Continue blood resuscitation and move to OR for definitive control.
- Large incision saves time - Stay anterior to phrenic nerve - Cardiac wound control is temporary - Aortic clamp time must be announced - Thoracotomy is a bridge to OR or a stop decision

- Penetrating thoracic traumatic arrest with signs of life or short CPR interval - Penetrating torso trauma with profound refractory shock - Penetrating non-thoracic traumatic arrest with short CPR where aortic control may bridge to source control - Selected blunt arrest with witnessed arrest, signs of life/cardiac motion, short CPR, and potentially correctable thoracic cause
- Blunt arrest without signs of life - Prolonged CPR/downtime without cardiac motion - Devastating nonsurvivable injury - No pathway to definitive source control
Exsanguinating subdiaphragmatic hemorrhage, empty heart despite blood resuscitation, or need to prioritize coronary/cerebral perfusion during open resuscitation.

Retract left lung, identify descending thoracic aorta just anterior/lateral to spine and above diaphragm, open pleura over the aorta, place vascular clamp across aorta while avoiding esophagus, announce clamp time, and move to definitive hemorrhage control.

In acutely hypotensive patients, bedside echo distinguishes RV failure (volume-overloaded, underfilled LV, may need pressors + inotropes ± reperfusion) from LV failure, tamponade, hypovolemia, and distributive shock. Treating undifferentiated shock with empiric fluids in RV failure worsens cardiac output.

Apical 4-chamber (A4C): • RV:LV ratio ≥ 1.0 → acute RV dilation • McConnell sign: free-wall akinesis with preserved apical contraction → 77% specific for acute PE • TAPSE < 17 mm by M-mode at lateral tricuspid annulus → systolic dysfunction (1) Parasternal long (PLAX): • RV outflow tract dilation; "D-sign" not seen here (use PSAX) Parasternal short (PSAX): • Septal flattening in systole (pressure overload, e.g. acute PE) or diastole (volume overload) → "D-sign" (3) • 60-T-AcT < 60 ms with mid-systolic notching of RVOT pulsed Doppler → acute pulmonary hypertension Subcostal: • IVC > 2.1 cm with < 50% inspiratory collapse → elevated CVP (RAP ~ 15 mmHg) • Look for pericardial effusion (RV strai

| Parameter | Cutoff | Interpretation | |-----------|--------|----------------| | RV:LV ratio (A4C) | ≥ 1.0 | Acute RV dilation | | TAPSE | < 17 mm | RV systolic dysfunction | | RV S' (TDI tricuspid annulus) | < 9.5 cm/s | RV systolic dysfunction | | FAC (fractional area change) | < 35% | RV systolic dysfunction | | 60-T-AcT (RVOT pulsed Doppler) | < 60 ms | Acute pulmonary HTN | | McConnell sign | Free-wall akinesis + apical sparing | 77% specific PE | | IVC | > 2.1 cm, < 50% collapse | Elevated CVP |

• Acute vs chronic: RV wall thickness > 5 mm at end-diastole suggests chronicity (cor pulmonale, PAH). Thin-walled, dilated RV with new strain = acute insult (PE, RVMI, ARDS, sepsis). • TAPSE in chronic PAH: can be preserved early; use TAPSE/PASP ratio (< 0.36 → poor RV-PA coupling). • Pseudo-McConnell: RV infarction can mimic — get a 12-lead and right-sided V4R. • Image placeholders: TAPSE M-mode reference · McConnell A4C example · D-sign PSAX · Plethoric IVC subcostal

Three mechanisms turn routine RSI into RV arrest in pre-existing RV failure: 1. Loss of catecholamine drive from sedatives → systemic hypotension → coronary perfusion gradient to the RV collapses → ischemia → further RV dilation. 2. Positive-pressure ventilation raises RV afterload by compressing pulmonary vasculature. 3. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acidosis during apnea → pulmonary vasoconstriction → acute RV afterload spike. Mortality of peri-intubation arrest in RV failure is reported as high as 19% — every second of hypotension matters.

• Get the BP up FIRST. Target MAP ≥ 65–70 before drugs go in. • Norepinephrine + vasopressin running before induction. • If RVMI: phenylephrine alone is dangerous (pure α can drop CO). • Inotrope if RV is failing on echo: dobutamine 2–5 mcg/kg/min OR milrinone (caution if hypotensive). Epinephrine 0.02–0.05 mcg/kg/min is a reasonable single-agent rescue. • Inhaled pulmonary vasodilator if available: epoprostenol 50 ng/kg/min or inhaled NO 20–40 ppm via mask before induction. • Do NOT bolus large-volume fluids in volume-overloaded RV (most acute RV failure is fluid-overloaded). Small 250 mL crystalloid challenge only if IVC is small. • Pre-oxygenate aggressively: NIV/HFNC, head-up 30°, apneic

| Agent | Dose | Notes | |-------|------|-------| | Etomidate | 0.15-0.3 mg/kg | Most hemodynamically neutral; reasonable first-line. Half-dose (0.15) if shocky. | | Ketamine | 0.5-1 mg/kg (reduced) | Preserves catecholamine drive; theoretical pulmonary vasoconstriction in adults is overstated. Reasonable. | | Propofol | AVOID bolus | Drops SVR + direct myocardial depression — high risk of arrest. | | Midazolam | AVOID as sole induction | Slow onset, unpredictable hemodynamics. | Paralytic: rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg or succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg if no contraindications.

• Tidal volume 6 mL/kg ideal body weight (lung-protective). • PEEP titrated to lowest workable — high PEEP kills the RV. Start at 5, raise only if clearly needed. • Plateau pressure < 30 cm H₂O. • Permissive hypercapnia is dangerous in RV failure — pCO₂ rise → pulmonary vasoconstriction → RV afterload. Target near-normal pH 7.30-7.45. • RR 14-20 to avoid breath-stacking and dynamic hyperinflation. • Sedation light — propofol drip is OK once on pressors; fentanyl + dexmedetomidine combo well tolerated.

1. Disconnect from vent — rule out auto-PEEP / breath-stacking. Allow full passive exhalation 15-20 sec. 2. Push-dose epi 10-20 mcg IV q1-2 min while the team troubleshoots. 3. Bedside echo — check tube position, RV size, pericardial effusion, septal motion. 4. Inhaled vasodilator if not already running. 5. Consider ECMO activation (V-A) if refractory — call early.

1. Restore coronary perfusion to the RV by raising systemic MAP above PA pressure (RV perfuses in systole AND diastole only when this gradient is preserved). 2. Augment RV contractility without increasing pulmonary vascular resistance. 3. Reduce RV afterload with selective pulmonary vasodilators when available. 4. Avoid further RV distension — minimize crystalloid in volume-overloaded patients. Target: MAP ≥ 65 (≥ 70 if RVMI), CVP no higher than necessary (typically 8-12), urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/hr, lactate trending down.

| Agent | Dose | Mechanism | Notes | |-------|------|-----------|-------| | Norepinephrine | 0.05-0.5 mcg/kg/min | α₁ + β₁ | First-line. Raises MAP without big rise in PVR. | | Vasopressin | 0.03-0.04 U/min fixed | V1 receptor | Add-on at norepi 0.3+; selective systemic vasoconstrictor, mild pulmonary vasodilation. | | Epinephrine | 0.02-0.2 mcg/kg/min | α₁ + β₁ + β₂ | Single-agent rescue; useful when both pressor + inotrope needed. Tachycardia/lactate at higher doses. |

| Agent | Dose | Notes | |-------|------|-------| | Dobutamine | 2-5 mcg/kg/min (start low) | β₁ inotrope + mild β₂ vasodilation; lowers PVR. Watch for hypotension — pair with norepi. | | Milrinone | 0.125-0.5 mcg/kg/min | PDE-3 inhibitor; potent pulmonary vasodilation. Caution: causes systemic hypotension; AVOID if SBP < 90. Renal-adjusted. | | Levosimendan | 0.05-0.2 mcg/kg/min × 24h | Calcium sensitizer; not FDA-approved in US but available in EU; useful in cardiogenic shock. |

• Phenylephrine alone — pure α; can drop CO in pure RV failure (especially RVMI). OK as bridge while titrating norepi. • Large-volume crystalloid bolus — most acute RV failure is volume-overloaded. • High-dose epinephrine — tachycardia worsens RV ischemia. • Beta-blockers — kills RV inotropy in acute setting.

• Acute PE (intermediate-risk): norepi → add dobutamine if low CO, monitor for arrhythmia. • RV infarction: maintain RV preload (cautious 250 mL bolus if IVC small), avoid nitrates/morphine, dobutamine first-line inotrope, consider PCI emergently. • PAH crisis: norepi + vasopressin + inhaled vasodilator (epoprostenol or NO); never stop home prostacyclin infusion. • Sepsis with RV strain: norepi titrated to MAP, add vasopressin early, inotrope only if echo confirms RV/LV dysfunction. • Post-LVAD RV failure: call CT surgery — may need RVAD; epinephrine + milrinone + iNO as bridge.

Inhaled vasodilators reach only well-ventilated alveoli, so they reduce pulmonary vascular resistance precisely where gas exchange occurs — which improves V/Q matching and oxygenation. IV pulmonary vasodilators (sildenafil, prostacyclin) cause systemic hypotension and worsen V/Q mismatch.

Most ED-friendly option. Rapid onset, short half-life (~3-5 min), no systemic accumulation. Dose: 50 ng/kg/min nebulized continuously (typical adult dose 30-50 ng/kg/min via in-line nebulizer with vent or mask). Wean: Step down by 10 ng/kg/min q4-6h once hemodynamics improve. Never stop abruptly — rebound pulmonary vasoconstriction is common. Monitoring: SpO₂, MAP, RR. Side effects rare given short half-life.

Dose: 20-40 ppm via specialized delivery system. Pros: Fastest onset (seconds), most selective. Cons: Expensive ($3000-5000/day), requires specialized equipment, methemoglobinemia risk, abrupt discontinuation → rebound PH crisis. Use: Severe acute PH crisis, post-cardiac surgery RV failure, when epoprostenol unavailable.

Longer half-life prostacyclins, less commonly used acutely. More relevant for chronic PAH on home therapy. Critical: If a patient is on home subcutaneous treprostinil or IV epoprostenol, NEVER stop the infusion. Abrupt cessation causes life-threatening rebound PH crisis. Continue the home pump and add ED therapy on top.

info.h: When to start in the ED
info.t: • PAH crisis with hemodynamic compromise (MAP < 65 despite pressors, refractory hypoxemia) • Bridge before high-risk RSI in known RV failure • Massive PE with refractory hypoxemia/shock as bridge to thrombolysis or thrombectomy • Post-cardiac surgery acute RV failure (rare in ED) Don't use as first-line — pressors/inotropes come first; vasodilators are layered on when available.

| Presentation | Disposition | |--------------|-------------| | Massive PE / cardiac arrest / refractory shock | ICU + activate PERT + cath lab + CT surgery | | Intermediate-high PE (positive troponin + RV dysfunction + hemodynamic strain) | ICU; consider catheter-directed thrombolysis or half-dose alteplase | | Intermediate-low PE (RV strain OR positive trop, hemodynamically stable) | Step-down or telemetry; PERT consult | | Low-risk PE (sPESI 0, no RV strain, normal trop) | Floor or outpatient (HESTIA criteria) on DOAC | | RVMI with shock | Cath lab activation, ICU | | Acute on chronic PAH crisis | ICU with pulmonary HTN team | | ARDS with acute cor pulmonale | ICU; lung-protective vent +

info.h: When to activate PERT (Pulmonary Embolism Response Team)
info.t: PERT is a multidisciplinary team — typically interventional cardiology, pulmonology/CC, vascular surgery, CT surgery — that meets emergently to decide on advanced therapies. Activate for: • Massive PE (sustained SBP < 90, vasopressor requirement, cardiac arrest) • Intermediate-high PE (RV dysfunction + positive troponin + clinical deterioration) • Contraindications to systemic thrombolysis where catheter-directed therapy may be option • Patients failing initial therapy Don't wait for the patient to crash. Early PERT activation in intermediate-high PE shortens time to decision and improves outcomes.

Patients meeting ALL of the following may be safely discharged on a DOAC after ED workup: • Hemodynamically stable (HR < 110, SBP > 100, no vasopressors) • No thrombolysis or embolectomy required • No active bleeding or high bleeding risk • SpO₂ > 92% on room air • No severe pain requiring IV analgesia • No medical/social reason for admission > 24h • No CrCl < 30 (apixaban OK to 25) • No severe liver dysfunction • No pregnancy • No HIT history • Reliable follow-up in 24-72 hours Pair with: apixaban 10 mg BID × 7d → 5 mg BID, or rivaroxaban 15 mg BID × 21d → 20 mg daily. PCP or hematology follow-up.

• No on-site PERT or interventional capability: transfer to tertiary center with extracorporeal life support if patient is sick enough to need advanced therapy. • PAH on home prostacyclin infusion: never stop pump during transfer; ensure infusion meds and backup pump travel with patient; alert receiving pulmonary HTN team. • RVMI: door-to-balloon for cath; do not delay for further imaging. • ECMO consideration: call early — cardiogenic shock from massive PE or RV failure may need V-A ECMO as bridge to recovery or thrombectomy.

Two or more findings + plausible mechanism = CUT. • Proptosis • IOP > 40 (or rock-hard globe) • Vision loss / RAPD • Limited or absent EOM • Severe orbital pain • Resistance to retropulsion 90-120 min vision-loss window. Do NOT wait for CT, ophthalmology, or transfer. This is an ED procedure. The downside of cutting an unindicated lid is small (heals well). The downside of waiting on an indicated cut is permanent blindness.

• 1-2% lidocaine with epi + 27G needle (or skip if catastrophic) • Hemostat (mosquito) • Straight iris/Stevens scissors • Toothed forceps • Saline + gauze • Gloves, eye shield for after • Topical antibiotic ointment for after

Step 1 — Anesthetize Inject 1-2 cc lido + epi SC into the lateral canthus. If patient is unstable or vision is collapsing in real time, do the procedure dry — local anesthetic loss of time is not worth waiting. Step 2 — Hemostat crush Clamp the lateral canthus horizontally with the hemostat for 60-90 seconds. This crushes tissue, reduces bleeding, and marks the cutting line. Tip of hemostat to orbital rim — about 1-1.5 cm. Step 3 — Canthotomy Release the hemostat. With straight scissors, cut horizontally along the crushed line from the lateral canthus to the orbital rim. This alone is not enough — must proceed to cantholysis. Step 4 — INFERIOR CANTHOLYSIS (the actual decompression) Grasp the

• Recheck IOP — should drop to < 30 mmHg • Apply topical antibiotic ointment to wound • Place rigid Fox shield over globe (NOT pressure patch) • Ice to forehead (reduces ongoing bleeding/swelling) • Reverse anticoagulation if applicable (PCC, vit K, idarucizumab; andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US) • CT orbits without contrast to confirm/characterize cause • Urgent ophthalmology and oculoplastics consult • Lid heals well; oculoplastics will close the wound when stable

Pearls: • The actual decompression is the tendon, not the skin. Canthotomy alone is insufficient. • Inferior crus first — most ED OCS is from retrobulbar hemorrhage in the inferior orbit. • Stabilize your hand on the patient's head/cheek for control. • Speak the procedure out loud — this calms patient and team. Pitfalls: • Cutting too superficial (skin only) — must go through tarsus + tendon. • Trying to use forceps without good lid traction — pull lid laterally first. • Not rechecking IOP after — if still > 30, do superior cantholysis or call oculoplastics for orbital decompression. • Cutting straight up/down (vertical) — cut should be HORIZONTAL from canthus to rim.

Time-to-irrigation is the strongest modifiable predictor of outcome. Alkali in particular saponifies cell membranes and can reach intraocular structures within minutes. Every minute spent on history, VA, or exam is a minute the chemical is still working.

1. Topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5%, 1-2 drops) — single use, allows tolerance. 2. Set up irrigation: • Morgan lens preferred (allows hands-free continuous flow) • OR wide-bore IV tubing taped to lid speculum • Both eyes if bilateral exposure • 1-2 L LR or NS minimum (alkali burns may need 4-6 L+) • Body-temperature fluid more comfortable 3. Sweep fornices: evert upper lid (Desmarres or cotton-swab eversion) and sweep with moistened cotton-tip applicator to remove particulate (cement, lime, magnesium fragments, drain cleaner crystals). 4. Continue until pH 7.0-7.4: • Check pH with litmus paper at lower fornix • Wait 5 min after stopping irrigation before checking — running fluid normali

info.h: Acid vs alkali — why alkali is worse
info.t: Acid burns: acid coagulates proteins, forming a barrier that limits deeper penetration. Less intraocular spread. • Common: hydrochloric acid, sulfuric (battery), nitric, acetic • Exception: hydrofluoric acid (HF) acts like alkali — small amount can perforate; needs calcium gluconate added Alkali burns: alkali saponifies cell membranes → tracks deep into AC, damages limbal stem cells, can reach iris, lens, ciliary body. Worse outcomes. • Common: lye/sodium hydroxide (drain cleaner), ammonia (cleaning), calcium hydroxide (cement, plaster, lime), magnesium hydroxide (fireworks, sparklers) • Cement and lime continue to release base when wet — sweep particulate aggressively

• Hydrofluoric acid: add calcium gluconate (10% solution) topically + IV — fluoride chelation prevents systemic toxicity (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, arrhythmia) • Pepper spray (OC) / mace: primarily inflammatory; copious irrigation, no specific antidote • Super glue: lid stuck shut — do NOT force open; mineral oil + erythromycin ointment, peel as it loosens, ophtho if cornea involved • Particulate (cement, fireworks): thorough lid eversion + sweeping is critical; particles trapped in fornix continue to react • Pediatric: don't skip irrigation because of crying — sedation/papoose if needed; outcomes depend on time-to-irrigation, not patient cooperation

Set up irrigation while you take history about the chemical, time of injury, eye protection, force/pressure (high-pressure spray vs splash), prior eye disease, and tetanus status. The team can run irrigation while you write the orders for slit lamp, antibiotics, and ophthalmology consult. Do not stop irrigation to do exam — exam happens after pH is normal.

Screen every Black, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Indian patient with hyphema. Even sickle trait (HbAS) carriers can decompensate. Why: AC has low pH and low pO2 → sickled RBCs → trabecular meshwork blockade → IOP spike → optic nerve ischemia. Sickled RBCs in AC also resist clearance. Workup: sickle prep + Hb electrophoresis (don't rely on prep alone — false negatives in trait). If sickle: • ❌ AVOID acetazolamide, methazolamide, dorzolamide (CAIs acidify AC, worsen sickling) • ❌ AVOID mannitol (raises AC osmolarity) • ❌ AVOID hyperventilation in intubated patients (alkalosis OK; respiratory acidosis bad) • ✅ For IOP: timolol 0.5% BID + brimonidine 0.2% TID + latanoprost qHS • Surgical AC wa

• Bedrest with HOB 30-45° (lets blood layer inferior, clears visual axis, reduces re-bleed risk) • Rigid Fox shield at all times • Topical cycloplegic — atropine 1% BID (prevents synechiae, comfort) • Topical steroid — prednisolone acetate 1% q2-4h (reduces inflammation, may reduce re-bleed) • Antifibrinolytic — tranexamic acid 25 mg/kg PO TID OR aminocaproic acid (Amicar) 50 mg/kg q4h × 5 days (reduces re-bleed ~30% incidence on day 2-5) • Avoid ASA, NSAIDs (re-bleed risk) • Daily ophthalmology follow-up for IOP, visual axis, re-bleed surveillance • IOP target: < 24 mmHg (non-sickle), < 20 mmHg (sickle)

Re-bleed occurs in ~30% of traumatic hyphemas, most often day 2-5. Risk factors: large initial hyphema, sickle trait/disease, anticoagulation, child < 6 yo, delay in care. Re-bleed signs: sudden visual axis darkening, increased pain, IOP spike, fresh blood layer above clotted darker blood ("cap and gown" appearance). Prevention: antifibrinolytic + bedrest + shield + activity restriction + sleep upright × 5-7 days. If re-bleed: call ophtho. Often needs admission and possible OR washout.

Non-sickle: • IOP > 50 mmHg × 5 days • IOP > 35 mmHg × 7 days • Total ("eight-ball") hyphema not resolving by day 6-9 • Corneal blood staining (early sign: rust hue at endothelium) Sickle: IOP > 24 mmHg × 24 hr OR optic nerve compromise Pediatric: lower threshold for OR — amblyopia risk if visual axis blocked > 7-10 d.
