info.pt: Pediatric Eye Findings in Abusive Head Trauma
info.t: Multilayered, multiquadrant retinal hemorrhages extending to the ora serrata in a child without a credible accidental mechanism is highly specific for abusive head trauma (AHT) — formerly "shaken baby syndrome." The combination of acceleration-deceleration forces, vitreous traction at the vitreoretinal interface, and direct trauma produces a pattern not seen in typical accidental injury (falls, MVCs at usual force, normal birth).

info.pt: Pediatric Eye Findings in Abusive Head Trauma
info.t: Retinal hemorrhages: • Bilateral (~85%) • Multilayered (preretinal + intraretinal + subretinal) • Multiquadrant • Extending to the ora serrata (peripheral retina) — distinguishes AHT from accidental • Too numerous to count in severe cases Other AHT eye findings: • Macular schisis (traumatic retinoschisis) — highly specific for shaking • Vitreous hemorrhage • Retinal folds (perimacular) • Optic nerve sheath hemorrhage on imaging • Papilledema (later, from elevated ICP) Findings that DON'T fit AHT (ddx): • Few flame-shaped hemorrhages at posterior pole only — usually accidental or birth-related • Linear pattern → consider chronic anemia, leukemia • Retinal hemorrhage from CPR alone is rare and

info.pt: Pediatric Eye Findings in Abusive Head Trauma
info.t: • Dilated fundus exam by ophthalmology (peds preferred) — RetCam imaging if available for documentation • CT brain — subdural hemorrhage (often interhemispheric), parenchymal injury, edema • MRI brain — better for parenchymal/diffusion injury, dating bleeds • Skeletal survey if < 2 yo (multiple bones, looking for healing fractures) • Coagulation studies — rule out bleeding diathesis (PT, PTT, INR, fibrinogen, vWF, platelets, factor activity if indicated) • Liver enzymes — abdominal injury surrogate • Toxicology as appropriate • Child Protection Team / SCAN team consult + DCFS report (mandatory in US)

info.pt: Pediatric Eye Findings in Abusive Head Trauma
info.t: • Document the mechanism as told by caregivers verbatim — words may change later • Document who was present at the time of injury and who brought the child in • Document developmental milestones — does the stated mechanism match the child's capability? (3-mo cannot roll off couch by themselves) • Document all injuries (skin, mouth, ears, genitalia, fontanelles) • Photo-document with consent and chain of custody if available • Be specific in language: "concerning for AHT" rather than diagnostic; let CPT make the call • Maintain therapeutic alliance with family — don't accuse, don't minimize • Brief other staff so caregivers don't accidentally have unsupervised access to the child until invest

info.pt: Pediatric Eye Findings in Abusive Head Trauma
info.t: • Missing AHT because the child is non-acutely ill ("she's just sleepy") — fundoscopy on every infant with unexplained AMS, vomiting, or seizure • Accepting a vague history without probing • Discharging without ophthalmology dilated exam • Not reporting because "it's probably not abuse" — your job is to report concern; investigators determine • Not consulting child neurology for non-accidental seizure workup

The Ocular Trauma Score (Kuhn et al, 2002) predicts 6-month visual acuity outcome from initial presentation variables. It was derived and validated on the United States Eye Injury Registry (USEIR) cohort. Use: counseling patients and families about likely outcomes; risk-stratification for research. DO NOT use to: decide whether to OR, whether to shield, whether to give antibiotics. Those decisions are independent of OTS.

Even Cat 1 patients deserve repair attempt; Cat 1 outcomes assume best surgical care. • Calculating before pediatric VA assessment is reliable — VA in pre-verbal children is approximate (CSM, fix-and-follow); OTS less validated. • Using initial VA when patient is too uncomfortable for accurate assessment — note this caveat in the chart. • Not recording OTS at all — this is medicolegally helpful documentation (you considered prognosis).

When a cancer patient presents to the ED, knowing what regimen they are on, when their last cycle was, and typical toxicity patterns dramatically narrows your differential. Always ask: 1. What is the cancer type? 2. What is the chemotherapy regimen (acronym)? 3. When was the last cycle? 4. Are they between cycles or on continuous therapy? 5. Any new immunotherapy? Typical nadir for most cytotoxics: day 7-14 post-cycle (lowest counts), recovery day 21-28. Plan ED workup accordingly.

info.h: CAR-T — Older Section Retained for Reference
info.t: CRS quick-reference: • Fever, hypotension, hypoxia, AMS • Onset: hours to days post-infusion (peak day 1-7) • Tx: tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV (max 800 mg) ± steroids; ICU for grade 3-4 ICANS quick-reference: • Confusion, aphasia, seizure, cerebral edema • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h, escalate per grade • Tocilizumab does NOT cross BBB — steroids preferred for ICANS • Anti-seizure prophylaxis (levetiracetam) commonly used See dedicated CRS / ICANS Protocol page for full management ladder.

STOP infusion immediately (do not flush) 2. Aspirate residual drug from cannula 3. Mark area, photograph 4. Cool or warm compress depending on agent 5. Plastic surgery consult for blistering or necrosis

Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity (ICANS) are the dominant acute toxicities of CAR-T cell therapy and increasingly seen with bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab, mosunetuzumab, teclistamab, talquetamab, glofitamab, epcoritamab). Time course: • CRS typically begins within hours to 14 days after CAR-T infusion (peak day 1-7). • ICANS typically follows CRS (median onset day 5, range 1-21). • Bispecifics: CRS is most common with the first dose / step-up dosing. Key principle: CRS and concurrent infection are clinically indistinguishable. Always pan-culture and start broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically with any febrile presentation in this p

Grade 1: Antipyretics (acetaminophen), IV fluids PRN. Pan-culture (blood, urine, CXR), empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefepime 2g IV q8h ± vancomycin if catheter/MRSA risk). Telemetry. Add dexamethasone 10 mg IV if no response in 24h. Grade 3: ICU. Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV + Dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h (or methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg IV q12h). Vasopressor for hypotension, high-flow O2/NRB. Echo + troponin + BNP. Cardiology consult. Grade 4 (life-threatening): ICU. Tocilizumab + Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily × 3 days then taper

| Grade | Severity | Treatment Principle | |-------|----------|---------------------| | 1 | Mild, asymptomatic / labs only | Continue ICI, supportive care | | 2 | Moderate, limits ADLs | Hold ICI, oral prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day | | 3 | Severe, limits self-care | Hold ICI, IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day, infliximab/MMF if no response in 48-72h | | 4 | Life-threatening | Discontinue ICI permanently, ICU, IV steroids 2 mg/kg/day + biologic | Steroid taper: Once Grade ≤1, taper over at least 4-6 weeks (premature taper → rebound). Add PJP prophylaxis (sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim) if steroids ≥20 mg prednisone-equivalent for >4 weeks.

Presentation: new dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxia. CT: ground-glass opacities, consolidation, NSIP/COP/AIP patterns. Workup: CT chest, infectious workup (sputum, blood cultures, viral PCR, PJP PCR), trend O2 sat. Management: • Grade 1 (radiographic only): hold ICI, repeat imaging 3-4 wk • Grade 2: prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, hold ICI • Grade 3-4: methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day IV, ICU if hypoxic; if no improvement in 48h → add infliximab 5 mg/kg IV OR mycophenolate 1g BID OR IVIG. Pulmonology consult. • Permanent ICI discontinuation for Grade 3-4

Presentation: ≥3 stools/day above baseline, abdominal pain, blood/mucus. Workup: stool studies (C. diff PCR + cultures + ova/parasites), CBC, BMP, lactate, CRP. Sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy if Grade 2+. Imaging if peritoneal signs (CT for perforation). Management: • Grade 1: loperamide, hydration, hold ICI if persistent • Grade 2: hold ICI, prednisone 1 mg/kg/day; if no improvement in 48-72h, infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or vedolizumab 300 mg IV • Grade 3-4: hospitalize, IV methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day, infliximab 5 mg/kg IV (avoid in perforation — use vedolizumab); GI + ID consult; permanent ICI discontinuation • Bowel perforation = surgical emergency — surgery consult, broad antibiotics

Presentation: asymptomatic LFT elevation → fulminant failure. Workup: AST/ALT/Alk Phos/T.bili/INR; viral hepatitis panel (HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, EBV, CMV); autoimmune workup (ANA, ASMA, AMA); RUQ US to exclude obstruction/mets. Management: • Grade 1 (AST/ALT ≤ 3× ULN): monitor, continue ICI cautiously • Grade 2 (3-5× ULN): hold ICI, prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day • Grade 3 (5-20× ULN): hold ICI, methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day IV, hepatology consult • Grade 4 (>20× ULN OR INR >1.5): ICU, MMF 1g BID added (avoid infliximab — hepatotoxic), transplant evaluation if fulminant

Hypophysitis (often ipi): headache, vision changes, fatigue, hypotension. MRI pituitary (enlarged stalk). Replace deficient hormones (cortisol FIRST then thyroid — reverse order can precipitate adrenal crisis). Steroids only for mass effect. Adrenal insufficiency: treat as adrenal crisis — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 50 mg q6h. See Adrenal Insufficiency consult. Thyroiditis: thyrotoxic phase (transient) → hypothyroid (often permanent). Levothyroxine replacement. Beta-blocker for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis. Type 1 DM: new DKA presentation. ICU, insulin drip, fluids, K replacement. Permanent insulin therapy after recovery.

Mortality 25-50%. Suspect with any new chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, or troponin elevation in ICI-treated patient. Workup: troponin (high-sensitivity), BNP, ECG, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI, endomyocardial biopsy (definitive), ID workup to rule out viral myocarditis. Management: • ICU admission immediately • Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily × 3-5 days (high-dose pulse), then taper • Add second-line if no response in 24h: mycophenolate 1g BID, infliximab 5 mg/kg (caution: increases mortality in CHF), abatacept 10 mg/kg, OR JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) • Anti-arrhythmics, mechanical support (IABP, ECMO) as needed • Permanent ICI discontinuation • Cardiology consult immediately

• Renal (interstitial nephritis): rising Cr, sterile pyuria, eosinophiluria. Hold ICI, prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. Renal biopsy if Grade 3+. • Neuro (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, encephalitis): ICU, IVIG, plasmapheresis, steroids. Neurology consult. Permanent ICI hold. • Skin (toxic epidermal necrolysis, SJS): burn unit, supportive care, IVIG; rare but life-threatening. • Hematologic: ITP, AIHA, aplastic anemia, HLH — hematology consult, steroids ± IVIG/rituximab.

Beck's Triad (full classic <30%): hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus: SBP drop >10 mmHg with inspiration — sensitive (>80%) for tamponade physiology in non-COPD patients. Other findings: dyspnea, tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans (specific but uncommon), water-bottle heart on CXR (chronic). Most common malignant causes: • Lung cancer (#1, ~33%) • Breast cancer (~25%) • Lymphoma • Leukemia • Melanoma • Mesothelioma Malignant effusions are typically chronic, accumulate slowly, and can reach >1 L before tamponade physiology develops (vs trauma where 100-200 mL causes acute tamponade).

Effusion size (parasternal long axis, end-diastole): • Small: <1 cm • Moderate: 1-2 cm • Large: >2 cm • Circumferential vs loculated Tamponade physiology (any of these = tamponade): 1. Right atrial systolic collapse — most sensitive (50-100%) 2. Right ventricular diastolic collapse — most specific (75-90%) 3. IVC plethora — IVC >2.1 cm with <50% inspiratory collapse 4. Septal bounce / D-shaped LV during inspiration (ventricular interdependence) 5. Mitral inflow respiratory variation >25% (tricuspid >40%) Pearl: Size doesn't equal tamponade. A small rapidly-accumulating effusion (post-procedure, type-A dissection) can tamponade; a slowly-growing 2-3 cm effusion may be hemodynamically tolerate

Avoid intubation if possible — positive pressure ventilation drops preload and can precipitate PEA arrest in tamponade. If intubation unavoidable: ketamine induction, no PEEP initially, gentle hand-bagging. Permissive hypertension — maintain MAP with norepinephrine (preserves contractility) or epinephrine (inotropy + chronotropy). Cautious IV fluids — 250-500 mL bolus may temporize by augmenting preload, but do not over-resuscitate (rises filling pressures further compress chambers). AVOID: • Beta-blockers (lose compensatory tachycardia) • Vasodilators / nitrates (drop preload) • Diuretics (drop preload) • PEEP / high tidal volumes

Indications (emergent in ED): • Tamponade physiology with hemodynamic instability • PEA arrest with known/suspected tamponade • Cannot wait for cards/CT-surgery Approach — Subxiphoid (most common in ED, no US): 1. Sterile prep, drape, lidocaine 2. Long 18-gauge needle attached to 10-mL syringe 3. Insert at angle of xiphoid + costal margin, 45° to skin, aim toward LEFT shoulder 4. Aspirate continuously while advancing 5. Stop when fluid returns; advance guidewire (Seldinger), upsize to drain US-guided (preferred when time allows): 1. Identify largest fluid pocket on subxiphoid OR parasternal OR apical view 2. Choose route avoiding lung, liver, internal mammary, LV apex 3. Apical or parasterna

• Cell count and differential • Cytology (3 separate sends increase yield to >90%) • Gram stain + culture (bacterial, AFB, fungal) • Cholesterol, triglycerides, glucose, LDH, protein • Light's criteria (exudate vs transudate) • ADA if TB suspected • Flow cytometry if lymphoma suspected • Hematocrit (if grossly bloody)

• Malignant effusion: pericardial drain + pericardial window (OR vs balloon pericardiotomy); intrapericardial chemotherapy (cisplatin, bleomycin, thiotepa) for sclerosis • Recurrent malignant: pericardial window or pericardiectomy • Bacterial: drainage + IV antibiotics + ID consult • Tuberculous: drainage + 4-drug RIPE; corticosteroids reduce constrictive pericarditis • Uremic: dialysis intensification • Post-MI / Dressler’s: NSAIDs + colchicine; avoid anticoagulation • Aortic dissection: DO NOT drain — increases shear, worsens dissection. Emergent CT-surgery for repair.

• ICU after pericardiocentesis (post-drainage pulmonary edema, recurrent effusion, dysrhythmia) • Cardiothoracic surgery consult for window • Oncology consult for primary cancer therapy • Repeat echo within 24h to assess re-accumulation • Goals of care discussion — malignant pericardial effusion median survival 2-4 months

High-risk tumors / situations (TLS prophylaxis indicated): • Burkitt lymphoma • T-cell ALL with WBC >100k • Bulky non-Hodgkin lymphoma • AML with WBC >50k • CLL starting venetoclax (especially during ramp-up) • Hepatocellular carcinoma during TACE • Spontaneous TLS in highly proliferative tumors (rare) Patient risk factors that worsen TLS risk: • Baseline elevated uric acid (>7.5) • Baseline renal dysfunction (Cr >1.5) • Dehydration / oliguria • Low urine output despite fluids Use the TLS Cairo-Bishop Calculator to classify lab vs clinical TLS.

Adults: Normal saline 2-3 L/m²/day → ~200-250 mL/hr in average adult. Pediatrics: 200 mL/m²/hr (max 3000 mL/m²/day). Goal urine output: >100 mL/hr in adults (or 3-5 mL/kg/hr in peds). Maintain even if oliguric — push fluids unless clear volume overload (then add diuretic + consider RRT). Avoid: • LR / Plasma-Lyte — contains potassium • Urine alkalinization (bicarbonate) — OBSOLETE. Promotes calcium phosphate precipitation. Was historical practice with allopurinol; abandoned with rasburicase era. • Dextrose-containing fluids — drives K intracellularly (masks hyperK), increases insulin requirement.

Allopurinol — prophylaxis (low-intermediate risk): • 300 mg PO daily, start 2-3 days before chemo • Xanthine oxidase inhibitor → prevents NEW urate formation • Does NOT lower existing urate • Renally adjusted (50% dose if CrCl <30) Rasburicase — high-risk OR established TLS: • 0.2 mg/kg IV × 1 dose (single dose effective in most cases) • Recombinant urate oxidase → converts urate → allantoin (water-soluble) • Drops urate within HOURS • CHECK G6PD if time allows — contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (causes severe hemolytic anemia) • Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding • Higher prevalence of G6PD deficiency in African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian populations — lower t

Hyperkalemia: • Calcium gluconate 3 g IV over 10 min (membrane stabilization, no effect on K) • Insulin regular 5 units IV, or 0.1 units/kg (max 10), if eGFR <60, dialysis-dependent, glucose <150, weight <60 kg, or no diabetes — 10 units if normal renal function AND adequate glucose. Give with 25 g dextrose (D50W 50 mL, or D10 250 mL drip) unless glucose >250. Check glucose at 30, 60, 120, 240 min • Albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized (additive) • Sodium polystyrene sulfonate or patiromer for elimination • RRT if K >6.5 refractory Hyperphosphatemia: • Sevelamer 800-1600 mg PO TID with meals (preferred; doesn't add Ca) • Aluminum hydroxide acutely (short-term only) • RRT for PO4 >10 or rapidly risin

• K >6.5 refractory to medical therapy • PO4 >10 or rapidly rising with symptomatic hypocalcemia • Symptomatic hypocalcemia with high Ca×PO4 product • Volume overload preventing adequate hydration • Uremia symptoms • Refractory metabolic acidosis • AKI with worsening despite optimal medical management Nephrology consult for any clinical TLS. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) often preferred over intermittent HD for ongoing electrolyte clearance.

Labs q4-6h initially: • BMP (Na, K, Cl, HCO3, BUN, Cr) • Phosphate, calcium (corrected), magnesium • Uric acid (on ice if post-rasburicase) • LDH (tumor burden marker) Strict I/O. Continuous cardiac monitoring. Disposition: • Clinical TLS (Cr/arrhythmia/seizure) → ICU • Lab TLS, high-risk tumor or worsening → ICU • Lab TLS, stable → Telemetry with q4-6h electrolytes • Transfer to oncology center if tertiary care unavailable

Three distinct stress diagnoses are gated entirely by time since the index trauma. Misdiagnosis at the wrong time window leads to wrong treatment. Never diagnose PTSD before 1 month post-trauma. A patient with severe symptoms 2 weeks post-trauma is NOT PTSD — they may meet ASD criteria, or they may be in normal acute reaction.

| Window | Diagnosis | Source | ED Action | |--------|-----------|--------|-----------| | 0-3 days | Acute Stress Reaction (ASR) | ICD term — NOT in DSM-5-TR | PFA + reassurance + 2-4 wk FU | | 3 days - 1 month | Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) | DSM-5-TR | PFA + early TF-CBT referral + sleep support if needed | | > 1 month | PTSD | DSM-5-TR | PCL-5 cluster scoring + warm handoff to TF-CBT (CPT/PE/EMDR) | | Full criteria not met until ≥6 months | PTSD with delayed expression | DSM-5-TR specifier | Same as PTSD pathway once criteria met |

Not a DSM-5-TR diagnosis. ICD-11 6B40. Normal acute response — sleep disturbance, intrusions, hypervigilance, irritability are EXPECTED in the first month and do not require pharmacotherapy. Management: Psychological First Aid + reassurance + written discharge materials. Follow-up at 2-4 weeks for re-screen.

DSM-5-TR criteria: • Same Criterion A (qualifying trauma) as PTSD • ≥9 of 14 symptoms required across five categories • Functional impairment required Categories: | Category | # Items | Examples | |----------|---------|----------| | Intrusion | 5 | Memories, dreams, flashbacks, distress at cues, physiological reactivity | | Negative mood | 1 | Persistent inability to experience positive emotions | | Dissociative | 2 | Altered sense of reality, dissociative amnesia | | Avoidance | 2 | Avoid memories/thoughts, avoid external reminders | | Arousal | 5 | Sleep, irritability, hypervigilance, concentration, startle | Critical: ASD is a TOTAL count (any combination across categories), NOT cluster-b

DSM-5-TR criteria require symptoms in EACH of four clusters: • B (Intrusion): ≥1 of 5 symptoms • C (Avoidance): ≥1 of 2 symptoms • D (Negative cognitions/mood): ≥2 of 7 symptoms • E (Arousal): ≥2 of 6 symptoms • Duration: >1 month • Functional impairment • Not attributable to substance/medical condition Specifiers: • With dissociative symptoms (depersonalization or derealization) • With delayed expression (full criteria not met until ≥6 months post-event) Subtypes recognized in clinical practice (not DSM): • Complex PTSD (ICD-11) — interpersonal/repeated trauma + disturbances in self-organization • Moral injury — distress from acts/witnessing acts that violate moral beliefs

| Tool | Items | Purpose | Cutoff | Time | |------|-------|---------|--------|------| | PC-PTSD-5 | 5 | Primary care/ED screen | ≥3 sensitive (94.8%) / ≥4 balanced | 2-3 min | | PCL-5 | 20 | Full DSM-5-TR characterization + tracking | 31-33 = probable PTSD | 5-10 min | | CAPS-5 | Structured interview | Gold-standard diagnosis | Clinician-rated | 45-60 min | Workflow: PC-PTSD-5 positive (≥3 or ≥4) → PCL-5 → if positive → CAPS-5 by trained clinician. ED reality: Most ED clinicians stop at PC-PTSD-5/PCL-5 and refer for CAPS-5 in outpatient setting.

PFA is the default early intervention for trauma in the ED. It is brief, evidence-based, and operationalized in NICE NG116, WHO guidance, and the NCTSN Field Operations Guide. Hobfoll 5 elements: 1. Safety — physical and psychological 2. Calming — reduce arousal 3. Self / community efficacy — restore agency 4. Connectedness — link to support 5. Hope — orient to recovery Evidence (Wang 2024 integrative review): • Reduces anxiety in immediate/intermediate term • Mixed evidence for PTSD prevention specifically • PFA > psychoeducation at 1 month in one trial; equivalent to EMDR/SMT in another • WHO, IASC, NICE NG116 all recommend

1. Listen and Validate • Open with: "I am sorry this happened. Take your time." • NO forced disclosure — patient leads, you follow • Reflect: "That sounds terrifying" • Tolerate silence 2. Provide Accurate Information • Normalize stress reactions: "Sleep disturbance, intrusions, avoidance, irritability are EXPECTED in the first month — they do not mean something is wrong with you." • Explain the time-window logic if PTSD comes up: "We do not diagnose PTSD before 1 month." • Written discharge materials (PTSD Coach app, free, NCPTSD) 3. Practical Assistance • Transportation home • Food / contacts / shelter • Phone calls to family • Coordinate childcare if needed 4. Connect to Social Support •

info.h: STRONG WARN: NEVER Do CISD / Single-Session Debriefing
info.t: Critical Incident Stress Debriefing (CISD) and similar single-session psychological debriefings are HARMFUL. Multiple international guidelines strongly recommend AGAINST. Cochrane review (Rose et al. 2002) — current standard: • Single-session debriefing does NOT prevent PTSD • One trial showed OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.24-5.09) for PTSD at 1 year in those who received debriefing • Conclusion: "Compulsory debriefing of victims of trauma should cease." WHO, NICE, ISTSS, APA, VA/DoD 2023 CPG all reaffirm: debriefing may worsen outcomes; PFA is the alternative. Why it harms: • Forces re-exposure before patient is ready • Disrupts natural recovery trajectory • May consolidate trauma memory in maladaptive

Developed at Harborview Level I Trauma Center; validated across 25 US trauma centers (Zatzick 2021). The American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma now mandates PTSD screening + referral as a best-practice standard. Step 1: Universal Screening + Post-Injury Case Management • PC-PTSD-5 at index visit and at follow-up • Care coordinator follows patient through transitions Step 2: Motivational Interviewing for Substance Use • Co-screen for AUD/SUD (high comorbidity) • Brief motivational intervention • SBIRT framework (Screening, Brief Intervention, Referral to Treatment) Step 3: Evidence-Based Pharmacotherapy / Trauma-Focused CBT • For patients with persistent symptoms at 3 months • CPT,

Trauma narratives, somatic presentations, and symptom expression vary across cultures. • Use trained medical interpreters for any patient with limited English proficiency. Family members should NOT interpret trauma content (re-traumatization, confidentiality, family dynamics). • Refugee / asylum seekers: Validated screening tools include the Harvard Trauma Questionnaire (HTQ) and the Hopkins Symptom Checklist-25 (HSCL-25). Multiple, repeated, and culturally complex traumas common. • IPV screening MUST occur in private — separate the patient from accompanying partner before any IPV question is asked. Use a clinical reason ("I need to do a confidential exam"). • Sexual assault disclosure is hi

Print or text these to every PTSD/ASD/SA/IPV patient before discharge: • Stress reactions in the first month are EXPECTED and do not mean something is wrong with you. • If symptoms persist >1 month or worsen, contact your primary care or mental health provider. • AVOID alcohol and drugs to cope — they make recovery harder. • Connect with a trusted person in the next 24-72 hours. • Free resources: 988 (call/text/chat), PTSD Coach app (free, NCPTSD). • Sexual assault: RAINN 1-800-656-HOPE • IPV: NDV 1-800-799-SAFE • Veterans: 988 → press 1 • In an emergency or if thinking of suicide: call 988 or come back to the ED immediately.

Most ED clinicians do NOT initiate chronic PTSD pharmacotherapy — defer to psychiatry or PCP follow-up. ED-relevant prescribing scenarios: • Established PTSD >1 month + reliable outpatient follow-up + patient willing to start • Trauma-related nightmares dominant — prazosin can be initiated • Sleep impairment without nightmares — short non-benzo bridge • AVOID benzodiazepines under any circumstance for PTSD/recent trauma

2023 VA/DoD CPG Recommendation 15 — three agents recommended (Hamblen 2024): | Drug | FDA | Start | Target | Notes | |------|-----|-------|--------|-------| | Sertraline (Zoloft) | ✓ PTSD | 25 mg PO daily x 1 wk | 50-200 mg/day | Best-tolerated of the three | | Paroxetine (Paxil) | ✓ PTSD | 10 mg PO daily | 20-50 mg/day | Watch discontinuation syndrome | | Venlafaxine XR (Effexor XR) | Off-label | 37.5 mg PO daily | 75-300 mg/day | BP monitoring (HTN at higher doses) | Notable change: Fluoxetine REMOVED from recommended list in 2023 CPG (no benefit in newer clinician-rated trial). Counseling points: • 4-6 weeks to full effect • Transient activation/anxiety/insomnia in first 1-2 weeks (warn e

Indication: Trauma-related nightmares + sleep disruption. Evidence picture (2025): • PACT trial (Raskind NEJM 2018): NEGATIVE in stable veterans (likely underpowered, over-selected) • 2025 meta-analysis (10 RCTs, n=648): improves insomnia (SMD -0.654) and nightmares (SMD -0.641); does NOT improve overall PTSD • 2023 VA/DoD CPG: SUGGESTS prazosin for PTSD nightmares specifically • Harvard South Shore 2024-2025 algorithm: remains first-line for PTSD-related sleep impairment Raskind dosing protocol: | Step | Day | Dose | |------|-----|------| | 1 | 1-2 | 1 mg PO qhs | | 2 | 3-7 | 2 mg PO qhs | | 3 | Week 2+ | Titrate weekly until nightmares absent or max dose | Maximum doses: • Men: 5 mg mid-mo

Reasonable bridge therapy when sleep is dominant complaint and nightmares are NOT prominent. | Agent | Dose | Notes | |-------|------|-------| | Hydroxyzine | 25-100 mg qhs | First-line PTSD sleep-onset (Harvard South Shore). Non-habit-forming. Anticholinergic — caution in elderly. | | Trazodone | 25-200 mg qhs (most 50-150) | PTSD-specific data: 72% reduction nightmares, 92% sleep onset (Palo Alto VA). WARN: 12% priapism rate — counsel and ask directly at FU. | | Mirtazapine | 7.5-30 mg qhs | Effective hypnotic. 2024 NMA: NO PTSD-specific benefit. Best when comorbid depression, weight loss. | AVOID for sleep in PTSD: • Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) — NMA found ineffective + depe

Critical safety teaching point — never give a BZD to a PTSD or recent-trauma patient. Evidence: • Guina 2015 meta-analysis (18 trials, 5236 participants) • 2023 VA/DoD CPG • APA, ISTSS, NICE all in agreement Findings: • BZDs are INEFFECTIVE for PTSD treatment AND prevention • Associated with: - WORSE overall PTSD severity - INCREASED risk of developing PTSD when given after trauma - Worse psychotherapy outcomes - Aggression, depression, substance use disorder - Cognitive impairment - Falls in elderly Mechanism of harm: • Interfere with extinction learning (Makkar 2010) — PTSD therapy DEPENDS on extinction learning • Reduce REM sleep (de Mendonca 2023) — REM is critical for trauma memory cons

WARN: Routine Acute Propranolol for PTSD Prevention • Failed in pooled meta-analyses (Argolo 2015, Steenen 2016, CADTH 2020, Raut 2022) • Attenuates HR without changing PTSD incidence • Neither ISTSS nor APA recommends WARN: Single-Session Debriefing (CISD) • Cochrane: OR 2.51 for PTSD at 1y in those who received debriefing • WHO and 2023 VA/DoD strongly against • See PFA Protocol page Currently NOT available outside research: • MDMA-assisted therapy: FDA REJECTED Lykos NDA Aug 9, 2024. Cited: functional unblinding, expectancy effects, ethical violations at one site, CV safety concerns. • Cannabis: Insufficient quality evidence. Risk of cannabis use disorder. Not recommended by VA/DoD or APA

| Scenario | Action | |----------|--------| | Trauma 0-3 days | NO pharm except medical stabilization | | Trauma 3 days - 1 month, sleep impairment | Hydroxyzine 25-50 mg qhs OR trazodone 25-50 mg qhs | | PTSD >1 month, willing to start | Sertraline 25 mg → 50-200 mg with outpatient FU | | Nightmares dominant | Prazosin 1 mg qhs → titrate (Raskind protocol) | | Anxiety / agitation in PTSD pt | NEVER give a BZD. Use hydroxyzine 25-50 mg PRN. Connect to crisis support. | | Comorbid depression | Sertraline (covers both) OR mirtazapine if weight loss / sleep dominant | | IPV survivor + sleep complaint | Hydroxyzine. NEVER BZD (impairs safety judgment). | | Veteran on existing BZD chronic | Do NO

PTSD Coach (NCPTSD, free, iOS/Android) — symptom tracking, coping skills, professional care connection. Evidence-based. PTSD Family Coach (NCPTSD, free) — for family members of PTSD patients. PE Coach (NCPTSD, free) — adjunct to Prolonged Exposure therapy. CPT Coach (NCPTSD, free) — adjunct to Cognitive Processing Therapy. Mindfulness Coach (NCPTSD, free) — mindfulness practice. Insomnia Coach (NCPTSD, free) — CBT-I support. Safety Plan apps (multiple) — Stanley-Brown Safety Plan format.

First-line per VA/DoD 2023 CPG (preferred OVER pharmacotherapy): • Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) — 12 sessions; addresses stuck points and trauma cognitions. Manualized. • Prolonged Exposure (PE) — 8-15 sessions; graded imaginal + in-vivo exposure. Strong evidence. • Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) — 8 phases; bilateral stimulation during trauma processing. WHO + APA endorsed. Second-line: • Brief Eclectic Psychotherapy (BEP) • Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) — for refugee/multiply-traumatized populations • Written Exposure Therapy (WET) Group format — available for CPT and other modalities; may help with stigma and isolation.

Find a CPT-certified provider: • https://cptforptsd.com — find-a-clinician directory Find an EMDR therapist: • https://emdria.org — EMDR International Association directory Find a PE therapist: • Penn CTSA (Center for Treatment and Study of Anxiety) directory VA & Vet Center locator: • https://www.va.gov/find-locations ISTSS Find-a-Clinician: • https://istss.org/clinical-resources/find-a-clinician SAMHSA treatment locator: • https://findtreatment.samhsa.gov OR call 1-800-662-HELP (4357)

info.t: ☐ DSM-5-TR criteria mapping (if Dx made) ☐ Index trauma description (HIPAA-minimum-necessary; do NOT detail more than needed) ☐ Screening tool result (PC-PTSD-5 / PCL-5 / ASD) ☐ C-SSRS suicide screen result (mandatory) ☐ Safety plan if any IPV/SI/SUD ☐ Mandatory reporting compliance: - Child abuse (all states, mandatory) - Elder abuse (most states) - Vulnerable adult abuse (varies) - IPV: NOT mandatory in most states for competent adult; do NOT report without consent unless mandatory in your state - Sexual assault: chain of custody for forensic evidence; reporting to LE is patient choice in most states ☐ Disposition rationale ☐ Follow-up appointment time + warm-handoff documentation ☐ Hotlin

| Population | Lifetime PTSD Risk | ED-Specific Action | |------------|--------------------|--------------------| | Sexual assault survivors | 30-50% | SANE within 72-120h; RAINN 1-800-656-HOPE; CBT/CPT/PE/EMDR all effective | | IPV / DV survivors | 30-60% | PRIVATE screen (HARK/HITS); NDV 1-800-799-SAFE; lethality assess; safety plan never shared | | Veterans / military | 10-30% | 988→1; Vet Center walk-in; assess for TBI overlap | | Pediatric post-injury | 15-25% | Parent psychoeducation per NICE NG116; screen at 1-mo FU; TF-CBT for kids | | Refugees / asylum | 30-60% | HTQ; trained interpreter; cultural adaptation; multiple traumas common | | First responders / ED staff (Crit A4) | Higher

DSI = Procedural sedation where the procedure is preoxygenation. Ketamine preserves spontaneous breathing and airway reflexes, allowing oxygen loading BEFORE paralysis. RSI: Trust the preoxygenation you already did DSI: Secure better preoxygenation in the patient who won't tolerate it

• Agitated delirium preventing preoxygenation • Patient refusing NC, NRB, BVM, or NIV • High-risk desaturator (SpO2 ≤93% on high-flow) • Combative patient on NIV • Needs pre-intubation procedures they won't tolerate

| Step | Dose | Notes | |------|------|-------| | Initial | 1-1.5 mg/kg IV | Slow push over 15-30 sec | | Redose | 0.5 mg/kg IV | Wait 60-90 sec between doses | | Goal | Dissociation | Calm, breathing, reflexes intact |
• NC 15 L/min (keep on entire procedure) • NRB 15 L/min OR BVM/CPAP with PEEP • Minimum 3 min once SpO2 >95% • 10-min abort rule if SpO2 <95%
• 15-20% avoid intubation after DSI • Slow ketamine push prevents apnea • Keep NC during paralysis • Have RSI drugs ready throughout
This is DISSOCIATIVE sedation, NOT full induction. Goal: Patient calm and compliant, still breathing spontaneously, airway reflexes intact. NOT: Unconscious and apneic.
| Parameter | Value | |-----------|-------| | Initial | 1.0-1.5 mg/kg IV | | Admin | Slow push 15-30 sec | | Redose | 0.5 mg/kg q5min PRN | | Onset | ~30 seconds | | Max total | 3-4 mg/kg |
Rapid IV push → transient apnea (defeats DSI purpose) Slow push → dissociation without respiratory depression Always push over 15-30 seconds
• Patient calm, not fighting • Tolerating oxygen delivery • Nystagmus present • Spontaneous breathing continues • May have subtle purposeful movements
• Hypersalivation — have suction ready • Transient HTN/tachycardia — expected • Emergence reactions — post-procedure, benzos if needed Apnea is rare but reported — have BVM ready
15 L/min O2 via nasal cannula • Keep on throughout ENTIRE procedure • Keep on during paralysis • Only remove at moment of intubation This is non-negotiable.
| If SpO2 | Use | |---------|-----| | >95% | Non-rebreather 15 L/min | | ≤95% | BVM + PEEP 5-15 cm H2O | | ≤95% | OR CPAP/NIV 5-15 cm H2O | PEEP prevents alveolar collapse, improves FRC
| Scenario | Time | |----------|------| | SpO2 >95% | Continue 3 more min | | SpO2 90-95% | Until >95%, then 3 min | | SpO2 <95% at 10 min | Abort to RSI |
• SpO2 >95% (target 98%) • Regular spontaneous respirations (RR 12-20) • Reduced work of breathing • Minimum 3 min for denitrogenation
☐ Head-up 30+ degrees ☐ Ramp if obese ☐ Auditory meatus above jugular notch
☐ Video laryngoscope + backup direct ☐ ETT sizes + stylet + bougie ☐ Suction x2 (ketamine hypersalivation) ☐ BVM with PEEP valve ☐ Supraglottic airway ☐ Surgical airway kit at bedside
DSI: ☐ Ketamine 1-1.5 mg/kg drawn RSI Backup (must be ready): ☐ Induction agent (etomidate/propofol) ☐ Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg OR ☐ Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg
☐ Continuous SpO2 ☐ Waveform capnography ☐ Continuous cardiac ☐ Blood pressure cycling
☐ Nasal cannula at 15 L/min ☐ NRB or BVM+PEEP ready ☐ CPAP/BiPAP available if needed
• Non-spontaneously breathing — DSI requires spontaneous ventilation • Absent airway reflexes — comatose, unresponsive • Ketamine allergy • Very high aspiration risk — DSI is not apneic
• Severe hypertension • Severe tachycardia • Active myocardial ischemia • Recent MI • Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism → Consider dexmedetomidine alternative

Dose: 1 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes Advantages: • No sympathomimetic surge • Less hypersalivation • Preserves airway reflexes Disadvantages: • Slower onset (3-5 min) • Less potent against severe agitation • May cause bradycardia/hypotension
DSI requires experienced airway provider. Not a technique for novices or first-year residents without direct supervision.

Pre-test probability exceeds contamination risk (~3%): • Sepsis / Septic Shock — 38-69% bacteremia rate • Suspected endocarditis — 3 sets from 3 sites • Meningitis / Encephalitis — before LP • Osteomyelitis / Septic arthritis — 30-50% yield • Healthcare-associated infections (HAP, CLABSI) • Complicated pyelonephritis (obstruction, catheter, shock) • Febrile neutropenia (ANC <500) • Immunocompromised (transplant, chemo, HIV CD4 <200)

False-positive rate may exceed true-positive rate: • Community-acquired pneumonia — 6-9% yield, changes management in <1% • Uncomplicated cellulitis — <2% bacteremia, contamination more likely • Simple UTI/pyelonephritis — same organism as urine 97% of time • Low-grade fever without risk factors (Shapiro <2) • Clear viral syndrome

Major criteria (3 points each): • Temperature >39.4°C (103°F) • Indwelling vascular catheter • Clinical suspicion of endocarditis Minor criteria (1 point each): • Temp 38.3-39.3°C • Age >65 • Rigors • Vomiting • SBP <90 • WBC >18,000 • Bands >5% • Platelets <150,000 • Creatinine >2.0 Score ≥2 points: 19% bacteremia → cultures indicated Score <2 points: <1% bacteremia → consider skipping

info.h: Organisms That Are ALMOST ALWAYS True Pathogens (>90%)
info.t: • *Staphylococcus aureus* • *Streptococcus pneumoniae* • *Escherichia coli* and other Enterobacteriaceae • *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* • ***Candida* species • Beta-hemolytic streptococci If you grow these → treat as true infection.**

• Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) — only 10-12% true infection • ***Corynebacterium* species (diphtheroids) • *Bacillus* species** (not *anthracis*) • *Propionibacterium acnes* • ***Micrococcus* species Single bottle CoNS in stable patient = likely contaminant.**

info.h: When to Suspect TRUE CoNS Infection
info.t: • ≥3 SIRS criteria present (probability 72.3%) • ≥2 SIRS criteria + central venous catheter • Multiple positive bottles from separate draws • Prosthetic valve or device • Time to positivity <14 hours If none of above: High probability of contamination. Consider observation without vancomycin.

• Unnecessary vancomycin therapy (resistance, nephrotoxicity) • Mean 2-4 extra hospital days • $1,000-$5,000 additional cost per episode • Drives antibiotic resistance • Delays appropriate disposition
• 20-30 mL total (10-15 mL per bottle pair) • Each additional mL increases yield by 3% • Under-filling is the most common error • Do NOT "save" bottles by under-filling
• Chlorhexidine/alcohol preferred over povidone-iodine • Allow to dry completely before venipuncture • Reduces contamination by 30-50% • Avoid touching the site after prep
• Initial ~0.5-1 mL of blood diverted away from culture bottle • Reduces contamination by average 64% • IDSA/ASM 2024: Strongly recommended • Worth the small additional cost

• 2 peripheral venipunctures preferred • Draw from separate anatomic sites • If must use line: draw peripheral + line simultaneously, note which is which • NEVER draw only from indwelling catheter (high false-positive rate)

• Obtain before antibiotics when possible • If already on antibiotics: draw at trough (just before next dose) • Do NOT delay antibiotics >1hr to obtain cultures in septic patients • All bottles can be drawn at same time (no need to wait between sets)

| Infection | Bacteremia Rate | |---|---| | Septic shock | 69% | | Severe sepsis | 38% | | Meningitis | 30-50% | | Endocarditis | 95% (3 sets) | | Osteomyelitis | 30-50% | | Febrile neutropenia | 20-30% | | CLABSI | High (variable) |
| Infection | Bacteremia Rate | |---|---| | Complicated pyelonephritis | 19-25% | | Cholangitis | 15-40% | | Healthcare-associated pneumonia | 10-20% | | Severe CAP (ICU) | 14-33% |

| Infection | Bacteremia Rate | Management Changed | |---|---|---| | CAP (non-ICU) | 6-9% | <1% | | Simple cellulitis | <2% | Rarely | | Simple UTI | <5% | Same organism 97% | | Simple pyelonephritis | 19-25% | 2.3% |

Order cultures when: • Pre-test probability exceeds contamination rate (~3%) • Result will change management • Patient has high-risk features (immunocompromised, indwelling device, rigors) Skip cultures when: • False-positive rate likely exceeds true-positive rate • Source-specific culture available (urine, wound) • Low-risk, immunocompetent patient with clear source

Sepsis / Septic Shock • 2 sets from 2 peripheral sites • 20-30 mL total volume • BEFORE antibiotics (but do not delay abx) Suspected Endocarditis • 3 sets from 3 separate sites • Over 1-24 hours (unless unstable) • Before antibiotics (critical for diagnosis) Meningitis / Encephalitis • Before or concurrent with LP • Critical for organism identification • Do not delay antibiotics

Febrile Neutropenia (ANC <500) • Pan-culture (blood, urine, consider fungal) • Low threshold for empiric broad-spectrum Immunocompromised • Solid organ transplant <1 year • Active chemotherapy • HIV with CD4 <200 • Chronic high-dose steroids Healthcare-Associated Infections • Hospital-acquired pneumonia • CLABSI suspected • Surgical site infection
• Rigors / shaking chills (LR 4.7 for bacteremia) • Temperature >39.4°C • Indwelling vascular device • Shapiro score ≥2 • Diastolic BP <40 mmHg (vasoplegia)

The "Big 3" — most specific: • Urinary retention (post-void residual >200 mL) • Saddle anesthesia (perineal numbness) • Bilateral leg weakness or numbness Other features: • Fecal incontinence • Decreased rectal tone • Sexual dysfunction • Progressive bilateral radiculopathy

Risk factors: • IVDU (most common) • Recent spinal procedure (injection, surgery) • Immunocompromised (diabetes, HIV, steroids, chemo) • Indwelling catheter / bacteremia Clinical: • Fever + localized back pain • Point tenderness over spine • Elevated ESR/CRP

• History of cancer (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma) • Unexplained weight loss >10 lbs • Pain worse at night or with rest • Age >50 with new, severe back pain • Failure to improve with conservative treatment
• Significant trauma • Age >65 (osteoporosis risk) • Chronic steroid use • Midline tenderness to palpation • History of osteoporosis
• Pulsatile abdominal mass • Tearing pain radiating to groin/flank • Age >60 with vascular risk factors • Known AAA
Post-void residual (PVR): • Use POCUS or bladder scanner • >200 mL is abnormal and raises suspicion for CES • Ask about urinary retention, hesitancy, incontinence
• Rectal tone — decreased or absent in CES • Perianal sensation — test light touch S2-S5 dermatomes • Voluntary squeeze — absent in severe CES

Saddle anesthesia: • Test light touch over perineum, buttocks, posterior thighs • S2-S5 distribution • Compare left to right Lower extremity: • L4: Medial leg/ankle • L5: Dorsum of foot, first web space • S1: Lateral foot

Test bilateral: • L4: Knee extension (quads) • L5: Great toe dorsiflexion (EHL), ankle DF • S1: Ankle plantarflexion, toe walking Look for: • Bilateral weakness (not just unilateral) • Progressive deficit
• Emergent MRI (gold standard) • POCUS bladder scan while awaiting MRI • Neurosurgery STAT consult • Decompression within 48 hours improves outcomes
Motor: Knee extension (quadriceps) Sensory: Medial leg, medial ankle Reflex: Patellar (knee jerk) Test: Squat and rise, heel walk
Motor: Great toe dorsiflexion (EHL), ankle dorsiflexion Sensory: Dorsum of foot, first web space Reflex: None (or internal hamstring) Test: Heel walk, great toe extension against resistance
Motor: Ankle plantarflexion, toe walking Sensory: Lateral foot, small toe, posterior calf Reflex: Achilles (ankle jerk) Test: Toe walk, single-leg heel raise
Positive: Radicular pain at <60° Sensitivity: 91% for L5/S1 disc herniation Specificity: ~26% Crossed SLR: Pain in affected leg when raising opposite leg • More specific (~88%) for disc herniation
Most effective for acute LBP • Ibuprofen 400-600 mg PO q6-8h • Naproxen 500 mg PO BID • Ketorolac 10 mg PO q4-6h (short-term) Cautions: GI bleed, renal impairment, cardiac disease
• 650-1000 mg PO q6h (max 3g/day) • Less effective than NSAIDs alone • Safe in most patients • Use as adjunct or if NSAIDs contraindicated
For muscle spasm: • Cyclobenzaprine 5-10 mg PO TID × 7-10 days • Methocarbamol 750-1500 mg PO QID • Baclofen 5-10 mg PO TID Cautions: Sedation, fall risk in elderly, abuse potential

Opioids: • No better than NSAIDs for acute LBP • Addiction, hyperalgesia, constipation • Reserve for severe pain refractory to first-line Benzodiazepines: • No evidence of benefit • Addiction risk, sedation Systemic steroids: • Conflicting evidence • Short-term benefit at best

"You have a muscle strain in your back. This is very common and not serious. Most back pain gets better on its own within 2-4 weeks." "Staying active helps you heal faster than bed rest. Light walking and gentle movement are good." "An MRI would show normal age-related changes that everyone has. It wouldn't help your treatment and might lead to unnecessary procedures."
• Stay active — avoid bed rest (harmful) • Light walking encouraged • Avoid heavy lifting for 1-2 weeks • Gradual return to normal activities • Heat or ice for comfort
• Take NSAIDs as prescribed (with food) • Acetaminophen can be used in addition • Muscle relaxants for significant spasm (short-term) • Avoid alcohol with medications

URGENT — Return immediately if: • Difficulty urinating or loss of bladder control • Loss of bowel control • Numbness in your groin or buttocks • Weakness in your legs getting worse • Fever with back pain • Severe pain not controlled by medications
• PCP in 2-4 weeks if not improving • Physical therapy if symptoms >2-4 weeks • No imaging needed unless red flags develop
• Patient supine, neck extended (unless C-spine) • Operator at patient's side • Laryngeal handshake: Non-dominant hand grips larynx (thumb + middle finger) • Index finger locates CTM from notch DOWN
• 4 cm VERTICAL incision through skin • Start above thyroid notch, extend below cricoid • Cut through skin and subcutaneous tissue • Vertical = more forgiving if landmarks are off
• Use finger to bluntly dissect to CTM • Palpate the soft "trampoline" of the membrane • Maintain laryngeal grip throughout
• HORIZONTAL stab through CTM with #10 scalpel • Cut ~2-3 cm across membrane • Rotate blade 90° caudally • Remove scalpel — keep finger in hole
• Slide bougie alongside finger into trachea • Direct caudally (toward feet) • Feel for "clicking" over tracheal rings • Hold-up at 15-20 cm confirms trachea
• Thread 6.0 ETT over bougie • Advance only until cuff passes incision • Remove bougie, inflate cuff • Confirm with ETCO₂ waveform
The cricothyroid membrane (CTM) is located between: • Thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple) — above • Cricoid cartilage — below It is the only avascular anterior access point to the airway.
• Height: ~9 mm • Width: ~30 mm • Just large enough for a 6.0 ETT (OD 8.2 mm) • Female and small patients may need 5.5 or 5.0

1. Stand at patient's side (not at head) 2. Grasp larynx with non-dominant hand 3. Thumb + middle finger on lateral thyroid cartilage 4. Index finger palpates from thyroid notch DOWN 5. Feel the "dip" of the CTM between cartilages Validated in RCT as superior to other localization methods.

• Superior thyroid artery/vein — at superior thyroid border • Anterior jugular veins — lateral to midline • Cricothyroid artery — crosses CTM superiorly (variable) Pearl: Keep incision in lower half of CTM to avoid vessels.

1. #10 scalpel (or #20) — large blade for CTM incision 2. Bougie (gum elastic bougie) — guides ETT placement 3. 6.0 cuffed ETT — fits through CTM; have 5.5 backup That's it. You can do this procedure with just these 3 items.

• CTM height = ~9 mm • 6.0 ETT outer diameter = 8.2 mm • 5.5 ETT OD = 7.5 mm (for small patients) • 5.0 ETT OD = 7.0 mm (smallest practical) Do not use tracheostomy tubes — they are shorter and may dislodge.
• 10 mL syringe (inflate cuff) • BVM • Waveform capnography (ETCO₂) • Suction • Tape or tie (secure tube) • Gauze (bleeding control)
• Tracheal hook (to elevate incision) • Trousseau dilator • Commercial cric kit (if familiar) Do NOT wait for a kit if you have scalpel, bougie, and tube.

Most common complication • Heavy bleeding reported in up to 50% of cases • IGNORE during procedure — this is tactile, not visual • Control with direct pressure AFTER airway secured • Rarely needs ligation or packing • Severe hemorrhage can cause aspiration (rare)
• ETT is longer than tracheostomy tube • Prevention: Advance only until cuff passes CTM • Detection: Absent left-sided breath sounds • Treatment: Withdraw ETT until bilateral breath sounds
• Bougie or ETT enters pre-tracheal soft tissue • Prevention: Feel for bougie "clicking" over tracheal rings • Hold-up should occur at 15-20 cm • Treatment: Remove and re-attempt with finger guidance
• From overly aggressive scalpel or deep insertion • Can cause esophageal injury • Prevention: Controlled horizontal incision, don't plunge • May lead to mediastinal air or infection
• Subglottic stenosis (long-term) • Voice changes • Scar formation This is why conversion to formal tracheostomy is recommended within 24-72 hours.

info.pt: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation — Quick Steps
info.t: - Video laryngoscope (hyperangulated preferred) - Flexible endoscope with ETT pre-loaded - Suction x2 - 4% lidocaine + atomizer - Glycopyrrolate 0.2mg IV (antisialagogue) - Low-dose ketamine drawn - Paralytic drawn and ready (rescue)

info.pt: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation — Quick Steps
info.t: VL Operator: Behind patient's LEFT shoulder FE Operator: Behind patient's HEAD Patient: Semi-Fowler (30-45 degrees) Monitor: Split-screen over bed

info.pt: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation — Quick Steps
info.t: 1. VL insertion - Obtain laryngeal view, hold with left hand, suction in right 2. FE insertion - Look in mouth, advance to blade tip, then use VL screen 3. Cord passage - Spray lidocaine, advance through cords to carina 4. Railroad ETT - Advance pre-loaded tube until visible on FE screen 5. Withdraw scope - Confirm ETT 2-3cm above carina 6. Confirm - Waveform capnography mandatory

info.pt: Video-Assisted Flexible Endoscopic Intubation — Quick Steps
info.t: "The right speed is SLOWER than your instincts." — Strayer & Caputo, ACEP Now 2022

9 mg/kg lean body weight (DAS ceiling); 7 mg/kg conservative target — calculate BEFORE starting! 70 kg lean body weight: - 7 mg/kg: max 490 mg (~12 mL of 4%) - 9 mg/kg: max 630 mg (~16 mL of 4%) - 4% lidocaine = 40 mg/mL - Toxicity has been reported at 6.0–9.3 mg/kg lean body weight
- 4% lidocaine, 4-5 mL - Low flow (4-8 L/min) - 10-15 minutes - Anesthetizes entire upper airway
- MAD device with 4% lidocaine - Spray tonsillar pillars - Spray posterior pharynx - Spray base of tongue/vallecula
"Spray as you go" - 2-3 mL of 4% lidocaine - Through FE working channel - Directly onto vocal cords - Wait 30-60 sec before advancing
- Perioral numbness, metallic taste - Tinnitus, visual changes - Lightheadedness, confusion - Seizures, arrhythmias If suspected: STOP lidocaine, support airway, consider lipid emulsion
Goal: Anxiolysis + comfort, maintains reflexes - 0.3-0.5 mg/kg IV (20-30 mg typical) - OR titrate 20 mg aliquots q2 min - Patient arousable, follows commands - Breathing preserved
Ketamine-Only Breathing Intubation - 1-2 mg/kg IV - OR 25 mg aliquots q15 sec until dissociated - Patient fully dissociated but breathing - Cannot follow commands

⚠️ ALWAYS have paralytic drawn and ready - Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg - OR Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg Why? - Laryngospasm can occur - Increased muscle tone may impair view - Patient may gag, cough, adduct cords
- Hypotension in catecholamine-depleted patients - Emergence reactions (midazolam can help) - Increased secretions (use antisialagogue) - May increase ICP (controversial)
Blood/secretions: - VL operator suctions aggressively - Clear pharynx before FE insertion Fogging: - Warm scope in warm water - Anti-fog solution - Wipe lens on mucosa

Awake patient: - More lidocaine to cords via FE channel - Wait 30-60 sec - Ask for deep breath, advance during inspiration Laryngospasm: - STOP, withdraw scope - Give paralytic (that's why it's drawn!)
Most common - catches on right arytenoid Solutions: 1. Rotate ETT 90° counterclockwise 2. Withdraw and re-advance 3. Jaw thrust by VL operator 4. Try smaller tube (6.5 or 6.0) DO NOT FORCE
1. STOP procedure 2. Remove FE and VL 3. BVM with 100% O2 4. If can't ventilate → SGA 5. If CICO → Cricothyrotomy

Anatomically Difficult/Distorted: - Angioedema (most common) - Ludwig angina / deep neck infection - Oropharyngeal abscess / hematoma - Laryngeal or orofacial trauma - Airway tumors / masses - Prior H&N surgery or radiation
- Micrognathia / retrognathia - Limited mouth opening (trismus) - Morbid obesity - Failed 3-3-2 rule - Mallampati IV - History of difficult intubation
- "Scared to paralyze" patients - Failed VL (can still oxygenate) - C-spine immobility + predicted difficult airway - Need continuous visualization (laryngeal trauma)
- Massive upper airway bleeding - Complete airway obstruction - Impending arrest / no time - Severely uncooperative patient Most are RELATIVE — aggressive suctioning can address secretions

Match technique to hook and location: | Technique | Success Rate | Best For | |-----------|--------------|----------| | Retrograde | 30-40% | Barbless, superficial | | String-yank | 65-90% | Small-medium hooks, fixed body parts | | Advance-and-cut | >95% | Large hooks, barb near surface | | Needle-cover | 60-70% | Sensitive areas (face, ear) |
Simplest but lowest success rate 1. Apply downward pressure on shank 2. Back hook out along entry path 3. Stop if resistance felt Best for: Barbless or minimally embedded hooks

Most commonly used, minimal trauma 1. Wrap string around hook bend 2. Press shank firmly DOWN toward skin 3. Quick jerk parallel to shank direction 4. Wear eye protection (hook flies!) CONTRAINDICATION: Earlobes, free-floating skin

Almost always successful 1. Anesthetize exit point 2. Advance hook through skin until barb exits 3. Cut barb off with wire cutters 4. Back remainder out through entry Best for: Large hooks, failed string-yank
For sensitive areas 1. Anesthetize thoroughly 2. Insert 18G needle along entry tract (bevel toward hook) 3. Engage barb in needle lumen 4. Back out hook and needle together Best for: Face, ear, nose

Understanding hook anatomy guides technique selection: Eye: Loop at top for line attachment Shank: Straight portion from eye to bend Bend: Curved portion (hook shape varies by design) Point: Sharp penetrating tip Barb: Angled projection preventing easy removal (key challenge) Gap/Gape: Distance from point to shank (determines penetration depth)

Single-barbed: Most common recreational hook. All techniques applicable. Treble hook: Three hooks joined at eye (lures). Tape uninvolved points. Use advance-and-cut: cut shank, pull through. Multiple-barbed: Commercial fishing. Often need advance-and-cut. Barbless: Catch-and-release. Simple retrograde removal usually works.

The barb is the key challenge: - Prevents simple backward removal - Must be disengaged (string-yank), sheathed (needle-cover), or removed (advance-cut) - Barb direction determines technique approach - Larger barbs = more tissue trauma Clinical tip: Have patient describe or draw the hook if not visible.
1. Explore wound for retained foreign body (bait, debris) 2. Irrigate thoroughly with saline or tap water 3. Leave wound open (do NOT suture) 4. Apply triple antibiotic ointment 5. Simple dressing

| Last Booster | Clean Wound | Contaminated | |--------------|-------------|---------------| | <5 years | No Td | No Td | | 5-10 years | No Td | Td | | >10 years | Td | Td + TIG | | Unknown | Td | Td + TIG |

NOT routinely indicated Consider antibiotics for: - Immunocompromised patients - Diabetes or PVD - Deep wounds (tendon, cartilage, bone) - Saltwater exposure (Vibrio coverage) - Heavily contaminated wounds - Delayed presentation (>24h)
Return to ED if: - Increasing pain, redness, swelling after 48h - Purulent drainage - Fever >101F (38.3C) - Red streaking from wound - Wound opening Follow-up: PCP in 3-5 days OR sooner if concerns

Tools: - [ ] Needle driver or hemostat - [ ] Wire cutters (MUST cut hook metal) - [ ] 18-gauge needle Anesthesia: - [ ] Lidocaine (without epinephrine) - [ ] 25-27 gauge needle for infiltration Antiseptic: - [ ] Povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine String-yank supplies: - [ ] 0-silk suture, fishing line, or umbilical tape (~18 inches) Safety: - [ ] Eye protection for patient AND provider

1. Remove all attached line, bait, lures 2. Clean area with antiseptic 3. Tape or cut uninvolved hooks on treble hooks 4. Position patient comfortably with good lighting 5. Put on eye protection (mandatory for string-yank) 6. Consider digital block for finger/toe involvement

String-yank: Often NO anesthesia needed (fastest, least painful) All other techniques: Local infiltration around hook Digital block: For finger/toe involvement TIP: Adequate anesthesia improves patient cooperation and technique success.

Bloody stool / "currant jelly" - mucus + blood + sloughed mucosa Bilious vomiting - indicates complete obstruction Abdominal distension - progressive obstruction Peritoneal signs - rebound, guarding, rigidity Shock - tachycardia, poor perfusion, hypotension
Lethargy or altered mental status - may be ONLY symptom in young infants Painless intussusception - rare but occurs Pallor and hypotonia - nonspecific but concerning
<3 months old: Higher risk of pathologic lead point (surgical consult early) >5 years old: Lead point in ~30% (consider CT to evaluate)
Peritonitis - rebound, guarding, rigidity Pneumoperitoneum - free air on X-ray Hemodynamic instability / Shock - despite resuscitation *These patients go directly to surgery*
Probe: Linear high-frequency (children), curvilinear for larger patients Approach: Systematic scan of all quadrants Focus: Right upper quadrant (most common location)

!Target Sign Appearance: Concentric rings of alternating echogenicity Size: Usually ~3 cm diameter Components: - Hypoechoic outer rim = edematous bowel wall - Hyperechoic center = mesentery and trapped fat - Multiple layers visible
When viewing along the length of the intussusception: - Elongated, kidney-shaped structure - Also called "sandwich" or "hayfork" sign - Layers visible along the length
Normal flow: Good prognostic sign Absent/reduced flow: Concerning for ischemia - higher risk *Absence of Doppler flow suggests vascular compromise - consider early surgical consultation*

- Free peritoneal fluid - prolonged/severe case - Absent Doppler flow - vascular compromise - Large trapped fluid - edema and ischemia - Left-sided location - advanced, harder reduction - Visible lead point - will likely need surgery
Sensitivity: >97% Specificity: >97% Negative Predictive Value: 99.7% *A negative US by experienced sonographer effectively rules out ileocolic intussusception*
Pathologic lead points occur in ~10% of pediatric intussusceptions overall. The vast majority (90%) are idiopathic - thought to be due to lymphoid hyperplasia (Peyer patches) from viral illness.
Higher risk of lead point even though intussusception is rare at this age. If intussusception occurs in this age group: - Idiopathic in ~75% - Lead point in ~25% - Obtain surgical consultation early
Peak age for intussusception Mostly idiopathic (viral-triggered lymphoid hyperplasia) Lead point in ~3-5% Good candidate for enema reduction

Lead point in ~30% - much higher! Common lead points: - Meckel diverticulum (most common, ~75%) - Polyps (~15%) - Lymphoma (especially older children) - Henoch-Schonlein purpura (intestinal involvement) - Duplication cysts Consider CT scan to evaluate for lead point before/after reduction Earlier surgical consultation recommended
Meckel Diverticulum - most common (75%) Polyps - 15% of lead points Lymphoma/Tumors - 3% Duplication cyst Lymphangioma Henoch-Schonlein purpura - vasculitis causing bowel wall hematoma

- Age <3 months or >5 years - Recurrent intussusception (3+ episodes) - Visible mass on ultrasound within intussusception - Failed reduction without obvious cause - Small bowel-small bowel intussusception with symptoms

Peritonitis - Rebound tenderness - Guarding - Rigidity - Exquisite tenderness Pneumoperitoneum - Free air on abdominal X-ray - Signs of perforation Hemodynamic Instability / Shock - Persistent tachycardia - Hypotension despite fluids - Poor perfusion - Altered mental status from shock *These patients require IMMEDIATE SURGICAL INTERVENTION*

These are NOT absolute contraindications, but reduction is more likely to fail: - Symptom duration >48 hours - Rectal bleeding or bloody stool - Severe dehydration - Small bowel obstruction on X-ray - Prolapsing intussusception (through rectum) - Left-sided location on imaging - Absent Doppler flow - Free fluid on ultrasound

Air (pneumatic) reduction: 80-95% success Hydrostatic (saline) reduction: 73-86% success Factors decreasing success: - Longer symptom duration - Younger age - Lethargy - Fever - Bloody diarrhea - SBO on X-ray - Left-sided intussusception - Pathologic lead point

Overall perforation rate during reduction: 0.5-1% If perforation occurs: - STOP the procedure - Decompress if tension pneumoperitoneum - Immediate surgical consultation - IV antibiotics - Emergent laparotomy
Minimum 4 hours observation after successful reduction (CHOP guideline) Some institutions observe 6-24 hours, but evidence supports shorter observation for stable patients.
Begin clear liquids 2 hours post-reduction Advance diet as tolerated If tolerating PO well - good sign for discharge
- Vital signs q1-2 hours initially - Serial abdominal exams - Watch for return of symptoms: - Episodic crying/pain - Vomiting - Abdominal distension - Lethargy
Recurrence rate: 8-10% Most recurrences occur within 24-48 hours If recurrence suspected: - Repeat ultrasound - Can attempt repeat enema reduction - After 3 recurrences: surgical intervention
- Observation period completed (4+ hours) - Tolerating oral intake - Asymptomatic - Reliable caregivers with transportation - Close follow-up available - Understand return precautions
- Age <36 months (some guidelines) - Unable to tolerate PO - Prolonged symptoms prior to reduction - Multiple reduction attempts required - Concern for lead point - Social concerns / poor follow-up
First-Line: DOACs (no bridging required) • Apixaban: 10 mg BID × 7 days → 5 mg BID • Rivaroxaban: 15 mg BID × 21 days → 20 mg daily *Both are single-drug approaches without parenteral bridging.*

CHEST 2021: DOAC or LMWH preferred over warfarin • Apixaban — preferred (lowest GI bleeding) • LMWH — if GI malignancy, drug interactions, or poor oral intake - Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BID - Dalteparin 200 U/kg daily × 30d → 150 U/kg daily Duration: Indefinite while cancer active
⚠️ DOACs and WARFARIN are CONTRAINDICATED • LMWH: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BID (weight-based) • Do NOT use once-daily dosing in pregnancy Duration: Throughout pregnancy + ≥6 weeks postpartum
CrCl 30-50: DOACs okay with dose adjustments CrCl 15-30: Apixaban preferred (5 mg BID) CrCl <15/Dialysis: Apixaban 5 mg BID, warfarin, or UFH *Avoid LMWH in dialysis (accumulates)*
⚠️ DOACs are INFERIOR to warfarin for APS • Use warfarin, target INR 2-3 • Triple-positive APS may need INR 3-4 • TRAPS trial showed higher thrombosis with rivaroxaban
• Apixaban — lowest GI bleeding among DOACs • Consider LMWH (partially reversible with protamine) • May need shorter duration therapy (3 months)
• Standard DOAC dosing appears effective • Consider drug-specific anti-Xa levels if concern • Alternative: warfarin or LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring

Compression Ultrasonography (CUS) • Compress vein with transducer every 1-2 cm • Normal: vein completely compresses (walls touch) • DVT: vein does NOT compress (thrombus visible) Standard locations: Common femoral → superficial femoral → popliteal

Definition: Popliteal vein or above (femoral, iliac) Risk: 40-50% have subclinical PE Management: • ALL proximal DVTs require anticoagulation • Minimum 3 months duration • Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis for iliofemoral DVT with: - Onset <14 days - Good functional status - Low bleeding risk

Definition: DVT limited to tibial, peroneal, or muscular veins Natural history: 15-25% propagate to proximal within 2 weeks Options: 1. Anticoagulate — severe symptoms, high extension risk 2. Serial imaging — repeat US at 1 week, then 2 weeks - If propagates → anticoagulate
Wells ≥2 + Negative US: • 5-7% still have DVT on repeat • Recommend repeat US in 5-7 days • Or whole-leg US • Consider CT/MR venography if iliac DVT suspected
May be missed on standard CUS Consider CT or MR venography if: • Bilateral leg swelling • Abdominal/back pain • Pregnancy (iliac compression) • Pelvic mass • Left leg DVT in young woman (May-Thurner)

Very Limited Indications: Absolute: • Acute proximal DVT/PE with TRUE contraindication to anticoag - Active major bleeding - Recent major surgery with high bleed risk - Hemorrhagic stroke NOT Indications: • "High bleeding risk" without active bleeding • Prophylaxis in trauma • Free-floating thrombus (anticoagulate) • Patient preference ⚠️ Filters do NOT reduce mortality and increase long-term DVT risk

First: Confirm compliance and therapeutic levels On DOAC: • Switch to LMWH, or • Increase dose, or switch DOAC On LMWH: • Increase dose by 25-33% • Check anti-Xa levels On Warfarin: • Switch to LMWH or DOAC Consider IVC filter only if recurs despite therapeutic anticoag

Limb-threatening DVT • Massive iliofemoral DVT • Triad: severe pain, cyanosis, massive edema • Risk of venous gangrene Management: • Immediate anticoagulation • Urgent vascular/IR consult • Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis • May need fasciotomy
• Often catheter-related or Paget-Schroetter syndrome • Similar anticoagulation principles • Consider catheter removal if related • Lower PE risk than lower extremity DVT
Examples: Major surgery, trauma, hospitalization >3 days, cast Duration: 3 months, then STOP Recurrence risk: <3% per year after stopping
Examples: Long flight, oral contraceptives, minor surgery, minor trauma Duration: 3 months minimum, consider extended Recurrence risk: ~5% per year after stopping

Definition: No identifiable risk factor Duration: Extended/indefinite (PREFERRED) • Or 3 months minimum, then reassess Recurrence risk: 10% at 1 year, 30% at 5 years • Males have higher recurrence than females
Duration: INDEFINITE while cancer active • Reassess if cancer in remission • Apixaban or LMWH preferred over warfarin
Duration: INDEFINITE anticoagulation
Reduced-dose DOAC: • Apixaban 2.5 mg BID • Rivaroxaban 10 mg daily *Similar efficacy with lower bleeding (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE)* Aspirin: Inferior but better than nothing if anticoag stopped
• Unprovoked DVT • Male sex • Positive D-dimer 1 month after stopping • Residual thrombus • Prior VTE • Active cancer • Antiphospholipid syndrome • Strong thrombophilia
• Provoked by major transient risk factor • High bleeding risk • Falls risk • Patient preference • Poor compliance expected

• New-onset psychiatric symptoms without prior history (63% have organic cause) • Age >45 with first psychiatric presentation • Age <12 with behavioral emergency • No prior psychiatric history • Abrupt onset (organic tends to be sudden) • Recent head trauma • Recent medication change (especially anticholinergics, steroids)

• Abnormal vital signs (T >100.4°F, HR <50 or >100, BP <100 or >180/110, RR <8 or >22, SpO2 <95%) • Altered level of consciousness (drowsy, obtunded, fluctuating) • Visual hallucinations (rare in primary psychiatric illness) • Disorientation to person, place, or time • Memory impairment (recent memory) • Focal neurologic deficits • Catatonia (immobility, mutism, posturing)

• Elderly (≥65) — delirium missed 76% of the time • Immunocompromised (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy) • Known chronic illness (diabetes, renal, hepatic, thyroid) • Substance use — intoxication or withdrawal • Polypharmacy — drug-drug interactions
Any red flag = organic until proven otherwise. Medical workup before psychiatric disposition.
• Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal • Metabolic acidosis (DKA, uremia, toxic alcohols) • Ammonia (hepatic encephalopathy)

• Hyponatremia (common with SSRIs, diuretics) • Hypercalcemia, hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia • Thyroid (hyper = anxiety; hypo = depression) • Cushing, Addison, pheochromocytoma • Postictal state, nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE)
• UTI (most common in elderly women) • Pneumonia, sepsis • Meningitis, encephalitis (autoimmune encephalitis increasing) • HIV-related CNS infections
• Intentional or accidental overdose • Hypoxia (PE, pneumonia, CO) • Opioid toxicity (respiratory depression, miosis)
• Uremic encephalopathy • Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
• Hypothermia, hyperthermia (heat stroke) • Head trauma, subdural hematoma • Wernicke encephalopathy (give thiamine before glucose)
• The "6th vital sign" — always check fingerstick glucose • Can mimic ANY psychiatric presentation • Insulinoma misdiagnosed as psych in 64% of cases
• Primary psychiatric illness (if all organic ruled out) • Toxins: CO, heavy metals, anticholinergics, serotonin syndrome, NMS
• Stroke (especially frontal, temporal) • Postictal state, NCSE • Tumor, abscess, subdural • SAH, VP shunt malfunction
Delirium present if BOTH of: 1. Acute onset or fluctuating course 2. Inattention PLUS EITHER: 3. Altered level of consciousness 4. Disorganized thinking
Ask family/caregiver: • "Is this a change from baseline?" • "Has the mental status fluctuated (come and go) today?"
Test with any of: • Spell WORLD backward • Say months of year backward (Dec → Jan) • Count backward from 20 to 1 Abnormal: >2 errors = inattention
RASS ≠ 0 (anything other than calm and alert) • Hyperactive: agitated, restless, combative • Hypoactive: drowsy, lethargic (MOST COMMONLY MISSED)

Ask questions: • "Will a stone float on water?" • "Are there fish in the sea?" • "Does one pound weigh more than two?" • "Can you use a hammer to pound a nail?" Observe for: • Rambling, irrelevant speech • Unclear or illogical flow of ideas
Original CAM: 94-100% sensitive, 90-95% specific bCAM (brief): 84% sensitive, 96% specific when done by physician Takes <2 minutes
Delirium: Acute (hours to days) Psychiatric: Chronic/subacute (days to weeks) or recurrent episodes
Delirium: Fluctuates throughout the day (waxes and wanes) Psychiatric: Relatively stable within a day
Delirium: Impaired (cannot focus, easily distracted) Psychiatric: Usually intact
Delirium: Altered (drowsy, agitated, or fluctuating) Psychiatric: Clear and stable
Delirium: Visual hallucinations common Psychiatric: Auditory hallucinations more common (command voices, commentary)
Delirium: Often disoriented (person, place, time) Psychiatric: Usually oriented
Delirium: Impaired recent memory Psychiatric: Memory usually intact
Delirium: Disrupted, often reversed day-night cycle Psychiatric: May have insomnia but no reversal
Delirium: Often abnormal (fever, tachycardia) Psychiatric: Usually normal
If visual hallucinations, fluctuating consciousness, or disorientation are present → assume delirium until proven otherwise.

• Encephalitis — autoimmune increasing; psychosis, catatonia, OCD-like behaviors • Complex partial seizures — temporal lobe; altered behavior, postictal state • Stroke/TIA — frontal or temporal; personality change, aphasia • Subdural hematoma — elderly on anticoagulants • Neurosyphilis — resurgence (70% increase); psychosis, mania, personality change • Parkinson disease — depression/anxiety precede motor symptoms • Huntington disease — psychiatric symptoms precede chorea

• Hyperthyroidism — anxiety (60%), panic, psychosis • Hypothyroidism — depression (treatment-resistant); severe = "myxedema madness" • Hypoglycemia — anxiety, confusion, bizarre behavior, seizures • Cushing syndrome — depression, anxiety in 50%+ • Pheochromocytoma — mimics panic attacks; episodic HTN + anxiety • Adrenal insufficiency — fatigue, depression

• Hyponatremia — common with SSRIs, diuretics; confusion, agitation • Hypercalcemia — cognitive impairment to obtundation • Uremia — encephalopathy with advanced renal disease • Hepatic encephalopathy — asterixis, confusion • B12 deficiency — depression, irritability, delirium, psychosis, OCD

• UTI — most common delirium cause in elderly women • Pneumonia — especially in elderly, immunocompromised • Sepsis — encephalopathy often first sign before fever • HIV/AIDS — CNS infections, dementia complex

• Alcohol withdrawal — delirium tremens, hallucinations • Benzodiazepine withdrawal — anxiety, seizures • Anticholinergic toxicity — agitation, hallucinations, dry/hot • Serotonin syndrome — agitation, hyperthermia, clonus • NMS — rigidity, hyperthermia, AMS with neuroleptics • CO poisoning — multiple affected people, headache
• ACS — can present as confusion in elderly • PE — sense of impending doom mimics panic • Arrhythmia — palpitations, anxiety

• Full vitals including orthostatic BP — POTS masquerades as vertigo • Fingerstick glucose, full neuro exam, gait test • Characterize the dizziness — true vertigo vs lightheaded vs disequilibrium • Focus on TIMING and TRIGGERS, not sensation quality

• AVS — Acute Vestibular Syndrome: constant hours-days + spontaneous nystagmus → HINTS pathway • t-EVS — Triggered Episodic: brief <1 min, positional → BPPV pathway • s-EVS — Spontaneous Episodic: min-hours, no trigger → VM / TIA pathway

• Deadly D's screen BEFORE HINTS — dysarthria, dysphagia, diplopia, dysmetria, dysphonia, downbeat nystagmus • Red flags: severe headache, neck pain, focal deficit, truncal ataxia, cannot walk • Any positive → immediate stroke workup

• BPPV history confirmation • Dix-Hallpike test — posterior canal = upbeat-torsional nystagmus • Epley maneuver for posterior canal — 80-95% single-session success • Horizontal canal — supine roll test + Gufoni/Barbecue (NOT Epley) • Verify cure → discharge with Brandt-Daroff if needed

• Confirm HINTS appropriateness — requires continuous vertigo + spontaneous nystagmus • Step 1: Nystagmus assessment — remove fixation! • Step 2: Head Impulse Test — Normal HIT = worrisome (counterintuitive) • Step 3: Test of skew — vertical skew = central • Step 4: Bedside hearing (HINTS+) — new unilateral loss = AICA stroke • All 4 reassuring → vestibular neuritis → treatment • Any central → stroke pathway
• VM criteria — 50% have NO headache! • Meets criteria → acute migraine treatment → discharge • Risk stratify for TIA if doesn't meet VM • High risk → TIA workup, low risk → outpatient
• VN admission criteria → admit or discharge • Vestibular medication principles — suppressants max 72h • Vestibular rehabilitation — most effective intervention

info.h: ⚠️ "Soup Nazi" Rules — HINTS only applies when ALL are true
info.t: • Continuous vertigo (AVS) — NOT episodic, NOT BPPV • Spontaneous nystagmus present at rest • No central red flags (already screened — Deadly D's) • Patient is currently symptomatic (not between episodes) Using HINTS on BPPV or asymptomatic patients will give dangerously misleading results. Normal HIT in a healthy person is normal — if you interpret it as worrisome, you will over-image. If you interpret a BPPV patient's transient positional nystagmus as "spontaneous," you will misclassify them.

Must remove visual fixation (peripheral nystagmus suppresses with fixation): • Frenzel goggles (ideal) • Ophthalmoscope trick (view one fundus while patient covers other eye) • "Paper trick" — blank paper 10 cm from face Peripheral pattern (reassuring): unidirectional, horizontal-torsional, follows Alexander's law Central pattern (worrisome): direction-changing, pure vertical (especially downbeat), pure torsional, does not suppress with fixation

• Patient fixates on your nose • Rapidly thrust head ~20° side to side (small amplitude, high velocity) • Watch for corrective saccade ⚠️ Counterintuitive rule: • Abnormal HIT (saccade) = peripheral lesion = REASSURING • Normal HIT (no saccade) in AVS = CENTRAL = WORRISOME Why: peripheral lesions impair the VOR on one side, so eyes fall off target. A patient with severe vertigo but intact VOR means the vestibular apparatus is working — so the lesion must be central.
• Alternate cover test — rapidly cover and uncover each eye • Watch for vertical refixation movement No skew = peripheral Vertical skew present = CENTRAL (most specific HINTS finding, spec ~98%)

• Finger rub bilaterally • Whisper test • Weber + Rinne if loss detected New unilateral SNHL + vertigo = AICA stroke until proven otherwise. The labyrinthine artery is a branch of AICA — infarction causes combined hearing + vestibular symptoms that mimic labyrinthitis.

Impulse Normal (HIT without saccade) Fast-phase Alternating (direction-changing nystagmus) Refixation on Cover Test (skew deviation) Any one of these = central = stroke workup. Peripheral (INFARCT-negative) = all 3 reassuring findings present.

HINTS sensitivity is 100% in expert hands (Kattah 2009). In non-neurologist hands, sensitivity is much lower (Nelson 2011). Practice on well patients with spontaneous-appearing peripheral-pattern nystagmus videos. If you are uncertain about your findings, default to imaging.

Purpose: diagnose posterior canal BPPV and identify the affected ear. Technique (testing right ear): 1. Patient seated on exam table, legs extended 2. Turn head 45° to the right 3. Rapidly lay patient supine with head extending 20° off the end of the table 4. Maintain head turn throughout 5. Observe the eyes for 30-45 seconds 6. Return to sitting, watch for reversal nystagmus 7. Rest 1 minute, repeat on left side Positive test (posterior canal BPPV): • Latency 5-20 seconds • Upbeat-torsional nystagmus (top poles beat toward downward ear) • Crescendo-decrescendo, <1 minute duration • Reverses on sitting up • Vertigo accompanies nystagmus

• Pure vertical (downbeat) nystagmus • Direction-changing nystagmus • No latency • Does not fatigue • Duration >1 minute • Associated focal neuro signs → consider central positional vertigo; image the posterior fossa.

For right-sided posterior canal BPPV: Position 1: Start in Dix-Hallpike right (head 45° right, supine with head hanging 20°). Hold 30-60 seconds or until nystagmus subsides. Position 2: Without lifting the head, rotate it 90° to the left so patient now faces left (head still extended). Hold 30-60 seconds. Position 3: Roll the entire body onto the left side while rotating the head another 90° so patient is looking at the floor (face-down position). Hold 30-60 seconds. Position 4: Slowly bring patient to seated position with head tilted down and turned 45° toward the affected (right) side. Hold 30 seconds. Success rate: 80-95% with a single maneuver (NNT=2 in Cochrane review). May repeat 2-3 t
