• Not extending the head enough off the edge (need 20°) • Lifting the head off the table between positions — breaks the maneuver • Not holding each position long enough for otoconia to migrate (30-60 sec minimum) • Testing on the wrong side • Waiting for the patient to "recover" between positions — actually worsens outcomes • Prescribing post-maneuver positional restrictions — not evidence-based Do NOT test for fatiguability (outdated, delays treatment).

Peripheral nystagmus suppresses with fixation. If you don't remove fixation, you may miss it entirely. Methods: • Frenzel goggles — high-plus lenses + light, blurs patient's vision while magnifying eyes for examiner. Gold standard but rarely available in ED. • Ophthalmoscope trick — ask patient to cover one eye. Look at the OTHER eye's fundus with a direct ophthalmoscope. Nystagmus direction appears reversed (horizontal movement of the posterior pole). • "Paper trick" — hold a plain white sheet of paper ~10 cm from patient's face. Nothing to fixate on. Less sensitive but accessible.

• Unidirectional — fast phase always in the same direction regardless of gaze • Horizontal + torsional (mixed pattern) • Suppresses with fixation • Alexander's law: amplitude increases on gaze toward the fast phase • Patient is "awake" and engaged • Associated with abnormal HIT and no skew

• Direction-changing — beats right on right gaze, left on left gaze (gaze-evoked) • Pure vertical — especially downbeat nystagmus (cerebellar/brainstem) • Pure torsional (without horizontal component) • Does NOT suppress with fixation • Out of proportion to vestibular symptoms (prominent nystagmus, minimal vertigo, or vice versa) • May be associated with saccadic abnormalities

Positional-only nystagmus (BPPV): transient, occurs only with specific positions, not spontaneous. Not used for HINTS. Downbeat nystagmus: cervicomedullary junction lesion (Chiari, MS, tumor, ischemia). Almost always central. Upbeat nystagmus: pontomedullary or cerebellar lesion. Central. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN): changes direction every 1-2 minutes. Central (cerebellum, Chiari, drugs). Pendular nystagmus: equal velocity in both directions (not fast/slow phases). Usually congenital or acquired from MS / brainstem stroke.

Diagnosis: Dix-Hallpike — upbeat-torsional nystagmus with latency Treatment: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning) Alternative treatment: Semont maneuver, Brandt-Daroff exercises (home) Success: 80-95% with single Epley

Diagnosis: Supine roll test (Pagnini-McClure) — purely horizontal nystagmus Subtypes: • Geotropic (canalithiasis): nystagmus beats toward the ground on both sides. Affected side = stronger nystagmus. More common, easier to treat. • Apogeotropic (cupulolithiasis): nystagmus beats toward the ceiling. Affected side = weaker nystagmus. Less common, harder to treat. Treatment: • Gufoni maneuver — easier to perform in ED • Barbecue Roll (Lempert) — alternative • Do NOT use Epley — specific to posterior canal Success: 70-80% for canalithiasis; lower for cupulolithiasis

Very rare. Diagnosis: downbeat-torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike. ⚠️ Warning: pure downbeat nystagmus is almost always central — anterior canal BPPV is a diagnosis of exclusion after imaging. Treatment: Reverse Epley or deep head-hanging maneuver. Specialist referral recommended.

Use when: ED maneuvers fail, refractory BPPV, patient cannot return for repeat treatment. Technique: 1. Sit on edge of bed, head 45° to LEFT 2. Quickly lie down on RIGHT side 3. Hold 30 seconds or until vertigo stops 4. Sit up, hold 30 seconds 5. Head 45° to RIGHT, lie down on LEFT side 6. Hold 30 seconds, sit up Regimen: 5 reps per session, 3 times daily, for 2 weeks or until 2 consecutive symptom-free days. Warn patients that initial symptoms worsen before improving.

• Failed 2-3 in-ED attempts • Horizontal canal (especially cupulolithiasis) • Suspected anterior canal • Multiple recurrences • Atypical features suggesting central cause • Fall risk in elderly requiring formal vestibular PT

Canalithiasis = loose crystals rolling in a canal. Cupulolithiasis = crystals stuck to the cupula sensor. Otolith dysfunction = the utricle/saccule level sensor is still giving imperfect balance signals after the canal problem is gone. Analogy: • Canalithiasis = gravel rolling in a hose • Cupulolithiasis = gravel stuck to a hinge • Otolith dysfunction = a wall level that still reads crooked

Free-floating otoconia move through a semicircular canal with gravity. Typical pattern: • Brief triggered vertigo • Positional nystagmus usually <1 minute • Latency before nystagmus starts • Fatigues with repeated testing • Responds well to canalith repositioning maneuvers

Otoconia adhere to the cupula, making the cupula gravity-sensitive. Typical pattern: • Positional nystagmus may start quickly • Nystagmus can persist >1 minute • Less fatigable • More refractory to standard maneuvers • Horizontal canal apogeotropic nystagmus often suggests cupulolithiasis For horizontal canal BPPV, apogeotropic nystagmus means the affected side is usually the side with LESS intense nystagmus.

The utricle and saccule detect gravity and linear acceleration. Dysfunction can leave the patient feeling off-balance even when the canalith problem is fixed. Clues: • Repeat Dix-Hallpike or supine roll test is negative • No positional nystagmus remains • Patient reports residual imbalance, rocking, veering, tilt, or motion sensitivity • Epley no longer reproduces the original BPPV pattern Do not keep repeating Epley without positional nystagmus. Consider vestibular PT or ENT/audiology follow-up.

Still positional nystagmus: think persistent BPPV, canal conversion, or cupulolithiasis. No positional nystagmus but still feels off: think residual dizziness or otolith dysfunction. Central red flags: pure downbeat nystagmus, direction-changing nystagmus, focal neuro findings, new severe headache/neck pain, inability to walk, or new hearing loss. These are not explained by BPPV nuance.
Peripheral: Often sudden but gradually improves. Patient feels better with stillness. Central: Sudden or gradual, may progress. Often no improvement with stillness.

Peripheral: Severe vertigo, prominent nausea/vomiting, patient often prefers to stay still with eyes closed. Central: Often less severe subjective vertigo but more imbalance and gait dysfunction. "Disconnect" between the vertigo severity and the exam findings is a red flag.

Peripheral: • Unidirectional • Horizontal-torsional (mixed) • Suppresses with fixation • Alexander's law Central: • Direction-changing • Pure vertical (especially downbeat) or pure torsional • Does NOT suppress with fixation • Gaze-evoked patterns
Peripheral: Abnormal (catch-up saccade) — reassuring Central: Normal (no saccade) in AVS patient — worrisome (counterintuitive)
Peripheral: Usually spared in vestibular neuritis. Affected in labyrinthitis (rare). Central: New unilateral SNHL = AICA stroke until proven otherwise.
Peripheral: Unsteady but can walk with assistance. Falls toward affected side. Central: Often cannot walk unaided. Truncal ataxia — cannot sit upright. "Cannot walk" is a critical red flag.

Peripheral: Isolated vestibular symptoms. No CN, cerebellar, sensory, or motor deficits. Central: May have Deadly D's, focal weakness, Horner syndrome, sensory loss, crossed signs (face on one side, body on the other), Wallenberg syndrome.

Peripheral: Negative MRI (vestibular neuritis has no imaging correlate). Central: MRI-DWI positive for ischemia — but 20-35% false-negative in first 24-48h for posterior fossa. Repeat MRI at 48-72h if clinical suspicion high.

1. ≥5 episodes of vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity, lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours 2. Current or previous history of migraine with or without aura (ICHD-3 criteria) 3. ≥50% of vestibular episodes accompanied by at least ONE migrainous feature: • Headache with migraine characteristics (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by activity) • Photophobia AND phonophobia • Visual aura 4. Not better explained by another vestibular or ICHD-3 diagnosis
• ≥5 episodes of vestibular symptoms 5 min-72 h • EITHER migraine history OR migrainous features during episodes (not both required) • Not attributable to another cause

~50% of vestibular migraine attacks occur WITHOUT headache. This is why the diagnosis is commonly missed in the ED. Ask specifically: • Any photophobia or sound sensitivity during the episodes? • Any visual disturbance (flashing lights, blind spots, zigzag lines)? • History of childhood motion sickness? • Personal or family history of migraine? • Trigger relationships (sleep, stress, hormones, foods)? A patient with recurrent episodic vertigo + history of migraine + no other explanation has vestibular migraine until proven otherwise.

• Most common cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo in adults • Lifetime prevalence ~1-3% • F:M ratio ~3:1 • More common than Ménière disease • Often starts after typical migraine has improved (e.g., perimenopause) • Underdiagnosed by a factor of 5-10x

• Ménière disease — requires fluctuating SNHL, tinnitus, aural fullness • BPPV — brief positional attacks • Posterior circulation TIA — vascular risk factors • Cardiac arrhythmia — ECG mandatory in recurrent s-EVS • Anxiety / panic — diagnosis of exclusion

Role: Rule out intracerebral hemorrhage or mass effect before thrombolytics or in altered patients. ⚠️ Sensitivity for acute posterior fossa ischemia: 7-16%. CT cannot rule out posterior circulation stroke. Do NOT reassure based on a negative CT. When to get CT: Suspected hemorrhage, altered mental status, anticoagulation, thunderclap headache, before LP or thrombolytics.

info.h: MRI with DWI — test of choice
info.t: Gold standard for posterior circulation stroke — but with important caveats: • False-negative rate ~20% in first 24 hours for small posterior strokes (Oppenheim 2000) • ~35% miss rate within first 6 hours in small lacunar or brainstem strokes • Repeat MRI at 48-72 hours if first study negative and clinical suspicion persists Do NOT discharge a patient with AVS and central features based on a negative early MRI alone.

Indications: • Suspected vertebrobasilar stenosis or occlusion • Suspected dissection (especially with neck pain, recent manipulation, trauma) • TIA workup in high-risk s-EVS • Assessment for thrombectomy eligibility CTA: Fast, widely available, good for bony anatomy and dissection. MRA: No radiation, no contrast (TOF), better for intracranial vessels. Time of flight (TOF) or contrast-enhanced.

• Classic BPPV — brief positional episodes, positive Dix-Hallpike, normal neuro exam. Imaging is unnecessary and low-yield. • Young patient with typical vestibular migraine — clinical diagnosis. • Clear orthostatic cause — treat, do not image. • Peripheral HINTS pattern with expert exam — HINTS is more sensitive than early MRI in these patients (Kattah 2009). ⚠️ Exceptions where you should still image: • Any new focal neurologic deficit • Age >60 with vascular risk factors and spontaneous episodic symptoms • First episode with atypical features • Progressive or crescendo pattern

Posterior circulation strokes are missed in ~35% of cases in US EDs (Arch 2016, Saber Tehrani 2014). Common reasons: • Reliance on negative CT • Anchoring on "labyrinthitis" diagnosis • Not performing HINTS correctly • Discharging without repeat imaging when clinical suspicion remains • Attributing symptoms to medications or anxiety Mitigation: systematic TITRATE approach + appropriate imaging + HINTS by trained examiners + willingness to admit diagnostic uncertainty.

• Posterior circulation strokes account for ~20-25% of all ischemic strokes • Brainstem strokes have 1-year mortality 20-30% • Vertebral artery dissection causes up to 20% of posterior strokes in patients <45 • Cerebellar strokes can cause fatal edema requiring decompression within 48-72 hours

CT sensitivity for acute posterior fossa ischemia: 7-16% (multiple studies). Reasons: • Posterior fossa bone artifact • Small stroke size • Limited early ischemic changes CT is useful to exclude hemorrhage but cannot rule out posterior circulation stroke.

Oppenheim 2000: ~20% false-negative rate for acute stroke in first 24 hours. Simonsen 2015: Sensitivity for posterior circulation stroke was lower than for anterior circulation, especially in first 48 hours. Saber Tehrani 2014: Small strokes (<10 mm) in pons, medulla, and lateral medulla had ~35% false-negative rate on first DWI within 48 hours of symptom onset. Implication: A single negative early MRI does not rule out stroke. Repeat imaging at 48-72 hours is the standard when clinical suspicion remains high.

Kattah 2009: In 101 AVS patients, HINTS examination by experienced neuro-ophthalmologists: • Sensitivity for stroke: 100% • Specificity: 96% • Superior to early MRI-DWI (sensitivity ~88% in first 48 hours) • All HINTS-central patients had stroke on repeat imaging Critical caveat: This was performed by neuro-ophthalmology specialists, not ED providers. Nelson 2011 showed much lower accuracy in non-specialists. Newman-Toker 2013: HINTS outperformed ABCD2 score for identifying stroke in acute continuous vertigo.

Arch 2016: Retrospective review of 465 patients ultimately diagnosed with ischemic stroke. ~35% were initially missed by ED or neurology services. Posterior circulation strokes were 2.3-fold more likely to be missed than anterior strokes. Common errors: • Misattribution to "labyrinthitis" or "vestibular neuritis" • Reliance on negative CT • Not performing HINTS (or performing it incorrectly) • Discharge without follow-up imaging when symptoms persist • Underweighting vascular risk factors Vulnerable populations: isolated vertigo without other neuro signs, young patients (dismissed as "benign"), patients with "normal" early MRI.

• Neck pain or occipital headache + vertigo = suspect vertebral dissection • Recent neck manipulation (chiropractic) or trauma (including minor) • Young patient (<50) • Horner syndrome • Crossed signs (Wallenberg syndrome) • CTA/MRA head and neck is essential

You have a condition affecting your inner ear or the balance system in your brain. Your doctor has examined you and determined this is most likely a benign (non-dangerous) cause. The dizziness should gradually improve over days to weeks as your brain adjusts.

• Meclizine (Antivert) 25 mg: take 1 tablet every 6-8 hours AS NEEDED for severe symptoms. Do not use for more than 3-5 days — longer use actually slows recovery. • Ondansetron (Zofran) 4 mg: dissolves on your tongue. Take as needed for nausea, up to 3 times per day. • Avoid sleeping pills, sedatives, and alcohol — they make balance worse.

info.h: The most important thing you can do
info.t: MOVE. Do NOT stay in bed. Bed rest makes dizziness last longer. The sooner you get up, walk around, and do your normal activities, the faster your brain will reset its balance system. • Walk around your home as soon as you feel able (with someone to help if unsteady) • Try turning your head from side to side while walking • Look up, down, and side to side throughout the day • Some brief dizziness with movement is normal and helpful — your brain is re-learning • Slowly increase activity each day

This is the single most effective treatment for your symptoms. It is more effective than any medication for long-term recovery. • Ask your primary care doctor for a referral to a vestibular-trained physical therapist • You can find certified therapists at vestibular.org • Start as soon as possible — earlier treatment means faster recovery • Even if you feel better, 2-3 PT sessions can significantly speed up your full recovery

• Remove loose rugs and clutter from walking areas • Use nightlights in bedroom and hallway • Hold handrails on stairs • Sit down when putting on pants or shoes • Ask for help with tasks requiring balance or reaching • Do not drive until your doctor says it is safe • Elderly patients: consider a cane or walker temporarily

info.h: Return to the ER immediately if you develop:
info.t: • New weakness in face, arm, or leg • Trouble speaking or slurred speech • Double vision or new vision loss • Severe headache or new neck pain • Hearing loss in one ear • Cannot walk at all • Persistent vomiting and cannot keep fluids down • Symptoms get much worse instead of gradually improving • Fall with injury

• Primary care doctor within 1 week • Vestibular physical therapy as soon as possible • ENT (ear/nose/throat) if your primary care doctor recommends • Neurology if your symptoms are not improving after 2 weeks

• TIF = catastrophic complication of tracheostomy (0.1-1% incidence) • Near-100% mortality without intervention; 50-70% mortality with surgery • Critical time window: 3 days to 6 weeks post-tracheostomy • Sentinel bleed precedes massive hemorrhage by 24-48 hours • Pathognomonic triad: sentinel bleeding, tube pulsating with heartbeat, stoma bleeding

• First-line maneuver for TIF bleeding • Add ~50 mL air to tracheostomy cuff balloon • Success rate: 85% for controlling hemorrhage • Goal: tamponade bleeding vessel by compressing against tracheal wall • This is temporizing only - surgery still required

• Utley maneuver: Insert finger through stoma, compress innominate artery against sternum • First secure airway with oral ETT • Remove tracheostomy tube • Insert index finger through stoma into pretracheal space • DO NOT release until surgeon takes over in OR

• Call CT surgery/vascular surgery STAT • All TIF patients go directly to OR • Definitive treatment: ligate AND divide innominate artery • Ligation without division = contraindicated (can re-fistulize) • Mortality without surgery approaches 100%

• Do NOT remove tracheostomy tube unless proceeding to finger tamponade • Do NOT delay for imaging (CTA/bronchoscopy only 20-30% sensitive) • Do NOT suction aggressively during active bleeding • Do NOT release finger tamponade before surgical takeover • Do NOT ligate without division (risk of re-fistulization)

The Utley maneuver is the lifesaving bedside intervention when cuff hyperinflation fails to control TIF hemorrhage. Success rate >80% for controlling hemorrhage via direct digital tamponade of the innominate artery.
• Deflate tracheostomy cuff • Insert cuffed oral ETT deep (cuff 2 cm past stoma) • Inflate ETT cuff • Confirm ventilation before proceeding
• With airway secured via oral ETT, remove tracheostomy tube • May need to extend stoma incision vertically for finger access • Do not hesitate to extend if stoma is too small
• Insert index finger through stoma into pretracheal space • Use blunt dissection to create space if needed • Advance finger anteriorly toward sternum
• Compress innominate artery anteriorly against posterior sternum/manubrium • Apply firm, steady pressure • Innominate crosses anterior to trachea at rings 6-9
• Place thumb in sternal notch • "Pinch" the artery between finger (internal) and thumb (external) • This provides additional tamponade
• Do NOT release until patient is in OR under surgical care • You are now physically attached to this patient • Transport to OR with finger in place • Surgeon must be ready to take over immediately

info.h: DO NOT Remove Tube Unless Doing Utley
info.t: • The tracheostomy tube provides tamponade and maintains airway • Removing it prematurely leads to uncontrolled hemorrhage and airway loss • Only remove if you are proceeding directly to finger tamponade with oral airway secured

• CTA, bronchoscopy, and angiography combined have only 20-30% sensitivity • Diagnosis is clinical - bleeding 3 days to 6 weeks post-tracheostomy = TIF until proven otherwise • Time spent imaging is time lost for definitive surgical management

• Ligation alone is contraindicated • Artery can re-fistulize if not divided • Surgical management requires ligate AND divide innominate artery proximal and distal to fistula • Cover tracheal defect with muscle flap

• Once Utley maneuver is started, you are committed • Maintain pressure until surgeon takes over in OR • You will be physically attached to the patient during transport • Releasing early = uncontrolled hemorrhage and death
• May dislodge protective clot • May worsen bleeding • Gentle suctioning only if needed for airway
• Sentinel bleed is a WARNING, not reassurance • Massive hemorrhage follows within 24-48 hours in 50% of cases • Use this window to prepare for surgery and OR

• Classic pentad (all 5 present in <5% of cases): MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic changes, renal dysfunction, fever • Modern diagnosis: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + no alternative explanation • Key labs: schistocytes on smear, elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, low/undetectable haptoglobin, normal coagulation studies • Direct Coombs test: negative (not immune-mediated hemolysis)

• Platelet count <30,000 (+1) • Combined hemolysis variable (reticulocyte >2.5%, haptoglobin undetectable, or indirect bilirubin >2) (+1) • No active cancer (Lack of malignancy) (+1) • No stem cell or organ transplant (Absence of transplant) (+1) • MCV <90 fL (Small MCV) (+1) • INR <1.5 (Mild coagulopathy) (+1) • Creatinine <2.0 mg/dL (Impaired renal function absent) (+1) Score interpretation: 0-4 = low risk (0-4%), 5 = intermediate (24%), 6-7 = high risk (72-96%)

• TTP: ADAMTS13 <10%, normal coags, often neurologic symptoms • HUS: Shiga-toxin associated (E. coli O157:H7), renal failure predominates, often pediatric • aHUS: Complement-mediated, ADAMTS13 normal, may have genetic predisposition • DIC: Abnormal coags (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen), elevated D-dimer • HELLP: Pregnancy-associated, elevated liver enzymes

• Do NOT wait for ADAMTS13 results to start treatment • TPE: 1-1.5 plasma volumes daily until platelet count >150,000 x 2 days • Methylprednisolone: 1 g IV daily x 3 days, then 1 mg/kg/day • If TPE unavailable: transfuse FFP as bridge (10-15 mL/kg) • Do NOT transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleeding or pre-procedure

• Caplacizumab: 11 mg IV load before first TPE, then 11 mg SC daily • Rituximab: 375 mg/m² weekly x 4 for refractory/relapsing disease • Hold rituximab infusion until 4+ hours after TPE to avoid drug removal • Consider caplacizumab for all patients (reduces time to platelet normalization and recurrence)

• All TTP patients require ICU admission • Daily CBC, LDH, haptoglobin to monitor response • ADAMTS13 activity at diagnosis and during treatment • Watch for neurologic changes (can fluctuate rapidly) • Troponin at baseline (cardiac involvement common) • Continue TPE until sustained remission (platelets >150K x 2 days)

Thrombotic microangiopathies (TMAs) share features of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and thrombocytopenia. Distinguishing the underlying cause is critical because treatments differ significantly.

• ADAMTS13: <10% (diagnostic) • Coagulation studies: Normal PT, PTT, fibrinogen • Renal involvement: Mild (Cr usually <2) • Neurologic symptoms: Common (50-70%): confusion, headache, seizure, stroke • Triggers: Idiopathic, autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, drugs (quinine, ticlopidine) • Treatment: TPE + steroids + caplacizumab

• ADAMTS13: Normal (>10%) • Coagulation studies: Normal • Renal involvement: Severe (dialysis often needed) • Neurologic symptoms: Less common than TTP • Typical HUS: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7), bloody diarrhea prodrome, often pediatric • aHUS: Complement-mediated, may have genetic mutations (CFH, CFI, MCP) • Treatment: Typical HUS = supportive. aHUS = eculizumab (complement inhibitor)

• ADAMTS13: Normal • Coagulation studies: Abnormal (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer) • Renal involvement: Variable • Neurologic symptoms: Variable • Triggers: Sepsis, malignancy, trauma, obstetric complications • Treatment: Treat underlying cause, transfuse products as needed

• ADAMTS13: Normal (usually >10%) • Coagulation studies: Usually normal (unless DIC develops) • Renal involvement: Variable • Neurologic symptoms: Headache, visual changes (associated preeclampsia) • Distinguishing features: Elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT), pregnancy (usually 3rd trimester or postpartum) • Treatment: Delivery of fetus

| Feature | TTP | HUS | DIC | HELLP | |---------|-----|-----|-----|-------| | ADAMTS13 | <10% | Normal | Normal | Normal | | PT/PTT | Normal | Normal | Prolonged | Normal | | Fibrinogen | Normal | Normal | Low | Normal | | D-dimer | Mild ↑ | Mild ↑ | Markedly ↑ | Mild ↑ | | Creatinine | Mild ↑ | Markedly ↑ | Variable | Variable | | LFTs | Normal | Normal | Variable | Elevated | | Pregnancy | Possible trigger | Rare | Possible | Required |

• Volume: 1-1.5 plasma volumes daily (typically 40-60 mL/kg) • Replacement fluid: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or cryosupernatant • Frequency: Daily until remission • Remission criteria: Platelet count >150,000/μL for 2 consecutive days + normalizing LDH • Taper: Some centers taper (every other day x 2-3) before stopping • If TPE unavailable: Transfuse FFP 10-15 mL/kg as temporizing measure

• Induction: Methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily x 3 days OR 10 mg/kg/day (max 1 g) • Maintenance: Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day PO after IV pulse • Taper: Gradual taper over weeks once in remission • Rationale: Suppresses autoantibody production against ADAMTS13 • Start steroids immediately with TPE - do not wait for ADAMTS13 confirmation

• Loading: 11 mg IV bolus before first TPE • Maintenance: 11 mg SC daily after each TPE, then continue for 30 days after last TPE • Extension: If ADAMTS13 <10% after 30 days, extend up to 28 additional days • Mechanism: Blocks vWF-platelet interaction (anti-vWF nanobody) • HERCULES trial: 74% reduction in TTP-related death/recurrence/major thromboembolism • Bleeding risk: Monitor for epistaxis (29%), gingival bleeding (16%)

• Refractory TTP: No response to TPE + steroids after 3-5 days • Relapsing TTP: Recurrence after initial remission • Prophylaxis: ADAMTS13 persistently <20% during remission (prevents relapse) • Dosing: 375 mg/m² IV weekly x 4 weeks • Timing with TPE: Administer immediately after TPE; hold next TPE for ≥4 hours to prevent drug removal • HBV screening: Required before starting (risk of reactivation)

• General rule: AVOID platelet transfusion in TTP • Concern: May worsen microvascular thrombosis ("fuel on the fire") • Exceptions: - Life-threatening hemorrhage - Required for central line placement or other urgent procedure - Active CNS hemorrhage • If transfusion required: use smallest effective dose, continue TPE aggressively

• Daily: CBC with platelet count, LDH, haptoglobin • ADAMTS13 activity: At diagnosis, during treatment, and at remission • Response indicators: Rising platelets, falling LDH, improving symptoms • Exacerbation: Platelets fall within 30 days of stopping TPE • Relapse: Platelets fall >30 days after stopping TPE • Long-term: Monitor ADAMTS13 q3-6 months (relapse risk if <10-20%)

Review prior CBCs, repeat the CBC if unexpected, and ask the lab to review a peripheral smear. Platelet clumping or EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia can create a false low count and should not trigger transfusion or admission by itself.

Critical bleeding, CNS or posterior eye bleeding, massive GI bleeding, obstetric hemorrhage, airway bleeding, shock, or urgent invasive procedure changes the first move. Resuscitate, call blood bank early, and use platelet targets based on bleeding site and procedure risk.
Before calling it ITP, actively exclude TTP/TMA, DIC/sepsis, HIT, pregnancy/postpartum emergencies, and marrow failure or acute leukemia. These are the diagnoses where delay changes outcome.

If the dangerous screen is negative, sort by pattern: isolated immune destruction, drug-induced thrombocytopenia, liver/splenic sequestration, alcohol or marrow suppression, infection/systemic illness, or chronic baseline.

info.h: 5. Disposition by risk, not by number alone
info.t: Admission is usually needed for bleeding, suspected TTP/TMA, DIC, HIT requiring non-heparin anticoagulation, pregnancy danger patterns, blasts/pancytopenia, platelets <10k, rapidly falling counts, unreliable follow-up, or need for IVIG/transfusion/procedure.
Pseudothrombocytopenia: platelet clumping on smear, unexpected isolated low count, no bleeding phenotype. Repeat in citrate or heparin tube.
ITP, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, HIT, TTP/TMA, DIC, post-transfusion purpura, autoimmune disease, viral-associated immune thrombocytopenia.
Acute leukemia, aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, chemotherapy/radiation, marrow infiltration, alcohol, B12/folate deficiency, severe infection, medication marrow suppression.
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension, splenomegaly, hypersplenism, massive transfusion, pregnancy-related dilution, chronic liver disease.

Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and well appearing. Severe thrombocytopenia, hypertension, RUQ pain, headache, renal injury, hemolysis, elevated LFTs, or bleeding should trigger HELLP, preeclampsia, AFLP, TTP/HUS, DIC, and ITP evaluation.

Repeat CBC with differential, peripheral smear, CMP with creatinine and LFTs, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer when ill/bleeding/pregnant or DIC concern, type and screen when severe or bleeding, pregnancy test when applicable.

LDH, haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, reticulocyte count, urinalysis, creatinine, and smear for schistocytes. Send ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor before plasma exposure if feasible, but do not delay hematology escalation.

Use 4Ts before testing. Low 4Ts should generally not be tested. Intermediate/high probability: stop heparin, send PF4/heparin immunoassay, and confirm with functional assay such as serotonin release assay when needed.

Add HIV and hepatitis C testing when unexplained. Add B12/folate, thyroid testing, autoimmune testing, tickborne/travel testing, or imaging for splenomegaly only when the clinical pattern supports it.

- Stable hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia: prophylaxis often at <10k. - Fever, sepsis, rapid fall, or added bleeding risk: consider <20k. - Active major bleeding or most invasive procedures: target at least 50k. - CNS bleeding, posterior eye bleeding, neurosurgery, or critical-site procedure: often target 100k with specialist input.

Avoid routine platelet transfusion in suspected TTP/TMA or HIT unless there is life-threatening bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure. In ITP, platelet transfusion is usually reserved for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedure and should be paired with disease-directed therapy such as IVIG and corticosteroids.

One adult apheresis unit often raises platelets by about 30k to 60k in a non-consuming patient. Response is lower with immune destruction, DIC, sepsis, splenomegaly, fever, ongoing bleeding, or alloimmunization.
Recheck CBC 10 to 60 minutes after transfusion when the response matters. Trend fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, calcium, temperature, pH, and bleeding source in major hemorrhage.

Platelet fall usually begins 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure, or sooner with recent exposure. Clues include >50% platelet fall, new thrombosis, skin necrosis, anaphylactoid reaction after IV heparin, and absence of a better explanation.

Low probability 4Ts 0 to 3: HIT unlikely, avoid reflex testing. Intermediate/high probability 4Ts 4 to 8: stop all heparin products, send PF4/heparin immunoassay, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant unless bleeding risk prohibits it.

Non-heparin options include argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or selected DOAC pathways depending on acuity, renal/hepatic function, thrombosis burden, procedure needs, and local protocol. Do not start warfarin until platelet recovery.
Do not transfuse platelets routinely in HIT. Reserve for life-threatening bleeding or urgent invasive procedure after specialist discussion.

ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise reassuring CBC and smear after exclusion of TTP/TMA, DIC, HIT, pregnancy emergencies, marrow disease, infection, liver/spleen disease, and drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
Adults with platelets generally >=30k and no significant bleeding are often observed with close hematology follow-up rather than treated immediately.

info.h: When ED treatment is more likely
info.t: Platelets <30k, significant mucosal bleeding, wet purpura, high-risk anticoagulated patient, critical bleeding, urgent procedure, or unreliable follow-up should prompt hematology discussion. Corticosteroids are common first-line therapy; IVIG is used when a faster platelet rise is needed.
Use platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedure, typically with IVIG plus corticosteroids because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed.

Admit or transfer for critical bleeding, recurrent bleeding, suspected TTP/TMA, DIC, intermediate/high probability HIT requiring non-heparin anticoagulation, pregnancy/postpartum danger pattern, blasts/pancytopenia, suspected acute leukemia/APL, severe sepsis, neurologic symptoms, renal injury, rapidly falling platelets, platelets <10k, or unreliable follow-up.

Observation is useful for uncertain trends, pending smear/coag/hemolysis labs, moderate thrombocytopenia with risk factors, post-transfusion response checks, medication washout, or heme/onc planning when the patient is not clearly safe for discharge.

Consider discharge only when the patient is well appearing, has no active bleeding or wet purpura, no schistocytes or blasts, no DIC/HIT/TMA/pregnancy danger pattern, noncritical stable platelet count or clear chronic explanation, medication review completed, and reliable near-term follow-up.

Return immediately for headache, confusion, focal neurologic symptoms, syncope, melena, hematemesis, hematuria, heavy vaginal bleeding, mucosal bleeding, wet purpura, fever, chest pain, dyspnea, new limb swelling/pain, or worsening weakness.

• DIC is always secondary — find and treat the trigger • Most common: sepsis, malignancy (incl. APL), trauma, obstetric, severe organ injury • Two phenotypes: bleeding-dominant (obstetric, trauma, APL) vs thrombotic-dominant (sepsis, Trousseau) • Bleeding from multiple sites + microvascular thrombosis + known trigger = suspect DIC

• ISTH score (≥5 = overt DIC): platelets, fibrin marker (D-dimer/FDP), PT prolongation, fibrinogen — sens 91%, spec 97% • JAAM score (≥4 = sepsis-DIC): adds SIRS criteria, more sensitive in early sepsis-DIC than ISTH • SIC score (≥4 with plt+INR ≥3): identifies progression risk in sepsis before overt DIC • ISTH 2024: trends matter — repeat scores every 6-12 hours during active disease

• Sepsis → source control + abx in 1h, goal-directed resus, SIC scoring • Malignancy → LMWH for Trousseau, treat cancer; APL is bleeding emergency • APL → ATRA 45 mg/m²/day immediately, fibrinogen >150-200, NO heparin or TXA • Obstetric → deliver/evacuate, MTP 1:1:1, cryo to keep fibrinogen ≥2 g/L, TXA 1g IV <3h • Trauma (TIC) → TXA 1g <3h, MTP 1:1:1, fibrinogen ≥1.5-2 g/L, calcium, normothermia

• Source control trumps every other intervention • Antibiotics within 1 hour for sepsis; surgical/IR/OB intervention as indicated • Definitive obstetric management; oncologic therapy; antivenom for snake bite • Most non-overt DIC resolves with trigger control alone — resist "treating the labs"

• Bleeding-dominant → aggressive replacement to thresholds • Platelets ≥0.05 × 10¹²/L if bleeding (≥0.1 if ICH/neuraxial); 1 apheresis unit raises by 30-50 • FFP 15 mL/kg if PT/PTT >1.5× ULN and bleeding (do NOT for labs alone) • Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or 0.06 u/kg) if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (<2 g/L in obstetric); raises by 0.5-1 g/L • 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg if volume-restricted or VKA reversal (selective use, discuss with heme) • Adjuncts: TXA in trauma/PPH/TBI; heparin only for thrombotic-dominant without bleeding

• ICU admission for nearly all DIC patients • Emergent hematology consult; source-specific consults (OB, oncology, surgery, IR) • Repeat CBC/PT/PTT/fibrinogen/D-dimer q4-6h during resuscitation, q12h stabilization, daily recovery • Resolution: ISTH <5 sustained ≥48h + trigger controlled + plt >100 + fibrinogen ≥2 g/L • Fibrinogen normalizes last — do not declare resolved on platelet count alone
Transfuse for active bleeding or pre-procedure — not for abnormal labs alone. Prophylactic product transfusion in non-bleeding DIC has not shown benefit and may worsen thrombosis.

• Bleeding: ≥50 × 10⁹/L • ICH / TBI / neuraxial procedure: ≥100 × 10⁹/L • Pre-procedure (LP, central line, surgery): ≥50 × 10⁹/L • Non-bleeding ICU prophylaxis: ≥20 × 10⁹/L • APL: ≥30-50 × 10⁹/L • Dose: 1 apheresis unit raises platelet count by ~30-50 × 10⁹/L; recheck 10-60 min post-transfusion

• Indication: PT or aPTT >1.5× ULN AND active bleeding (or pre-procedure) • Dose: 15 mL/kg IV (typically 4 units for 70 kg adult) • Each unit: ~250 mL • Recheck PT/PTT 30 min post-infusion • Volume burden: caution in CHF, ARDS, pediatrics — consider 4F-PCC alternative • ABO-compatible plasma; AB plasma is universal donor

• Non-pregnant DIC with bleeding: fibrinogen ≥1.5 g/L • Obstetric DIC / PPH: fibrinogen ≥2 g/L (higher because pregnant baseline is 4-6 g/L) • APL / leukemia DIC: fibrinogen ≥1.5-2 g/L • Massive transfusion / TIC: fibrinogen ≥1.5-2 g/L • Dose: 10 units (or 0.06 units/kg) raises fibrinogen by ~0.5-1 g/L in adult; each unit ≈5-10 mL • Contains: fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII, fibronectin • Fibrinogen concentrate (RiaSTAP): 25-100 mg/kg IV; pathogen-reduced and volume-sparing

• Indication: volume-restricted patient with severe coagulopathy + bleeding, or VKA reversal on top of DIC • Dose: 25-50 units/kg IV (Kcentra, Beriplex, Octaplex) - 25 units/kg if INR 2-4 - 35 units/kg if INR 4-6 - 50 units/kg if INR >6 or major bleed - Max 5000 units regardless of weight • Caution in DIC: procoagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X) carry theoretic thrombosis risk in already-procoagulant state — discuss with hematology • Vitamin K co-administration: 10 mg IV if VKA reversal (PCC effect fades in 6-24h)

• Activate early for major hemorrhage (trauma, OB, GI bleed) • Ratio: 1:1:1 (RBC:FFP:platelets) until viscoelastic-guided • Calcium replacement: citrate from products chelates ionized Ca — maintain iCa ≥1.1 mmol/L • Avoid hypothermia: warm fluids, blankets, forced-air warmers (<35°C impairs platelet function and enzyme kinetics) • Correct acidosis: pH <7.2 impairs coagulation enzyme function • Notify blood bank early

• Recheck CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen 30-60 min after each round • Repeat scoring (ISTH) every 6-12 hours during active resuscitation • Adjust products based on viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) when available • De-escalate as trigger is controlled and trends improve
DIC is always secondary. Identify the trigger and jump directly to the etiology-specific pathway. All four converge on the hemostatic resuscitation principles in Module 4.

• Most common etiology — gram-negative > gram-positive • Phenotype: thrombotic / microvascular dominant • Priorities: source control + appropriate antibiotics within 1 hour, goal-directed resuscitation, SIC scoring • Hemostatic support only if bleeding or pre-procedure • Anticoagulation controversial — SIC-positive without bleeding may benefit → Jump to: dic-sepsis

• Solid tumor (Trousseau): chronic, thrombotic-dominant; LMWH first-line • Hematologic (APL): bleeding emergency — 5-10% early death from hemorrhage • Other AML/ALL with high blast counts can also cause DIC • Treat the cancer; LMWH > warfarin for Trousseau • Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion in stable thrombotic-dominant cases → Jump to: dic-malignancy → dic-apl if APL suspected

• Triggers: placental abruption (most common), Amniotic Fluid Embolism, retained products, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, PPH, sepsis (chorioamnionitis, septic abortion) • Phenotype: rapid-onset, bleeding-dominant • Key threshold: fibrinogen ≥2 g/L (pregnant baseline is 4-6 g/L — not <1) • Priorities: definitive obstetric management, MTP 1:1:1, cryo early, TXA 1g IV within 3 hours (WOMAN trial), avoid heparin → Jump to: dic-obstetric

• Mechanism: tissue injury + shock + acidosis + hypothermia + hemodilution; activated protein C-mediated hyperfibrinolysis • Recognition: major trauma, massive transfusion need, lactate >4, abnormal TEG/ROTEM • Priorities: damage control resuscitation, TXA 1g IV bolus + 1g over 8h within 3 hours (CRASH-2), MTP 1:1:1, fibrinogen ≥1.5-2 g/L, calcium replacement, normothermia • TBI exception: permissive hypotension contraindicated — keep MAP ≥80, SBP ≥110; TXA within 3h (CRASH-3) → Jump to: dic-trauma

Reconsider differential: TTP, HIT, primary fibrinolysis, severe liver failure, vitamin K deficiency, transfusion reaction, snake envenomation, heat stroke, Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. → See: dic-ddx and dic-rare

5-10% of APL patients die from hemorrhage in the first days of presentation — usually intracranial. Early death is the leading cause of treatment failure. Suspicion alone is enough to start ATRA. Do NOT wait for cytogenetic confirmation.

• Pancytopenia + circulating promyelocytes • Auer rods, faggot cells on smear • Severe bleeding diathesis at presentation (epistaxis, gum bleeding, mucosal bleeding, ICH) • Markedly elevated D-dimer, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/PTT • PML-RARα fusion (t(15;17)) — confirmed by FISH/PCR (results in hours-days) • Hyperfibrinolysis pattern in addition to consumption

• ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid) 45 mg/m²/day in 2 divided doses — start IMMEDIATELY on suspicion, do NOT wait for cytogenetics • Aggressive cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL (1.5-2.0 g/L) — much higher than non-APL DIC • Platelets to keep ≥30-50 × 10⁹/L; higher if active bleeding or ICH • FFP to correct PT/PTT prolongation • AVOID heparin — historical use abandoned, increases bleeding mortality • AVOID tranexamic acid — controversial, may increase thrombosis (not part of standard APL bundle) • Arsenic trioxide (ATO) is added per oncology protocol once stabilized

• Occurs in 5-25% of patients within 2-21 days of ATRA initiation • Symptoms: fever, weight gain, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, hypotension, AKI • Treatment: dexamethasone 10 mg IV q12h × 3+ days; continue ATRA unless severe • Without prompt treatment, can be fatal

• Emergent heme/onc consult — transfer to tertiary center capable of managing APL after stabilization • ICU admission • Blood bank notification — anticipate massive product needs • Neurology if any neurologic symptoms — low threshold for head CT (ICH most common cause of early death) • Outcomes: with prompt ATRA + arsenic, modern APL has cure rate >90% in patients who survive the first weeks

• PT/INR — extrinsic + common (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen) • aPTT — intrinsic + common (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogen) • Platelets — number • Fibrinogen — substrate for clot • D-dimer — fibrinolysis marker Add peripheral smear; mixing study, anti-Xa, factor assays, TEG/ROTEM as needed.
• Bleeding-dominant — mucosal (platelet/vWF) vs deep tissue (factor) • Thrombotic-dominant — unprovoked, unusual site, young age, recurrent • Mixed — DIC, HIT, APS, TTP — jump to dedicated tree

• Isolated PT — warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, mild liver, FVII def • Isolated PTT — hemophilia A/B, FXI, vWD, lupus AC, heparin, dabigatran, acquired hem A • Both prolonged — severe vitamin K def, liver failure, DIC, supratherapeutic anticoag • Low platelets + bleeding — ITP, DITP, HIT, DIC, TTP, marrow disease • Low fibrinogen + high D-dimer — DIC, primary fibrinolysis, severe liver

• Corrects (≤4 sec of normal) → factor deficiency → specific assays • Does NOT correct → inhibitor (heparin contamination, lupus AC, factor inhibitor, dabigatran) • Incubation 37°C ×1-2 h → lupus AC (immediate non-correction) vs factor inhibitor (time-dependent) • Always rule out heparin contamination first

• Vitamin K / warfarin — vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg if bleeding • Dabigatran — idarucizumab 5 g IV (RE-VERSE AD) • FXa-DOAC — 4F-PCC per local PCC protocol (off-label for DOACs; andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US) • Heparin — protamine 1 mg per 100 units • Low fibrinogen — cryo 10 units (or 0.06 u/kg) raises 0.5-1 g/L • Hemophilia A/B — recombinant factor concentrate; DDAVP for mild hem A • vWD — DDAVP (type 1) or vWF/FVIII concentrate • Hyperfibrinolysis — tranexamic acid 1 g IV

• Cirrhosis — "rebalanced" hemostasis; PT/INR does NOT predict bleeding • Pregnancy — fibrinogen baseline 4-6 g/L; treat <2 g/L (not <1) • HIT — 4Ts ≥4: stop ALL heparin, NO platelet transfusion, start argatroban/bivalirudin • APS triple-positive — warfarin (NOT DOACs) • Thrombophilia testing — 4-6 wk after stopping anticoag, only if would change management

• Pro-coagulant: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X • Anti-coagulant: Protein C, Protein S • Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues, enabling factor binding to phospholipid surfaces

• Factor VII — 6 hours (falls FIRST in vitamin K deficiency → isolated PT prolongation initially) • Factor IX — 24 hours • Factor X — 40 hours • Factor II (prothrombin) — 60 hours (falls last) • Protein C falls fast (6-8 h) — important when starting warfarin (transient hypercoagulable state)

• Warfarin or vitamin K antagonist — most common • Malabsorption — cystic fibrosis, IBD, biliary obstruction, pancreatic insufficiency • Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics — kills gut flora that produce vitamin K • Malnutrition / starvation • Newborn — give vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth (prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn) • Cholestyramine and other bile-acid binders

• Oral: 1-10 mg PO; effect in 6-24 hours • IV (slow infusion over ≥20 min): 10 mg IV; effect in 6-12 hours; risk of anaphylactoid reaction with rapid IV (rare) • SC absorption is unreliable — not preferred • Avoid IM in anticoagulated patients (hematoma risk)

| Scenario | Management | |---|---| | INR <4.5, no bleed | Hold warfarin; recheck | | INR 4.5-10, no bleed | Hold; vitamin K 1-2.5 mg PO if high risk | | INR >10, no bleed | Hold; vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO | | Active bleeding (any INR >1.5) | Vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4F-PCC 25-50 u/kg | | Life-threatening bleed | 4F-PCC + vitamin K immediately, hold warfarin | 4F-PCC dosing (Kcentra): • INR 2-4: 25 units/kg (max 2500) • INR 4-6: 35 units/kg (max 3500) • INR >6: 50 units/kg (max 5000)

• 4F-PCC preferred — onset 10-30 min, low volume (~100-200 mL), reliable INR correction, low TRALI/TACO risk • FFP — onset hours, high volume (15 mL/kg ≈ 1 L for 70 kg), often partial correction; use only if PCC unavailable or multifactorial deficiency • Always co-administer vitamin K — PCC effect fades in 6-24 hours; vitamin K provides durable reversal
Use this overlay to identify the platelet disorder and jump to the right consult or workup pathway.

• Diagnosis of exclusion — isolated thrombocytopenia, no other cytopenias, well-appearing patient • Often post-viral in children; chronic autoimmune in adults • Treatment: observe if plt >30 × 10⁹/L and no bleeding; steroids ± IVIG if bleeding or plt <30 • Avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding (transient effect)

• 4Ts score — Thrombocytopenia, Timing (5-10 days from heparin start), Thrombosis, Other cause • Score ≥4 → stop ALL heparin, anti-PF4 ELISA, start argatroban/bivalirudin/fondaparinux • Do NOT transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleeding • Bridge to warfarin only after platelet recovery (warfarin alone in HIT → venous limb gangrene) • Lifelong heparin avoidance; document in chart → See: coag-hit node

• MAHA + thrombocytopenia with normal coags (PT/PTT/fibrinogen) • ADAMTS13 <10% confirms • Pentad rarely complete: MAHA, thrombocytopenia, AKI, neuro, fever • Emergency → plasma exchange + steroids + caplacizumab • Avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding → See: TTP tree

• Common offenders: quinine, vancomycin, sulfa drugs, heparin (HIT), abciximab, linezolid, beta-lactams, NSAIDs • Onset days-weeks after exposure; resolves with drug discontinuation • Treatment: stop offending drug; supportive • Specific antibody testing rarely needed; clinical correlation

• Aplastic anemia, MDS, leukemia, marrow infiltration • Other cytopenias usually present (anemia, leukopenia) • Smear: blasts, dysplastic features, pancytopenia • Workup: peripheral smear, retic count, B12, folate, viral studies (HIV, hepatitis), bone marrow biopsy

• Hypersplenism — cirrhosis, portal hypertension; usually plt 50-100 • Massive transfusion — dilutional thrombocytopenia after 10-15 RBC units • No specific treatment for sequestration; product replacement for dilutional
Most thrombophilia testing does NOT change management. Only test if the result would alter duration of anticoagulation or guide family screening.

• Unprovoked VTE before age 50 • Recurrent unprovoked VTE • VTE in unusual location (cerebral, splanchnic, mesenteric, hepatic, renal vein) • Strong family history (first-degree relative <50 with VTE) • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (suspect protein C deficiency) • Recurrent pregnancy loss • Arterial thrombosis at young age (suspect APS) • VTE despite therapeutic anticoagulation

• NOT during acute thrombosis — alters protein C, S, antithrombin, lupus AC results • NOT on anticoagulation — warfarin lowers protein C/S; heparin lowers antithrombin • 4-6 weeks after stopping anticoagulation is optimal • Genotype tests (FV Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) can be sent anytime

| Test | Method | |---|---| | Factor V Leiden | Genotype (no timing constraint) | | Prothrombin G20210A | Genotype (no timing constraint) | | Protein C activity | Functional assay (time off warfarin) | | Protein S activity | Functional assay (time off warfarin) | | Antithrombin activity | Functional assay (time off heparin) | | Lupus anticoagulant | dRVVT, hexagonal phase (time off anticoag; confirm at 12 wk) | | Anti-cardiolipin IgG/IgM | ELISA (confirm at 12 wk) | | Anti-β2-glycoprotein-I IgG/IgM | ELISA (confirm at 12 wk) | | Homocysteine | Less commonly tested |

• Factor V Leiden (heterozygous) — 5-10% population, 3-8× risk • Factor V Leiden (homozygous) — 1 in 5000, 50-80× risk • Prothrombin G20210A — 2-4% population, 2-3× risk • Protein C deficiency — 7-10× risk; warfarin-induced skin necrosis • Protein S deficiency — 5-10× risk • Antithrombin deficiency — 25-50× risk; rare; severe phenotype

• Sapporo criteria: clinical event (thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity) + lab (lupus AC, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2GP-I) on 2 occasions ≥12 weeks apart • Triple positive = highest thrombosis risk • Treatment: lifelong warfarin (target INR 2-3, or 3-4 in arterial/recurrent) • Avoid DOACs in triple-positive APS (TRAPS, RAPS trials) • Catastrophic APS (CAPS): anticoagulation + steroids + plasmapheresis ± rituximab
• <6 hours → salvage >90% • 6–12 hours → salvage ~50% • 12–24 hours → salvage ~20% • >24 hours → salvage near 0% Every additional 30 minutes of imaging delay measurably reduces testicular survival.

• TWIST 5–7 with cooperative urologist → OR direct • Classic clinical presentation in adolescent (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric) → OR direct • OR available within 30 minutes Ready-room the OR while you call urology — do not wait for the call back to start the process.

• TWIST 3–4 → Doppler ultrasound, but call urology in parallel • Ambiguous presentation in adult • Trauma history that could explain findings • Pediatric atypical presentation Do NOT serially repeat imaging — if Doppler is equivocal in a clinically suspicious patient, that's a surgical exploration indication.

Time-stamp these in the chart: • Pain onset (per patient) • Triage / arrival • First MD eval • TWIST score • Urology contact time • Imaging order → imaging complete • OR time Torsion is the #1 urological malpractice diagnosis. The chart wins or loses the case.

• Patient supine, examiner at the foot of the bed • Adequate analgesia: opioid + spermatic cord block at the external ring (10 mL of 1% lidocaine without epinephrine) • Reassure the patient — procedure is brief but uncomfortable

• Visualize as if reading a book — testicles are the pages • Rotate the affected testicle outward (lateral) from the midline - Right testis → counterclockwise from your view at the foot of the bed - Left testis → clockwise from your view • Torsion is typically 360–720° — plan for 1–3 full rotations • Reassess pain after each rotation
• Sudden pain relief — most reliable sign • Testicle drops to a lower / more horizontal position • Doppler shows return of intratesticular flow • Testicle softens on palpation

• You may be detorsing in the wrong direction • Reverse direction (medial rotation) for the same number of turns • If still worse, stop and proceed to OR • Document direction tried, response, and time

• Even successful detorsion still requires bilateral orchidopexy — ~30% retort • Manual detorsion is a bridge, not a definitive treatment • Do not delay surgical consult to attempt the maneuver — attempt while the OR is being readied • Document direction, turns, pain before/after, Doppler before/after

• Loss of consciousness more than ~30 seconds • Worsening headache, repeated vomiting • Seizure or seizure-like activity • Persistent confusion, agitation, or unequal pupils • Focal neurologic deficit (weakness, numbness, vision change) • Neck pain or midline c-spine tenderness • Suspected skull fracture (Battle sign, raccoon eyes, otorrhea, rhinorrhea) • GCS < 15 at any point or trending down

• Maintain inline immobilization until cleared • Apply NEXUS or Canadian C-Spine Rule once awake and cooperative • Any midline tenderness, neuro deficit, intoxication, distracting injury, or dangerous mechanism = full immobilization and CT cervical spine • If helmet on and properly fitted: do not remove unless airway compromised — transport with helmet in place

• Apply Canadian CT Head Rule or New Orleans Criteria to all minor head injuries • Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs, antiplatelets) lowers threshold dramatically — most experts CT all anticoagulated patients with any head trauma • Children: PECARN rules • Suspected skull base fracture, depressed skull fracture, or focal deficit = CT now

• Catastrophic cerebral edema after a second concussion sustained before symptoms of the first have resolved • Mortality up to 50%; survivors often severely disabled • Largely a pediatric and adolescent phenomenon • Hard rule: no athlete returns to contact same day, ever, after suspected concussion

• All concussions need same-day removal from play and a structured graded RTP protocol • Provide written discharge instructions, observer for 24 h, return precautions (worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, weakness, seizure) • Outpatient concussion clinic or sports medicine follow-up within 1–2 weeks if symptoms persist

• Any blow to head, face, neck, or body with force transmitted to head • Visible signs: dazed, vacant stare, balance issues, clutching head, slow to get up • Reported symptoms: headache, dizziness, fogginess, nausea, photophobia, sensitivity to noise • If suspected — remove from play immediately. "When in doubt, sit them out."

• What venue are we at today? • Which half is it now? • Who scored last in this match? • What team did you play last week? • Did your team win the last game? Any incorrect answer suggests concussion until proven otherwise.
• GCS • Pupils equal and reactive • Cranial nerves • Strength symmetric in 4 limbs • Tandem gait, finger-to-nose • Cervical exam: tenderness, range of motion (only if no red flags)

• Step 1: Symptom-limited daily activity (24–48 h relative rest, then light cognitive activity) • Step 2: Light aerobic exercise (walking, stationary bike) — no impact • Step 3: Sport-specific exercise (running drills, no head impact) • Step 4: Non-contact training drills (more complex; resistance training) • Step 5: Full contact practice (after medical clearance) • Step 6: Return to play Minimum 24 h per stage. If symptoms recur, drop back one stage. Total minimum 6 days, often 1–4 weeks. Pediatric athletes return slower than adults.

• Cognitive rest first 24–48 h: reduce screens, schoolwork, video games • Sleep is therapeutic — normal sleep patterns • No alcohol, no driving until symptom-free at rest • Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin first 24–48 h (bleeding risk) • Acetaminophen okay for headache • Return precautions: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, weakness, seizure, confusion

Use the GINA severity assessment to classify as mild, moderate, severe, or life-threatening. Key indicators: ability to speak (sentences vs. words vs. single words), respiratory rate, heart rate, accessory muscle use, SpO2, and peak flow if obtainable.

• Albuterol continuous nebulization (10-15 mg/hr) or back-to-back MDI (4-8 puffs q20min) • Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized q20min x 3 doses in moderate-severe • Magnesium sulfate 2g IV over 20 min if severe/life-threatening • Consider epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg IM if not responding

• Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 16 mg) PO/IV x1 dose OR • Prednisone/methylprednisolone 1-2 mg/kg (max 60-125 mg) • Give within first hour of presentation • Single-dose dexamethasone is equivalent to 5-day prednisone for most patients

Non-invasive ventilation can buy time and may prevent intubation. Start IPAP 10-12, EPAP 3-5. Titrate to patient comfort and work of breathing. Ketamine sedation may help if patient is too agitated for BiPAP.

Delayed Sequence Intubation (DSI) uses ketamine 1-2 mg/kg to dissociate the patient before paralysis, allowing preoxygenation in patients too agitated to tolerate it. This preserves spontaneous respirations while optimizing conditions.

• Low RR (10-14/min) with long expiratory time (I:E 1:4 or 1:5) • Low tidal volume (6-8 mL/kg IBW) • Permissive hypercapnia is acceptable (pH >7.15) • Watch for auto-PEEP and breath stacking • Target plateau pressure <30 cmH2O
• Talks in sentences • Prefers sitting to lying • Not agitated • RR increased (but <30) • HR <100 • SpO2 >95% • PEF >70% predicted
• Talks in phrases • Prefers sitting, hunched forward • May be agitated • Accessory muscle use • RR 20-30 • HR 100-120 • SpO2 90-95% • PEF 50-70% predicted

• Talks in single words • Sitting hunched forward, tripod position • Agitated • Accessory muscle use prominent • RR >30 • HR >120 • SpO2 <90% • PEF <50% predicted • May have paradoxical thoracoabdominal movement

• Unable to speak / not talking • Drowsy, confused, or exhausted • Silent chest on auscultation • Bradycardia or hypotension • Cyanosis • SpO2 <90% despite O2 • PEF <25% predicted or unable to perform • Respiratory arrest imminent

A "silent chest" in severe asthma is ominous—it indicates such severe airflow obstruction that no wheeze can be generated. Absence of wheeze in a severe asthmatic is a pre-arrest sign, not a reassuring finding.

• IPAP: 10-12 cmH2O (start low, titrate up to 15-20 as tolerated) • EPAP: 3-5 cmH2O (keep low to avoid increasing air trapping) • FiO2: Titrate to SpO2 92-95% • Backup rate: 10-12 if available (not always needed)

• Decrease work of breathing (less accessory muscle use) • Improved patient comfort and decreased agitation • RR trending down toward 20-25 • Able to speak in longer phrases • Improving SpO2 and mental status • Increase IPAP by 2 cmH2O every 5-10 min until improvement (max 20)

• Patient too agitated or uncomfortable to tolerate mask • Ketamine dissociative dose (1-1.5 mg/kg IV): Creates calm, dissociated state while preserving respirations • Low-dose ketamine (0.2-0.5 mg/kg): For anxiolysis without full dissociation • Avoid benzodiazepines and opioids—respiratory depression risk • Ketamine also provides direct bronchodilation

• Altered mental status / unable to protect airway • Facial trauma or burns preventing mask seal • Hemodynamic instability / impending arrest • Vomiting or high aspiration risk • Patient refusal • Upper airway obstruction

• Continuous SpO2, RR, HR monitoring • Reassess every 15-30 minutes • VBG at 1 hour to assess CO2 trend (not required before starting) • Failure to improve in 1-2 hours or worsening = prepare for intubation • Watch for air swallowing (gastric distension)

info.h: Why Asthma Intubation Is High Risk
info.t: • Patients are often hypoxic and cannot tolerate apnea for preoxygenation • Air trapping leads to rapid desaturation post-intubation • Breath stacking and auto-PEEP cause hemodynamic collapse • Post-intubation arrest is common if ventilator settings are wrong • Goal: Avoid intubation if at all possible

DSI uses ketamine to create a dissociated state BEFORE paralysis, allowing: • Apneic oxygenation via high-flow nasal cannula (40-70 L/min) or NRB • Preoxygenation in a patient too agitated to cooperate • Time to optimize conditions before committing to paralysis • Patient breathes spontaneously while dissociated • Once SpO2 optimized, proceed with paralysis and intubation

Dissociative Dose: 1-2 mg/kg IV push • Onset: 30-60 seconds • Duration: 10-20 minutes • Patient will appear "awake" but is dissociated Infusion (if needed): 0.5 mg/kg/hr after initial bolus Bronchodilatory effect: Ketamine causes smooth muscle relaxation—beneficial in asthma independent of sedation

• Preserves respiratory drive (unlike propofol, benzos) • Maintains airway reflexes • Direct bronchodilation via catecholamine release • Inhibits vagal-mediated bronchoconstriction • Does not cause histamine release (unlike morphine, fentanyl) • Maintains hemodynamic stability

Induction: • Propofol 1-1.5 mg/kg (causes bronchodilation but hypotension) • Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg (hemodynamically stable) Paralytics: • Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg (preferred) • Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg (may cause histamine release—less ideal) Avoid: Morphine, meperidine, atracurium (histamine release)
The intubated asthmatic dies from breath stacking and auto-PEEP, not hypoxia. The priority is allowing complete exhalation, even at the cost of permissive hypercapnia. "Low and slow" is the mantra.

| Parameter | Target | |-----------|--------| | Mode | Volume control (AC/VC) | | Tidal Volume | 6-8 mL/kg IBW | | Respiratory Rate | 10-14/min | | I:E Ratio | 1:4 to 1:5 | | PEEP | 0-5 cmH2O (start low) | | FiO2 | Titrate to SpO2 88-92% |

• Target pH >7.15 (not a specific CO2 number) • pCO2 of 60-80 is acceptable and often unavoidable • Higher CO2 is tolerable if pH is maintained • Avoid sodium bicarbonate unless pH <7.10—bicarb generates CO2 • Paralysis reduces CO2 production and may improve pH

Signs of auto-PEEP (breath stacking): • Flow on expiratory limb of vent waveform does not return to zero before next breath • Rising plateau pressures despite unchanged tidal volume • Hypotension (auto-PEEP reduces venous return) • Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony Management: • Decrease RR (longer time for exhalation) • Decrease I:E ratio • Brief ventilator disconnect to allow full exhalation (30-60 sec) • Deep sedation +/- paralysis

• Plateau pressure <30 cmH2O (goal) • Peak pressure will be high (often 40-60) due to airway resistance—this is expected • Plateau pressure reflects alveolar pressure—this is what matters for barotrauma • If plateau >30: decrease tidal volume, increase expiratory time • Check auto-PEEP with inspiratory hold maneuver

• Auto-PEEP causing decreased venous return: disconnect vent briefly • Tension pneumothorax: check for absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation • Sedation-related vasodilation: judicious fluids, vasopressors if needed • Mucus plugging: consider bronchoscopy if unilateral decreased breath sounds • Dynamic hyperinflation: use apnea test (disconnect for 30-60 sec)

- Check POC glucose immediately. - If altered, seizing, or unsafe to swallow: IV dextrose if access, glucagon if no access. - If awake and able to swallow: 15-20 g fast carbohydrate PO. - Do not delay dextrose for confirmatory labs in an unstable patient.

- Recheck glucose in 15 minutes. - Repeat therapy until glucose is >70 mg/dL and symptoms improve. - Once corrected, give longer-acting carbohydrate or meal if medication effect remains active. - If recurrent, start D10W infusion and move to rebound-risk assessment.

- Medication mismatch: insulin, sulfonylurea, meglitinide, pump, duplicate dose. - Intake or substrate: missed meal, vomiting, alcohol, malnutrition, exercise. - Clearance: renal failure, hepatic failure. - Illness: sepsis, shock, hypothermia. - Endocrine: adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism. - Unexplained or non-diabetic: apply Whipple triad and consider critical sample.

- Insulin effect: food if awake, dextrose infusion if recurrent, electrolyte monitoring if overdose. - Sulfonylurea/meglitinide: dextrose for immediate correction plus octreotide for recurrent or high-risk cases. - Critical illness or endocrine cause: treat glucose and the underlying condition in parallel.

Discharge only if glucose remains stable, the cause is clear and reversible, the patient is eating, medications are adjusted, supplies and food access are realistic, and follow-up is reliable. Observe or admit recurrent, medication-driven, unclear, critical illness, renal failure, poor intake, or unsafe cases.

Most common ED bucket. - Insulin: wrong dose, duplicate dose, meal missed after bolus, pump basal error, renal failure reducing clearance. - Sulfonylureas/meglitinides: glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride, repaglinide, nateglinide. - Poor intake, vomiting, alcohol, exercise, frailty, food insecurity, medication confusion.

- Sepsis, shock, hypothermia. - Liver failure or acute hepatic injury. - Renal failure or missed dialysis. - Malnutrition or depleted glycogen stores. These patients often need admission even if the initial glucose corrects.

- Adrenal insufficiency or adrenal crisis. - Hypopituitarism. - Insulinoma or non-islet cell tumor. - Post-bariatric or post-prandial hypoglycemia. - Surreptitious insulin or secretagogue exposure. - Medication effects beyond diabetes drugs, including quinolones, pentamidine, quinine, beta blockers masking symptoms, and other patient-specific exposures.

Consider when fingerstick is discordant with clinical picture or lab delay is plausible: - Poor peripheral perfusion. - Delayed sample processing. - Severe leukocytosis or erythrocytosis. - Capillary meter error. Confirm with plasma glucose if the patient is stable, but do not delay treatment of symptomatic hypoglycemia.

Send during a documented low glucose episode when hypoglycemia is unexplained, recurrent, non-diabetic, medication history is unreliable, or the clinical picture does not fit the stated cause. Draw before dextrose only if doing so does not delay treatment.

- Plasma glucose. - Insulin. - C-peptide. - Proinsulin. - Beta-hydroxybutyrate. - Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen. - Cortisol if adrenal insufficiency is plausible. - Ethanol, renal function, liver panel, lactate, and sepsis labs as clinically indicated.

- High insulin + high C-peptide: endogenous insulin or secretagogue. - High insulin + low C-peptide: exogenous insulin. - Low beta-hydroxybutyrate during hypoglycemia: hyperinsulinemic pattern. - High ketones with low insulin: fasting, alcohol, malnutrition, adrenal or critical illness pattern. Endocrinology input is appropriate for unexplained, recurrent, non-diabetic, or suspected hyperinsulinemic cases.

info.h: Single normal glucose is not disposition
info.t: A corrected glucose proves treatment worked once. It does not prove the medication effect, organ failure, poor intake, or intentional overdose risk has resolved.

info.h: Repeated D50 can worsen sulfonylurea cycling
info.t: Dextrose is required for immediate correction, but recurrent sulfonylurea or meglitinide hypoglycemia needs octreotide because secretagogues continue to drive insulin release.

info.h: Food access and med access matter
info.t: Discharge can fail if the patient cannot eat reliably, cannot check glucose, has no fast carbohydrate, has medication confusion, or cannot adjust the culprit drug.

info.h: Critical illness hypoglycemia is high risk
info.t: Sepsis, liver failure, renal failure, adrenal crisis, hypothermia, and malnutrition are not benign hypoglycemia causes. Treat the glucose and the underlying illness together.

Acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, altered arousal, or sudden loss of baseline function is delirium or medical illness until proven otherwise. Check glucose, oxygenation, vitals, temperature, medication/toxin exposure, pain, urinary retention, constipation, trauma, stroke signs, seizure, and infection clues.

info.h: 2. Put the differential before the label
info.t: Dementia is a syndrome. Consider Alzheimer disease, vascular cognitive impairment, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia, Parkinson disease dementia, normal pressure hydrocephalus, depression, sleep apnea, sensory impairment, medication toxicity, alcohol/substance effects, B12/thyroid/metabolic disease, and rapidly progressive neurologic disease.

Ask family, caregiver, facility, or prior records about baseline cognition, time course, ADLs, IADLs, medication management, finances, driving, wandering, falls, stove/firearms, scams, caregiver capacity, and supervision. Functional loss is the line between cognitive concern/MCI and dementia-level impairment.

Mini-Cog, MoCA, SLUMS, clock drawing, or brief recall/attention testing can support the assessment, but no single ED screen diagnoses dementia. Note hearing, vision, language, education, pain, intoxication, delirium, and fatigue.

Discharge requires medical stability, reliable supervision, medication safety, ability to eat and transfer/ambulate safely, no active wandering or dangerous behavior, and follow-up. Observe, admit, or arrange protected placement when delirium, falls, caregiver failure, unsafe home, poor intake, agitation danger, or capacity limits make discharge unsafe.

- Alzheimer disease: gradual episodic memory and learning decline. - Vascular cognitive impairment: executive dysfunction, stepwise decline, stroke/TIA history, focal signs. - Lewy body dementia: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonism, neuroleptic sensitivity. - Frontotemporal dementia: early behavior, personality, disinhibition, apathy, compulsions, or language-predominant syndrome. - Parkinson disease dementia: parkinsonism established before cognitive syndrome.

- Delirium from infection, hypoxia, dehydration, metabolic disease, medication toxicity, pain, retention, constipation, intoxication, or withdrawal. - Stroke/TIA, ICH/subdural, seizure, CNS infection, tumor, normal pressure hydrocephalus. - Depression, grief, psychosis, sleep apnea, severe hearing/vision loss, isolation. - B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, renal/hepatic failure, sodium/calcium disorders, alcohol use disorder.

Weeks-to-months decline, young onset, focal deficits, seizures, myoclonus, ataxia, early parkinsonism, severe headache, cancer/immunosuppression, systemic inflammatory symptoms, or prominent gait-first presentation should trigger a higher urgency diagnostic pathway.

Use "suspected dementia" or "major neurocognitive disorder pattern" when there is acquired decline from prior baseline, persistent/progressive course, objective cognitive abnormality, functional impact on IADLs or ADLs, collateral support, and reasonable exclusion of delirium or major reversible mimics.

Mild cognitive impairment has objective cognitive concern but preserved functional independence. Dementia-level impairment means cognition is interfering with independence: meds, finances, cooking, shopping, transportation, phone use, bathing, dressing, toileting, eating, or safe supervision.

Preferred wording: "Pattern concerning for dementia; formal outpatient longitudinal evaluation is needed to confirm type and stage." Avoid diagnosing a dementia subtype from one acute visit unless prior documentation already supports it.

An abnormal cognitive screen during infection, intoxication, withdrawal, severe pain, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, or acute hospitalization documents impairment today. It does not establish chronic dementia until the acute syndrome resolves and baseline is reassessed.

info.h: Confusion alone is not a UTI
info.t: Older adults with dementia can have bacteriuria without infection. IDSA recommends assessment for other causes and observation rather than antibiotics when bacteriuria occurs with delirium/confusion but without urinary symptoms or systemic infection signs.

Treat when there are urinary symptoms, flank or suprapubic pain, catheter obstruction/trauma, fever, hypothermia, sepsis physiology, leukocytosis with clinical source, respiratory findings, cellulitis/wound, abdominal source, meningismus, or another convincing source pattern.

Correct dehydration, hypoxia, fever, pain, urinary retention, constipation, medication toxicity, and sleep disruption. Avoid anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and sedatives unless specifically indicated.

- Active delirium or unstable medical illness. - Unsafe gait, recurrent falls, inability to transfer, unsafe ambulation. - Wandering, elopement, stove/firearms/driving risk. - Medication mismanagement with insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, sedatives, or polypharmacy. - Poor intake, dehydration, dysphagia, aspiration risk, failure to thrive. - No reliable caregiver, caregiver burnout, suspected neglect, abuse, or exploitation. - Lacks capacity for discharge decision and no safe surrogate plan.

- Confirm supervision and transportation. - Review medication list and remove high-risk nonessential deliriogenic meds when possible. - Give caregiver return precautions. - Arrange PCP/geriatrics/neurology/neuropsychology follow-up. - Address driving, weapons, wandering, stove safety, fall risk, hydration, nutrition, and med administration.

Use case management/social work for caregiver failure, placement, home health, APS concern, food/med access, transportation, or unsafe discharge. Use PT/OT for gait, transfer, falls, DME, or rehab/SNF questions. Use pharmacy for medication simplification and high-risk drug reconciliation.

info.h: 1. First pass: sick and dangerous screen
info.t: Start with vitals, fever/toxic appearance, immunocompromise, visual acuity, pupils, red eye, EOM, proptosis, cranial nerves, gait, Horner pattern, oral/dental exam, floor of mouth, trismus, dysphagia, skin, ear, and age >50 GCA symptoms.

- Eye/orbit: acute angle closure, keratitis/uveitis, orbital cellulitis, HZO, cavernous sinus process. - Neurovascular: cervical artery dissection, stroke/TIA, SAH/ICH, cavernous sinus thrombosis. - Infection: odontogenic abscess, deep neck infection, Ludwig angina, complicated sinusitis, mastoiditis. - Inflammatory: giant cell arteritis. - Zoster: HZO, Ramsay Hunt, pre-eruptive neuralgia.

Red painful eye, neurologic/vascular symptoms, deep infection signs, age >50 GCA symptoms, or dermatomal zoster signs should move directly to the relevant urgent lane before calling the pain sinus, dental, TMJ, migraine, cluster, or trigeminal neuralgia.

- Triggered electric shocks: trigeminal neuralgia pattern. - Orbital/temporal attacks with autonomic signs and restlessness: cluster/TAC pattern. - Tooth percussion, biting pain, swelling: dental pattern. - Persistent >10 days, severe purulent/febrile, or double-worsening URI: bacterial rhinosinusitis pattern. - Jaw clicking, bruxism, chewing pain: TMJ/myofascial pattern. - Photophobia, nausea, movement sensitivity: migraine/headache pattern.

Admit or consult for ocular emergency, neurovascular concern, deep infection or airway risk, vision-threatening GCA, immunocompromised zoster/complicated infection, toxic appearance, uncontrolled pain, inability to hydrate, unsafe home, or uncertain diagnosis with objective abnormality.

Red painful eye, halos, vomiting, fixed or mid-dilated pupil, decreased vision, photophobia, corneal findings, proptosis, diplopia, painful or restricted EOM, V1 rash, nose-tip lesions, or fever with eyelid/orbital swelling.

Thunderclap onset, focal neurologic deficit, aphasia, diplopia, ataxia, transient monocular vision loss, Horner syndrome, unilateral neck pain, posterior headache, trauma/manipulation, severe sudden headache, anticoagulation, or cancer/immunosuppression.

Toxic appearance, fever, rigors, trismus, dysphagia, drooling, muffled voice, floor-of-mouth elevation, neck swelling, odontogenic swelling, diabetes, immunocompromise, periorbital spread, or pain out of proportion.
Age >50 plus new temporal/scalp/facial pain, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, diplopia, PMR shoulder/hip symptoms, fever, weight loss, scalp tenderness, or abnormal temporal artery.

Dermatomal burning/allodynia, V1 rash, ear vesicles, facial weakness, hearing symptoms, vertigo, immunocompromise, disseminated rash, or ocular symptoms. Pre-eruptive zoster may have pain before visible lesions.

- Acute angle closure glaucoma, keratitis, uveitis, orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis. - Cervical artery dissection, stroke/TIA, SAH, ICH. - Odontogenic deep-space infection, Ludwig angina, mastoiditis, complicated sinusitis. - Giant cell arteritis. - HZO, Ramsay Hunt, disseminated zoster. - Malignancy, invasive fungal sinusitis, osteomyelitis in selected hosts.

- Trigeminal neuralgia: brief electric shocks, V2/V3, triggered by light touch or chewing. - Cluster headache/TAC: strictly unilateral orbital/temporal attacks with autonomic signs or restlessness. - Migraine: unilateral pain with photophobia, nausea, movement sensitivity, prior pattern. - Occipital/cervicogenic referral can involve face/head but should not bypass vascular red flags.

- Dental pulpitis, apical periodontitis, cracked tooth, abscess, cellulitis. - Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis only when persistent, severe purulent/febrile, or double-worsening criteria are met. - Otitis externa/media, mastoiditis, malignant otitis externa in high-risk hosts. - TMJ dysfunction or myofascial pain after dental, eye, infection, and neurovascular threats are addressed.

Unilateral facial pain is commonly mis-labeled as sinus, dental, migraine, or TMJ. The diagnostic task is to prove no eye, vascular, deep infection, GCA, or zoster danger signal is present before settling on a benign phenotype.

Visual acuity is a vital sign for facial pain with eye symptoms. Add fluorescein/slit lamp, IOP when angle closure is plausible, EOM/proptosis exam, and CT orbit/sinuses with contrast when orbital cellulitis, abscess, or cavernous sinus process is possible.

CTA head/neck for dissection, stroke/TIA, Horner plus pain, transient monocular vision loss, thunderclap with vascular concern, or focal neurologic symptoms. Non-contrast CT head first when ICH/SAH is the immediate question. MRI/MRA can follow when suspicion persists.

CT face/neck with IV contrast for deep-space infection, trismus, dysphagia, floor-of-mouth swelling, facial cellulitis, abscess, immunocompromise, or complicated odontogenic disease. Add CBC/CMP/lactate/cultures by sepsis severity, not as a reflex for simple dental pain.

ESR, CRP, CBC with platelets, and CMP support the diagnosis but do not replace clinical judgment. Start steroids before confirmatory biopsy/ultrasound when suspicion is meaningful, especially with visual symptoms.
Do not CT uncomplicated bacterial rhinosinusitis, classic TMJ pain, or classic recurrent migraine without red flags. Do not use normal dental or sinus findings to close a neurovascular presentation.

info.h: Admit, transfer, or urgent specialty care
