info.t: - Vision threat, AACG, orbital cellulitis, HZO with eye involvement, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or decreased visual acuity. - Dissection, stroke/TIA, SAH/ICH concern, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or objective neuro deficit. - Deep neck/odontogenic infection with airway risk, trismus, dysphagia, toxic appearance, diabetes/immunocompromise, or need for IV antibiotics/source control. - GCA with visual symptoms, diplopia, or high suspicion requiring urgent steroid pathway. - Inability to hydrate, uncontrolled pain, unsafe social situation, or unclear diagnosis with objective abnormality.

Use observation when pain is severe or diagnosis is evolving, CT/CTA/MRI or specialty assessment is pending, oral intake is uncertain, infection response needs reassessment, or discharge safety depends on symptom control and repeat exam.

Dangerous eye/neurovascular/infection/GCA/zoster features are absent or addressed, vitals stable, neuro and eye exams documented as appropriate, pain controlled, patient can eat/drink, follow-up is specific, and return precautions cover vision change, focal neuro symptoms, fever, swelling, trismus, dysphagia, rash, and worsening pain.

Do not only document the final label. Document the negative danger screen: visual acuity/eye exam, neurovascular clues, dental/deep infection screen, GCA screen when age >50, and zoster/skin/ear exam.

1. Triage by glucose level: - <70 mg/dL: Hypoglycemia pathway - 70-300 mg/dL: Assess for DKA/HHS - >300 mg/dL: Evaluate for diabetic emergencies 2. Screen for DKA/HHS: - DKA: pH <7.3, AG >12, ketones positive - HHS: Glucose >600, Osm >320, minimal ketones - Euglycemic DKA: SGLT2 inhibitor use 3. Assess diabetes type and insulin status: - Type 1 vs Type 2 - Pump vs injections - Current regimen and doses

Alert patient (glucose <70): - 15-20g fast-acting carbs PO - Recheck in 15 min, repeat PRN Severe/AMS: - IV: D50W 25-50 mL or D10W 100-250 mL - No IV: Glucagon 1 mg IM or 3 mg intranasal - Thiamine first in alcoholics Sulfonylurea-induced: - Prolonged monitoring (12-72h) - D10W infusion - Consider octreotide 50-100 mcg q6-8h

Target: 140-180 mg/dL (general and ICU) Basal-Bolus Protocol: 1. Meta-analyses demonstrate that DOACs are associated with a 39% relative reduction in major bleeding compared to vitamin K antagonists while maintaining similar efficacy for preventing recurrent VTE. In low-risk PE patients specifically, DOACs showed absolute differences in symptomatic VTE recurrence ranging from −0.4% to 0.3% compared to conventional therapy, with reduced bleeding risk (absolute risk difference −0.6%).

Apixaban and rivaroxaban offer the advantage of single-drug oral therapy without requiring initial heparin, making them particularly convenient for outpatient management of low-risk PE. The choice among DOACs is guided by pharmacologic properties, patient characteristics (particularly renal function), concomitant medications, and patient preference for once versus twice-daily dosing.

Higher initial energy reduces need for repeat cardioversion — critical in non-intubated patients where sedation may wear off. • Ensure shock delivery is synchronized to the QRS complex • If initial attempt unsuccessful, escalate energy and reconfirm pad contact

• Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min infusion to maintain sinus rhythm • IV Magnesium Sulfate 2–4 g to augment cardioversion success • Continue amiodarone until critical illness significantly improved — stopping early risks reversion to A-Fib (42% reversion rate in one study) • Monitor for post-cardioversion bradycardia (especially if baseline HR was <100)

• WPW + A-Fib: Cardioversion is first-line. Do NOT use AV nodal blockers (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, IV amiodarone) • Critically ill patients: Standalone DC cardioversion often fails — patients frequently revert to A-Fib. Pre/post-treatment with amiodarone + magnesium improves sustained conversion • Anticoagulation: If AF duration >48 hours and not anticoagulated, consider TEE to exclude atrial thrombus before elective cardioversion

info.h: Call 911 or Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If Your Child Has
info.pt: When to Return to the Emergency Department
info.t: Breathing Problems: • Difficulty breathing that is getting worse • Struggling to breathe (chest pulling in deeply between or below the ribs with each breath) • Fast breathing or working very hard to breathe • Noisy breathing when resting (stridor) that doesn't improve or gets worse • Pauses in breathing or stops breathing briefly Serious Warning Signs: • Blue or gray color around the lips, mouth, or fingernails • Extreme drowsiness or difficulty waking up • Confusion or unusual behavior • Drooling or difficulty swallowing • Unable to drink fluids or refusing all liquids

info.h: Return to Your Doctor or Emergency Department If Your Child Has
info.pt: When to Return to the Emergency Department
info.t: • Symptoms that don't improve after taking the prescribed steroid medicine • Barking cough that lasts more than 3 days • Fever above 103°F (39.4°C) or fever that lasts more than 3 days • Symptoms that improve and then suddenly get worse • Trouble sleeping due to breathing problems

info.pt: When to Return to the Emergency Department
info.t: • Symptoms are often worse at night and may improve during the day • The barking cough typically lasts 1-2 days but can continue for up to 5-7 days • Your child may sound worse than they actually are — the barking cough can be scary but doesn't always mean severe illness • Keep your child calm, as crying and agitation can make breathing more difficult

info.pt: When to Return to the Emergency Department
info.t: • Give the steroid medicine exactly as prescribed • Keep your child comfortable and calm • Offer plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration • Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or discomfort (follow dosing instructions) • Keep your child's head elevated during sleep if comfortable

info.pt: When to Return to the Emergency Department
info.t: Most children start feeling better within 2-3 hours after receiving steroid medication. The cough should gradually improve over the next 2 days. If your child is not improving as expected, contact your doctor. Trust your instincts. If you are worried about your child's breathing or overall condition, seek medical attention right away. It's always better to be checked and reassured than to wait too long.

info.h: Return to the ED Immediately If You Experience
info.t: Serious Warning Signs: • Chest pain or pressure • Severe shortness of breath or difficulty breathing • Fainting or loss of consciousness • Severe dizziness or lightheadedness • Confusion or difficulty speaking • Weakness or numbness on one side of your body (signs of stroke) • Heart rate that feels extremely fast or irregular and does not improve with rest • Coughing up blood • Severe bleeding (especially if you are taking blood thinners) Other Concerning Symptoms: • Palpitations (racing or fluttering heartbeat) that are much worse than usual or do not go away • Swelling in your legs, ankles, or abdomen that is new or worsening • Persistent nausea or vomiting • Inability to take your prescri

Take Your Medications: • Take all medications exactly as prescribed, including rate control medications (beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers), blood thinners (anticoagulants) if prescribed, and any other heart medications • Do not stop or change your medications without talking to your doctor first • Set reminders to help you remember to take your medications on time Monitor Your Symptoms: • Check your pulse regularly as instructed by your doctor • Rest and stay calm if you feel your heart racing • Keep a log of any symptoms you experience, including when they occur and how long they last Lifestyle Modifications: • Limit or avoid alcohol — it can trigger atrial fibrillation episodes •

Appointments: • Schedule follow-up with your primary care doctor or cardiologist within 1–2 weeks (or as directed) • Keep all scheduled appointments, even if you are feeling better • Bring a list of your current medications and any questions Blood Work: • If you are taking blood thinners, you may need regular blood tests to monitor their effectiveness • Follow your doctor’s instructions about when to have these tests done Questions to Ask Your Doctor: • What is my target heart rate? • How often should I check my pulse? • What activities are safe for me? • Do I need to make any changes to my diet? • When can I return to work or normal activities?

• Atrial fibrillation increases your risk of stroke — this is why blood thinners may be prescribed • Even if you feel better, continue taking all medications as prescribed • Call your doctor’s office if you have questions or concerns that are not emergencies • Wear a medical alert bracelet if you are taking blood thinners

info.pt: PEP: What You Need to Know
info.t: PEP stands for post-exposure prophylaxis. It is a 28-day course of HIV medications taken after a possible exposure to HIV. PEP can prevent HIV infection if started within 72 hours of exposure. The sooner you start, the better it works.

info.pt: PEP: What You Need to Know
info.t: The risk of getting HIV from a single exposure varies by type: • Receptive anal intercourse: ~1.4% per exposure (highest sexual risk) • Receptive vaginal intercourse: ~0.08% per exposure • Insertive anal or vaginal intercourse: ~0.04–0.11% per exposure • Needlestick injury: ~0.23% per exposure • Mucous membrane splash: ~0.09% per exposure • Sharing injection drug needles: ~0.63% per exposure Risk is higher if the source person has a high viral load (not on treatment) and lower if the source person is on HIV treatment with an undetectable viral load.

info.pt: PEP: What You Need to Know
info.t: PEP is highly effective when taken correctly: • Reduces HIV risk by approximately 80% or more • Most effective when started within hours of exposure — ideally within 2 hours • Must be taken every day for the full 28 days to work • Missing doses or stopping early significantly reduces effectiveness • PEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections

info.pt: PEP: What You Need to Know
info.t: Most people tolerate PEP well. Side effects are usually mild and improve over the first 1–2 weeks: • Nausea (most common — take with food to help) • Fatigue or tiredness • Headache • Diarrhea or stomach discomfort • Difficulty sleeping When to call your doctor: • Severe nausea or vomiting that prevents you from taking the medication • Yellowing of skin or eyes • Dark-colored urine • Rash • Any severe or worsening symptoms

info.pt: PEP: What You Need to Know
info.t: • Take your medication at the same time every day • Complete all 28 days — do not stop early even if you feel fine • You will need follow-up HIV testing at 4–6 weeks and 3 months • Visit your doctor at 2 weeks to check for side effects and blood work • Use condoms and safe practices during and after PEP until your final HIV test is negative • If you have ongoing risk for HIV, ask your doctor about PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) — a daily medication to prevent HIV before exposure

HBsAg (Surface Antigen) — present on the virus surface. Positive = active infection (acute or chronic). HBsAb (Surface Antibody) — also called anti-HBs. Positive = immunity (from vaccination or resolved infection). HBcAb (Core Antibody) — also called anti-HBc. Positive = prior or current infection (does not develop from vaccination).

If exposed patient is susceptible (all markers negative): • Source HBV-positive or unknown: give HBIG (0.06 mL/kg IM) + start HBV vaccine series • Source HBV-negative: start HBV vaccine series (no HBIG needed) • HBIG is most effective within 24 hours; give within 7 days of exposure If exposed patient was previously vaccinated (HBsAb+): • HBsAb ≥10 mIU/mL: protected, no treatment needed • HBsAb <10 mIU/mL (non-responder): give HBIG + vaccine booster If exposed patient has chronic HBV (HBsAg+): • HBIG and vaccine will not help — refer hepatology • Ensure patient is connected to HBV care
• Standard: 0, 1, and 6 months (3-dose series) • Accelerated: Heplisav-B (HepB-CpG) — 2 doses, 1 month apart • Check HBsAb 1–2 months after final dose to confirm response (≥10 mIU/mL)

• Confirm disabling deficit, last-known-well/time window, and no hemorrhage on initial imaging. • Do not delay IV thrombolysis for CBC/coags/chemistry if there is no anticoagulant use, bleeding history, thrombocytopenia concern, or other reason to suspect an abnormal result. • If IV thrombolysis is contraindicated, keep the stroke pathway moving: CTA/CTP or MRI/MRA for LVO/EVT selection. • Use local stroke protocol for agent choice and dose. Tenecteplase and alteplase eligibility rules overlap but are not identical by institution.

info.h: Hard Stop / Do Not Give IV Thrombolysis
info.t: • Any intracranial hemorrhage on baseline imaging. • Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, even if initial CT is normal. • Active internal bleeding or known major bleeding diathesis. • Platelets <100,000, INR >1.7, PT >15 sec, or aPTT elevated from heparin/direct thrombin inhibitor effect. • Therapeutic LMWH within 24 hours. • DOAC use within ~48 hours unless sensitive testing and renal function show no clinically relevant anticoagulant effect. • Persistent BP >185/110 despite treatment. • Blood glucose <50 mg/dL until corrected and stroke mimic excluded. • Significant head trauma, intracranial/spinal surgery, or ischemic stroke within 3 months. • Intracranial neoplasm, AVM, aneurysm, or other

• Rapidly improving but still disabling deficit: consider treatment if disabling symptoms persist. • Minor non-disabling deficit: usually no IV thrombolysis; use DAPT pathway when appropriate. • Seizure at onset: treat if persistent deficit is believed to be stroke, not postictal paralysis. • Pregnancy/postpartum: individualized risk-benefit; not an automatic exclusion. • Recent major surgery, serious trauma, GI/GU bleed, arterial puncture at noncompressible site, or lumbar puncture: discuss urgently with stroke team. • Large early infarct/hypodensity or large core: higher hemorrhage risk; neuro/stroke team decision.

Before thrombolysis: BP must be <185/110 mmHg • Labetalol 10–20 mg IV bolus • Nicardipine 5 mg/hr IV infusion if repeated boluses are not enough • Clevidipine 1–2 mg/hr IV alternative If BP cannot be lowered and maintained <185/110: do not give IV thrombolysis. After thrombolysis: maintain BP <180/105 for 24 hours and avoid antithrombotics for the first 24 hours unless a stroke specialist directs otherwise. Required now: fingerstick glucose. CBC/coags/chemistry are targeted when history, medication list, or exam suggests they matter.

• Do not end the stroke alert. • Get CTA/CTP or MRI/MRA if not already done and the patient may have LVO. • Mechanical thrombectomy may still be indicated even when IV thrombolysis is unsafe. • Start antiplatelet/anticoagulant decisions only after hemorrhage is excluded and timing is clear. If thrombolysis was given, hold antithrombotics for 24 hours pending repeat imaging/protocol. • Document the exact exclusion: medication, lab, BP, bleeding risk, imaging finding, or time/imaging mismatch.

info.h: When to Choose CT Over MRI (Even if MRI is Available)
info.t: Suspected LVO / thrombectomy candidate • CTA is faster; delays to EVT worsen outcomes Severe/disabling deficits within 4.5 hours • NCCT sufficient to exclude hemorrhage and initiate thrombolysis; DWI not necessary Unstable or agitated patient • CT faster, less motion artifact, no sedation needed MRI contraindications (pacemaker, cochlear implant, metallic foreign body, severe claustrophobia) • CT is safe alternative • MRI Safety Screening — full checklist and device protocol Collateral assessment needed • Multiphase CTA provides collateral status for thrombectomy selection Perfusion imaging in extended window (6–24h) • CT perfusion is faster than MRI perfusion in most settings

info.h: When MRI is Preferred Over CT
info.t: Wake-up stroke / unknown onset • DWI-FLAIR mismatch determines thrombolysis eligibility TIA or minor stroke with resolved symptoms • DWI detects infarct in ~40% of TIAs (CT only ~4%) Posterior fossa stroke • CT limited by bone artifact; MRI superior Stroke mimics suspected • MRI better differentiates ischemia from mimics Renal insufficiency or contrast allergy • Time-of-flight MRA avoids iodinated contrast Small/lacunar infarcts • DWI more sensitive for small lesions Large infarct assessment for EVT eligibility • DWI may be needed to determine core volume

Hemorrhage detection • CT: High sensitivity/specificity • MRI: Equivalent with GRE/SWI Acute infarct detection (≤3h) • CT: 47–53% sensitive • MRI (DWI): 88% sensitive LVO detection (CTA vs MRA) • CTA: 92–100% sensitive • MRA: Slightly inferior, especially distally Acquisition time • CT (NCCT + CTA + CTP): ~5–10 min • MRI: ~20–30 min Perfusion imaging • CT: Validated thresholds; faster • MRI: Equivalent accuracy; slower

In the hyperacute setting with disabling deficits and suspected LVO, CT-based protocols (NCCT + CTA ± CTP) should be the default due to speed, even when MRI is available. Reserve MRI for wake-up strokes, TIA workup, posterior circulation strokes, stroke mimics, or when contrast is contraindicated.

info.h: Early Treatment: Benefit Out of 100 Patients

info.t: A blood clot is blocking blood flow to part of the brain. Without rapid reperfusion, threatened brain tissue can become permanently injured.

We are recommending an IV clot-dissolving medication, either tenecteplase or alteplase depending on local stroke protocol. The goal is to improve the chance of recovery with less disability. The earlier the medication is given, the larger the expected benefit. Tenecteplase and alteplase are both guideline-supported options within the standard 4.5-hour treatment window.

• Treatment within 3 hours: about 10 additional patients per 100 reach disability-free survival or no/minimal deficit. • Treatment from 3 to 4.5 hours: about 5 additional patients per 100 reach a good outcome. • Selected wake-up or 4.5-9 hour patients with favorable advanced imaging may still benefit, but this requires stroke-team imaging criteria. • IV thrombolysis does not replace thrombectomy when a large vessel occlusion is present.

The main risk is bleeding: • Symptomatic bleeding into the brain is usually discussed as about 2-7 patients per 100, depending on trial, definition, imaging selection, and patient-specific risk. • Fatal intracranial bleeding excess in pooled alteplase trials is about 2 patients per 100. • Bleeding risk is higher with large infarct/core, severe deficit, uncontrolled blood pressure, anticoagulant effect, bleeding disorder, recent major surgery/trauma, or frailty. • Other risks include systemic bleeding, allergic reaction, and tongue/lip swelling (angioedema), which is uncommon but can threaten the airway. • After treatment, the team monitors neurologic status and blood pressure closely for 24

info.h: What Happens If We Do Not Treat?
info.t: Without IV thrombolysis, the stroke may improve on its own, but it may also leave permanent disability or worsen. Possible outcomes include weakness or paralysis, speech or language difficulty, vision loss, loss of independence, need for long-term care, or death. Supportive stroke care and thrombectomy evaluation still continue when appropriate.

Because time is critical, treatment should not be delayed for a prolonged consent search when the patient lacks decision-making capacity and no surrogate is immediately available. In that setting, emergency consent may apply. Document the indication, risk/benefit discussion, decision-maker, and consent status.

This page supports, but does not replace, the formal eligibility screen: hemorrhage excluded, disabling deficit, blood pressure within protocol, glucose checked, no active anticoagulant effect or other hard-stop contraindication, and stroke-team workflow active.

info.h: Verbal Screening — Ask Patient or Surrogate
info.t: Run through ALL questions. Any "Yes" or "Unknown" requires investigation before proceeding. 1. Cardiac device? • Pacemaker, ICD (defibrillator), or loop recorder? • Any prior cardiac surgery or heart procedure? 2. Brain or spine stimulator? • Deep brain stimulator (DBS)? • Spinal cord stimulator? • Vagus nerve stimulator (VNS)? 3. Cochlear or hearing implant? • Internal ear device (not a hearing aid) 4. Brain aneurysm clips or coils? • Prior brain surgery for an aneurysm? • Neurosurgical hardware in the head? 5. Implanted pump? • Insulin pump (external = safe; internal = screen) • Intrathecal pain pump • Baclofen pump 6. Metal in or near the eyes? • Welding or grinding history without protec

When patient cannot communicate, order films to identify unknown implants. Step 1 — Portable Chest X-Ray (always first) • Pacemaker/ICD: generator in pectoral area + leads into heart • Loop recorder: small oblong density, left parasternal, NO leads • LVAD: large pump + driveline visible • Sternotomy wires: prior cardiac surgery (sternal hardware visible) • Prosthetic heart valves: metallic density at valve position Step 2 — Skull X-Ray (if neurological device suspected) • Deep brain stimulator: generator in chest + leads through scalp + electrodes in brain • Cochlear implant: metallic density in mastoid/temporal bone • VP shunt: radiopaque tubing from skull into abdomen • Aneurysm clips: sma

info.h: Pacemaker vs ICD vs Loop Recorder — X-Ray Differentiation
info.t: These must be distinguished before any MRI decision. Pacemaker (PPM) • Generator: rectangular metallic box, 4–5 cm, left pectoral • Leads: 1–3 thin wires entering subclavian vein → right heart • Single lead (VVI): tip at right ventricular apex • Dual lead (DDD): one to RA, one to RV apex • Biventricular (CRT-P): three leads — RA, RV, and left lateral (via coronary sinus) • Generator has characteristic X-ray marker identifying manufacturer ICD (Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator) • Generator: LARGER and THICKER than pacemaker (high-energy capacitor) • Shocking coil: thick, dense segment on RV lead — the key distinguishing feature • Coil appears as a dense, ribbed segment 2–5 cm long on th

ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATIONS — Do NOT scan • Pacemaker or ICD — NOT MRI-conditional (most devices implanted before 2011) • Cochlear implant — most models (some newer are MRI-conditional; confirm) • Ferromagnetic aneurysm clips (pre-1990 era clips — titanium clips are safe) • Metallic intraocular foreign body • Most implanted neurostimulators not labeled MRI-conditional • Magnetic ossicular prostheses (inner ear) CONDITIONAL — Safe only with proper protocol • MRI-conditional pacemaker/ICD — requires EP reprogramming before scan (see protocol below) • Loop recorder (most models) — MRI-conditional at 1.5T; check model • Coronary stent — generally safe after 6–8 weeks post-placement (earlier if he

MANDATORY: Do not scan a pacemaker/ICD patient without EP involvement. Step 1 — Confirm MRI-conditional status • Must be explicitly labeled "MRI-conditional" by the manufacturer • Common MRI-conditional brands: Medtronic SureScan, Abbott Assurity MRI, Boston Scientific Incepta MRI, Biotronik ProMRI • Unknown device → treat as NOT conditional until proven otherwise Step 2 — Page Cardiology/EP STAT • EP must interrogate the device with a programmer wand • Confirms: model number, MRI-conditional status, battery life, pacemaker-dependency • Pacemaker-dependent patients — highest risk; discuss benefit vs. risk carefully before proceeding Step 3 — Pre-scan programming • EP reprograms device to MRI

Unknown cardiac device → Cardiology/EP • Device interrogation + MRI-conditional confirmation • Required for all pacemaker/ICD MRI decisions Unknown neurostimulator → Neurosurgery • DBS, VNS, spinal cord stimulators • Many require manufacturer tech support for programming Cochlear implant → ENT or Audiology • Very few models are MRI-conditional; most require magnet removal before scan Intrathecal pump → Neurosurgery or Pain Management • Device must be aspirated before scan in most protocols Model lookup → MRIsafety.com • Shellock MRI Safety Database • Search by manufacturer + model number • Lists field strength limits, SAR limits, and special conditions Scan safety questions → MRI technologis

info.h: How to Use This at Bedside
info.t: Use the syndrome to predict the likely vascular territory, decide whether CTA/CTP or MRI/MRA is urgent, and avoid being falsely reassured by a low NIHSS. Do not use this to rule out stroke. Clinical localization is imperfect, especially with posterior circulation, thalamic, lacunar, and multifocal embolic strokes. Sudden focal neurologic deficit still needs the stroke pathway. High-yield rule: cortical signs point to cortex or large-vessel territory; absence of cortical signs with pure motor/sensory/ataxic patterns points toward lacunar or brainstem disease.

• Face/arm > leg weakness + aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation, or visual field cut: MCA / ICA until proven otherwise. • Leg > arm weakness + abulia, urinary incontinence, gait apraxia, grasp reflex: ACA. • Homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, memory disturbance, alexia, or cortical blindness: PCA. • Vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, crossed sensory/motor findings, or decreased consciousness: posterior circulation / vertebrobasilar. • Pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand without aphasia/neglect/visual cortical signs: lacunar pattern. • Monocular curtain/vision loss: retinal or ophthalmic artery ischemia, a stroke-equivalent pat

Proximal MCA / ICA terminus / tandem ICA-MCA Territory: lateral frontal, parietal, temporal cortex; insula; deep basal ganglia/internal capsule branches. Pattern: dense contralateral face/arm > leg weakness and sensory loss, gaze preference toward lesion, homonymous field cut, aphasia if dominant hemisphere, neglect/anosognosia if nondominant hemisphere. ED pitfall: severe right MCA neglect can look like confusion or intoxication; NIHSS is usually high but not always. MCA superior division Territory: lateral frontal cortex, precentral region, Broca area when dominant. Pattern: face/arm weakness > leg, gaze preference, expressive/nonfluent aphasia if dominant hemisphere, neglect if nondominan

ACA cortical territory Territory: medial frontal and parietal lobes; leg motor/sensory cortex; supplementary motor area; corpus callosum. Pattern: contralateral leg > arm weakness or sensory loss, gait apraxia, abulia, apathy, impaired judgment, mutism, grasp reflex, urinary incontinence. ED pitfall: ACA strokes can present as weakness plus odd behavior rather than classic FAST findings. Bilateral ACA / azygos ACA pattern Territory: bilateral medial frontal lobes. Pattern: paraparesis, akinetic mutism, profound abulia, frontal release signs, urinary incontinence. ED pitfall: may be misrouted as metabolic encephalopathy or psychiatric disease if the leg-predominant weakness is not tested.

PCA superficial territory Territory: occipital cortex and medial temporal lobe. Pattern: contralateral homonymous hemianopia, quadrantanopia, visual agnosia, prosopagnosia, color/reading disturbance; dominant left PCA can cause alexia without agraphia; bilateral PCA can cause cortical blindness or Anton syndrome. ED pitfall: a complete hemianopia is disabling but only scores 2 NIHSS points. PCA deep / thalamic territory Territory: thalamus, posterior internal capsule, midbrain connections. Pattern: hemisensory loss, sensory pain syndrome, hypersomnolence, confusion, memory impairment, dysarthria, ocular movement abnormalities, ataxia. ED pitfall: thalamic strokes can mimic intoxication, seiz

Basilar artery occlusion Territory: pons, midbrain, cerebellar branches, top-of-basilar PCA/SCA territory. Pattern: dizziness/vertigo may be early; dysarthria, diplopia, gaze palsy, cranial nerve deficits, bilateral weakness, quadriparesis, decreased consciousness, coma, or locked-in syndrome. ED pitfall: early symptoms can be nonspecific. Rapid impaired consciousness plus motor or brainstem signs is basilar occlusion until proven otherwise. PICA / lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) Territory: dorsolateral medulla, inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular nuclei, spinal trigeminal nucleus, sympathetic fibers, nucleus ambiguus. Pattern: vertigo, nausea/vomiting, ipsilateral ataxia, ipsil

Pure motor hemiparesis Territory: posterior limb internal capsule, corona radiata, or ventral pons. Pattern: contralateral face/arm/leg weakness without sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, or visual field deficit. Pure sensory stroke Territory: thalamus, especially VPL. Pattern: contralateral face/arm/leg numbness, paresthesia, or pain without weakness or cortical signs. Sensorimotor lacunar stroke Territory: thalamocapsular region, internal capsule, putamen-capsule-caudate region. Pattern: combined contralateral sensory and motor loss without cortical signs. Ataxic hemiparesis Territory: internal capsule, corona radiata, or pons. Pattern: mild contralateral weakness with disproportionate ipsila

Central retinal artery / ophthalmic artery ischemia Territory: retina or ophthalmic branch of ICA. Pattern: sudden painless monocular vision loss, curtain/gray-out, afferent pupillary defect, retinal whitening/cherry-red spot when visible. ED pitfall: treat as acute retinal ischemia / stroke-equivalent. Look for carotid disease, atrial fibrillation, embolic source, and giant cell arteritis when age and symptoms fit. Open CRAO or Monocular Vision Loss Hub when this pattern is present.

Cortical watershed (ACA-MCA or MCA-PCA border) Territory: border zones between major cortical arteries. Pattern: proximal arm/leg weakness, higher cortical deficits, or transcortical aphasia patterns; often after hypotension, severe carotid stenosis, or embolic shower. Internal watershed Territory: deep white matter border zone between superficial and deep perforator systems. Pattern: "man-in-the-barrel" proximal arm weakness or stepwise/fluctuating deficits. ED pitfall: recurrent hypotension or over-aggressive BP lowering can worsen symptoms in flow-dependent stenosis.

Suggested note language: "Deficit localizes clinically to _ territory based on _. Stroke pathway activated; CTA/CTP or MRI/MRA used to confirm vascular target and treatment eligibility. NIHSS interpreted in context because posterior circulation, visual, thalamic, and lacunar syndromes may be underweighted."

• PLATO trial: 16% relative reduction in CV death/MI/stroke vs clopidogrel (NNT 54) • Reversible P2Y12 inhibition — offset in ~3-5 days • Not dependent on CYP2C19 metabolism • KEY: Aspirin must be ≤100 mg/day (higher doses reduce ticagrelor efficacy) • Side effects: dyspnea (~14%, usually mild), bradycardia • Twice-daily dosing may reduce adherence • Loading: 180 mg → Maintenance: 90 mg BID × 12 months

• TRITON-TIMI 38: 19% relative reduction in CV death/MI/stroke vs clopidogrel (NNT 46) • More potent and less variable platelet inhibition • ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: Prior stroke or TIA (net clinical harm) • Generally avoid if age ≥75 (no net benefit) or weight <60 kg (consider 5mg maintenance) • Irreversible — offset ~7 days (longest of the three) • Best for: diabetic patients, prior stent thrombosis on clopidogrel • Loading: 60 mg at PCI → Maintenance: 10 mg daily × 12 months

• Least potent P2Y12 inhibitor but lowest bleeding risk • Preferred for triple therapy (OAC + DAPT) • Prodrug requiring CYP2C19 activation — ~30% of population are poor metabolizers with reduced efficacy • Avoid concurrent omeprazole/esomeprazole (CYP2C19 inhibition) — use pantoprazole • Loading: 300-600 mg → Maintenance: 75 mg daily × 12 months
• TIMI score 0-2 • No hemodynamic instability • No refractory angina • No sustained arrhythmias • No heart failure signs • Low-risk troponin trajectory (trending down)

Anticoagulation: Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily preferred (lowest bleeding — OASIS-5 trial) Antiplatelet: Aspirin 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg (or ticagrelor 90 mg BID) Anti-ischemic: Metoprolol — target HR <70. Nitroglycerin PRN. Statin: Atorvastatin 80 mg immediately ACE inhibitor: Within 24h if no contraindications

Options (in order of preference): • Exercise treadmill test (if can exercise and ECG interpretable) • Stress echocardiography • Pharmacologic stress MRI/nuclear Timing: Before discharge or within 72 hours If positive: Upgrade to invasive strategy (catheterization) If negative: Discharge with medical therapy and close follow-up
• Positive stress test • Recurrent angina at rest or with minimal exertion • New/worsening heart failure • New sustained arrhythmia • Hemodynamic instability • Rising troponin trajectory

Regional Wall Motion Abnormalities (RWMA): • Hypokinesis (reduced movement) • Akinesis (absent movement) • Dyskinesis (paradoxical movement) • Distribution suggests culprit vessel territory Global LV Function: • Visual EF estimate (normal >55%, reduced <40%) • E-point septal separation (EPSS) — >10mm suggests EF <40% RV Assessment: • RV dilation (RV:LV ratio >0.6 suggests RV involvement) • RV free wall motion — McConnell sign (RV free wall akinesis with apical sparing) = acute RV strain • TAPSE <16mm = RV dysfunction

• Free wall rupture: pericardial effusion + tamponade physiology • VSD: new color flow across interventricular septum; step-up in O₂ saturation PA vs RA • Papillary muscle rupture: severe acute MR with flail leaflet • LV aneurysm: thin, akinetic wall segment (late complication) All mechanical complications require emergent surgical consultation.

• Parasternal long axis (PLAX): Global LV function, MR, pericardial effusion, EPSS • Parasternal short axis (PSAX): Segmental wall motion (sweep base to apex) • Apical 4-chamber (A4C): Comparative RV/LV size, TAPSE, regional WMA • Subxiphoid: Pericardial effusion, RV size • IVC: Volume status (collapsibility guides fluid management) For detailed echo technique, see Basic Echo Views

Cardiac MRI (within 7 days): • Distinguishes ischemic vs non-ischemic patterns • T2 mapping: identifies edema (acute injury) • Late gadolinium enhancement: scar pattern — Subendocardial: ischemic (plaque, spasm, embolism) — Subepicardial/mid-wall: myocarditis — Absent with edema: Takotsubo Additional testing as indicated: • OCT/IVUS during index cath (plaque erosion, dissection) • Provocative testing (acetylcholine challenge for spasm) • Hypercoagulability panel if embolic etiology suspected • Screening for pheochromocytoma if Takotsubo

Do not reflexively apply standard ACS therapy. Each MINOCA etiology has specific management — some standard ACS medications can cause harm: • Beta-blockers worsen coronary spasm • Anticoagulation extends SCAD dissection • Catecholamines worsen Takotsubo • NSAIDs worsen myocarditis Determine etiology FIRST, then tailor therapy accordingly.
Peaked T-waves — narrow-based, symmetric, tall. Most sensitive early finding but not specific. Best seen in precordial leads V2-V4. Flattened P-waves. ST-segment depression.
PR interval prolongation → first-degree AV block. Further P-wave flattening or complete loss of P-waves. Continued T-wave peaking.

QRS widening (> 120 ms) — intraventricular conduction delay. Loss of P-waves. Bradycardia from prolonged PR and QRS. Bundle branch block patterns. Junctional or escape rhythms. Second- or third-degree AV block.
Sine wave pattern — merged wide QRS complexes with peaked T-waves. Pathognomonic. Ventricular fibrillation. Asystole or pulseless electrical activity. Complete heart block.

The following findings are associated with serious adverse events (VF, cardiac arrest, death within 6 hours): • Bradycardia — RR 12.3 • Junctional rhythm — RR 7.5 • Prolonged QRS — RR 4.7 Frequency in severe hyperkalemia (K+ ≥ 6.5): • Peaked T-waves: 35.7% • Prolonged PR: 12.1% • Bradycardia: 12.0% • Widened QRS: 7.8% • Escape rhythm: 7.1% • High-degree AV block: 3.5% • Ventricular arrhythmias: 0.7%

ECG changes typically do not manifest until K+ exceeds 6.5 mEq/L. ECG changes have low sensitivity for detecting hyperkalemia and do not correlate reliably with specific K+ levels. The rate of potassium rise is often more important than the absolute level — patients with lower baseline K+ who experience rapid increases are at higher risk. Chronic hyperkalemia (e.g., dialysis patients) is better tolerated — these patients may have elevated K+ with fewer ECG manifestations. Never rule out dangerous hyperkalemia based on a normal ECG. Sensitivity for peaked T-waves is only ~34%.

The earliest change is decreased T-wave amplitude, progressing as potassium declines. • T-wave flattening/inversion (27% of patients) — most common finding • ST-segment depression (16%) — upsloping morphology • QTc prolongation (14%) — often actually QTU prolongation with T-U wave fusion • Prominent U waves (> 1 mm amplitude) — most specific finding • U waves larger than T-waves in same lead (U:T ratio > 1) Best seen in leads V2 and V3. ECG changes are present in only about 40% of hypokalemic patients.

For each 1 mmol/L decrease in potassium within the low range (2.0-4.1): • QTc prolongation: +12.8 ms • T-wave amplitude reduction: -43.1 μV • PR interval prolongation: +4.6 ms • P-wave duration prolongation: +2.7 ms

QTc prolongation increases risk of Torsades de Pointes. AVOID QT-prolonging drugs in hypokalemia: • Amiodarone, sotalol • Fluoroquinolones • Ondansetron • Haloperidol, droperidol • Methadone Other arrhythmias: • First- or second-degree AV block • Atrial fibrillation • PVCs • Ventricular tachycardia • Ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest Digitalis toxicity is potentiated by hypokalemia — monitor carefully in patients on digoxin.

Characteristic findings include: • Prominent U waves with T-U fusion • ST-segment depression • T-wave flattening or inversion • Apparent QT prolongation (often QTU interval) • Widened QRS in severe cases Life-threatening arrhythmias may occur: VT, Torsades de Pointes, VF, cardiac arrest.

ECG changes do NOT reliably correlate with specific K+ levels. The rapidity of decline is more predictive of ECG changes than the absolute level. Consider hypokalemia in any patient with new-onset AF or VT. U waves are a classic teaching point but present in only ~20% of hypokalemic patients — QTc prolongation is the most clinically significant finding. Always obtain ECG when hypokalemia is identified to determine treatment urgency.

The presence of pyuria and/or bacteriuria on urinalysis AND a positive urine culture. • Pyuria: ≥5 WBCs/hpf in centrifuged specimen (DCMC uses centrifuged specimens) or ≥10 WBCs/hpf in counting chamber • Urine culture positive: ≥50,000 CFU/mL by catheterization or suprapubic aspiration • Clean catch: ≥100,000 CFU/mL optimal, 50,000-100,000 acceptable with decreased sensitivity/specificity

The presence of Leukocyte Esterase OR Nitrites OR microscopic analysis positive for leukocytes or bacteria is suggestive of active UTI. When more than one finding is present simultaneously, sensitivity and specificity increase significantly. • Urine dipstick alone cannot report WBC count and bacterial presence — use with caution • If bag specimen UA is positive, obtain catheterized specimen for culture to avoid contamination

Defined as UTI with any of the following: • Functional or anatomic abnormality of the urinary tract • Indwelling urinary catheter • Recent urinary tract instrumentation • Recent antibiotic use • Immunosuppression

For infants <48 weeks PMA and >7 days of life: • UTI defined as >50,000 CFU/mL in catheter obtained specimen • Exclusions: History of Candida infection (consult ID), concomitant bacteremia or meningitis • ESBL: Bacteria with particular resistance to penicillins — requires expanded antibiotic coverage
Order urinalysis with reflex culture. Midstream clean-catch is standard for most patients. Catheterized specimen if unable to provide clean-catch or concern for contamination.

Uncomplicated: premenopausal, non-pregnant female with cystitis and no structural abnormalities. Complicated: male sex, pregnancy, diabetes, immunocompromised, structural abnormality, recent instrumentation, or healthcare-associated infection.

Pregnancy: always treat, use safe agents. Elderly: distinguish ASB from true UTI, avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. CAUTI: remove catheter when possible, treat only if symptomatic. Males: always complicated, consider prostatitis.
Uncomplicated cystitis: Nitrofurantoin (1st line), TMP-SMX, or Fosfomycin. Pyelonephritis: Fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX with culture guidance. Follow local resistance patterns and IDSA guidelines.

Uncomplicated cystitis: PCP follow-up if symptoms persist >48-72 hours. Pyelonephritis: Close follow-up within 24-48 hours if discharged. Complicated UTI: Consider urology referral for structural abnormalities or recurrent infections.

Sensitivity: 75-96% Specificity: 94-98% Produced by neutrophils. A positive result indicates pyuria and supports the diagnosis of UTI. False negatives can occur with dilute urine, glycosuria, or proteinuria.

Sensitivity: 35-85% Specificity: 95-98% Indicates presence of gram-negative bacteria (Enterobacteriaceae) that convert urinary nitrate to nitrite. Requires 4+ hours of bladder incubation. False negative with frequent voiding, non-nitrate-reducing organisms (Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus saprophyticus), or low dietary nitrate.

>5 WBC/hpf is abnormal and suggests pyuria. >10 WBC/hpf strongly supports UTI. Pyuria without bacteriuria: consider urethritis (Chlamydia, gonorrhea), interstitial cystitis, renal TB, or recent antibiotic use.
Any bacteria on unspun urine correlates with >10^5 CFU/mL. Gram stain can help guide empiric therapy (gram-negative rods vs gram-positive cocci).

High squamous epithelial cells (>5/hpf): suggests contamination from vaginal or perineal flora. Consider repeat specimen with better technique or catheterized sample. Mixed flora on culture: typically indicates contamination rather than true infection.

Positive LE + positive nitrites: PPV >90% for UTI Negative LE + negative nitrites: NPV >95% for UTI In symptomatic patients with negative dipstick, send culture and consider empiric treatment based on clinical presentation.

Definition: Acute cystitis or pyelonephritis in a premenopausal, non-pregnant woman with no known urological abnormalities, no recent instrumentation, and no recent healthcare exposure. Key features: - Female sex - Premenopausal - Non-pregnant - No structural abnormalities - No recent instrumentation - No recent antibiotics - Community-acquired - Normal renal function

Definition: UTI associated with factors that increase the risk of treatment failure or serious outcomes. Complicating factors: - Male sex (always complicated) - Pregnancy - Diabetes mellitus - Immunocompromised state - Structural urinary tract abnormality - Functional abnormality (neurogenic bladder) - Indwelling urinary catheter - Recent urinary tract instrumentation - Recent antibiotic use - Healthcare-associated infection - Renal insufficiency - Renal transplant

Uncomplicated cystitis: - Short course antibiotics (3-5 days) - Narrow-spectrum agents appropriate - No imaging required Complicated UTI: - Longer treatment course (7-14 days) - Broader empiric coverage - May require imaging to rule out obstruction/abscess - Higher risk of resistant organisms - May require urology consultation

FDA black box warning: Fluoroquinolones are associated with disabling and potentially permanent adverse effects including tendinitis/rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects. Reserve for infections without alternative treatment options. Avoid fluoroquinolones in: - Uncomplicated cystitis (when alternatives exist) - Patients >60 years (higher tendon rupture risk) - Concurrent corticosteroid use - History of tendon disorders - Renal/cardiac/lung transplant recipients

Always treat UTI in pregnancy (including asymptomatic bacteriuria) due to risk of pyelonephritis and adverse fetal outcomes. Safe agents: - Nitrofurantoin (avoid at term >36 weeks - hemolysis risk) - Cephalexin 500 mg QID x 7 days - Amoxicillin-clavulanate 500 mg BID x 7 days Avoid: - TMP-SMX in 1st trimester (neural tube defects) and at term (kernicterus) - Fluoroquinolones (cartilage toxicity) - Nitrofurantoin at term (neonatal hemolysis if G6PD deficient) Duration: 7 days minimum for cystitis. Always obtain test of cure culture 1-2 weeks after treatment.

Key principle: Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in the elderly. ASB is common (up to 50% in institutionalized elderly) and treatment does not improve outcomes but increases resistance and adverse effects. True UTI requires: - Urinary symptoms (dysuria, urgency, frequency, suprapubic pain) AND - Positive UA/culture Non-specific symptoms (confusion, falls, weakness) should prompt search for other causes before attributing to UTI. Altered mental status alone is not an indication for UTI treatment. Consider UTI if: new or worsening urinary symptoms, fever, flank pain, rigors.

Definition: UTI in patient with indwelling catheter or within 48 hours of removal. Management principles: 1. Remove or replace catheter if possible (reduces treatment failure) 2. Treat only if symptomatic (fever, rigors, flank pain, acute mental status change) 3. Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients 4. Obtain culture from new catheter before starting antibiotics Duration: - 7 days if prompt resolution - 10-14 days if delayed response - 5 days may be sufficient in women with catheter removed Common organisms: E. coli, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Candida

All male UTIs are considered complicated. Rationale: Anatomic abnormality, prostatitis, or obstruction is often present. Workup: - UA with culture - Consider prostate exam - Consider STI testing in sexually active men - Consider imaging if recurrent, severe, or concern for obstruction Treatment: - Duration: 7-14 days (longer if prostatitis suspected) - Agents with good prostate penetration preferred: - TMP-SMX - Fluoroquinolones - Avoid nitrofurantoin (poor tissue penetration) Refer to urology if: recurrent infections, structural abnormality, suspected prostatitis, or age >50 (prostate evaluation).

• Skin vesicles (mouth, scalp, trunk) — most specific finding • Seizures (especially focal) • Lethargy or irritability out of proportion to fever • Hepatosplenomegaly • Temperature instability (hypothermia or hyperthermia) • Apnea or respiratory distress • Poor feeding • Bulging fontanelle
• Thrombocytopenia • Transaminitis (elevated AST/ALT) • Coagulopathy (elevated PT/INR) • CSF pleocytosis (especially lymphocytic) • Elevated CSF protein

• Maternal history of genital HSV (especially primary outbreak near delivery) • Vaginal delivery with active lesions • Prolonged rupture of membranes • Fetal scalp electrode use • Age <21 days (highest risk period)

• HSV PCR — blood (plasma) • HSV PCR — CSF • Surface cultures: conjunctiva, throat, nasopharynx, rectum • Vesicle fluid: viral culture and/or PCR (if lesions present) • AST, ALT (hepatic involvement screen)

• Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h • Duration: minimum 5 doses or until HSV PCR results negative • If PCR not resulted after 5 doses → contact Infectious Disease • Ensure adequate hydration (crystalline nephropathy risk)

• Gestational age <37 weeks (any postnatal age) • Postnatal age <7 days (any gestational age) • Receiving calcium-containing IV products (risk of fatal Ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates in lungs/kidneys) • Known cephalosporin anaphylaxis

• Total bilirubin >10 mg/dL • Risk factors for hyperbilirubinemia: • ABO incompatibility • G6PD deficiency • Significant bruising/cephalohematoma • East Asian ethnicity • Exclusive breastfeeding with weight loss >10% • Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin → increased free bilirubin → kernicterus risk

• Cefepime — 4th-generation cephalosporin • Dosing 0-28 days: 50 mg/kg IV q12h • Dosing >28 days: 50 mg/kg IV q8h • Broader gram-negative spectrum than Ceftriaxone • No calcium interaction, no significant bilirubin displacement
• Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q8h + Gentamicin 4 mg/kg IV q24h • Covers: GBS, Listeria, E. coli, Enterococcus • Duration: 48h rule-out period (d/c if cultures negative + well-appearing)
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q24h (or Cefepime if CI) • Duration: 48h rule-out period
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q24h (or Cefepime if CI) • Duration: 24-36h rule-out period
• Ampicillin 100 mg/kg IV q8h + Cefepime 50 mg/kg IV q12h • D/C Gentamicin when switching to meningitic dosing • Consider adding Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h + Ampicillin 75 mg/kg IV q6h • Consider adding Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h
• Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h + Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q6h • Consider adding Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h

• Cefazolin 17 mg/kg IV q8h (without bacteremia) • Cefazolin 33 mg/kg IV q8h (with bacteremia) • Step-down: Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID • Low-risk 29-60d UTI: Cephalexin 17 mg/kg PO TID (oral from start) • Total treatment: 10 days (IV + PO combined)

• Gentamicin: trough before 3rd dose if >2 doses anticipated (goal <1 mcg/mL) • Vancomycin: trough before 4th dose (goal 15-20 mcg/mL for meningitis) • If extended antibiotic course anticipated, monitor renal function (BMP)
• All febrile infants 0-2 months should have UA obtained • If UA positive → send catheterized urine culture • Bag specimens: acceptable for screening UA only, NEVER for culture
UTI probability increases with number of risk factors: • Non-Black race • Temperature ≥39°C (102.2°F) • Fever ≥2 days • No other source identified • Age <12 months ≥2 risk factors → screen with UA
• Uncircumcised → always screen with UA • Circumcised → screen if ≥3 of the female risk factors present • UTI prevalence in circumcised males is ~0.2% vs ~2% in uncircumcised

Gram-negative (most common): • E. coli (80-90% of pediatric UTIs) • Klebsiella • Proteus (more common in males) • Enterobacter • Pseudomonas (consider if recent instrumentation) Gram-positive: • Enterococcus • Group B Streptococcus (neonates) • Staphylococcus saprophyticus (rare in infants) Non-pathogens (likely contaminant): • Lactobacillus • Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus • Corynebacterium

ANY of the following: • Leukocyte esterase (LE): trace or greater • Nitrites: positive (very specific but low sensitivity in infants) • WBC: >5/hpf (centrifuged) or >10/hpf (uncentrifuged) • Bacteria on Gram stain Note: In neonates <30 days, LE and nitrites have lower sensitivity. A negative UA does not rule out UTI in this age group if clinical suspicion is high.

• Catheterized specimen: ≥50,000 CFU/mL (single organism) = positive • Suprapubic aspirate: any growth = positive • Bag specimen: NEVER use for culture (high false-positive rate, 85% contamination) • Mixed flora or multiple organisms → likely contamination → repeat if clinically indicated
• Cell count with differential (automated) • WBC >20 cells/µL suggests UTI • Bacteria >50,000/mL on flow cytometry • More sensitive than standard dipstick in young infants

• Positive UA + positive culture = confirmed UTI → treat • Positive UA + negative culture = possible early/partially treated UTI or contamination • Negative UA + positive culture = possible UTI (especially neonates) → treat • Negative UA + negative culture = UTI excluded

info.h: ED Discharge Criteria (ALL must be met)
info.t: • Well-appearing on exam • Tolerating oral liquids • Reliable caregiver with transportation • PCP or ED follow-up within 24 hours confirmed • Caregiver comfortable with home observation • Good social support (telephone access, reasonable proximity to ED) • Return precaution education completed and understood

Bring your baby back to the emergency department immediately if: • Temperature rises above 100.4°F (38°C) again • Baby becomes difficult to wake or unusually sleepy • Baby stops eating or drinking, or has fewer than 3 wet diapers in 24 hours • Baby develops a rash, especially blisters or purple spots • Baby has trouble breathing (fast breathing, grunting, ribs showing) • Baby is crying inconsolably and cannot be comforted • Baby seems limp, floppy, or weaker than usual • You are worried for any reason — trust your instincts

• PCP or ED follow-up in 24 hours for repeat assessment • If blood cultures were sent: results typically available at 24-48h. If positive, you will be called to return. • If on antibiotics: complete the full course as prescribed • Monitor temperature at home: rectal thermometer is most accurate for infants
Confirmed viral syndrome (bronchiolitis, RSV, influenza) REDUCES but does NOT eliminate the risk of invasive bacterial infection (IBI). The management varies significantly by age.

IBI RISK: 1.1% bacteremia, 0.8% meningitis, 5.2% UTI ⚠️ This is NOT negligible risk. • FULL SEPSIS WORKUP REQUIRED — same as FWS pathway • CBC, blood culture, CMP • Procalcitonin, CRP • Catheterized UA + urine culture • LP required at this age • Respiratory viral panel to confirm ADMIT + Empiric antibiotics pending cultures Discontinue abx if cultures negative at 24–36h and infant well-appearing.

IBI RISK with RSV: ~0.7% bacteremia, <0.5% meningitis, 5–7% UTI • CBC, blood culture, procalcitonin • Catheterized UA + urine culture — always required (UTI risk unchanged) • Respiratory viral panel LP DECISION: • If ALL inflammatory markers normal → LP can be deferred • If ANY marker abnormal → LP recommended Low-risk criteria (ALL must be met): • PCT <0.5 ng/mL • ANC <4,000 cells/mm³ • T ≤38.5°C • CRP <2.0 mg/dL If low-risk + UA negative → home observation, no antibiotics needed.

IBI RISK with RSV: <0.5% bacteremia, ~0% meningitis, 5–7% UTI This is VERY LOW risk for IBI. • Catheterized UA + urine culture — always required • Blood culture optional but reasonable • Procalcitonin optional NO LP REQUIRED for well-appearing infants with confirmed viral syndrome. If UA negative → supportive care, home observation, no antibiotics.
IBI RISK: Very low (<0.3% bacteremia) • UA only if UTI risk factors present • No blood work required if clear viral diagnosis • Supportive care • Home observation

UTI risk remains 5–7% even with confirmed viral syndrome. Always obtain catheterized UA for febrile infants <60 days, regardless of viral diagnosis. Bag specimens are NOT acceptable for culture — 85% contamination rate.

• No bronchodilators — no benefit in bronchiolitis • No steroids — do not reduce admission rates • No antibiotics for the bronchiolitis itself • Gentle nasal suctioning PRN • Maintain hydration (PO or IV) • Monitor for apnea in infants <6 weeks • Supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ <90% sustained

The Step-by-Step approach identifies febrile infants at LOW risk for invasive bacterial infection (IBI). Originally validated for infants 22–90 days, it uses sequential evaluation of clinical appearance, inflammatory markers, and urinalysis.
1. Well-appearing (no toxic appearance) 2. Age ≥21 days 3. Procalcitonin <0.5 ng/mL 4. ANC <4,000 cells/mm³ 5. Temperature ≤38.5°C (at home or ED) 6. CRP <2.0 mg/dL (if obtained) 7. UA negative

• Age 22–28 days: LP can be deferred (shared decision). Home observation reasonable. • Age 29–60 days: No LP needed. Home observation with 24h follow-up. • Age 61–90 days: No LP, no blood work needed. Home observation. No antibiotics required if all criteria met.
• Higher risk for IBI • LP recommended (except age >60 days where risk remains low) • Consider empiric antibiotics pending cultures • Disposition per clinical judgment
• Sensitivity for IBI: 92% • Specificity: 48% • NPV for bacteremia: 99.7% • NPV for meningitis: 99.9% When all criteria are met, IBI risk is <0.3%.

The following are NOT recommended in routine bronchiolitis: • Chest X-ray — Does not change management. Leads to inappropriate antibiotic use • Viral testing — Does not change management in uncomplicated bronchiolitis • CBC / Blood culture — Not recommended in well-appearing infants >90 days of age

• Albuterol / bronchodilators — No benefit in bronchiolitis. Not the same mechanism as asthma • Epinephrine (racemic) — Not recommended for routine use • Systemic or inhaled corticosteroids — No benefit. Do not reduce admission rates or LOS • Antibiotics — Bronchiolitis is viral. Antibiotics do not help unless secondary bacterial infection confirmed • Hypertonic saline (3%) — Mixed evidence, not recommended in the ED setting • Chest physiotherapy — No benefit. May worsen respiratory distress • Deep suction beyond nasopharynx — Harmful. Use gentle superficial nasal suction only
• <7 kg: 4 LPM • 7–9 kg: 6 LPM • >9 kg: 6 LPM Start FiO₂ at 21%, titrate to maintain SpO₂ ≥90% awake or ≥88% asleep.
• ≤7 kg: 2 LPM/kg (e.g., 5 kg = 10 LPM, 7 kg = 14 LPM) • >7 kg: 14 LPM Escalate by 2 LPM at a time. Monitor for signs of excess flow.
• Initiation: Q15 min assessment — BAS score, RR, pulse ox, WOB • Maintenance: Continuous pulse ox. Suction PRN. BAS Q4h or per PEWS. • Document HR, RR, pulse ox.

• Nasal obstruction • Ingestion/toxins • Life-threatening hypoxia, apnea, or hemodynamic instability • Trauma (maxillofacial, suspected base of skull fracture, chest) • Pneumothorax • Foreign body aspiration
• Decreased level of consciousness • Congenital heart disease • Asthma • Chronic lung disease

• Any patient worsening after 60 minutes on HFNC • Severe respiratory distress on HFNC • FiO₂ >50% • Flow rates above recommended parameters • Apnea • NICU consideration: <44 weeks corrected gestational age, prematurity <32 weeks and <44 weeks post-menstrual age
• Stable on current HFNC settings for ≥4 hours • BAS consistently <9 • Adequate oral intake or stable on NG/IV fluids

• O₂ wean first — decrease FiO₂ to maintain SpO₂ goals • Flow wean by physician order — generally not until stabilized 8–12 hours • Decrease flow by 2 LPM every 4 hours • Change to nasal cannula when on 2 LPM for 4 hours • If BAS ≥9 after decrease, return to previous flow rate

All must be met: • FiO₂ <40% • SpO₂ >90% awake and >88% asleep • HR within normal limits while calm • BAS <9 Exclusions: • Born <32 weeks gestation • Cardiac disease requiring home medications • Chronic lung disease or on home oxygen • Significant neuromuscular disease

Start Holiday BID: • FiO₂ >21%: change to 2 LPM at 100% • FiO₂ at 21%: take off HFNC, keep on room air • Monitor in room minimum 5 minutes — if immediate deterioration, return to previous settings Reassess within 30–60 minutes:

PASS: HR, RR, WOB acceptable AND SpO₂ >90% → Wean NC 1 LPM or stay on room air PASS TO LFNC: HR, RR, WOB acceptable BUT SpO₂ <90% awake / 88% asleep → Titrate nasal cannula up to 2 LPM NO PASS (Clinical Decompensation): Severe WOB, HR increase >20 bpm, RR increase by 10 → Return to previous HFNC settings
Upon initiation of HFNC, the child should remain NPO for approximately 1 hour to assess clinical response. The attending physician will then determine the appropriate method of nutrition.
If hydration status is of concern: • Nasogastric tube (NGT) — recommend initial trial of Pedialyte before EBM or formula • IV fluids (IVF) • NGT + IVF • Nasojejunal tube (NJT)
• Mild (BAS 0–3): May resume PO feeds. First feed observed by staff. • Moderate to Severe (BAS 4–12): Consider NG feeds.

If PO feeds have been started, make NPO and consider alternatives if: • Choking/gasping and/or increased WOB during or acutely after PO feeding • Respiratory rate consistently >60 beyond 15 minutes • Child is titrated to maximum HFNC flow rate for weight At any time, the physician may make the child NPO and hydrate by other means.
• Routine bronchiolitis management • FiO₂ <50% to maintain SaO₂ ≥90% awake or ≥88% asleep • Continuation of care when transferred from higher acuity unit • HFNC at standard flow rates

info.h: Acute Care Unit with High Acuity Status
info.t: • Significant cardiac or pulmonary comorbidities • Moderate to severe symptoms (see BAS scoring) • Worsening clinical status despite increasing flow rates • Comorbidities requiring discussion between provider and charge RN

• Any patient with worsening clinical status after 60 minutes of HFNC • Requiring positive pressure ventilation • Witnessed episode of apnea • Flow rates above maximum recommended levels • Severe dehydration or shock
• Patients not meeting acute care or high acuity criteria and currently <44 weeks corrected gestational age • Prematurity ≤32 weeks gestation and currently <44 weeks post-menstrual age

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: Bronchiolitis is an infection of the small airway tubes (bronchioles) in the lungs. The airways become swollen and fill with mucus, causing a stuffy nose, coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing. It is caused by a virus — the same viruses that cause common colds. It mostly affects children under 2 years old because they have smaller airways. It usually goes away on its own in 2 to 3 weeks.

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: • Breathing harder or faster • Runny or stuffy nose • Wheezing • Fever • Cough that may get worse

info.h: What Can I Do at Home?
info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: 1. Watch your child’s breathing. Always call your doctor if you are not comfortable caring for your child at home. 2. Fluids are important. Offer small amounts often. Ask your doctor about Pedialyte if your child is not drinking milk or formula well. 3. Suction the nose to help your child breathe, eat, and sleep better. Use saline drops (2–3 drops in each nostril) before suctioning with a bulb syringe.

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: Watch for: • No tears when crying • Fewer wet diapers • Dark-colored urine • Dry mouth, tongue, or lips

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: 1. No cough or cold medicines — they do not work for bronchiolitis and are not safe for young children. 2. No antibiotics — they do not kill viruses. 3. No breathing treatments (such as albuterol) — they do not help bronchiolitis.

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: • Having a harder time breathing • Not eating or drinking as usual • Sleepy, drowsy, or less active • Crying or restless and cannot be calmed • Fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C) or higher

info.h: Call 911 or Go to the ER If Your Child:
info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: • Has pale skin or a blue color around nails or lips • Is breathing fast and shallow • Is struggling for each breath • The space between ribs sinks in with each breath • Is making a grunting sound when breathing • Has a limp or floppy body • Is sleepy all the time, even after a nap

info.pt: Bronchiolitis: What You Need to Know
info.t: Wash your hands: • After caring for your child • Before cooking or eating • After blowing your nose, coughing, or sneezing No smoking around your child. Cigarette smoke irritates infected airways and makes it harder to breathe.

La bronquiolitis es una infección de las pequeñas vías respiratorias (bronquiolos) en los pulmones. Las vías respiratorias se inflaman y se llenan de mucosidad, causando tos, sibilancia o dificultad para respirar. Es causada por un virus — los mismos virus que causan los resfriados comunes. Afecta principalmente a niños menores de 2 años. Generalmente desaparece por sí misma en 2 a 3 semanas.
• Respiración más rápida o difícil • Secreción o congestión nasal • Sibilancia o silbido • Fiebre • Tos que podría empeorar

1. Observe la respiración de su hijo/a. Siempre llame a su médico si no se siente cómodo cuidando a su hijo/a en casa. 2. Los líquidos son importantes. Ofrezca pequeñas cantidades con frecuencia. Pregunte a su médico sobre Pedialyte si su hijo/a no está tomando bien la leche o fórmula. 3. Limpie la nariz para ayudar a su hijo/a a respirar, comer y dormir mejor. Use gotas de solución salina (2–3 gotas en cada fosa nasal) antes de succionar con la pera de succión.
Preste atención a: • Ausencia de lágrimas al llorar • Menos pañales mojados • Orina de color oscuro • Boca, lengua o labios secos

1. No use medicamentos para la tos o el resfriado — no funcionan contra la bronquiolitis y no son seguros para niños pequeños. 2. No use antibióticos — no matan los virus. 3. No use tratamientos respiratorios (como albuterol) — no ayudan con la bronquiolitis.

• Tiene mucha dificultad para respirar • No come ni bebe como lo hace normalmente • Está adormitado, mareado o menos activo • Llora o está inquieto y no puede calmarlo • Tiene fiebre de 100.4°F (38.0°C) o más

info.h: Llame al 911 o Vaya a Urgencias Si Su Hijo/a:
info.t: • Se ve pálido o tiene un color azul en las uñas o alrededor de los labios • Su respiración es rápida o superficial • Se esfuerza en cada respiración • Tiene un espacio entre las costillas que se hunde con cada respiración • Hace un sonido como gruñido cuando respira • Tiene el cuerpo débil o flácido • Está somnoliento todo el tiempo, incluso después de una siesta

Lávese las manos: • Después de atender a su hijo/a • Antes de comer • Después de sonarse, toser o estornudar No fume cerca del niño/a. El humo de cigarro es muy irritante para las vías respiratorias infectadas.
• Page OB and Pediatrics STAT — assign team roles • Gather delivery equipment and position patient • Confirm vertex presentation with bedside U/S if time permits

• Coach pushing: deep breath → bear down 10 sec × 3 per contraction • Support perineum, control occiput — slow, controlled head delivery • Sweep finger around neck — check for nuchal cord • If tight cord → double clamp and cut • Deliver shoulders: gentle downward then upward traction • If turtle sign → Shoulder Dystocia emergency
• Clamp cord in two places, cut between — delayed clamping 30–60 sec if vigorous • Place baby skin-to-skin, dry and stimulate, APGAR at 1 and 5 min • If not breathing or HR <100 → initiate NRP

• Gentle cord traction + counter-pressure on fundus — never force • Inspect placenta for completeness — save for pathology • Start Oxytocin 20 units in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr — bimanual massage • Assess lacerations: repair 1st/2nd degree, defer 3rd/4th to OB • Monitor mom × 1 hour: uterine tone, bleeding, vitals q15 min

Labor is regular uterine contractions that produce cervical effacement and dilation. ACOG recommends considering 6 cm cervical dilation the start of the active phase of the first stage of labor. Cervical dilation at or beyond 6 cm is therefore active-phase labor; complete dilation at 10 cm marks the transition to the second stage and delivery efforts.

info.h: What 6 cm does and does not mean
info.t: The 6-cm threshold identifies the phase of labor; it does not by itself mean that delivery is imminent or that transfer is automatically unsafe. Also assess contraction pattern, rate of cervical change, effacement, fetal station and presentation, pushing or crowning, rupture of membranes, bleeding, maternal status, fetal status, and the time required for a safe transfer.

Under EMTALA, a pregnant patient having contractions has an emergency medical condition when there is inadequate time to complete a safe transfer before delivery or when transfer may threaten the health or safety of the patient or unborn child. Confirm an accepting facility with appropriate obstetric capability. If delivery is imminent or transfer cannot be completed safely, prepare for local delivery and activate OB and neonatal support.

Assess maternal vital signs, fetal heart rate, bleeding, uterine tenderness, contractions, cord prolapse, fetal movement, and whether delivery is imminent. Call OB/L&D immediately for instability, suspected abruption, nonreassuring fetal status, suspected intra-amniotic infection, active labor, or imminent birth. Do not delay definitive care for an ROM test.

Clarify the time and character of leakage, gestational age, contractions, bleeding, fever, fetal movement, urinary leakage, vaginal infection symptoms, intercourse/semen exposure, GBS status, cerclage, and prior PPROM. Perform a sterile speculum examination to look for pooling, fluid from the cervical os, blood, purulence, and cord. Avoid digital examination unless delivery is imminent or OB directs it. Speculum examination

Frank pooling or fluid passing through the cervical os supports a clinical diagnosis and does not require an additional ROM test. If pooling is absent or equivocal, use the local biochemical test and/or ferning. At Dell Seton, order Rupture of Fetal Membranes for AmniSure/PAMG-1. Ultrasound can support the diagnosis when fluid is low, but normal fluid does not exclude a small or intermittent leak. AmniSure | Ferning

info.h: 4. Route by gestational age and condition
info.t: Term PROM, PPROM, and previable/periviable PPROM have different OB pathways. Confirmed ROM generally needs an OB/L&D plan, not routine ED discharge. Infection, abruption, active labor, maternal deterioration, or fetal compromise can override gestational-age-based expectant management. Disposition

info.pt: Ferning: What a Positive Pattern Looks Like
info.t: During the sterile speculum examination, collect fluid from the posterior fornix or visible pooling site. Smear a thin sample on a clean glass slide and allow it to air-dry before microscopy. Do not interpret a wet preparation as the final fern result. Speculum examination

info.pt: Ferning: What a Positive Pattern Looks Like
info.t: Fine, branching, leaf-like arborization across the dried specimen supports the presence of amniotic fluid. Ferning is an adjunct to the history and examination, not a substitute for assessing maternal and fetal status.

info.pt: Ferning: What a Positive Pattern Looks Like
info.t: Cervical mucus and semen can create branching patterns. Blood, scant fluid, a dry swab, technical error, or contamination can obscure or prevent arborization. Ferning is less reliable when the patient is not in labor, so a negative slide does not overrule ongoing high suspicion. Reassess

When the sterile speculum examination does not establish ROM, search the Dell Seton order menu for Rupture of Fetal Membranes. This is the local order used for the AmniSure/PAMG-1 immunoassay. Confirm the current order name and collection instructions in the live EHR if the menu changes.

AmniSure detects placental alpha-microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1) in cervicovaginal fluid. A positive result supports that amniotic fluid is present. Diagnostic studies generally show higher sensitivity than nitrazine or ferning, but performance varies with the population, sampling, and reference standard. Evidence

A positive result does not diagnose intra-amniotic infection, abruption, labor, fetal compromise, or imminent delivery. A negative result lowers the likelihood but does not rule out a small/intermittent leak or a poorly collected sample. Correlate with history, sterile speculum findings, gestational age, maternal condition, and fetal monitoring. Persistent high suspicion requires reassessment and OB/MFM input. High suspicion

AmniSure does not replace the emergency triage, fetal monitoring, sterile speculum examination, infection assessment, or OB/L&D disposition plan. Never delay treatment of cord prolapse, hemorrhage, suspected infection, fetal compromise, active labor, or imminent delivery while waiting for the result.

• Urinary incontinence or urine leakage • Physiologic leukorrhea of pregnancy • Cervical mucus or mucus plug • Semen after intercourse • Bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, or cervicitis • Vaginal bleeding or blood-tinged discharge • Sweating or fluid from cleansing products

Amniotic fluid is more alkaline than normal vaginal fluid, but nitrazine can be falsely positive with blood, semen, urine, cervical mucus, vaginitis, and alkaline antiseptics. Do not use pH alone to establish ROM.
Cervical mucus and semen can mimic arborization. Blood, scant fluid, a dry swab, or poor slide technique can cause a false-negative or uninterpretable result. Ferning photo
Oligohydramnios supports the diagnosis in the right clinical context. A normal amniotic-fluid volume does not exclude a recent, small, or intermittent membrane leak.

info.h: Do NOT perform a routine digital cervical examination
info.t: Use a sterile speculum when ROM is suspected. Avoid digital examination unless delivery is imminent or OB directs it because examination can increase infection exposure and shorten latency in PPROM. Speculum examination

info.h: Do NOT delay an obstetric emergency for testing
info.t: Cord prolapse, heavy bleeding/abruption, suspected intra-amniotic infection, nonreassuring fetal status, maternal instability, active labor, and imminent birth outrank AmniSure, ferning, nitrazine, and ultrasound.

info.h: Do NOT call a single negative test definitive
info.t: A negative result can occur with scant or intermittent leakage or poor sampling. If the history remains convincing, reassess the specimen and involve OB/MFM. Reassess

info.h: Do NOT use test results as a substitute for disposition
info.t: A positive ROM test does not assess fetal status, infection, abruption, labor, or neonatal capability. Route by gestational age and maternal/fetal condition, with an explicit OB/L&D plan. Gestational-age routing
• Peripartum + sudden hypoxia + hypotension + DIC • ~30% have prodrome: agitation, "sense of doom", paresthesias • Rule out PE, anaphylaxis, sepsis, hemorrhage, eclampsia
• Call OB, anesthesia, ICU, NICU, blood bank (MTP), ECMO • Announce the diagnosis — bring OR to patient, do NOT transport • Immediate intubation, 100% FiO₂, PEEP 5–10, ETT 6.0–7.0

• If arrest → CPR with standard hand position + manual LUD • Two-handed push-to-left over tilt — continuous through CPR • 2× large-bore IV above diaphragm, A-line, IO if no IV in 60s • Draw fibrinogen, platelets, PT/PTT, TEG, ABG, lactate, type+cross 6 U

• A-O-K: Atropine 0.2 mg + Ondansetron 8 mg + Ketorolac 15 mg IV push together • Alternative 50-50-500: Diphenhydramine 50 mg + Famotidine 50 mg + Hydrocortisone 500 mg IV • Start norepinephrine 0.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min — add vasopressin 0.04 U/min early

• If arrest + ≥23 wk and no ROSC by 4 min → start resuscitative hysterotomy NOW • Bedside — do NOT transport to OR; midline vertical, CPR continuous • Full procedural detail in Resuscitative Hysterotomy consult

• Activate MTP — do not wait for labs; 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets • Fibrinogen target ≥150–200 mg/dL — cryoprecipitate 10 U or fibrinogen concentrate 2–4 g • TXA 1 g IV over 10 min × 2 doses (second at 30 min if bleeding) — <3 h window • Avoid rFVIIa — thrombotic death in Amniotic Fluid Embolism series

• Call ECMO team DURING resus, not after — survival 60–80% with vs ~30% without • Impella RP / RVAD if ECMO delayed • Extended CPR in Amniotic Fluid Embolism has produced neurologically intact survivors — do not terminate early
• ICU, TTM 32–36 °C × 24 h if comatose • Trend fibrinogen, TEG, platelets q1–2 h — watch delayed DIC × 24 h • Report to AFE Foundation registry

1. Sudden cardiorespiratory arrest OR hypotension (SBP <90) + respiratory compromise (dyspnea, cyanosis, SpO₂ <90%) 2. Documented DIC (ISTH obstetric score ≥3) after the initial event — BEFORE significant hemorrhage-related dilution 3. Clinical onset during labor, C-section, D&E, or within 30 minutes postpartum 4. No other clinical explanation for findings Amniotic Fluid Embolism is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion — treat empirically, meet criteria retrospectively. Do NOT delay resuscitation to establish the diagnosis.

Hypoxia + Hypotension + Coagulopathy occurring in peripartum period. Prodrome in ~30% of cases — precedes collapse by seconds to minutes: • Agitation, restlessness • "Sense of impending doom" • Shivering, chills • Paresthesias, metallic taste • Numbness of lips, fingers

Platelet count: >100 = 0, 50–100 = 1, <50 = 2 Prolonged PT: <25% = 0, 25–50% = 1, >50% = 2 Fibrinogen: >200 = 0, ≤200 = 1 Total score ≥3 = overt DIC (obstetric-specific — lower than the ≥5 threshold for general DIC).

• Pulmonary embolism — echo: RV strain without fibrinolytic DIC • Anaphylaxis — urticaria, clear trigger, responds to epi alone • Septic shock — slower onset, source + fever/WBC • Myocardial infarction — ECG changes, troponin • Eclampsia — seizure, proteinuria, HTN • Hemorrhagic shock — identifiable bleeding + fluid-responsive • Peripartum cardiomyopathy — subacute, LV dysfunction, no DIC • Air embolism / LAST — context-specific

• Incidence: 1 in 15,200 to 1 in 53,800 deliveries (varies by registry) • Maternal mortality: 20–60% • Neurologically intact maternal survival: ~70% of survivors • Perinatal mortality: ~20–25% • ~50% of deaths occur within first hour — recognition and action in minutes matters

• Hand position: standard — center of sternum (NOT higher, despite older teaching) • Rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil — same as non-pregnant • Rotate compressor q2 min — fatigue drops quality fast • Mechanical CPR device if available — frees a team member for other tasks

info.h: Manual Left Uterine Displacement (LUD) — MANDATORY if fundus ≥ umbilicus
info.t: Two-handed push-to-left is preferred over tilt. Technique: Dedicated provider stands at patient's left, cups uterus with both hands, pushes up and to the patient's LEFT. Continuous throughout CPR — do NOT stop for rhythm checks. Why: IVC compression by gravid uterus reduces venous return up to 30%. CPR is ineffective without LUD. Tilt (Cardiff wedge, rolled blanket) is inferior — compression quality drops ~30% on any tilt. Use only if LUD cannot be maintained.

• Standard joules — biphasic 120–200 J or monophasic 360 J • Standard pad placement — anterolateral; no change for pregnancy • Remove fetal monitors BEFORE defibrillation — external and internal (scalp electrode) • Energy absorbed by fetus is negligible — do not under-dose

• Early intubation — higher aspiration risk + airway edema + difficult airway • Smaller ETT (6.0–7.0) — laryngeal and mucosal edema • Cricoid pressure during bagging until intubated • Expect difficult airway — full-term body habitus, large breasts, Mallampati worsening • Waveform capnography immediately post-intubation — ETCO₂ >20 = adequate CPR

• IV above the diaphragm — IVC compression below • IO if no IV within 60 sec — humeral (above-diaphragm) preferred • All ACLS drugs at standard doses — epinephrine 1 mg IV q3–5 min, amiodarone 300 mg bolus • No drug contraindicated in maternal arrest — fetal risk is irrelevant if mother dies

If ROSC not achieved by 4 minutes of arrest AND fundus ≥ umbilicus OR ≥23 wk: start resuscitative hysterotomy at minute 4, deliver by minute 5. Relieves aortocaval compression → restores maternal venous return and CPR effectiveness. Maternal survival is the primary goal, not fetal rescue. Bedside procedure — do NOT transport. → Resuscitative Hysterotomy consult for full procedure.

Rationale: Blocks three pulmonary vasoconstrictor/platelet pathways simultaneously. Case-report evidence; reasonable adjunct to ACLS, pressors, MTP, and perimortem C/S. Give all three together, IV push, within 1 minute of recognition: • Atropine 0.2 mg IV — vagolytic → reverses pulmonary reflex bradycardia/hypotension • Ondansetron 8 mg IV — 5-HT3 antagonist → reduces serotonin-mediated pulmonary vasoconstriction • Ketorolac 15 mg IV — COX inhibitor → blocks thromboxane, preserves platelets Mnemonic: "All Of these in a Kiss" — give together.

Based on the older anaphylactoid hypothesis for Amniotic Fluid Embolism pathophysiology (complement activation + mast cell degranulation). Still reasonable if A-O-K drugs unavailable or as an addition. • Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV — H1 antihistamine • Famotidine 50 mg IV (or 20 mg per hospital formulary) — H2 antihistamine • Hydrocortisone 500 mg IV — stress-dose corticosteroid

info.h: What these drugs DO NOT replace
