info.t: • ACLS — CPR, defibrillation, standard resuscitation drugs • Perimortem C/S at 4 minutes of arrest • Massive transfusion 1:1:1 with fibrinogen replacement • Vasopressors (norepinephrine + vasopressin) • Mechanical circulatory support (ECMO) for refractory cases A-O-K and 50-50-500 are adjuncts. The core resuscitation must continue in parallel.

Both protocols are based on case reports and small case series. No RCTs exist — Amniotic Fluid Embolism is too rare (~1:50,000 deliveries) for randomization. The mechanistic rationale is plausible, the drugs are cheap and available, and the risk profile in the peri-arrest setting is favorable. Rezai 2017 reports maternal and neonatal survival in an atypical Amniotic Fluid Embolism case using A-O-K. Subsequent case reports have shown varying outcomes.

Do NOT wait for labs. Amniotic Fluid Embolism coagulopathy is fibrinolytic PLUS consumptive — it will develop rapidly. Initial order set: • PRBC : FFP : Platelets = 1:1:1 (standard MTP pack) • Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or 2 pooled bags) • Fibrinogen concentrate 2–4 g IV if available (faster, volume-sparing) • Tranexamic acid (TXA) 1 g IV over 10 min • Type and crossmatch 6 U PRBC if not already

FIBRINOGEN: ≥150–200 mg/dL • Higher than trauma (<200 predicts ongoing obstetric hemorrhage — Charbit 2007) • Each 10 units cryo raises fibrinogen ~50–100 mg/dL • 1 g fibrinogen concentrate raises fibrinogen ~30–40 mg/dL in 70 kg patient PLATELETS: >50 ×10⁹/L (>75 if ongoing bleeding, >100 if CNS hemorrhage) PT/INR: <1.5 × control pH: >7.2 — bicarb for pH <7.1 with hemodynamic instability iCa²⁺: >1.1 mmol/L — check after every 4 units PRBC (citrate chelates calcium) Temperature: >35 °C — fluid warmer + forced-air rewarmer mandatory

Tranexamic acid (TXA): • 1 g IV over 10 min → repeat 1 g IV over 10 min at 30 minutes if bleeding continues • Must be given <3 h from onset of hemorrhage/Amniotic Fluid Embolism — effect diminishes after • WOMAN trial (Lancet 2017): NNT 267 for death from bleeding in PPH; no increase in thromboembolic events • Do NOT rapid-push — causes hypotension

If available, TEG/ROTEM is superior to static fibrinogen for real-time decision making: • FIBTEM A5 <12 mm → give fibrinogen (cryo or concentrate) • EXTEM CT prolonged → FFP or 4-factor PCC • LY30 >3% → TXA for hyperfibrinolysis • EXTEM A10 low + FIBTEM normal → platelets

Avoid recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) — Leighton 2011 systematic review showed increased thrombotic death in Amniotic Fluid Embolism patients receiving rFVIIa. Reserve only for refractory bleeding AFTER maximal standard MTP has failed AND surgical bleeding is controlled. Avoid prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) routinely in Amniotic Fluid Embolism — unlike in anticoagulation reversal, it adds procoagulant load to an already prothrombotic complication. TEG-guided use only. Avoid crystalloid overload — dilutes remaining factors, worsens RV distension, and triggers abdominal compartment syndrome if >3 L given.

Oxytocin 20 U in 1 L NS at 250 mL/hr — never IV push (hypotension) Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM — avoid if HTN/preeclampsia Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) 250 mcg IM q15 min × 8 doses — avoid in asthma Misoprostol 800–1000 mcg PR or SL — safe in HTN and asthma Bakri balloon or uterine packing for refractory atony Hysterectomy — do not delay for the dying patient

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transport to OR for perimortem C/S
info.t: Resuscitative hysterotomy is a bedside procedure. Transport wastes the 4-minute window and degrades CPR quality. Bring a scalpel, not a gurney. Perimortem C/S decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay hysterotomy waiting for anesthesia
info.t: A patient in cardiac arrest needs no anesthesia. Waiting for an anesthesiologist to "confirm" she is in arrest before cutting violates the 4-minute rule. Start hysterotomy NOW.
IV push causes profound hypotension and can re-arrest a post-ROSC Amniotic Fluid Embolism patient. Always dilute 20 units in 1 L NS at 250 mL/hr or give 10 U IM. Uterine atony management.
The 50 mcg/kg bolus drops SBP by 10–20 mmHg — catastrophic in Amniotic Fluid Embolism shock. Start infusion at 0.25 mcg/kg/min without a bolus. Hemodynamic support.

Leighton 2011: recombinant Factor VIIa was associated with increased thrombotic death in Amniotic Fluid Embolism. Reserve only for refractory bleeding after maximal standard MTP has failed. MTP targets.

Amniotic Fluid Embolism shock is RV failure physiology. Fluid worsens RV distension and septal shift. Limit crystalloid to 500 mL during initial resuscitation; use blood products after. RV-first strategy.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT place chest compressions higher than normal
info.t: Older teaching recommended higher hand position in pregnancy. The AHA 2015 statement confirms: standard center-of-sternum position. Hand position is not the problem — aortocaval compression is. Pregnancy-modified ACLS.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT tilt instead of manual LUD
info.t: Any tilt (Cardiff wedge, rolled blanket, left lateral decubitus) degrades compression quality ~30%. Two-handed push-to-left by a dedicated provider is the standard. LUD technique.

Amniotic Fluid Embolism is one of the few arrest scenarios where prolonged, "futile-appearing" CPR has produced neurologically intact survivors. Reversible physiology + ECMO eligibility = extended resuscitation is appropriate. Extended resuscitation.

NICU team must be at the bedside BEFORE hysterotomy. Neonatal outcomes depend on time from maternal arrest to delivery — have the team, the warmer, and the equipment ready when you cut. Team activation.

• Blood loss ≥1000 mL OR signs of hypovolemia within 24h of delivery • Shock Index >0.9 abnormal in pregnancy; >1.0 = hemorrhagic shock • Call OB, anesthesia, blood bank, charge nurse — announce clearly • Designate a timekeeper — call out every 5 min
• 2 large-bore IVs (16-18g), IO if access fails • CBC, fibrinogen, PT/PTT, T&C 4-6 units — fibrinogen <200 = severe PPH • Emergency-release O-neg blood; activate MTP if SI >1.0
• Fundal massage + empty bladder (Foley) • Tranexamic Acid 1 g IV within 3h — repeat at 30 min if bleeding continues • Bimanual uterine compression — 5-10 min

• Tone (70-80%) — boggy uterus → uterotonics • Trauma (20%) — speculum every quadrant, check fundus • Tissue (10%) — retained products; manual exploration • Thrombin (<1%) — coagulopathy; MTP + balanced transfusion

• Oxytocin 20u in 1L at 250 mL/hr — NEVER IV push • Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM q2-4h — AVOID in HTN/preeclampsia • Carboprost 0.25 mg IM q15-90 min — AVOID in asthma • Misoprostol 800-1000 mcg PR/SL — few CIs, useful when other agents blocked

• Bakri balloon 300-500 mL saline under U/S — 75-86% success • Activate [Massive Transfusion Protocol — 1:1:1 + cryo + Ca + warm](#/node/pph-mtp) • IR for UAE (stable); OR for B-Lynch, O'Leary, hysterectomy • Hysterectomy is the final life-saving step — do not delay

• ICU if ≥4 units transfused, hysterectomy, or instability • VTE prophylaxis mechanical immediately; pharmacologic once hemostatic • RhoGAM within 72h if Rh-negative mother • [Discharge Instructions for return precautions](#/node/pph-controlled)

Clinical clue: Boggy, soft uterus; fundus palpable above umbilicus. Risk factors: Prolonged labor, augmented labor, chorioamnionitis, overdistension (multiples, polyhydramnios, macrosomia), grand multiparity, rapid precipitous delivery, general anesthesia, magnesium sulfate. Management: • Fundal massage + empty bladder • Bimanual compression • Uterotonic ladder: Oxytocin → Methylergonovine → Carboprost → Misoprostol • Persist → Bakri balloon

Clinical clue: Firm, well-contracted uterus but ongoing bleeding. Types: • Cervical laceration — most common at 3 and 9 o'clock; use ring forceps to inspect every quadrant • Vaginal laceration / sulcus tear — side walls, posterior fornix • Perineal laceration — 1st-4th degree grading • Vulvar / paravaginal hematoma — disproportionate pain, expanding mass, hemodynamic decline • Uterine inversion — absent/dimpled fundus abdominally, fleshy mass at introitus • Uterine rupture — severe pain, loss of fetal station, hemoperitoneum Management: • Speculum exam with adequate light, analgesia, assistants • Repair 1st/2nd degree perineal in ED; defer 3rd/4th and cervical to OB • Uterine inversion → sto

Clinical clue: Incomplete placenta on inspection; persistent bleeding despite firm uterus; placenta not delivered within 30 min. Types: • Retained cotyledon / fragment — torn edge or ragged membranes • Retained succenturiate lobe — check for torn vessels at placental edge • Placenta accreta spectrum — resistant to separation; DO NOT force • Blood clot retention — evacuate manually Management: • Manual uterine exploration under analgesia • Ultrasound-guided D&C if needed • Antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin) • Accreta → leave placenta in situ, transfer to OR for controlled delivery ± hysterectomy

Clinical clue: Oozing from IV sites, mucosal bleeding, petechiae, non-clotting blood. Causes: • Dilutional coagulopathy (large crystalloid or unbalanced resuscitation) • DIC — severe PPH, sepsis, abruption, IUFD • Amniotic Fluid Embolism — cardiopulmonary collapse + DIC + respiratory failure • HELLP / severe preeclampsia • Pre-existing — vWD, hemophilia carrier, anticoagulation Management: • Balanced transfusion 1:1:1 (pRBC:FFP:platelets) — MTP • Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <200 mg/dL • Calcium gluconate 1-2 g per 4 units blood • Keep warm, correct acidosis, treat the lethal triad

Always check tone first. It's the most common cause. If the uterus is firm and well-contracted but bleeding continues, pivot immediately to trauma and tissue. Thrombin is the quietest but easiest to miss — watch the IV sites and the drapes.

Dose: 20 units in 1 L NS/LR at 250 mL/hr (~10 mU/min) — or 10 units IM if no IV Onset: 1-2 min IV, 3-5 min IM Contraindications: None significant at PPH doses Cautions: • NEVER IV push — causes profound hypotension, can re-arrest • Water intoxication with prolonged high-dose infusion Full drug detail →

Dose: 0.2 mg IM, may repeat q2-4h up to 5 doses (1 mg total) Onset: 2-5 min Contraindications (absolute): • Hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP • Coronary artery disease, recent MI, CVA • Raynaud's phenomenon • Sepsis (vasospasm → gangrene) Cautions: • NEVER IV — fatal hypertensive emergencies • Premedicate with ondansetron (nausea/vomiting common) Full drug detail →

Dose: 0.25 mg (250 mcg) IM, may repeat q15-90 min up to 8 doses (2 mg total) Onset: 3-5 min Contraindications (absolute): • Asthma — ANY history • Pulmonary hypertension • Significant cardiac, hepatic, renal disease Cautions: • Stop if bronchospasm develops • Premedicate with ondansetron + loperamide (GI side effects in 20-30%) • Fever, flushing common Full drug detail →

Dose: 800-1000 mcg PR or SL, single dose Onset: 10-15 min PR, faster SL Contraindications: Essentially none at PPH doses Cautions: • Fever, shivering expected (~30-50%, not infection) • Diarrhea common When to use: First choice when HTN + asthma both present (methylergonovine AND carboprost contraindicated). Cheap, shelf-stable — widely used globally. Full drug detail →

No HTN, no asthma → Oxytocin → Methergine → Hemabate → Miso HTN / preeclampsia → Oxytocin → Hemabate (if no asthma) → Miso Asthma → Oxytocin → Methergine (if no HTN) → Miso HTN + Asthma → Oxytocin → Miso (only agent without absolute CI) Always use drugs in parallel with mechanical measures (massage, bimanual compression) and TXA.

• Persistent uterine atony despite maximal medical therapy • Bleeding from the lower uterine segment (e.g., after placenta previa) • Temporizing measure during transport to OR or interventional radiology • Coagulopathy with ongoing hemorrhage (while correcting)

• Known uterine anomaly preventing balloon placement • Uterine rupture (do not balloon-tamponade a torn uterus) • Active uterine infection • Inability to identify the source (e.g., undiagnosed laceration — rule out first)

• Bakri balloon (specific brand — max 500 mL; alternatives: ebb balloon 750 mL, or Foley 30-60 mL if Bakri unavailable) • Sterile 60 mL syringe or IV tubing • 500 mL sterile saline • Speculum, ring forceps • Ultrasound for placement confirmation • Foley catheter (empty bladder prior to placement)

1. Empty the bladder (Foley). 2. Place patient in lithotomy, expose cervix with speculum. 3. Insert deflated balloon through the cervix into the uterine cavity — grasp anterior cervical lip with ring forceps to stabilize. 4. Confirm intrauterine placement with bedside ultrasound — the balloon tip should be above the level of the cervix, within the uterine fundus. 5. Inflate with sterile saline: 300-500 mL (do not exceed 500 mL for Bakri). Stop at the volume that controls bleeding and provides firm resistance. 6. Apply gentle downward traction on the drainage port — tape stem to the patient's thigh. 7. Monitor the drainage port: blood draining at >100 mL/hr = tamponade failure → escalate to s

Bakri balloon tamponade achieves hemostasis in 75-86% of atonic PPH cases, reducing the need for hysterectomy. Best outcomes when applied early — before massive transfusion cascade. Failure (>100 mL/hr drainage continuing) → move rapidly to surgical options: B-Lynch suture, uterine artery embolization (IR), or hysterectomy.

• Bakri-style condom catheter (Akhter method) — MacGyver'd from a Foley + condom + IV saline; 85–95% success in published series; WHO-endorsed for low-resource and bridge use • Foley catheter alone (30–60 mL balloon) — widely available; weakest option but useful as immediate bridge while building a condom catheter • Sengstaken-Blakemore / Rüsch / ebb balloon — larger-volume alternatives; off-label use of esophageal balloons • Uterine packing with gauze — older technique (rolled gauze soaked in saline ± thrombin), largely replaced by balloons but still valid if nothing else available

Indications — same as Bakri: • Persistent atonic PPH despite uterotonics + bimanual compression • Lower-uterine-segment bleeding (placenta previa site) • Bridge to OR / IR / transfer when commercial balloon is unavailable or not on formulary Settings where this is standard of care: • Low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) — originally published in Bangladesh by Dr. Sayeba Akhter • Rural US hospitals without L&D or IR • Disaster / austere / field medicine • Any ED where the Bakri is locked in L&D and the patient is bleeding now — the condom catheter can be assembled at bedside in 2–3 minutes Same contraindications as Bakri: uterine rupture, uterine anomaly preventing placement, active infect

• Foley catheter, 16–18 Fr with 30 mL bulb (standard bladder catheter — pick the largest your ED stocks) • 1 condom — any latex male condom; unlubricated preferred but any will work. If latex allergy → polyurethane/polyisoprene condom or sterile surgical glove finger as substitute • 2–3 lengths of silk suture, umbilical tape, or sterile string — to tie the condom to the catheter • IV bag of normal saline (500 mL or 1 L) + standard IV tubing • Three-way stopcock (optional but helpful — allows clamping without disconnecting) • Ring forceps × 2 (sponge forceps) • Bivalve speculum (Graves or Sims) • Sterile gloves, lube, Betadine • Second Foley catheter for the bladder (always empty the bladder

1a. Open the Foley catheter aseptically. Do NOT insert it into the bladder. 1b. Unroll the condom over the distal tip of the Foley catheter — the condom covers the drainage eyes AND the 30 mL bulb. The Foley should sit entirely inside the condom with only the proximal shaft (with the inflation port and drainage port) exposed. 1c. Tie the open end of the condom tightly to the catheter shaft just proximal to the Foley bulb using 2–3 wraps of silk suture or umbilical tape. Pull tight — leaks here defeat the whole device. A second tie 1 cm proximal to the first adds security. 1d. Test the assembly on the back table: inflate the Foley bulb with 10 mL of air first, then push 50 mL of saline into t

2a. Lithotomy position, Betadine prep, sterile drapes. 2b. Empty the bladder with a second Foley — uterine distension from the balloon will compress the bladder and cause retention if not drained. 2c. Bimanual exam to confirm the uterus is atonic and to rule out uterine rupture or retained placenta (both are absolute contraindications — tamponading a rupture is lethal, tamponading retained products delays definitive treatment). 2d. Insert the bivalve speculum and visualize the cervix. Grasp the anterior cervical lip with ring forceps to stabilize and straighten the cervical canal.

3a. Hold the assembled catheter with the second pair of ring forceps at the distal (condom-covered) end. Guide the condom tip through the cervix into the uterine cavity. 3b. Advance until the condom is entirely above the internal os — feel for loss of resistance as you pass the internal os. The entire Foley bulb and the condom should sit in the uterine body. 3c. Inflate the Foley bulb with 10 mL of saline (through the balloon port) — this anchors the catheter and helps prevent the condom from being pushed out. 3d. If ultrasound is available, confirm intrauterine placement — the balloon should be visible as a fluid-filled structure within the uterine cavity, above the level of the internal os

4a. Connect IV tubing from the 500 mL or 1 L NS bag to the drainage port of the Foley (not the balloon port). A three-way stopcock between tubing and catheter makes clamping easier. 4b. Hang the saline bag 1–1.5 meters above the patient or squeeze with both hands to drive flow. 4c. Fill gradually, watching for: • Hemorrhage slowing or stopping — the primary endpoint • Firm resistance against the uterine wall • Return of normal uterine tone on abdominal palpation 4d. Typical fill volume: 250–500 mL (range 100–750 mL depending on uterine size — a post-term or twin uterus can take more). Stop when bleeding stops or when you feel firm resistance — do not chase an arbitrary volume. 4e. Clamp the

5a. Apply gentle downward traction on the catheter shaft and tape it to the patient's inner thigh — tension keeps the condom seated against the lower uterine segment. 5b. Pack the vagina with a sterile gauze roll if the condom appears to be prolapsing through the cervix. A Sims or Deaver retractor supported by vaginal packing also works. 5c. Start or continue Oxytocin 20 units in 1 L NS at 250 mL/hr — uterotonic support improves tamponade efficacy by adding myometrial contraction. 5d. Prophylactic antibiotics: ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV, cefazolin 2 g IV, or (in resource-limited settings) ampicillin 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV. 5e. Bladder Foley stays in throughout the procedure and fo

6a. Leave in place 12–48 hours — most protocols use 24 hours. Longer is tolerated in LMIC settings while waiting for transfer. 6b. Before removal: ensure bleeding has stopped, vitals are stable, fibrinogen and platelets are within safe range, and any coagulopathy has been corrected. 6c. Deflate the condom gradually — open the clamp and allow saline to drain by gravity over 10–20 minutes (not all at once — a rapid deflation can trigger rebound bleeding). 6d. Observe for 30 minutes with the empty catheter still in place — if re-bleeding starts, re-inflate immediately and plan definitive surgical management (B-Lynch, UAE, or hysterectomy). 6e. Deflate the Foley bulb (remove the 10 mL saline fro

• Akhter 2003 (original description, 23 patients, Bangladesh): 100% hemostasis in atonic PPH refractory to uterotonics. No hysterectomies in the case series. • Tindell 2012 (systematic review, 13 studies, 369 patients): pooled success ~92% for uterine balloon tamponade across commercial and improvised devices — condom catheter outcomes comparable to Bakri. • Rathore 2012 (RCT, 32 patients in India): condom catheter controlled bleeding in 94% vs. conventional management in 62%. • WHO 2017 Updated PPH Recommendations: uterine balloon tamponade (including improvised devices) is recommended when uterotonics fail and before resorting to surgery. Caveat: Most high-quality evidence is from LMIC coh

🛑 Leak at the tie — the single most common failure. Test on the back table before insertion. Use 2–3 ties, not one. If you see saline seeping during fill, stop, deflate, re-tie. 🛑 Under-filling — stopping at 100 mL because "that seemed like enough." The endpoint is bleeding stopped AND firm resistance — not a number. A term-pregnancy uterus can easily accept 500 mL. 🛑 Over-filling — forcing past resistance risks uterine rupture, especially in an already-overdistended atonic uterus. Stop when bleeding stops. 🛑 Missed uterine rupture — tamponading a torn uterus is fatal. Always bimanual-exam first; if any suspicion of rupture (shoulder-tip pain, hemoperitoneum on FAST, unstable vitals out

Failure = >100 mL/hr continued drainage OR unstable vitals despite resuscitation OR rising fundus above the balloon. Escalate immediately: • Massive Transfusion Protocol — 1:1:1 + cryoprecipitate if not already running • OR for B-Lynch suture, O'Leary ligation, or hysterectomy • Interventional Radiology for uterine artery embolization if patient is stable enough to transport • Hysterectomy is the definitive answer — do not delay for fertility preservation if the patient is dying

Accreta — chorionic villi attached to myometrium (most superficial) Increta — villi invade into myometrium Percreta — villi penetrate through uterine serosa, may invade bladder, bowel, or adjacent organs Collectively called placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). Incidence: 1 in 500-1000 deliveries in the US; rising sharply with cesarean delivery rates.

• Placenta previa over a prior cesarean scar — >50% risk with 3+ prior C-sections • Prior cesarean delivery (risk ↑ with each) • Prior uterine surgery (myomectomy, D&C, endometrial ablation) • Advanced maternal age, multiparity • Prior uterine radiation • IVF pregnancy

• Placenta fails to deliver within 30 minutes of birth • No plane of cleavage on manual extraction — resistance to separation • Heavy bleeding when separation is attempted • Ultrasound before delivery may show loss of retroplacental clear space, placental lacunae

DO NOT FORCE placental separation — catastrophic hemorrhage (average blood loss with forced separation: 3-5 L). If PAS is discovered during delivery: 1. Stop — do not pull harder 2. Leave the placenta in situ 3. Resuscitate aggressively — 2 large-bore IVs, T&C 4-6 units, activate MTP 4. Transfer to OR immediately for controlled cesarean hysterectomy (if no ability to deliver in-place vaginally with accreta-specialized team) 5. Consult interventional radiology for possible preoperative uterine artery balloon occlusion 6. Consult urology if bladder involvement suspected (percreta)

When PAS is diagnosed antepartum by ultrasound or MRI, delivery should be planned at 34-35 weeks in a tertiary center with: • Accreta-experienced OB surgeon • IR availability (preoperative balloon occlusion catheters) • ICU bed • Blood bank with 4-6 units crossmatched and MTP ready • Cell saver • Urology on standby Planned cesarean hysterectomy is the standard of care for diagnosed percreta.

info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: You had a postpartum hemorrhage — heavier-than-normal bleeding after delivery. The team acted quickly to stop the bleeding, replace blood if needed, and make sure you and your baby are safe. It is normal to feel shaken, tired, or emotional for days to weeks afterward.

info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: • Vaginal bleeding (lochia) — normal for 4-6 weeks. Starts red, becomes pink, then yellow/white. • Fatigue — you may feel tired for weeks, especially if you needed a transfusion. Iron supplements help. • Cramping — especially with breastfeeding; this is your uterus contracting back down, a good sign. • Emotional changes — mood swings, tearfulness, even flashbacks to the event are common after severe PPH. You are not alone.

info.h: 🚨 Return to the ED Immediately If:
info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: • Heavy bleeding — soaking more than one full pad per hour for 2+ hours • Passing large blood clots (bigger than a golf ball, or multiple clots in a row) • Sudden flood of bright red blood after bleeding had slowed • Foul-smelling vaginal discharge or fever >100.4°F (38°C) • Severe abdominal or pelvic pain that is getting worse • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting when standing up • Fast heartbeat (>110/min at rest), pale skin, cold sweat • Calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath (blood clot warning signs — higher risk after PPH) • Severe headache, vision changes, or confusion (preeclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum)

info.h: Medications You Will Continue at Home
info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: • Iron supplements — take with vitamin C or orange juice; avoid with coffee/tea/dairy. Constipation is common — stool softener helps. • Antibiotics — finish the full course even if you feel better. • Pain medicine — take as directed; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs if you have a bleeding history. • Prenatal vitamins — continue, especially if breastfeeding.

info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: • OB visit — in 1-2 weeks (earlier if you had a hysterectomy or major surgery). Bring a list of questions. • Blood count check — often done at your 2-week visit. • Future pregnancies — tell your next pregnancy doctor you had a PPH; this changes how they plan your next delivery. • Mental health — ask about counseling or support groups. Severe PPH can cause post-traumatic stress and postpartum depression.

info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: • Rest as much as possible for the first 2 weeks — avoid heavy lifting, stairs if possible. • Walk short distances several times a day to reduce blood clot risk. • No driving for at least 1 week after discharge (or longer if you had surgery). • No sexual intercourse, tampons, or douching until cleared by your OB (usually 4-6 weeks). • Stay hydrated — especially if breastfeeding.

info.pt: After a Postpartum Hemorrhage — Patient Information
info.t: Surviving a postpartum hemorrhage is physically and emotionally hard. Many people feel scared, guilty, or overwhelmed afterward. This is normal. Talk to your doctor, partner, or a counselor. Organizations like Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773) can help. https://www.postpartum.net

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give oxytocin IV push
info.t: IV bolus of oxytocin causes profound hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias — documented cardiac arrests have occurred, especially in patients with any underlying cardiac compromise. Always give as an infusion (20 units in 1 L at 250 mL/hr) or IM (10 units). See oxytocin node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methylergonovine in HTN or preeclampsia
info.t: Methergine causes severe vasoconstriction and has triggered fatal hypertensive emergencies, MI, and CVA when given to patients with any hypertension, preeclampsia, or CAD. Always check BP before every dose. If HTN, skip to misoprostol or (if no asthma) carboprost. See methergine check.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give carboprost (Hemabate) in asthma
info.t: Carboprost is a PGF2α analog — bronchospasm is the dose-limiting adverse effect and has caused fatal status asthmaticus. Any history of asthma is an absolute contraindication. Use misoprostol instead. See carboprost check.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT pull harder on a placenta that won't separate
info.t: Forceful traction on an adherent placenta can cause uterine inversion (life-threatening emergency) or catastrophic hemorrhage from placenta accreta (average EBL with forced separation: 3-5 L). If resistance is felt, stop immediately — leave the placenta in situ and transfer to OR. See tissue node and accreta page.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give uterotonics to a uterine inversion
info.t: Uterotonics contract the cervical ring, trapping the inverted uterus and making manual reduction impossible. Stop all uterotonics immediately if you suspect inversion (dimpled/absent fundus, fleshy mass at introitus). Use tocolytics (NTG, terbutaline, or magnesium) to relax the uterus, perform manual reduction (Johnson maneuver), then resume uterotonics only AFTER the uterus is reverted. See uterine inversion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on visual estimation of blood loss
info.t: Visual EBL underestimates true blood loss by 30-50%. By the time hypotension develops in a pregnant patient, she has often lost ≥25% of her blood volume (~1500 mL). Use Shock Index >0.9 (abnormal) / >1.0 (shock), calibrated under-buttocks drapes, and weighed sponges. See initial assessment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay TXA past 3 hours
info.t: TXA reduces death from bleeding in PPH only when given within 3 hours of delivery (WOMAN trial, RR 0.69 for death from bleeding when given <1 hour). Given >3 hours has no benefit and may increase mortality in some subgroups. Don't wait on labs — give 1 g IV over 10 min as soon as PPH is diagnosed. See TXA node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interpret a "normal" fibrinogen as reassuring
info.t: Pregnancy baseline fibrinogen is 400-600 mg/dL at term. A fibrinogen of 300 mg/dL — "normal" in non-pregnant adults — actually reflects significant consumption in a postpartum bleed. <200 mg/dL is the earliest lab marker of severe PPH and predicts massive transfusion. Replete with cryoprecipitate aggressively. See labs.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay hysterectomy out of fertility preservation when life is threatened
info.t: Peripartum hysterectomy is the final life-saving step. Every additional hour of uncontrolled hemorrhage raises maternal mortality. When uterotonics + Bakri + MTP + IR/B-Lynch fail, do not delay hysterectomy out of inappropriate attachment to future fertility. Discuss with the patient's partner/family when possible, document indication, and proceed. See hysterectomy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget RhoGAM, VTE prophylaxis, and mental health follow-up
info.t: After the crisis: Rh-negative mothers need Rh Immune Globulin within 72 hours. PPH + immobility + massive transfusion dramatically raises VTE risk — start mechanical prophylaxis immediately and pharmacologic once hemostasis is confirmed (fibrinogen ≥200). Severe PPH is a traumatic event — screen for postpartum depression and PTSD at follow-up. See post-PPH care.
• Suspect breech: HR above umbilicus, head at fundus, soft presenting part • Confirm with bedside POCUS — takes <60 seconds • Classify: Frank (best), Complete, Footling (highest cord prolapse risk)

• Not imminent → OR for C-section (Term Breech Trial, ACOG 745) • Imminent (body delivering, full dilation, active pushing) → vaginal with maneuvers • Transverse lie → C-section only; tocolysis to buy time
• Call OB + Peds/NICU + Anesthesia STAT; OR must be available as backup • Check immediately for cord prolapse (footling = 15-20%) • Dorsal lithotomy, bladder empty, IV ×2, type and screen, warmer on

• Hands off the breech until scapulae visible — traction causes head extension • Body delivers to umbilicus via maternal pushing only • Keep back anterior; rotate if posterior (grip iliac crests, thumbs on sacrum) • Pinard maneuver for extended legs (frank breech): finger behind knee → reflex flexion • Loop cord down after umbilicus delivers; 5-10 min to head
• Flexed arms deliver spontaneously • Nuchal arm → Løvset maneuver: 180° rotate → sweep across chest; reverse for 2nd arm

• Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit: body on forearm, finger in MAXILLA (not mandible), other hand on shoulders • Burns-Marshall if MSV fails: hold ankles, body hangs, arc upward over abdomen • Head entrapment: Terbutaline tocolysis → emergent OR for C-section rescue

• Neonate: APGAR, brachial plexus exam, limb palpation, hip assessment • Oxytocin 20u in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr after placenta delivers • Inspect cervix carefully (higher laceration rate in breech) • Admit mom to OB ×24h min, neonate to nursery/NICU

ANATOMY: Hips flexed, both knees extended — fetal feet are up near the face ("pike position"). PRESENTING PART: Buttocks only; feels like a smooth oval on vaginal exam. DELIVERY IMPLICATIONS: • Most favorable type for vaginal delivery • Buttocks dilate cervix like a wedge — reduces risk of head entrapment • Lower cord prolapse risk (~0.5%) • May require Pinard maneuver to flex each extended leg for delivery

ANATOMY: Hips AND knees both flexed ("cannonball" or cross-legged position). PRESENTING PART: Both buttocks and feet together at the pelvic outlet. DELIVERY IMPLICATIONS: • Acceptable for vaginal delivery in selected cases • Cord prolapse risk ~5% • Legs deliver spontaneously — no Pinard needed

info.h: Incomplete / Footling Breech (10-40% at term, more common preterm)
info.t: ANATOMY: One or both hips extended — foot or feet present first. PRESENTING PART: Single foot (single footling) or both feet (double footling). DELIVERY IMPLICATIONS: • HIGHEST cord prolapse risk (~15-20%) — foot does not occlude cervix • Relative contraindication to vaginal delivery — cervix may not fully dilate around the small foot, trapping body/head • Strong preference for C-section even if delivery seems imminent
ANATOMY: Hips extended, knees flexed — knees present first. MANAGEMENT: Managed similarly to footling breech — high complication risk, prefer C-section.

SACRO-ANTERIOR (preferred): Fetal sacrum faces maternal pubic symphysis (anteriorly). This allows normal mechanism of labor, with proper head flexion during delivery. SACRO-POSTERIOR (avoid): Fetal sacrum faces maternal spine (posteriorly). Head is likely extended; vaginal delivery becomes dangerous. Gently rotate to sacro-anterior using iliac crest grip (thumbs on sacrum — never on abdomen). See Keep Back Anterior for rotation technique.

PURPOSE: Flex an extended fetal leg at the knee to deliver one foot at a time — used in frank breech with legs extended above the body. TECHNIQUE: 1. Two fingers into the vagina alongside the extended leg 2. Press behind the knee (popliteal fossa) — triggers reflex knee flexion 3. Sweep the foot laterally and deliver it 4. Repeat on the contralateral leg CAUTION: Do not pull on the leg. Reflex flexion from popliteal pressure, not traction. Named for Adolphe Pinard (1844-1934).

PURPOSE: Deliver fetal arms that are trapped behind the head ("nuchal arms"). GRIP: Thumbs on fetal sacrum, fingers wrapped around iliac crests. Never grip the abdomen. TECHNIQUE: 1. Gentle downward traction + rotate body 180° clockwise → brings posterior arm anteriorly under pubic arch 2. Sweep the now-anterior arm across the fetal face/chest and out 3. Rotate body 180° counter-clockwise → brings other arm anteriorly 4. Sweep second arm out the same way CAUTION: Always sweep arm across chest, not laterally — lateral sweep risks humerus fracture. Named for Jørgen Løvset (1896-1981).

PURPOSE: Deliver the aftercoming fetal head in controlled, flexed position. SETUP: Fetal body straddles operator's dominant forearm (face down). HAND POSITIONING: • Dominant hand (body-supporting): Middle finger into fetal mouth on the MAXILLA (upper jaw — NOT mandible). Index and ring fingers on malar/cheek bones. Purpose: flex the head. • Non-dominant hand (shoulder): Middle finger on occiput; index and ring fingers on each scapula. Purpose: downward shoulder traction. TECHNIQUE: 1. Gentle downward traction while mouth-finger keeps head flexed 2. As occiput emerges under symphysis, elevate body upward toward maternal abdomen 3. Head delivers over the perineum ASSISTANT: Gentle suprapubic p

PURPOSE: Alternative technique for the aftercoming head when MSV fails or is not preferred. TECHNIQUE: 1. Grasp fetal ankles with one hand 2. Let the body hang vertically from the perineum — body weight encourages head flexion 3. Wait 30-60 seconds for the occiput to appear under the symphysis 4. Once occiput visible, arc the body upward over the maternal abdomen in a slow wide sweep 5. Head delivers as chin → mouth → nose → forehead → occiput CAUTION: Move slowly — rapid decompression of the head causes tentorial tears and intracranial hemorrhage.

PURPOSE: Alternative hands-off technique used in European/German obstetric practice — promotes physiologic delivery with minimal manipulation. TECHNIQUE: 1. When the body has delivered to the scapulae, do not pull or manipulate 2. With the next contraction, grasp the body around the pelvis and gently hyperflex it upward over the maternal abdomen (symphysis as pivot) 3. This hyperflexion helps the head flex and deliver in one continuous motion 4. Assistant may apply suprapubic pressure CAUTION: Requires strong maternal contractions; may not work if uterine tone is poor. Most familiar to European providers.

PURPOSE: Relax uterus to allow head delivery or buy time for OR transfer. AGENTS: • Terbutaline 0.25 mg SQ × 1 — onset 1-5 min, duration 15-30 min • Nitroglycerin 50-200 mcg IV boluses — onset <1 min, duration 1-2 min (requires BP monitoring) USE: When head is entrapped and you need immediate uterine relaxation while preparing for rescue maneuvers or emergent C-section.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply traction to the fetal body
info.t: Traction causes the fetal head to extend — an extended head cannot pass through the pelvis, causing catastrophic head entrapment. Let uterine contractions and maternal pushing deliver the body. Hands off until scapulae visible.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT grip the fetal abdomen
info.t: Squeezing the abdomen damages the spleen, kidneys, and adrenal glands — adrenal hemorrhage is a known breech delivery complication. Always grip the bony pelvis: thumbs on sacrum, fingers on iliac crests. Correct grip.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt vaginal delivery if breech is NOT imminent
info.t: Per the Term Breech Trial (Hannah 2000) and ACOG Committee Opinion 745, planned C-section reduces perinatal mortality by 67%. If you have time for OR, use it. Transfer to OR.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to check for cord prolapse
info.t: Footling breech has a 15-20% cord prolapse rate. A sterile vaginal exam at first contact should rule this out. Missed cord prolapse = rapid fetal death. Cord check.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT pull on the fetal mandible during MSV
info.t: The Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit maneuver requires finger pressure on the MAXILLA (upper jaw) to flex the head. Pulling on the mandible dislocates the jaw and does NOT achieve head flexion. MSV technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT sweep Løvset arms laterally
info.t: When delivering nuchal arms with the Løvset maneuver, always sweep the arm across the fetal chest. Lateral sweep risks humerus fracture. Løvset technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rush the aftercoming head
info.t: Rapid head decompression causes tentorial tears and intracranial hemorrhage. Whether MSV or Burns-Marshall, move slowly and deliberately. Burns-Marshall.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt vaginal delivery of transverse lie
info.t: Transverse lie cannot be delivered vaginally. Attempts cause uterine rupture and fetal death. Tocolysis + emergent C-section only. Transverse management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt internal podalic version in the ED
info.t: Internal podalic version (rotating the fetus by pulling on the feet) is beyond ED scope. Historically performed, but carries high maternal and fetal morbidity. For transverse lie or compound presentation, go to OR.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT commit to vaginal breech without OR backup
info.t: Breech deliveries can convert to head entrapment, nuchal arms, or cord prolapse within minutes. Without available OR for C-section rescue, the risk is unacceptable. Always call OB + Anesthesia STAT before proceeding. Call for help.
• Maternal cardiac arrest confirmed • Fundus at or above umbilicus → RH indicated • If unsure of GA, assume ≥20 weeks and proceed

• Manual Left Lateral Uterine Displacement — continuous, dedicated provider • IV access ABOVE the diaphragm — IVC is compressed • Anticipate difficult airway — VL, small ETT, aspiration risk • Start the timer — timekeeper calls out every 30 seconds • Page OB, neonatology, anesthesia, blood bank

info.h: 3. Cardiac Arrest Response (standard ACLS, with modifications)
info.t: • Same drugs, same energies, same pad placement as non-pregnant • Compressions: standard midsternal position, 100-120/min, 5-6 cm depth • Seek reversible causes — BEAU-CHOPS mnemonic • Remove fetal monitors before defibrillation

• At 4 minutes without ROSC: begin incision • Target: fetus delivered by 5 minutes • Past 4 min already? Start NOW — later still beats never (Rose 2015, Benson 2016) • Scalpel is the only tool you need

info.h: 5. The Procedure (at the bedside, CPR ongoing)
info.t: • Do NOT move patient, do NOT wait for OB, do NOT stop CPR • Vertical midline skin incision: xiphoid → symphysis pubis • Classical (vertical) uterine incision — shallow entry, extend with fingers • Deliver fetus — head first (vertex) or presenting part (breech) • Clamp and cut cord — hand to neonatal team • Deliver placenta with gentle cord traction + fundal counter-pressure • Continue CPR throughout — do NOT close abdomen yet

• Reassess maternal pulse — ROSC often happens now • If ROSC: pressors, uterotonics, TXA, cefazolin 2g, transfer to OR • Uterine atony: Oxytocin drip + TXA 1g IV + bimanual massage • Neonate: vigorous? routine care. Depressed? initiate NRP • APGAR at 1, 5, 10 minutes — use the calculator • ICU + NICU — formal closure in OR — debrief team + family

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT move the patient to the OR
info.t: Transport degrades CPR quality and adds 5-15 minutes of delay. The procedure is performed at the bedside, wherever arrest occurred. Every minute of transport worsens maternal and neonatal outcomes. SOAP 2014, AHA 2015, EMCrit.
Most obstetricians have never performed RH outside the OR. The EM physician is the correct operator. OB can do formal closure later. Waiting for OB wastes the 4-minute window. Perform at bedside now.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop CPR during the procedure
info.t: CPR and LUD continue throughout incision and extraction. The delivery IS part of the resuscitation. Stopping compressions defeats the purpose. Continue CPR.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use tilted-board positioning during CPR
info.t: The 30° left tilt degrades chest compression quality by ~30%. Use manual LUD instead — patient flat supine, dedicated provider pulls uterus up and to the left continuously. Manual LUD technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT place IV access below the diaphragm
info.t: Femoral and lower-extremity access delivers drugs into a compressed IVC — they never reach the central circulation. Upper extremity or humeral IO only. Vascular access.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the procedure because you're past 4 minutes
info.t: The 4-minute rule is a starting gun, not a finish line. Rose 2015 and Benson 2016 demonstrate maternal and neonatal survival well beyond 5 minutes. Longer arrest is not a contraindication — do the procedure. Evidence on timing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use Pfannenstiel or low transverse uterine incision
info.t: These are obstetric-convenience incisions. For RH use vertical midline skin (xiphoid to symphysis) and classical vertical uterine — fastest, best exposure, no bladder mobilization, works with anterior placenta. Incision choice.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give oxytocin IV push post-delivery
info.t: IV bolus oxytocin causes profound hypotension, tachycardia, and can re-arrest the patient. Run it as an infusion: 20 units in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr. PPH management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methylergonovine in HTN/preeclampsia
info.t: Methylergonovine (Methergine) is contraindicated in hypertension, preeclampsia, and eclampsia — patients very likely to be the ones needing RH. Use oxytocin, TXA, misoprostol, and carboprost instead. Carboprost avoided in asthma. Uterotonic choice.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget magnesium toxicity as a cause
info.t: If the patient was on MgSO4 for eclampsia or preterm labor, magnesium toxicity may be the cause of arrest. Give Calcium Gluconate 1 g IV or Calcium Chloride 1 g IV. BEAU-CHOPS causes.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT close the abdomen during ongoing arrest
info.t: Pack with clean/saline-soaked gauze and continue resuscitation. Formal closure happens in the OR only after ROSC. Closing during arrest wastes time and conceals bleeding. Post-procedure.

This is emergent life-saving surgery during cardiac arrest. No consent is required. Brief communication with family if present is appropriate but should not delay the procedure. Document the clinical scenario. Proceed with RH.

SAME AS NON-PREGNANT: • Position: center of chest, midsternal (older teaching to move hands cephalad is no longer recommended — AHA 2015/2023) • Rate: 100-120/min • Depth: at least 5 cm (2 inches) • Recoil: allow full chest recoil • Interruptions: minimize (<10 sec for pulse check) WHAT'S DIFFERENT: • Patient flat supine (no tilted board) • Manual LUD continuously — dedicated provider

SAME AS NON-PREGNANT: • Energy: 200J biphasic (same as standard) • Pad placement: anterolateral (standard) • Shocks are safe at all gestational ages — fetus tolerates defibrillation without issue WHAT'S DIFFERENT: • Remove fetal/tocodynamometer monitors before shocking (arcing risk) • Continue LUD through the shock

NO DOSE MODIFICATIONS IN PREGNANCY: • Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min • Amiodarone 300 mg IV for refractory VF/VT (150 mg if second dose) • Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV if amiodarone unavailable • Calcium if hyperkalemia/hypocalcemia/magnesium toxicity • Sodium bicarbonate only for specific indications (not routine) PRINCIPLE: Fetal medication exposure concerns do not apply during arrest — "what is best for the mother is best for the baby." Give full doses. Medications

CRITICAL: IV/IO access must be above the diaphragm. PREFERRED SITES: • Antecubital fossa • External jugular • Humeral IO • Subclavian (if trained) AVOID: • Femoral lines • Lower extremity IVs • Lower extremity IO WHY: The gravid uterus compresses the IVC — drugs given below the compression point do not reach the heart. Medications appear to "not work" until the patient has a sustainable return of circulation.

PREGNANT AIRWAY IS 8× MORE LIKELY TO BE DIFFICULT: • Mucosal edema — friable, bleeds with manipulation • Increased O2 consumption + reduced FRC → rapid desaturation • Delayed gastric emptying → high aspiration risk • Breast tissue can obstruct blade insertion PREPARATION: • Video laryngoscopy first-line • Smaller ETT — try 6.0-7.0 mm (not 7.5-8.0) • Avoid nasal intubation (nasal mucosa bleeds) • Short handle if breast tissue interferes • Bougie, suction, cricoid pressure ready • Standard RSI meds acceptable (etomidate, ketamine, succinylcholine, rocuronium)

MANDATORY from 20 weeks onward during any resuscitation. MANUAL LUD > TILT: • Patient flat supine → optimal compression quality • Dedicated provider on patient's left side • Two-handed pull: reach across and pull the uterus toward you (up and to the left) • Alternative: one-handed push from the right, palm pushing uterus up and leftward • Continuous — not periodic, not optional WHY NOT TILT: • 30° tilt degrades compression quality ~30% • Makes intubation, defibrillation, IV access harder • Patient slides off tilted surface during prolonged resuscitation

UNIQUE TO PREGNANT ARREST: • At 4 minutes without ROSC → begin resuscitative hysterotomy • Fetus delivered by 5 minutes ideal • Past 4 min? Start NOW anyway — Rose 2015 and Benson 2016 demonstrate benefit at much longer intervals TIMEKEEPER: Designate one person to call out every 30 seconds. Under stress, teams underestimate elapsed time by 30-50%.

In addition to standard H's and T's, seek pregnancy-specific causes: • Bleeding / DIC (placenta, atony, rupture, Amniotic Fluid Embolism-DIC) • Embolism (PE, amniotic fluid embolism, air, fat) • Anesthetic complications (high spinal, LAST) • Uterine atony • Cardiac disease (MI, PPCM, aortic dissection) • Hypertension (eclampsia, HELLP, ICH) • Other standard H's and T's + Mg toxicity • Placenta previa / abruption • Sepsis Full BEAU-CHOPS with treatments

CAUSES: • Placental abruption, placenta previa, accreta • Uterine rupture (especially prior C-section) • Vaginal/cervical laceration • Postpartum atony hemorrhage • Amniotic Fluid Embolism-associated DIC MANAGEMENT: • Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol — 1:1:1 pRBC:FFP:platelets • TXA 1g IV over 10 min (within 3h of bleeding) • Fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate) — goal >200 mg/dL • Surgical source control — OR emergent laparotomy

PULMONARY EMBOLISM: • 5-10x higher risk in pregnancy • PE in Pregnancy • Consider systemic thrombolysis if confirmed and arrested AMNIOTIC FLUID EMBOLISM: • Uniquely pregnancy-related • Sudden cardiovascular collapse + DIC + respiratory failure during labor/delivery or immediate postpartum • Mortality 40-60% • Treatment: supportive, MTP, consider ECMO if available • Case reports of atropine + ondansetron + ketorolac ("A-OK") with anecdotal benefit

HIGH / TOTAL SPINAL: • Sudden hypotension, bradycardia, apnea after neuraxial anesthesia • Treatment: intubation, pressors, LUD, resuscitation LOCAL ANESTHETIC SYSTEMIC TOXICITY (LAST): • Seizures, arrhythmias, arrest after local anesthetic (epidural, paracervical block) • Treatment: Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion • AVOID propofol (worsens LAST) FAILED AIRWAY: Anticipate difficult airway in pregnancy — see ACLS Mods

UTERINE ATONY (after delivery): • Oxytocin 20 U in 1L NS at 250 mL/hr (NO IV push) • TXA 1g IV • Misoprostol 800-1000 mcg PR • Methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM (AVOID in HTN/preeclampsia) • Carboprost 250 mcg IM q15 min (AVOID in asthma) • Bimanual uterine massage UTERINE RUPTURE: • Sudden abdominal pain, fetal distress, hemodynamic collapse • MTP + emergency laparotomy

MI IN PREGNANCY: • Rare but increasing (older maternal age, obesity) • Treatment: aspirin, cardiac cath, PCI — do not withhold life-saving interventions due to pregnancy PERIPARTUM CARDIOMYOPATHY: • Presents late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum • HF with EF ≤45%, no prior cardiac disease AORTIC DISSECTION: • Aortic Dissection • Increased risk in pregnancy (especially connective tissue disease) ARRHYTHMIA / CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE: Standard ACLS, no dose modifications

STANDARD H's: • Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, H+ (acidosis), Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia STANDARD T's: • Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary) PREGNANCY-SPECIFIC: • Magnesium toxicity — if on MgSO4 infusion, give Calcium Gluconate 1g IV • Insulin-induced hypoglycemia in gestational diabetics • Thyroid storm in hyperthyroid patients

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give diltiazem or verapamil in HFrEF
info.t: Calcium channel blockers are Class 3: Harm in patients with EF ≤40%. They worsen heart failure and increase mortality. Use beta-blockers or amiodarone instead.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give AV nodal blockers in WPW
info.t: Beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin, and adenosine are contraindicated in AFib with WPW (pre-excitation). They block the AV node, forcing conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. Procainamide or cardioversion.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT cardiovert AFib >48h without anticoagulation
info.t: Cardioverting AFib of unknown or >48h duration without 3+ weeks of anticoagulation or TEE-confirmed no thrombus risks stroke. Rate control + anticoagulation + cardiology.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT combine beta-blocker + CCB IV
info.t: Giving IV metoprolol + IV diltiazem together causes severe bradycardia and hypotension. Choose one agent first, add the other cautiously if needed. Rate control approach.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on digoxin alone for acute RVR
info.t: Digoxin takes 2-6 hours to achieve rate control — too slow for acute RVR. Use beta-blockers or CCBs first; digoxin is an adjunct for CHF patients.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to check TSH
info.t: Thyrotoxicosis is a reversible cause of AFib. Rate control will fail if hyperthyroidism is not treated. Check TSH + troponin in ALL patients.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge new AFib without cardiology follow-up
info.t: New-onset AFib needs evaluation for underlying cause, long-term anticoagulation decision, and rhythm vs rate control strategy. Arrange cardiology follow-up.

• Assign team roles — leader, airway, compressor, meds, recorder • Monitoring setup: SpO2 right wrist (preductal), temp over liver • Equipment: radiant warmer ON, T-piece, pulse ox, suction, intubation kit, UVC kit • Cord management plan: DCC 30-60s vigorous, ICM ≥35wk non-vigorous
• Three questions: Term? Breathing/Crying? Good Tone? • Yes to ALL → routine care (skin-to-skin, DCC, warmth) • No to ANY → proceed to initial steps
