• Hematoma block (preferred) — 5–10 mL 1% lidocaine into fracture, fastest discharge • Procedural sedation — ketamine/propofol, requires NPO + monitoring team • Regional — Bier block or US-guided nerve blocks, superior but longer setup

• Apply longitudinal traction — waterski position, lean back, steady pull • Make circles to free fragment — recreate length before reducing • Finger traps for sustained traction — frees hands for splinting
• Exaggerate the deformity FIRST — unlocks dorsal periosteal hinge • Push distal fragment palmar (volar) with thumbs • Ulnar deviate to restore radial inclination
• Plaster NOT fiberglass — fiberglass sets too fast to mold • 10 layers, 6-inch, measure on uninjured side, cut thumb hole • MINIMAL padding at fracture (2 layers Webril) — padding defeats mold
• Flat hands (thenar eminences) — NEVER fingertips • Oval cross-section, 3-point pressure: dorsal at fracture, volar proximal + distal • Do NOT squeeze. Do NOT move hands while plaster sets
• 10° flexion + ulnar deviation — counteracts dorsal displacement • Elbow, MCPs, and thumb must remain FREE

• X-ray: 2nd metacarpal line parallel to radius, cast index <0.80 • "Straight cast = crooked bone" — round cast = inadequate mold • If inadequate: remove cast, top up analgesia, re-attempt full TRAMP • If 2 attempts fail → ortho consult

Standard approach: Identify fracture site on dorsal wrist. Prep with chlorhexidine. Insert 20-gauge needle at dorsal fracture line. Aspirate — dark blood confirms placement in fracture hematoma. Inject 5–10 mL of 1% plain lidocaine. Wait 5–10 minutes for full effect. Ultrasound guidance: Real-time visualization of needle entering fracture gap improves accuracy, reduces pain during injection, and may improve block success. Particularly valuable in pediatric patients and those with difficult anatomy. Combined fractures: For radius + ulna, a second injection into the ulnar fracture hematoma is required for complete analgesia.

Max dose: Lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg without epinephrine (1% lidocaine = 10 mg/mL). Critical safety point: The fracture hematoma is contiguous with the medullary canal — lidocaine is absorbed directly into marrow vasculature. Systemic absorption is rapid, similar to intraosseous (IO) administration. Respect weight-based dosing limits strictly. Signs of toxicity: Perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus → seizures → cardiac arrest. Have lipid emulsion available for LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity).

ED length of stay: Hematoma block patients discharge in a mean of 1.5 hours vs 4.6 hours for procedural sedation — a 3-hour time savings. ENP-led reductions: Emergency nurse practitioners using hematoma blocks achieved 87.2% successful first-attempt reduction rate, comparable to physician-led sedation results. Mean pain scores were acceptable (VAS 3.2 during reduction). No NPO requirement: Hematoma block does not require fasting assessment, dedicated monitoring nurse, or capnography — reducing resource utilization significantly. Wilderness/austere settings: Hematoma block is the preferred analgesia technique for fracture reduction in resource-limited environments where sedation monitoring is

Bier's block comparison: Oakley et al. (2023) found hematoma block and Bier's block provided equivalent reduction quality and patient satisfaction for distal radius fractures, with hematoma block requiring fewer resources and shorter setup. US-guided nerve blocks: Christensen et al. (2025) found US-guided nerve blocks achieved 94% first-attempt reduction success vs 74% for hematoma block, with lower pain scores during reduction. However, nerve blocks required ultrasound proficiency and additional setup time. Axillary block comparison: Rook et al. (2025) demonstrated superior analgesia with US-guided axillary nerve block vs hematoma block, but at the cost of longer preparation and higher tech

• Speed: Can be performed in <5 minutes, full effect in 5–10 min • Simplicity: No specialized equipment beyond needle and syringe (US optional) • No fasting required: Can proceed immediately on arrival • No monitoring team: Single provider can perform block and reduction • Cost-effective: Minimal supplies, shorter ED stay • Pediatric safe: Well-studied in adolescents, US guidance helpful for precision • Difficult airway patients: Avoids sedation risks entirely

• Incomplete analgesia: Some patients report moderate pain during reduction (VAS 3–5) — less complete than sedation or regional blocks • Marrow absorption risk: Rapid systemic uptake requires strict weight-based dosing • Single-site only: Each fracture site requires a separate injection • No muscle relaxation: Unlike sedation, does not relax forearm musculature — may make reduction technically harder in muscular patients • Lower first-attempt success: 74% vs 94% compared to US-guided nerve blocks in one RCT • Not suitable for: Open fractures, severely comminuted fractures requiring prolonged manipulation, or patients requiring general anesthesia for other reasons

Plaster — moldable, sets in 3–5 min, exothermic reaction. Better for fractures requiring 3-point molding. Standard: 8–12 layers depending on site. Fiberglass — lighter, stronger, water-resistant, sets faster. Better for stable fractures where molding is not critical. More expensive. Stockinette — cotton tube applied directly to skin. Protects from plaster irritation. Fold over edges for a clean finish. Webril (cast padding) — soft cotton roll. Provides cushioning between skin and plaster. Standard: 2–4 layers. Elastic bandage (ACE wrap) — secures the splint. Wrap distally to proximally. Should be snug but not tight.

• 2–4 layers Webril over the entire splinted area • Extra padding over bony prominences (malleoli, olecranon, styloids, calcaneus) • Minimal padding directly over the fracture site when molding is needed — excessive padding defeats the mold • Cotton between fingers for gutter splints to prevent maceration

1. Dip plaster in lukewarm water (not hot — the exothermic reaction adds additional heat and can burn) 2. Squeeze out excess water gently — do not wring 3. Smooth layers together on a flat surface to remove air pockets 4. Apply to the limb and mold with flat palms (thenar eminences) 5. Never use fingertips — creates pressure points → skin necrosis 6. Hold the mold until plaster sets (3–5 minutes) — do NOT move hands during setting 7. Secure with elastic bandage — snug, not constricting

Position of function (unless otherwise specified): • Wrist: 15–20° extension • MCP joints: 70–90° flexion (for gutter splints — prevents collateral ligament contracture) • IP joints: slight flexion (10–20°) • Elbow: 90° flexion • Ankle: 90° dorsiflexion (neutral — prevents equinus contracture) • Thumb: abducted, slightly opposed ("holding a can")

Before AND after splinting — document both. • Sensation: Light touch in each nerve distribution (median, ulnar, radial for upper; deep peroneal, superficial peroneal, tibial, sural for lower) • Motor: Thumb opposition (median), finger abduction (ulnar), wrist/finger extension (radial), toe dorsiflexion (deep peroneal), toe plantarflexion (tibial) • Vascular: Capillary refill <2 seconds, pulses palpable (radial/ulnar for upper; dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial for lower) • Color and temperature: Compare to uninjured side

Our institution prefers A+P (anterior + posterior) splints over sugar tong for forearm fractures. • Two separate plaster slabs (one dorsal, one volar) rather than one continuous slab wrapping around the elbow • Provides equivalent AP stability without restricting elbow motion • Less bulky, better patient comfort, easier to adjust • Use sugar tong only when rotational control (pronation/supination) is specifically required

• Elevate above the level of the heart — reduces swelling • Ice 20 minutes on / 20 minutes off (over padding, not directly on skin) • Finger/toe exercises — wiggle frequently to prevent stiffness and monitor for compartment syndrome • Loosen elastic bandage if swelling increases — mark the outer edge so patient knows where to unwind Return immediately for: • Increasing pain not relieved by elevation and medication • Numbness, tingling, or inability to move fingers/toes • Fingers/toes turning blue, white, or cold • Splint feels too tight, causes pressure pain • These are compartment syndrome warning signs — a surgical emergency
• Proximal humerus → Sling / Cuff & Collar • Humeral shaft → Coaptation Splint (→ functional brace at 1–2 wk) • Supracondylar → Long Arm Posterior or Double Sugar Tong

• Olecranon / coronoid → Long Arm Posterior • Radius/ulna proximal or midshaft → Long Arm Posterior or Double Sugar Tong • Radius distal, isolated → Thumb Spica or Volar • Radius/ulna distal, complex → Sugar Tong (A+P preferred) • Ulna styloid → Sugar Tong (A+P preferred)

• Scaphoid / trapezium / lunate fracture → Thumb Spica • Lunate dislocation → Sugar Tong (A+P preferred) • Triquetrum / pisiform / trapezoid / capitate / hamate → Volar • UCL injury / thumb MCP dislocation / De Quervain → Thumb Spica • 1st metacarpal → Thumb Spica • 2nd / 3rd metacarpal → Radial Gutter or Volar • 4th / 5th metacarpal (boxer) → Ulnar Gutter • 1st phalanx → Thumb Spica • 2nd / 3rd prox/mid phalanx → Radial Gutter or buddy taping • 4th / 5th prox/mid phalanx → Ulnar Gutter or buddy taping • Distal phalanx → Aluminum U-shaped (stack) splint

• Distal tibia / distal fibula → Posterior Short Leg (± Stirrup) • Ankle sprain grade 2/3 → Stirrup • Talus / calcaneus / navicular / cuboid / cuneiform → Posterior Short Leg • Metatarsal → Posterior Short Leg • Lisfranc → Posterior Short Leg (non-weight bearing)
• Wrist: 15–20° extension • MCP (gutter splints): 70–90° flexion • Elbow: 90° flexion • Ankle: 90° dorsiflexion (neutral) • Thumb: abducted, slightly opposed

Troponin is released from the myocardium as early as 2–4 hours after symptom onset in acute MI. However, depending on the assay, values may not become abnormal for up to 12 hours. Diagnostic accuracy increases progressively with time from symptom onset. Sensitive troponin assays maintain excellent diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.90–0.94) even within 2 hours of symptom onset, while standard assays show markedly inferior performance (AUC ~0.71) at these early time points.

hs-cTn assays have superior sensitivity compared to conventional assays, particularly in early presenters. The time from chest pain onset to detectable troponin concentration is shorter with hs-cTn, enabling more rapid rule-in or rule-out. Approximately one-third of NSTEMI patients take longer than 3 hours from symptom onset to exceed common rule-out thresholds (5 ng/L).

Fourth Universal Definition of MI: • Conventional assays: sample at 0h, repeat at 3–6 hours • hs-cTn assays: sample at 0h, repeat at 1–2 hours Single-measurement rule-out (select patients): • In early presenters (≤2h from onset), a single hs-cTn below the limit of detection (2 ng/L) achieves 99.4% sensitivity and 99.7% NPV • This strategy should NOT be used in very early presenters (<2h) or high-risk patients • hs-cTn sensitivity remains consistently high across subgroups including early presenters

A single negative troponin does not rule out ACS in early presenters. Serial troponin measurements are essential, especially when symptom onset is <3 hours before presentation. hs-cTn assays narrow the diagnostic window but do not eliminate it.
• Classify as hyponatremia or hypernatremia • Assess symptom severity for hyponatremia • Order initial labs: serum osm, urine osm, urine Na
• 3% Hypertonic Saline 100-150 mL bolus x3 — target 4-6 mEq/L rise • Correction limits: max 10 mEq/L in 24h (8 for high-risk) • DDAVP clamp-bolus protocol for controlled correction

• Serum Osm >275 → non-hypotonic (check glucose, lipids) • Urine Osm <100 → water excess (potomania, polydipsia) • Urine Na <30 → volume assessment (hypo- vs hypervolemic) • Urine Na >30 → SIAD, diuretics, or adrenal insufficiency
• SIAD → fluid restriction → oral urea → salt tabs + loop • Diuretic-induced → hold thiazide, DDAVP clamp if Na <120 • Hypovolemic → NS resuscitation, watch for autocorrection

• Volume depleted → Free Water Deficit calculator → enteral or D5W replacement • Polyuria → DI workup (central vs nephrogenic) • Central DI → DDAVP + free water • Volume overloaded → natriuretic diuresis + free water

The DDAVP clamp separates the water problem from the sodium problem. DDAVP blocks renal free water excretion via V2 receptors, preventing dangerous autocorrection. Then 3% NaCl boluses raise Na at a predictable, controlled rate. This is especially critical in patients at HIGH risk of overcorrection: alcoholics, malnourished, hypokalemia, thiazide-induced, beer potomania.

Step 1: Give Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2 mcg IV as first dose. Step 2: Start DDAVP 2 mcg IV q6-8h (scheduled, not PRN). Step 3: Give Thiamine 100 mg IV empirically (ODS prophylaxis). Step 4: Check serum Na q2h from initiation. Do NOT wait for labs before starting DDAVP in high-risk patients — start the clamp immediately.

While DDAVP clamp is active: • Give 3% NaCl 100 mL IV bolus to raise Na. • Each 100 mL bolus raises Na ~2 mEq/L in a 70 kg adult. • Check Na 2 hours after each bolus. • Target correction: 4-6 mEq/L in the first 6 hours for severe symptoms. • Max: 8 mEq/L in 24h for high-risk, 10 mEq/L for standard risk. If Na rises too fast: Hold 3% boluses. DDAVP will prevent further rise. If already overcorrected → Overcorrection Rescue Protocol.

During active DDAVP clamp: • Serum Na q2h • Urine output and volume • Urine osmolality (should be concentrated if DDAVP working) • Neurological status • Serum K+ (correct hypokalemia — ODS risk factor)

Stop DDAVP clamp when: • Na >125 mEq/L AND stable • Underlying cause has been addressed • Patient tolerating oral intake After stopping DDAVP: • Continue Na monitoring q4-6h for 24-48h • Watch for rebound — free water excretion may resume rapidly • If Na rises >2 mEq/L in first 4h after stopping → consider restarting DDAVP

• Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg • Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg (usually >300) • Urine sodium >30 mEq/L (on normal salt intake) • Euvolemic on clinical exam • Normal thyroid and adrenal function • No recent diuretic use

• SSRIs/SNRIs — most common drug cause, especially in elderly • Carbamazepine / Oxcarbazepine — potent ADH stimulators • NSAIDs — reduce renal free water clearance • Opioids — stimulate ADH release • Cyclophosphamide — direct ADH-like effect • Desmopressin — iatrogenic when given for other indications • Ecstasy (MDMA) — stimulates ADH + excessive water intake
• Small cell lung cancer — most classic association (ectopic ADH production) • Head and neck cancers • Lymphoma • GI malignancies • GU malignancies
• Stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, TBI • Meningitis, encephalitis • Brain tumors • Multiple sclerosis • Guillain-Barré syndrome
• Pneumonia (any cause) • Tuberculosis • Positive pressure ventilation • Asthma exacerbation • COPD exacerbation

• SIAD is a diagnosis of exclusion — rule out hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency first • Many "euvolemic" patients are actually mildly volume depleted — trial of NS can help distinguish • Urine Na may be low in SIAD if patient is on severe salt restriction • The term "SIAD" is preferred over "SIADH" because not all cases involve elevated ADH

• Elderly with impaired thirst — by far the most common ER presentation • Altered mental status / intubated patients • Restricted access to water (nursing homes, ICU) • Infants dependent on caregivers
• Hypertonic saline infusions • Sodium bicarbonate boluses • Excessive TPN sodium content • Oral sodium ingestion (soy sauce, salt tablets)
• Central DI — deficient ADH production (post-neurosurgery, TBI, tumors, idiopathic) • Nephrogenic DI — renal resistance to ADH (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, post-obstructive)
• Osmotic diuresis (hyperglycemia, mannitol, urea) • Loop diuretics (produce hypotonic urine) • Post-obstructive diuresis
• Diarrhea (especially osmotic — lactulose, sorbitol) • Vomiting with inadequate replacement • Nasogastric suction • Enterocutaneous fistulas
• Burns • Fever (each degree above 37°C increases free water loss ~100 mL/day) • Mechanical ventilation with dry gas • Exercise / environmental heat exposure

• Hypernatremia is always hyperosmolar — no pseudohypernatremia exists • In hospitalized patients, hypernatremia is usually iatrogenic (inadequate free water provision) • Community-acquired hypernatremia is usually chronic and associated with higher mortality than hospital-acquired • Mortality ranges from 40-60% in severe cases — often a marker of severe underlying illness

Activate rescue if: • Na rises >10 mEq/L in 24 hours (standard risk) • Na rises >8 mEq/L in 24 hours (high-risk patients) • Na correction rate exceeds 1 mEq/L per hour sustained High-risk patients: Alcoholics, malnourished, hypokalemia, thiazide-induced, beer potomania, Na <105 mEq/L.

Step 1: Desmopressin (DDAVP) 2 mcg IV stat — blocks free water excretion immediately. Step 2: D5W 3 mL/kg/hr IV — provides free water to re-lower Na back to safe trajectory. Step 3: Check Na q1-2h until correction rate is back within limits. Step 4: Once Na back on safe trajectory, transition to DDAVP clamp protocol for controlled correction.

Re-lower Na to bring the 24-hour correction back to within 8-10 mEq/L from baseline. Example: If baseline Na was 112 mEq/L and rose to 126 mEq/L in 12 hours (+14 mEq/L), give DDAVP + D5W to re-lower Na toward ~120-122 mEq/L.

• Proactive DDAVP clamp in all high-risk patients — do not wait for overcorrection to occur • Thiamine 100 mg IV empirically — reduces ODS susceptibility • Correct hypokalemia — K+ correction raises Na (1 mEq K+ repleted = ~1 mEq Na rise) • Avoid NS boluses in patients with reversible ADH excess — can trigger rapid autocorrection • Monitor Na q2h during active treatment

Osmotic demyelination syndrome (formerly "central pontine myelinolysis") is a devastating neurologic injury caused by overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia. Brain cells that adapted to hypo-osmolality cannot readapt fast enough, leading to myelin destruction. Onset is delayed 2-6 days after overcorrection — clinicians may falsely believe the patient is improving when the damage is already done.

• Alcoholism — most common risk factor • Malnutrition — depleted organic osmolytes • Hypokalemia — K+ correction raises Na (double hit) • Thiamine deficiency — overlaps with alcohol/malnutrition • Liver disease / cirrhosis • Na <105 mEq/L — severely adapted brain • Chronic hyponatremia (>48h) — brain has fully adapted • Thiazide-induced — high autocorrection risk when drug stopped

Biphasic course: 1. Initial improvement with Na correction (hours to days) 2. Delayed deterioration (2-6 days): • Dysarthria, dysphagia • Paraparesis or quadriparesis • "Locked-in" syndrome (worst case) • Behavioral changes, confusion • Seizures MRI findings: T2 hyperintensity in central pons ("trident sign") — may not appear for 1-2 weeks.

• Proactive DDAVP clamp for all high-risk patients • Thiamine 100 mg IV empirically • Correct hypokalemia alongside Na (but account for K+ effect on Na) • Max correction: 8 mEq/L in 24h for high-risk, 10 mEq/L for standard • Avoid NS boluses in reversible causes — triggers autocorrection • If overcorrection occurs → immediate DDAVP + D5W rescue • Do NOT give vaptans — unpredictable, uncontrolled aquaresis

Osm >275 mOsm/kg → Non-hypotonic hyponatremia • Check glucose → Corrected Na Calculator — add 1.6 mEq/L to Na for every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100 (factor 2.4 if glucose >400) • Check lipids, total protein — pseudohyponatremia (artifact of indirect ISE method) • Check for mannitol, glycine, sorbitol infusions Osm <275 mOsm/kg → True hypotonic hyponatremia → proceed to Step 2

Urine Osm <100 mOsm/kg → Dilute urine (ADH appropriately suppressed) • Primary polydipsia (>15-20 L/day intake) • Beer potomania (low solute intake, high free water) • "Tea-and-toast" diet in elderly • Marathon runners / dilutional HIGH overcorrection risk — once water intake normalizes, kidneys excrete massive free water volumes. Proactive DDAVP clamp recommended. Urine Osm >100 mOsm/kg → Concentrated urine (ADH active) → proceed to Step 3

Urine Na <30 mEq/L → Avid Na retention • Hypovolemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhea), third-spacing, poor intake • Hypervolemic: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (effective arterial volume depletion) • Distinguish by clinical volume assessment Urine Na >30 mEq/L → Na wasting or euvolemia • SIAD (most common euvolemic cause) • Diuretic-induced (thiazides >> loops) • Adrenal insufficiency (cortisol/ACTH deficiency) • Cerebral salt wasting (rare, post-neurosurgery) • Hypothyroidism (rare cause, usually requires severe TSH elevation)

• Urine Osm 100-300: Overlap zone — could be partial ADH suppression or partial concentration • Urine Na 20-40: Borderline — may reflect mixed etiology or recent volume status changes • Diuretics confound all urine values — urine Na and Osm are uninterpretable while on diuretics • Fractional excretion of urate (FEua) can help distinguish SIAD (>12%) from volume depletion (<12%) when urine values are ambiguous

Effective osmoles draw water out of cells, diluting plasma Na. • Hyperglycemia (most common): For every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100, Na is artifactually lowered by ~1.6 mEq/L. Corrected Na = measured Na + 1.6 × [(glucose - 100) / 100]. Some experts use factor of 2.4 for glucose >400. • Mannitol infusion: Osmotic drag effect similar to hyperglycemia. • Glycine / Sorbitol: TURP syndrome, hysteroscopy irrigation — can cause severe dilutional hyponatremia. Treatment: Correct the underlying osmole. Na normalizes as glucose falls / mannitol is cleared.

Lab artifact from indirect ion-selective electrode (ISE) analyzers. High concentrations of lipids or paraproteins expand the non-aqueous plasma fraction, causing the analyzer to underestimate Na concentration in the aqueous phase. • Severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1500 mg/dL) • Paraproteinemia (multiple myeloma, Waldenström) • Extreme hypercholesterolemia Diagnosis: Serum osmolality is normal (measured directly). Or use direct ISE method (blood gas analyzer, POC chemistry) — gives true Na. Treatment: None needed for the Na itself. Treat the underlying condition.

• Serum osmolality >275 mOsm/kg rules out true hypotonic hyponatremia • POC (point-of-care) Na uses direct ISE and gives the true value — compare with lab Na • If POC Na is normal but lab Na is low → pseudohyponatremia • If calculated Osm is normal but measured Osm is high → osmol gap (unmeasured osmoles like mannitol, ethylene glycol)

ALL of the following must be met: ✅ Na ≥130 mEq/L OR Na 125-129 with known chronic stable cause ✅ Completely asymptomatic (no confusion, gait instability, headache, nausea) ✅ Cause identified or workup can be completed outpatient ✅ Not high-risk for ODS: no alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease ✅ Reliable follow-up available (PCP or nephrology within 1 week) ✅ Patient understands fluid restriction instructions if indicated ✅ Not on medications requiring adjustment (thiazides, SSRIs)

🚨 Admit if ANY of the following: • Na <125 mEq/L (any cause) • Na <130 mEq/L with any symptoms • Severe or moderate symptoms regardless of Na level • Requiring hypertonic saline • Requiring DDAVP clamp for controlled correction • High overcorrection risk (beer potomania, thiazide-induced, alcoholic, malnourished) • Underlying cause needs inpatient workup (new SIAD, concern for malignancy) • Unable to follow fluid restriction or no reliable follow-up

ALL of the following must be met: ✅ Na <150 mEq/L ✅ Asymptomatic (no altered mental status, weakness, lethargy) ✅ Cause is simple dehydration with intact thirst mechanism ✅ Patient can drink adequate free water (PO intake intact) ✅ No underlying DI or complex metabolic cause ✅ Able to access free water independently ✅ Follow-up Na check available within 1-3 days

🚨 Admit if ANY of the following: • Na ≥150 mEq/L • Any neurologic symptoms (confusion, lethargy, weakness) • Unable to drink or swallow safely • Diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic) • Requires IV free water replacement • Elderly with impaired thirst or dependent on caregivers • Underlying cause unclear or needs workup • Hospital-acquired hypernatremia (reflects severe illness)

For patients discharged with mild hyponatremia (Na 130-134): • Fluid restriction: Limit total fluids to 1-1.5 L/day • Avoid: Excessive water intake, electrolyte-free beverages • Stop offending medications if identified (thiazides, SSRIs) • Recheck Na: Within 1 week at PCP or lab • Return immediately if: confusion, severe headache, nausea/vomiting, gait problems, seizure • Follow up with: PCP (1 week), Nephrology if SIAD suspected

For patients discharged with mild hypernatremia: • Drink water regularly: Set a schedule (do not rely on thirst alone) • Goal intake: At least 2-3 L/day of free water (water, not juice/soda) • Avoid: Caffeine, alcohol (increase water losses) • Recheck Na: Within 3 days • Return immediately if: confusion, severe weakness, unable to drink • Elderly/caregivers: Ensure someone provides water on a schedule

⚠️ Mild hyponatremia (130-134) is NOT benign: • Associated with increased falls, fractures, cognitive impairment • Increased mortality in outpatient settings • Requires follow-up even if "asymptomatic" ⚠️ Most patients leave hospital still hyponatremic: • Despite effective therapy, discharge often premature • Ensure cause is addressed, not just the number ⚠️ ODS symptoms are delayed: • May not appear until 1-2 weeks after discharge • Counsel patients on warning signs: speech changes, dysphagia, quadriparesis

• Recognize clinical forms: furious (80%), paralytic (20%), atypical • Prodromal clue: pain/paresthesia at prior bite site • Collect 4 specimens: saliva, nuchal biopsy, CSF, serum • Contact CDC/public health — testing not available at most labs • Management: palliative (most) vs aggressive/ICU (select)

• Classify WHO exposure category: I (intact skin), II (minor), III (severe/bite) • Bat exposure — lower threshold: sleeping, child, intoxicated = exposure • Dog/cat/ferret — 10-day observation if healthy and available • Raccoon, skunk, fox, coyote — high risk, immediate PEP • Rodents/rabbits — generally NOT indicated
• Wash wound with soap and water ≥15 minutes • Irrigate with povidone-iodine if available • Delay suturing — if needed, infiltrate RIG first

• Unvaccinated: RIG 20 IU/kg (infiltrate wound) + vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14 • Previously vaccinated: vaccine days 0 and 3 only, no RIG • Immunocompromised: 5-dose series (add day 28) + serology + RIG even if prev. vaccinated
• Schedule remaining vaccine doses — do NOT restart if delayed • Monitor observation animal (dogs/cats/ferrets) • Deltoid only (adults) — NEVER gluteal • Report to animal control / public health

Bats — #1 cause of human rabies in US. Bites can be invisible. PEP for any direct contact unless bite/scratch definitively excluded. Raccoons — Most commonly reported rabid wild animal in eastern US. Skunks — Second most common rabid wild animal. Foxes — Regional risk varies; high in Arctic and some southern states. Coyotes — Increasing rabies cases in recent years.

Dogs — Leading cause of human rabies globally, uncommon in US due to vaccination. 10-day observation if healthy domestic dog. Stray/feral dogs in rabies-endemic areas = higher risk. Cats — Most commonly reported rabid domestic animal in US (more than dogs). 10-day observation if healthy. Ferrets — Can be observed 10 days. Uncommon rabies vector.

Small rodents — Mice, rats, squirrels, hamsters, gerbils, guinea pigs, chipmunks. Almost never found rabid. PEP not routinely recommended. Rabbits/hares — Very low risk. Consult public health for unusual circumstances. Exception: Woodchucks (groundhogs) — Higher rabies risk than other rodents. Consult public health.

Livestock (cattle, horses, sheep, goats) — Consider individually. Consult public health/veterinarian. Reported rabid livestock cases occur annually. Non-human primates — Consult public health and infectious disease. Unknown/escaped animal — Treat as if rabid unless species is known low-risk. Consult public health.

HSV Encephalitis — Fever (80%), temporal lobe involvement on MRI, CSF pleocytosis (10-200 cells). Lacks hydrophobia/aerophobia. No fluctuating consciousness with lucid intervals. Tetanus — Continuous muscle rigidity between spasms (absent in rabies). Normal consciousness until late. No hydrophobia/aerophobia. Shorter incubation (3-21 days). Identifiable wound often present. Autoimmune Encephalitis (anti-NMDAR) — Prominent psychiatric symptoms (psychosis, behavioral changes). Seizures in 85% (vs 20% in infectious encephalitis). Lower CSF pleocytosis (median 6 cells). Responds to immunotherapy. Epileptiform EEG discharges. Arboviruses (West Nile, Japanese encephalitis) — Consider based on geog

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) — The most important differential. Key distinguishing features: • Consciousness: preserved throughout in GBS vs preserved until preterminal in paralytic rabies • Sensory: distal paresthesias (GBS) vs pain at bite site (rabies) • CSF: albuminocytologic dissociation in GBS vs minimal pleocytosis in rabies • Progression: 12 hours to 28 days in GBS vs more rapid with fever/dysautonomia in rabies Botulism — Descending (not ascending) flaccid paralysis. Consider when paralysis begins cranially.

Pathognomonic features: • Hydrophobia and aerophobia (furious form) • Pain/paresthesia/pruritus at a prior bite site • Fluctuating consciousness with lucid intervals CSF: Typically minimal or no pleocytosis — this distinguishes rabies from most viral encephalitides which typically show moderate pleocytosis. Epidemiologic clues: • Animal exposure (especially bats, dogs, wild carnivores) • Travel to rabies-endemic areas • Lack of post-exposure prophylaxis Important: Rabies diagnosis in the US is almost always missed at the first clinical encounter. Up to 30% of patients may not recall animal exposure.

No single test is sufficient. Collect all 4 specimen types for maximum sensitivity (100% combined). 1. Saliva — Sterile, preservative-free tube. Transport at room temperature within 24 hours. • Test: RT-PCR (nucleic acid amplification) + viral isolation • Sensitivity: ~70% single sample; ≥3 serial samples increases to >98% • Intermittent viral shedding — may cease after seroconversion 2. Nuchal Skin Biopsy — Full-thickness from nape of neck with hair follicles (~4mm diameter, 20mm³). Sterile container, room temperature, 24 hours. • Test: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) + immunohistochemistry • Sensitivity: Nearly 100% with adequate tissue — most reliable single specimen 3. CSF — Sterile, p

Early illness (first week): Viral detection methods have higher yield → Prioritize saliva RT-PCR + nuchal skin biopsy Later illness (>7-12 days): Antibody detection becomes more reliable → CSF and serum antibody testing have higher yield Median time from symptom onset to first positive sample: 8 days Median time to death: 16 days

Diagnostic: Finding rabies virus antigen or nucleic acid in ANY antemortem sample. In unvaccinated patients, rabies-neutralizing antibodies in CSF confirm diagnosis. Sequential sampling is essential if initial testing is negative but suspicion remains high. Important caveats: • Prior IVIG can be a passive source of donor-derived rabies antibodies → false-positive serology • Paralytic rabies has lower sensitivity across all specimen types vs furious rabies • Dog rabies variants may produce minimal antibody responses compared to bat variants

CSF analysis: Typically minimal or no pleocytosis (distinguishes from other viral encephalitides). Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis can occur. MRI: Nonspecific. May show T2 hyperintensity in brainstem, hippocampi, basal ganglia, hypothalamus, spinal cord. Possible enhancement of nerve roots and brachial plexus on bitten limb side. Postmortem: Brain histopathology shows Negri bodies (pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusions), mononuclear infiltration, perivascular cuffing.

Rabies testing is NOT available at most hospital labs. You MUST: • Contact local public health laboratory or CDC immediately • CDC serves as the national rabies reference laboratory • Obtain approval and complete requisite paperwork before submitting samples • Rabies is a nationally notifiable disease — report to state/local health department

Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a series of shots that prevent rabies infection after an animal exposure. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear, but PEP is nearly 100% effective when given correctly.

You will receive shots on specific days. Your doctor will tell you which schedule applies to you: Standard schedule: Day 0 (today), Day 3, Day 7, Day 14 Extended schedule (if immune system is weakened): Day 0, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 28 If previously vaccinated: Day 0 and Day 3 only Do NOT miss your scheduled doses. If you miss a dose, get it as soon as possible — the series does NOT need to be restarted.

Common side effects (not dangerous): • Pain, redness, or swelling at injection site • Headache • Nausea or dizziness • Muscle aches Seek medical attention if you develop: • Difficulty breathing or swallowing • Hives or widespread rash • Swelling of face, lips, or throat • Fever > 103°F (39.4°C)

• Keep the wound clean and dry • Watch for signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, pus, red streaks, fever • You can take acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) for pain • Avoid strenuous activity with the injected arm/leg for 24 hours • Return to the emergency department if your wound shows signs of infection

• Bring this information to each follow-up visit • Vaccines can be given at your primary care doctor, urgent care, local health department, or emergency department • If you were told an animal is being observed for 10 days, contact your local animal control for updates • Call your doctor or return to the ED if the animal becomes sick or dies during the observation period

• Stop the burning process — remove clothing, irrigate • Identify burn mechanism (thermal, chemical, electrical, radiation) • ABCDE primary survey — burns are trauma patients first • Screen for inhalation injury (enclosed space, facial burns, soot, stridor)
• Assess for hard signs of inhalation injury — intubate early if in doubt • CO poisoning — co-oximetry on ALL enclosed-space fire patients • Cyanide — clinical diagnosis, do not wait for levels
• Classify burn depth (epidermal → full thickness) • Calculate TBSA — Rule of 9's (adult) or Lund-Browder (peds) • Only count partial thickness and full thickness in TBSA

• Select protocol: Rule of 10's, Parkland, or Dell-Seton • Calculate from TIME OF BURN, not arrival • Monitor UOP: 0.5 mL/kg/hr (adult), 1 mL/kg/hr (peds) • Pediatric: add maintenance D5½NS to resuscitation volume
• Cool with running water 20 min (within 3 hours of injury) • Select dressings by depth — avoid SSD on superficial burns • Multimodal pain management (morphine, ketamine, fentanyl IN for peds)
• Assess for circumferential deep partial/full thickness burns • Extremity: medial/lateral mid-axial incisions • Chest: bilateral anterior axillary lines — "clamshell" pattern
• Apply ABA burn center transfer criteria (10 indications) • Disposition: transfer / admit / discharge

• Power off first — confirm the source is de-energized before anyone touches the patient • Pulseless? Reverse triage in lightning — treat the apparently dead first • Ventilate after ROSC — respiratory center recovers after the heart; prolonged CPR is reasonable • C-spine precautions, IV access, baseline neurovascular exam, find every contact point
• Pregnant or pediatric cord bite? Route first • Low voltage <1000 V / high voltage ≥1000 V / lightning / CEW • Low voltage: AC tetany, transthoracic path, wet contact, prolonged contact, LOC

• 12-lead ECG on everyone; measure QTc; troponin only if chest pain, instability, or ischemic ECG • Normal ECG + no criteria = discharge without telemetry • Any criterion (high voltage, LOC, abnormal ECG, arrest, chest pain, cardiac history, high-risk path, pregnancy) = 24 h telemetry

• Skin is the tip of the iceberg — TBSA underestimates • CK, urine myoglobin, BMP q6 h, lactate; trauma imaging by mechanism • LR titrated to UOP 1 mL/kg/h (1–2 if myoglobinuria) — not Parkland; no diuretics until resuscitated • Hourly compartment checks — 5 Ps unreliable • Emergent fasciotomy / escharotomy • Posterior shoulder dislocation, spine fractures; Tdap ± TIG; opioid + ketamine, no NSAIDs

• Flashover, not deep burn — no burn-formula fluids; Lichtenberg figures fade in 24 h • Keraunoparalysis vs real neurologic injury • CT head for AMS / deficit / seizure; CT spine for persistent paralysis or fall • Otoscopy on everyone (TM rupture 50–80%); eye exam and cataract counseling; check under metal

• Pregnancy: fetal monitoring ≥4 h at ≥20 wk, OB consult, watch for abruption • Cord bite: labial artery bleed 5–21 days in up to 25% — teach pinch compression, plastics/ENT in 1 wk • CEW: asymptomatic awake patient needs no ECG, labs, or monitoring • Probe removal; eye / genital / neck probes to specialist; assess the fall

• ABA: all high-voltage and lightning to burn center; low-voltage gets follow-up; wound care; tetanus • Discharge / telemetry admit / burn ICU • Discharge counseling: neuropathy, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cataracts, return precautions

info.h: What to expect over the next 3 weeks
info.pt: Electrical Burn to the Lip — Parent Instructions
info.t: • Days 1–3: the lip swells and the burn turns gray-white. This is normal. • Days 3–10: a firm scab (eschar) forms over the burn. • Days 5–21: the scab loosens and falls off. This is when bleeding can happen. A small artery in the lip sits right under the scab and can bleed heavily — it happens in roughly 1 in 4 to 1 in 10 children with this injury. It is most common in the second week.

info.h: IF THE LIP BLEEDS — do this immediately
info.pt: Electrical Burn to the Lip — Parent Instructions
info.t: 1. Pinch the lip firmly between your thumb and index finger — one finger inside the mouth, one outside — squeezing the bleeding spot from both directions. Use a folded piece of gauze or a clean cloth if you have one. 2. Hold constant pressure for a full 10 minutes by the clock. Do not peek. Do not let go early. 3. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department while holding pressure. Do not wait to see if it stops. Even if the bleeding stops, your child still needs to be seen the same day. 4. Keep your child sitting upright and leaning slightly forward so blood is not swallowed.

info.pt: Electrical Burn to the Lip — Parent Instructions
info.t: • Keep the area clean. Gently dab with water after meals; do not scrub. • Apply a thin layer of the antibiotic ointment you were given, as instructed. • Do not pick, pull, or rub the scab — let it fall off on its own. • Soft, cool foods. Avoid hard, sharp, hot, or salty foods that irritate the burn. A cup or spoon is easier than a bottle nipple or straw. • Pain medicine as directed (acetaminophen or ibuprofen by weight). • Keep the follow-up appointment with the plastic surgeon or ENT — usually within 1 week. Some children need a small mouth splint to prevent the corner of the mouth from tightening as it heals.

info.h: Return to the emergency department for
info.pt: Electrical Burn to the Lip — Parent Instructions
info.t: • Any bleeding from the lip (see above) • Difficulty breathing, drooling, or trouble swallowing • Refusing to drink, or fewer wet diapers than usual • Fever, spreading redness, pus, or a bad smell from the burn • Increasing swelling of the lip, tongue, or face

info.pt: Electrical Burn to the Lip — Parent Instructions
info.t: Unplug cords when not in use, use outlet covers, keep cords out of reach, and replace frayed cords. Toddlers explore with their mouths — this injury is common and is not a reflection on your parenting.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT touch the patient until the power is confirmed off
info.t: A rescuer who contacts an energized patient or the ground near a downed high-voltage line becomes the second casualty. Utility confirmation or a trained rescuer with insulated tools — then approach. Scene safety.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT triage lightning casualties normally
info.t: Standard triage abandons the pulseless. In lightning, the pulseless victim is the one who can be saved and the walking wounded will survive without you. Reverse triage — treat the apparently dead first. Resuscitation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop ventilating after ROSC, and do NOT call death on fixed pupils
info.t: The medullary respiratory center stays paralyzed after cardiac automaticity returns; an unventilated post-ROSC patient re-arrests from hypoxia. Fixed dilated pupils after lightning are autonomic, not a death sign. Resuscitation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT admit a low-voltage patient with a normal ECG to telemetry "just in case"
info.t: Zero delayed malignant arrhythmias in 480- and 465-patient cohorts and a 1,234-patient systematic review. Routine monitoring and routine troponin add cost and delay with no yield. Reserve telemetry for the listed criteria. Monitoring decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT resuscitate a high-voltage injury by TBSA / Parkland
info.t: The skin burn is a fraction of the injured tissue. Formula volumes underestimate; titrate LR to urine output 1 mL/kg/h (1–2 if myoglobinuria). Fluids.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give diuretics or bicarbonate before volume is restored
info.t: Mannitol and furosemide in a hypovolemic rhabdomyolysis patient mask under-resuscitation and worsen AKI. These are burn-attending decisions after resuscitation. Fluids.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on the 5 Ps to exclude compartment syndrome
info.t: Paresthesias come from nerve injury and pulselessness is a late sign. A tense compartment or pain with passive stretch is enough — call surgery. Check every hour. Compartment checks.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform fasciotomy for keraunoparalysis
info.t: The cold, mottled, pulseless limb after lightning is vasospasm and resolves within hours. Cutting it open converts a self-limited phenomenon into a surgical wound. Reserve fasciotomy for a tense compartment or measured pressure. Lightning neuro.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT run a burn-formula resuscitation on a lightning victim
info.t: Flashover burns are superficial; aggressive volume causes cerebral edema in an already injured brain. Maintenance fluids unless deep burns, hypotension, or myoglobinuria. Lightning.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip otoscopy and the eye exam after lightning
info.t: TM rupture in 50–80%; cataracts develop later and are only compensable if documented absent at baseline. Both exams are WMS 1C recommendations. Lightning exam.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a cord-bite child without teaching pinch compression
info.t: The labial artery bleeds 5–21 days later in up to 25% of cases, at home, at night. Parents must know the bidirectional pinch and to come straight back. Cord bite.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order ECG, labs, or monitoring for an awake, asymptomatic CEW patient — and do NOT pull a probe from the eye, genitals, or neck
info.t: CEW current causes no arrhythmia or troponin rise; the injuries are the probes and the fall. Sensitive-site probes go to the specialist. CEW.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give NSAIDs to a high-voltage injury
info.t: AKI risk with rhabdomyolysis plus pending operative intervention. Opioids and sub-dissociative ketamine instead. Analgesia.

• Unstable or bleed screen = CT first; stable + brainstem, cord, marrow, infection question = MRI • Run the safety screen before Zone IV • Devices, orbital metal, implants • Pregnancy: non-contrast MRI is fine; avoid gadolinium • Claustrophobia and the critically ill • Group II gadolinium can be given at any eGFR when needed

• Protocol picker — region, emergency, exact order • Stroke/TIA: MRI brain without + MRA head and neck • Dizzy: thin posterior fossa DWI — central HINTS outranks a negative early DWI • Cauda equina: MRI L-spine without, emergently • Epidural abscess: whole spine with and without
• T1 = fat bright (anatomy); T2 = water bright (pathology) • DWI bright + ADC dark = true restriction • SWI/GRE: blood black and blooming • T1 post-contrast: ring patterns
• SWI most sensitive, FLAIR for SAH, CT still first • It Be, Iddy Biddy, Baby Doody
• Step 0: right patient, right sequence label • Brain: DWI/ADC → FLAIR/T2 → SWI → T1 post • Spine: sagittal T2 → STIR → axial T2 → T1 • Traps: motion, shine-through, partial volume, flow, metal
• Stroke, abscess, HSV, PRES, CVST, epidural abscess, cord compression
• Your read is not the final read; how to talk to radiology • When a negative MRI does not clear the patient • Disposition by finding
• Authors, sources and licenses for every scan and photo
Bright DWI + dark ADC = true restriction (acute infarct, pus). Bright DWI + bright ADC = T2 shine-through (not acute). Open the DWI card.

Modern group II agents carry a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) so low that the ACR and National Kidney Foundation (2021) say a clinically needed scan should not be withheld because of kidney function — including eGFR <30, AKI, and dialysis.

• Hemodialysis patients: when practical, time the scan shortly before a scheduled dialysis session; otherwise dialyze on the usual schedule. Do not start or change dialysis because of the gadolinium dose. • AKI or eGFR <30: use a group II agent; do not withhold or delay a needed scan.
Reactions are uncommon. A prior reaction to a gadolinium agent → radiology chooses a different agent and decides on premedication per its contrast-reaction protocol.

Small amounts of gadolinium stay in the brain, bone, and skin after exposure (FDA class warning, December 2017). No harm has been proven, and macrocyclic agents retain less — but give contrast only when it adds diagnostic value.

Safe in any trimester — no ionizing radiation and no reported harmful fetal effects. It is the preferred cross-sectional test after ultrasound (appendicitis, other abdominal pain) and should not be delayed or withheld because of pregnancy.

Crosses the placenta. In a population study of over 1.4 million births (Ray 2016), first-trimester MRI without gadolinium showed no significant increase in stillbirth or neonatal death, anomalies, cancer, or vision or hearing loss; gadolinium at any point in pregnancy was associated with more rheumatologic, inflammatory, or infiltrative skin conditions (adjusted HR 1.36) and with stillbirth or neonatal death (adjusted RR 3.70, based on few events). Use it only when it will clearly change management, after discussion with radiology.
Very little gadolinium reaches the infant. Breastfeeding should not be interrupted after gadolinium (ACOG); a mother who still prefers to can pump and discard for 12–24 h (ACR).

• Tell radiology the gestational age • Document the indication and the discussion with the patient • Order the specific protocol without gadolinium unless the radiologist advises otherwise • Appendicitis in pregnancy order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send an unstable patient to MRI
info.t: You cannot resuscitate in Zone IV, and scans take 5–60 minutes or more. Stabilize, or use CT. CT or MRI?

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT let MRI delay a stroke treatment decision
info.t: In a stroke code, non-contrast CT ± CTA is the default unless your center runs a rapid MRI pathway. Stroke order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send a patient into Zone IV without a completed screen
info.t: Unknown device, unknown implant, or possible orbital metal = not cleared. Oxygen tanks, IV poles and monitors become projectiles. Safety screen

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT be reassured by a negative early DWI in a dizzy patient with a central exam
info.t: Early DWI misses up to half of small brainstem strokes in the first 48 hours. The exam wins. Posterior stroke order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for MRI to start acyclovir
info.t: Suspected HSV encephalitis gets acyclovir immediately; early MRI can be normal. HSV order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgery for MRI in suspected necrotizing infection
info.t: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, gas, or shock goes to the operating room. Infection order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order an MRI brain alone for dissection or CVST
info.t: The brain images do not show the neck vessels or venous sinuses. Add MRA with T1 fat-sat, or MRV. Dissection order card · CVST order card

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold a needed contrast MRI for low eGFR
info.t: Group II gadolinium agents can be given at any eGFR, including dialysis, when the scan is needed. Contrast and the kidneys

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge on your own read
info.t: Act on your read; discharge on the radiologist's. Your read is not the final read

• The "fifth recurrent abscess" in the same fold is HS — average 7–10 year diagnostic delay • Three criteria: typical lesions + typical sites + ≥2 flares in 6 months • First or second episode in a fold: document "possible HS" and refer

• Toxic perineal patient, pain out of proportion, crepitus = Fournier / NSTI • Fournier: emergent surgery, IV antibiotics within 1 h, LRINEC unreliable with chronic inflammation • Chronic non-healing ulcer or mass in Hurley III = SCC until biopsied • Mimics: simple abscess, Crohn, pilonidal, Bartholin, epidermoid cyst, LGV / granuloma inguinale
• Hurley I no tunnels / scars; II tunnels + scars, separated; III diffuse interconnected • IHS4 = nodules + 2 × abscesses + 4 × draining tunnels; mild ≤ 3, moderate 4–10, severe ≥ 11

• Abscess → drain; nodule → inject; sick → workup; chronic → ladder • I&D is rescue only (recurrence ~100%); punch debridement preferred • Punch debridement: field block, 5–7 mm punch removes roof + follicular unit, leave open, no packing • Simple I&D: small linear incision, no packing, counsel that it does not treat the disease • Inflamed nodule < 2 cm: triamcinolone 10 mg/mL, 0.5–1 mL intralesional • NSAID + acetaminophen, opioid ≤ 3 days only if needed; culture only for systemic signs, cellulitis, immunosuppression, atypical pattern • Systemic signs: labs, ultrasound, culture, empiric antibiotics for true secondary infection

• Choose the rung by Hurley / IHS4 • Mild: topical clindamycin BID + antiseptic wash, doxycycline or minocycline × 8–12 wk, smoking cessation • Moderate: clindamycin 300 + rifampin 300 BID × 10–12 wk (contraceptive failure), spironolactone / metformin, name the biologic • Severe: adalimumab, secukinumab, or bimekizumab via dermatology in 2–4 wk; bridge; surgical referral in parallel
• Screen: metabolic syndrome / T2DM, PCOS, IBD, depression and suicide risk, anemia, arthritis, smoking • Complications: fistulae, lymphedema, contractures, amyloidosis, SCC, chronic pain

• Discharge / surgical referral / admit • Discharge: diagnosis on paper, dated derm referral, ladder scripts, written flare plan, return precautions • Surgical referral: deroofing for Hurley II tunnels, wide excision for Hurley III • Admit: sepsis, Fournier, extensive cellulitis, uncontrolled pain, IV antibiotics; inpatient derm + surgery

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: The four options at a glance:

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: Inflamed tissue is acidic and neutralizes local anesthetic. Field block, not direct injection: infiltrate 1% lidocaine with epinephrine (buffered 9:1 with 8.4% bicarbonate) in a ring 1–2 cm outside the erythema and beneath the lesion, then wait 5–10 minutes. Add or substitute 0.25% bupivacaine for 4–8 h of post-procedure analgesia. Stay under maximum doses — 7 mg/kg lidocaine with epinephrine, 2.5 mg/kg bupivacaine — when treating several sites. Consider procedural sedation or intranasal analgesia for extensive Hurley III drainage.

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: 1. Prep and drape; mark the lesion and any tunnel opening you can probe 2. Field block as above 3. Center a 5–7 mm disposable biopsy punch on the lesion; twist down through dermis into the cavity — or unroof with iris scissors / electrocautery for a larger lesion 4. Remove the plug: this takes the roof and the folliculopilosebaceous unit, which is the source of the lesion 5. Blunt-probe the cavity; unroof any short communicating tunnel by cutting along the probe 6. Curette or gauze-scrub the gelatinous base; irrigate with saline 7. Hemostasis with pressure, aluminum chloride, or light cautery 8. Leave open. Petrolatum gauze or an absorbent foam dressing; no wick Healing by secondary intentio

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: Reserve for the tense abscess when a punch is not feasible (no equipment, patient cannot tolerate, extensive disease going to the OR anyway). Smallest effective linear incision along skin tension lines over maximal fluctuance; express; irrigate; no packing; non-adherent dressing. Say out loud that this will likely recur and that the fix is the ladder plus dermatology.

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: A randomized trial of simple cutaneous abscesses found packing increased pain and analgesic use with no reduction in treatment failure or recurrence (O'Malley 2009); a pediatric trial found the same (Kessler 2012). In HS the packing strip also sits inside a tunnel network and keeps it open. North American guidelines recommend against packing HS wounds. Daily showers, gentle irrigation, and an absorbent dressing are the standard.

info.pt: HS Procedures — I&D vs Punch Debridement vs Deroofing
info.t: • Multiple interconnected tunnels or a whole Hurley III region — wide excision in the OR • Perineal, perianal, or genital tunnels — colorectal, urology, or plastic surgery; fistula and sphincter risk • Lesions overlying neurovascular structures in the axilla or groin • Chronic non-healing ulcer or mass — biopsy by dermatology, not an ED punch through inflamed tissue • Any patient on a biologic with an infected lesion — coordinate with the prescriber; procedures are usually still appropriate

• Hurley I / IHS4 ≤ 3: routine, 6–12 weeks; start topicals and a tetracycline course from the ED • Hurley II / IHS4 4–10: 4–6 weeks; start clindamycin + rifampin or a tetracycline; name the biologic • Hurley III / IHS4 ≥ 11, or failed ≥ 1 antibiotic course: 2–4 weeks; biologic candidate; bridge • Adolescent (≥ 12 y): adalimumab (≥ 30 kg, 2018) and secukinumab (≥ 30 kg, March 2026) are FDA-approved from age 12 — refer pediatric dermatology early; tetracyclines only ≥ 8 years • Pregnant or breastfeeding: topical clindamycin and washes; tetracyclines, rifampin, spironolactone, and methotrexate are contraindicated; adalimumab can be continued in pregnancy under dermatology / MFM guidance; refer

• Recurrent disease at the same site despite ≥ 8–12 weeks of medical therapy • Established tunnels (Hurley II) — deroofing • Whole-region Hurley III involvement — wide excision • Contracture limiting motion, chronic lymphedema, fistula • Urgent (1–2 weeks): suspected squamous cell carcinoma — chronic non-healing ulcer, verrucous mass, new bleeding or induration in long-standing gluteal / perineal disease

info.h: Other referrals triggered in the ED
info.t: • Gastroenterology: perianal fistula, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, blood in stool — Crohn overlap • Colorectal / urology: anal, rectal, urethral, or vaginal fistula • Behavioral health: positive depression screen; emergency psychiatric evaluation for suicidal ideation • Primary care: metabolic syndrome, diabetes, PCOS, anemia, smoking cessation, weight management • Pain or addiction medicine: chronic opioid use

• Sepsis or systemic toxicity • Fournier gangrene or necrotizing infection — surgical service • Extensive cellulitis, failed outpatient antibiotics, or infection in an immunosuppressed patient (biologic, diabetes, HIV) • Pain uncontrolled with oral multimodal analgesia • Need for IV antibiotics, operative drainage or deroofing under general anesthesia, or perineal disease preventing self-care • Positive suicide screen with inadequate safety plan Order an inpatient dermatology consult on every HS admission — it is the visit that finally stages the disease and starts definitive therapy.

• Diagnosis, Hurley stage, and IHS4 written on the discharge paperwork • Dermatology referral with a date or a phone number, urgency as above • Prescriptions from the treatment ladder (topical clindamycin + wash for all; the 8–12-week oral course for moderate disease) • Analgesia plan: scheduled NSAID + acetaminophen; opioid ≤ 3 days only if required • Wound care sheet: daily showers, absorbent dressing, no packing • Written flare plan and return precautions • Smoking cessation offered; comorbidity screen forwarded

Fever or rigors; rapidly spreading redness; pain out of proportion or a dusky, numb, or crepitant area in the groin or perineum; pain not controlled by the plan; feculent, urinary, or vaginal drainage from a skin lesion; a lesion that ulcerates and will not heal; suicidal thoughts.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a recurrent fold abscess as "abscess"
info.t: Two or more flares in 6 months in the axilla, groin, inframammary, perineal, or gluteal skin is hidradenitis suppurativa. Every visit that ends without the diagnosis adds to a 7–10 year delay. Recognize it.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume the toxic perineal patient "just has an HS flare"
info.t: HS rarely causes systemic illness. Fever, hypotension, pain out of proportion, crepitus, or rapid spread in perineal or genital disease is Fournier gangrene until surgery says otherwise — and chronic scarring hides the early skin changes. Red flags.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust a low LRINEC in an HS patient
info.t: Chronic inflammation raises CRP and WBC at baseline, so the score is neither sensitive nor specific here. Exam and surgical consultation drive the decision. Fournier.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss a non-healing ulcer or new mass in Hurley III
info.t: Squamous cell carcinoma arises in 1–4% of long-standing severe disease, mostly gluteal and perineal, mostly men, and is usually diagnosed late. Urgent referral for biopsy. SCC.
Packing increases pain without reducing failure or recurrence in simple abscesses, and in HS it keeps the tunnel network open. Leave the cavity open with an absorbent dressing and daily showers. I&D.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reach for the scalpel on a non-fluctuant nodule
info.t: An inflamed nodule under 2 cm is injected with triamcinolone 10 mg/mL, not incised. Cutting it creates a scar and a future tunnel and does not shorten the flare. Intralesional steroid.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat HS with a 7-day antibiotic course
info.t: HS lesions are sterile or polymicrobial; a short course neither treats the disease nor prevents the next flare. Disease-modifying regimens are 8–12 weeks of a tetracycline or clindamycin + rifampin, prescribed as such. Ladder.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prescribe rifampin without counseling on contraceptive failure
info.t: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 and renders oral, patch, ring, and implant contraception unreliable, and drops levels of DOACs, warfarin, antiretrovirals, and many others. Backup contraception for the course and 4 weeks after. Moderate rung.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give tetracyclines, rifampin, or spironolactone in pregnancy
info.t: Tetracyclines stain fetal teeth and bone; rifampin and spironolactone are contraindicated. Pregnant and breastfeeding patients get topical clindamycin, antiseptic washes, and an expedited dermatology referral. Mild rung.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the suicide question
info.t: Depression affects roughly one in four HS patients and completed suicide risk is roughly doubled. Ask directly at every visit; a positive answer changes the disposition. Comorbidity screen.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT tell a patient on a biologic to stop it because they have a flare
info.t: Flares occur on therapy and stopping causes rebound. Ask the timing of the last dose, treat the lesion, and route infection concerns through the prescribing dermatologist. Severe rung.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT write an open-ended opioid prescription
info.t: HS pain is chronic and recurrent; chronic opioid use and opioid use disorder are over-represented. Scheduled NSAID + acetaminophen, a short opioid course (≤ 3 days) only when needed, and a single prescriber. Analgesia.

Appearance: Red, dry, no blisters Sensation: Painful Cap refill: Brisk blanching Healing: 5-7 days, no scarring Treatment: Moisturizer, cool compresses, OTC analgesics TBSA: NOT counted in TBSA calculation Example: Sunburn

Appearance: Pink/red, moist, blisters present Sensation: Very painful (intact nerve endings) Cap refill: Brisk Healing: 10-14 days, minimal scarring Treatment: Nonadherent dressing + bacitracin — avoid SSD (delays healing) TBSA: Counted

Appearance: Dark pink/red, moist or dry Sensation: Reduced (partial nerve damage) Cap refill: Sluggish Healing: 14-21 days, moderate scarring Treatment: Silver dressings (Mepilex Ag, Aquacel Ag) or SSD. May need grafting. TBSA: Counted

Appearance: Mottled red and white, dry Sensation: Minimal pain (significant nerve destruction) Cap refill: None Healing: >21 days, significant scarring, contracture risk Treatment: Requires excision and skin grafting TBSA: Counted

Appearance: White, brown, or black; waxy or leathery Sensation: Painless (complete nerve destruction) Cap refill: None Healing: Cannot heal by re-epithelialization — always needs grafting Treatment: Excision and grafting. Escharotomy if circumferential. TBSA: Counted

• Capillary refill is the single best predictor of depth • Initial assessment often underestimates depth — reassess at 48h • Zone of Stasis tissue may convert to deeper injury over 24-72h • Scald burns in children are often deeper than they appear initially • Laser Doppler imaging (if available) is most accurate for indeterminate depth

• Remove all clothing, jewelry, and constrictive items (rings EARLY — edema makes later removal difficult) • Thermal: Remove from heat source. Cool with running water 15-25°C for 20 min (most effective within 3 hours of injury) • Chemical: Copious water irrigation (exceptions: elemental metals — brush off first) • Electrical: Ensure power source disconnected before contact • Do NOT use ice — causes vasoconstriction and deepens injury

• Running tap water (15-25°C) for 20 minutes — single most impactful prehospital intervention • Effective up to 3 hours post-burn (still beneficial, diminishing returns) • Cool the burn, NOT the patient — limit cooling to <20% TBSA at a time to prevent hypothermia • No ice, no butter, no toothpaste, no home remedies

• Assess for inhalation injury BEFORE transport: facial burns, soot, singed hair, hoarse voice, stridor • Airway edema peaks at 12-24 hours — a patent airway now may occlude later • If concern for airway compromise, intubate BEFORE transport if possible • Humidified 100% O₂ via NRB for all enclosed-space fires

• Establish large-bore IV access en route (through burned skin if necessary) • IO access if IV not achievable • For burns >20% TBSA: start LR at Rule of 10's rate (%TBSA × 10 mL/hr) • Do NOT delay transport for IV access
• Burns patients lose thermoregulation rapidly • Dry sterile sheets (not wet) • Warm ambulance environment • Limit wound cooling to 20 min — then cover • No wet dressings during transport

• Burn center if available within 60-90 min and meets ABA criteria • Nearest trauma center if hemodynamically unstable or major associated injuries • Any ED if airway compromised — secure first, transfer later • Contact receiving facility early with TBSA estimate and mechanism
No formula-based LR or FFP resuscitation under this institutional protocol. Assess other hydration needs separately.

1. Administer 1 unit of FFP upon arrival 2. Initial fluid: Lactated Ringer's at 10 × %TBSA mL/hr, after the FFP unit. 30% TBSA → 300 mL/hr LR. No weight adjustment. 3. Titrate LR up or down by 20% every hour based on UOP goal 4. UOP goal: 0.5 cc/kg/hr (adults), 1 cc/kg/hr (peds) 5. At cumulative volume of 15 cc × %TBSA × kg → switch ALL fluid to FFP 6. At cumulative volume of 20 cc × %TBSA × kg → do NOT increase hourly rate further regardless of UOP 7. Check bladder pressure (abdominal compartment syndrome screening) 8. Place a trialysis catheter (IJ or subclavian preferred) 9. Consult nephrology for CRRT — once started, decrease FFP to 125 cc/hr regardless of UOP

1. Initial fluid: FFP ONLY at 10 × %TBSA mL/hr (NO crystalloid). 50% TBSA → 500 mL/hr FFP. No weight adjustment. 2. Titrate FFP up or down by 20% every hour based on UOP goal 3. Place a triple lumen dialysis catheter (trialysis) 4. At cumulative volume of 20 cc × %TBSA × kg → do NOT increase hourly rate further 5. Consult nephrology — once CRRT started, decrease FFP to 125 cc/hr regardless of UOP

• Excessive crystalloid → third-spacing → airway edema, abdominal compartment syndrome, extremity compartment syndrome • FFP provides oncotic pressure, maintaining intravascular volume with less total fluid • The 15cc and 20cc thresholds are cumulative volume triggers, not hourly rates • CRRT manages fluid overload while continuing resuscitation

• Foley catheter — UOP hourly (primary endpoint) • Bladder pressure — q4-6h or if abdominal distension (>25 mmHg = ACS) • Labs q4-6h: BMP, lactate, Hgb, glucose, coags • Hourly I/O documentation with cumulative totals • Reassess airway, extremity perfusion, abdominal exam each nursing shift

Use the map as the procedural anchor. Mark the intended cut lines before incision. For limbs, cut the medial and lateral mid-axial lines between flexor and extensor surfaces. For chest/trunk restriction, cut the bilateral anterior/mid-axillary lines from clavicle to costal margin and connect across the costal margin when needed. For hand involvement, use dorsal intermetacarpal incisions rather than palmar cuts. The bedside question is: does the circumferential eschar behave like a tourniquet? If perfusion or ventilation is threatened, open the eschar now and involve burn surgery early.

Screen every circumferential deep partial/full-thickness burn early and repeatedly. Edema worsens during the first hours of resuscitation, so a limb that looked acceptable on arrival can declare later. 6 P's of Compartment Syndrome: • Pain — out of proportion, or paradoxically absent in full-thickness • Pressure — tense, woody compartment • Paresthesias — early neurologic compromise • Paralysis — late, ominous • Pulselessness — very late, pre-amputation • Pallor/Poikilothermia Objective measures: • Doppler: absent or diminished pulses • Compartment pressure >30 mmHg • Capillary refill >3 seconds • Undetectable SpO2 on digit • Rising ventilator pressures / poor chest excursion for chest escha

• Call burn surgery/trauma surgery, but do not delay decompression for a threatened limb or restricted ventilation • Remove jewelry, watches, circumferential dressings, and constrictive splints • Baseline and post-procedure: pulses, Doppler, cap refill, motor/sensory, digit pulse ox when possible • Prep widely; expose the entire involved limb/chest • Analgesia/sedation as needed; full-thickness eschar may be insensate, but margins are not • Prefer electrocautery for hemostasis if available; scalpel is acceptable when time-critical

• Medial and lateral mid-axial lines — incise through full thickness of eschar to subcutaneous fat • Adequate depth: tissue gapes open and subcutaneous fat is visible • Start and finish about 1 cm into healthy skin when possible; anesthetize viable skin margins • Eschar in full-thickness areas is insensate — no anesthesia needed within the eschar itself (sedation/analgesia still usually needed) • Use electrocautery (preferred — hemostasis) or scalpel • Avoid crossing flexor creases directly; curve/Z/S across joints when needed Upper extremity: Axilla to wrist along medial and lateral mid-axial lines. Pass anterior to the medial epicondyle to avoid the ulnar nerve. If hand involved, use dorsa

• Indication: Circumferential trunk burns restricting ventilation — rising peak airway pressures, decreasing tidal volumes • Incision pattern: Bilateral anterior axillary lines from clavicle to costal margin • Connect superiorly across clavicles and inferiorly across costal margin = "clamshell" or "H" pattern • May extend to iliac crests if abdominal compartment syndrome concern • Expect immediate improvement in tidal volumes • If no improvement → consider fasciotomy or decompressive laparotomy

• Doppler pulse check immediately after and q1h • Control bleeding with electrocautery, hemostats, or direct pressure • Apply topical antimicrobial to exposed tissue • Elevate burned extremities above heart level • If perfusion does not improve → escalate to fasciotomy (requires OR) • Reassess neurovascular status q1h for first 6 hours

• Persistent vascular compromise after adequate escharotomy • Electrical burns (deep tissue injury exceeds surface appearance) • Compartment pressure >30 mmHg post-escharotomy • Requires OR and surgical consultation — not a bedside procedure • 4-compartment fasciotomy of the leg is most common
• Moisturizer (aloe vera, petroleum-based) • Nonadherent dressing only if friction area • No antimicrobials needed • OTC analgesics sufficient

• Nonadherent (Adaptic, Xeroform) + Bacitracin + gauze wrap • Do NOT use silver sulfadiazine — delays epithelialization by 1-2 days • Alternative: hydrogel dressings (Burnaid, Intrasite) for pain relief • Change dressings daily or BID • Modern silver dressings (Mepilex Ag, Aquacel Ag) if available — less painful changes

• Silver dressings preferred: Mepilex Ag, Aquacel Ag (can stay in place 3-7 days) • Silver Sulfadiazine 1% cream BID — acceptable alternative • Mafenide acetate (Sulfamylon) — better eschar penetration, but painful on application • Surgical consultation for grafting planning

Face: Bacitracin only — NO dressings (impair assessment, uncomfortable). Clean gently BID. Hands: Xeroform or nonadherent + loose gauze. Individual finger wrapping. Elevate. Early ROM exercises — splint in functional position (wrist extended, MCPs flexed, IPs extended). Ears: Bacitracin only. No pressure (pillow, headband) — risk of chondritis. Watch for auricular chondritis. Perineum/Genitalia: Bacitracin. Foley for urethral meatus burns. Frequent dressing changes. Circumferential: Do NOT apply tight circumferential dressings — risk of tourniquet effect with edema.

• Tetanus prophylaxis: Tdap if >5 years or unknown status • No prophylactic systemic antibiotics — increases resistance without benefit • Debridement: Remove loose/devitalized tissue gently. Leave intact blisters that are small, <24h old, and not impeding ROM. Debride ruptured blisters. • No home remedies: butter, toothpaste, egg whites — all worsen outcome • Pain management before dressing changes — see Burn Pain Management

• <5%: Normal (nonsmokers) • <10%: Normal for smokers • 5-15%: Headache, nausea, dizziness • 15-25%: Confusion, visual changes, tachycardia • 25-40%: Severe confusion, syncope, tachypnea • 40-60%: Coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse • >60%: Usually fatal CRITICAL: Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal — it cannot distinguish COHb from OxyHb. Order ABG with co-oximetry on ALL enclosed-space fire patients.
• Room air (21% O₂): ~320 minutes (5.3 hours) • 100% O₂ NRB: ~75 minutes (1.25 hours) • Hyperbaric O₂ (2-3 ATA): ~23 minutes Continue 100% O₂ until COHb <5% and asymptomatic.

• COHb >25% • Loss of consciousness (even if transient) • Neurologic deficits (confusion, ataxia, seizure) • Cardiac ischemia (ECG changes, troponin elevation) • Pregnancy with COHb >15% • Persistent symptoms despite 100% O₂ • Refractory metabolic acidosis Contact nearest HBO facility early — benefit diminishes >6h post-exposure.

There is no rapid confirmatory test. This is a CLINICAL diagnosis. Suspect cyanide when: • Enclosed-space fire (synthetic materials produce HCN) • Persistent metabolic acidosis despite adequate O₂ therapy • Lactate >8-10 mmol/L (strong predictor) • AMS out of proportion to COHb level • Cardiovascular collapse • PaO₂ and SpO₂ may be NORMAL (cells can't use O₂) Do NOT wait for cyanide levels — results take hours and patient may die waiting.

First-line: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) 5g IV over 15 min • Repeat 5g ×1 if persistent instability • Pediatric: 70 mg/kg (max 5g) • Turns skin/urine RED 2-3 days • Draw all labs BEFORE giving — interferes with colorimetric assays Alternative: Sodium thiosulfate 12.5g IV (slower onset) AVOID: Sodium nitrite if concurrent CO poisoning — creates methemoglobin, further reducing O₂ carrying capacity

• Occurs in 15-40% of significant CO poisoning cases • Onset: 2-40 days after exposure • Symptoms: cognitive deficits, personality changes, memory impairment, parkinsonism, incontinence • HBO may reduce incidence (controversial) • Warn patients and arrange neuropsych follow-up at discharge

Mechanism: Coagulation necrosis — protein denaturation creates eschar that limits penetration depth Common agents: Sulfuric acid (battery), hydrochloric acid (muriatic/pool), nitric acid Treatment: • Copious water irrigation 20-30 min • Do NOT neutralize (exothermic reaction worsens injury) • Check skin pH with litmus paper until 7.0-7.5 • Remove all contaminated clothing/jewelry Special acids: • Phenol: Wipe with PEG (polyethylene glycol) or glycerol FIRST, then water irrigation. Water alone may spread phenol. • Chromic acid: Irrigation + topical 10% ascorbic acid. Monitor for systemic chromium toxicity (renal failure).

Mechanism: Liquefaction necrosis — saponifies fats, NO self-limiting eschar → penetrates deeply. More dangerous than acids. Common agents: NaOH (lye/drain cleaner), KOH, cement, ammonia, bleach Treatment: • Prolonged irrigation 30-60+ minutes — alkali penetrates much deeper • Cement: brush dry powder off first, then irrigate • Check pH q15 min during irrigation • Do NOT neutralize with acid Eye exposure: Emergency — continuous Morgan lens irrigation until pH neutral. Immediate ophthalmology consult.

Uniquely dangerous. Fluoride ion penetrates tissue and binds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ → progressive deep necrosis, severe pain out of proportion to appearance, and life-threatening hypocalcemia (burns >2% TBSA or >50% concentration can be fatal). Treatment ladder: 1. Water irrigation × 20 min 2. Calcium Gluconate 2.5% Gel — apply and massage continuously. Pain relief = successful fluoride binding. 3. If pain persists: Calcium Gluconate SQ 5% solution, 0.5 mL/cm² 4. Digital/refractory: Intra-arterial CaGluc via radial catheter (10 mL 10% CaGluc in 40 mL NS over 4h) 5. Systemic hypocalcemia: IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride Monitor: Serial iCa, Mg, K, ECG (QT prolongation → VF). Admit ALL HF burn

Na, K, Li: React violently with water → H₂ gas + alkali burn • Cover with mineral oil to prevent air/water contact • Remove all metal fragments with forceps • Irrigate with water ONLY after all metal is removed White phosphorus: Ignites spontaneously in air • Keep submerged in water at all times • CuSO₄ 1% solution turns particles black (aids identification — use sparingly as copper is toxic) • Remove all visible particles under water Magnesium: Burns extremely hot (>2000°C) • Cover with sand or dry chemical extinguisher • Do NOT use water until fire is extinguished • X-ray if penetrating injury suspected

• Default to copious water irrigation (safe for vast majority of agents) • Contact Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222 • Full PPE for all responders (gloves, gown, eye protection, N95 minimum) • If powder: brush off first, then irrigate • Continue irrigation 20+ min, check pH until neutral • Collect/photograph agent container for identification

• Chemical burns often appear superficial initially and progress over 24-72 hours — serial reassessment is mandatory • Lower threshold for burn center transfer with chemical burns • Watch for systemic toxicity specific to the agent (especially HF, chromic acid, phenol) • Diphoterine (amphoteric chelating solution) is emerging as a universal chemical burn decontaminant — available in some EDs
• Non-contrast CT head — confirm ICH, estimate volume (ABC/2) • Labs: CBC, BMP, INR/PTT/fibrinogen, anti-Xa level if on DOAC • CTA for nearly all patients (mandatory if lobar <70y or deep <45y)

• Identify anticoagulant — do NOT wait for labs before reversing • Warfarin → 4-Factor PCC + Vitamin K 10 mg IV • Dabigatran → Idarucizumab 5 g IV • Xa inhibitor → 4-Factor PCC 50 IU/kg • Heparin/LMWH → Protamine sulfate
• Treat pain/anxiety FIRST • SBP 150–220 → target 130–150 mmHg • SBP >220 → target 140–180 mmHg • Avoid SBP <130 and drops >70 mmHg in first hour
• Supratentorial: limited evidence for early evacuation — consult neurosurgery • Cerebellar >15 mL with brainstem compression → IMMEDIATE surgical evacuation • IVH with hydrocephalus → EVD placement
• Seizure prophylaxis NOT recommended — treat if witnessed/EEG-confirmed • ICP management, sodium monitoring, fever treatment • DVT prophylaxis: IPC immediately, chemical ppx after 24–48h if stable
• ICU admission for all ICH patients • Serial CT at 6h and 24h • Early goals-of-care discussion

Swirl sign — Areas of varying density within the hematoma. Fresh unclotted blood is hypodense relative to clotted blood. Indicates active hemorrhage. Black hole sign — Relatively dark area within the hematoma not connected to adjacent brain tissue. Predicts hematoma growth (32% sensitivity, 94% specificity). Blend sign — Hematoma contains both hyperdense and hypodense regions. Fluid-fluid level — Highly specific for coagulopathy or anticoagulant use. If present and no anticoagulant identified, search aggressively for occult coagulopathy. Island sign — ≥3 small hemorrhages separated from the main hematoma. Isodense/hypodense blood — On initial CT, may indicate coagulopathy (clotting retarded

Spot sign — Leakage of contrast into the hematoma. 51% sensitivity, 85% specificity for predicting expansion. Must NOT be in anatomic continuity with adjacent blood vessels. The spot sign is a key indicator for early hematoma expansion risk and may influence aggressiveness of BP management and reversal strategy.

Edema takes several hours to develop — usually not seen on initial CT. Unusually extensive or irregular edema raises suspicion for: • Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) with secondary hemorrhage • Ischemic stroke with hemorrhagic transformation • Tumor with intratumoral hemorrhage Perihematomal edema peaks at ~5–6 days. This is cytotoxic edema — does NOT respond to steroids.

Hypertensive ICH — most common cause. Same arterial lipohyalinization that causes lacunar strokes. • Basal ganglia / external capsule (60–65%) • Thalamus (15–20%) • Pons or deep cerebellar nuclei (10%) Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) — ~15% of all spontaneous ICH. Most common cause of lobar hemorrhage in normotensive elderly patients. Beta-amyloid deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels. Associated with Alzheimer disease. See CAA details

Most common cause of ICH in young adults. Often require surgical or endovascular intervention. • Aneurysmal rupture — usually has subarachnoid component; frontal (ACA/AComm) or temporal (MCA) location • Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) — key in young patients • Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) — consider if younger patient, hypercoagulable state, bilateral hemorrhages, or excess edema • Cavernous malformation — popcorn-like appearance on T2 MRI • Dural arteriovenous fistula (dAVF) • Mycotic aneurysm — endocarditis/bacteremia • Moyamoya disease
