• Malignancy — primary brain tumor or hemorrhagic metastasis • Ischemic stroke with hemorrhagic conversion • RCVS (reversible cerebral vasospasm syndrome) • Coagulopathy — warfarin, DOACs, liver disease, DIC • Sympathomimetic drug use — cocaine, amphetamines • Vasculitis — PAN, lupus, ANCA vasculitis, drug-induced

Cerebrovascular disorder caused by beta-amyloid deposition in small-to-medium cortical and leptomeningeal arteries. Prevalence ~5% in people >65 years. Accounts for ~15% of all spontaneous ICH. Associated with Alzheimer disease. Most common cause of lobar hemorrhage in normotensive elderly patients. However, half of lobar ICH in the elderly is NOT due to CAA.

• Location: Lobar hemorrhage (occipital and parietal lobes most common) • Finger-like projections extending from the hemorrhage • Extension may involve subarachnoid, subdural, or intraventricular spaces • MRI GRE/SWI: Multiple microhemorrhages at grey-white junction and/or convexity, with hemosiderosis Clinical hint: Elderly patient + cognitive decline + lobar hemorrhage + small amount of cortical subarachnoid hemorrhage = likely amyloid angiopathy.

Short-term prognosis is often favorable, but high recurrence risk (~7.5%/year) and progressive cognitive decline. Critical: Patients diagnosed with CAA should generally NOT be restarted on anticoagulation due to very high risk of recurrent hemorrhage. This is a key management decision that differs from non-CAA ICH. Antiplatelet monotherapy may be considered with careful risk-benefit analysis.

Rare variant where perivascular beta-amyloid triggers inflammation. Mean onset in 70s. Presentation: Acute/subacute headache, reduced consciousness, behavioral change, focal neurologic signs, seizures. MRI: Vasogenic edema in subcortical white matter with mass effect + underlying CAA features (microhemorrhages). Treatment: May respond to steroids followed by cyclophosphamide.

30-day mortality: ~40% 1-year survival: ~50% 5-year survival: ~30% Functional independence at 1 year: ~20% Predictors of poor outcome: • Hematoma volume >60 mL • GCS <8 • Deep or infratentorial location • Intraventricular extension • Increasing age

Components (0–6 points): • GCS 3–4: +2 pts | GCS 5–12: +1 pt | GCS 13–15: 0 pts • Hematoma volume ≥30 mL: +1 pt • Intraventricular hemorrhage: +1 pt • Infratentorial origin: +1 pt • Age ≥80: +1 pt Mortality by score: • ICH 0: ~0% • ICH 1: ~13% • ICH 2: ~26% • ICH 3: ~72% • ICH 4: ~97% • ICH 5–6: ~100%

• Transient impairment (sedation, hypercapnia) may inflate the score • Hydrocephalus may cause reversible consciousness impairment — treatable with EVD • No distinction between tiny vs massive IVH • No distinction between pontine (poor) vs cerebellar (treatable) infratentorial bleeds • No distinction between age 18 and 79 • Does not account for pre-existing functional status/frailty Caution: These scores should NOT be used to justify withdrawal of care. Self-fulfilling prophecy bias is a known limitation — aggressive early treatment may improve outcomes beyond what the scores predict.

Components (0–11 points): • ICH volume: <30 mL (+4) | 30–59 mL (+2) | ≥60 mL (0) • Age: <70 (+2) | 70–79 (+1) | ≥80 (0) • Location: Lobar (+2) | Deep (+1) | Infratentorial (0) • GCS: ≥9 (+2) | <9 (0) • Pre-ICH cognitive impairment: No (+1) | Yes (0) Probability of functional independence at 90 days: • FUNC 0–4: 0–2% • FUNC 5–7: 6–29% • FUNC 8: 42% • FUNC 9–10: 55–66% • FUNC 11: 80%

A positive screening result comprises: • Heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche PLUS one of the following: • Postpartum hemorrhage • Surgery-related bleeding • Bleeding associated with dental work OR two or more of the following: • Bruising 1–2 times per month • Epistaxis 1–2 times per month • Frequent gum bleeding • Family history of bleeding symptoms

• Order: von Willebrand factor antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, Factor VIII • Consult hematology for interpretation • Up to 13% of women with heavy menstrual bleeding have von Willebrand disease • Up to 20% may have some underlying coagulation disorder • Also consider: other coagulation factor deficiencies, platelet function disorders, hemophilia carriers

• Systemic diseases (leukemia, liver failure) can impair coagulation • Medications (anticoagulants, chemotherapy) should be reviewed • Adolescents with heavy menses since menarche presenting with acute AUB should undergo vWD testing regardless of screening result

Polyp (AUB-P) Endometrial or endocervical growths. Often asymptomatic but can cause intermenstrual or heavy bleeding. Diagnosed by US or hysteroscopy. Treatment: polypectomy. Adenomyosis (AUB-A) Endometrial tissue within the myometrium. Causes heavy, painful periods with diffuse uterine enlargement. Diagnosed by MRI or US. Treatment: medical or hysterectomy. Leiomyoma (AUB-L) Benign smooth muscle tumors. Submucosal fibroids (AUB-LₛM) most likely to cause AUB. Size and location guide management. Treatment: medical, myomectomy, UAE, or hysterectomy. Malignancy & Hyperplasia (AUB-M) Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Diagnosed by endometrial biopsy. Risk factors: age, obesity, unopposed estr

Coagulopathy (AUB-C) Inherited or acquired bleeding disorders. vWD most common (up to 13% of HMB). Screen with structured tool. Ovulatory Dysfunction (AUB-O) Most common cause of dysfunctional uterine bleeding (~80%). Anovulatory cycles lead to unopposed estrogen → endometrial proliferation → irregular shedding. Common in: PCOS, obesity, perimenarchal, perimenopausal, stress, weight changes. Endometrial (AUB-E) Primary endometrial disorder with normal ovulatory cycles. Defects in local hemostasis, inflammation, or angiogenesis. Iatrogenic (AUB-I) Medication-related: anticoagulants, hormonal therapy, IUD, chemotherapy, steroids. Not Yet Classified (AUB-N) Rare or poorly understood etiologies

• Increasing age — 1.4% prevalence in women 50–70 • Unopposed estrogen therapy — RR 2–10 • Tamoxifen therapy — RR 2 • Early menarche — increased risk • Late menopause (after age 55) — RR 2 • Nulliparity — RR 2 • PCOS (chronic anovulation) — RR 3 • Obesity — RR 2–4 • Diabetes mellitus — RR 2 • Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — 22–50% lifetime risk • Cowden syndrome — 13–19% lifetime risk • Family history of endometrial, ovarian, breast, or colon cancer

• Age ≥45 with AUB — first-line test • Age <45 with any of: — Obesity or PCOS (unopposed estrogen exposure) — Chronic anovulation — Failed medical management of AUB — Persistent AUB • Postmenopausal bleeding (always evaluate) Obese patients are at particularly high risk — adipose tissue converts androgens to estrogen via aromatase, creating chronic unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium.

Dose: 25 mg IV q4–6h for up to 24h Efficacy: 72% stop bleeding within 8h Key CI: Active VTE, breast cancer, hepatic disease Notes: Only FDA-approved treatment for acute AUB. Must follow with progestin (MPA 10 mg PO × 10d). Premedicate with antiemetic.

Dose: Monophasic OCP with 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol, 1 tab TID × 7 days Efficacy: 88% stop bleeding (median 3 days) Key CI: Smoking + age >35, HTN, VTE history, migraine with aura, breast cancer Notes: Preferred for ovulatory dysfunction AUB. Provides cycle regulation. Can transition to daily OCP for maintenance.

Dose: 20 mg PO TID × 7 days Efficacy: 76% stop bleeding (median 3 days) Key CI: Active VTE, breast cancer, hepatic disease Notes: Preferred when estrogen contraindicated. Good for obese/PCOS patients. Alternative progestins (norethindrone acetate) may also be effective.

Dose: Tranexamic Acid 1.3 g PO TID × 5 days OR 10 mg/kg IV (max 600 mg) q8h Efficacy: Reduces menstrual blood loss 30–55% Key CI: Active thrombosis, impaired color vision Notes: Antifibrinolytic — can use alone or as adjunct. Does not affect fertility. Caution with concurrent OCPs (additive thrombotic risk).

Method: 26F Foley catheter inflated with 30 mL saline in uterine cavity. Bakri balloon (up to 300 mL) for enlarged uterus. Alternative: gauze packing with thrombin. When: GYN unavailable and medical therapy insufficient Notes: Temporizing measure while arranging definitive care. Consult GYN STAT.
• Clinically unstable despite medical management • Failed medical therapy • Contraindications to all medical therapies • Suspected structural pathology requiring tissue diagnosis • Known malignancy

Diagnostic + therapeutic. Preferred if intrauterine pathology suspected (polyp, submucosal fibroid). D&C alone (without hysteroscopy) is inadequate for evaluation and provides only temporary reduction — subsequent cycles are not improved. Preserves fertility.

Destroys the endometrial lining. Only if: • Other treatments ineffective or contraindicated • Childbearing complete (pregnancy after ablation is dangerous) • Endometrial/uterine cancer reliably ruled out Multiple techniques: thermal balloon, radiofrequency, cryoablation.

Interventional radiology procedure. Most effective for fibroid-related AUB. Reduces blood supply to fibroids. May affect future fertility — discuss with patient. Case reports show successful use for acute AUB control.

Definitive treatment for controlling heavy bleeding. Reserved for: • Failure of all medical and less-invasive surgical options • Completed childbearing • Known malignancy • Patient preference after counseling May be performed vaginally, laparoscopically, or via laparotomy depending on clinical context.

Most effective medical option for long-term AUB management. Reduces menstrual blood loss by up to 97%. Lasts 5–8 years. Especially beneficial for obese/PCOS patients — provides continuous endometrial suppression and reduces endometrial cancer risk.
Monthly or extended-cycle regimens. Regulate ovulation, thin endometrium, reduce blood loss. Good first-line for younger patients who also need contraception. Review CDC MEC for eligibility.

• Oral progestins (MPA, norethindrone) — cyclic (days 14–25) or continuous • Depo-medroxyprogesterone (DMPA) 150 mg IM q3 months • Etonogestrel implant (Nexplanon) Preferred when estrogen is contraindicated. Critical for obese/PCOS patients to prevent endometrial hyperplasia from chronic unopposed estrogen.
1.3 g PO TID during menses (first 5 days). Non-hormonal option. Can be combined with hormonal therapies. Does not affect fertility or cycle regularity.

Ibuprofen, naproxen, mefenamic acid. Reduce menstrual blood loss by 20–50% via prostaglandin inhibition. Take during menses only. Avoid in patients with bleeding disorders (impair platelet aggregation).
You were seen in the emergency department for abnormal uterine bleeding. You have been started on medication to help control the bleeding.

• Take your prescribed medication exactly as directed • Complete the full course (usually 7 days) even if bleeding improves • You may experience nausea with hormonal medications — take with food • If prescribed iron supplements, take on an empty stomach with vitamin C for best absorption (or with food if nausea occurs)

info.h: Return to the ED Immediately If
info.t: • Soaking through more than 1 pad or tampon per hour for 2 or more hours in a row • Feeling dizzy, lightheaded, or faint • Passing out (syncope) • Chest pain or difficulty breathing • Fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C) • Severe abdominal or pelvic pain • Bleeding does not improve after completing your medication course

• See a gynecologist (OB/GYN) within 1–2 weeks • Your doctor may recommend additional testing or long-term treatment to prevent future episodes • If you have obesity or irregular periods, long-term hormonal management is important to reduce your risk of future complications • Continue iron supplements if you were told you are anemic

• Do not skip doses of your medication • Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen unless approved by your doctor (they can worsen bleeding) • Stay well hydrated • Rest as needed — you may feel tired from blood loss • Keep track of your bleeding pattern to share with your gynecologist

• Confirm SE: seizure >5 min or recurrent without recovery • ABCs — left lateral decubitus, O2, IV access × 2, monitor • Fingerstick glucose STAT — treat hypoglycemia immediately • Obtain labs: BMP (Na, Ca, Mg), CBC, UDS, lactate, ASM levels
• IV access: Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg), repeat × 1 • No IV: Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM (max 10 mg) • Assess response 5 min after BZD — up to 2 doses allowed
• Pregnant / eclampsia → Magnesium sulfate first • Toxic ingestion (INH) → Pyridoxine is specific antidote • Pediatric → same algorithm, weight-based dosing

• Select 2nd-line agent — ESETT: all three are equivalent • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg) — fewest interactions • Valproate 40 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg) — avoid in pregnancy/liver disease • Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (max 1500 mg PE) — cardiac monitoring required • Phenobarbital 15-20 mg/kg IV — if above unavailable

• Intubate — RSI with short-acting paralytic • Start continuous EEG monitoring — MANDATORY • Select continuous infusion: midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital, or ketamine • Target burst suppression on EEG × 24-48h before wean attempt
• All SE → ICU admission with continuous EEG • Complete etiology workup: MRI, LP if indicated, autoimmune panel • Neurology consultation for all SE patients
• Fingerstick glucose — hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia (non-ketotic hyperosmolar) cause seizures • Point-of-care electrolytes if available — Na, Ca, glucose

• Complete blood count — leukocytosis may indicate infection (transient leukocytosis common post-seizure) • Comprehensive metabolic panel — Na, Ca, Mg, Phos as metabolic seizure etiologies • Urine drug screen — cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA, marijuana, heroin all associated with seizures • Serum toxicology — acetaminophen, salicylate, ethanol levels • Lactate — excess from muscle tissue; if elevated >1h post-seizure, monitor for persistent acidosis. Lactate >2.45 mmol/L distinguishes GTC from syncope/PNES (sensitivity 88%, specificity 87%) • Blood gas (VBG/ABG) — respiratory acidosis, hypercarbia in depressed mental status • Pregnancy test — positive test limits certain ASMs due to teratogenic

• ASM levels — assess medication compliance in known epilepsy patients • Prolactin — draw 10-20 min post-seizure. Sensitivity 53%, specificity 93% for convulsive SE. Limited by narrow collection window. • Creatine kinase (CK) — rises 1-12h, peaks 24-72h. Trend for rhabdomyolysis and AKI. Sensitivity 14-87%, specificity 85-100%. • Troponin — can be elevated with seizures (autonomic features). Prompt cardiac evaluation if elevated. • Cultures — blood, urine, CSF if infection suspected

• CT head non-contrast — first-line after stabilization. Evaluate for hemorrhage, mass, edema, herniation. Normal CT does not rule out elevated ICP. • CT/MR venogram — consider if risk for cerebral venous thrombosis (hypercoagulability, recent pregnancy, OCP use, headache, papilledema) • MRI brain — superior for structural causes. Obtain when stable. DWI for acute ischemia, FLAIR for edema/encephalitis.

• Indications: Signs of meningitis, critically ill patients, age ≤18 months with febrile seizure, new-onset seizures without obvious cause, antibiotics given prior to evaluation, incomplete/unknown vaccination history • Obtain CT head before LP if altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit • CSF pleocytosis should prompt further investigation — seizures alone do NOT cause CSF pleocytosis • Low threshold to test CSF for infectious causes — delays in treating CNS infection worsen outcomes

• Continuous EEG recommended when: patient does not return to baseline, concern for NCSE, clinical evaluation limited by sedation or paralysis • ESETT: 48% of patients with altered consciousness post-SE had NCSE on EEG • Intermittent EEG (30-60 min) may miss up to 10% of subclinical seizures • High-risk populations for NCSE: ICU patients on neurotoxic medications, history of epilepsy, prior GTC, prior head injury/stroke, female sex

Levetiracetam — Best overall safety profile • Fewest drug interactions • No cardiac effects (no telemetry needed during infusion) • Safe in hepatic failure, renal impairment (dose adjust) • Safe in pregnancy (preferred 2nd-line) • Caution: psychiatric side effects (irritability, agitation) Valproate — Broad-spectrum efficacy • Well-tolerated even at rapid infusion rates • AVOID in: pregnancy (Category X), liver disease, mitochondrial disorders, thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, urea cycle disorders • Check ammonia if AMS persists Fosphenytoin — When specific indication exists • Requires cardiac monitoring during/after infusion • INEFFECTIVE for drug/alcohol-induced seizures • AVOID in: cardiac

• Levetiracetam: Psychiatric symptoms, drowsiness. Caution in mood disorders. • Valproate: Thrombocytopenia, hyperammonemia, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. Caution in liver disease, pregnancy. • Fosphenytoin: Cardiac arrhythmia, hypotension, Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Caution in cardiac disease. • Lacosamide (adjunct): PR prolongation, cardiac arrhythmia. Caution in cardiovascular disease. Not yet standard of care. • Phenobarbital: Respiratory depression, hypotension. Caution with concurrent BZDs.

Choose midazolam when: • Hemodynamic instability is a concern • Short duration of suppression anticipated • Easier ICU nursing management Choose propofol when: • Need for rapid onset and frequent neuro assessments • Younger patients (lower PRIS risk) • Shorter anticipated duration (<48h) Choose pentobarbital when: • Other agents have failed • Deepest level of suppression required • Hemodynamic support is available Choose ketamine when: • GABAergic agents have failed (different mechanism) • Hemodynamic support is limited (sympathomimetic effect) • Consider early trial to potentially avoid intubation

• Burst suppression: 3-10 second bursts, <50% suppression ratio • Seizure suppression: Complete absence of electrographic seizures • Maintain for 24-48 hours before first wean attempt • Wean by reducing infusion 25% every 4-6 hours with continuous EEG monitoring • Seizure recurrence on wean → restart at effective dose, extend 24h, retry

• RSI is indicated — secure airway before starting continuous anesthetic infusions • Use short-acting paralytic (succinylcholine preferred over rocuronium) to allow ongoing clinical seizure assessment • Avoid prolonged paralysis — masks clinical seizure activity • Once paralyzed, continuous EEG is the ONLY way to monitor seizure activity • Post-intubation sedation with the chosen anesthetic infusion

• MANDATORY for all RSE patients — cannot assess seizure activity in sedated/paralyzed patient • Target: burst suppression or complete seizure suppression (per clinical scenario) • Duration: maintain suppression × 24-48 hours before first wean attempt • Automated seizure detection algorithms exist but are not yet available in most EDs • If continuous EEG unavailable, intermittent EEGs (30-60 min) are helpful but may miss up to 10% of subclinical seizures

• Anesthetic agents cause significant hypotension — arterial line for continuous BP monitoring • Central venous access for vasopressor infusions • Pentobarbital almost always requires vasopressors • Propofol and midazolam may require vasopressors at higher doses • Goal: MAP >65 mmHg (or higher if concern for elevated ICP)

• Nutrition: enteral feeding when feasible (propofol contributes 1.1 kcal/mL toward caloric intake) • DVT prophylaxis (SCD + pharmacologic when safe) • Stress ulcer prophylaxis • Head of bed elevation 30° • Temperature management — fever worsens neuronal injury; target normothermia • Daily labs: CBC, CMP, CK, lactate, triglycerides (if propofol), drug levels

• After 24-48h of seizure suppression on EEG: • Reduce infusion rate by 25% every 4-6 hours • Maintain continuous EEG monitoring throughout wean • If seizures recur → restart at prior effective dose, extend suppression 24h, retry wean • Super-refractory SE (SRSE): SE that persists/recurs despite 24h of anesthetic therapy • SRSE options: switch anesthetic agent, add lacosamide, immunotherapy (if autoimmune suspected), therapeutic hypothermia (32-35°C), ketogenic diet

• Unexplained altered mental status / coma • Failure to return to baseline after convulsive seizure treatment • Subtle motor signs: nystagmus, gaze deviation, eyelid fluttering, lip smacking, subtle facial twitching, myoclonus • Fluctuating level of consciousness • Unexplained aphasia or cognitive decline • ICU patients on neurotoxic medications (cephalosporins, methotrexate, baclofen, lithium, opioids) • History of epilepsy, prior GTC, prior head injury or stroke

EEG criteria for diagnosing NCSE: Primary criteria (any one sufficient): • Epileptiform discharges (EDs) >2.5 Hz • EDs ≤2.5 Hz OR rhythmic delta/theta activity with ONE of: — EEG AND clinical improvement after IV BZD — Subtle clinical ictal phenomena during EEG pattern — Typical spatiotemporal evolution (frequency, morphology, or location change) Absent primary criteria: The recording does NOT show NCSE

Protocol: • Administer lorazepam 1-2 mg IV while monitoring EEG (if available) and clinical status • Positive trial: Clinical improvement (increased responsiveness, improved cognition) AND/OR EEG improvement (reduction/cessation of epileptiform activity) • A positive trial confirms NCSE and initiates treatment • Negative trial: No clinical or EEG change — does not definitively rule out NCSE but makes it less likely • Even without EEG, clinical improvement after BZD trial supports NCSE diagnosis

• Same escalating algorithm as convulsive SE (BZD → 2nd-line ASM → anesthetic infusions) • Urgency of aggressive treatment is debated — NCSE generally has lower mortality than convulsive SE • Weigh risks of anesthetic agents and intubation against ongoing subclinical seizure activity • Treat underlying etiology aggressively (infection, metabolic, structural) • Continuous EEG monitoring throughout treatment to guide escalation/de-escalation • Maintain a high index of suspicion — NCSE accounts for up to 48% of post-SE altered consciousness (ESETT)

• Hematemesis vs melena vs hematochezia • History: NSAIDs, anticoagulants, alcohol, liver disease • Hemodynamic status: Shock? Active bleeding? • TXA is NOT recommended (HALT-IT trial: no benefit, increased harm)

• Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS): Best for identifying low-risk - GBS 0-1 = <1% need intervention, consider outpatient EGD • AIMS65: Predicts mortality/ICU need - Score ≥2 = high risk (31% mortality) • Cirrhosis? Variceal bleeding in 59% of cirrhotic patients

• Restrictive transfusion: Hgb <7 g/dL threshold • Target Hgb 7-8 g/dL (exception: ACS target >8) • Villanueva trial: 45% mortality reduction with restrictive • Avoid over-resuscitation (increases portal pressure in varices) • Coagulation targets: Plt >50k, fibrinogen >150

• PPI: 80 mg IV bolus, then 40 mg IV Q12h or 8 mg/hr infusion • Erythromycin: 250 mg IV 20-90 min pre-EGD (improves visualization) • Endoscopy timing: Within 24 hours (earlier does NOT improve outcomes)

• Octreotide: 50 mcg bolus, then 50 mcg/hr x 2-5 days • Start BEFORE EGD if varices suspected • Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily x 7 days (ALL cirrhotics) • Avoid excessive fluid (worsens portal pressure)

• Indications: Exsanguinating bleed, bridge to TIPS, failed EGD • INTUBATE FIRST (aspiration risk) • CXR before inflation • Gastric balloon: 250-300 mL (SBT) or 450-500 mL (Minnesota) • Esophageal balloon: NEVER exceed 45 mmHg
• GBS 0-1: Outpatient EGD 24-48h • Floor: GBS ≥2, stable after resuscitation • ICU: AIMS65 ≥2, unstable, cirrhosis + varices, intubated
• Assess hemodynamic stability — ABCs if unstable • Resuscitate: 2 large-bore IVs, NS/LR 20 mL/kg, cardiac monitor • Targeted history: stool character, duration, travel, meds, contacts

• Bloody diarrhea — stool culture, avoid antimotility, avoid abx if STEC • Febrile (>38.5°C) — fecal leukocytes/lactoferrin, stool culture • Severe dehydration — IV rehydration, monitor urine output • Immunocompromised — broader workup, O&P, lower admission threshold • Surgical concern — appendicitis, ischemic bowel, CT abdomen

• Selective lab testing — fecal markers, stool culture, C. diff toxin • C. difficile — stop offending abx, oral vancomycin first-line • Traveler's diarrhea — fluoroquinolone or azithromycin ± loperamide • Mild/self-limited — ORS, loperamide, ondansetron PRN • Empiric antibiotics — ciprofloxacin (adults), TMP-SMX (children)

• Pregnant — loperamide safest, avoid fluoroquinolones • Pediatric — ORS, ondansetron, no antimotility, watch for HUS • Elderly — higher risk etiologies, drug interactions, lower admit threshold • Disposition — discharge criteria, admit criteria, follow-up

info.h: Return to the ED Immediately If
info.t: • You are very thirsty, weak, dizzy, or feel faint • You have a fever over 101.5°F (38.6°C) • You have blood, pus, or mucus in your stool • You have black or wine-colored stool • You have severe pain in your stomach or abdomen • You are vomiting and cannot eat or drink for more than 24 hours • Your diarrhea lasts more than 7 days • You are not getting better or you are getting worse • Your skin is dry, loose, or you feel confused

First 1-2 days: • Drink lots of fluids — caffeine-free sodas, oral rehydration solutions (available at pharmacy), or flavored mineral water • Nibble on salted crackers or pretzels (your body needs the salt) • Drink orange juice or eat bananas for potassium • You are drinking enough if you are not thirsty and your urine is pale yellow After the first 1-2 days: • Try plain potatoes, noodles, rice, bread, and other bland foods • Return to your regular diet as your diarrhea improves Avoid: • Milk and dairy products for 2-3 days • Caffeine (tea, cola, coffee) • Alcohol • Fruit juices like prune, apple, or grape juice (these can worsen diarrhea)

• Use an oral rehydration solution (such as Pedialyte) from the pharmacy or supermarket • Let your child eat a regular diet as soon as possible • If your child is vomiting, try very small, frequent sips of liquid until the vomiting stops Do NOT: • Do not use plain water or sports drinks to rehydrate your child — use oral rehydration solution instead • Do not withhold dairy products from your child • Do not give fruit juices (prune, apple, grape) — these can worsen diarrhea

• Take all medications exactly as your doctor prescribed • Anti-diarrheal medicine (like Imodium) can help adults — take as directed • Do NOT use anti-diarrheal medicine if you have a high fever, bloody diarrhea, or if your doctor told you not to • Do NOT give anti-diarrheal medicine to children unless prescribed by a doctor

• Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after using the bathroom and before eating • Do not prepare food for others while you are sick • Clean and disinfect bathroom surfaces frequently • Do not return to work or school until you have been diarrhea-free for at least 24 hours • Keep sick children home from day care
• See your own doctor in 2-3 days if you are not improving • See your doctor sooner if you are getting worse • If you were prescribed antibiotics, finish the entire course even if you feel better

• Vomiting typically follows abdominal pain in appendicitis (precedes pain in gastroenteritis) • Appendicitis: 1-2 loose stools, NOT voluminous • 15% of appendices are in atypical locations • 27% of children with appendicitis are initially misdiagnosed — diarrhea is a common confounding symptom • 57% of children under 3 with appendicitis are initially misdiagnosed • Serial abdominal exams are key — gastroenteritis improves with fluids, appendicitis does not • Gastroenteritis can cause higher fevers (>103°F) than appendicitis

• Consider in adults >50 years or with peripheral vascular disease • Severe pain out of proportion to physical findings — classic presentation • Voluminous diarrhea (small bowel ischemia) or bloody diarrhea (ischemic colitis) • Occult blood in up to 75% of patients • Risk factors: arrhythmias, CHF, hypovolemia, sepsis, vasoconstrictors (digitalis, pseudoephedrine, cocaine, amphetamines) • May progress to infarction unless detected early

• Antibiotics — especially C. difficile risk within past 3 months • Magnesium/calcium antacids • Colchicine • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol) — abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea • Sorbitol/mannitol (artificial sweeteners) — osmotic diarrhea • Laxative abuse — consider in patients with eating disorders or weight loss attempts • Enteral tube feedings • Herbal preparations may also cause diarrhea

• Melanotic stools are usually liquid — patients may describe as "diarrhea" • Always ask specifically about black or tarry stools • Rectal exam can determine stool characteristics • GI bleed requires completely different management — see GI Bleeding consult

• Fecal impaction — chronic constipation followed by watery diarrhea (overflow) • IBD first presentation — chronic/recurrent bloody diarrhea, family history, young patient • Hyperthyroidism — diarrhea as part of thyrotoxicosis • Intussusception (pediatric) — currant jelly stool, episodic crying • DKA, pneumonia — extra-abdominal conditions that can present with abdominal complaints

1. Fever >38.5°C (101.3°F) PLUS one of: • Guaiac-positive stools • Fecal leukocytes or fecal lactoferrin positive 2. Acute dysentery (bloody diarrhea with fever and cramping) 3. Moderate-to-severe traveler's diarrhea 4. Diarrhea lasting >48 hours (higher probability of non-viral cause) 5. Nosocomial diarrhea with suspected C. difficile — stop offending antibiotic, start metronidazole or vancomycin

• Suspected STEC (E. coli O157:H7) — antibiotics increase HUS risk. Suspect if: bloody diarrhea + afebrile + exposure to undercooked beef or unpasteurized products • Vomiting as prominent symptom — viral etiology more likely, antibiotics will have low yield • Mild, self-limited diarrhea in healthy patient • Salmonellosis (non-typhoidal) — antibiotics can prolong carrier state and increase relapse rate

Antibiotics shorten illness duration by 1-2 days when effective. This benefit must be weighed against drug side effects, expense, and antibiotic resistance concerns. Studies show that patient satisfaction with diarrheal illness care correlates poorly with receiving antibiotics — physicians are not adept at identifying which patients expect them.

• High fever (>38.5°C / 101.3°F) • Bloody diarrhea or suspected dysentery • Suspected inflammatory diarrhea (positive fecal leukocytes/lactoferrin) • Suspected Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC) — can worsen HUS • Sepsis or severe systemic illness • Immunocompromised patients • Pediatric patients — not recommended for children with acute gastroenteritis

• Delayed clearance of enteric pathogens • Prolonged fever in invasive bacterial diarrhea • Toxic megacolon risk — especially with C. difficile and inflammatory bowel disease • Increased HUS risk with STEC infection Some authorities argue antimotility agents may be used in non-dysenteric forms of diarrhea caused by enteroinvasive pathogens as long as antibiotics are also prescribed — but this remains controversial.

• Afebrile patients with non-bloody, non-inflammatory diarrhea • Chronic diarrhea associated with inflammatory bowel disease (with appropriate IBD treatment) • Traveler's diarrhea — loperamide as adjunct WITH antibiotics reduces duration by 1 additional day • Preferred agent: Loperamide (Imodium) — peripheral opioid, no CNS effects, not habit-forming • Alternative: Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) — also has antimicrobial and antiemetic properties

Most reliable findings: • Dry axilla — supports hypovolemia diagnosis • Moist mucous membranes + tongue without furrows — argues against hypovolemia Unreliable in adults: • Capillary refill time — no proven diagnostic value • Skin turgor — no proven diagnostic value Other indicators: • Orthostatic vital signs (SBP drop >20 or HR rise >20) • Urine output and color • BUN/Creatinine ratio >20:1 suggests dehydration • Thirst, dizziness, syncope

Gold standard: Acute body weight change (compare to recent known weight) Next best measures: • Mucous membrane hydration • Capillary refill time (>2 seconds) • Absence of tears when crying • Altered mental status (lethargy, irritability) Also assess: • Sunken anterior fontanelle (infants) • Sunken eyes • Skin turgor (tenting) • Urine output (fewer wet diapers) Severity: • Mild (3-5%): slightly dry mucous membranes, mildly decreased urine • Moderate (6-9%): dry mucous membranes, decreased tears, tachycardia, oliguria • Severe (≥10%): absent tears, sunken eyes, very delayed capillary refill, altered mental status, anuria

WHO ORS composition: • Sodium 75 mmol/L • Potassium 20 mmol/L • Glucose 75 mmol/L • Total osmolarity 245 mOsm/L Commercial options: Pedialyte, Lytren, Rehydrolyte Sports drinks (Gatorade, etc.) have inadequate sodium for diarrheal losses. Can supplement with salted crackers or pretzels. Plain water is NOT appropriate for rehydration in children — risk of hyponatremia. IV rehydration: NS or LR 20 mL/kg bolus, repeat as needed. Consider in moderate-severe dehydration or when vomiting prevents oral intake.

Preformed toxin — vomiting predominates Staphylococcus aureus • Source: Meats, dairy, cream-filled pastries left at room temperature • Onset: 1-6 hours • Duration: 24-48 hours • Key: Vomiting > diarrhea, no fever Bacillus cereus (emetic form) • Source: Fried rice, pasta left at room temperature • Onset: 1-6 hours • Duration: <24 hours • Key: "Fried rice syndrome" — vomiting predominant, self-limited

Bacillus cereus (diarrheal form) • Source: Meats, vegetables, sauces • Onset: 8-16 hours • Duration: 24-48 hours • Key: Watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, minimal vomiting Clostridium perfringens • Source: Beef, poultry, gravies kept warm for extended periods • Onset: 8-16 hours • Duration: 24-48 hours • Key: "Cafeteria germ" — watery diarrhea, cramping, rarely vomiting

Salmonella (non-typhoidal) • Source: Poultry, eggs, unpasteurized dairy, reptile contact • Onset: 12-72 hours • Duration: 4-7 days • Key: Fever, bloody diarrhea possible. NO antibiotics unless severe (prolongs carriage) Campylobacter jejuni • Source: Undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, puppies/kittens • Onset: 2-5 days • Duration: 5-7 days • Key: Most common bacterial cause of diarrhea in US. Bloody stools, high fever. Guillain-Barre risk (1:1000) STEC (E. coli O157:H7) • Source: Undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized juice/milk, contaminated produce • Onset: 3-4 days • Duration: 5-10 days • Key: Bloody diarrhea + afebrile = suspect STEC. NO ANTIBIOTICS (increases HUS risk). Watch for H

Cryptosporidium • Source: Swimming pools, lakes, contaminated drinking water • Onset: 2-10 days • Duration: 1-2 weeks (longer in immunocompromised) • Key: Chlorine-resistant. Profuse watery diarrhea, can be prolonged. Nitazoxanide for treatment. Giardia lamblia • Source: Streams, lakes ("beaver fever"), day care centers • Onset: 1-2 weeks • Duration: 2-6 weeks if untreated • Key: Foul-smelling, greasy stools, bloating, flatulence. Metronidazole or tinidazole. Norovirus • Source: Contaminated water/food, person-to-person, cruise ships • Onset: 12-48 hours • Duration: 24-72 hours • Key: Highly contagious. Vomiting + diarrhea. "Winter vomiting disease." Self-limited.

Shigella • Source: Fecal-oral (low infectious dose ~10 organisms), day care, MSM • Onset: 1-3 days • Duration: 5-7 days • Key: Dysentery (bloody mucoid stools), fever, tenesmus. Treat with azithromycin (resistance to FQ/TMP-SMX) Norovirus • Source: Cruise ships, nursing homes, schools, hospitals • Onset: 12-48 hours • Duration: 24-72 hours • Key: Explosive outbreaks. Environmental contamination persists. Supportive care only. Rotavirus • Source: Day care centers, pediatric wards • Onset: 1-3 days • Duration: 3-8 days • Key: Leading cause of severe pediatric diarrhea pre-vaccine. Watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever.

Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) • Source: Contaminated food/water in developing countries • Onset: 1-3 days • Duration: 3-5 days • Key: "Traveler's diarrhea" — watery, no blood. Treat with azithromycin or fluoroquinolone + loperamide Cyclospora cayetanensis • Source: Fresh produce (raspberries, basil) from endemic areas • Onset: 1-2 weeks • Duration: Weeks if untreated • Key: Relapsing/remitting watery diarrhea. Treat with TMP-SMX. Entamoeba histolytica • Source: Endemic areas (Mexico, Central/South America, South Asia) • Onset: 2-4 weeks • Duration: Weeks to months • Key: Bloody diarrhea, "anchovy paste" liver abscess. Treat with metronidazole + paromomycin.

Clostridioides difficile • Source: Hospital/nursing home, recent antibiotics (especially clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins) • Onset: Days to weeks after antibiotic exposure • Duration: Variable, can recur • Key: Watery diarrhea (rarely bloody), fever, leukocytosis. Stop offending antibiotic. Treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Risk factors: Recent hospitalization, PPI use, age >65, immunosuppression, inflammatory bowel disease

Additional pathogens to consider: • Cryptosporidium — severe, prolonged, can be fatal in AIDS • Microsporidia — chronic diarrhea, wasting • Isospora belli — watery diarrhea, treat with TMP-SMX • CMV colitis — bloody diarrhea, fever, treat with ganciclovir • MAC (Mycobacterium avium complex) — chronic diarrhea, weight loss, when CD4 <50 Always check CD4 count in HIV patients with diarrhea
• Pregnancy test in ALL reproductive-age women with abdominal pain/bleeding • Hemodynamic stability assessment • Unstable → assume ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise
• Bedside US + quantitative beta-hCG • IUP confirmed → rules out ectopic (except ART patients) • Pregnancy of unknown location → 48h beta-hCG recheck • Ectopic confirmed → methotrexate vs surgery
• Classify type: threatened, complete, missed, inevitable, incomplete, septic • Nonviable → expectant vs medical (misoprostol) vs surgical (D&C) • Rh status → consider RhoGAM if Rh-negative

• Severity assessment — tolerating PO? • Mild: pyridoxine ± doxylamine (ACOG first-line) • Moderate: add dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine, or promethazine • Severe/IV: metoclopramide or ondansetron + D5NS + thiamine • Hyperemesis gravidarum → OB consult, admit
• UTI / bacteriuria — MUST treat in pregnancy • Pyelonephritis — admit ALL for IV ceftriaxone • Appendicitis — surgical, imaging: US → MRI → CT

• PUL → discharge with 48h beta-hCG recheck • Miscarriage → discharge with management plan + grief resources • NVP → discharge with prescriptions if tolerating PO • Admit: ruptured ectopic, pyelonephritis, appendicitis, hyperemesis, septic abortion

98% of ectopic pregnancies are tubal • Distal third (ampullary): most common (~40%) • Middle third (isthmic): ~37% • Proximal third: ~12% • Fimbrial: ~5% • Fimbrial-ovarian: ~1.5% • Interstitial (cornual): ~1.2% — high rupture morbidity due to increased vascularity • Abdominal: ~1.4% • Cervical: ~0.15% • Ovarian: ~0.15%

• Prior ectopic pregnancy — strongest predictor of recurrence • History of salpingitis / PID — tubal damage • History of sexually transmitted infections — chlamydia, gonorrhea • Prior tubal surgery — sterilization, reversal, salpingostomy • Smoking — dose-response relationship (>1 pack/day: OR 4) — ciliary dysmotility impairs ovum transport • IUD in situ — if pregnancy occurs despite IUD, >50% are ectopic • Assisted reproductive technology (ART) — also increases heterotopic risk to 1 in 100 • DES exposure in utero • Endometriosis

Nearly half of patients with ectopic pregnancy will have NO identifiable risk factors. Presence or absence of risk factors should NOT alter the standard diagnostic approach. No historical or physical exam features can reliably rule in or rule out ectopic pregnancy.

Coexistence of IUP + ectopic pregnancy: • General population: 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 30,000 • ART patients: ~1 in 100 Confirming an IUP does NOT exclude ectopic in ART patients. Maintain clinical suspicion if IUP + lateral pain/adnexal mass.

100% specific (any of these = ectopic confirmed): • Extrauterine gestational sac with yolk sac • Extrauterine embryo (with or without cardiac activity) These are RARE findings. Most ectopics show indirect signs only.

Hyperechoic ring surrounding a small anechoic center in the adnexa, separate from the ovary. • Specificity: 88-95% for ectopic pregnancy • Represents the echogenic trophoblastic tissue surrounding the gestational sac • Must distinguish from corpus luteum cyst (CL is ON the ovary, tubal ring is SEPARATE) Pearl: Slide the probe to confirm the mass moves independently from the ovary.

Any adnexal mass separate from the ovary raises suspicion for ectopic: • Complex mass (cystic + solid) — most common finding • Blob sign — inhomogeneous adnexal mass without clear ring structure • Hyperechoic mass — may represent hematosalpinx or clot Probe tenderness: Pain when pressing adnexal mass with transvaginal probe strongly suggests ectopic.

Echogenic (complex) free fluid in cul-de-sac suggests hemoperitoneum: • Simple anechoic fluid — physiologic or hemorrhagic (less specific) • Echogenic fluid with debris — blood/clot, highly suspicious • Moderate-to-large volume + no IUP → assume ruptured ectopic FAST exam: In unstable patient, any free fluid + positive pregnancy test = OR for presumed ruptured ectopic.

Intrauterine fluid collection WITHOUT the double decidual sign or yolk sac: • Present in 10-20% of ectopic pregnancies • Represents decidual reaction to ectopic pregnancy hormones • Differentiating features: - Pseudosac: centrally located, single layer, no double ring - True IUP: eccentric, double decidual sign, yolk sac visible by 5.5 weeks Pearl: If unsure whether IUP or pseudosac, do NOT reassure patient. Treat as PUL with close follow-up.

Multiple findings increase diagnostic certainty: • Adnexal mass + free fluid + no IUP → PPV 97% for ectopic • Tubal ring sign + free fluid → very high specificity • Even small free fluid with adnexal mass significantly raises ectopic probability Clinical decision: High-risk US findings warrant urgent OB consultation even if beta-hCG is low. DO NOT discharge without definitive plan.

Absent findings do NOT rule out ectopic: • No adnexal mass visible — small ectopics are often not visualized • No free fluid — unruptured ectopics have no hemoperitoneum • Normal-appearing uterus — expected in early ectopic Key point: "Normal" ultrasound + positive pregnancy test + no IUP = Pregnancy of Unknown Location. Requires serial beta-hCG monitoring.

Cervical os: Closed Ultrasound: Viable IUP (fetal cardiac activity present) Presentation: Vaginal bleeding with viable pregnancy Prognosis: If FCA present, only 3.4% progress to miscarriage. Heavy bleeding → 11-18% miscarriage rate.
Cervical os: Closed Ultrasound: No IUP (previously confirmed) Presentation: Passage of all products of conception Management: Confirm with US. Serial beta-hCG to zero. OB follow-up.

Cervical os: Closed Ultrasound: CRL ≥7 mm without cardiac motion; OR gestational sac ≥25 mm without embryo Presentation: Nonviable uterine gestation — often discovered incidentally Management: Expectant, medical (misoprostol), or surgical (D&C)
Cervical os: Open Ultrasound: IUP present, no passage of products yet Presentation: Open os indicates process will proceed Management: Expectant, medical, or surgical — consult OB

Cervical os: Open Ultrasound: Partially expelled products of conception Presentation: Some tissue has passed, but retained products remain Management: If tissue visible in cervix — remove with ring forceps at bedside. Medical or surgical management for retained products.

Cervical os: Any (open or closed) Ultrasound: Any finding possible Presentation: Intrauterine infection — fever, uterine tenderness, purulent discharge Management: EMERGENT — IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + surgical evacuation. May progress rapidly to sepsis/septic shock.

Pyridoxine (B6) 10-25 mg PO TID ± Doxylamine 12.5 mg PO TID Adjuncts: • Ginger 250 mg PO QID • P6 acupressure wristband • Convert prenatal vitamin to folic acid only 💊 Generic pyridoxine + OTC doxylamine (Unisom SleepTabs) is significantly cheaper than Diclegis/Bonjesta.
Add one of: • Dimenhydrinate 50 mg PO QID (max 200 mg/day if taking doxylamine) • Diphenhydramine 25-50 mg PO QID • Prochlorperazine 25 mg PR q12h • Promethazine 12.5 mg PO or PR q6h

Rehydration: D5NS preferred (slightly better than NS for nausea) Thiamine 100 mg IV before dextrose if protracted vomiting IV antiemetics — choose one: • Metoclopramide 10 mg IV q8h — preferred (no fetal malformation risk) • Ondansetron 4-8 mg IV over 15 min q12h — effective but exhaust other options first • Dimenhydrinate 50 mg IV in 50 mL NS over 20 min q6h • Promethazine 12.5 mg IV q6h (dilute, slow push — tissue necrosis risk)

If no improvement after IV therapy: • OB consultation • Admit for continued IV rehydration • Electrolyte monitoring • Daily thiamine • Parenteral antiemetic regimen • Nutritional assessment Definition: ≥5% loss of prepregnancy body weight + persistent nausea/vomiting + ketonuria

• No high-quality evidence supports one specific drug over another for NVP • Pyridoxine + doxylamine is superior to pyridoxine alone • Ondansetron: possible small risk of fetal cardiac abnormalities — use after exhausting alternatives • Metoclopramide: no association with fetal malformations — reasonable first-line IV agent • NVP is actually protective against pregnancy loss (HR 0.20 for nausea + vomiting)

• Do not withhold indicated imaging for fear of radiation — missed/delayed diagnosis may cause worse fetal outcomes • Ultrasound and MRI (without gadolinium) are preferred first-line modalities • Single CT study does not exceed threshold dose for fetal harm • Document risks/benefits discussion with patient for studies involving direct fetal radiation
These produce negligible fetal exposure: • Head or neck imaging (any modality) • Extremity radiography or CT (except possibly hip) • Chest radiography (first and second trimesters)

Very low (<0.1 mGy): • C-spine XR: <0.001 mGy • Extremity XR: <0.001 mGy • Chest XR (2 views): 0.0005-0.01 mGy Low to moderate (0.1-10 mGy): • Abdominal XR: 0.1-3.0 mGy • Chest CT / CTPA: 0.01-0.66 mGy • Head/neck CT: 1.0-10 mGy • Bone scan: 4-5 mGy Higher (10-50 mGy): • Abdominal CT: 1.3-35 mGy • Pelvic CT: 10-50 mGy Reference: Annual background radiation = 1.1-2.5 mGy

Iodinated contrast (CT): • Crosses placenta but no known harm in limited data • ACOG: use only if "absolutely required" — precautionary, not evidence-based Gadolinium (MRI): • AVOID unless absolutely necessary • Associated with increased stillbirth, neonatal death, and rheumatologic/inflammatory skin conditions • MRI for appendicitis should always be ordered WITHOUT contrast MRI without gadolinium is safe — no fetal risk demonstrated through age 4 years in >1.4 million pregnancies

1. Ultrasound first — but visualization rate as low as 7%, sensitivity only 18% in pregnancy 2. MRI without contrast — sensitivity 94%, specificity 97%. Preferred if available. 3. CT abdomen/pelvis — if US indeterminate and MRI unavailable. High sensitivity/specificity. Single study does not exceed threshold. Both US and MRI have high specificity (97-99%) — a positive result can be relied upon.

• Amoxicillin — first-line for UTI in pregnancy • Cephalosporins (cephalexin, ceftriaxone, cefazolin) — widely used, well-studied • Penicillins — extensive safety record • Azithromycin — safe for atypical coverage

info.h: Use with Caution in First Trimester
info.t: • Nitrofurantoin — ACOG 2017: safe in 2nd/3rd trimester but use in 1st trimester only "when no other suitable alternative antibiotics are available" • Sulfonamides (TMP-SMX) — same ACOG caveat as nitrofurantoin. Theoretical risk of folate antagonism.

• Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — cartilage damage in animal studies; avoid if alternatives exist • Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) — tooth discoloration and bone growth effects after first trimester • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) — ototoxicity risk; use only when benefits clearly outweigh risks (e.g., septic abortion) • Metronidazole — generally avoided in first trimester (conflicting data, likely safe but alternatives preferred)

Preferred regimens (7-day course): • Amoxicillin 875 mg PO BID • Cephalexin 500 mg PO q6h • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID (if no alternatives — 1st trimester only) Key points: • ALWAYS send urine culture — negative UA does not exclude bacteriuria • Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria when found — reduces pyelonephritis risk from 2.4% to 0.6% • Shorter courses may be less effective than 7-day regimens • Local antibiograms should guide empiric therapy

Admit ALL pregnant patients for initial IV antibiotics: • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily • Continue until afebrile 48 hours • Transition to oral agent guided by sensitivities Insufficient evidence for outpatient management in pregnancy.

You have experienced a miscarriage (also called early pregnancy loss). This is unfortunately common — it occurs in up to 1 in 4 pregnancies. Most miscarriages are caused by genetic abnormalities in the pregnancy and are not caused by anything you did or did not do.

• Bleeding: You may have vaginal bleeding and cramping for 1-2 weeks. This is normal. • Pain: Cramping is expected. Take ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) 600 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. • Passing tissue: You may pass blood clots or tissue. This is part of the natural process. • Bleeding should gradually decrease over the next 1-2 weeks.

• Rest as needed — there is no strict bed rest requirement • Avoid placing anything in the vagina (tampons, douching, intercourse) for 2 weeks or until bleeding stops • Hydrate well and eat as tolerated • You may shower and bathe normally

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department If
info.t: • Heavy bleeding — soaking more than 1 pad per hour for 2 or more hours in a row • Fever greater than 100.4°F (38°C) • Foul-smelling vaginal discharge • Severe abdominal pain not relieved by ibuprofen • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting • Persistent heavy bleeding beyond 2 weeks

• See your OB/GYN within 1-2 weeks • Your doctor may check a blood test (beta-hCG) to confirm the miscarriage is complete • Discuss future pregnancy planning with your OB/GYN when you are ready • Most women who have a miscarriage go on to have healthy pregnancies in the future

• A miscarriage is a loss, and it is normal to grieve • Everyone experiences grief differently — there is no "right way" to feel • Talk to your partner, family, or a trusted friend • Your doctor can refer you to a grief counselor or pregnancy loss support group • National support: Share Pregnancy & Infant Loss Support — www.nationalshare.org
• Determine HIV status — CD4 count, viral load, current ART regimen • Route to appropriate pathway based on immune status and presentation

• Recognize acute retroviral syndrome: fever + rash + lymphadenopathy + NO respiratory symptoms • 4th generation Ag/Ab test (2-week window period) • Send HIV RNA viral load if 4th gen negative but clinical suspicion remains high • Never rely on antibody-only test in the acute setting

• Treat like immunocompetent patient for most acute complaints • Watch for chronic inflammatory complications (CAD, COPD, osteoporosis) • Screen for ARV medication side effects and drug interactions • Verify ART adherence and recent viral load

• High risk for opportunistic infections — low threshold for imaging and admission • PJP (CD4 <200): dyspnea, dry cough, bilateral GGOs, elevated LDH • Toxoplasmosis (CD4 <100): ring-enhancing lesions, focal neuro deficits • Cryptococcal meningitis (CD4 <100): headache, altered mental status, elevated opening pressure • CMV (CD4 <50): retinitis, colitis, esophagitis • TB: any CD4 — atypical presentations with low CD4

• Know ARV drug classes and their signature toxicities • NRTI: TDF → Fanconi syndrome, renal tubular acidosis, bone loss • NNRTI: efavirenz → neuropsychiatric effects, vivid dreams, SJS • PI: atazanavir → jaundice, radiolucent kidney stones, CYP3A4 drug interactions • INSTI: generally well-tolerated, fewest interactions
• PEP: post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours of exposure • PrEP: refer high-risk patients for pre-exposure prophylaxis • Document exposure time, source HIV status, and risk level

• Fever — present in 80–90% of cases, often high-grade • Sore throat — pharyngitis WITHOUT exudate (unlike strep or EBV) • Macular rash — erythematous, non-pruritic; face, trunk, and upper extremities; appears day 2–3 of illness • Lymphadenopathy — diffuse, non-tender, symmetric • Mucocutaneous ulcers — oral and/or genital; shallow, painful • Myalgia / arthralgia — widespread, non-specific • Headache — may be severe; consider aseptic meningitis if meningismus present • Weight loss / diarrhea — in some cases

• NO respiratory symptoms — absence of cough, rhinorrhea, and congestion distinguishes ARS from influenza and URI • NO exudative pharyngitis — unlike strep and mononucleosis • Mucocutaneous ulcers — highly specific; rare in other viral syndromes • Rash + fever + lymphadenopathy + sore throat without respiratory symptoms should trigger HIV testing • Ask about sexual exposure or needle sharing in the preceding 2–6 weeks

• Lymphopenia initially (transient CD4 drop), followed by lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes • Thrombocytopenia — mild, self-limited • Elevated transaminases — hepatitis in 20–50% of cases • Elevated ESR/CRP — non-specific but supports viral syndrome

• 4th generation Ag/Ab test (preferred) — detects p24 antigen + HIV-1/2 antibodies; window period ~2 weeks • If 4th gen negative but clinical suspicion high — send HIV RNA viral load (detectable within 10–12 days of infection) • Never rely on antibody-only (3rd gen) test alone — window period 3–4 weeks; will miss acute seroconversion • Rapid point-of-care tests are antibody-only — useful for screening but CANNOT rule out acute infection • If ARS confirmed: refer for immediate ART initiation (reduces reservoir size and transmission risk)

• Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — exudative pharyngitis, splenomegaly, positive heterophile • Influenza — respiratory symptoms predominate • Secondary syphilis — palmar rash, condylomata lata, positive RPR • Strep pharyngitis — exudate, anterior cervical LAD, positive rapid strep • CMV mononucleosis — heterophile-negative, less pharyngitis • Drug reaction — medication exposure history

• Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) — Fanconi syndrome (proximal renal tubular acidosis, glycosuria, phosphaturia, proteinuria), decreased bone mineral density • Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) — less renal and bone toxicity than TDF; preferred in renal impairment • Abacavir (ABC) — HLA-B*5701 hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, GI symptoms — can be fatal on rechallenge); associated with increased MI risk in some studies • Lamivudine (3TC) / Emtricitabine (FTC) — well-tolerated; active against hepatitis B (HBV flare risk if discontinued in co-infected patients) • Zidovudine (AZT) — macrocytic anemia, neutropenia, myopathy (legacy drug, rarely used) • Class effect: lactic acidosis with hepa

• Efavirenz (EFV) — neuropsychiatric effects (vivid dreams, depression, psychosis, suicidality), dizziness, Stevens-Johnson syndrome • Nevirapine (NVP) — severe hepatotoxicity (fulminant hepatitis, especially in women with CD4 >250 or men with CD4 >400), SJS/TEN • Doravirine (DOR) — fewer CNS side effects than efavirenz; better tolerated • Rilpivirine (RPV) — requires food and gastric acid for absorption; avoid PPIs (reduced efficacy) • Class effect: rash (usually mild, self-limited); low barrier to resistance

• Atazanavir (ATV) — indirect hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice without hepatotoxicity), radiolucent kidney stones (invisible on plain film, visible on CT), cholelithiasis, nephrolithiasis • Darunavir (DRV) — rash (contains sulfonamide moiety), GI intolerance; requires pharmacokinetic booster • Ritonavir / Cobicistat — used as pharmacokinetic boosters (not for antiviral effect); potent CYP3A4 inhibitors causing major drug interactions • Critical interactions: Contraindicated with simvastatin, lovastatin, ergot alkaloids, oral midazolam, triazolam, rifampin, St. John’s wort. Significant interactions with calcium channel blockers, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, immunosuppressants. • Class ef

• Bictegravir (BIC) — available only as co-formulated Biktarvy (BIC/TAF/FTC); well-tolerated, high barrier to resistance • Dolutegravir (DTG) — neural tube defect concern in periconception period (risk ~0.3%); insomnia, weight gain; rare hypersensitivity • Raltegravir (RAL) — fewest drug interactions of any ARV class; CK elevation, myopathy (rare) • Elvitegravir (EVG) — requires cobicistat boosting (carries CYP3A4 interaction liability) • Class effect: generally the best-tolerated ARV class; weight gain (especially with DTG); insomnia and headache

• Enfuvirtide (T-20) — subcutaneous injection-site reactions (nearly universal); used only in heavily treatment-experienced patients • Maraviroc (MVC) — CCR5 antagonist; hepatotoxicity (with allergic features), postural hypotension; requires tropism testing before use • Ibalizumab (IBA) — monoclonal antibody; IV infusion; hypersensitivity reactions; reserved for multidrug-resistant HIV • Fostemsavir (FTR) — attachment inhibitor; QTc prolongation; reserved for multidrug-resistant HIV • Lenacapavir — first-in-class capsid inhibitor; subcutaneous q6 months; injection-site reactions

• Do not stop ART in the ED unless directed by HIV specialist — interruptions promote resistance • Check drug interactions before prescribing any new medication to a patient on ART (especially PIs and cobicistat-boosted regimens) • Radiolucent stones: if patient on atazanavir presents with renal colic and negative plain film, order CT • Lactic acidosis: consider in any HIV patient with unexplained metabolic acidosis, especially on older NRTIs • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS): paradoxical worsening within weeks of ART initiation — unmasking of latent OIs

• CDC (2006): Opt-out HIV screening for all patients aged 13–64 in healthcare settings, including EDs; repeat at least annually for high-risk patients • USPSTF (2019): Grade A recommendation for screening all adolescents and adults aged 15–65; younger and older if at increased risk • ACEP (2022): Supports routine opt-out ED-based HIV screening as a public health strategy • Separate written consent is NOT required in most states — general medical consent covers HIV testing • Pre-test counseling requirements have been eliminated in most jurisdictions to reduce barriers

• Men who have sex with men (MSM) • Injection drug use (IDU) or needle sharing • Transactional sex or sex work • Sexual contact with known HIV-positive partner • Diagnosis of another sexually transmitted infection • Diagnosis of tuberculosis or hepatitis B/C • Occupational exposure (needlestick, mucous membrane splash) • Sexual assault • Pregnancy (all trimesters — opt-out) • Patients requesting PEP or PrEP • Incarcerated populations • Homeless individuals

• 4th generation Ag/Ab combination immunoassay (preferred) — Detects HIV-1 p24 antigen + HIV-1/2 antibodies simultaneously — Window period: ~2 weeks (14–18 days) — Sensitivity 99.7%, specificity 99.5% — Laboratory-based; turnaround time typically 1–2 hours • 3rd generation antibody-only immunoassay — Detects HIV-1/2 antibodies (IgM and IgG) — Window period: 3–4 weeks (21–28 days) — Will MISS acute seroconversion during the window period • Rapid point-of-care tests (e.g., OraQuick, INSTI) — Antibody-only (most are 3rd generation equivalent) — Results in 1–20 minutes — Useful for screening but CANNOT rule out acute HIV infection — All reactive rapid tests require confirmatory laboratory testin

• HIV RNA (NAAT): 10–12 days • 4th gen Ag/Ab: 14–18 days (p24 antigen appears first) • 3rd gen Ab-only: 21–28 days • Rapid POC tests: 21–90 days (depending on test) • Self-test (OraQuick Home): ~90 days A negative test within the window period does NOT exclude infection. Counsel patients with recent high-risk exposure to retest at appropriate intervals.

CSF Lactate: Independent of serum level (crosses BBB slowly). >35.1 mg/dL strongly favors bacterial cause. Particularly useful in healthcare-associated infections where postoperative inflammation alters conventional markers. CSF PCR: Detects bacterial DNA even days after antibiotics (87–100% sensitive, 98–100% specific). Gold standard for viral pathogen identification. Serum PCT: >0.25–0.5 ng/mL has 90–95% sensitivity, 98–100% specificity for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis. More sensitive than any CSF marker for this purpose.

CT is NOT sensitive for detecting meningitis or encephalitis. Its purpose is to exclude mass lesions that could cause herniation with LP. Most patients do NOT need CT before LP. Herniation after LP is rare: only 0.1% of patients deteriorated within 1 hour of LP. Of those who deteriorated, 91% had a prior normal CT.
