Why: Reticulocytes are immature red blood cells. The retic count tells you if the bone marrow is working. Normal response to anemia: Reticulocyte count should be ELEVATED (bone marrow compensating for hemolysis). LOW reticulocyte count (<1%) with anemia = APLASTIC CRISIS • Usually caused by Parvovirus B19 infection • Bone marrow suppressed — patient cannot make new RBCs • Self-limited (7–10 days) but may need transfusion In summary: • High retic + low Hgb = hemolysis (expected in SCD) • Low retic + low Hgb = aplastic crisis (Parvovirus B19) • Low retic + dropping Hgb = CRITICAL — patient cannot compensate

Why: Assess renal function, electrolytes, and hemolysis markers. • Creatinine/BUN: SCD nephropathy is common; baseline renal function important for medication dosing • Bilirubin (indirect): Elevated in hemolysis — helps confirm ongoing hemolytic crisis • LDH: Another hemolysis marker; very elevated in acute hemolytic crisis • Electrolytes: K+ may be elevated with hemolysis; Na+ for hydration status

Why: SCD patients require EXTENDED antigen-matched blood (C, E, Kell negative) due to alloimmunization risk. • Type and screen early if ANY chance of transfusion • Blood bank needs extra time to find compatible units • 30% of chronically transfused SCD patients develop alloantibodies • Standard uncrossmatched blood can cause severe hemolytic transfusion reactions

Why: Determines current HbS percentage — guides transfusion targets. • Target HbS <30% for stroke, severe ACS • Helps differentiate SCD genotypes • Tracks response to chronic transfusion therapy • Important for patients who have had recent transfusions

Why: SCD patients have functional asplenia — cannot clear encapsulated organisms. • ALWAYS obtain before antibiotics in febrile SCD patient • S. pneumoniae most common pathogen • A positive viral test does NOT exclude bacteremia in SCD • Historical bacteremia risk was 15–20%; now ~1% with vaccines + penicillin prophylaxis

Exercise Collapse Associated with Sickle Cell Trait • Associated with competitive athletics and military training • 28× increased risk of exercise-related death (Kark 1987) • Metabolic crisis: dehydration + acidosis + hypoxia + hyperthermia → sickling Progression: Extremity pain → rhabdomyolysis → AKI → AMS → shock → arrhythmias → DIC Management: • STOP exercise immediately • Cool the patient • Aggressive IV fluids (target UO 200–300 mL/hr) • Continuous cardiac monitoring • Serial: BMP, CK, blood gas, coagulation studies Note: 2016 study of ~48,000 Black US Army soldiers found mortality similar to those without SCT when risk mitigation employed.

Most common cause of hematuria in SCT. • Painless gross hematuria • Microinfarctions in renal medulla — hypoxic, acidotic environment of vasa recta promotes sickling Workup: UA, urine culture, BMP, renal ultrasound with bladder Management: • Mild: outpatient — bed rest, oral hydration, urine alkalinization • Severe: inpatient — desmopressin infusion, ureteroscopic tamponade, or epsilon aminocaproic acid

Rare but highly aggressive malignancy. • Almost exclusively in SCT carriers • Predominantly young adults • Median survival: 15 weeks (usually disseminated at diagnosis) Red Flag: Flank pain + hematuria in SCT patient → CT urography to evaluate Do not assume hematuria is benign renal papillary necrosis if flank pain is present.

• Hyposthenuria — inability to concentrate urine → chronic dehydration risk. Counsel on increased fluid intake. • Splenic infarction at altitude — can occur at >8,000 feet; presents with LUQ pain • Exertional rhabdomyolysis — even without full ECAST, can develop isolated rhabdomyolysis during intense exercise Prevention Counseling: • Gradual acclimatization to altitude and heat • Adequate hydration before, during, and after exercise • Avoid extreme exertion without preparation • Routine physical activity IS safe and beneficial

You were evaluated in the emergency department for syncope (fainting) — a temporary loss of consciousness caused by a brief drop in blood flow to the brain. Based on your evaluation, including your history, physical exam, and heart tracing (ECG), your fainting episode appears to be low risk.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Fainting again, especially during exercise or while lying down • Chest pain or pressure • Rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations) • Shortness of breath • Sudden severe headache • Weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking • Fainting without any warning signs beforehand

Avoid known triggers: • Prolonged standing in hot environments • Dehydration — drink plenty of fluids daily • Skipping meals • Sudden position changes — sit up slowly, pause before standing If you feel faint (warning signs like lightheadedness, sweating, nausea): • Sit or lie down immediately • Cross your legs and squeeze your thigh muscles • Grip your hands together tightly • These "counterpressure" maneuvers can prevent fainting General health: • Increase fluid and salt intake (unless your doctor has restricted salt) • Avoid alcohol and excessive caffeine • Take all medications as prescribed

• See your primary care doctor within 1–2 weeks • Bring a list of all your medications to your appointment • If fainting happens again, try to note what you were doing, how you felt before, and how long it lasted • Your doctor may recommend additional heart monitoring or testing

After a fainting episode, you should not drive until you have been evaluated by your doctor. Some states have specific laws about driving after syncope. Ask your doctor when it is safe to drive again, especially if you drive for work.

• Most fainting episodes are not dangerous and do not indicate a serious heart problem • About 1 in 10 people who faint will faint again within 6 months • Avoiding triggers and staying hydrated are the best ways to prevent future episodes • If you have a history of heart disease, follow up with your cardiologist
You were treated in the emergency department for a burn injury. Your burn has been cleaned, treated, and bandaged. Follow these instructions to help your burn heal properly and prevent infection.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Increasing redness spreading away from the burn • Pus or foul-smelling drainage from the wound • Fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C) • Increasing pain not controlled by your medication • Numbness or tingling near the burn • Burns on the face, hands, feet, or genitals that worsen

Daily dressing changes: • Wash your hands before and after touching the wound • Gently remove the old dressing • Clean the wound with mild soap and water • Pat dry with a clean towel • Apply prescribed ointment and a fresh sterile non-stick dressing • Secure with medical tape or wrap Pain management: • Take pain medication 30 minutes before dressing changes • Cool water (not ice) can help with pain • Keep the burned area elevated when possible

• Partial-thickness (second-degree) burns typically heal in 1–3 weeks • Do NOT pop blisters — they protect healing skin • Do NOT pick at peeling or healing skin • Minimize friction on the healing area • Protect healed skin from sun exposure for at least 1 year (use SPF 30+)

• Return to your doctor or burn clinic in 3–5 days for a wound check • Return sooner if you notice any signs of infection • If your burn is not healing after 2 weeks, you may need a referral to a burn specialist • Once healed, ask about scar prevention options
You had a chest tube placed to treat a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) or fluid around your lung. The tube has been removed and your lung is re-expanded on x-ray.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Sudden chest pain or worsening shortness of breath • Difficulty breathing or feeling like you cannot get enough air • Rapid heartbeat • Dizziness or lightheadedness • Fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C) • Redness, swelling, or drainage from the tube site

• Keep the dressing clean and dry for 48 hours • After 48 hours, remove the dressing and gently clean with soap and water • Apply a clean bandage until the site is fully healed • Do not submerge in water (no baths, pools, or hot tubs) until healed

• No heavy lifting or straining for 1–2 weeks • No air travel until cleared by your doctor (minimum 2 weeks) • No scuba diving until cleared by a lung specialist • Gradually return to normal activities as tolerated • Avoid contact sports until cleared by your doctor

• Follow-up chest x-ray in 2–4 weeks to confirm your lung remains fully expanded • See a lung specialist (pulmonologist) if your doctor recommends it • If you smoke: This is the most important time to quit — smoking greatly increases the risk of another collapsed lung

• A collapsed lung can happen again — about 30% chance within the first year • Seek immediate care if you develop sudden chest pain or shortness of breath in the future • Tall, thin individuals and smokers are at higher risk for recurrence

You were treated in the emergency department for a broken wrist (distal radius fracture). Your wrist has been set and placed in a splint or cast to hold the bones in the correct position while they heal.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: These could be signs of a serious complication (compartment syndrome): • Increasing pain that is not relieved by elevation and medication • Numbness, tingling, or loss of feeling in your fingers • Inability to move your fingers • Fingers turning blue, white, or cold • The cast or splint feels too tight

First 48 hours are most important: • Elevate — keep your hand above the level of your heart as much as possible • Ice — apply ice over the cast padding for 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off • Finger exercises — wiggle and bend your fingers frequently to prevent stiffness • Check circulation — make sure your fingers stay pink, warm, and have normal feeling Cast/splint care: • Keep the cast or splint dry • Do not stick anything inside the cast to scratch • Do not remove or modify the splint yourself

• See an orthopedic doctor (bone specialist) in 5–7 days for repeat x-rays • X-rays in the first 2 weeks are important to make sure the bones stay aligned • Bring your discharge paperwork and x-ray images to the appointment • Cast duration is typically 4–6 weeks for adults, 3–4 weeks for children

• Take pain medication as prescribed — staying ahead of pain helps recovery • Do not drive while in a cast or splint on your dominant hand • Avoid using the injured arm for lifting or carrying • Physical therapy may be recommended after the cast is removed

You were evaluated in the emergency department. Your HIV-related concern has been addressed and you are being discharged home. It is very important that you continue your medications and follow up with your HIV care provider.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Fever above 100.4°F (38°C) that does not go away • New confusion, severe headache, or vision changes • Difficulty breathing or worsening cough • Inability to keep food or medications down for more than 24 hours • New rash that is spreading or blistering • Severe abdominal pain or bloody diarrhea

Do NOT stop your HIV medications unless your doctor tells you to. Stopping medications can cause the virus to become harder to treat. • Take all medications exactly as prescribed • If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember (unless it is almost time for your next dose) • Tell your doctor about ALL other medications, vitamins, and supplements you take • If you are having side effects, talk to your HIV provider before making changes

• See your HIV care provider within 1–2 weeks (or sooner if directed) • If you do not have an HIV provider, ask the ED staff for a referral • Keep all lab appointments — regular blood work monitors your treatment • If you were started on PEP, follow up in 3–7 days

• Consistent medication use is the single most important thing you can do for your health • When HIV is well-controlled (undetectable viral load), you cannot transmit HIV to sexual partners • Stay up to date on vaccinations — ask your provider about flu, pneumonia, and hepatitis vaccines • Seek care promptly for any new symptoms — do not wait for your next scheduled appointment

You were evaluated for meningitis (inflammation of the lining around the brain and spinal cord). Based on your test results, your meningitis appears to be caused by a virus. Viral meningitis is usually much less serious than bacterial meningitis and typically gets better on its own within 7–10 days.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Worsening headache that is not relieved by medication • Fever above 101.3°F (38.5°C) or fever that returns after improving • Confusion, unusual behavior, or difficulty staying awake • Seizures or jerking movements • Stiff neck that is getting worse • Vomiting that prevents you from keeping down fluids or medications • Rash — especially one that does not fade when you press on it • Sensitivity to light that is worsening

• Rest in a quiet, dimly lit room • Drink plenty of fluids to stay hydrated • Take over-the-counter pain relievers (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for headache and fever • You may feel fatigued for several weeks — this is normal • Viral meningitis can be mildly contagious — wash hands frequently and avoid close contact for the first few days

• See your primary care doctor within 3 days for reassessment • If your spinal fluid test results are still pending, your doctor will contact you • If symptoms are not improving after 1 week, follow up sooner

• Most people with viral meningitis recover completely • Recovery can take 1–2 weeks, sometimes longer for fatigue • If any warning signs develop, do not wait for your follow-up — go to the emergency department immediately

• Screen for persistent abnormal vital signs, neuro deficit, chest pain, abdominal pain, hemorrhage • Any positive finding → evaluate for specific life-threatening etiology • Syncope is a diagnosis of exclusion when red flags present

• Differentiate based on postictal state, tongue laceration, movement pattern, and prodrome • Myoclonic jerks are common in syncope — do not assume seizure • Serum lactate within 2 hours aids differentiation (LR+ 5.8)
• Obtain 12-lead ECG and place on telemetry • Review for conduction disease, ischemia, prolonged QTc, Brugada, HCM • 50% of arrhythmic causes detected within 2 hours (low-risk)
• Assess triggers, prodrome, position, duration, cardiac history, medications, family history • History is the single most important tool • Classic vasovagal or situational → low risk
• Neurally mediated (reflex) — most common, benign prognosis • Orthostatic hypotension — medication-related ~40% • Cardiac syncope — highest morbidity
• Apply CSRS or SFSR for unexplained syncope • High risk → admit to monitored bed • Intermediate → observation vs. outpatient with close follow-up • Low risk → discharge with reassurance

Neurally Mediated (Reflex) • Vasovagal — pain, emotions, blood, medical procedures • Situational — Valsalva, post-exercise, coughing, swallowing, defecation • Carotid sinus — head-turning, shaving (age >40) Orthostatic Hypotension • Drug-induced (most common cause) • Volume depletion • Autonomic failure (diabetes, Parkinson, MSA) Cardiac • Arrhythmia — bradycardia, tachycardia, channelopathies • Structural — aortic stenosis, HCM, PE, aortic dissection, tamponade

info.h: Life-Threatening Conditions That Present with TLOC
info.t: • Subarachnoid hemorrhage — thunderclap headache, neuro deficit • Pulmonary embolism — dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, recent surgery/immobilization • Aortic dissection — tearing chest/back pain, BP differential between arms • Ruptured AAA — abdominal/back pain, pulsatile mass, hypotension • Acute MI — chest pain, ST changes, elevated troponin • Tension pneumothorax — unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension • Ectopic pregnancy — abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, positive βhCG • GI hemorrhage — melena, hematemesis, rectal bleeding • Cardiac tamponade — JVD, muffled heart sounds, hypotension • High-grade AV block — persistent bradycardia, syncope without warning

• Seizure — postictal confusion >few seconds, tongue laceration, rhythmic jerks >20 • Psychogenic pseudosyncope — prolonged duration, eyes closed, no injury, psychiatric history • Hypoglycemia — diabetic medications, altered mentation, rarely resolves spontaneously • Posterior circulation TIA — vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia (rare cause of TLOC) • Toxicologic — overdose, poisoning (uncommonly resolves spontaneously) • Metabolic — severe electrolyte derangement, hypoxia

Seizure vs. Syncope: • Postictal disorientation >few seconds → seizure • Prodrome (lightheadedness, diaphoresis) → syncope • Tongue laceration → seizure • <10 jerks → syncope; >20 jerks → seizure • Urinary incontinence → does NOT differentiate • Serum lactate within 2h: elevated → seizure (LR+ 5.8) 45% of unexplained syncope patients may have past or current substance abuse history. Men with psychiatric illness are more likely to have unexplained syncope.

info.h: ECG Findings Associated with Serious Arrhythmias Within 30 Days
info.t: • Nonsinus rhythm (atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter) • Mobitz II or third-degree AV block • Bundle branch block (especially new LBBB) • QTc > 460 ms (concerning); > 500 ms (high risk in elderly — predicts 30-day and 1-year mortality) • Pre-excitation (delta wave, short PR = WPW) • ST depression or T-wave inversions (ischemia) • Ventricular ectopy (frequent PVCs, NSVT) Atrial fibrillation, IVCD, LVH, and ventricular pacing are independent predictors of mortality. The ECG is more likely to be diagnostic in patients >40 years.

Type 1 Brugada pattern is the only diagnostic pattern — characterized by coved ST-segment elevation ≥2mm in V1-V3 followed by negative T wave. Types 2 and 3 (saddleback morphology) are suggestive but not diagnostic. Patients with spontaneous type 1 Brugada morphology + syncope are at high risk for ventricular fibrillation and may need ICD evaluation. Family history is NOT an independent predictor for future arrhythmic events in the setting of a diagnostic type 1 Brugada pattern.

"Dagger" Q waves — narrow, deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and/or V4-V6 with associated LVH voltage criteria suggest HCM. Exertional syncope in a young patient with HCM features on ECG is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent echocardiography and cardiology evaluation. Family history of sudden cardiac death in young relatives (including those classified as drowning or unexplained MVC) may indicate undiagnosed inheritable arrhythmogenic conditions.

QTc > 460 ms on multiple ECGs is concerning for inherited long QT syndrome, especially with family history of sudden cardiac death. In pediatric patients, syncope associated with a loud noise should prompt evaluation for long QT syndrome (LQTS type 2). QTc > 500 ms in elderly patients predicts both 30-day and 1-year mortality. 25% of elderly patients may have QTc prolongation — age-related and medication-related causes are common.

• Epsilon waves — small positive deflections at the end of QRS in V1-V3, pathognomonic for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) • Early repolarization — previously considered benign, but inferior or lateral early repolarization with horizontal/descending ST segment may be associated with increased risk • Ventricular pacing — may mask underlying conduction disease or ischemia • Short QT interval (QTc < 340 ms) — rare but associated with SCD risk

• Triggered by pain, blood, emotional distress, medical procedures • Prolonged standing (especially in warm environments) • Prodrome present: nausea, sweating, warmth, lightheadedness, tunnel vision • Younger patient (< 40 years) • Recurrent episodes with similar triggers • Rapid return to baseline • Occurs during or after meals (postprandial)

• During or immediately after coughing, sneezing, laughing • During or after micturition (especially nocturnal) • During defecation or straining • During swallowing • Post-exercise (not during exertion) • After prolonged standing at attention (military, choir)

• Occurs on standing from sitting or lying position • After prolonged recumbency • Temporal relationship with starting or increasing antihypertensives, diuretics, vasodilators • History of autonomic neuropathy (diabetes, Parkinson disease) • Dehydration, hot weather, alcohol • Post-prandial in elderly

• No prodrome — abrupt onset, no warning • Syncope during exertion • Syncope while supine or sitting (rules out orthostatic) • Palpitations immediately preceding syncope • History of structural heart disease, prior arrhythmia • Family history of sudden cardiac death at young age • Family history of drowning, unexplained MVCs, or SIDS

• Syncope during exertion (HCM, aortic stenosis) • Known valvular disease or murmur • Recent surgery or immobilization (PE) • Dyspnea + chest pain + syncope (PE, aortic dissection) • History of heart failure • Audible murmur on exam
• Obtain ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact • Identify ECG pattern — standard STEMI, posterior, LBBB, aVR

• Clear STEMI — activate cath lab immediately • Posterior MI — obtain V7-V9 leads • LBBB/Paced — apply Sgarbossa criteria • aVR elevation — assess hemodynamic stability • Nondiagnostic — serial ECGs q15-30 min
• Aspirin 162-325 mg chewed + P2Y12 loading • P2Y12 selection — prasugrel vs ticagrelor vs clopidogrel • Anticoagulation — UFH or bivalirudin for PCI
• PCI available ≤90 min → primary PCI • Transfer achievable ≤120 min → transfer for PCI • PCI not available → fibrinolytic therapy • Post-fibrinolysis — transfer for angiography 3-24h

• Cardiogenic shock — emergent PCI regardless of time • RV involvement — right-sided leads, avoid nitrates • Reperfusion arrhythmias — AIVR is benign • Special populations — women, elderly, cocaine, post-arrest
• All STEMI patients admitted ICU/CCU
Leads: V1, V2, V3, V4 Artery: Left anterior descending (LAD) Reciprocal changes: ST depression in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) Largest territory. Anterior STEMI carries highest mortality risk.

Leads: II, III, aVF Artery: Right coronary artery (85%) or left circumflex (15%) Reciprocal changes: ST depression in aVL (most sensitive early sign), lead I 33-50% involve the right ventricle — get right-sided leads (V4R).
Leads: I, aVL (high lateral) and V5, V6 (low lateral) Artery: Left circumflex (LCx) Reciprocal changes: ST depression in inferior leads (III, aVF)

Standard ECG clue: ST depression in V1-V3 with upright T waves and prominent R wave Posterior leads (V7-V9): STE ≥0.5 mm diagnostic Artery: Left circumflex, occasionally RCA Accounts for ~3% of acute MIs. Frequently missed because posterior leads are not routinely obtained.

Pattern: STE in aVR with diffuse ST depression in multiple leads Note: Only 10% have acute thrombotic occlusion — pattern also seen in triple vessel disease, diffuse subendocardial ischemia, and tachycardia. Hemodynamic instability strongly favors emergent catheterization.

Posterior → Anterior (V1-V3 depression) Anterior → Inferior (II, III, aVF depression) Inferior → Lateral (I, aVL depression) Lateral → Inferior + Septal (II, III, aVF + V1 depression) Reciprocal changes help differentiate true STEMI from mimics (e.g., pericarditis has NO reciprocal changes). Presence indicates larger myocardial territory at risk.

• Regional ST elevation following arterial distribution • Convex (dome-shaped) ST morphology • Reciprocal ST depression present • Hyperacute T waves • Q waves developing • Dynamic ECG changes over minutes to hours

• Diffuse ST elevation (not following arterial distribution) • Concave (scooped) ST morphology • No reciprocal changes (except aVR) • PR depression (highly specific, seen in >80% of pericarditis) • ST elevation in II > III (suggestive but not reliable alone) • Pain worse supine, improved sitting forward • Pericardial friction rub on exam
Phase I: Diffuse STE + PR depression (>80% of cases) Phase II: ST and PR normalize Phase III: T-wave inversion Phase IV: T-wave normalization Phase I changes must be differentiated from AMI.

If the clinical picture is ambiguous, consider bedside echocardiography to assess for wall motion abnormalities (93% sensitive for AMI) or pericardial effusion. Discuss with cardiology before cath lab activation.

• Any prior intracranial hemorrhage • Known structural cerebrovascular lesion (AVM, aneurysm) • Known malignant intracranial neoplasm • Ischemic stroke within 3 months • Suspected aortic dissection • Active bleeding or bleeding diathesis (excluding menses) • Significant closed-head or facial trauma within 3 months • Intracranial or intraspinal surgery within 2 months • Severe uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >180 or DBP >110) unresponsive to therapy

• Chronic severe poorly controlled hypertension • Significant hypertension on presentation (SBP >180 or DBP >110) • Prior ischemic stroke >3 months ago • Dementia or known intracranial pathology not covered in absolute CI • Traumatic or prolonged CPR (>10 minutes) • Major surgery within 3 weeks • Recent internal bleeding (2-4 weeks) • Noncompressible vascular punctures • Pregnancy • Active peptic ulcer • Current use of anticoagulants (higher INR = higher bleeding risk)

Patient MUST be transferred for PCI regardless of anticipated time delay. Fibrinolysis cannot be given. If relative contraindication exists, weigh bleeding risk against benefit of reperfusion. Consider PCI transfer as alternative.

• Tenecteplase preferred for ease of single-bolus dosing • Fibrin-specific agents have significant mortality reduction vs streptokinase (GUSTO trial) • Streptokinase is no longer available in the United States • Maximum benefit when given within 120 minutes of symptom onset • After fibrinolysis: transfer to PCI center for angiography within 3-24 hours (NOT within first 2-3 hours)
ECG diagnosis of STEMI (or STEMI equivalent) + ischemic symptoms. Activate cath lab and start initial therapies simultaneously.

At PCI-capable hospital? • YES → Primary PCI. Goal: FMC-to-device ≤90 min. • NO → Can transfer achieve FMC-to-device ≤120 min? - YES → Transfer for PCI. DIDO ≤30 min. - NO → Fibrinolytic therapy. Door-to-needle ≤30 min.

<12 hours: PCI or fibrinolysis indicated 12-24 hours: PCI reasonable if ongoing ischemia or hemodynamic instability >24 hours, stable, asymptomatic: PCI NOT recommended (no benefit) Exception: Cardiogenic shock or severe HF → PCI regardless of time from onset

• Transfer to PCI-capable center • Angiography within 3-24 hours (pharmaco-invasive approach) • NOT within first 2-3 hours after fibrinolytic administration • Rescue PCI if fibrinolysis fails (persistent symptoms or STE)

• Cardiogenic shock: Immediate PCI regardless of time delay or facility • Absolute lytic CI: Must transfer for PCI regardless of time • Age >75y: Half-dose tenecteplase if lytics indicated • Cocaine-associated: PCI strongly preferred (higher ICH risk with lytics)

Posterior → look for reciprocal changes in Anterior leads (V1-V3) Anterior → look for reciprocal changes in Inferior leads (II, III, aVF) Inferior → look for reciprocal changes in Lateral leads (I, aVL) Lateral → look for reciprocal changes in Inferior + Septal leads

• aVL is almost completely opposite lead III — reciprocal changes in aVL are the most sensitive early sign of inferior STEMI • Reciprocal changes indicate a significantly larger myocardial territory at risk • May identify patients with greater potential for salvage with revascularization • Early ST depression or T-wave inversion in aVL may appear before STE develops in inferior leads

• Benign early repolarization — concave STE, young healthy patients, stable • Normal variant — persistent juvenile pattern, athlete's heart • Left ventricular hypertrophy — strain pattern in lateral leads

• Pericarditis — diffuse concave STE, PR depression, no reciprocal changes • Myocarditis — focal or diffuse STE, may mimic STEMI closely • Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy — anterior STE, apical ballooning on echo • Aortic dissection — may cause STEMI if dissection involves coronary ostium • Pulmonary embolism — right heart strain, STE in V1, S1Q3T3 • Hyperkalemia — peaked T waves, widened QRS, pseudo-STEMI pattern

• Reciprocal changes strongly favor true STEMI (absent in pericarditis) • Regional vs diffuse STE — regional follows arterial distribution (STEMI) • Convex vs concave ST morphology — convex more concerning for STEMI • Dynamic changes on serial ECGs — evolving pattern favors STEMI • Point-of-care echo — RWMA in 93% of AMI (but also 43% of non-AMI) • Check serum potassium if hyperkalemia suspected — rapid POC testing
Order labs and choose approach • ABG or VBG, BMP (Na, Cl, HCO3, BUN, Cr, Glucose) • Lactate, albumin, beta-hydroxybutyrate, serum osmolality

Assess pH — acidemia / alkalemia / normal Determine pCO2 — respiratory vs metabolic primary Calculate Anion Gap — AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3), correct for albumin Apply Delta Gap — detect mixed metabolic disorders Winter's Formula — check respiratory compensation Treatment & Disposition

Assess pH & CO2 — respiratory component Calculate SID (Na − Cl) — strong ion difference Evaluate Lactate — lactate contribution Calculate SIG — unmeasured anions Check Osmolar Gap — if SIG elevated and source unclear Treatment & Disposition

• AG > 12 with normal pH → mixed AG acidosis + metabolic alkalosis • Delta < 1 → concurrent non-AG acidosis • Delta > 2 → concurrent metabolic alkalosis • Actual pCO2 > Winter's → concurrent respiratory acidosis • SIG > 2 → unmeasured anions (ketones, uremia, toxins) • Osm gap > 10 → consider toxic alcohol

Rule 1 — Acute Respiratory Acidosis: Expected HCO3 = 24 + 1 × (pCO2 − 40)/10 HCO3 rises ~1 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in pCO2 Calculate Rule 1 Rule 2 — Chronic Respiratory Acidosis (> 3-5 days): Expected HCO3 = 24 + 3.5 × (pCO2 − 40)/10 HCO3 rises ~3.5 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in pCO2 Calculate Rule 2

Rule 3 — Acute Respiratory Alkalosis: Expected HCO3 = 24 − 2 × (40 − pCO2)/10 HCO3 drops ~2 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg drop in pCO2 Calculate Rule 3 Rule 4 — Chronic Respiratory Alkalosis (> 3-5 days): Expected HCO3 = 24 − 5 × (40 − pCO2)/10 HCO3 drops ~5 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg drop in pCO2 Calculate Rule 4

Rule 5 — Winter's Formula: Expected pCO2 = 1.5 × [HCO3] + 8 ± 2 Ventilatory compensation begins within minutes but takes up to 24 hours for maximal effect. A more robust response is observed in acidemia than in alkalemia. Calculate Rule 5
Rule 6 — Metabolic Alkalosis: Expected pCO2 = 40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24) pCO2 rises ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L increase in HCO3 Maximum compensatory pCO2 is approximately 55 mmHg Calculate Rule 6

For base excess users, expected pCO2 changes can also be estimated: Metabolic disturbance: Expected pCO2 ≈ 40 + Base Excess Chronic respiratory disturbance: Expected Δ BE ≈ 0.4 × (Chronic change in pCO2) If measured values differ from expected → a mixed disturbance is present.

If the observed compensation matches the expected range → pure disturbance. If the observed compensation is more than expected → an additional process in the same direction. If the observed compensation is less than expected → an opposing disturbance is also present. These rules apply to simple, single disturbances. Complex patients often have multiple overlapping processes.

• Methanol • Uremia (renal failure — phosphate, sulfate, hippurate) • Diabetic ketoacidosis (also SGLT2 inhibitor-induced euglycemic DKA) • Paraldehyde / Phenformin • Iron / INH (isoniazid) — both also cause lactic acidosis • Lactic acidosis (Type A: hypoperfusion; Type B: aerobic glycolysis) • Ethylene glycol • Salicylates (also causes concurrent respiratory alkalosis) Most HAGMA is ultimately attributable to lactate, ketone bodies, or renal acids.

GI losses (negative urine AG): • Diarrhea (most common) • Pancreatic/biliary fistula • Ureteroenterostomy Renal (positive urine AG — RTA): • Type I (Distal): urine pH > 5.5 — autoimmune, sickle cell, cirrhosis, idiopathic • Type II (Proximal): urine pH < 5.5 — myeloma, Wilson's, Vit D deficiency, heavy metals • Type IV (Hyperkalemic): urine pH < 5.5 — aldosterone deficiency, diabetes Iatrogenic: • Normal saline resuscitation (>2L in <24h) • Acetazolamide

Chloride-responsive (UCl < 20): • Vomiting / NG suction • Diuretic use (after effect) • Post-hypercapnia • Laxative abuse Chloride-resistant (UCl > 20): • Primary hyperaldosteronism • Cushing syndrome • Bartter / Gitelman syndrome • Severe hypokalemia • Licorice ingestion

Acute: Airway obstruction, CNS depression (opioids, sedatives, stroke), neuromuscular disease (GBS, myasthenia), pneumothorax, massive PE, acute chest wall trauma Chronic: COPD, obesity hypoventilation, kyphoscoliosis, chronic neuromuscular disease
Acute: Anxiety, pain, PE, early sepsis, salicylates, pregnancy, hepatic failure Chronic: High altitude, chronic liver disease, pregnancy

• Hypoalbuminemia (most common — correct AG for albumin) • Bromide intoxication (displaces Cl in lab assays) • Multiple myeloma (paraproteins exist as cations) • Hypercalcemia, hypermagnesemia • Lithium intoxication • Free water excess (dilutional)

Gokel et al. (2000) — 152 patients with uremia or DKA: mean pH difference between ABG and VBG was only up to 0.05. Malatesha et al. (2007) — 95 heterogeneous ED patients: excellent agreement between arterial and venous pH, pCO2, and bicarbonate. McKeever et al. (2016) — 234 patients with COPD: good agreement between arterial and venous pH and bicarbonate. In the absence of hypercapnia, differences in pH are negligible.

VBG is sufficient for most ED acid-base assessment: • pH difference typically ≤ 0.03-0.05 • HCO3 correlates well between arterial and venous samples • pCO2 correlates less well but adequate for screening ABG is still useful when: • Precise pCO2 is needed for ventilatory management decisions • A-a gradient is required to differentiate causes of hypoxemia • PaO2/FiO2 ratio needed for ARDS classification or lung injury assessment • Oxygenation index calculation for respiratory failure management DKA guidelines (ADA) recommend VBG for serial monitoring after initial ABG.

A VBG with pulse oximetry can replace ABG in most clinical scenarios. This avoids arterial puncture discomfort and complications while providing adequate acid-base data. Consider end-tidal capnography for rapid noninvasive estimation of pCO2 when significant pulmonary disease is absent.

Lactate serves as a fuel for cellular metabolism, including brain and myocardium. It is the conjugate base of lactic acid. Accumulation does not necessarily result in acidosis as long as buffer systems compensate. Mortality is associated with lactic acidosis (buffer failure), not simple hyperlactatemia. The liver clears ~70% of lactate via the Cori cycle (gluconeogenesis). The kidneys clear the remainder via gluconeogenesis and urinary excretion.

info.h: Type A Lactic Acidosis — Tissue Hypoxia
info.t: Poor perfusion and acute tissue hypoxia drive anaerobic glycolysis. Causes: Septic shock, cardiogenic shock, hemorrhagic shock, mesenteric ischemia, seizures, cardiac arrest, severe hypoxemia. 44% of ICU patients with acidosis have a lactic acidosis — this subgroup has the highest mortality (56%).

info.h: Type B Lactic Acidosis — Aerobic Glycolysis
info.t: Lactate generated WITHOUT overt hypoperfusion or hypoxia. Mechanisms: • Hyperadrenergic states (sepsis hyperdynamic phase, pheochromocytoma) — beta-2 receptor activation increases glycolysis, overwhelms TCA cycle • Exogenous epinephrine/vasopressors — same mechanism • Metformin — reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis, impairs lactate clearance • Hepatic failure — reduced Cori cycle capacity • Malignancy (Warburg effect) • Thiamine deficiency — impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase D-lactic acidosis: Seen in short-gut syndrome/jejunoileal bypass. Colonic bacteria metabolize carbohydrates to D-lactate, which standard L-lactate assays do NOT measure. Presents as AG acidosis with normal serum lactate.

Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) are produced via beta-oxidation of fatty acids in the liver when carbohydrates are scarce. In healthy fed states, ketone levels rarely exceed 0.1-2 mmol/L. Fasting raises levels ~20× normal. Ketoacidosis occurs when levels exceed ~70× normal, overwhelming buffer capacity. Ketosis (elevated ketones) ≠ ketoacidosis (ketones + acidemia).

Severe acidemia in DKA is NOT solely from ketone bodies. Concomitant hypovolemia, renal failure, and lactic acidosis compound the acidemia. Net bicarbonate loss occurs via both buffering AND renal excretion of ketone body salts (sodium/potassium ketonuria). This indirect bicarbonate loss may not be reflected in the AG and often becomes apparent only after volume re-expansion with saline. Euglycemic DKA: Can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors — severe ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. Maintain high suspicion in patients on empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin. Pitfall: Check K+ before starting insulin — patients with K+ < 3.3 should receive potassium supplementation FIRST.

Complex but often rapidly reversible. Chronic alcohol consumers have depleted glycogen stores. Without adequate glycogenolysis, starvation and hormonal cascades → increased lipolysis → fatty acid oxidation → ketogenesis → acidemia. Patients may present with absent serum ethanol levels. Shares the parallel insults of profound hypovolemia and lactic acidosis seen in DKA. Treatment: Dextrose-containing IV fluids (D5NS or D5LR) + thiamine 100mg IV + volume repletion. Most patients improve rapidly (3-4 hours). Insulin is NOT indicated.

Lactic acidosis is the most common cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis in hospitalized patients. The Cohen-Woods system divides it by mechanism: • Type A — impaired tissue oxygenation (oxygen supply/demand mismatch → anaerobic glycolysis) • Type B — lactate accumulation WITHOUT overt hypoperfusion or hypoxia (B1 disease, B2 drugs/toxins, B3 inborn errors) Many critically ill patients have BOTH (e.g., septic shock = Type A hypoperfusion + Type B accelerated aerobic glycolysis). Lactate > 4 mmol/L or a rising lactate carries high mortality regardless of category.

Shock (all forms): • Septic shock • Cardiogenic shock • Hypovolemic / hemorrhagic shock • Obstructive shock (massive PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax) Regional / tissue ischemia: • Mesenteric ischemia (lactate may be normal early — do NOT exclude) • Acute limb ischemia, compartment syndrome • Necrotizing soft tissue infection • Major burns, crush injury / trauma • Volvulus, incarcerated bowel Global oxygen delivery failure: • Cardiac arrest / post-ROSC • Severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ very low) • Severe anemia • Carbon monoxide poisoning (impaired O₂ delivery) Markedly increased demand: • Generalized seizures / status epilepticus (usually clears in 1-2 h) • Extreme exertion, severe shiver

• Sepsis (hyperdynamic/early phase — accelerated aerobic glycolysis, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase upregulation, often before hypoperfusion) • Hepatic failure / cirrhosis — impaired lactate clearance (Cori cycle) • Malignancy — leukemia, lymphoma, bulky solid tumors (Warburg effect / aerobic glycolysis); consider in unexplained lactate • Thiamine (B1) deficiency — impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase; alcoholics, malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric, TPN without thiamine • Diabetes mellitus / DKA • Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-driven glycolysis) • Severe renal failure (reduced clearance) • HIV / AIDS (disease and antiretroviral-related)

Mitochondrial / clearance-impairing: • Metformin (MALA) — inhibits gluconeogenesis + Complex I; risk ↑ with renal failure, sepsis, contrast • Linezolid — disrupts mitochondrial protein synthesis (prolonged use) • Propofol (propofol infusion syndrome — high dose/prolonged) • NRTIs (stavudine, didanosine, zidovudine) — mitochondrial γ-polymerase toxicity Catecholaminergic (β₂-driven glycolysis): • Epinephrine (endogenous or infused), norepinephrine • β₂-agonists — albuterol, terbutaline • Theophylline, cocaine / sympathomimetics Toxic alcohols & osmoles (check osmolar gap): • Methanol, ethylene glycol • Propylene glycol — diluent in IV lorazepam, diazepam, phenobarbital, nitroglycerin • Ethano

info.h: TYPE B3 — Inborn Errors of Metabolism
info.t: Usually present in infancy/childhood but can surface in adults under metabolic stress: • Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke / GSD type I) • Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency • Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency • Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency • Mitochondrial myopathies — e.g., MELAS • Defects of oxidative phosphorylation / respiratory chain

Standard lactate assays measure only the L-isomer. D-lactic acidosis produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with a *normal* measured (L-)lactate. Setting: Short bowel syndrome / jejunoileal bypass — malabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented by colonic bacteria to D-lactate. Clue: Episodic encephalopathy (confusion, slurred speech, ataxia) after a high-carbohydrate meal, with an unexplained AG acidosis. Order a specific D-lactate level. Treat with carbohydrate restriction ± non-absorbable antibiotics.

• Repeat / trend lactate — clearance predicts outcome better than a single value. • Venous lactate is adequate for screening; a tourniquet, delayed processing, or struggling/seizing limb falsely elevates it. • Normal lactate does not exclude mesenteric ischemia early. • Unexplained Type B lactate → review the med list (metformin, propofol, linezolid, β-agonists, propylene-glycol vehicles), give empiric thiamine, and consider occult malignancy. • Treat the cause — bicarbonate does not improve hemodynamics and is reserved for pH ≤ 7.20 with AKI (BICAR-ICU).

Peter Stewart (1978) argued that it is NOT the gain or loss of HCO3 or H+ that determines pH, but rather three independent variables that influence water dissociation: 1. Dissolved CO2 (pCO2) — respiratory component 2. Strong Ion Difference (SID) — the gap between strong cations and anions 3. Total Weak Acids (ATOT) — primarily albumin and phosphate Bicarbonate and H+ are DEPENDENT variables — their concentrations are consequences of changes in the independent variables, not causes.

Strong ions dissociate completely in solution at physiologic pH. SID = (Na + K + Ca + Mg) − (Cl + Lactate + other strong anions) Simplified: SID ≈ Na − Cl (normal ~35 mEq/L) The excess positive charge (SID) is balanced by buffer anions (primarily HCO3 and albumin). A decreased SID forces bicarbonate down → acidosis. An increased SID allows bicarbonate to rise → alkalosis. The Gamblegram — A visual tool (developed by James Gamble) showing paired columns of cations and anions. Strong anions (Cl, lactate) "squeeze out" bicarbonate to maintain electroneutrality.

Albumin is the most important weak acid in plasma. It has an overall negative charge from histidine residue dissociation. Albumin effect ≈ 2.5 × (4.2 − measured albumin g/dL) For every 1 g/dL decrease in albumin → base excess increases by 2.5 mEq/L (alkalosis). Hypoalbuminemia is the most common weak acid change in critically ill and surgical patients. It causes a metabolic alkalosis that can mask a concurrent acidosis. This is why albumin-corrected AG is essential.

The simplified Stewart approach combines routine plasma chemistry with acid-base analysis using simple arithmetic: Base Excess = (Na−Cl−35) + (1−Lactate) + 2.5×(4.2−Albumin) + Other Ions Rearranged to find unmeasured ions: Other Ions (SIG) = BE − (Na−Cl−35) − (1−Lactate) − 2.5×(4.2−Albumin) This tells you quantitatively HOW MUCH each component contributes to the metabolic disturbance.

• Identifies hyperchloremic component quantitatively — traditional AG misses relative hyperchloremia in hyponatremic patients • Better in hypoalbuminemia — traditional AG is falsely normal; Stewart automatically accounts for albumin • Predicts fluid therapy effects — switching from NS (SID 0) to PlasmaLyte (SID 50) will widen Na-Cl and improve acidosis • From a Stewart perspective: sodium bicarbonate is chloride-free sodium that increases the SID • Integrates with base excess — routine blood gas machines already calculate BE via the Van Slyke equation

Patient with cirrhosis, sepsis, saline resuscitation: Na 133, Cl 110, Albumin 2.2 g/dL, Lactate 5, BE −11.5 • Na-Cl effect = 133−110−35 = −12 (acidosis from relative hyperchloremia) • Lactate effect = 1−5 = −4 (lactic acidosis) • Albumin effect = 2.5×(4.2−2.2) = +5 (alkalosis from hypoalbuminemia) • Other Ions = −11.5 − (−12) − (−4) − (+5) = −0.5 (minimal unmeasured anions) This tells us the acidosis is primarily from hyperchloremia (saline resuscitation) and lactic acidosis, partially offset by hypoalbuminemic alkalosis. Unmeasured anions are not significant. Switching to PlasmaLyte would improve the Na-Cl component.

Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl): Na 154, Cl 154 mEq/L | SID = 0 | pH 5.5 | 308 mOsm/L Lactated Ringer's (Hartmann's): Na 130, Cl 109, K 4, Ca 3, Lactate 28 mEq/L | Effective SID ≈ 28 | pH 6.5 | 273 mOsm/L PlasmaLyte (Plasma-Lyte A): Na 140, Cl 98, K 5, Mg 3, Acetate 27, Gluconate 23 mEq/L | SID ≈ 50 | pH 7.4 | 294 mOsm/L Plasma: Na ~140, Cl ~105 | SID ≈ 35-42 | pH 7.40 | ~290 mOsm/L

Normal saline has equal concentrations of Na and Cl (154 mEq/L each) — a SID of 0. The disproportionately greater rise in plasma chloride vs sodium narrows the strong ion difference, "squeezing out" bicarbonate and causing a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. This also impairs renal perfusion and alters bicarbonate resorption from the kidneys, potentially contributing to acute kidney injury.

SMART Trial (Semler et al., NEJM 2018) — 15,802 critically ill ICU patients. Balanced crystalloids reduced the composite of death, new renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction (MAKE-30) compared to NS: 14.3% vs 15.4% (p = 0.04). Self et al. (NEJM 2018) — 13,347 non-critically ill patients. Benefits of balanced crystalloids were less robust in non-critically ill patients. Cochrane Review (Bampoe et al., 2017) — Perioperative patients receiving < 2L of NS for trauma, burns, sepsis, or surgery are unlikely to suffer lasting consequences. The clinical significance of saline-induced acidosis remains debated and is an area of active research.

Prefer balanced crystalloids (LR or PlasmaLyte) when: • Large-volume resuscitation anticipated (> 2L) • Critically ill / ICU patients • Known metabolic acidosis (avoid worsening with NS) • Liver disease (already acidotic, low albumin) Prefer NS when: • Hyperkalemia (LR contains 4 mEq/L K+) • Traumatic brain injury / neurocritical care (LR is hypotonic — 273 mOsm/L — may worsen cerebral edema) • Mixing with blood products (Ca in LR can cause clotting in the tubing) Avoid expensive resuscitation fluids — gelatin, starch colloids, and albumin products should not routinely replace inexpensive crystalloids.

• Ensure scene safety — team preparation, security if needed • Fingerstick glucose, SpO2, temperature — correct immediately • RASS score — determine delirium subtype (hypoactive vs hyperactive) • CAM screening — acute onset + inattention + altered consciousness OR disorganized thinking

• Infection: UTI, pneumonia, skin/soft tissue, bacteremia • Metabolic: Na, Ca, glucose, hepatic/renal, thyroid • Intracranial: stroke, SDH, SAH, meningitis, seizure/NCSE • Toxic/Medication: anticholinergics, BZDs, opioids, withdrawal • Directed workup: BMP, CBC, UA, VBG, ECG (QTc baseline)

• Verbal de-escalation — 10 elements (AAEP Project BETA) • Environmental modification — reduce stimuli, reorient, glasses/hearing aids • TADA: Tolerate, Anticipate, Don't Agitate • Physical restraints — last resort, proper technique, continuous monitoring

• Young adult: haloperidol 5-10 mg IM + midazolam, OR droperidol 5 mg, OR olanzapine 10 mg IM • Elderly: half-dose antipsychotic, AVOID benzodiazepines • Parkinson's/Lewy Body: quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO (lowest D2 affinity) • Intoxication/withdrawal: benzodiazepines preferred • Excited delirium: cool, fluids, midazolam/ketamine, monitor for rhabdo

• Post-sedation: continuous SpO2, ETCO2, telemetry if antipsychotic, RASS q15 min • QTc monitoring after haloperidol/droperidol — stop if >500 ms or Δ>60 ms • Admit: undifferentiated delirium, persistent AMS, elderly with infection • Discharge: clear reversible cause corrected, returned to baseline, safe follow-up

• Hypoxia / respiratory failure • Hypoglycemia • Hypertensive encephalopathy • Intracranial hemorrhage (SDH, SAH, ICH) • Meningitis / encephalitis • Status epilepticus / NCSE • Sepsis / septic shock • Myocardial infarction (delirium is ONLY symptom in up to 5% of elderly STEMI) • Poisoning (carbon monoxide, cyanide, ethylene glycol)

• Infection (16-67% of cases) — UTI and pneumonia most common • Electrolyte disorders — hypo/hypernatremia, hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia • Hepatic encephalopathy • Uremia / renal failure • Thyroid disorders (myxedema, thyroid storm) • Acute stroke (especially posterior circulation) • Pulmonary embolism • Dehydration / malnutrition • Acute urinary retention / fecal impaction • Uncontrolled pain

High-risk medications for delirium in elderly: • Anticholinergics — diphenhydramine, promethazine, scopolamine, oxybutynin, tricyclic antidepressants • Benzodiazepines — independent risk factor for delirium • Opioids — especially meperidine (highest delirium risk of all opioids) • Sedative-hypnotics — zolpidem, eszopiclone • H2-receptor antagonists — ranitidine, famotidine • Corticosteroids — especially high-dose pulse therapy • Thioridazine / chlorpromazine — first-gen antipsychotics with high anticholinergic load • Fluoroquinolones — CNS effects underrecognized ED recommendation: Avoid meperidine. If opioids necessary, use oxycodone. For other classes, weigh risks vs benefits using clinica

• Alcohol withdrawal — tremor → hallucinations → seizures → delirium tremens • Benzodiazepine withdrawal — similar progression to alcohol • Sympathomimetic intoxication — cocaine, methamphetamine, synthetic cathinones • Anticholinergic toxidrome — diphenhydramine, jimsonweed, TCA overdose • Serotonin syndrome — SSRIs + MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid • Opioid intoxication — decreased consciousness, not typically "delirious"

• Physical restraints • Bladder catheterization • Addition of ≥3 new medications • Sleep disruption • Malnutrition / NPO status • Immobilization • Sensory deprivation (missing glasses/hearing aids) Often multiple precipitants coexist. In 13% of cases, no precipitating factor is identified.

info.h: Major Risk Factors (ACEP Geriatric ED Guidelines)
info.t: Presence of 1-2 factors increases delirium risk by 2.5× Presence of 3-4 factors increases delirium risk by >9× 1. Vision or hearing impairment 2. Decreased cognitive ability (baseline dementia) 3. Severe illness (high APACHE score) 4. Dehydration (elevated BUN:Cr ratio)

• Age ≥65 years • Pre-existing cognitive impairment / dementia — strongest association with delirium. Two-thirds of geriatric delirium patients have underlying dementia. • Visual or hearing impairment • Multiple comorbidities • Male sex • History of prior delirium episodes • Functional impairment (Katz ADL Score ≤4) • Malnutrition / poor nutritional status • Depression

• Severity of acute illness • Number of medications (polypharmacy ≥5) • Presence of infection • Dehydration (BUN:Cr >18) • Metabolic derangements • Surgery or anesthesia • Pain (undertreated) • Sleep deprivation

Delirium results from the interaction between vulnerability factors and precipitating factors. • A highly vulnerable patient (elderly, demented, sensory-impaired) may develop delirium from a minor precipitant (UTI, single dose of diphenhydramine, Foley catheter) • A low-vulnerability patient (young, healthy) requires a major precipitant to develop delirium (severe sepsis, major intoxication, ICU stay) This model explains why delirium is so common in the elderly and why seemingly minor events can trigger it in vulnerable patients.

Onset: • Delirium: Acute (hours to days) • Dementia: Insidious (months to years) Course: • Delirium: Fluctuating — waxes and wanes throughout the day • Dementia: Progressive — gradual decline, relatively stable day-to-day Attention: • Delirium: Impaired — this is the HALLMARK feature • Dementia: Preserved until late stages Level of Consciousness: • Delirium: Altered — clouded, hyperalert, or obtunded • Dementia: Usually clear until late stages Hallucinations: • Delirium: Common — especially visual hallucinations • Dementia: Less common — except Lewy body dementia Psychomotor Activity: • Delirium: Variable — hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed • Dementia: Usually normal until late stages Durati

• Dementia is the single strongest risk factor FOR delirium — they frequently coexist • Without proper history, differentiating acute vs chronic cognitive change may be impossible • Obtaining baseline mental status from family, caregivers, or prior documentation is ESSENTIAL • Lewy body dementia is particularly challenging — fluctuating cognition and hallucinations are baseline features, mimicking delirium • When in doubt, assume delirium and search for a medical precipitant — delirium is treatable, and missing it carries significant mortality risk • Document current cognitive findings — this becomes the baseline for future clinicians

Haloperidol — 5-10 mg IM/IV (elderly: 0.5-2 mg) • Onset: 10-20 min IM, 3-5 min IV • Most studied ED agent. High D2 selectivity. • Side effects: QTc prolongation, EPS/dystonia, akathisia • Contraindicated: Parkinson's, Lewy body, QTc >500 ms Droperidol — 2.5-5 mg IM/IV • Onset: 3-10 min (faster than haloperidol) • More sedating. ~2-3× more potent than haloperidol. • FDA black box for QTc (2001) — but real-world risk appears very low • May be preferred when rapid sedation is the goal

Olanzapine — 10 mg IM (elderly: 2.5-5 mg) • Onset: 15-45 min IM • No QTc prolongation. No dystonia. • ⚠️ DO NOT combine with parenteral BZDs — fatal respiratory depression risk • Use when QTc is borderline/prolonged Quetiapine — 25-100 mg PO • Onset: 30-60 min (PO only) • Lowest D2 affinity — safest for Parkinson's / Lewy body • Primarily sedating at low doses (H1 blockade) • Not useful for acute severe agitation Risperidone — 1-2 mg PO • Onset: 30-60 min (PO only) • Less sedating than quetiapine/olanzapine • Available as orally disintegrating tablet

Midazolam — 2.5-5 mg IM • Onset: 5 min IM. Shortest acting BZD. • Preferred for intoxication/withdrawal syndromes • More rapid and adequate sedation than droperidol or haloperidol in one RCT Lorazepam — 1-2 mg IV • Onset: 2-3 min IV. Duration 10-20 hours. • Preferred IV BZD for alcohol withdrawal • Unpredictable IM absorption — IV preferred • Independent risk factor for delirium in elderly — AVOID

Ketamine — 4 mg/kg IM or 1-2 mg/kg IV • Onset: 5 min IM • For refractory agitation only — when antipsychotics and BZDs fail • Reliable, rapid sedation • Prepare for intubation (29% rate in one prehospital study) • Avoid in elderly, heart disease, schizophrenia

Combination therapy is superior to either class alone for rapid resolution of acute agitation. • Haloperidol + Lorazepam — classic combination. More rapid symptom resolution than either agent alone. • Haloperidol + Midazolam — "B52" variant (+ diphenhydramine). Effective for undifferentiated severe agitation. • Droperidol or Olanzapine + Midazolam — adjunctive midazolam achieves more rapid sedation than midazolam alone. ⚠️ Do NOT combine olanzapine with parenteral BZDs — use haloperidol instead if both classes needed. Low-dose combinations minimize side effects of both classes while maximizing efficacy.

• "Start low and go slow" — especially in elderly • Treat the underlying etiology first — pharmacological treatment is for behavioral symptom management • Wait ≥20 min before redosing antipsychotics • If 10 mg cumulative of an agent is ineffective, reconsider diagnosis — try a different class • QTc >500 ms? Use olanzapine or BZDs (no QTc effect) • Parkinson's/Lewy body? Use quetiapine PO • Intoxication/withdrawal? Use BZDs • Antipsychotics are NOT beneficial for hypoactive delirium

Verbal de-escalation is a first-line intervention for agitated patients. The American Association for Emergency Psychiatry (AAEP) recommends a 3-step approach: 1. Verbally engage the agitated patient 2. Establish a collaborative relationship with the patient 3. Verbally de-escalate the patient out of agitation A show of force (security presence) avoided sedation in 27% of cases in one study. One-to-one observation had a perceived efficacy of 48% among surveyed EDs.

1. Respect the patient's personal space Maintain ≥2 arm lengths distance. Do not tower over the patient. Get at eye level if safe. 2. Do not be provocative Use a calm, even tone. Avoid authoritative posture or commands. Uncross arms. Hands visible. 3. Establish verbal contact One person speaks to the patient. Introduce yourself by name. Use the patient's name. 4. Be concise Use short, simple sentences. Avoid jargon. Repeat key messages if needed. 5. Identify the patient's wants and feelings "What brought you here today?" "What do you need right now?" Validate emotions. 6. Listen closely to what the patient is saying Active listening. Paraphrase to demonstrate understanding. Do not interrupt.

If verbal de-escalation fails or if the patient presents with severe agitation posing immediate danger to self or staff: • Show of force — security activation may de-escalate without physical intervention • Physical restraints — temporizing measure only. Follow proper technique. • Pharmacological management — indicated when safety cannot be maintained nonpharmacologically De-escalation is an ongoing process — continue verbal engagement even after pharmacological or physical interventions.

Avoid using "excited delirium" as a diagnostic label when documenting. Describe the clinical syndrome and treat the immediately reversible threats. High-risk findings: 1. Severe agitation or combativeness with altered mental status 2. Tachypnea — rapid, labored breathing 3. Sweating / tactile hyperthermia — temperature >104°F (40°C) is a major danger sign 4. Adrenergic overdrive — tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis 5. Prolonged physical struggle or inability to tire 6. Disorientation, bizarre behavior, or stimulant toxidrome Deaths are usually related to hyperthermia, acidosis, dysrhythmia, restraint-associated asphyxia, or underlying intoxication/medical illness.

• Often associated with sympathomimetic intoxication (cocaine, methamphetamine), delirium, severe psychiatric agitation, or mixed medical causes • Results in dangerous hyperthermia, severe metabolic acidosis, and autonomic instability • Rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia are common complications • Sudden unexpected death can occur even after apparent clinical stabilization

1. Remove from prone position — positional asphyxia is a major cause of death during restraint 2. Aggressive cooling — target temperature <101°F (38.3°C) • Ice packs to axillae, groin, neck • Cold IV fluids • Mist and fan evaporative cooling • Consider cold water immersion if available 3. IV access and fluids • Large-bore IV × 2 • Aggressive normal saline (goal: prevent renal failure from rhabdomyolysis) 4. Sedation • Benzodiazepines when feasible: Midazolam 5 mg IM, repeat as needed • Ketamine 4-5 mg/kg IM if immediate safety threat or failed benzodiazepines • Avoid prolonged physical struggle — it worsens hyperthermia and acidosis 5. Cardiac monitoring — continuous telemetry. Anticipate PE

• CK — rhabdomyolysis (often massive: >10,000 IU/L). Aggressive IV hydration, target UOP >200 mL/hr. • Potassium — hyperkalemia from rhabdomyolysis. Treat aggressively (calcium, insulin/glucose, bicarbonate if acidotic). • VBG with lactate — metabolic acidosis • Core temperature q15 min — continue cooling until <101°F • Creatinine — acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis • Continuous telemetry — monitor for arrhythmia • Urine drug screen — identify causative substance

ICU admission is recommended for severe hyperactive delirium with hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, organ injury, or ongoing sedation/airway risk. • Cardiac monitoring minimum 24 hours for severe cases • Continue aggressive IV hydration for rhabdomyolysis • Serial CK, electrolytes, creatinine • Temperature management • Psychiatric evaluation when medically stable

Quick initial screen — can be performed by trained nonclinicians with similar performance to clinicians. RASS Assessment: • If RASS is anything other than 0 (alert and calm) → DTS is POSITIVE → proceed to Step 2 • If RASS is 0 → assess for inattention: ask patient to recite months of the year backward from December to July • If unable to do so correctly → DTS is POSITIVE → proceed to Step 2 • If RASS 0 and passes attention screen → DTS is NEGATIVE — delirium unlikely

Confirmatory test — takes ~2 minutes. Administer when DTS is positive. Feature 1: Acute Onset or Fluctuating Course ✓ required • Is there an acute change in mental status from baseline? OR • Has the mental status fluctuated in the past 24 hours? Feature 2: Inattention ✓ required • "Squeeze my hand when I say the letter A" then recite: S-A-V-E-A-H-A-A-R-T • ≥2 errors (failed to squeeze on A, or squeezed on non-A) = inattention present Feature 3: Altered Level of Consciousness • RASS ≠ 0 Feature 4: Disorganized Thinking • Ask: "Will a stone float on water?" "Are there fish in the sea?" "Does 1 pound weigh more than 2 pounds?" "Can you use a hammer to pound a nail?" • ≥1 incorrect answer + unab

2-Tier DTS + bCAM approach: • Sensitivity: 82% (95% CI: 69-90%) • Specificity: 95.8% (95% CI: 93-97%) • Comparable performance when administered by trained nonclinician raters • Feasibility: 76.5% adherence rate in pilot study CAM alone (all clinical settings): • Sensitivity: 94% (range 46-100%) • Specificity: 89% (range 63-100%) • Performance is better when formal cognitive testing is incorporated CAM-ICU (validated for ED use): • Sensitivity: 72% • Specificity: 98.6%

• The 2-tier approach (DTS → bCAM) is the current recommended screening strategy • Low recognition rates (54-89% missed) are attributed to lack of education and heavy ED workflow — not inadequacy of available tools • Fluctuating course means some patients may screen negative initially but positive on re-evaluation • Baseline cognitive status is critical — obtain from family, caregivers, or prior documentation • Altered mental status as chief complaint, when documented, has been noted to be specific for delirium • If unable to determine baseline, assume acute change and screen
• Assess clinical presentation • Confirm crisis features — SBP ≤100 or ≥20 below baseline • Immediate IV fluids — 1L NS (peds: 20 mL/kg) • Emergency steroids — Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV
• Ongoing management — HC 200 mg/24h • Response assessment at 1-2 hours • Identify and treat precipitant • Refractory shock — broaden differential
• PAI vs SAI vs TAI • Primary AI — Addison's disease • Secondary AI — pituitary • Tertiary AI — steroid-induced
• Morning cortisol + ACTH • Cosyntropin stimulation test
• Maintenance therapy — HC 15-25 mg PO daily • Sick-day rules — double/triple dose • Medication-related triggers • Crisis prevention & patient education
• ICU — active crisis / hemodynamic instability • Floor — acute illness / new diagnosis • Discharge — stable with follow-up

Infection — #1 trigger overall (viral in children, bacterial in adults) GI illness — vomiting prevents oral steroid absorption Surgery / trauma — inadequate stress dosing perioperatively Steroid withdrawal — abrupt cessation of chronic glucocorticoids CYP3A4 inducers — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital accelerate cortisol metabolism Adrenal hemorrhage — anticoagulation, meningococcemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen), antiphospholipid syndrome Emotional stress — significant psychological stressors Temperature extremes — heat or cold exposure No identifiable trigger — ~10% of cases

Shock — septic, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive Endocrine emergencies — thyroid storm, myxedema coma, DKA, HHS GI — acute abdomen, gastroenteritis, dehydration Cardiac — acute MI, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Other — anorexia nervosa, TCA overdose (can mimic adrenal crisis)

• Shock refractory to fluids AND vasopressors • Hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, buccal mucosa) • Hyponatremia + hyperkalemia (PAI) • Hypoglycemia without diabetes or insulin use • Known chronic steroid use with missed doses • History of autoimmune disease • Rapid improvement after parenteral hydrocortisone (1-2 hours)

Only in PAI: Hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation, elevated ACTH, elevated renin, low aldosterone Only in SAI: Other pituitary deficits (TSH, LH/FSH, GH, prolactin abnormalities), visual field defects Suggests TAI: History of chronic exogenous steroid use (oral, inhaled, topical, intra-articular, opioids)

info.h: When to Increase Your Steroid Dose
info.t: Your body needs MORE cortisol when you are sick, injured, or under stress. You must increase your steroid dose to prevent a dangerous drop in cortisol called an adrenal crisis.

• Fever over 100.4°F (38°C): DOUBLE your daily dose • Fever over 102.2°F (39°C): TRIPLE your daily dose • Continue the increased dose for 2-3 days until you feel better • Then return to your normal dose
• TRIPLE your daily dose or take hydrocortisone 50 mg by mouth twice a day • Seek medical attention • Continue increased dose until illness resolves, then taper back to normal over 2-3 days

• If you vomit within 30 minutes of taking your steroid pill, you need your EMERGENCY INJECTION • Give yourself hydrocortisone 100 mg into your outer thigh muscle (IM injection) • GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY after the injection • You will need IV steroids and fluids

• Tell your surgeon and anesthesiologist that you have adrenal insufficiency • You will need extra steroids before, during, and after the procedure • Your endocrinologist or surgeon should provide specific dosing instructions

• Medical alert bracelet or necklace • Steroid emergency card with your diagnosis and medications • Emergency hydrocortisone injection kit • Written copy of these sick-day rules • Extra supply of your oral steroid medication

info.h: When to Go to the Emergency Room
info.t: • Vomiting and unable to keep your steroid pills down • Fever not improving despite increased steroid dose • Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting • Confusion or difficulty staying awake • Severe abdominal pain • After using your emergency injection

Hydrocortisone is the glucocorticoid of choice — inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2 (minimal fetal exposure). • Increase HC by 20-40% in third trimester (physiologic cortisol rises in late pregnancy) • Morning sickness/hyperemesis may prevent oral absorption — use IM HC if vomiting • Labor/delivery: Stress-dose HC 100 mg IV at onset of labor, then 50 mg IV q8h until 24-48h postpartum • Cesarean section: treat as major surgery • Fludrocortisone may need increase (progesterone competes for mineralocorticoid receptor) • Interpret cortisol levels with caution — total cortisol rises in pregnancy due to increased cortisol-binding globulin

Most common cause of PAI in children — 21-hydroxylase deficiency (>90% of cases). • Maintenance: HC 6-10 mg/m²/day divided TID (lowest effective dose) • Fludrocortisone 50-200 μg/day for salt-wasting forms • Salt supplementation 1-2 g/day in infants • Monitor growth velocity — overtreatment suppresses linear growth • Newborn screening available in all US states (but can be missed) • Stress dosing: 30-50 mg/m²/day for illness, 50-100 mg/m² IV bolus for surgery • Parents must be trained in emergency IM injection technique • Sick-day rules education at every visit

Mechanism: Opioids suppress hypothalamic CRH release → tertiary AI. • Prevalence: ~15% of chronic opioid users • Higher risk with higher doses (>20 MME/day) and longer duration • No patient on <20 morphine milligram equivalents/day developed opioid-induced AI • Symptoms overlap with opioid side effects (fatigue, nausea) — easy to miss • Screen with AM cortisol in chronic opioid patients with fatigue or hypotension • May recover weeks to months after opioid cessation • Stress dosing needed until HPA recovery confirmed (AM cortisol >18 μg/dL off replacement)

Ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4): Hypophysitis → secondary AI (highest risk, ~10% incidence). Pembrolizumab/nivolumab (anti-PD-1): Primary adrenalitis → primary AI (less common). Combined checkpoint therapy: Highest overall endocrine toxicity risk. • Usually irreversible — lifelong hormone replacement needed • Do NOT hold cancer therapy — manage with hormone replacement and oncology co-management • Screen with AM cortisol + ACTH if new fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia • MRI pituitary for suspected hypophysitis • Full anterior pituitary panel if SAI confirmed

• Physiologic — structurally identical to endogenous cortisol • Dual activity — provides both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid effect • Short half-life (~8-12h) — allows physiologic diurnal dosing (high AM, low PM) • Lower growth suppression in children vs longer-acting steroids • Crisis doses (≥50 mg/day) provide sufficient mineralocorticoid effect — no fludrocortisone needed

Dexamethasone: When cosyntropin stimulation test is planned (no cortisol assay interference). Once-daily dosing for adherence. Avoid in children long-term (growth suppression). Prednisolone: Once-daily dosing improves adherence. Liquid formulation for young children. Widely available. Methylprednisolone: IV alternative when hydrocortisone is unavailable in crisis setting. NOTE: All non-hydrocortisone alternatives lack adequate mineralocorticoid activity — patients with PAI on these agents MUST also take fludrocortisone.

1. Obtain PLAX view — Parasternal long axis at 3rd-4th ICS 2. Activate M-mode — Place cursor through mitral valve leaflet tips 3. Identify E-point — The peak of the anterior mitral leaflet during early diastole 4. Measure — Distance from E-point to the interventricular septum

• EPSS < 7 mm — Normal systolic function likely • EPSS 7–10 mm — Grey zone (add B-lines/IVC assessment) • EPSS > 10 mm — Reduced EF likely (LVEF ≤30%) 100% sensitivity for detecting LVEF ≤30% when EPSS >7 mm. Specificity is moderate (52%).
EPSS may be inaccurate in: • Aortic regurgitation • Mitral stenosis • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy • Non-sinus rhythms (A-Fib) Pediatric thresholds: 6.0 mm for children, 4.9 mm for ages 0–3 years.

Airway & Supportive Care — passive rewarming only, avoid sedatives Step 1: Steroids FIRST — HC 100 mg IV before T4 Step 2: IV Levothyroxine — 200-400 mcg IV load Step 3: Consider IV Liothyronine — for critically ill only Lab Workup & Monitoring Disposition — ICU vs monitored floor

Step 1: Evaluation & Sepsis Workup — echo BEFORE beta-blockers Step 2: Steroids — HC 300 mg IV load → 100 mg q8h Step 3: Thionamide — methimazole 40 mg load or PTU 500-1000 mg Step 4: Iodine — SSKI 5 drops q6h (≥1hr after thionamide) Step 5: Cholestyramine — 4 g q6h Step 6: Hyperthermia — acetaminophen, NO aspirin Step 7: Agitation — olanzapine preferred Step 8: Cardiovascular — echo first, then decide on beta-blocker
AFib in Thyroid Storm Pregnancy — PTU mandatory in 1st trimester Refractory Storm — plasmapheresis, thyroidectomy
Incidental Lab Abnormality TSH ≥10 — Start Treatment TSH 4.5-10 — Observation Suppressed TSH — Urgent Referral

Beta-adrenergic blockade is recommended for patients with symptomatic thyrotoxicosis, especially elderly patients and those with resting HR >90 or coexisting cardiovascular disease. Propranolol is preferred — at high doses (>160 mg/day), it also inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion. Beta-blockers are the mainstay of treatment for AFib secondary to hyperthyroidism. For critically ill patients, esmolol infusion provides titratable, ultra-short-acting rate control.

Beta-blockers can be lethal in thyroid storm. Some patients develop severe thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy with reduced EF. In this context, beta-blockade may cause cardiac arrest or cardiogenic shock. In one multi-center study, 38% of thyroid storm patients developed cardiogenic shock. Japanese guidelines cite increased mortality with propranolol vs esmolol. Retrospective data show no difference between beta-1-selective agents and propranolol — arguing against the clinical relevance of propranolol's T4→T3 blocking. The concept that beta-blockers are a "cornerstone therapy" needs to be debunked. Beta-blockers are excellent for chronic, compensated hyperthyroidism — but potentially lethal in acute,

1. Echo BEFORE beta-blockers — mandatory. Assess EF and volume status. 2. If preserved EF + hypertension: Beta-blockers are reasonable. Esmolol preferred (titratable, ultra-short acting). Start low, titrate carefully. 3. If reduced EF or decompensated HF: Do NOT give beta-blockers. Treat the thyroid storm aggressively (steps 2-7). Sinus tachycardia may be compensatory — targeting HR <130 is more realistic than <110. 4. Do not use beta-blockers to intentionally slow sinus tachycardia — treat the underlying cause instead. 5. If patient deteriorates after beta-blocker: Stop immediately. This is likely iatrogenic cardiogenic shock.

• One meta-analysis concluded that beta-blocker use in thyroid storm was linked to cardiogenic collapse and cardiac arrest • A multi-center French study found 38% of thyroid storm patients developed cardiogenic shock • Retrospective Japanese data: mortality was independently associated with non-use of antithyroid drugs, but NOT with non-use of beta-blockers • No RCTs exist comparing beta-blocker use vs no beta-blocker in thyroid storm

Both inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking new thyroid hormone synthesis. Methimazole: Binds irreversibly to thyroperoxidase → longer duration of action, less frequent dosing. PTU: Binds reversibly → shorter duration, requires q4-8h dosing. Additional benefit: Blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion (~45% reduction in 24h). However, IBCC notes no clinical evidence this additional effect is clinically meaningful.

Hepatotoxicity: • Methimazole: Lower risk. Cholestatic pattern (less severe). Mean onset ~30 days. • PTU: Higher risk (~1/1000 severe injury). FDA Black Box Warning. Hepatocellular pattern — can cause fulminant liver failure. Median onset ~120 days. Dose-dependent. Agranulocytosis (~0.2% for both): • Risk is dose-dependent for both drugs • Higher risk with PTU at equivalent doses • Almost always within 90 days of therapy • Presents with high fever + pharyngitis • Cross-reactivity between agents — do not switch if agranulocytosis occurs ANCA-associated vasculitis: Higher risk with PTU. Overall: Methimazole is safer for long-term use. Transition from PTU to methimazole once stable.

1st trimester: PTU is MANDATORY • Methimazole crosses placenta → teratogenic (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, cardiac malformations) • PTU: lower risk and less severe anomalies (preauricular cysts, urinary tract defects) 2nd/3rd trimester: Switch to methimazole • Risk of congenital anomalies decreases after 1st trimester • Methimazole preferred to reduce maternal hepatotoxicity risk Both drugs: Use lowest effective dose — both cross placenta and can cause fetal hypothyroidism.

ATA: Favors PTU in acute thyroid storm (earlier onset + T4→T3 blocking). IBCC: Favors methimazole overall (safer, no robust evidence PTU is clinically superior). Japanese Endocrine Society: No significant outcome benefit of one over the other. Pragmatic choice: Either is acceptable. Use PTU if pregnant (1st trimester) or if specifically preferred by consulting endocrinologist.

Both decompensated hypothyroidism and thyroid storm are CLINICAL diagnoses. Lab values reflect the chronic thyroid state, not acute severity. If clinical suspicion is high, initiate treatment regardless of lab availability.

Primary Hypothyroidism (most common): TSH: ↑↑ High | Free T4: ↓ Low | T3: ↓ Low Central (Secondary) Hypothyroidism: TSH: Low, normal, or slightly ↑ | Free T4: ↓ Low | T3: ↓ Low → Consider panhypopituitarism, pituitary tumor, or secondary AI Overt Hyperthyroidism / Thyroid Storm: TSH: ↓↓ Very low (<0.01 mU/L) | Free T4: ↑ High | T3: ↑↑ Often disproportionately elevated → T3 may be more elevated than T4 due to preferential T3 secretion by hyperthyroid gland Subclinical Hypothyroidism: TSH: ↑ Mildly elevated (4.5-10+) | Free T4: Normal | T3: Normal Subclinical Hyperthyroidism: TSH: ↓ Low (<0.1) | Free T4: Normal | T3: Normal Euthyroid Sick Syndrome (Nonthyroidal Illness): TSH: Low or normal | F

Decompensated Hypothyroidism: • Hyponatremia (~50%) — SIADH + decreased renal blood flow • Hypoglycemia — may indicate concurrent adrenal insufficiency • Elevated CK — rhabdomyolysis from hypothermia/immobility • Hypercapnia on ABG — depressed respiratory drive • Low voltage ECG, bradycardia, QT prolongation • Elevated cholesterol/LDL • Anemia, leukopenia • Acquired von Willebrand syndrome (coagulopathy) Thyroid Storm: • Hyperglycemia (catecholamine-mediated glycogenolysis) • Hypercalcemia (hemoconcentration + bone resorption) • Hypokalemia (especially in thyrotoxic periodic paralysis) • Abnormal LFTs / jaundice (hepatic congestion or hypoperfusion) • DIC (elevated INR, low fibrinogen, throm

Always obtain in suspected decompensated hypothyroidism. Draw BEFORE giving steroids if possible. • <10 µg/dL during crisis: virtually diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency • <18 µg/dL during acute stress: suggestive of AI • >18 µg/dL: AI less likely (steroids may be tapered once confirmed)

• Levothyroxine noncompliance (#1 cause — 28% in one series) • Infection / sepsis (15%) — viral in children, bacterial in adults • Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism (11%) • Cold exposure (90% of cases present in winter) • Surgery, trauma, burns • MI, heart failure, stroke, GI bleed • Medications: lithium, immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), IV iohexol contrast • Sedatives, opioids (can trigger decompensation) • Beta-blockers, diuretics, antipsychotics

• Infection (#1) • Antithyroid medication noncompliance • Acute iodine load (contrast dye, amiodarone) • Thyroid surgery or radioiodine therapy • Trauma, surgery • DKA, hypoglycemia • Pregnancy, labor, postpartum • PE, MI, stroke • Aspirin intoxication (increases free thyroid hormone) • Checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors • No identifiable trigger in ~30% of cases

Amiodarone (most important): • Can cause BOTH hypothyroidism AND hyperthyroidism • Type 1 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis: excess iodine → increased hormone synthesis (treat with thionamide) • Type 2: destructive thyroiditis → hormone release (treat with steroids) • ~30% of thyroid storm cases in some series are amiodarone-related Lithium: Inhibits thyroid hormone release → hypothyroidism in 20-40% of users Checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab): Immune-mediated thyroiditis → can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism. Myxedema coma has been reported.

Decompensated hypothyroidism mimics: • Sepsis / septic shock • Stroke • Adrenal crisis • DKA • Drug intoxication (carbon monoxide, beta-blocker, CCB, clonidine, opioid, benzodiazepine) • Environmental hypothermia • Malnutrition • Panhypopituitarism Thyroid storm mimics: • Sepsis / septic shock • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) • Serotonin syndrome • Sympathomimetic intoxication (cocaine, amphetamines) • Drug/alcohol withdrawal • Pheochromocytoma • Heat stroke • Malignant hyperthermia • Psychiatric crisis (mania, psychosis)
