Thyroid physiology changes in pregnancy: • TSH reference range decreases in 1st trimester (reduce upper limit by ~0.5 mIU/L) • Total T4/T3 increase 50% after 16 weeks (increased TBG) — use free levels • Gestational transient hyperthyroidism is common (HCG cross-reacts with TSH receptor) — usually benign Hypothyroidism in pregnancy: Untreated → pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, placental abruption, stillbirth. Adequate T4 replacement minimizes risks. Thyroid storm in pregnancy: • Treatment similar to non-pregnant + key modifications • PTU is mandatory in 1st trimester (methimazole is teratogenic) • Switch to methimazole after 1st trimester (lower hepatotoxicity) • Iodine: cautious use — crosses p

Thyroid storm is rare in children. Most pediatric hyperthyroidism is Graves disease (onset usually during puberty, ~80% after age 11). Presentation: Fever, tachycardia, failure to gain weight, chronic diarrhea, altered mental status. Febrile seizures reported. Treatment: Based on adult literature + expert opinion. No standard pediatric recommendations exist. • Sepsis workup + resuscitation • Consult pediatric endocrinology • Thionamide dosing: Methimazole 0.25-1 mg/kg/day divided q8-12h • PTU if methimazole not tolerated: 5-10 mg/kg/day divided q8h • Propranolol 0.5-2 mg/kg/day divided q6-12h

Congenital hypothyroidism: 1 in 2000-4000 newborns. Part of standard newborn screening. Often asymptomatic at birth (maternal T4 present). If symptomatic: lethargy, feeding difficulty, macroglossia, hypothermia, jaundice. Treatment: oral Levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg daily. Neonatal thyrotoxicosis: Rare. Seen in babies born to mothers with Graves disease (maternal TRAb crosses placenta). May present at end of first week (after maternal antithyroid drugs clear). Signs: failure to thrive, persistent tachycardia, heart failure. Treatment: PTU 5-10 mg/kg/day divided q8h, or Methimazole 0.25-1 mg/kg/day.

Decompensated hypothyroidism: Most common in women 60-85 years. Higher mortality with age. • Start T4 at lower doses (200 mcg load, 50 mcg/day maintenance) • Higher risk of arrhythmias during thyroid replacement • Lower threshold for T3 — may exacerbate cardiac disease Thyroid storm in elderly: • May present atypically — "apathetic thyrotoxicosis" (lethargy rather than agitation) • Higher prevalence of AFib (35% in older vs younger patients) • Greater cardiac sensitivity to beta-blockers — start low, monitor closely • Goiters more common in younger patients (94% vs 50%)

Two types (require different treatment): Type 1 (excess iodine → increased synthesis): • Occurs in patients with pre-existing thyroid disease (Graves, toxic adenoma) • Treatment: thionamide (methimazole) • May need potassium perchlorate to block iodine uptake Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis → hormone release): • Occurs in normal thyroid glands • Treatment: corticosteroids (prednisone 40-60 mg/day) • Thionamides are ineffective (not a synthesis problem) Mixed/uncertain: Treat with both thionamide + steroids. Amiodarone has extremely long half-life (~40-55 days) — thyroid effects persist for months after discontinuation.

Decompensated hypothyroidism: • Macroglossia (myxedema of tongue) • Posterior pharyngeal myxedema / angioedema • Vocal cord edema • Reduced neck mobility Goiter (hypo or hyper): • Tracheal compression and deviation • Laryngeal displacement • Hypopharynx displacement • May make surgical airway technically challenging Approach: Video laryngoscopy as first device. Fiberoptic available as backup. If stable + predicted difficult airway → awake intubation with ENT/anesthesia standby. In cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate → surgical airway needed (technically challenging with large goiter — may need urgent tracheostomy in OR).

Decompensated hypothyroidism: • Severe respiratory muscle weakness • Depressed central ventilatory drive → CO₂ narcosis • Decreased lung elasticity • Pleural effusions → hypoxemia • Patients may have respiratory alkalosis DESPITE low minute ventilation (due to decreased CO₂ production) Thyroid storm: • Significant muscle weakness + high metabolic rate → progressive respiratory failure • Hemodynamic instability → peri-intubation arrest risk All thyroid emergencies: • Extreme sensitivity to sedatives and opioids • Use smallest effective doses for RSI medications • Pre-oxygenate aggressively • Have vasopressors ready (anticipate peri-intubation hypotension)

Decompensated hypothyroidism: • Prolonged ventilator weaning expected — respiratory muscle weakness + impaired central drive improve slowly with thyroid replacement • Address respiratory alkalosis by decreasing tidal volume or rate (CO₂ production is low) • Consider increased aspiration risk from neurogenic oropharyngeal dysphagia Thyroid storm: • Increased CO₂ production from hypermetabolic state — may need higher minute ventilation • Temperature management critical — hyperthermia worsens metabolic demand
• Assess presentation — multi-organ involvement? • Apply WAO 2020 diagnostic criteria • Differential: vasovagal, scombroid, ACE-I angioedema
• Source control + IM Epi 0.5 mg anterolateral thigh • Pediatric: 0.01 mg/kg IM (max 0.5 mg) • Repeat every 5 min up to 3 doses
• Assess response to IM epinephrine • Good response → adjunctive therapies • Poor response → IV epinephrine infusion • Peri-arrest → push-dose epi 20-50 mcg IV
• Aggressive IV fluids — up to 35% plasma extravasates • Airway assessment — stridor, edema, intubation prep • Critical airway — video laryngoscopy, smaller ETT, neb epi
• Beta-blocked patient — methylene blue, higher epi doses • Refractory anaphylaxis — methylene blue, vasopressin, ECMO • Persistent bronchospasm — albuterol, terbutaline

• H1 + H2 antihistamines (second-line only) • Steroids — controversial, single dose if giving • Tryptase — draw within 3 hours • Disposition — 4-6h observe vs admit vs ICU • Discharge Rx — EpiPen x2 + allergist referral

IM epinephrine takes ~10 minutes to reach peak blood levels (Simons 2001). Absorption is erratic with biphasic serum levels. Repeating IM epi at 5-minute intervals risks dose-stacking — the second dose is given before the first takes effect, leading to inappropriately large total doses. Patients in shock may have poor muscle perfusion, further reducing IM absorption.

Based on Abboud et al (septic shock PK data): • Volume of distribution (Vd) = 8 liters • Half-life = ~3.5 minutes • Elimination constant (Ke) = 0.2/min Loading dose = Vd × therapeutic concentration = 8000 mL × 0.005 mcg/mL = ~40 mcg Maintenance = Vd × concentration × Ke = ~8-10 mcg/min

Brown et al 2014: Prospective study of 19 patients with bee sting anaphylaxis treated with IV epinephrine infusion at 5-15 mcg/min. • All patients responded rapidly (within 5 minutes) • No appreciable adverse effects • 9 patients required re-initiation after stopping (recurrence) • One patient needed 30 mcg/min (dysfunctional IV line)

Peri-arrest: 20-50 mcg IV bolus (push-dose) Loading: 20 mcg/min × 2 minutes (~40 mcg total = 1 Vd loading dose) Maintenance: 10 mcg/min — titrate based on response AGGRESSIVELY WEAN after resolution (~2 hours). The greatest weakness of IV epi infusion is reluctance to wean. If symptoms recur during wean → resume immediately, attempt again in 1-2 hours.

This approach applies ONLY to: • Patients with pre-existing IV access • Managed by experienced resuscitationist • IM epinephrine remains first-line for the vast majority Dosing errors: IV bolus overdose risk is 61× greater than IM. Never give cardiac arrest dose (1 mg) to a patient with a pulse. The 1 mg/mL concentration must be further diluted before IV use.

Key distinction: Vasovagal = bradycardia with hypotension. Anaphylaxis = tachycardia with hypotension (distributive shock). Vasovagal: pallor, diaphoresis, no urticaria/wheezing. Resolves rapidly with supine positioning.

Caused by histamine in poorly refrigerated fish. Symptoms within minutes to hours: flushing, headache, peppery taste, GI symptoms. Clues: Multiple people affected after same meal. Patient has eaten same fish before without reaction. Responds to antihistamines alone. Not a true allergy — does NOT require EpiPen or allergist referral.

Bradykinin-mediated (not IgE). Epinephrine is ineffective. Isolated angioedema (lips, tongue, oropharynx) WITHOUT urticaria. Can occur at any time during treatment course — weeks to years after starting ACE-I. Management: Stop ACE-I permanently. Airway management. Consider icatibant or FFP for severe cases.

C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency → excess bradykinin. Recurrent episodes, family history. Lacks pruritus of allergy. High GI involvement (93%). Epinephrine ineffective. Diagnosis: C4 level (low), C1-INH level and function.

Abnormal mast cell proliferation → endogenous histamine release. Recurrent "idiopathic" anaphylaxis, flushing, pruritus, GI symptoms, hypotension. Male predominance. Severe anaphylaxis with hypotension but absence of urticaria. Suggestive: elevated baseline tryptase (>8 ng/mL). Definitive: bone marrow biopsy.

• Asthma — wheeze + dyspnea in known asthmatic may mask anaphylaxis • Carcinoid — flushing syndrome with diarrhea, wheezing • MSG reaction — nausea, diaphoresis, headache after MSG foods • Panic attack — dyspnea, tachycardia, but no urticaria/angioedema/hypotension • Vocal cord dysfunction — stridor without other systemic findings • Pulmonary embolism — dyspnea + hypotension without skin findings • Sepsis / toxic shock — distributive shock with skin findings (but different rash)

Biphasic reactions occur in ~5% of anaphylaxis cases (range 3-20% depending on definition). Majority occur within 8-10 hours of initial reaction resolution. Median time: 10-11 hours. No deaths have been reported from biphasic reactions in published studies. Although the absolute rate is ~5%, clinically significant biphasic reactions may be <2%.

• Multiple epinephrine doses required for initial stabilization • IV fluid bolus required (initial hypotension) • Delayed initial administration of epinephrine • Inhaled beta-agonist treatment needed • Unknown anaphylaxis trigger • Severe initial presentation • Wheezing at presentation • History of biphasic reactions

Uniphasic — Most common. Resolves within ~1 hour. Usually does not require ICU. Biphasic — Recurrence >1 hour after resolution without re-exposure. ~5% of cases. Usually mild. Persistent — Ongoing anaphylaxis >4 hours. ~4% of cases. Refractory — Ongoing despite appropriate epinephrine + adjuncts. Rare (<0.5%). Associated with drug etiology.

Standard (most patients): 4-6 hours from peak reaction. Extended (12-24 hours) for: • Multiple risk factors above • Severe initial reaction requiring IV epi • Late-evening presentation (biphasic would occur overnight) • Asthma history (risk factor for fatal anaphylaxis) • Unknown trigger UK guidelines: Minimum 6 hours for adults, minimum 6-12 hours for severe or risk factors.

• Medications (34%) — beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, monoclonal antibodies, radiocontrast, paralytics, protamine, local anesthetics • Food (31%) — peanuts, tree nuts, seafood, shellfish, egg, red meat (alpha-gal) • Insect stings (20%) — Hymenoptera (bees, wasps, hornets, ants) • Environmental (7.5%) — latex, cold/heat exposure • Exercise (1.2%) — food-dependent, within 1-4 hours of eating trigger foods • Idiopathic (11%) — no identifiable trigger

Food is the most common cause in children (~8% prevalence of food allergy). Most common foods: Peanuts and tree nuts (responsible for 94% of fatal food anaphylaxis). Vaccine anaphylaxis: Very rare (~1.5 per million vaccinations). Anaphylaxis may be missed in infants — flushing, vomiting, loose stool are nonspecific and easily attributed to other causes.

Death from anaphylaxis is rare (<1% of cases, ~1 death per million people/year). Time from exposure to death: • IV medications: ~5 minutes • Insect venom: ~15 minutes • Food: ~30 minutes Risk factors for fatal anaphylaxis: • Asthma (especially uncontrolled) • Adolescents/young adults (less likely to carry/use EpiPen) • Peanut or tree nut allergen • Delayed epinephrine • Upright posture during symptoms • Known allergen re-exposure In fatal cases, <15% had cutaneous symptoms — absence of urticaria should NOT delay treatment.

Food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FDEIA) occurs during exercise within 1-4 hours of eating trigger foods. More common in women. Most common triggers: Wheat, corn, garlic, celery, vegetables, shellfish. Neither food NOR exercise alone causes symptoms. Prevention: avoid trigger foods within 4-6 hours before exercise. Carry EpiPen during exercise.
You had a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. This is a serious, potentially life-threatening condition that requires immediate treatment with epinephrine (EpiPen).

You have been prescribed two EpiPen auto-injectors. Carry both with you at ALL times. How to use: • Remove the blue safety cap • Hold the orange tip against your outer thigh (through clothing is OK) • Press firmly until you hear a click • Hold in place for 3-10 seconds • Call 911 immediately after using

info.h: When to Use Your EpiPen and Call 911
info.t: Use your EpiPen immediately AND call 911 if you experience ANY of the following: • Difficulty breathing or wheezing • Swelling of lips, tongue, or throat • Feeling faint or dizzy • Widespread hives or rash • Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain after exposure to your trigger • Any combination of the above Do NOT wait to see if symptoms get worse. Early use of epinephrine saves lives.

If your allergic trigger was identified, strictly avoid it: • Read food labels carefully • Inform restaurants about your allergy • Tell all healthcare providers • Avoid areas where your trigger may be present • Consider a medical alert bracelet

• Allergist appointment within 2-4 weeks — for trigger testing and long-term management plan • Primary care follow-up within 1 week • Replace your EpiPen before the expiration date • Teach family members how to use your EpiPen

• Allergic reactions can recur within 24-72 hours without new exposure (biphasic reaction) • Always carry TWO EpiPens — you may need a second dose • Never hesitate to use your EpiPen — the risk of not treating is far greater than the risk of the medication • If you used your EpiPen, ALWAYS go to the emergency department even if you feel better

• Assess airway: signs of compromise (stridor, voice change, dyspnea)? • Secure airway: dual setup, awake fiberoptic, avoid RSI • Monitor: supplemental O2, avoid positive pressure, frequent reassessment

• Classify: histamine-mediated (urticaria) vs bradykinin-mediated (no urticaria) • Bradykinin screen: ACEi? HAE? Post-tPA? Acquired? Idiopathic? • Undifferentiated: empiric histamine treatment, reassess in 30-60 min
• Severity assessment: anaphylaxis features vs isolated angioedema • Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM + H1/H2 blockers + methylprednisolone + IVF • Isolated: antihistamines, observe 4-6 hours

• ACEi-induced: STOP ACEi, TXA or icatibant or FFP, observe • HAE acute: C1-INH concentrate (Berinert) first-line, icatibant/ecallantide alternatives • First presentation: send C4 level, treat empirically • Acquired angioedema: low C1q distinguishes from HAE, screen for malignancy • Post-tPA: icatibant or C1-INH, AVOID TXA • Pediatric: smaller airway, C1-INH preferred, US over CT for abdominal • Pregnancy: Berinert preferred, variable disease course
• GI involvement in up to 73% of HAE — mimics acute abdomen • Treat underlying cause — improvement confirms diagnosis, avoid unnecessary surgery

• Ishoo staging: Stage 1-4 by anatomic location • Stage 1-2 (face/lip/palate): observe 4-6h, discharge with precautions • Stage 3 (tongue/floor of mouth): admit for monitoring • Stage 4 (laryngeal): ICU — 67% require airway intervention

Histamine-mediated: Rapid onset (minutes to hours). Episodes typically resolve within 24-37 hours. Bradykinin-mediated: Slow onset (evolves over hours to days). Episodes typically last 48-72 hours, occasionally up to 5 days.

Histamine-mediated: Diffuse, symmetric. Lips 30%, tongue 33%, eyelids 4%, larynx 3%, extremities 11%. Bradykinin-mediated: Often focal and asymmetric. Tongue 42%, lips 24%, eyelids 2%, larynx 17%, extremities 4%.

Histamine-mediated: Urticaria and/or pruritus often present. Flushing may occur. Bradykinin-mediated: NO urticaria or pruritus. HAE may cause erythema marginatum (non-pruritic erythematous rings on torso).

Histamine-mediated: Allergic triggers — foods, insect stings, medications, environmental allergens. IgE type I hypersensitivity, direct mast cell degranulation (contrast, opioids), or COX inhibition (NSAIDs). Bradykinin-mediated: Trauma, infections, stress, estrogens (pregnancy). ACEi use (any time from hours to 10+ years after starting). Often no obvious trigger.

Histamine-mediated: Other organs commonly involved — hypotension, wheezing (strong indicator of histamine involvement), GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting, diarrhea). Bradykinin-mediated: Usually does NOT involve other organs. GI involvement (bowel edema) may occur in HAE but often not synchronous with upper airway symptoms.

Histamine-mediated: Responds rapidly to epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids. Bradykinin-mediated: Does NOT respond to epinephrine, antihistamines, or corticosteroids. Requires targeted therapy: C1-INH concentrate, icatibant, TXA, or FFP.

C4 is the best screening test for C1-INH-mediated angioedema. • 96% sensitive during an acute attack (81% between attacks) • Low C4 found in: HAE Type 1, HAE Type 2, Acquired angioedema • Normal C4 in: HAE Type 3 (normal C1-INH), ACEi-induced, Idiopathic Obtain C4 in the ED during acute attack if personal/family history suggests HAE — testing is most sensitive during attacks.

• HAE Type 1: Low (<30%) — most common type (85% of HAE) • HAE Type 2: Normal — the protein is present but dysfunctional • HAE Type 3: Normal • Acquired angioedema: Low or normal • ACEi-induced: Normal • Idiopathic: Normal

• HAE Type 1: Low (<30%) • HAE Type 2: Low (<30%) — THIS is the key finding (normal antigen but low function) • HAE Type 3: Normal • Acquired angioedema: Low • ACEi-induced: Normal • Idiopathic: Normal

C1q distinguishes HAE from Acquired Angioedema (AAE): • HAE (all types): Normal C1q • Acquired angioedema: Low C1q (in ~75% of patients) — the KEY differentiator • ACEi-induced: Normal • Idiopathic: Normal

Tryptase: Elevated in anaphylaxis/histamine-mediated angioedema (but NOT always — may be normal even in severe cases). Not elevated in bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Draw within 1-4 hours of symptom onset. Paraprotein: Present in most acquired angioedema cases (associated with lymphoproliferative disorders). CRP: Some studies suggest elevation in ACEi-induced angioedema, but not widely adopted for diagnosis. NOTE: There is no rapid point-of-care test to definitively diagnose the type of angioedema in the ED. Definitive testing requires days to weeks.
Stage 1: Facial rash, facial edema, lip edema Stage 2: Soft palate edema Stage 3: Tongue edema, floor of mouth edema Stage 4: Laryngeal edema (voice change, hoarseness, stridor, dyspnea)

Stage 1: • ED discharge: 85% • Admission without airway intervention: 2.5% • Airway intervention: 0.1% Stage 2: • ED discharge: 65% • Admission without airway intervention: 8% • Airway intervention: 1% Stage 3: • ED discharge: 30% • Admission without airway intervention: 12% • Airway intervention: 8% Stage 4: • ED discharge: 0% • ICU without airway intervention: 17% • Airway intervention: 67%

• Voice change, hoarseness, dyspnea, and stridor are significantly correlated with need for ICU admission • Voice change, hoarseness, dyspnea, and stridor predict need for airway intervention • Edema localized to lips alone = low intubation risk • The AJEM 2023 intubation-risk score adds objective clinical predictors: hypertension, anterior tongue swelling, pharyngeal swelling, drooling, and shortness of breath • Approximately 40-60% of all angioedema patients are admitted for observation

Open Angioedema Airway Risk Calculator Use the calculator when the patient is stable enough to score but not clearly low-risk. Do not delay intubation for stridor, hypoxemia, secretion failure, rapidly progressive symptoms, or laryngeal edema.

• All patients: Strict return precautions if symptoms worsen or airway compromise develops • All patients: PCP follow-up recommended (ideally next day) • Allergic/immunologic component: Short course of antihistamines + epinephrine autoinjector • ACEi-induced: Discontinue ACEi permanently, PCP for alternative antihypertensive • Known HAE: Discharge with targeted therapy for recurrence prevention, refer to allergist/immunologist • Unknown cause: Send C4 level (from ED or via PCP), refer for further evaluation

Layer 1: hard airway triggers. Intubate now if stridor, hypoxemia, inability to handle secretions, rapidly progressive tongue/floor-of-mouth swelling, altered mental status, exhaustion, or confirmed laryngeal edema. Layer 2: structured risk estimate. If the patient is stable enough to score, combine Ishoo anatomic stage with the AJEM 2023 ED intubation-risk score.

Predictors and point values: • Hypertension: +2 • Anterior tongue swelling: +2 • Pharyngeal swelling: +3 • Drooling: +4 • Shortness of breath: +5 Risk bands: • Score <5: low risk, ~5% intubation in derivation cohort • Score 5-7: moderate risk, ~16% intubation • Score >7: high risk, ~68% intubation Open Calculator

• Stage 1: face/lip/facial rash only. Usually observation/discharge candidate after stability. • Stage 2: soft palate. Observation or admission depends on trajectory and mechanism. • Stage 3: tongue or floor of mouth. Admit for close airway monitoring. • Stage 4: laryngeal involvement, stridor, or clear laryngeal symptoms. ICU/airway territory.

• Call the most experienced airway operator early. • Notify anesthesia/ENT/trauma airway when available. • Keep the patient upright and spontaneously breathing if oxygenation allows. • Prepare awake flexible endoscopic or awake video-assisted intubation with topical lidocaine. • Open cricothyrotomy tray and identify surgical-airway operator before the first attempt. • Avoid paralytic until anatomy is visualized and a rescue plan is ready, unless the patient is crashing. • Do not transport away from airway backup until the airway plan is secure.

Moderate-risk patients are not discharge airways. Use continuous monitoring, q15 minute reassessment, airway cart and cric tray immediately available, senior airway operator aware, and flexible laryngoscopy when available or when laryngeal involvement is uncertain. Escalate immediately for worsening voice, dyspnea, drooling, tongue/floor-of-mouth edema, stridor, hypoxemia, or AJEM score rising above 7.

Low-risk discharge requires stable or improving symptoms after observation, no tongue/floor-of-mouth/pharyngeal/laryngeal involvement, no voice change, no dyspnea, no drooling, ability to tolerate oral intake, reliable return precautions, and a mechanism-specific medication plan. Isolated lip/facial edema is the classic low-risk anatomy.

Deficient C1-INH level (<30% of normal). Most common form. Autosomal dominant inheritance — but 25% arise from de novo mutations (no family history). Prevalence: 1:100,000 to 1:150,000. Lab findings: Low C4, Low C1-INH antigen, Low C1-INH function, Normal C1q.

Normal C1-INH level but decreased C1-INH function (<30% of normal). The protein is present but dysfunctional. Key diagnostic clue: normal C1-INH antigen but low C1-INH function. Lab findings: Low C4, Normal C1-INH antigen, Low C1-INH function, Normal C1q.

Previously known as "HAE with normal C1-INH." Linked to genetic mutations in: • Factor XII (increases prekallikrein → kallikrein conversion) • Angiopoietin-1 • Plasminogen gene Clinically associated with predominantly tongue edema. All complement levels are normal — diagnosis requires genetic testing. C1-INH concentrate efficacy is variable.

Very rare (~1.5 per million). Typically presents after age 40. Acquired C1-INH deficiency. Type I: Associated with lymphoproliferative disorders (CLL, NHL, Waldenstrom, MGUS). Due to increased consumption of C1-INH. Type II: Associated with autoimmune disease (lupus). Due to autoantibodies against C1-INH. Key differentiator from HAE: Low C1q (normal in HAE, low in ~75% of AAE).

• Infection (most common trigger in adults — bacterial; in children — viral) • Trauma (dental procedures, surgery) • Emotional stress • Estrogens (oral contraceptives, pregnancy — enhance bradykinin signaling) • Physical stimuli (cold, pressure, vibration) • Medications (ACE inhibitors can unmask/worsen subclinical HAE)

• 50-75% of HAE patients have first attack by age 12 (mean onset 5-11 years) • 25% of cases arise from de novo mutations — no family history • Up to 44% of HAE patients are initially misdiagnosed • GI involvement in up to 73% — can mimic acute abdomen • Mean delay to diagnosis: 8-10 years

You had swelling beneath the skin, called angioedema. This can be caused by an allergic reaction, a medication side effect, or a genetic condition. Your emergency team treated your swelling and monitored you to make sure it improved.

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department Immediately If
info.t: • Your swelling returns or gets worse • You develop a change in your voice or hoarseness • You have difficulty breathing or swallowing • You develop swelling of your tongue or throat • You feel lightheaded, dizzy, or faint • You develop a widespread rash or hives with difficulty breathing

info.h: If You Were Taking an ACE Inhibitor
info.t: Your blood pressure medication (such as lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, or benazepril) may have caused your swelling. This is a side effect, not an allergy. You must STOP this medication permanently. Do NOT restart it or take any other ACE inhibitor. Contact your primary care doctor within 1-2 days to discuss a different blood pressure medication. There are many safe alternatives available.

info.h: If You Were Given an Epinephrine Auto-Injector
info.t: You have been prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector (such as an EpiPen). Carry it with you at all times. If you develop sudden swelling, hives, or difficulty breathing, use it immediately and call 911.

• See your primary care doctor within 1-2 days • If a hereditary or genetic cause is suspected, you may be referred to an allergist or immunologist for further testing • Keep a record of your episodes — note what you were eating, doing, or taking before the swelling started

• ACEi-induced angioedema is a class effect — ALL ACE inhibitors carry this risk • It is NOT dose-dependent — symptoms can occur at any dose, hours to years after starting • The patient must discontinue ALL ACE inhibitors permanently

ARBs (losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, etc.) have historically been quoted as having ~10% cross-reactivity with ACEi for angioedema. However, more recent data suggest the risk is much lower. ARBs do NOT inhibit ACE directly (they block the angiotensin II receptor), so bradykinin accumulation is less of a concern. ARBs may be considered as an alternative antihypertensive, but this decision should be made by the patient's primary care provider with close monitoring, not in the ED.

• Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine) — no cross-reactivity concern • Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) — first-line per JNC guidelines • Beta-blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol) — no cross-reactivity concern • Direct renin inhibitors (aliskiren) — CAUTION: may also affect bradykinin metabolism The choice of alternative should be made by the patient's PCP based on comorbidities, not in the ED.

• Stop the ACEi today — do not take any more doses • Follow up with PCP within 1-2 days for medication adjustment • Inform the patient this is a side effect (not an allergy) — document as "ACEi intolerance" not "ACEi allergy" in the medical record • Educate that angioedema can recur even after stopping the ACEi (rare, usually within first few weeks)
• Identify presentation and chief complaint • Screen for neurologic, ocular, or otic symptoms • Assess for pregnancy and congenital risk

• Classify by stage: primary, secondary, early latent, late latent, tertiary • Primary: painless chancre, 10-90 days after exposure • Secondary: rash (palms/soles), condylomata lata, systemic symptoms • Tertiary: gummatous, cardiovascular — rule out neurosyphilis
• Risk factor assessment and co-testing (HIV, GC/CT, Hep B/C) • Order RPR (quantitative) + treponemal test • Interpret NTT/TT combination in clinical context

• Early syphilis: Benzathine PCN-G 2.4M IM × 1 • Late syphilis: Benzathine PCN-G 2.4M IM weekly × 3 • Neurosyphilis: IV Penicillin G × 10-14 days • PCN allergy: Doxycycline or Ceftriaxone alternatives • Pregnancy: PCN ONLY — desensitize if allergic
• Discharge: mandatory reporting, partner notification, RPR follow-up • Admit: neurosyphilis, ocular/otic, desensitization, pregnancy complications

Incubation: 10-90 days (average 21 days) Classic presentation: Single, painless, firm, round, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation. Clean base, raised edges. Key features: • Usually single — multiple chancres possible (especially HIV+) • Sites: penis, vulva, cervix, anus, mouth, fingers • Bilateral painless inguinal lymphadenopathy in ~70% • Heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks even without treatment • Often unnoticed by patient (painless, may be in non-visible location) Atypical: Painful, multiple, or atypical-appearing lesions can occur

Timing: 4-10 weeks after chancre (which may still be present) Rash: Diffuse, symmetric, maculopapular. Red to red-brown, flat, scaly. Classically involves palms and soles (50-80%). Non-pruritic. Can be difficult to identify on darker skin. Other findings: • Condylomata lata: moist, flat, broad-based lesions in warm/moist areas — highly infectious • Mucous patches: painless, silvery-gray oral/genital erosions • Moth-eaten alopecia: patchy, non-scarring hair loss • Malignant syphilis (lues maligna): rare — cutaneous ulcers with central necrosis Systemic: fever, malaise, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, arthralgias, hepatitis, uveitis Resolves in 3-12 weeks untreated → enters latent phase

Asymptomatic — diagnosed by serologic testing only. Early latent (< 1 year): Documented seroconversion or exposure within 12 months. Still sexually transmissible — ~25% may relapse to secondary. Late latent (> 1 year or unknown): Not sexually transmissible (except vertical in pregnancy). Can progress to tertiary in ~30% untreated. If timing unknown → classified as late latent (conservative treatment).

Timing: 3-15+ years after initial infection. Rare in developed countries. Gummatous (~15%): Granulomatous nodular lesions — skin, bone, liver, testes. Destructive but treatable. Cardiovascular (~10%): Aortitis, ascending aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation, coronary ostial stenosis. Typically 15-30 years post-infection. Neurosyphilis: Can occur at any stage. See Neurosyphilis Evaluation.

Vertical transmission from infected mother to fetus. Higher risk with primary/secondary syphilis in pregnancy but can occur at any stage. Early congenital (< 2 years): hepatosplenomegaly, rash, rhinitis ('snuffles'), pseudoparalysis, osteochondritis, anemia, low birthweight Late congenital (> 2 years): Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, eighth nerve deafness (Hutchinson triad), saber shins, saddle nose, frontal bossing 12% higher risk for miscarriage, preterm labor, or stillbirth. ~40% of infected newborns are symptomatic at birth.

1. Screen with NTT (RPR or VDRL) 2. If reactive → confirm with TT (TP-PA, FTA-ABS) 3. Both reactive → active or past syphilis — quantitative RPR for staging 4. NTT reactive + TT nonreactive → biologic false positive Advantages: NTT provides quantitative titers for monitoring. Cost-effective screening. Limitations: May miss early primary (NTT not yet reactive) and late latent (NTT may revert).

1. Screen with TT (EIA or CIA — automated, high-throughput) 2. If reactive → reflex NTT (RPR) 3. Both reactive → active or past syphilis 4. TT reactive + NTT nonreactive → confirm with second, different TT • Second TT reactive → prior treated or late latent • Second TT nonreactive → likely false-positive initial TT Advantages: Higher sensitivity for early primary and late latent. Automated testing. Limitations: Cannot distinguish active from past infection with TT alone.

Nontreponemal tests (RPR/VDRL): • Become reactive 3-4 weeks after infection (1-2 weeks after chancre) • Peak during secondary syphilis • Decline after treatment (4-fold drop = cure) • May decline even without treatment in late disease • ~10% remain low-titer positive for life (serofast state) Treponemal tests (TP-PA/FTA-ABS): • Seroconvert slightly earlier than NTTs • Remain positive for life regardless of treatment • Cannot monitor treatment response Window period: Both tests may be nonreactive in up to 30% of primary syphilis. If clinical suspicion is high and both negative → treat empirically and repeat in 2-4 weeks.

• Prozone phenomenon: Very high NTT titers in secondary syphilis can saturate the assay → false negative. Request diluted RPR if clinically suspected. • BFP (biologic false positive): NTT reactive + TT nonreactive. Causes: pregnancy, SLE, IVDU, HIV, vaccination, liver disease. • Serofast state: ~10% of treated patients maintain persistently low NTT titers despite adequate treatment. • RPR vs VDRL: Not interchangeable. RPR titers run slightly higher. Always compare same test type.

First-line: Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM × 1 dose PCN allergy (non-pregnant): • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 14 days • Ceftriaxone 1-2g IM/IV daily × 10-14 days (limited data) Follow-up: RPR at 6 and 12 months. Expect 4-fold titer decline.

First-line: Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly × 3 weeks (total 7.2M units) • Missed dose > 14 days → restart 3-dose series • Rule out neurosyphilis before treating (especially if RPR ≥ 1:32 or HIV+) PCN allergy (non-pregnant): • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 28 days • Must exclude neurosyphilis first (doxycycline has poor CSF penetration) Follow-up: RPR at 6, 12, and 24 months.

First-line: Penicillin G IV 18-24 million units/day (3-4M units q4h) × 10-14 days Alternative: Procaine Penicillin 2.4M units IM daily + Probenecid 500mg PO QID × 10-14 days PCN allergy: Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily × 10-14 days (limited data) See Neurosyphilis Evaluation for full workup. Follow-up: CSF re-examination at 6 months.

Penicillin is the ONLY acceptable treatment. Same dosing as non-pregnant by stage. If PCN-allergic → desensitization is mandatory (no alternatives proven for congenital syphilis prevention). Monitor for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with fetal monitoring × 24h if viable gestational age. Inadequate for preventing congenital syphilis: • Non-penicillin regimen used • Treatment < 30 days before delivery • No documented 4-fold titer decline

Emerging evidence (not yet standard practice): Single 200mg oral doxycycline dose within 72 hours (preferably 24 hours) of unprotected intercourse reduced syphilis by 87% in the DoxyPEP trial (MSM and transgender women). Further research needed before becoming standard recommendation.

Acute febrile reaction caused by cytokine release from dying spirochetes after treatment initiation. This is NOT an allergic reaction — it is an inflammatory immune response to treatment. Do NOT withhold future doses of treatment.
• Primary syphilis: 10-35% • Secondary syphilis: 75-90% • Late/latent syphilis: uncommon but possible More common with higher spirochete burden.

Timing: Onset 2-8 hours after treatment, resolves within 24 hours. Symptoms: • Fever, rigors, chills • Headache, myalgias, arthralgias • Tachycardia, mild hypotension • Flushing, worsening of existing rash Treatment: Supportive care only • Antipyretics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) • Oral fluids • Rest • Reassurance — self-limited

Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can precipitate: • Preterm contractions and labor • Fetal distress (variable decelerations) • Rarely, fetal demise Management: • Continuous fetal monitoring × 24 hours if viable gestational age • OB consultation before or immediately after treatment • Should NOT prevent or delay treatment — untreated syphilis poses greater risk to fetus Treatment earlier in pregnancy (especially first trimester) is associated with better fetal outcomes and lower Jarisch-Herxheimer severity.

Syphilis is a reportable sexually transmitted infection in all 50 US states. All positive cases must be reported to the state or local public health department. Provide accurate patient contact information — public health agencies conduct partner notification and facilitate treatment.

Evaluate and test sexual partners within these exposure windows: • Primary syphilis: 3 months + symptom duration • Secondary syphilis: 6 months + symptom duration • Early latent: 1 year Presumptive treatment: Partners exposed within 90 days should be treated presumptively, even if seronegative (may be in window period). Partners exposed > 90 days ago: Test and treat based on results.

During treatment: • Avoid all sexual contact until 7 days after treatment AND until all lesions have fully resolved • Syphilis lesions are infectious — any skin contact can spread the disease Prevention: • Consistent condom use reduces transmission risk (but does not eliminate it — lesions outside the condom area can transmit) • Regular STI screening for high-risk individuals • Monogamous sexual relationships lower risk • If on PrEP for HIV: test for syphilis at least every 6 months Follow-up: • Return for RPR testing at 6, 12, and 24 months • Return immediately if new symptoms develop (vision changes, hearing changes, neurologic symptoms, new rash or lesion) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction: Fev

Congenital syphilis cases in the US have increased 755% from 2012 to 2022 (from ~335 to 3,761 cases), with 282 stillbirths and infant deaths in 2022 alone. This increase mirrors rising syphilis rates among reproductive-age women and reflects gaps in prenatal screening and treatment.

• Primary/secondary syphilis in pregnancy: highest vertical transmission risk (60-100%) • Early latent: moderate risk (40%) • Late latent: lower but still present (10%) Risk is reduced by: • Treatment before or early in pregnancy (ideally first trimester — 0% congenital syphilis if treated in first trimester in a Chinese cohort of 682 patients) • Treatment ≥ 30 days before delivery • Documented 4-fold titer decline after treatment

Approximately 40% of infected newborns are symptomatic at birth. Clinical findings: • Hepatosplenomegaly • Diffuse rash, desquamation • Rhinitis ('snuffles') — bloody/mucoid nasal discharge • Pseudoparalysis of Parrot (painful limb immobility from osteochondritis) • Anemia, thrombocytopenia • Low birthweight, failure to thrive • Jaundice, nephrotic syndrome Neurologic: Seizures, cranial nerve deficits, hearing loss, blindness

Hutchinson Triad: 1. Hutchinson teeth — smaller, widely spaced teeth with notching along biting surface 2. Interstitial keratitis — corneal inflammation causing pain, photophobia, vision loss 3. Eighth nerve deafness — sensorineural hearing loss Other findings: • Saber shins — anterior tibial bowing from periostitis • Saddle nose — nasal bridge collapse from cartilage destruction • Frontal bossing — prominent forehead • Clutton joints — painless bilateral knee effusions • Mulberry molars — defective first molars

Screen ALL pregnant women: • First prenatal visit • Third trimester (28 weeks) • At delivery (in high-prevalence areas) Treatment: Penicillin is the ONLY acceptable treatment in pregnancy. Desensitize if allergic. Inadequate treatment (infant at risk): • Mother received non-penicillin regimen • Treatment completed < 30 days before delivery • No documented 4-fold titer decline • No treatment during pregnancy Newborn treatment: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 units/kg IV q12h (< 7 days old) or q8h (> 7 days) × 10 days.

Syphilis (T. pallidum): • Painless, firm, indurated ulcer (chancre) • Usually single, clean base • Bilateral painless lymphadenopathy • Heals in 3-6 weeks Herpes Simplex (HSV-1/2): • Painful, grouped vesicles on erythematous base • May coalesce into shallow ulcers • Recurrent episodes common • Tender inguinal lymphadenopathy Chancroid (H. ducreyi): • Painful, ragged, undermined ulcer with purulent base • Soft, non-indurated edges • Unilateral tender inguinal bubo (may suppurate) • Rare in US Lymphogranuloma Venereum (Chlamydia L1-L3): • Small painless papule/ulcer (often unnoticed) → heals • Followed by painful unilateral inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy (2-6 weeks later) • 'Groove sign' — e

Fixed drug eruption: • Recurrent, well-demarcated round lesion in same location • Often related to NSAIDs, tetracyclines, sulfonamides Behçet disease: • Recurrent painful oral AND genital ulcers • Associated with uveitis, skin lesions, pathergy Traumatic ulcer: • History of trauma, friction, or sexual activity • Irregular borders, painful Squamous cell carcinoma: • Persistent, non-healing ulcer or nodule • Irregular borders, induration • Risk factors: HPV, immunosuppression • Biopsy indicated for non-healing lesions > 4 weeks

When in doubt, test for syphilis. The chancre of primary syphilis is painless and often missed. Consider syphilis testing in ANY sexually active patient with a genital lesion, especially in high-risk populations (MSM, HIV+, PrEP users). Multiple STIs can coexist — always test for HIV, GC/CT, and syphilis together.

• Identify exposure: acute ingestion, chronic toxicity, or unknown timing • Estimate dose: <150 mg/kg minimal, 150-300 moderate, >300 severe • Chronic toxicity: lower levels can kill — clinical status > level

• Volume resuscitate with D5W or LR — NEVER normal saline • Seizures: benzodiazepines + empiric dextrose for neuroglycopenia • CRITICAL: The dangerous airway — avoid intubation if possible • If must intubate: pre-bolus bicarb, RR 30-35, call for emergent HD
• Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if within 1-2 hours • MDAC or WBI for enteric-coated or massive ingestion

• NaHCO3 bolus 1-2 mEq/kg then infusion in D5W (CORNERSTONE) • CRITICAL: Replete K+ ≥ 4.0 or alkalinization fails • Dextrose D50W for neuroglycopenia even with normal glucose • Monitor: urine pH hourly, ABG/BMP q2h, salicylate level q2h
• EXTRIP indications: level >100, pH <7.2, AMS, pulm edema, renal failure • Continue NaHCO3 during and after HD — rebound is expected • Consult nephrology EARLY — HD takes time to arrange
• Serial levels q2h until declining, then q4h • ICU: any HD, intubation, seizures, ongoing alkalinization • Psychiatric evaluation mandatory for all intentional ingestions

Early: Primary respiratory alkalosis from direct medullary stimulation — one of the first signs of toxicity. Late: Anion gap metabolic acidosis develops from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation → lactic acidosis + ketoacidosis. Most of the AG elevation is NOT from salicylate itself (<5 mEq/L contribution). Typical presentation: Mixed respiratory alkalosis + AG metabolic acidosis with a nearly normal pH.

info.h: Why Bicarb Still Works in Alkalosis
info.t: Even when the serum pH is already alkalemic (7.45-7.55) from respiratory alkalosis, sodium bicarbonate is still beneficial. The goal is urinary alkalinization, not serum. Alkaline urine traps ionized salicylate in the renal tubules. This works regardless of the serum pH, as long as the kidneys are producing alkaline urine.

A 'normal' pH of 7.40 may mask severe poisoning if respiratory alkalosis is offsetting metabolic acidosis. Always check the anion gap and HCO3 independently. A patient with pH 7.40, pCO2 20, HCO3 12, AG 22 is severely poisoned — the normal pH is misleading.

Acidemia in salicylate toxicity is a DANGER sign indicating imminent demise without intervention. At lower pH, more salicylic acid exists in its non-ionized form → freely crosses the blood-brain barrier → worsens CNS toxicity → further respiratory depression → more acidosis. This is the death spiral. Children and severe/late presentations may present with pure metabolic acidosis (worse prognosis).

Adults: Classic mixed picture (respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis). Children: Metabolic acidosis may predominate — may not develop the initial respiratory alkalosis phase. Children are at higher risk for rapid deterioration.

Salicylic acid is a weak acid (pKa 3.0). At alkaline pH, it exists primarily in its ionized form, which cannot cross cell membranes or be reabsorbed by renal tubules. Urinary alkalinization to pH 8.0 increases renal salicylate clearance approximately 10-fold compared to pH 6.0.

Bolus: 1-2 mEq/kg IV (2-3 amps of 8.4% NaHCO3). Infusion: 150 mEq NaHCO3 (3 amps of 8.4%) in 1L D5W. Run at 150-200 mL/hr. Add KCl: 20-40 mEq per liter of infusion. D5W carrier provides dual benefit: vehicle for bicarb AND CNS glucose support.

• Urine pH: 7.5-8.0 (check hourly via Foley catheter) • Serum pH: 7.45-7.55 (check q2h, do NOT exceed 7.60) • Potassium: ≥ 4.0-4.5 mEq/L (check q2h) • Salicylate level: q2h until peaked and declining • Glucose: Fingerstick q1h if AMS

This is the #1 reason alkalinization fails. When K+ is low, the distal collecting duct reabsorbs K+ in exchange for H+ secretion — producing acidic urine regardless of how much bicarbonate you infuse. Two simultaneous measures are required for urinary alkalinization: 1. Adequate bicarbonate delivery 2. Aggressive K+ repletion (target ≥ 4.0-4.5 mEq/L) Bicarbonate infusion itself tends to drop K+ further — preemptive repletion is essential.

Acetazolamide: ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED. Causes systemic metabolic acidosis (promotes bicarb excretion from the wrong side) AND displaces salicylate from albumin binding sites, increasing free (toxic) salicylate levels. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl): Acidifying solution (strong ion difference = 0). Use D5W or LR for volume resuscitation. Do NOT use NS as carrier for bicarb infusion.

Discontinue alkalinization when: • Two consecutive salicylate levels showing decline • Level < 30 mg/dL (< 2.2 mmol/L) • Patient asymptomatic with normal respiratory rate Taper slowly — abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound acidosis. After stopping, follow labs for 2-4 additional hours to ensure no rebound (especially important in chronic toxicity).

Hemodialysis is strongly recommended for: • Salicylate level > 100 mg/dL (7.2 mmol/L) in acute ingestion • Salicylate level > 90 mg/dL (6.5 mmol/L) with impaired renal function • Altered mental status attributable to salicylate (including need for intubation) • pH ≤ 7.20 despite adequate resuscitation and bicarbonate • New hypoxemia requiring supplemental O2 (non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema) • Progressive clinical deterioration despite aggressive treatment

Hemodialysis is suggested for: • Salicylate level > 80 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L) in acute ingestion • Salicylate level > 60 mg/dL (4.4 mmol/L) in chronic or elderly patients • Renal failure limiting salicylate clearance • Volume overload preventing adequate alkalinization • Clinical deterioration despite appropriate treatment

Salicylate is an ideal dialysis candidate: • Small molecule (MW 138 Da) — easily crosses dialysis membrane • Low volume of distribution (0.1-0.3 L/kg) — accessible in blood compartment • Protein binding saturated in overdose (90% → 50%) — more free drug available for removal • Water-soluble — efficiently removed by aqueous dialysate HD simultaneously removes salicylate AND corrects metabolic acidosis.

• Standard intermittent HD preferred over CRRT — much more efficient clearance • HD is safe even in hypotensive patients (no fluid removal, so no hemodynamic compromise) • Continue NaHCO3 during and after HD — tissue redistribution continues • Typical session duration: 4-6 hours • Expect rebound — recheck level 2h post-HD • Some patients need 2-3 sessions for massive ingestions
Stop HD when: • Salicylate level < 30 mg/dL with no rebound at 2h post-HD • AND clinical improvement (resolving AMS, normalizing acid-base) Continue alkalinization between/after HD sessions.

info.pt: The Dangerous Airway — Salicylate Death Spiral
info.t: A salicylate-poisoned patient's compensatory hyperventilation (often RR 30-40) is the ONLY thing maintaining their pH. The respiratory alkalosis offsets the metabolic acidosis, keeping the patient alive.

info.pt: The Dangerous Airway — Salicylate Death Spiral
info.t: 1. Apneic period during RSI → CO2 rises rapidly 2. pH crashes → more salicylic acid shifts to non-ionized form 3. Non-ionized salicylate crosses the blood-brain barrier freely 4. CNS salicylate concentration rises → brainstem depression 5. Further loss of respiratory drive → more CO2 retention 6. Worsening acidosis → more CNS penetration → cardiac arrest This cascade can happen within minutes of losing respiratory compensation.

info.pt: The Dangerous Airway — Salicylate Death Spiral
info.t: Even with aggressive ventilator settings (RR 30-35), matching a patient's own hyperventilatory response is extremely difficult: • Mechanical dead space reduces effective alveolar ventilation • Circuit compliance absorbs tidal volume • Sedation/paralysis eliminates any spontaneous respiratory effort • Auto-PEEP limits achievable respiratory rate The result: post-intubation pH is almost always lower than pre-intubation pH.

info.pt: The Dangerous Airway — Salicylate Death Spiral
info.t: Pre-intubation: • Bolus NaHCO3 1-2 mEq/kg IV — give 5-10 minutes before paralysis so the patient can blow off the CO2 generated by bicarbonate • Pre-oxygenate with BVM at high rate Intubation: • Most experienced operator available • Ketamine preferred (maintains respiratory drive longest) • Minimize apneic time — this is the critical window Post-intubation: • Immediately connect ventilator: TV 8 mL/kg, RR 30-35 • Target pH, NOT pCO2 — get ABG within 10 minutes • Continue NaHCO3 boluses • Switch to spontaneous mode (pressure support) ASAP • Call for EMERGENT hemodialysis

info.pt: The Dangerous Airway — Salicylate Death Spiral
info.t: Intubation in salicylate toxicity should be a last resort. Hemodialysis is almost always a better option than intubation for deteriorating patients. A patient who needs intubation almost certainly needs HD too — and HD without intubation is far safer than intubation without HD. HFNC may help support breathing without the risks of intubation.

Elderly patients on chronic aspirin therapy are most commonly affected. Often unintentional — gradual accumulation from renal impairment, dehydration, or drug interactions. Also seen with chronic use of: • Bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) • Topical salicylate products (Ben-Gay, Icy Hot) • Combination cold medicines containing aspirin • Oil of wintergreen preparations

info.h: Why It's More Deadly Than Acute
info.t: Chronic toxicity has HIGHER mortality than acute toxicity despite LOWER serum levels. Reasons: • Greater tissue accumulation — salicylate has had time to distribute into brain and other compartments • Cerebral and pulmonary edema are more common than in acute toxicity • Diagnosis is frequently delayed (misidentified as sepsis, CHF, dementia) • Underlying comorbidities compound the toxicity The Done nomogram does NOT apply to chronic toxicity.

Chronic salicylate toxicity is frequently confused with: • Sepsis (tachypnea, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, AMS) • CHF exacerbation (pulmonary edema, dyspnea) • Dementia/delirium (confusion, agitation) • Simple UTI (elderly with AMS — don't stop at the UA) Include salicylate level in your AMS/delirium workup, especially in elderly patients.

• Unexplained anion gap metabolic acidosis in elderly • Tachypnea out of proportion to clinical picture • Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema without clear cause • AMS + tinnitus (or new hearing loss in elderly) • Metabolic acidosis in a patient taking chronic aspirin • Confusion that doesn't fit other diagnoses Ask about ALL medications — including OTC products.

• Analgesic/antiplatelet: 5-15 mg/dL • Anti-inflammatory (therapeutic): 15-30 mg/dL (1.1-2.2 mmol/L) • Mild toxicity: 30-50 mg/dL • Moderate toxicity: 50-80 mg/dL • Severe toxicity: 80-100 mg/dL • Potentially lethal: > 100 mg/dL (> 7.2 mmol/L) Unit conversion: mg/dL × 0.0724 = mmol/L. Some labs report in mg/L (= mg/dL × 10).

A single salicylate level can be dangerously misleading: • Timing: Peak levels may not occur until 6+ hours (standard) or 12-24 hours (enteric-coated) after ingestion • Chronic toxicity: Levels may be only mildly elevated while tissue toxicity is severe • pH dependence: The same total level produces different tissue penetration at different pH values — a level of 46 mg/dL at pH 7.2 has the same CNS penetration as 100 mg/dL at pH 7.55 • Bezoar formation: Levels may continue to rise for 12+ hours

Serial levels are essential — check q2h until peaked and clearly declining: • Rising levels → ongoing absorption (bezoar, enteric-coated, large ingestion) • Plateau → approaching peak, continue monitoring • Declining levels × 2 → absorption complete, switch to q4h • After stopping treatment → follow 2-4 additional hours for rebound

The Done nomogram plots salicylate level vs time after ingestion. Limitations — NOT valid for: • Chronic toxicity (tissue stores far exceed blood level) • Enteric-coated or sustained-release formulations • Unknown time of ingestion • Co-ingestions • Renal impairment Clinical assessment always takes priority over nomogram predictions.

WARNING: A declining serum level with WORSENING clinical status suggests tissue redistribution — salicylate is moving from blood into cells (especially brain) where it causes damage. This patient needs hemodialysis, not reassurance. The falling level is false comfort — the salicylate is in a worse place, not a better one.

• Assess clinical severity — mild vs moderate vs severe • Anticholinergic toxidrome features • Immediate resuscitation for critical patients • GI decontamination — activated charcoal decision • Intubation considerations — avoid hypoventilation
• 12-lead ECG assessment — QRS duration • Normal QRS — monitoring plan • R wave in aVR — sensitive marker • Serial ECG monitoring protocol
• NaHCO₃ bolus — cornerstone of treatment • Aggressive bicarb for QRS >160 ms • Treatment goals and monitoring • Maintenance infusion • Bicarbonate-refractory management
• Seizure assessment — lethal feedback loop • First-line BZD treatment • Refractory seizure escalation • Contraindicated antiepileptics
• Hypotension assessment — 3 mechanisms • Volume resuscitation • Vasopressor selection by heart rate • Wide-complex tachycardia management • Lipid emulsion — rescue therapy • ECMO — final rescue
• Disposition decision — ICU vs monitor vs discharge • ICU admission criteria • Discharge criteria + psychiatric clearance

• QRS <100 ms — Low risk. Monitor with serial ECGs • QRS 100-120 ms — Increased seizure risk (~10-33%). Give sodium bicarbonate • QRS 120-160 ms — Significant sodium channel blockade. Seizure risk ~30%. Aggressive bicarb • QRS >160 ms — High risk of ventricular arrhythmias (~50%). Immediate aggressive treatment ⚠️ In toxicology, "wide QRS" = anything >100 ms (not the standard >120 ms)

• R wave >3 mm in aVR — sensitive marker of sodium channel blockade • R/S ratio >0.7 in aVR — additional marker • aVR may be more sensitive than QRS duration for predicting seizures and arrhythmias (sensitivity 81%) • Can be positive even when QRS is <100 ms • Reflects preferential right bundle branch blockade by sodium channel blockers

• Rightward axis deviation of terminal 40 ms of QRS — characteristic finding • Sodium channel blockade preferentially affects the right bundle branch • Results in terminal rightward forces visible in leads I and aVR • May be the earliest ECG sign of sodium channel blockade

• Coved ST elevation in V1-V3 with RBBB morphology • Important NOT to confuse with true Brugada syndrome • TCA-induced pattern resolves with treatment (unlike genetic Brugada) • Present in up to 15% of significant TCA overdoses

• Present due to potassium channel blockade (separate from sodium channel effects) • Less prognostically significant than QRS widening for TCA toxicity • Risk of torsades de pointes, but uncommon as long as patient remains tachycardic • Treat with magnesium 2g IV if polymorphic VT develops

• Serial 12-lead ECGs every 15-30 min for first 2 hours • Then q2h for minimum 6 total hours • Continuous telemetry throughout observation period • Check ECG after each bicarbonate bolus • Check ECG after any clinical change (seizure, hypotension, arrhythmia) • Minimum 6 hours after LAST ECG abnormality resolves before considering discharge

1. Sodium loading — hypertonic NaHCO₃ (1000 mOsm/L) increases extracellular sodium, which competes for cardiac sodium channels blocked by TCA 2. Alkalosis — increasing serum pH shifts TCA to its protein-bound (non-toxic) form, reducing free drug concentration Both mechanisms are clinically important — neither alone is sufficient

• 1-2 mEq/kg IV push over 1-2 minutes • Repeat every 3-5 minutes until QRS narrows • 1 amp = 50 mEq/50 mL of 8.4% solution • Most patients need 1-3 boluses; severe cases may need 5-10+ • Case report: 2650 mEq (53 amps) total in severe case with survival

• 150 mEq (3 amps) in 1L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr • This is isotonic bicarbonate — less effective than hypertonic boluses for acute QRS widening • Use for maintenance AFTER initial boluses have narrowed the QRS • Continue until QRS normal × ≥6 hours, then wean while monitoring ECG • Central line preferred for large volumes (8.4% is extremely hypertonic)

• QRS < 100 ms (may not be achievable if severely/chronically prolonged) • pH 7.50-7.55 — achieve via bicarb ± hyperventilation (if intubated) • Serum Na ≤ 155 mEq/L — excessive hypernatremia is dangerous • Avoid excessive alkalinization — pH >7.55 may paradoxically increase arrhythmia or seizure risk

If QRS not narrowing despite adequate bicarb: 1. Hyperventilation (if intubated) — fastest way to alkalinize. Target ETCO₂ ~25-30 mmHg 2. Hypertonic saline 3% — additional sodium loading if Na <155 mEq/L 3. Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg IV — Class IB antiarrhythmic that competes for Na channel binding sites 4. Lipid emulsion — rescue for cardiac arrest (see separate protocol) 5. ECMO — final rescue for refractory cardiac arrest ⚠️ If QRS doesn't respond despite 100-200 mEq, question the diagnosis

• Hypokalemia — alkalosis shifts K⁺ intracellularly. Replete K⁺ simultaneously • Hypocalcemia — ionized Ca²⁺ drops with alkalosis. Monitor and replete • Hypernatremia — each 50 mEq amp delivers 50 mEq sodium. Monitor Na closely • Volume overload — significant fluid load with multiple boluses • Paradoxical CNS acidosis — CO₂ crosses BBB faster than HCO₃⁻ • Metabolic alkalosis — if pH >7.55, hold further bicarb and rely on hyperventilation

• Amitriptyline, Nortriptyline, Imipramine, Desipramine • Doxepin, Clomipramine, Trimipramine, Protriptyline • Most commonly discussed sodium channel blockers • Often dominate the clinical picture with combined Na channel + anticholinergic + alpha blockade
• Bupropion, Citalopram, Fluoxetine • Maprotiline, Paroxetine, Venlafaxine • Generally less cardiotoxic than TCAs but can cause sodium channel blockade in overdose

• Type Ia: Procainamide, Quinidine, Disopyramide • Type Ic: Flecainide, Propafenone • These are CONTRAINDICATED in TCA overdose — worsen sodium channel blockade • Amiodarone also avoided (QTc prolongation)
• Diphenhydramine — common, can cause TCA-like toxicity in overdose • Chlorpheniramine, Dimenhydrinate • Doxepin (also classified as TCA) • Combined anticholinergic + sodium channel effects

• Cocaine — Na channel blockade + sympathomimetic effects • Beta-blockers: Propranolol, Acebutolol (membrane-stabilizing activity) • Antimalarials: Chloroquine, Hydroxychloroquine, Quinine • Antiepileptics: Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Phenytoin, Lacosamide • Antipsychotics: Thioridazine, Loxapine • Muscle relaxants: Cyclobenzaprine (TCA analogue), Orphenadrine • Miscellaneous: Amantadine, Tramadol, Topiramate, some insecticides

⚠️ Combinations of multiple sodium channel blockers potentiate toxicity. A "subclinical" dose of diphenhydramine + cyclobenzaprine may produce significant blockade together. With decreased TCA prescribing, most patients presenting with Na channel blockade today do NOT have TCA overdose — diphenhydramine, cocaine, and antiarrhythmics are more common causes. The management principles (bicarbonate, lidocaine, avoid Class IA/IC) apply to ALL sodium channel blockers.

• Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide) • Cocaine • Diphenhydramine (common — false positive on TCA screen) • Carbamazepine • Cyclobenzaprine (structural TCA analogue — usually mild cardiac effects) • See Agents That Block Sodium Channels for complete list

• Antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) • Antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine) • Antiparkinsonian agents (benztropine, trihexyphenidyl) • Mydriatics (atropine, cyclopentolate) • Plants (jimsonweed / Datura, deadly nightshade) • Mushrooms (Amanita muscaria)

• Hyperkalemia — peaked T waves, sine wave (give calcium + bicarb empirically if unsure) • True Brugada syndrome — genetic, does NOT resolve with bicarbonate • Pre-excitation (WPW with atrial fibrillation) • Ventricular tachycardia (ischemic, structural heart disease) • Bundle branch block with SVT • Drug-induced: digoxin, theophylline

• TCA + SSRI/SNRI coingestion can cause serotonin syndrome • Key differentiator: clonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis (wet, not dry like anticholinergic) • Mydriasis present in both • Treat with cyproheptadine and benzodiazepines

⚠️ Urine drug screen for TCA has many false positives: • Diphenhydramine • Cyclobenzaprine • Carbamazepine • Phenothiazines (chlorpromazine, thioridazine) • Quetiapine TCA levels are NOT useful for acute management — do not correlate with toxicity

🛑 The acidosis death spiral: 1. TCA blocks sodium channels → QRS widens 2. Seizure → lactic acidosis → pH drops 3. Acidosis increases free (unbound) TCA → more sodium channel blockade 4. More blockade → wider QRS → arrhythmias → more seizures 5. Vicious cycle → cardiac arrest Seizures must be treated aggressively — every minute of ongoing seizure worsens cardiac toxicity
Choose one:

• Give sodium bicarbonate WITH benzodiazepines — not instead of • Alkalinization reduces free TCA crossing the blood-brain barrier • Counteracts seizure-induced lactic acidosis • Do not wait for seizure to stop before giving bicarb
If BZDs fail after 2-3 doses:

Do NOT use these — they worsen sodium channel blockade: • Phenytoin / Fosphenytoin — may precipitate cardiac arrest • Carbamazepine — sodium channel blocker • Lamotrigine — sodium channel blocker • Lacosamide — enhances slow inactivation of sodium channels Phenytoin contraindication is ABSOLUTE in TCA overdose — this is a universally agreed-upon principle across all toxicology guidelines

Any of the following: • QRS widening (current or resolved within last 6h) • Ventricular arrhythmias (current or resolved) • Seizures (current or resolved) • Hypotension requiring vasopressors • Altered mental status • Requiring sodium bicarbonate infusion • Required intubation In the ICU: • Continuous telemetry minimum 6h after last ECG abnormality • Serial ABGs and electrolytes to guide bicarbonate therapy • Wean bicarb slowly while monitoring ECG

Criteria: • Asymptomatic or mild anticholinergic features only • Normal ECG (QRS <100 ms) at presentation • Reported significant ingestion requiring observation Protocol: • Serial ECGs q2h for minimum 6 hours • Continuous telemetry • If ANY QRS widening → escalate to bicarb protocol and ICU

ALL criteria must be met: • Asymptomatic for ≥6 hours of observation • QRS persistently <100 ms on serial ECGs • Normal mental status • Normal hemodynamics (no hypotension, stable HR) • Psychiatric clearance obtained (MANDATORY for intentional ingestions) Before discharge: • Document lethal means counseling • Counsel family to remove access to TCAs and other toxic medications • Consider safer antidepressant alternatives (SSRIs, SNRIs) • Ensure psychiatric follow-up is arranged • Provide safety plan
National Poison Control Center: 1-800-222-1222 Available 24/7 for consultation on any suspected poisoning. Consider toxicology consultation for all severe cases.
• Classify ingestion pattern: acute vs chronic vs unknown • Gather history: dose, timing, formulation, coingestants, risk factors • Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion — nomogram does NOT apply

• Draw APAP level at 4h post-ingestion — plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram • Extended-release / coingestant — serial levels if >10 mcg/mL • Chronic ingestion — use (ALT)(APAP) product, treat if ALT elevated or APAP detectable • GI decontamination — activated charcoal within 4 hours

• IV NAC 21-hour 3-bag protocol (preferred) • Oral NAC 72-hour protocol (alternative) • Anaphylactoid reaction management — slow rate, antihistamines, NEVER stop permanently • Stopping criteria: APAP <10 + INR <2 + AST/ALT improving + clinically well
• High-dose NAC — Hendrickson protocol (2-4× standard Bag 3 rate) • Fomepizole — CYP2E1 inhibitor, blocks NAPQI formation • Hemodialysis — EXTRIP indications, removes APAP and NAPQI

• Established hepatic failure — continue NAC indefinitely • King's College Criteria — transplant referral • Supportive care — coagulopathy, cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, renal failure • Disposition — admit vs ICU vs discharge criteria

Often asymptomatic or nonspecific: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, diaphoresis. Labs generally normal during this period. ⚠️ Symptoms during this period (altered mental status, lactic acidosis) suggest massive ingestion (>30g) or coingestant — evaluate for high-risk protocol.

Stage 1 symptoms resolve or improve — patient may appear well (the "treacherous calm"). Right upper quadrant pain can develop. Labs: AST elevation nearly universal by 36 hours. AST is the most sensitive early marker. ALT:AST ratio typically 1:1 initially. Nephrotoxicity may begin.

Systemic symptoms reappear: nausea/vomiting, malaise, jaundice. Hepatic failure emerges: encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR elevation), hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis. AST/ALT may exceed 10,000 IU/L. Peak occurs 3-4 days post-ingestion. Greatest risk of death — usually from cerebral edema, multi-organ failure, or sepsis. Key pearl: Patients with peak AST/ALT <1,000 usually do NOT develop clinically significant hepatic dysfunction. AST:ALT ratio pearl: An AST:ALT ratio <0.4 suggests aminotransferases have peaked and are falling — a reassuring sign.
Patients who survive make a complete recovery — the liver regenerates fully without chronic sequelae. Transaminases normalize over 1-2 weeks. No increased risk of chronic liver disease.

The nomogram is valid ONLY when ALL of the following are true: • Acute ingestion — ingestion within a period of <24 hours • Reliable history — dose, time, and formulation are known • Time since ingestion is defined as time since the end of the ingestion period • APAP level drawn at ≥4 hours post-ingestion

Treatment Line (150 mcg/mL at 4h): Levels above this line indicate risk of hepatic failure — start NAC. High-Risk Line (300 mcg/mL at 4h): Levels above this line indicate massive overdose — high-dose NAC protocol, consider fomepizole and hemodialysis. Both lines follow exponential decay with an approximate 4-hour half-life. The US uses the 150-line (lowered from the original 200-line for added safety margin).

info.h: When the Nomogram Does NOT Apply
info.t: • Chronic/repeated supratherapeutic ingestion (ingestions spanning >24 hours) — use (ALT)(APAP) product instead • Unreliable history — conflicting statements, insufficient detail, symptoms inconsistent with history • Late presentation (>24 hours post-ingestion) • Unknown timing of ingestion • Extended-release formulations — may have delayed peak; if below treatment line but >10 mcg/mL, redraw in 4-6 hours

CYP2E1 inducers (increase toxic NAPQI production): • Isoniazid, rifampin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin • Chronic alcohol ingestion Glutathione depletion: • Chronic alcohol use, chronic APAP use, chronic liver disease • Malnutrition, fasting Decreased glucuronidation: • Gilbert disease, zidovudine, TMP-SMX ⚠️ Lower treatment thresholds in these patients — consider treating below the line if risk factors present.

Extended-release tablets: If level at 4-12h is below treatment line but >10 mcg/mL → redraw in 4-6 hours. Opioid/anticholinergic coingestants: Delay gastric emptying → delayed absorption peak. Same redraw logic if >10 mcg/mL. Level <4h post-ingestion: Undetectable level after >2h typically excludes significant ingestion. If detectable, redraw at ≥4h.

Bag 1: 150 mg/kg in 200 mL D5W over 60 min Bag 2: 50 mg/kg in 500 mL D5W over 4 hours Bag 3: 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL D5W over 16 hours Total: 300 mg/kg over 21 hours Advantages: 100% bioavailability, faster completion, avoids vomiting, preferred in pregnancy. Disadvantage: Anaphylactoid reactions (~10-20%, usually mild, during loading dose).

Loading: 140 mg/kg PO Maintenance: 70 mg/kg PO q4h × 17 additional doses Total: 1,330 mg/kg over 72 hours Advantages: No IV access needed, no anaphylactoid risk, higher hepatic first-pass delivery. Disadvantages: 72-hour duration, vomiting common (mix with cola), terrible smell/taste, lower systemic bioavailability (4-10%). Repeat dose if vomiting within 1 hour.

Bag 1: 200 mg/kg in D5W over 4 hours Bag 2: 100 mg/kg in D5W over 16 hours Total: 300 mg/kg over 20 hours Used in Australia/New Zealand. Lower rate of anaphylactoid reactions than the standard 3-bag protocol (slower initial infusion rate).

Pregnancy is NOT a contraindication to NAC. • Acetaminophen poses risk of hepatic failure to both mother and fetus • NAC is safe and beneficial in pregnancy • IV route preferred — achieves higher serum levels and avoids vomiting • Delayed treatment associated with increased miscarriage and fetal death

Cap the dose at 100 kg body weight per consensus guidelines. Using actual weight in morbidly obese patients leads to unnecessarily high doses with increased risk of fluid overload and anaphylactoid reactions.

NAC anaphylactoid reactions are histamine-mediated (direct drug effect), NOT IgE-mediated allergic reactions. They are NOT a contraindication to continuing NAC. Liver failure from inappropriately stopping NAC is far more dangerous than the anaphylactoid reaction itself. In a study of 6,455 treatment courses, no deaths were attributed to anaphylactoid reactions.
Usually occur during the loading dose (first 60 minutes). Almost always within the first 2 hours, and invariably within 6 hours of initiation.

Flushing only: → Continue NAC at same rate. Monitor closely. Urticaria: → Diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg IV (max 50 mg). Consider a corticosteroid. Continue NAC. Angioedema: → Diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg IV + corticosteroid. Hold NAC for 1 hour, then resume at slower rate. Respiratory symptoms or hypotension: → Diphenhydramine 1 mg/kg IV + corticosteroid + epinephrine (IM bolus or infusion). Hold NAC for 1 hour, then resume at slower rate.

• ALWAYS resume NAC — this is NOT a true allergy • Resume at a lower initial rate, then titrate up • Previous anaphylactoid reaction does NOT preclude future NAC use — can pre-treat with antihistamines • Document as "anaphylactoid reaction to NAC" — NOT as an allergy

• >30 grams ingested (or >0.5 g/kg if <60 kg) • APAP level above the 300 line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram These patients may present with early lactic acidosis and altered mental status within 12 hours — due to mitochondrial dysfunction, BEFORE liver damage occurs.

Standard NAC may be inadequate — NAC neutralizes NAPQI in a 1:1 molar ratio, so the dose must scale with the amount of acetaminophen. Keep Bag 1 + Bag 2 standard. Increase Bag 3 infusion rate based on severity: • Above 300 line: 12.5 mg/kg/hr (2× standard) • Above 450 line: 18.75 mg/kg/hr (3× standard) • Above 600 line: 25 mg/kg/hr (4× standard) During hemodialysis: Double the rate you would otherwise use (HD removes ~50% of NAC). Maximum rate: 25 mg/kg/hr. Doubling the rate is increasingly accepted; tripling/quadrupling is more controversial — consult toxicology.

Fomepizole inhibits CYP2E1, which prevents the conversion of acetaminophen to toxic NAPQI. Complementary mechanism to NAC (which detoxifies NAPQI after it forms). Dosing: 15 mg/kg IV over 30 min loading → 10 mg/kg IV q12h × 48h or until APAP undetectable. Generally safe. Main drawback is cost. Use for established high-risk ingestions alongside high-dose NAC.

EXTRIP indications for extracorporeal treatment: • APAP level >900 mcg/mL • Altered mental status + lactate >3 + pH <7.1 • Clinical deterioration despite adequate NAC Dialysis removes both APAP and toxic NAPQI metabolites. NOT a substitute for NAC — patients on dialysis require HIGHER NAC doses (at minimum 12.5 mg/kg/hr).

• Isoniazid (INH) — most clinically significant • Rifampin • Phenobarbital • Carbamazepine • Phenytoin • Chronic alcohol ingestion (NOT acute intoxication — acute alcohol actually competes with APAP for CYP2E1 and may be protective) These patients produce more NAPQI per dose of acetaminophen, overwhelming glutathione stores faster.

• Chronic alcohol use (double risk: CYP2E1 induction + glutathione depletion) • Chronic acetaminophen use (subacute glutathione depletion) • Chronic liver disease • Malnutrition / fasting — even brief fasting reduces hepatic glutathione Depleted glutathione stores cannot neutralize NAPQI, leading to hepatocellular necrosis at lower APAP doses.

• Gilbert's disease (genetic decrease in UDP-glucuronosyltransferase) • Zidovudine • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) Reduced glucuronidation shifts more acetaminophen through the CYP2E1 pathway → more NAPQI production.

Lower threshold for NAC treatment in patients with any of these risk factors. • Consider treating even if APAP level is below the nomogram treatment line • The "150 line" was already lowered from the original "200 line" to add a safety margin — but high-risk patients may need treatment even below 150 • Chronic alcohol + chronic APAP = "alcohol-tylenol syndrome" — hepatotoxicity at doses generally considered safe

Repeated supratherapeutic ingestion = multiple ingestions spanning >24 hours. This includes acute-on-chronic acetaminophen use. More common than acute overdose in clinical practice. Often more dangerous than appreciated due to subacute depletion of hepatic glutathione stores.

Chronic alcohol use + chronic acetaminophen ingestion can cause hepatotoxicity at doses that are generally considered safe (<4 g/day). Mechanism: chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 (more NAPQI) + depletes glutathione (less NAPQI neutralization) — a "double hit."

info.h: Why the Nomogram Does Not Apply
info.t: The Rumack-Matthew nomogram was validated for a single acute ingestion with known timing. In repeated ingestions: • There is no single "time of ingestion" to plot • Glutathione stores may already be depleted • APAP levels may be deceptively low despite significant hepatic injury Use the (ALT)(APAP) product instead: >10,000 strongly predicts hepatotoxicity, <1,500 makes it very unlikely.

Start NAC if: • APAP level is detectable AND ALT is elevated • (ALT)(APAP) product >10,000 • Clinical concern despite normal initial labs (consider risk factors) Consult toxicology/poison control — these cases are often complex. Monitor: Serial APAP levels, AST/ALT, INR q6h. The (ALT)(APAP) product can be recalculated with each set of labs to track trajectory.

Assess hemodynamic status and severity • Sepsis-3: infection + organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2) • Septic shock: vasopressor-dependent + lactate >2 Source evaluation by organ system Order labs, cultures, imaging Identify suspected infectious source

Airway & breathing stabilization 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid (LR preferred) Empiric antibiotics within 1 hour • Beta-lactam FIRST when also giving vancomycin MRSA coverage if risk factors present Source control within 6-12 hours Reassess at 1-3 hours

Norepinephrine — first-line vasopressor • Can start peripherally for <6 hours Second-line: vasopressin or epinephrine MAP targets & personalization Fluid responsiveness assessment Inotrope for low cardiac output Refractory shock management
Stress-dose hydrocortisone for vasopressor-dependent shock Septic cardiomyopathy recognition Transfusion threshold: Hgb ≤7 g/dL Sepsis mimics & differential
Resuscitation endpoints — MAP, CRT, UOP, lactate Antibiotic de-escalation at 48-72h Fluid & vasopressor weaning ICU admission criteria Floor admission criteria

• Administer within 1 hour of sepsis recognition • Beta-lactam FIRST when also giving vancomycin (improved survival) • Full loading dose regardless of renal function • Extended infusion for beta-lactam maintenance doses

Beta-lactam backbone (choose one): • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h (broadest anaerobic coverage) • Cefepime 2g IV q8h (antipseudomonal, less anaerobic) • Meropenem 1g IV q8h (reserve for MDR risk) Add MRSA coverage if risk factors: Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg IV load

Beta-lactam (ceftriaxone 2g IV or ampicillin-sulbactam) PLUS atypical coverage: • Doxycycline 100 mg IV q12h (preferred) OR • Azithromycin 500 mg IV If Pseudomonas risk (structural lung disease, recent abx, immunocompromised): Use antipseudomonal beta-lactam instead
Uncomplicated: Ceftriaxone 2g IV Complicated / Pseudomonas risk: Piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime ESBL risk: Meropenem 1g IV q8h Review prior urine cultures for resistance patterns

Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h (covers anaerobes) OR Meropenem 1g IV q8h (if ESBL/MDR concern) OR Cefepime + Metronidazole (alternative combination) C. difficile: Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID +/- IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h

Non-necrotizing: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam Necrotizing fasciitis: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin (toxin suppression) IVDU / line infection: Vancomycin + antipseudomonal beta-lactam

Vancomycin (MRSA coverage) + antipseudomonal beta-lactam • Remove suspected infected catheter after establishing alternative access • Draw cultures through line AND peripherally before removal Endocarditis suspected: Add gentamicin for synergy (consult ID)

• Prior MRSA infection or colonization • Recent hospitalization or long-term care • Hemodialysis • IV drug use • Central line or indwelling device • Soft tissue infection with purulence • Nosocomial / surgical site infection

• Structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, CF) • Recent broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure • Prolonged hospitalization or ICU stay • Neutropenia or immunosuppression • Known prior Pseudomonas cultures

Source control within 6-12 hours when feasible. Undrained foci may not respond to antibiotics alone. Balance: risk of intervention vs. patient stability. Decisions should consider diagnostic uncertainty regarding the source.

• Intravascular catheter infection: Remove catheter after establishing alternative access • Abscess (any site): Percutaneous or surgical drainage (thoracic empyema, peritoneal, joint, perirectal) • Ascending cholangitis: ERCP or percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography • Obstructing nephrolithiasis with infection: Percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteral stent • Bowel perforation/obstruction: Surgical repair • Necrotizing fasciitis: Emergent surgical debridement (do not delay) • Fulminant C. difficile colitis: Colectomy • Infected implantable device/hardware: Removal when feasible • Toxic shock syndrome: Drain or excise any toxin-producing focus, even minor
