Receptors: Alpha-1 >> Beta-1 Effect: Vasoconstriction + mild inotropy Dose: 0.01-3 mcg/kg/min Evidence: Multiple meta-analyses favor NE over dopamine. Standard of care. Pros: Reliable, well-studied, improves MAP without excessive tachycardia Cons: Digital/splanchnic ischemia at high doses

Receptors: V1 (vascular smooth muscle), V2 (renal) Effect: Non-adrenergic vasoconstriction Dose: 0.03-0.04 units/min (FIXED, non-titratable) Evidence: VASST — NE-sparing, no mortality benefit. VANISH — no renal benefit. Meta-analysis: lower AF risk (RR 0.77) Pros: NE-sparing, lower AF risk, no tachycardia Cons: No inotropy, splanchnic ischemia risk

Receptors: Alpha-1, Beta-1, Beta-2 Effect: Vasoconstriction + inotropy + chronotropy Dose: 0.01-0.5 mcg/kg/min Evidence: CAT trial — outcomes similar to NE Pros: Combines vasopressor + inotrope. Good for bradycardia/cardiac dysfunction Cons: Increases lactate (aerobic), tachyarrhythmia risk, worsens acidosis if lactate >5

Receptors: Pure Alpha-1 Effect: Vasoconstriction only — no inotropy, no chronotropy Dose: 100-200 mcg IV push; infusion 40-200 mcg/min Evidence: Limited. NOT recommended as primary vasopressor Use: Push-dose temporizer while preparing NE infusion. Consider for severe tachyarrhythmia (e.g., rapid AF) where beta stimulation is undesirable

DO NOT USE for septic shock Evidence: SOAP-II trial (n=1679) — dopamine associated with increased arrhythmias and mortality vs norepinephrine Reason: Dose-dependent receptor profile (dopaminergic → beta-1 → alpha-1) is unreliable. Higher rates of tachyarrhythmia. No role in modern sepsis management.

Receptors: Beta-1 >> Beta-2 Effect: Inotropy + mild vasodilation Dose: 2-20 mcg/kg/min Use: Low cardiac output despite adequate vasopressors (septic cardiomyopathy) Caution: May cause hypotension — up-titrate NE if BP drops. Not for supranormal cardiac index.

Mechanism: iNOS/eNOS inhibition → restores vascular tone Dose: 1-2 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.5 mg/kg/h infusion Evidence: Ibarra-Estrada 2023 RCT — shorter time to vasopressor discontinuation, more pressor-free days Use: Refractory shock on multiple vasopressors + glucocorticoids

30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within first 3 hours • Administer in 500 mL boluses, reassess between each • Stop if pulmonary edema develops or no further response • CLOVERS trial: restrictive vs liberal — similar mortality • CLASSIC trial: restrictive approach safe, trend toward less intubation

Balanced crystalloid preferred (Lactated Ringer's) • SMART trial: lower composite of death/RRT/persistent renal dysfunction vs 0.9% NaCl • AVOID HES — 6S trial: increased mortality (51 vs 43%) and RRT • No benefit to albumin vs crystalloid (SAFE trial) • No role for hypertonic saline • If bicarb indicated: isotonic bicarbonate (150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1L D5W)

• Obesity (BMI >30): Use ideal body weight for 30 mL/kg calculation • Heart failure: Smaller initial bolus acceptable — document rationale for CMS • ESRD: Same initial bolus recommended despite dialysis status • Pneumonia with mild hypotension: Fluid-conservative + early vasopressors • CMS SEP-1 allows <30 mL/kg if clinician documents reasoning

RESTRICT further fluids — most crystalloid extravasates (~95% leaves vasculature) • ICU patients receive ~1.5L/day from infusions + antibiotics alone • Track net fluid balance — avoid >4-5L net positive • Use dynamic measures for fluid responsiveness (PLR, IVC, PPV) • Fluid responsiveness is NORMAL — it does NOT mean give more fluid • Absence of fluid responsiveness suggests volume overload
• No clear infectious source identified • Procalcitonin unexpectedly low • Atypical clinical course • Not responding to appropriate antibiotics and resuscitation

• Endocarditis causing valve failure → cardiogenic shock (not distributive) • Tick-borne illness — anaplasmosis, babesiosis (exposure, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis) • Invasive candidiasis — ongoing critical illness, central line, colonization, TPN • Invasive aspergillosis — prolonged neutropenia, heme malignancy, steroids • PJP pneumonia — diffuse infiltrates, HIV, chronic steroids, immunosuppression

• Adrenal crisis — recent steroid d/c, vasopressor-refractory, eosinophilia, abdominal pain • Thyroid storm — tremors, thyromegaly, tachycardia, encephalopathy • DKA — hyperglycemia, anion gap (may coexist with sepsis!)

• Acute mesenteric ischemia — AF, vasculopathy, pain out of proportion → CTA • Bowel obstruction → CT abdomen • Pancreatitis — epigastric pain, elevated lipase • Fulminant hepatic failure — LFTs • Decompensated cirrhosis — does not exclude concurrent sepsis

• Salicylate intoxication — tachypnea, delirium, elevated AG → check salicylate level • Beta-blocker/CCB overdose — disproportionate bradycardia • Carbon monoxide — exposure history → carboxyhemoglobin • Metformin toxicity — disproportionate lactate elevation

• Anaphylaxis — rapid onset, hives, bronchospasm (treat both if uncertain) • HLH — cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, very high fevers → ferritin • DRESS/AGEP — skin exam, medication review • Aspiration pneumonitis — rapid onset AND often rapid recovery

Occurs in up to 50% of septic shock patients. Acute, biventricular myocardial dysfunction that is reversible within 7-10 days. Often under-recognized because systemic vasodilation may mask low EF (pseudo-normal LVEF).

• Low cardiac output (cool extremities) despite adequate MAP • Vasopressor-refractory shock • Preload unresponsiveness (not fluid responsive) • Narrow pulse pressure (<40 mmHg) • Profound systemic inflammation (toxic shock, gram-negative sepsis) • Prior history of heart failure • Abrupt vasopressor escalation without clear clinical trigger

LV Systolic: • LVEF <45% (may be pseudo-normal from vasodilation) • Reduced global longitudinal strain (GLS <-17%) • Reduced MAPSE LV Diastolic: • Lateral e' <8 cm/s (strongly predicts mortality) • Lateral E/e' >13 cm/s (suggests elevated LVEDP) RV Dysfunction: • TAPSE <16 mm • RV/LV ratio >0.6 • TDI S' <10 cm/s

• Avoid excessive vasoconstrictors — NE + vasopressin without inotropy is suboptimal • Inotrope: Dobutamine (first choice) or epinephrine • Stress-dose steroids (inflammatory cytokines worsen cardiomyopathy) • Treat fever, agitation, shivering (reduce O₂ demand) • Thiamine if deficiency possible • Fluid removal if significant congestion • Consider ECMO for pure cardiogenic failure phenotype • Do NOT discontinue dexmedetomidine without considering its sympatholytic effects on HR

• Acute MI (check ECG, troponin trend) • Myocarditis • Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy (usually no RV involvement) • LVOTO (LV outflow tract obstruction) • RV failure from PE • Chronic HF with superimposed septic cardiomyopathy

CMS SEP-1 uses Sepsis-2 definitions (not Sepsis-3). "Severe sepsis" = infection + organ dysfunction or lactate >2. "Septic shock" = SBP <90 not responsive to fluids, OR lactate ≥4 (regardless of hypotension). SEP-1 is currently pay-for-reporting, becoming pay-for-performance in 2026.

1. Measure serum lactate 2. Obtain 2 sets of blood cultures prior to antibiotic administration 3. Administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (within 1 hour when possible) 4. If hypotensive OR lactate ≥4 mmol/L: Administer 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid Notes: • Ideal body weight acceptable for BMI >30 • <30 mL/kg acceptable if clinician documents reasoning (e.g., CHF concern) • Blood cultures should not delay antibiotics in critically ill patients

1. Remeasure lactate if initial >2 mmol/L 2. If hypotensive OR lactate ≥4 in first 6 hours: • Administer IV vasopressors to achieve MAP ≥65 mmHg • Reassess intravascular volume status and tissue perfusion Reassessment options: • Repeat focused exam (vitals, cardiopulmonary, CRT, skin, UOP) • Any two of: CVP, ScvO2, bedside echo, PLR, or fluid challenge

• SEP-1 does NOT require vasopressor dependence for "septic shock" • SEP-1 uses lactate ≥4 as standalone shock criterion • Sepsis-3 requires both vasopressor need + lactate >2 • SSC 2021 guidelines largely align with Sepsis-3, not CMS criteria

Assess for hard signs vs soft signs • Hard signs: Hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis • Soft signs: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity Risk factors: DM, immunocompromise, IVDU, recent surgery LRINEC Score — adjunct only, does NOT rule out CT imaging if diagnosis uncertain

Call surgery IMMEDIATELY • Each hour of surgical delay increases mortality 2-3% • Do NOT wait for imaging, labs, or hemodynamic stability Bedside finger test if surgery delayed Anatomic location guides microbiology • Fournier gangrene — perineal NSTI • Head/neck NSTI — airway threat

Triple therapy within 1 hour • Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h (or meropenem) • Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h (or vancomycin for MRSA) • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h (CRITICAL for toxin suppression) Vibrio — saltwater: add doxycycline + cephalosporin Aeromonas — freshwater: add doxycycline + fluoroquinolone De-escalate based on culture results at 48-72h

Clindamycin for toxin suppression • Beta-lactams may paradoxically increase toxin release IVIG for streptococcal TSS • 1 g/kg day 1, then 0.5 g/kg days 2-3 Hyperbaric oxygen — controversial • Never delay surgery for HBO
Serial wound exams every 4-6 hours • Mark borders with time at each exam Return to OR every 24-48 hours All NSTI patients require ICU admission Mortality: 25-35% overall, 40% Fournier, >50% Vibrio

At least 2 organisms, often 4-5+ Organisms: • Anaerobes: Bacteroides, Clostridium, Peptostreptococcus • Aerobic streptococci (non-Group A) • Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Klebsiella) • Enterococci Clinical associations: • Diabetes mellitus • Post-operative infections • Fournier gangrene • Trunk/torso involvement • Older patients with comorbidities

Single organism, often more virulent Most common organisms: • Group A Streptococcus (GAS) — most common, associated with toxic shock • MRSA — up to 1/3 of Type II infections • Clostridium perfringens — traumatic, contaminated wounds Clinical associations: • Extremity involvement • Younger, healthier patients • Often no clear entry point • Higher association with TSS

Proposed separate category Vibrio vulnificus: • Saltwater exposure (Gulf Coast, warm coastal waters) • Raw oyster ingestion • Liver cirrhosis = 100x increased risk • Extremely rapid progression • >50% mortality Vibrio parahaemolyticus: • Similar exposure risks • Generally less severe than V. vulnificus

Distinct entity with muscle involvement Organisms: • Clostridium perfringens (most common) • C. septicum (associated with colon cancer — get colonoscopy) • C. novyi, C. histolyticum Characteristics: • Gas production in tissues (crepitus) • Extremely rapid progression • Bronze skin discoloration • Sweet, foul odor • Traumatic or post-surgical

Polymicrobial perineal NSTI Sources: • Urologic (UTI, instrumentation) • Colorectal (perianal abscess, fistula) • Dermatologic (skin infection, trauma) Risk factors: • Diabetes mellitus (most common) • Alcoholism • Immunocompromise Mortality: ~40%

Triple therapy: 1. Broad-spectrum beta-lactam: • Pip-tazo 4.5g IV q6h — preferred • Meropenem 1g IV q8h — if MDR risk 2. MRSA coverage: • Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h — preferred • Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg load — alternative 3. Toxin suppression (ALWAYS include): • Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h Give antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition.

Saltwater (Vibrio vulnificus): • ADD Doxycycline 100 mg IV q12h • ADD Ceftriaxone 2g IV q24h (or ceftazidime) Freshwater (Aeromonas): • ADD Doxycycline 100 mg IV q12h • ADD Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h

When cultures finalize (48-72 hours): Group A Streptococcus: • Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h • PLUS Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h MRSA: • Vancomycin or Linezolid • PLUS Clindamycin if toxin-producing Clostridial: • Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h • PLUS Clindamycin 900 mg IV q8h

Total duration: 7-14 days Continue IV therapy: • 48-72 hours after final debridement • Until clinical improvement evident Transition to oral: • When tolerating oral intake • Appropriate oral options based on culture • Complete remainder of course as outpatient if stable

• Assess for classic signs: mydriasis, yawning, diaphoresis, piloerection, rhinorrhea, lacrimation • History: craving, dysphoria, myalgias, GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping) • Calculate COWS score to grade severity

• Rule out ethanol/sedative withdrawal (seizures, hyperthermia = NOT opioid WD) • Labs: BMP if significant vomiting/diarrhea (hypoK, hypoMg → QT risk) • ECG if methadone use or combining QT-prolonging meds
• Buprenorphine: 8 mg SL → reassess 30–60 min → repeat to max 32 mg • Microdosing: 0.5–2 mg if on full agonist or fentanyl-dependent • Methadone: 20 mg PO or 10 mg IM (QT risk, not preferred)

• Clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg PO q1h (max 0.8 mg/day) for autonomic symptoms • Lofexidine 0.54 mg PO q5–6h (FDA-approved for OW) • Diazepam 5–10 mg IV or lorazepam 1–2 mg IV for anxiety • Ondansetron 4 mg for nausea; loperamide 4 mg for diarrhea • NSAIDs/acetaminophen for body aches
• Naloxone-precipitated: buprenorphine 16–32 mg SL (short-acting, resolves 1–2h) • Naltrexone-precipitated: aggressive non-opioid adjuncts, IV fluids, consider ICU

• Discharge with bridge Rx (3–7 day buprenorphine) + MOUD referral within 72h • Harm reduction: naloxone kit, fentanyl test strips, overdose risk counseling • Admit if: hemodynamic instability, intractable vomiting, naltrexone depot WD, pregnancy

0–4: No Withdrawal — Observe. Do not initiate buprenorphine (risk of precipitated withdrawal if full agonist still active). Reassess in 1–2 hours. 5–12: Mild Withdrawal — May initiate buprenorphine if COWS ≥ 8 (traditional threshold). Consider symptomatic treatment alone if patient prefers. 13–24: Moderate Withdrawal — Initiate opioid agonist therapy. This is the recommended threshold for fentanyl-dependent patients to reduce BPOW risk. 25–36: Moderately Severe — Aggressive treatment. High-dose buprenorphine (up to 32 mg) or methadone + adjunctive medications. 37–47: Severe Withdrawal — Emergent treatment. IV fluids for dehydration. Close monitoring for hemodynamic instability.

Fentanyl is highly lipophilic with slow tissue clearance. Traditional COWS ≥ 8 threshold carries higher risk of buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal (BPOW) in fentanyl-dependent patients. Many experts now recommend: • Wait for COWS ≥ 13 before standard buprenorphine induction • Consider microdosing (0.5–2 mg) as alternative to avoid BPOW entirely • BPOW rate remains < 1% even in fentanyl-era studies with standard dosing • If BPOW occurs: treat with MORE buprenorphine (up to 16–32 mg), not less
Most reliable signs for clinical assessment (interrater κ): • Piloerection: 0.94 • Yawning: 0.93 • Mydriasis: 0.90 • Perspiration: 0.88 • Rhinorrhea: 0.87

info.pt: QT Prolongation Risk in Opioid Withdrawal
info.t: • Methadone — dose-dependent QT prolongation. Highest risk among OW medications. ECG recommended at doses > 100 mg/day. • Ondansetron — dose-dependent QT prolongation, particularly IV route • Loperamide — QT prolongation at supratherapeutic doses (used recreationally as “poor man’s methadone” at high doses) • Lofexidine — mild QT prolongation; ECG monitoring recommended

info.pt: QT Prolongation Risk in Opioid Withdrawal
info.t: • Hypokalemia — from vomiting, diarrhea. Directly prolongs QT. • Hypomagnesemia — from GI losses. Prevents correction of hypokalemia. • Both exacerbate drug-induced QT prolongation • BMP with Mg level recommended before starting methadone

info.pt: QT Prolongation Risk in Opioid Withdrawal
info.t: • All patients receiving methadone (especially > 40 mg) • When combining 2+ QT-prolonging medications • Significant vomiting or diarrhea (electrolyte depletion) • History of cardiac disease, syncope, or known long QT • QTc > 450 ms: discuss risks/benefits of QT-prolonging agents • QTc > 500 ms: avoid or discontinue QT-prolonging agents

info.pt: QT Prolongation Risk in Opioid Withdrawal
info.t: • Buprenorphine does NOT significantly prolong QT — preferred opioid agonist • Clonidine does NOT prolong QT • Benzodiazepines do NOT prolong QT • NSAIDs/acetaminophen do NOT prolong QT

When: COWS ≥ 8–12, short-acting opioid use (heroin, oxycodone) 1. Administer 8 mg SL buprenorphine 2. Observe 30–60 minutes 3. If withdrawal persists: give additional 4–8 mg SL 4. Repeat until symptom control or COWS < 8 5. Maximum Day 1 total: 32 mg 6. Discharge with 3–7 day bridge prescription + follow-up Key: If buprenorphine precipitates withdrawal, treat with MORE buprenorphine (not less) — up to 16–32 mg total.

When: Fentanyl-dependent patients, severe withdrawal (COWS ≥ 13) • Starting dose up to 16 mg SL (vs traditional 4–8 mg) • Total Day 1 dose up to 32 mg SL • 579-patient case series: no respiratory depression at ≥ 12 mg starting doses • 439-patient study: safe and effective in confirmed fentanyl exposure • High-dose approach increasingly preferred in the fentanyl era • BPOW rate < 0.5% with 7-day extended-release SQ buprenorphine 24 mg

When: Patient still on full agonist, early/mild withdrawal, cannot abstain long enough for standard induction • Start 0.5–2 mg SL while patient continues opioid use • Gradually increase buprenorphine while tapering full agonist • Dosing frequency based on COWS score • Avoids precipitated withdrawal entirely • Feasibility confirmed in ED setting • Outpatient protocols typically span 6–10 days • Particularly valuable for methadone-to-buprenorphine transitions

• Prescribe buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) for outpatient use • Bridge supply: 3–7 days minimum (longer if follow-up barriers exist) • Typical maintenance: 16 mg/day SL • Follow-up with addiction medicine within 72 hours • No X-waiver required since December 2022 • Any clinician with DEA Schedule III authority can prescribe

Many patients in opioid withdrawal have a pulse and blood pressure within normal limits. Only a small minority manifest both hypertension AND tachycardia, and when present, these are almost always from iatrogenically precipitated withdrawal (naloxone/naltrexone). In contrast, normal vital signs in ethanol or sedative withdrawal are the exception rather than the rule.
You were treated in the emergency department for opioid withdrawal. Your symptoms have improved, and you are being discharged with a plan for follow-up care.

If you were started on buprenorphine (Suboxone/Subutex): • Take your medication exactly as prescribed • Place the tablet/film under your tongue and let it dissolve completely • Do not swallow, chew, or cut the tablet • Wait at least 30 minutes before eating or drinking • Do NOT use other opioids, benzodiazepines, or alcohol while on this medication — this can cause life-threatening breathing problems

• Keep your follow-up appointment with addiction medicine / opioid treatment program • If you were given a bridge prescription, you have a limited supply — attend your follow-up before it runs out • If you cannot reach your follow-up provider, call the SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 (free, 24/7)

Your risk of overdose is highest right now. When you go through withdrawal, your body loses its tolerance to opioids. If you use the same amount you were using before, it can cause a fatal overdose. • If you use again, start with a much smaller amount • Never use alone • Keep your naloxone (Narcan) kit nearby at all times • Teach someone close to you how to use naloxone

Nasal spray: 1. Lay the person on their back 2. Insert the nozzle into one nostril 3. Press the plunger firmly to release the dose 4. If no response in 2–3 minutes, give a second dose in the other nostril 5. Call 911 immediately 6. Stay with the person — naloxone wears off in 30–90 minutes and overdose symptoms may return

info.h: Return to the Emergency Department If
info.t: • You cannot keep any food or liquids down • You feel dizzy, weak, or faint when standing • You develop chest pain or difficulty breathing • You develop a fever (temperature > 100.4°F / 38°C) • You have a seizure • You feel you may harm yourself

• SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 (free, 24/7, English/Spanish) • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 • Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222 • Ask your provider about fentanyl test strips and safe use supplies

• Verify alcohol history — pattern, timing, prior withdrawal/seizures/DT • Fingerstick glucose, electrolytes (Ca/Mg/Phos), CBC, INR, LFTs • CXR, consider CT head (exclude SDH) • Thiamine 100-500 mg IV • Exclude alternatives — infection, trauma, hepatic encephalopathy, drug OD

• PAWSS score ≥4 predicts clinically significant withdrawal • Assess severity — minor vs moderate-severe vs seizure vs DT • Minor → outpatient with oral chlordiazepoxide or phenobarbital taper • Asymptomatic at-risk → prophylactic phenobarbital 10-15 mg/kg

• Screen contraindications • Loading: 10 mg/kg IV over 30 min (ideal body weight) • Titration: 130 mg IV q30 min PRN, target RASS 0 to -1 • Soft stop: 20 mg/kg — re-evaluate diagnosis • Hard stop: 30 mg/kg — symptoms likely NOT withdrawal • Auto-tapers over ~3-4 days — minimal additional therapy needed

• Select agent: diazepam (most) or lorazepam (cirrhosis) • Symptom-triggered: diazepam 5-10 mg IV q5-10 min when CIWA-Ar ≥8 • Front-loading for high-risk patients • Refractory DT: add phenobarbital 130-260 mg IV q15-20 min • If still refractory: propofol infusion (requires intubation)

• Phenobarbital 15-20 mg/kg IV — treats seizure AND withdrawal • Phenytoin is NOT effective for withdrawal seizures • Consider pyridoxine 100 mg IV/PO • Seizures tend to recur — up to 1/3 progress to DT if untreated

• Thiamine: 500 mg IV q8h if altered (Wernicke), 100 mg IV daily if normal • Magnesium: aggressively replete (often severely depleted) • Potassium and phosphate repletion • IV fluids until euvolemic • Monitor glucose — risk of hypoglycemia • Watch for refeeding syndrome in malnourished patients

• ICU: DT, refractory withdrawal, intubated, significant comorbidities • Floor: controlled withdrawal needing monitoring/taper • Discharge: resolved, tolerating PO, safe disposition • Consider initiating AUD medication before discharge • Naltrexone (first-line) or acamprosate (cirrhosis-safe)

• Half-life: ~3-4 days — allows gradual auto-taper • Volume of distribution: ~0.65 L/kg • Bioavailability: ~100% by all routes (IV, PO, IM) • IV onset: <30 minutes for full distribution • PO onset: Slower, risk of dose stacking if doses given <60 min apart • Serum level = cumulative dose ÷ (0.65 × weight in kg)

• 10 mg/kg → ~15 μg/mL (low therapeutic — minimal sedation) • 15 mg/kg → ~23 μg/mL (mid therapeutic) • 20 mg/kg → ~30 μg/mL (high therapeutic — SOFT STOP) • 25 mg/kg → ~38 μg/mL (near upper limit) • 30 mg/kg → ~46 μg/mL (HARD STOP) Therapeutic range (epilepsy): 15-40 μg/mL Mild toxicity (ataxia, nystagmus): ~50 μg/mL Stupor/coma: >65 μg/mL

1. Dual mechanism: ↑ GABA (duration of channel opening) + ↓ glutamate (AMPA/kainate receptors) — well matched to withdrawal pathophysiology 2. Uniform efficacy: No patient is truly phenobarbital-refractory (unlike benzos, which fail in ~5-10%) 3. No paradoxical agitation: Benzos can cause paradoxical reactions (~2% in alcoholics) 4. Predictable pharmacokinetics: Linear dose-level relationship, measurable levels 5. Greater therapeutic index: Toxic dose (>40 mg/kg) is far above therapeutic dose (10-25 mg/kg) 6. Auto-taper: Long half-life provides days of ongoing protection 7. Superior seizure prophylaxis: More potent anti-epileptic activity than benzos 8. Levels can be checked: If lost, check

• Synergistic with benzodiazepines — never titrate both simultaneously • After large phenobarbital load (>15 mg/kg), patients are sensitive to ANY benzodiazepine • Communicate total dose to all subsequent providers • Use ideal body weight for dosing (water-soluble drug) • Induces hepatic CYP enzymes with prolonged use — affects methadone, other drug metabolism

Some patients with alcohol withdrawal evolve into a non-alcohol-related delirium (NARD). This is well-described with benzodiazepines (benzodiazepine-induced delirium) and can also occur with phenobarbital. The critical danger: Continuing GABAergic medications for NARD creates a vicious cycle of over-medication → worsening delirium → more medication → stupor/coma.

• Patient remains agitated/belligerent but NO other signs of withdrawal (no tremor, normal BP, no tachycardia) • Symptoms persist >2-3 days after admission — increasingly likely to be nonspecific delirium • Already received >20 mg/kg phenobarbital (or equivalent high-dose benzodiazepines) without improvement • Delirium without hyperadrenergic signs • Patient becomes somnolent after moderate-low doses of benzodiazepine

1. STOP escalating GABAergic medications (phenobarbital AND benzodiazepines) 2. Evaluate for other causes of delirium: • Infection (pneumonia, UTI, meningitis) • Metabolic (hepatic encephalopathy, electrolyte derangements, hypoglycemia) • Medication-induced (propylene glycol toxicity from IV lorazepam, anticholinergics) • Structural (subdural hematoma, stroke) 3. Treat symptomatically: • Haloperidol 2-5 mg IV PRN for agitation • Dexmedetomidine for overnight sedation — stop in morning and reassess • Address contributing factors (sleep deprivation, pain, constipation) 4. Consider flumazenil if benzodiazepines were used — 84% of patients improved in one case series

• NNT: 12 (prevent return to heavy drinking), 20 (prevent any drinking) • Dosing: 25 mg PO daily × 3-7 days → 50 mg PO daily • Strengths: Once daily, reduces cravings, supports abstinence OR reduced consumption • Limitations: Requires LFT monitoring q6 months • Contraindications: Current opioid use, LFTs >5× normal, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, GFR <45

• NNT: 9-12 (prevent return to any drinking) • Dosing: 666 mg PO TID (1998 mg/day) • Strengths: Not hepatically metabolized — safe in cirrhosis. May improve sleep • Limitations: TID dosing challenging for adherence. Best for abstinence goal only • Contraindications: GFR <30 mL/min

• Evidence: Weakest among AUD medications. One large RCT failed to find benefit • Dosing: Variable (typically 300-1800 mg/day in divided doses) • Strengths: Safe in cirrhosis (renally cleared). May help with residual withdrawal, neuropathy • Limitations: ~1% misuse/abuse risk in general population • Contraindications: Renal failure, concurrent opioid use

• Evidence: OR 1.88 for maintaining abstinence, decreased heavy drinking days by 9% • Dosing: Slow titration required to minimize side effects • Strengths: May help comorbid seizure disorder • Limitations: Hard to tolerate (metabolic acidosis, somnolence, paresthesia). Hepatically cleared • Contraindications: Moderate-advanced cirrhosis, nephrolithiasis, narrow-angle glaucoma

• Mechanism: Aversion therapy — blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → severe reaction with alcohol • Dosing: 250 mg PO daily (supervised) • Strengths: Effective with supervised administration • Limitations: Most toxic agent. Hepatotoxicity, disulfiram reactions (flushing, chest pain, hypotension). Multiple contraindications • Contraindications: Cirrhosis, renal dysfunction, seizure disorder, CAD, psychosis, impulsivity

• If one agent fails, stop and try another — combination therapy has not been shown superior • Optimal duration: at least 6 months • Medical therapy should be combined with psychosocial interventions • Hospitalization provides a useful opportunity to initiate MAUD — associated with reduced ED visits and readmissions

• If altered mental status or Wernicke possible: 500 mg IV q8h × 2-3 days • If normal mental status: 100 mg IV daily to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy • Always give thiamine BEFORE or WITH glucose — glucose metabolism consumes thiamine • Transition to PO (100 mg daily) at discharge • Wernicke encephalopathy can mimic alcohol withdrawal — when in doubt, treat with high-dose thiamine

Magnesium: • Alcoholics often have severe total-body magnesium deficit • May require multiple IV doses or continuous infusion • Hypomagnesemia predisposes to dysrhythmias and seizures, inhibits thiamine response Potassium: • Hypokalemia common from renal/extrarenal losses and aldosterone changes • Correct Mg first — hypokalemia is refractory if Mg is low Phosphate: • Monitor closely — risk of refeeding syndrome in malnourished patients • Severe hypophosphatemia can cause cardiac failure and rhabdomyolysis

• IV fluids: Isotonic saline until clinically euvolemic. Nearly all patients are hypovolemic from diaphoresis, vomiting, decreased intake • Glucose: Monitor fingerstick intermittently. Patients with cirrhosis have impaired glycogen reserves — higher hypoglycemia risk • Do NOT use "banana bags" — may not meet individual patient needs for specific substrates

• Patients with chronic alcoholism are frequently malnourished with high metabolic needs • Initially NPO if aspiration risk is present • Parenteral glucose initially, but plan enteral nutrition within 1-2 days • Refeeding syndrome risk: Monitor phosphate, potassium, magnesium. Start feeds slowly in severely malnourished patients • Folate and multivitamin supplementation

6+ hours — Minor withdrawal: • Tremulousness, anxiety, insomnia • GI upset, anorexia, headache • Diaphoresis, palpitations • Can begin while BAL is still elevated • Resolves within 24-48 hours if withdrawal does not progress 8-12 hours — Alcoholic hallucinosis: • Visual hallucinations (most common), auditory, tactile • Patient is AWARE they are hallucinating and often distressed • Clear sensorium — NOT the same as delirium tremens • Vital signs usually normal • Resolves within 24-48 hours 12-48 hours — Withdrawal seizures: • Generalized tonic-clonic, usually brief, self-limiting • Peak risk at 12-24 hours • Tend to cluster (2-6 seizures) • Up to 1/3 progress to DT if untreated • Recurrent or

• Age >65 • Concurrent illness or comorbid conditions (especially TBI) • Physiologic dependence on GABAergic agents (benzodiazepines) • Long duration of heavy, regular consumption • Multiple prior withdrawal episodes • History of withdrawal seizures, DT, or intubation • Elevated BAL on admission with active withdrawal symptoms • Longer time since last drink at presentation • Marked autonomic hyperactivity on presentation • PAWSS score ≥4

• Delirium tremens • Refractory withdrawal requiring phenobarbital + benzodiazepine combination • Need for or anticipated need for intubation/mechanical ventilation • Significant comorbidities that could be exacerbated by withdrawal (cardiovascular disease, sepsis) • Recurrent seizures or status epilepticus • Temperature >40°C (104°F) • Cumulative phenobarbital >15 mg/kg with concurrent benzodiazepines • Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support • Concurrent medical/surgical emergency

• Continuous: vitals, SpO2, cardiac rhythm • Frequent: neurologic assessment, fluid balance, urine output • Use RASS (not CIWA-Ar) for intubated patients — target RASS 0 to -2 • Reassess medication regimen daily — wean sedation and reassess • Monitor for complications: aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac dysrhythmias

• Hepatic encephalopathy — patients have excess GABA stimulation, extremely sensitive to GABAergics. Risk of prolonged coma • Severe respiratory depression without ventilatory support • Porphyria • Wrong diagnosis — if diagnostic uncertainty exists, phenobarbital's long half-life means side effects will also be long-lasting

• Already received large dose of benzodiazepines — synergistic sedation risk. Reduce or omit loading dose • Advanced cirrhosis (without encephalopathy) — reduced metabolism • Age >65 — increased sensitivity • Cardiovascular disease — monitor closely • COPD — respiratory depression risk • Volume depletion — correct before loading • Morbid obesity — use ideal body weight for dosing • Complex neurologic problems — may need close attention with ongoing dose titration; consider benzodiazepines for more flexible management

• Diagnostic uncertainty (use short-acting midazolam test dose first) • Hepatic encephalopathy risk • Advanced cirrhosis (use lorazepam — no active metabolites) • Already committed to benzodiazepine regimen with significant doses given • Complex patient with multiple fluctuating neurologic issues

• Determine diagnosis status — known hemophilia, known vWD, or suspected • If suspected: CBC, PT/PTT, fibrinogen → isolated prolonged PTT suggests hemophilia • Classify severity: Severe <1%, Moderate 1–5%, Mild 5–40% • 30% of hemophilia is de novo — no family history

• Hemarthrosis: 40–60% — single dose often adequate • Muscle/soft tissue: 40–60% — q12–24h × 2–3 days • Iliopsoas: 80% × 3 days, then >50% — admit, strict bed rest • ICH: 100% STAT — factor BEFORE imaging • Mucosal: 30–50% + antifibrinolytics • GI hemorrhage: 80–100% • Hematuria: 50% + hydration 1.5×, NO antifibrinolytics • Major trauma: 100% STAT

• FVIII: 1 unit/kg → +2% level. Dose = (Target% − Baseline%) ÷ 2 × Weight • FIX: 1 unit/kg → +1% level. Dose = (Target% − Baseline%) × Weight • Half-life: FVIII 8–12h, FIX 18–24h • Round up to nearest whole vial
• Inhibitors: ≥5 BU → bypassing agents (FEIBA or rFVIIa) • Mild hemophilia A: DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV may suffice • vWD: Desmopressin if documented responder, otherwise vWF concentrate

info.t: • von Willebrand disease (most types) • Qualitative platelet disorders • Factor XIII deficiency (not detected by standard PT/PTT) • Fibrinolytic disorders If vWD suspected: Send vWF:Ag, vWF:RCo activity, and factor VIII level. Interpret with caution — vWF is an acute phase reactant (false negatives during acute illness).

info.pt: Bleeding Disorder Differential by Lab Pattern
info.t: Primary hemostasis: Platelet plug formation (vWF mediates platelet adhesion + aggregation) Secondary hemostasis: Coagulation cascade reinforces platelet plug with fibrin • Initiation: Tissue factor + Factor VII → activates Factor X and IX • Amplification: Thrombin activates Factors V, VIII, IX (positive feedback) • Propagation: Factor X-V complex generates large-scale thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin • Factor XIII crosslinks fibrin strands → stable clot

Recombinant (preferred): • Advate (octocog alfa) • Kogenate FS / Kovaltry (octocog alfa) • Xyntha / Xyntha Solofuse (moroctocog alfa) • Nuwiq (simoctocog alfa) Extended half-life (~1.5× standard): • Eloctate / Elocta (efmoroctocog alfa — Fc fusion) • Adynovate (rurioctocog alfa pegol — PEGylated) • Jivi (damoctocog alfa pegol — PEGylated) • Esperoct (turoctocog alfa pegol) • Altuviiio (efanesoctocog alfa — VWF-XTEN fusion, ~4× half-life) Plasma-derived: • Humate-P (also contains vWF — usable for vWD) • Koate-DVI • Hemofil M

Recombinant (preferred): • BeneFIX (nonacog alfa) • Rixubis (nonacog gamma) Extended half-life (~3× standard): • Alprolix (eftrenonacog alfa — Fc fusion) • Idelvion (albutrepenonacog alfa — albumin fusion) • Rebinyn (nonacog beta pegol — PEGylated) Plasma-derived: • AlphaNine SD • Mononine

FEIBA (anti-inhibitor coagulant complex) • Contains activated vitamin-K-dependent factors • 50–75 U/kg (joints) to 100 U/kg (life-threatening) • Max 200 U/kg/day rFVIIa — NovoSeven (eptacog alfa) • 90 mcg/kg q2–3h × 3 doses OR 270 mcg/kg × 1 • Preferred for FIX inhibitors (allergic risk to FIX in FEIBA) Equally efficacious (FENOC trial). Some patients respond better to one.

Emicizumab (Hemlibra): • Bispecific antibody — bridges FIXa and FX (mimics FVIII function) • Hemophilia A prophylaxis only (with or without inhibitors) • Does NOT treat acute bleeds — still need factor or bypassing agents • Interferes with aPTT-based coagulation assays Resource-limited alternatives: • Cryoprecipitate: 1 bag/6 kg (max 10) for hemophilia A or severe vWD • FFP: 15 mL/kg for hemophilia B

No clear evidence that switching factor brands increases inhibitor risk. In emergencies where the patient's specific brand is unavailable: • Use an alternative brand of the same factor type • Prefer recombinant over plasma-derived when switching • Document the switch for the patient's hematologist

Alloantibodies against infused clotting factor that neutralize its hemostatic activity. Development is the most significant complication of hemophilia treatment. • Hemophilia A: ~33% develop inhibitors • Hemophilia B: ~6.5% develop inhibitors Risk factors: specific genotypes, young age at first exposure, early intensive therapy.

Low titer: <5 Bethesda Units (BU)/mL • Can often be overcome with higher-dose factor replacement • Loading dose: [Weight × 80 × (1−Hct) × titer BU] + 50 U/kg additional • Check post-infusion levels — if poor response, reclassify as high titer High titer: ≥5 BU/mL • Factor replacement is INEFFECTIVE • Requires bypassing agents (FEIBA or rFVIIa) Low-responding: Inhibitor stays <5 BU despite repeated factor exposure High-responding: Inhibitor rises ≥5 BU after factor exposure (anamnestic response)

FEIBA: • Joint bleeds: 50–75 U/kg IV • Life-threatening: 100 U/kg IV • Repeat q12h as needed • ⚠️ Maximum 200 U/kg/day (thrombotic risk) rFVIIa (NovoSeven): • Standard: 90 mcg/kg IV q2–3h × 3 doses • Single high dose: 270 mcg/kg IV × 1 • After single high dose: subsequent doses 90 mcg/kg, separated by ≥6h Administer within 1 hour of bleeding onset when possible.

• FENOC trial: equally efficacious for joint bleeds • Some patients respond better to one vs the other • Prefer rFVIIa for: — Factor IX deficiency with inhibitors (allergic reaction risk to FIX in FEIBA) — Factor VIII deficiency if limiting FVIII exposure while awaiting inhibitor titer decrease • Refractory bleeds (10–20% of cases): Sequential alternating FEIBA and rFVIIa q6h — Reserve for life/limb-threatening bleeds — Hematology guidance mandatory — Series of 20 patients: safe (no thrombosis, DIC, or thrombocytopenia)

• Inhibitor titers are NOT useful acutely (results take days) • Suspect inhibitor if: Factor infusion produces little-to-no response • Check post-infusion factor levels at 30–60 min — poor rise suggests inhibitor • Patients on emicizumab: aPTT will be falsely normal — NOT reliable for monitoring • If inhibitor suspected in previously uninhibited patient: treat the acute bleed, then arrange hematology follow-up for formal Bethesda assay

Requirements: Documented prior desmopressin challenge response Contraindicated in: Type 2B vWD (worsens thrombocytopenia) • IV: 0.3 mcg/kg (dilute in 50 mL NS, infuse over 20–30 min) • Intranasal: 150 mcg (<50 kg) or 300 mcg (≥50 kg) • Use HIGH-CONCENTRATION spray (Stimate® 150 mcg/spray) • Max 2–3 doses (tachyphylaxis) • Restrict fluids to maintenance × 24h • Use NS if IV fluids needed • Monitor electrolytes with repeated doses • Side effects: facial swelling, headache, water retention

For patients NOT responsive to desmopressin: • Loading: 30–60 RCo units/kg IV • Maintenance: 20–40 RCo units/kg q12–48h • Target: vWF:RCo and FVIII >50 IU/dL • Duration: 3–5 days • Monitor daily trough levels

info.h: vWF Concentrate — Major Bleeding or Surgery
info.t: • Loading: 40–60 RCo units/kg IV • Maintenance: 20–40 RCo units/kg q8–24h • Target: vWF:RCo and FVIII >50 IU/dL • Duration: at least 7 days • Monitor daily trough levels • ⚠️ Watch for excessive FVIII accumulation (thrombotic risk)

Antifibrinolytics (for mucosal bleeding): • Aminocaproic acid: 50–60 mg/kg PO/IV q6h (max 5 g) × 5–7 days • Tranexamic acid: 10–15 mg/kg PO/IV q8–12h • ⚠️ CONTRAINDICATED with hematuria (renal thrombi risk) • Check UA before starting Menorrhagia: • First-line: Hormonal contraceptives (OCPs) • Adjuncts: DDAVP (if responsive) + antifibrinolytics Resource-limited settings: • Cryoprecipitate: 1 bag/6 kg (max 10 bags) — contains both vWF and FVIII

Type 1 (80%): Usually responds to DDAVP. Concentrate if non-responder. Type 2A: DDAVP may partially work. Concentrate preferred for significant bleeds. Type 2B: DDAVP CONTRAINDICATED. Use vWF concentrate. Type 2M: Variable DDAVP response. Test before relying on it. Type 2N: Mimics hemophilia A (low FVIII). Concentrate required. Type 3: Undetectable vWF. Severe phenotype. Concentrate always required.

• Factor BEFORE imaging for ICH/trauma — do NOT delay • Assume severe if baseline factor level unknown • Antifibrinolytics CONTRAINDICATED with hematuria • Check post-infusion levels at 30–60 min for major bleeds • Poor factor response → suspect inhibitor → switch to bypassing agent • Round dose UP to nearest whole vial • FVIII half-life: 8–12h (redose q8–12h) • FIX half-life: 18–24h (redose q18–24h)

• Chest radiography interpretation • AFB smear + NAA testing • Interpret AFB/NAA results • Mycobacterial culture + drug susceptibility • Diagnosis confirmed — select treatment pathway
• RIPE regimen — standard 6-month treatment • 2-month sputum culture check • 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen • Hepatotoxicity assessment • Hepatotoxicity management — stepwise rechallenge

• Resistance classification — mono, MDR, XDR • INH monoresistance treatment • MDR-TB approach • BPaL / BPaLM regimens

Presumptive TB — Initiate Treatment • Highest confidence for TB diagnosis • Start empiric RIPE regimen immediately • Isolate with airborne precautions • Await culture for species confirmation and drug susceptibility • Notify public health department

GeneXpert MTB/RIF: Simultaneously detects M. tuberculosis AND rifampin resistance. Results in 2 hours. WHO-recommended initial diagnostic test. AFB Smear Sensitivity: 50–80% for pulmonary TB (higher with cavitary disease). Fluorochrome staining preferred over Ziehl-Neelsen. NAA Sensitivity: 95–98% in smear-positive specimens, 60–77% in smear-negative. Culture: Gold standard. Liquid media (BACTEC MGIT 960) — 1–3 weeks. Solid media (LJ) — 3–6 weeks.
Intensive Phase (2 months — daily):

Daily: INH 5 mg/kg + RIF 10 mg/kg 3×/week (DOT only): INH 15 mg/kg + RIF 10 mg/kg Duration: • Standard: 4 months (6 months total) • Cavitary + negative 2-month culture: consider 7 months (9 total) • Cavitary + positive 2-month culture: 7 months minimum (9 total)
All daily × 4 months (17 weeks):

ALL criteria must be met: • Age ≥12 years • Drug-susceptible, non-cavitary pulmonary TB • HIV-negative (or HIV+ with CD4 >100 on compatible ARVs) • Not pregnant or breastfeeding • No fluoroquinolone resistance • Sputum AFB smear grade ≤2+ • QTc monitoring required (moxifloxacin prolongs QTc)
Preferred rifamycin-based regimens:

• Monoresistant: Resistance to ONE first-line drug only • Polyresistant: Resistance to >1 first-line drug (but NOT both INH + RIF) • MDR-TB: Resistance to at least isoniazid AND rifampin • Pre-XDR-TB: MDR-TB + resistance to any fluoroquinolone • XDR-TB: MDR-TB + fluoroquinolone resistance + bedaquiline or linezolid resistance

Group A — Include ALL (unless contraindicated): • Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin (fluoroquinolone) • Bedaquiline • Linezolid Group B — Add NEXT: • Clofazimine • Cycloserine or Terizidone Group C — Add when Groups A+B insufficient: • Ethambutol • Delamanid • Pyrazinamide • Imipenem-cilastatin or Meropenem • Amikacin (or Streptomycin) • Ethionamide or Prothionamide • p-aminosalicylic acid
Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid:
Add moxifloxacin when fluoroquinolone susceptibility confirmed:

QTc (bedaquiline + moxifloxacin): • Baseline ECG before starting • At least monthly ECGs throughout treatment • Hold if QTc >500 ms • Correct electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca) before starting and monthly CBC (linezolid): • Weekly CBC — thrombocytopenia and anemia are dose-limiting • If platelets <75,000 or Hgb drops >2 g/dL → reduce linezolid to 600 mg • If severe → hold linezolid temporarily Visual acuity + neuropathy (linezolid): • Monthly visual acuity testing — optic neuritis is irreversible if missed • Monthly peripheral neuropathy assessment LFTs (all agents): • Monthly hepatic function tests • Hold if ALT >5× ULN or >3× ULN with symptoms
• CDC Division of Tuberculosis Elimination: 404-639-8120 • Regional TB Centers of Excellence • State/local TB control programs • WHO drug-resistant TB resources

Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer — reduces levels of many ARVs: Compatible with rifampin: • Efavirenz (EFV) — standard dose, no adjustment • Dolutegravir (DTG) — increase to 50 mg BID (from daily) • Raltegravir (RAL) — increase to 800 mg BID INCOMPATIBLE with rifampin: • All protease inhibitors (boosted or unboosted) • Cobicistat-boosted regimens (elvitegravir/c) • Most NNRTIs except efavirenz • Doravirine Alternative: Rifabutin instead of rifampin — fewer drug interactions, compatible with some PIs at adjusted doses

When to start ART after TB diagnosis: • CD4 <50: Start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment • CD4 ≥50: Start ART within 8 weeks of TB treatment • CNS TB (TB meningitis): Delay ART to 8 weeks regardless of CD4 count (high IRIS risk) Key principle: Never delay TB treatment while waiting for ART. Start TB treatment immediately upon diagnosis.

Definition: Paradoxical clinical worsening after starting ART, caused by recovering immune system mounting exaggerated response to TB antigens Timing: 1–4 weeks after ART initiation Risk factors for IRIS: • Low baseline CD4 (<50) • High TB burden (disseminated, cavitary) • Early ART initiation • Large drop in HIV viral load Features: • New/worsening fever • Enlarging lymph nodes • Worsening pulmonary infiltrates • New pleural/pericardial effusions Management: • Continue BOTH TB treatment AND ART • Mild: NSAIDs • Moderate-severe: Prednisone 1.5 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks, then taper over 2–4 weeks • Life-threatening: High-dose corticosteroids, consider temporary ART interruption with specialist guid

Standard duration: Same RIPE regimen as HIV-negative patients Extend to 9 months total if: • Cavitary disease on initial CXR • Positive sputum culture at 2 months • Slow clinical response 4-month regimen in HIV: • May be used if CD4 >100 and on compatible ARVs • Not recommended if CD4 ≤100 Treatment failure (positive cultures at 4+ months): • Repeat drug susceptibility testing • Assess adherence + drug interactions • Consider therapeutic drug monitoring • Consult TB specialist

Drug-induced hepatotoxicity during TB treatment: • AST/ALT >3× ULN WITH symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, dark urine) • AST/ALT >5× ULN WITHOUT symptoms Most common cause: pyrazinamide > isoniazid > rifampin

• Age >35 years • Alcohol use • Pre-existing liver disease (hepatitis B/C, cirrhosis) • HIV co-infection • Pregnancy or immediate postpartum • Concurrent hepatotoxic medications • INH acetylator status (slow acetylators at higher risk)

Stop ALL hepatotoxic TB drugs: INH, RIF, PZA Continue: Ethambutol (NOT hepatotoxic) Bridge therapy: Consider adding moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily to maintain at least 2 active drugs while hepatotoxic agents are held

Monitor LFTs weekly until AST/ALT <2× ULN • Also monitor bilirubin, INR • Assess for other causes of hepatotoxicity (viral hepatitis, alcohol, other drugs) • If fulminant hepatic failure → discontinue all TB drugs, hepatology consult

Reintroduce ONE drug at a time, 1 week apart: 1. Rifampin FIRST — least hepatotoxic of the 3, most important for efficacy → Start at full dose, check LFTs after 1 week → If LFTs stable → add next drug 2. Isoniazid SECOND — recheck LFTs after 1 week → If LFTs stable → consider PZA 3. Pyrazinamide LAST — most commonly implicated → May choose to omit permanently if severe hepatotoxicity occurred If PZA permanently discontinued: Extend total treatment to 9 months If hepatotoxicity recurs on rechallenge: • Use non-hepatotoxic regimen: ethambutol + fluoroquinolone ± injectable • Consult TB specialist • Consider therapeutic drug monitoring

Obtain baseline LFTs BEFORE starting TB treatment if: • Age >35 years • HIV co-infection • Hepatitis B or C • Alcohol use • Pregnancy or ≤3 months postpartum • Concurrent hepatotoxic medications • History of liver disease Monthly LFTs recommended for these patients throughout treatment

TB is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most commonly affects the lungs but can affect other parts of the body. TB spreads through the air when someone with active TB coughs, sneezes, or talks.

• Active TB disease: You have symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss) and can spread TB to others. You need treatment right away. • Latent TB infection: The TB bacteria are in your body but are not making you sick. You do not have symptoms and cannot spread TB. Treatment prevents it from becoming active.

• TB treatment involves taking multiple medications for several months • It is critical to take ALL your medications exactly as prescribed for the full course • Stopping treatment early or missing doses can cause the bacteria to become drug-resistant, which is much harder to treat • Your healthcare team may use Directly Observed Therapy (DOT), where a health worker watches you take each dose

• Orange-colored body fluids (urine, tears, sweat) — this is NORMAL with rifampin and not harmful • Nausea, stomach upset — take medications with a small snack if needed • Fatigue, joint aches • Skin rash or itching Contact your doctor IMMEDIATELY if you experience: • Yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice) • Dark urine or pale stools • Persistent nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite • Abdominal pain • Numbness or tingling in hands/feet • Vision changes or blurred vision • Fever lasting more than 3 days • Easy bruising or unusual bleeding

• Cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing • Stay home from work/school until your doctor says you are no longer contagious (usually after 2–3 weeks of treatment with improving symptoms and smears) • Open windows for ventilation when possible • Wear a mask when around others until cleared by your doctor • Close contacts should be tested for TB

• Keep ALL scheduled appointments • Bring your medications to every visit • Monthly sputum tests to check your progress • Blood tests to monitor for side effects • Contact your doctor or local health department if you have questions or concerns Remember: TB is curable with proper treatment. The most important thing you can do is complete your entire course of treatment.

• Born in or travel to TB-endemic country (Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Eastern Europe, Central Asia, Latin America) • Close contact with active TB case • Residence in congregate settings (shelters, correctional facilities, long-term care) • Healthcare workers with TB exposure • Immigration from high-burden country within 5 years • History of prior TB infection or incomplete treatment

• HIV infection (greatest risk factor — 20–30× increased risk) • Immunosuppressive therapy (TNF-α inhibitors, chronic corticosteroids ≥15 mg/day prednisone, chemotherapy) • Organ transplant recipients • End-stage renal disease / hemodialysis • Diabetes mellitus • Silicosis • Malnutrition / low body weight • Injection drug use • Gastrectomy or jejunoileal bypass • Head and neck cancer

• Prior TB treatment (especially incomplete treatment) • Contact with known drug-resistant TB case • Birth in or travel to area with high MDR-TB prevalence: → Eastern Europe (Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Moldova) → Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan) → Parts of Sub-Saharan Africa → India, China, Philippines • HIV co-infection • Cavitary disease with positive cultures after 2 months of treatment • Treatment failure on standard regimen

Reversal: Vitamin K 10 mg IV over 30 min + 4-Factor PCC PCC dose: INR 2-4 → 25 u/kg | INR 4-6 → 35 u/kg | INR >6 → 50 u/kg (max 5,000 u) Alt: 4 units FFP if PCC unavailable Monitor: INR at 30 min, 6h, 24h Pearl: PCC + FFP wear off in 6-8h. ALWAYS give Vitamin K simultaneously or INR rebounds.

Reversal: Idarucizumab 5 g IV (2 × 2.5 g, ≤15 min apart) Alt: 4-Factor PCC | Hemodialysis (80% renal, low protein binding) If <2h ingestion: Activated Charcoal 50 g Monitor: PTT or Thrombin Time at baseline, 2-4h, q12h Pearl: Normal thrombin time excludes clinically significant dabigatran effect.

Reversal: 4-Factor PCC Dose: CNS bleed → 50 u/kg (max 5,000) | Non-CNS → dose per local PCC protocol If <2h ingestion: Activated Charcoal 50 g Monitor: Anti-Xa level (best); INR after PCC, then q6h Pearl: PCC does NOT change anti-Xa level. These agents are NOT dialyzable (>90% protein bound).

Reversal: Protamine — most cases, just stop the infusion Dose: 1 mg per 100 units UFH given in last 2h (max 50 mg). Give slowly over 15 min. Monitor: PTT at 10-15 min, 2h, then q4h × 24h Pearl: Excess protamine causes paradoxical anticoagulation. Never >50 mg at once.

Reversal: Protamine — only ~50% reversal Dose: <8h → 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin | 8-12h → 0.5 mg per mg | >12h → unlikely to help Fondaparinux: Protamine NOT effective → consider PCC Pearl: Don't expect normalization of anti-Xa level with protamine.

Reversal: TXA 1 g IV load + 1 g/hr OR Aminocaproic acid 4-5 g IV + 1 g/hr Plus: Cryoprecipitate 10 units (target fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL) Optional: FFP ~2 units | Platelets if thrombocytopenic Pearl: tPA is gone in minutes, but clotting factor depletion persists. Target fibrinogen >200 for ICH.

First-line: DDAVP 0.3-0.4 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min Consider: Higher fibrinogen target (>200 mg/dL) AVOID: Platelet transfusion (PATCH trial: no benefit, possible harm) Desperate: TXA as adjunct Pearl: Ticagrelor is reversible — platelet transfusion won't work (new platelets get inhibited too).
• Hold warfarin • Resume at lower dose when INR is therapeutic • No Vitamin K needed in most cases
• Hold 1-2 doses of warfarin • Vitamin K 1-2.5 mg PO or IV if risk for bleeding • Resume at lower dose when INR is therapeutic • Small titrated doses are compatible with ongoing warfarin use
• Hold 1-2 doses of warfarin • Vitamin K 2.5-5 mg PO or IV • Repeat Vitamin K in 24h if INR remains elevated • Resume at lower dose when INR is therapeutic

• Vitamin K 10 mg IV over 30 minutes — ONE dose, ONE route • 4-Factor PCC simultaneously (INR-based dosing) • For ICH: give PCC immediately WITHOUT waiting for INR • Follow INR q3-6h for ICH • FFP cannot achieve INR <1.7 — don't try

IV: Preferred for emergent reversal. Infuse over 30 min. Anaphylactoid risk ~1/30,000 (rate-related — infuse slowly to minimize). This is NOT a true allergy (anaphylactoid, not anaphylactic). Fear of this reaction should NEVER delay treatment. PO: Acceptable for non-urgent supratherapeutic INR. Slower onset (12-24h). Variable bioavailability (~15%). Subcutaneous: AVOID — erratic absorption. Intramuscular: AVOID — hematoma risk in anticoagulated patient.

INR in cirrhosis does NOT reliably reflect bleeding risk — reflects rebalanced hemostasis. • A single dose of Vitamin K 10 mg IV may be tried to exclude concurrent vitamin K deficiency • No benefit to repeated dosing — studies show no difference between single and multiple doses • TEG is more accurate than INR for assessing coagulation in cirrhosis • Do NOT give FFP to "correct" the INR in cirrhosis — it improves the number but not clinical hemostasis

A full 10 mg IV dose will make the patient warfarin-resistant for 1-2 weeks. • Hepatic vitamin K reserves are small and turn over rapidly • Appropriate for emergent reversal where re-anticoagulation is not immediately planned • For patients who need to resume warfarin soon, use smaller PO doses (1-2.5 mg)
Order: INR Interpretation: INR directly reflects warfarin effect. Standard monitoring test. Goal for reversal: INR <1.4 (ICH per AHA/ASA 2022) or <1.5 (per ESO/EANS 2025 for INR ≥1.3)

Crude assay: PTT • Normal PTT argues against clinically significant dabigatran effect, but doesn't completely exclude it Better assay: Thrombin Time (TT) • Excellent correlation with dabigatran levels • May be unmeasurably elevated at therapeutic concentrations • Normal TT excludes clinically significant dabigatran effect — this is the key test • TT >25 seconds: suggests significant dabigatran level • Availability varies — often not available STAT Best assay: Diluted thrombin time (dTT) or Ecarin clotting time (ECT) — quantitative

Crude assay: INR • Normal INR argues against significant drug level but doesn't entirely exclude it Better assay: Anti-Factor Xa level • Correlates well with DOAC drug level • Normal anti-Xa excludes clinically relevant Xa inhibitors • The anti-Xa assay optimized for LMWH detection may be more sensitive, but any anti-Xa assay is probably fine Best assay: Drug-specific level (apixaban level, rivaroxaban level) — most accurate but availability limited

Order: PTT or Anti-Xa level • PTT: traditional monitoring, widely available • Anti-Xa: more accurate, especially if PTT is unreliable (lupus anticoagulant, factor deficiencies) After protamine: Check PTT at 10-15 min to confirm reversal Watch for: Heparin rebound at 8-18h (protamine has shorter half-life than UFH)

Order: Anti-Xa level (calibrated for LMWH) • PTT is unreliable for LMWH monitoring • After protamine, don't expect normalization — protamine only neutralizes ~50% of anti-Xa activity Peak levels: 3-5h after subcutaneous injection

Order: INR, PTT, Fibrinogen, CBC • Don't wait for results before giving reversal to actively bleeding patients • Fibrinogen is the critical lab — target >150-200 mg/dL (>200 for ICH) • Consider TEG for comprehensive hemostasis assessment • Each 10 units cryoprecipitate raises fibrinogen ~50 mg/dL

Platelet Functional Assay (PFA): More widely available, useful for aspirin effect TEG with platelet mapping: Superior for P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) In practice: Decisions are often based on clinical history (which drug, when was last dose) rather than lab results, due to poor availability and turnaround times Reversible vs irreversible: • Irreversible (aspirin, clopidogrel, prasugrel): platelet function recovers when new platelets are made (~1 week) • Reversible (ticagrelor): platelet function recovers after 3-5 half-lives

INR 2.5 on warfarin = expected therapeutic anticoagulation INR 2.5 on apixaban = suggests HIGH bleeding risk (apixaban doesn't typically elevate INR this much) INR 2.5 in cirrhosis = likely rebalanced hemostasis, NOT necessarily increased bleeding risk The same INR number means completely different things depending on the clinical context. Any study or guideline based predominantly on INR values is fundamentally flawed when applied across these different populations.
• Scene safety, ABCs, fingerstick glucose, security • Severity: Is patient redirectable? • Immediate threat → restrain + sedate simultaneously

• Verbal de-escalation first • Etiology-based drug selection: – Psych: antipsychotics preferred – EtOH intoxication: butyrophenones (droperidol/haloperidol) – Withdrawal: benzos mandatory – Anticholinergic: benzos + physostigmine, NO antipsychotics – Undifferentiated: benzos first-line

• Combination therapy: antipsychotic + benzo • Droperidol 5 mg + Midazolam 5 mg IM (preferred) • OR Haloperidol 5 mg + Midazolam 5 mg ± Diphenhydramine 50 mg IM ("B52") • Refractory → Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM / Dexmedetomidine / RSI
• Last resort — bridge while meds take effect • 5-person team, arms first, supine only • Monitoring: q15 min circulation, q1-2h physician reassess • Order limits: 4h adults, 2h teens, 1h children
• SpO₂, ECG (QTc after antipsychotics) • Watch for dystonia and akathisia • Complete medical workup — do NOT attribute to "psych" prematurely • Disposition: ICU / floor / psych eval / discharge

E — Empathy: "I can see you are upset" R — Respect: "I want to help you" A — Active listening: nod, reflect, do not interrupt S — Safety: "You are safe here" E — Environment: reduce stimulation, lower lights R — Rapport: "What can I do for you right now?"

1. Respect personal space (≥2 arm lengths) 2. Do not be provocative 3. Establish verbal contact — one person speaks 4. Be concise, use simple language 5. Identify wants and feelings 6. Listen actively 7. Agree or agree to disagree 8. Lay down the law and set clear limits 9. Offer choices and optimism 10. Debrief the patient and staff afterward

• Reduce stimulation: dim lights, reduce noise, single room • Remove potential weapons and sharps • Offer food, drink, blanket, phone charger • Allow one trusted person present if safe • Show of force (security presence) — nonverbal limit-setting, avoids sedation in up to 27% of cases

• De-escalation failing after 5-10 minutes of active attempt • Patient is escalating despite verbal engagement • Patient has made a direct physical threat or assault • Patient is at risk for self-harm • Environmental safety compromised (weapons, barricading)

"B52": Haloperidol 5 mg + Midazolam 5 mg + Diphenhydramine 50 mg — all compatible in one syringe IM Droperidol 5 mg + Midazolam 5 mg IM — fastest combination ⚠️ Do NOT combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzos — respiratory depression risk
Half-dose ALL agents. Avoid benzos (paradoxical agitation, falls). Max haloperidol 5 mg/24h. Max olanzapine 15 mg/24h. Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg preferred for Parkinson's/Lewy body.

• Patient is immediate danger to self or staff • Verbal de-escalation failed • Chemical sedation not yet effective or insufficient • Restraints are a BRIDGE — always administer medications concurrently

• Soft limb restraints (4-point): Standard for acute agitation — allows IV access, monitoring • Mittens / hand covers: Supplement when pulling IVs/tubes • Vest / torso: Prevent sitting up — ⚠️ asphyxiation risk, monitor closely • Hard restraints (leather): Extreme agitation — increased injury risk, reserve for refractory • Spit mask / hood: Spitting/biting biosafety — must allow adequate ventilation

• Minimum 5 people (1 per limb + 1 team leader) • Team leader does NOT touch patient — directs and monitors • Arms first (greatest threat), then legs • Each limb secured to BED FRAME (not side rails) • Patient SUPINE — NEVER prone (asphyxiation risk) • Diagonal pattern: R wrist → R upper rail, L wrist → L lower rail • Remove watches, glasses, potential weapons from reach

• Hogtie (wrists/ankles bound behind back) • Prone restraint • Stack mattresses on patient • Place knee on chest or back • Restrain without concurrent chemical sedation • Leave restrained patient unmonitored

Every 15 min: • Circulation — distal pulses, capillary refill • Sensation and skin integrity under restraints • Respiratory status • Offer food, water, toileting Every 1-2 hours: • Physician reassessment — document ongoing need • Attempt partial release (1 limb) as patient calms

• Adults (≥18 years): 4 hours maximum per order • Adolescents (9-17 years): 2 hours • Children (<9 years): 1 hour • Face-to-face physician evaluation within 1 hour of initiation • New order required before each expiration • Physician must see patient in person before each renewal

1. Behavior necessitating restraints 2. Less restrictive alternatives attempted 3. Type of restraint applied 4. Time applied 5. Names of all staff involved 6. • Half-dose ALL agents • Avoid benzodiazepines — paradoxical agitation, falls, respiratory depression • First-line IM: Haloperidol 0.5-2 mg or Olanzapine 2.5-5 mg • First-line PO: Quetiapine 25-50 mg or Risperidone 0.5-1 mg • FDA black box: all antipsychotics increase mortality in dementia-related psychosis (1.6-1.7×) • Max haloperidol 5 mg/24h, olanzapine 15 mg/24h • Midazolam: highest adverse event rate in elderly (53%, OR 5.25 vs haloperidol)

• AVOID typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol) — worsen motor symptoms • Lewy body: extreme neuroleptic sensitivity — even "safe" agents can trigger life-threatening reactions • First-line: Quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO (lowest D2 affinity) • If IM needed: Low-dose midazolam 1-2 mg or olanzapine 2.5 mg • Consult neurology early

• Benzodiazepines preferred for acute agitation • Lorazepam 1-2 mg IM/IV — most pregnancy safety data among benzos, no active metabolites • Midazolam 2.5-5 mg IM if rapid onset needed • If antipsychotic required: Haloperidol has most safety data (FDA category C) • Avoid droperidol • Fetal monitoring after sedation • OB consult • Left lateral tilt positioning to prevent aortocaval compression

• Benzodiazepines only — NO antipsychotics (worsen anticholinergic toxicity) • Physostigmine 0.5-2 mg IV is definitive antidote • Contraindications: QRS >120 ms, TCA ingestion, reactive airway disease • Pre-treat with glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg IV • May need large cumulative benzo doses

• Lorazepam preferred benzo — no active metabolites, glucuronidation (not hepatic CYP) • Reduce antipsychotic doses in hepatic impairment • Avoid diazepam in liver disease — long-acting active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam)

- Guest dosing: OTP patient who missed their clinic - Initiation: New patient with OUD, not on methadone - Unclear dose: Patient claims methadone but cannot verify - Inpatient bridging: Hospitalized maintenance patient

- Always verify dose with OTP before administering claimed dose - Call the OTP directly (patient should have contact info) - Confirm: enrollment status, last dose date, daily dose - If unverified: Give conservative 30 mg dose regardless of claimed dose - Risk: overstatement can lead to fatal respiratory depression

- Any DEA-registered provider may administer or dispense up to 3-day supply - Purpose: Emergency withdrawal management while arranging OTP linkage - 2023 Update: May now dispense (provide take-home) not just administer - Initiation: 30 mg PO Day 1, may add 10 mg if COWS >= 13 (max 40 mg) - Days 2-3: 40 mg PO daily - OTP appointment required within 72 hours

- ECG not required for single dose <= 40 mg in healthy patient - Get ECG if: dose >100 mg/day, QT-prolonging drugs, cardiac history, electrolyte abnormalities - QTc < 450 ms: Low risk - QTc 450-499 ms: Moderate risk (discuss, monitor) - QTc >= 500 ms: High risk (avoid methadone if possible)

- Post-dose: RR q15-30 min x 2h, SpO2, sedation level, COWS - First dose observation: minimum 2-4 hours - Guest dosing (verified): 30 minutes minimum - Red flags: RR <10, SpO2 <92%, excessive sedation - Respiratory depression: Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV titrated to RR

- Discharge with OTP appointment within 72 hours - Provide naloxone kit - Return precautions: difficulty breathing, excessive drowsiness, palpitations - SAMHSA OTP Locator: 1-800-662-4357 - Document 72-hour rule use in chart
1. Identify phase: Prodromal / Hyperemetic / Recovery 2. Confirm diagnostic criteria (Simonetto) 3. Key feature: compulsive hot water bathing (~90%)
4. Screen for red flags 5. Order labs: BMP, Mg, lipase, UDS, pregnancy, ECG 6. Check QTc before butyrophenones
7. IV access, NS bolus, NPO 8. First-line: Haloperidol 0.05 mg/kg IV OR Droperidol 0.625-2.5mg IV 9. Adjunct: Topical capsaicin 0.075% to abdomen 10. AVOID opioids and benzodiazepines
11. Reassess response at 30-60 min 12. Olanzapine 5-10mg IM/PO as second-line
13. Discharge if tolerating PO, hydrated, counseled 14. Admit if AKI, refractory vomiting, severe electrolyte derangement 15. Cannabis cessation = ONLY definitive cure

CHS: • Requires chronic cannabis use (usually daily, >1 year) • Hot water bathing is pathognomonic (~90%) • Resolves with cannabis cessation • TRPV1 receptor pathway implicated CVS (Rome IV): • No cannabis association required • Hot water bathing less common • Stereotypical episodes since childhood possible • May respond to triptans • Comorbid migraine common

CHS: • Occurs DURING active cannabis use • Relieved by cessation • Hot water bathing compulsion Cannabis Withdrawal: • Occurs AFTER cessation (24-72h after last use) • Irritability, insomnia, decreased appetite • Nausea is milder, no vomiting episodes • Resolves within 1-2 weeks

• Gastroparesis — worse postprandially, delayed gastric emptying • Biliary disease — RUQ pain, Murphy sign, abnormal LFTs • Pancreatitis — elevated lipase, epigastric pain radiating to back • Bowel obstruction — distension, absent bowel sounds, imaging • Pregnancy — hCG positive • Adrenal insufficiency — morning nausea, check cortisol • Intracranial pathology — headache, neurological signs • Superior mesenteric artery syndrome — thin patients, postprandial

Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS) is a condition caused by long-term cannabis (marijuana) use. It causes repeated episodes of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The only proven cure is to stop using cannabis completely.

• Cannabis is the direct cause of your symptoms • Symptoms will return every time you use cannabis • Symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks after stopping • No medication can permanently prevent episodes while continuing use

• Capsaicin cream (OTC): Apply 0.025-0.1% cream (Zostrix, Capzasin-HP) to your abdomen during episodes — this works on the same pathway as hot showers • Stay hydrated with small, frequent sips of water or electrolyte drinks • Avoid prolonged hot showers — while they provide temporary relief, they can worsen dehydration

• You cannot keep any fluids down for more than 12 hours • You see blood in your vomit • You have severe abdominal pain that is worsening • You notice very dark urine or no urine output • You feel dizzy, confused, or faint • You develop chest pain

• See your primary care provider within 1 week • Ask about substance use counseling resources • SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357 (free, 24/7) • Bring this information to your follow-up appointment

L — Look Externally: facial trauma, short neck, small mouth, prominent teeth, large tongue, beard, obesity E — Evaluate 3-3-2: 3 fingers mouth opening, 3 fingers mentum→hyoid, 2 fingers hyoid→thyroid notch M — Mallampati: I (full view) → IV (hard palate only) O — Obstruction: tumor, abscess, angioedema, epiglottitis, Ludwig angina N — Neck Mobility: c-spine injury, ankylosing spondylitis, arthritis, radiation Score ≥4 = predicted difficult intubation
M — Mask seal (beard, blood, disrupted anatomy) O — Obesity/Obstruction (BMI >26, angioedema) A — Age >55 N — No teeth (leave dentures in for seal) S — Stiff lungs/Sleep apnea (COPD, ARDS, asthma)
R — Restricted mouth opening (<2 cm) O — Obstruction (supraglottic mass, edema) D — Disrupted/distorted anatomy S — Stiff lungs / cervical Spine immobility

S — Surgery (prior neck surgery) H — Hematoma/infection in neck O — Obesity/fixed flexion R — Radiation to neck T — Tumor involving airway No absolute contraindications exist for emergency cricothyrotomy.

Grade I — Full glottis visible → standard intubation Grade IIa — Partial cords → standard intubation Grade IIb — Only arytenoids → bougie indicated Grade III — Only epiglottis → bougie strongly indicated Grade IV — No view → bougie or rescue pathway

Ketamine — 1.5-2 mg/kg IV | Onset 30-60s | Duration 10-20 min • Hemodynamically supportive (sympathomimetic) • Preferred in hypotension • NOT contraindicated in head injury (myth debunked) • KeNIK trial: equivalent to etomidate Etomidate — 0.3 mg/kg IV | Onset 15-45s | Duration 5-15 min • Hemodynamically neutral • Single-dose adrenal suppression — clinically insignificant • No longer preferred over ketamine per KeNIK Propofol — 1.5-2.5 mg/kg IV | Onset 15-45s | Duration 5-10 min • CAUSES HYPOTENSION • Reduce to 0.5-1 mg/kg if hemodynamically fragile • Less commonly used for ED RSI

Succinylcholine — 1.5 mg/kg IV (2 mg/kg IM) | Onset 30-60s | Duration 3-8 min • Depolarizing — fastest onset • Contraindicated: hyperkalemia, burns >24h, crush >24h, denervation, MH hx, myopathies Rocuronium — 1.2 mg/kg IV (RSI dose) | Onset 60-90s | Duration 40-60 min • Non-depolarizing — no succinylcholine contraindications • Reversible with sugammadex 16 mg/kg (immediate reversal) • Preferred for difficult airway (longer working time)

Fentanyl — 1-3 mcg/kg IV | Give 3 min before induction • Blunts sympathetic response • Consider for: elevated ICP, aortic dissection Lidocaine — 1.5 mg/kg IV | Give 3 min before induction • Theoretically attenuates ICP response (weak evidence) • NOT routinely recommended Atropine — 0.02 mg/kg IV (min 0.1 mg) • Pediatric patients <1 year • Repeat succinylcholine dosing
• Scalpel: #10 blade (broad) • Bougie: 15 Fr coude-tip, lubricated • ETT: 6.0 mm cuffed • Other: 10 mL syringe, capnography, ties for securing

1. Announce: "Can't intubate, can't oxygenate — performing cricothyrotomy" 2. Assign second provider to continue rescue oxygenation 3. Full head extension (unless c-spine precaution) 4. PPE / eye protection

Step 1: Stabilize larynx — laryngeal handshake (thumb + 3rd finger on thyroid cartilage, index finger palpates CTM) Step 2: Vertical skin incision (~4 cm) over CTM. If anatomy clear, single horizontal stab may suffice. Step 3: Palpate CTM with finger through incision — confirm the depression Step 4: Horizontal stab through CTM (lower half — avoid superior vessels and cords) Step 5: Extend incision — rotate scalpel 180° and extend opposite direction Step 6: Finger in — replace scalpel with index finger through CTM into airway lumen Step 7: Bougie — slide alongside finger into trachea, advance until resistance (10-15 cm) Step 8: Railroad 6.0 mm ETT over bougie until cuff disappears into airway

• Secure tube with ties (not tape — blood prevents adhesion) • CXR — confirm position, rule out pneumothorax • Continuous waveform capnography monitoring • Convert to formal tracheostomy within 24-72 hours (ENT/surgery consult) • Monitor for: subcutaneous emphysema, bleeding, posterior wall perforation
NAP4 Audit (Cook 2011): • Needle cricothyrotomy: 60% failure rate • Surgical cricothyrotomy: 100% success rate DAS 2015 explicitly recommends scalpel-bougie over needle/cannula technique.
• Failed intubation / failed BVM • Cardiac arrest airway • Bridge while preparing definitive airway
• Restricted mouth opening • Obstruction at/below glottis • Distorted/disrupted anatomy • Stiff lungs or fixed cervical spine
• Prefer second-generation SGA with gastric drainage • Use i-gel adult sizing: 3 = 30-60 kg, 4 = 50-90 kg, 5 = >90 kg • Follow package guidance for cuffed LMA devices
• Suction ready, EtCO2 attached, oxygen source connected • Insert along hard palate until seated • Confirm chest rise, EtCO2, SpO2 trend, breath sounds, and leak
• If oxygenation restored: choose definitive plan • If ventilation fails: failed SGA pathway • Failed tube + failed SGA + failed BVM = CICO
Trismus, angioedema, mandibular fracture, wiring, or severe pain may prevent passage of the device. If the mouth cannot accept the SGA, move to BVM/intubation/cric plan.
An SGA sits above the glottis. It will not bypass laryngeal, subglottic, tracheal, or foreign-body obstruction. Stridor or known distal obstruction should lower confidence.
Facial trauma, laryngeal fracture, neck hematoma, tumor, radiation distortion, or surgical anatomy may prevent the mask from seating.

ARDS, severe asthma, pulmonary edema, obesity with poor compliance, or fixed cervical position may require pressures above the SGA seal. If pressure is the problem, a better seal may not fix ventilation.
RODS does not forbid rescue SGA in a dying patient. It tells you whether to prepare early for a different rescue path.
