Use the device package or local airway cart card. Do not overinflate. If leak persists after correct seating and cuff pressure check, change size or device rather than repeatedly reinserting the same setup.
At i-gel overlaps, use anatomy and ventilation result. A short 88 kg patient may behave differently than a tall 88 kg patient. If seal is poor, reassess position and size.

• Suction on and within reach • BVM/PEEP valve attached to oxygen • EtCO2 ready before first ventilation • Backup SGA size above/below • Cric kit visible if this is rescue airway • Gastric tube if the device supports drainage

• Lubricate posterior surface only • Insert along hard palate with gentle continuous pressure • Seat until definite resistance • For cuffed devices, inflate per manufacturer guidance and check pressure if available • Secure once ventilation is confirmed
• Chest rise • EtCO2 waveform or colorimetric change • Improving SpO2 trend • Bilateral breath sounds • Acceptable leak at planned ventilation pressure • Gastric insufflation absent/minimal
• Re-seat deeper or withdraw slightly • Jaw thrust • Reposition head/neck if safe • Check cuff pressure if cuffed • Change size or device • Lower inspiratory pressure if clinically acceptable
• Check circuit and oxygen source • Check for biting, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, ARDS, or distal obstruction • If pressures exceed seal capacity, the SGA may not be the right airway
• Suction aggressively • Turn if feasible • Reassess whether the SGA still ventilates • Prepare cuffed tracheal airway if oxygenation allows • If oxygenation fails, treat as active failed airway
Limit to 3 insertion attempts. If SGA and BVM both fail, declare CICO and proceed to emergency front-of-neck access.
• Why extubate now? • If the original indication has not improved, keep the tube • Goals-of-care extubation follows the documented patient-specific plan
• Hard stop screen • Delay if difficult reintubation risk, shock, severe hypoxemia, paralysis, deep sedation, or incomplete reversal is present
• Assess airway protection • Adequate cough, manageable secretions, and adequate mental status are required • A passed SBT does not override poor airway protection
• Run or confirm SBT • Pass requires stable vitals, acceptable oxygenation/ventilation, and comfortable work of breathing
• Assess failure risk • Assess stridor risk • Choose NIV, HFNC, or standard oxygen before tube removal
• Tube removal • First 30 minutes • Reintubate early for severe or worsening post-extubation failure

• Original indication for intubation not improved • Predicted difficult reintubation without airway-skilled backup • Ongoing shock or escalating vasopressors • Severe hypoxemia or high ventilator requirements • Persistent severe acidosis or uncontrolled bronchospasm • Deep sedation, residual paralysis, or incomplete reversal • Poor cough, heavy secretions, vomiting, or aspiration risk • Inadequate monitoring, staffing, or rescue equipment

Required bedside checks: • Awake enough for airway reflexes or following simple commands • Coughs against suction or command • Secretions are manageable by bedside suctioning • No active emesis or uncontrolled bleeding into airway • Reintubation plan is explicit before tube removal

Common options: • T-piece • CPAP • Low pressure support Run for about 30 minutes when feasible. Fail for distress, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hypoxemia, rising CO2, arrhythmia, hypotension, or worsening mental status.
RSBI can support the assessment, but extubation decisions should not rest on RSBI alone. Combine the SBT result with airway protection, secretion burden, mental status, and rescue feasibility.

info.h: Who Needs a Cuff Leak Test?
info.t: Use for patients at increased risk of post-extubation stridor: traumatic or multiple intubation attempts, airway edema, prolonged intubation, large ETT relative to patient, prior failed extubation from stridor, or concerning airway exam.

• Leak present: lower risk, not zero risk • Absent or low leak: increased risk for laryngeal edema and stridor • Test quality matters: secretions, tube size, positioning, and ventilator method can affect results

If extubation is not urgent, delay and give systemic corticosteroids before extubation. If extubation cannot wait, do it with airway-skilled help at bedside, stridor meds ready, and immediate reintubation plan.

Sit upright, oxygen, call airway help, consider nebulized racemic epinephrine and systemic steroid, and prepare to reintubate. Do not rely on transient medication response if obstruction is worsening.

Use when the risk phenotype is hypercapnic or cardiogenic: COPD, obesity hypoventilation, OSA with hypercapnia, CHF/pulmonary edema, or hypercapnia during SBT. Place mask immediately after tube removal.
Use for high-risk hypoxemic patients who do not clearly need NIV. HFNC provides high FiO2, flow support, dead-space washout, and better tolerance than mask-based support.
Reasonable for low-risk patients with minimal oxygen requirement, good cough, low secretion burden, and no major failure-risk features.
Prophylactic support is different from rescue support. If established post-extubation respiratory failure develops and the patient is severe or worsening, reintubate early.

Treat as upper airway obstruction. Sit upright, oxygen, call airway help, use nebulized racemic epinephrine and systemic steroid as temporizing therapy, and prepare for reintubation if severe or worsening.
Red flags: severe work of breathing, fatigue, shock, altered mental status, rising CO2, persistent hypoxemia, aspiration, or inability to clear secretions. These should trigger early reintubation.
A short NIV bridge can be reasonable only when the phenotype fits, usually COPD or CHF, and improvement is immediate. Reassess in minutes while preparing the airway setup.
Do not let noninvasive support delay definitive airway control in severe post-extubation failure. The safest reintubation is before crash physiology develops.

• Is patient in cardiac arrest? → If yes, go directly to arrest protocol • Contact VAD coordinator immediately — every ED visit • Auscultate for pump hum — absence = pump failure = emergency • Measure MAP via Doppler — goal 70-90 mmHg
• Read controller parameters — Speed, Power, Flow, PI • Interpret alarms — Hazard (red) vs Advisory (yellow) • Treat hypertension if MAP >90 • Evaluate low flow — assess JVP/IVC to differentiate

• Triage by chief complaint — bleeding, thrombosis, infection, RV failure, suction, stroke, arrhythmia • Suction event — volume challenge first • Stroke — CT head, NO tPA (on warfarin), mechanical thrombectomy may be option

• Bleeding — leukoreduced/irradiated blood ONLY; desmopressin for acquired vWD; octreotide for GI AVMs • Pump thrombosis — high power + hemolysis labs; heparin + transfer for pump exchange • Infection — driveline site vs BSI; never manipulate driveline • RV failure — milrinone + dobutamine; AVOID intubation

• Assess perfusion, NOT pulse — MAP <50 AND ETCO₂ <20 = start CPR • Defibrillation is SAFE — anterior-posterior pads, avoid device • Bedside echo in arrest — LV/RV size guides the differential • Post-arrest — if refractory, consider ECMO
• Nearly all VAD patients require admission or transfer • Transfer criteria — pump failure, thrombosis, stroke, device infection • Discharge is rare — requires VAD team approval

Life-threatening — require immediate action: • Red heart (flashing): Low flow (<2.5 LPM) or pump stoppage → Emergent VAD team contact • Red battery icon: <5 minutes power remaining → Connect to AC or swap battery immediately • Driveline disconnected: Pump stops → Reconnect immediately, check cable integrity • Controller fault: Internal malfunction → Use backup controller (patient should carry one) • Electrical fault: Possible driveline wire fracture → Immediate VAD team consultation

Important but non-life-threatening: • Yellow battery (diamond): <15 minutes power remaining → Replace battery promptly • Yellow triangle: Various advisory conditions including: – High watts (may indicate pump thrombosis) – Low flow advisory – Speed change (automatic adjustment for suction) • Battery charging: Normal operational state when connected to AC power

• Red alarm + constant tone: Critical — low flow, pump stop, battery depleted • Yellow alarm: Advisory — battery low, power deviation • Controller displays: Speed, Power, Flow, PI (same as HM3) • Older device (axial flow) — higher thrombosis rates than HM3

Discontinued 2021 — ~4,000 patients still implanted • Solid yellow: Low priority • Flashing yellow: Medium priority • Red: High priority ("VAD Stopped," "Critical Battery") • Controller displays Speed and Power only (no PI) • Known safety concern: Pump restart failures (106 complaints, 14 deaths) • If pump fails to restart → use patient's backup controller with modified software • Medtronic provides ongoing support with 20 global specialists

1. Check all connections — driveline to controller, controller to power source 2. Ensure batteries are charged; switch to backup battery if needed 3. Position patient flat before replacing battery (prevents suction event) 4. Connect to hospital base unit or patient's own AC power unit 5. If controller fault → use patient's backup controller 6. Auscultate for pump hum — confirm pump is running 7. Call VAD coordinator for any alarm you cannot quickly resolve Low battery may trigger automatic speed reduction → can cause syncope or hemodynamic instability. Always ensure adequate power supply.

1. Place pencil Doppler probe over brachial artery 2. Inflate standard BP cuff on ipsilateral arm 3. Inflate >30 mmHg above last audible flow signal 4. Slowly deflate cuff 5. Record pressure at first return of flow signal = MAP This value approximates MAP — there is no systolic/diastolic. Goal MAP: 70-90 mmHg • MAP >90 → treat (stroke risk) • MAP <50 → arrest protocol • MAP <70 → hypoperfusion workup

No pulse does NOT mean cardiac arrest in a VAD patient. Continuous-flow LVADs produce minimal or zero pulsatility — absent pulse is the normal baseline state. Unreliable in VAD patients: • Pulse palpation • Pulse oximetry waveform • Oscillometric (automated) blood pressure cuffs Reliable perfusion indicators: • Level of consciousness • MAP by Doppler (>50 = some perfusion) • ETCO₂ (>20 = some perfusion) • Skin color, temperature, capillary refill • Arterial line waveform

Initiate CPR if ALL of the following: 1. Patient is unresponsive 2. MAP <50 mmHg by Doppler (or undetectable) 3. ETCO₂ <20 mmHg (in intubated patient) AND/OR: • LVAD is non-functioning (no hum, pump stopped) Do NOT rely on: • Absent pulse alone (normal in LVAD) • Low SpO₂ alone (unreliable without pulsatile flow)

info.h: Chest Compressions — Safe in VAD Patients
info.t: AHA 2017 Scientific Statement officially endorsed chest compressions in VAD patients. Historical concerns about cannula dislodgement have been debunked — autopsy studies found no disruption or dislodgement of inflow/outflow cannulas after compressions. Technique: • Standard chest compressions — no modification needed • High quality: rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4 inches • Minimize interruptions • Rotate compressors every 2 minutes

Defibrillation is SAFE and NOT contraindicated. Pad placement: Anterior-posterior preferred • Do NOT place pads directly over the LVAD device or driveline • Standard biphasic energy (200J) • Disconnect controller from AC power before shock (run on batteries) • Never disconnect LVAD components before cardioversion/defibrillation Patients with ICD: may fire appropriately or inappropriately — does not change external defibrillation management.

1. Assess responsiveness and perfusion (NOT pulse) 2. Verify LVAD function — listen for hum, check controller 3. Troubleshoot device — check power, connections, batteries 4. If LVAD non-functioning AND no perfusion → Begin CPR 5. If LVAD functioning but MAP <50 AND ETCO₂ <20 → Begin CPR 6. Attach defibrillator — anterior-posterior pads, away from device 7. Standard ACLS — epinephrine, amiodarone, defibrillation per rhythm 8. Bedside echo — assess LV/RV size, contractility, tamponade 9. Address reversible causes (Hs and Ts + device-specific) 10. Contact VAD team emergently 11. Consider VA-ECMO for bridge-to-transplant patients 12. Post-arrest: TTM, early PCI if indicated, ICU admission

• Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min • Amiodarone 300 mg IV (first dose), 150 mg (second) • Lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg (alternative antiarrhythmic) • Vasopressin may be used • Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia • Standard doses — no LVAD-specific modifications needed

Order a hemolysis panel when pump thrombosis is suspected: • High power on controller (>9-10 W for HM3) • Rising power trend • Abnormal pump sound (clunking, grinding) • Device feels warm to touch • Unexplained hemodynamic deterioration • Dark urine (hemoglobinuria) • New AKI

LDH >2.5× ULN + Low haptoglobin + High power: → Pump thrombosis until proven otherwise LDH mildly elevated + Normal haptoglobin: → Consider other causes (infection, hepatic congestion) LDH normal + High power: → Less likely thrombosis; consider increased demand state Rising LDH trend (even within normal range) is concerning — serial monitoring q4-6h is recommended when thrombosis is suspected.

info.h: Additional Labs for All VAD ED Visits
info.t: Standard panel: • CBC — anemia assessment, platelet count • CMP — electrolytes, renal function, liver function • PT/INR/PTT — critical for anticoagulation management • Troponin — myocardial injury • BNP/NT-proBNP — device malfunction, RV failure • Lactate — perfusion adequacy • Type & screen — anticipate bleeding If infection suspected: • Blood cultures ×2 (before antibiotics) • Driveline site culture • CRP, procalcitonin If critically ill: • ABG — cannot rely on pulse oximetry • TEG (thromboelastography) if available

• 48% six-month mortality without intervention • Average onset: ~1 year post-implantation • Incidence: 1.5% at 2 years (HM3), higher for HMII and HVAD • LDH >1,150 IU/L is highly suggestive • tPA thrombolysis: 70% hemolysis resolution, 10% hemorrhagic stroke

Bedside echocardiography is the primary imaging modality for acute LVAD assessment. Compare all findings to the patient's baseline echo (available from the VAD center). MRI is CONTRAINDICATED in all current LVAD patients — ferromagnetic components.

• LV size — compare to baseline; over- or under-distension • RV size and function — RV:LV ratio, TAPSE, RV free wall motion • Inflow cannula — position, flow velocity (normal <2 m/s) • Outflow graft — flow pattern • Aortic valve — opening frequency, regurgitation • IVC — size and collapsibility for volume status • Pericardial effusion — tamponade assessment • Septal position — bowing suggests pressure differential

| Echo Finding | LV | RV | Likely Diagnosis | |-------------|-----|-----|------------------| | Small LV + Small RV | ↓ | ↓ | Hypovolemia / bleeding | | Small LV + Large RV | ↓ | ↑ | PE, RV infarct, pulmonary HTN | | Large LV + Large RV | ↑ | ↑ | Pump thrombosis / obstruction | | Small LV + Septal shift | ↓↓ | — | Suction event (septum pulled toward cannula) | | Normal LV + Large RV | — | ↑ | RV failure | | Pericardial effusion | — | — | Tamponade (diastolic collapse) |

Normal: Cannula tip in mid-LV cavity, directed toward mitral valve, unobstructed. Abnormal findings: • Flow velocity >2 m/s — suggests obstruction (thrombus, malposition) • Cannula abutting septum — suction event • Rocking/mobile cannula — partial dehiscence (surgical emergency) Tip: Color Doppler across the cannula confirms flow direction and velocity.

Normal in LVAD: Aortic valve opens intermittently or not at all (continuous flow bypasses the valve). Concerning findings: • Aortic regurgitation — creates recirculation loop (blood pumped to aorta regurgitates back into LV → re-pumped). Incidence: 6-32% at 1 year. • Commissural fusion — leaflets fuse from chronic non-opening. Progressive. AR in LVAD patients causes: • Elevated pump flow (recirculated, not forward flow) • Decreased effective cardiac output despite "adequate" flow readings • Progressive heart failure symptoms despite mechanical support

| Parameter | Normal | RV Failure | |-----------|--------|------------| | RV:LV ratio (A4C) | <0.6 | >0.6 | | TAPSE | >17 mm | <17 mm | | IVC | <2.1 cm, >50% collapse | >2.1 cm, <50% collapse | | Hepatic vein flow | Normal | Systolic reversal | | RV free wall motion | Normal | Hypokinetic/akinetic | RV failure is present in 9-40% of LVAD patients. Echo is the first-line diagnostic tool.

• Identify TdP on ECG — polymorphic VT with "twisting of points," short-long-short initiation • Assess hemodynamic stability — pulseless vs unstable vs stable • Pulseless: unsynchronized defibrillation — do NOT give amiodarone • Unstable: synchronized cardioversion + IV Mg

• Determine etiology — acquired (most common) vs congenital LQTS vs unknown • Acquired TdP — drug-induced, electrolytes, structural heart → proceed to Mg protocol • Congenital LQTS — OPPOSITE treatment: beta-blockers BENEFICIAL, isoproterenol CONTRAINDICATED • Unknown: treat as acquired (safer default)

• Magnesium protocol — EMCrit: 4g bolus → 1g/hr ×4h → 0.5g/hr ×20h. Target Mg 3.5–5.0 • If recurrent despite Mg — overdrive pacing 90–110 bpm OR isoproterenol (acquired ONLY) • Lidocaine — 1–1.5 mg/kg IV, Class IB (shortens QT) • AVOID — amiodarone, procainamide, sotalol, beta-blockers (acquired)

• Stop ALL QT-prolonging drugs — use QT Drug Checker tool • Correct electrolytes aggressively — K+ >4.5, Mg 3.5–5.0, normalize Ca • Review risk factors — female sex, age >65, CYP inhibitors, structural heart
• All TdP patients require ICU admission • Resolved: ICU + telemetry + Mg infusion + cardiology • Recurrent: ICU + overdrive pacing + EP consult • Refractory: ECMO consideration + emergent EP

• Pulseless → Unsynchronized defibrillation (standard ACLS energy) • Do NOT give amiodarone — it prolongs QT • IV Magnesium 4g bolus over 20 min (faster if unstable) • Stop ALL QT-prolonging drugs immediately

• Bolus: 4 g IV over 20 min • Infusion: 1 g/hr × 4 hours, then 0.5 g/hr × 20 hours • Target serum Mg: 3.5–5.0 mg/dL • Give even if serum Mg is normal — intracellular stores depleted • Covers drug washout period (e.g., dofetilide t½ = 10h) • Toxicity antidote: Calcium gluconate 1 g IV
• K+ >4.5 mEq/L (most important modifiable factor) • Mg 3.5–5.0 mg/dL (much higher than standard repletion) • Normalize calcium • Recheck electrolytes every 2 hours during active management

• Overdrive pacing 90–110 bpm (transvenous preferred, up to 140 bpm) • Isoproterenol 1–10 mcg/min IV (ACQUIRED LQTS only — CONTRAINDICATED in congenital) • Lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV push, then 1–4 mg/min infusion (Class IB — shortens QT)

• Amiodarone — prolongs QT, worsens TdP • Procainamide — prolongs QT • Sotalol — Class III antiarrhythmic, prolongs QT • Beta-blockers — in acquired TdP (can worsen bradycardia-dependent TdP) • Any Class IA or Class III antiarrhythmic

Acquired (most common): • Mg + overdrive pacing + isoproterenol + lidocaine • Beta-blockers: AVOID • Prognosis: good with drug removal + correction Congenital LQTS: • Mg + IV beta-blocker (esmolol/propranolol) + pacing • Isoproterenol: CONTRAINDICATED (paradoxical QT lengthening) • Genetics/EP consult + ICD evaluation • Untreated mortality >50%; treated <10%

info.h: Key ECG Features of Torsades de Pointes
info.t: • Polymorphic QRS complexes — continuously varying axis (the "twisting") • Sinusoidal waxing and waning of QRS amplitude around the isoelectric line • Rate typically 150–300 bpm • Self-terminating in most episodes (seconds to minutes) • Degeneration to VF is the lethal risk

Classic trigger pattern: 1. Short interval — a premature ventricular complex (PVC) 2. Long interval — a compensatory pause after the PVC 3. Short interval — another PVC landing on the T wave ("R-on-T phenomenon") 4. TdP initiates — the R-on-T PVC triggers the arrhythmia This pause-dependent mechanism explains why bradycardia and early afterdepolarizations (EADs) are the substrate for TdP.

info.h: TdP vs Polymorphic VT (No QT Prolongation)
info.t: Critical distinction: • TdP = polymorphic VT + prolonged QT on baseline ECG (QTc >500 ms) → Treatment: Magnesium, overdrive pacing, isoproterenol → AVOID: Amiodarone, procainamide • Polymorphic VT without QT prolongation = different entity (often ischemic) → Treatment: Standard ACLS, amiodarone IS appropriate → Must rule out ACS Always check baseline QTc to distinguish these two conditions — treatment is opposite.

• Normal: ≤440 ms (male), ≤450 ms (female) • Prolonged: 441–500 ms (male), 451–500 ms (female) • High TdP Risk: >500 ms — 2–3× increased risk of TdP • Critical: >600 ms — very high risk, treat urgently Note: Bazett formula overcorrects at high heart rates. Consider Fridericia (FDA-preferred) or Rautaharju (ACEP Tox recommended) for ED use.

1. Confirm CCHR eligibility (GCS 13-15, LOC/amnesia/disorientation, within 24h) 2. Assess HIGH-RISK criteria (GCS <15 at 2h, skull fracture signs, vomiting ≥2, age ≥65) 3. If no high-risk → assess MEDIUM-RISK (amnesia ≥30 min, dangerous mechanism) 4. Any positive → CT indicated. All negative → CT not indicated.

≥ 2 years: Check GCS <15 or basilar skull fracture signs → if yes, CT. If no → check LOC, vomiting, severe mechanism, severe headache → if yes, observe vs CT (shared decision). If none → no CT. < 2 years: Check GCS <15 or palpable skull fracture → if yes, CT. If no → check LOC ≥5s, non-frontal hematoma, severe mechanism, not acting normally → if yes, observe vs CT. If none → no CT.

1. Any HIGH-RISK factor? (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, paresthesias) → Image 2. Any LOW-RISK factor allowing ROM? (simple rear-end MVC, sitting, ambulatory, delayed pain, no midline tenderness) → If no low-risk factors → Image 3. Active ROM 45° left AND right? → If yes, cleared. If no → Image.

1. Assess pre-test probability (gestalt) 2. LOW risk → Apply PERC (all 8 met = ruled out) 3. PERC fails → D-dimer (age-adjusted if ≥50) 4. MODERATE risk → Wells score → if ≤4, D-dimer; if >4, CTPA 5. HIGH risk → CTPA directly (do NOT use PERC or D-dimer)

Appendicitis: Calculate Alvarado (MANTRELS). 0-4 = unlikely (discharge). 5-6 = possible (observe/image). 7-8 = probable (surgery ± CT). 9-10 = very probable (surgery). Renal Colic: Known stones + typical symptoms + young/healthy → may not need CT. First episode, fever, or AKI → CT indicated.
Ankle/Foot: Ottawa Ankle Rules → X-ray if criteria met. CT rarely needed. Knee: Ottawa Knee Rules or Pittsburgh Knee Rules → X-ray if criteria met. CT rarely needed.

CT Head: 2 mSv (20 CXR equivalents, ~4 months background) CT C-Spine: 3-4 mSv (30-40 CXR, ~6 months background) CT Chest: 7 mSv (70 CXR, ~1.1 years background) CT Abdomen/Pelvis (single phase): 10 mSv (100 CXR, ~1.6 years) CT Abdomen/Pelvis (multiphase): 31 mSv median (310 CXR, ~5 years) CT Pulmonary Angiogram: 10-15 mSv (100-150 CXR) Chest X-ray (reference): 0.1 mSv US average background radiation: ~6.2 mSv/year.

CT Head: 0.23 cancers per 1,000 (range 0.03-0.70) CT Chest: 1.5 cancers per 1,000 Multiphase Abdomen/Pelvis: 4.0 cancers per 1,000 (range 0.83-11.1) Overall: ~103,000 projected cancers/year from 93 million CT scans in the US (2023 data).

13-fold dose variation between highest and lowest dose for each CT study type at different facilities. Widest range: multiphase abdomen/pelvis CT (6.4 to 90.4 mSv). ALARA Principle: As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Key strategies: • Weight-based protocols • Automatic exposure control • Iterative reconstruction • Limiting scan phases • Limiting scan range Children are more radiosensitive than adults — higher cell proliferation, longer remaining lifespan for cancer to manifest.

Image Gently Campaign (est. 2008) — 4 principles: 1. Child-size the radiation dose (weight/size-based protocols) 2. Scan only when necessary (use PECARN, clinical decision rules) 3. Scan only the indicated region (limit scan length) 4. Scan once (avoid multiphase scanning) Children <10 years are several times more radiosensitive than adults. Best practices: • Use PECARN before head CT in minor trauma • Consider observation period for intermediate-risk PECARN • Ultrasound first for appendicitis, pyloric stenosis, intussusception • MRI when available for non-emergent conditions

Fetal radiation thresholds: • < 50 mGy: No identifiable developmental defects. Pregnancy interruption NOT warranted. • 50-100 mGy: Threshold for teratogenic effects (first 15 weeks only) • > 100 mGy: Increased malformation risk — extremely rare from diagnostic imaging Typical fetal doses from CT: • CT Head: < 0.01 mGy (negligible) • CT Chest / CTPA: 0.01-0.66 mGy (minimal) • CT Abdomen/Pelvis: 10-25 mGy (modern scanners ~13 mGy) All typical fetal doses are well below the 50 mGy threshold. Key principles (ACR/ACOG): • Do NOT withhold medically indicated CT from pregnant patients • Risk of missed diagnosis far exceeds radiation risk • Iodinated contrast: crosses placenta but no proven teratoge

Major paradigm shift (ACR 2024 + ACR/AAAAI 2025): Mild prior reactions (hives, nausea, limited urticaria): • Premedication no longer routinely recommended • Primary strategy: switch to a different contrast agent • Breakthrough rate: 25.8% same agent → 6.9% different agent Moderate prior reactions: • Shared decision-making between provider, patient, radiologist • Premedication may be considered but NOT always needed • Agent switching preferred when feasible Severe prior reactions (anaphylaxis, laryngeal edema, hypotension): • Premedication still recommended when no alternative study exists Traditional premedication (when indicated): *13-hour oral:* Prednisone 50 mg PO at 13h, 7h, and 1h befor

1. Clinical indication: Specific signs/symptoms prompting the study 2. Pre-test probability: Decision rule applied and result (e.g., "Wells score = 6, PE likely") 3. Clinical question: Specific diagnosis being evaluated 4. Risk-benefit discussion: Especially for pregnant, pediatric, or patients with recent CTs 5. Contrast decision: Why contrast is/is not needed; allergy status; eGFR 6. Alternative imaging considered: Why CT was chosen over US, MRI, or plain films 7. Medical necessity language: Tie order to presenting complaint and clinical findings

1. Clinical decision rule applied and result (e.g., "PECARN negative — no high-risk features") 2. Shared decision-making: Discussion with patient/family about observation vs imaging 3. Return precautions given: Specific instructions for when to return 4. Follow-up plan: Who to see and when 5. Understanding confirmed: Patient/family demonstrated understanding

Ordering: "CT head ordered per CCHR: patient meets high-risk criteria (GCS 14 at 2h post-injury, age 72). Clinical question: intracranial hemorrhage or fracture. No contrast needed. Risks of radiation discussed." Not ordering: "Canadian CT Head Rule applied: no high-risk or medium-risk criteria met (GCS 15, no basal skull fracture signs, no vomiting, age 34, no amnesia >30 min, simple fall from standing). CT not indicated. Shared decision-making with patient. Return precautions provided for worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, weakness, or seizure. Follow-up with PCP in 2-3 days if symptoms persist." Key principle: Document the rule, not just the conclusion.

CT is used in 27 per 100 ED encounters — nearly matching ECG usage (28 per 100). An estimated 103,000 new cancers annually may be attributable to CT imaging. Vulnerable populations relying on EDs for primary care face disproportionate radiation exposure. Clinical decision rules can reduce unnecessary imaging by 20-40% without missing clinically significant pathology.

• Identify DFSA red flags — amnesia, unexplained injuries, incapacitation • Assess medical stability — treat life threats before forensic workup • Determine time since assault — drives specimen collection urgency

• Informed consent framework — each element independent • Consent for exam — patient may decline any component • Consent for specimens — no police report required • Photo consent — injury documentation

• Collection priority by time window • <6h: GHB still detectable — gray-top tube (NaF) STAT • 6-12h: Urine urgently, blood for other agents • 12-72h: Urine primary, blood secondary • >5 days: Plan hair collection at 4-6 weeks
• Hospital UDS is INADEQUATE — must use forensic lab • Lab ordering — baseline clinical labs + forensic specimens
• SANE availability check • Clothing evidence — paper bags, NOT plastic • Documentation — objective findings only

• STI prophylaxis — ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole • Emergency contraception — ulipristal preferred • HIV PEP assessment — link to PEP consult • Safe discharge — screen for ongoing threat • Follow-up plan — STI 2wk/3mo, hair 4-6wk

Blood: 4-6 hours Urine: 3-12 hours Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Most time-critical agent. Endogenous GHB exists at low levels — forensic labs use cutoffs of >10 mcg/mL (blood) and >10 mcg/mL (urine) to distinguish exogenous dosing. Gray-top tube (NaF preservative) is MANDATORY — NaF inhibits in vitro GHB production that occurs in standard blood tubes.

Blood: 24-72 hours Urine: Up to 72 hours (as 7-aminoflunitrazepam metabolite) Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Parent drug has short half-life. Forensic labs target the 7-aminoflunitrazepam metabolite, which standard immunoassay does NOT detect.

Blood: 24-48 hours Urine: 72-96 hours (as norketamine metabolite) Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Low facilitative doses may fall below standard immunoassay cutoffs. LC-MS/MS targets both ketamine and norketamine.

Blood: 4-8 hours (zolpidem), 2-4 hours (zaleplon) Urine: Up to 24 hours Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure NOT detected by standard benzodiazepine immunoassay — structurally different. Requires specific LC-MS/MS targeting.

Blood: 6-12 hours (short-acting) to 24-48 hours (long-acting) Urine: 24-72 hours (short-acting) to 1-2 weeks (long-acting) Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Standard immunoassay detects some but has poor sensitivity for clonazepam, lorazepam, and midazolam. Forensic labs use targeted LC-MS/MS.
Blood: Up to 24 hours Urine: 48-72 hours Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Emerging DFSA agents. NOT included in standard UDS panels. Easy to administer covertly (OTC, tasteless in food/drink).

Blood: 10-12 hours Urine: 12 hours (parent) / EtG up to 80 hours / EtS up to 48 hours Hair: Not standard for alcohol Ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS) are alcohol metabolites that persist much longer than ethanol. EtG in urine can confirm alcohol consumption up to 80 hours post-ingestion.

Blood: 24-48 hours (most agents) Urine: 48-96 hours Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Fentanyl and synthetic opioids may not be detected by standard immunoassay. Forensic labs use expanded panels with norfentanyl and other metabolites.
Blood: Limited data, likely <24 hours Urine: 24-72 hours Hair: Limited data Emerging DFSA agent. Can cause amnesia, sedation, and confusion at supratherapeutic doses. NOT included in standard panels.

Blood: Up to 72 hours (single use) to 1 month (chronic) Urine: 3-30+ days depending on use pattern Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Longest standard detection window in urine. Presence alone does not confirm facilitation — must correlate with clinical presentation.

Blood: 24-48 hours Urine: 48-96 hours Hair: 4-6 weeks post-exposure Not commonly considered DFSA agents but included in SOFT-recommended panels. Carisoprodol (Soma) has abuse potential and sedative effects.

Window: 4-6 weeks after exposure (allows incorporation into hair shaft) Collection: Pencil-thickness bundle from posterior vertex, cut at scalp Wrap in aluminum foil, label proximal (scalp) end Detects: GHB, flunitrazepam, ketamine, zolpidem, benzodiazepines, opioids, cannabinoids, antihistamines, and most DFSA agents Hair analysis is the only option for presentations >5 days post-assault.

Sedative-Hypnotics: • GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) + GBL • Benzodiazepines (full panel including clonazepam, lorazepam, midazolam, flunitrazepam) • Zolpidem, zaleplon, zopiclone • Barbiturates Dissociatives: • Ketamine + norketamine • PCP + metabolites Opioids: • Natural: morphine, codeine • Semi-synthetic: oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone • Synthetic: fentanyl + norfentanyl, tramadol, methadone Stimulants: • Amphetamines, methamphetamine, MDMA • Cocaine + benzoylecgonine Antihistamines: • Diphenhydramine, doxylamine, hydroxyzine, chlorpheniramine Muscle Relaxants: • Carisoprodol + meprobamate • Cyclobenzaprine Other: • Scopolamine • Cannabinoids (THC + metabolites) • Alcohol + EtG/EtS (

Forensic labs specifically target these metabolites that hospital UDS misses: • 7-aminoflunitrazepam — primary Rohypnol metabolite • Norketamine — persists longer than parent ketamine • Norfentanyl — confirms fentanyl exposure • EtG/EtS — alcohol metabolites detectable 48-80h post-ingestion • Benzoylecgonine — cocaine metabolite • Meprobamate — carisoprodol metabolite

• Immunoassay cutoffs too high — designed for clinical use (detecting overdose), not forensic use (detecting facilitative doses) • Missing analytes — GHB, Z-drugs, and many benzodiazepines not included • No confirmation testing — GC-MS/LC-MS/MS required for forensic admissibility • No chain of custody — standard clinical specimens lack forensic documentation • Cross-reactivity — false positives from common medications Bottom line: A negative hospital UDS does NOT rule out drug facilitation.

• NMS Labs (Willow Grove, PA) — nmslab.com • Axiom Testing (San Diego, CA) • Redwood Toxicology Laboratory (Santa Rosa, CA) • Your state/regional crime lab Contact for specimen requirements, shipping instructions, and turnaround times. Most accept gray-top blood + first-void urine with chain of custody documentation.

Gray-top tube (NaF/KOx) — MANDATORY for GHB: • Sodium fluoride inhibits in vitro GHB production • Without NaF, GHB is generated post-collection, causing false positives • Collect at least 5 mL Lavender-top tube (EDTA) — standard forensic tox: • 10 mL minimum • For benzodiazepines, ketamine, opioids, Z-drugs, antihistamines Red-top tube (no additive) — clinical baseline: • HIV, Hepatitis B/C, RPR, CMP • Separate from forensic chain of custody

First-void urine is critical: • Do NOT have patient void and discard before collection • Minimum 50-100 mL in clean, additive-free container • Do NOT use standard UA cups with preservatives • Label immediately with tamper-evident seal Urine has longer detection windows than blood for most DFSA agents and is the primary specimen for presentations >6 hours post-assault.

Collect at 4-6 weeks post-assault (allows drug incorporation into shaft) • Pencil-thickness bundle (~100 strands) • From posterior vertex (back of crown) — most consistent growth rate • Cut at scalp — do NOT pluck (damages root) • Wrap in aluminum foil • Mark proximal (scalp) end — orientation is critical for timeline • Store at room temperature in paper envelope Hair growth rate: ~1 cm/month. The proximal 1-3 cm segment corresponds to the assault timeframe.

Every specimen requires: 1. Label: patient name, DOB, date/time of collection, collector name/signature 2. Tamper-evident seal across container lid 3. Chain of custody form initiated at collection 4. Every transfer documented: who, when, where, signature 5. Specimens refrigerated (2-8°C), NOT frozen 6. Stored in locked, access-controlled location 7. Transport to forensic lab as soon as possible Break in chain = evidence may be inadmissible. Document meticulously.

• Each clothing item in a separate PAPER bag • NEVER plastic — promotes bacterial growth, degrades DNA • Place paper sheet under patient during undressing to catch trace evidence • Seal each bag with tamper-evident tape • Label: item description, patient name, date/time, collector • Store in evidence locker or secure location Fingernail scrapings: Wooden stick under each nail, separate envelopes for each hand. Indicated if patient reports scratching assailant.
Gonorrhea: • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 dose Chlamydia: • Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days Trichomoniasis: • Metronidazole 2 g PO × 1 dose All three can be given simultaneously in the ED.

Gonorrhea alternative: • Gentamicin 240 mg IM × 1 dose + Azithromycin 2 g PO × 1 dose Chlamydia and trichomoniasis: Same as standard (doxycycline + metronidazole) If IgE-mediated cephalosporin allergy, azithromycin + gentamicin avoids all beta-lactams.

Chlamydia in pregnancy: • Azithromycin 1 g PO × 1 dose (replaces doxycycline — contraindicated in pregnancy) Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM × 1 (same — safe in pregnancy) Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole 2 g PO × 1 (CDC category B — safe in pregnancy)

• 2 weeks: NAAT for GC/CT (nucleic acid amplification test) • 3 months: Full STI panel — GC, CT, syphilis (RPR), HIV (4th gen), Hep B/C • Test of cure not routinely needed unless symptoms persist or pregnancy • Pelvic exam if symptoms develop (discharge, pain, bleeding)

• No police report required — patients can receive a forensic exam and have specimens collected without filing a police report • No insurance billing — forensic examination costs cannot be billed to the patient's insurance • Specimens can be held — evidence can be stored by the hospital or crime lab while the patient decides whether to involve law enforcement • Cannot condition exam on cooperation — facilities cannot deny a forensic exam based on willingness to cooperate with law enforcement • Patient may decline any component — each element of the exam and evidence collection is independently consentable

• Some states have mandatory reporting requirements for sexual assault (especially for minors, dependent adults, and certain weapon injuries) • Evidence retention periods vary by state (typically 20-50 years for untested kits) • Victim compensation programs vary — most cover forensic exam costs regardless of LE cooperation • Check your state's specific VAWA implementation and mandatory reporting statutes When in doubt: Contact your hospital's social work department or patient advocate for guidance on local requirements.

• Document that VAWA rights were explained to the patient • Document each consent/declination separately • Do NOT include language implying the patient must cooperate with LE • Do NOT delay forensic exam pending LE arrival unless patient requests it • The medical record may be subpoenaed — document objectively

You received a medical evaluation in the emergency department. Depending on what you consented to, the following may have been done: • Medical examination and treatment of injuries • Collection of specimens for evidence • Medications to prevent sexually transmitted infections • Emergency contraception (if applicable) • Medications to prevent HIV (if applicable) • Referral to a victim advocate

Physically: • Soreness or bruising may develop over the next few days • Medications may cause nausea (especially metronidazole) — take with food • If you received emergency contraception, your next period may be early or late Emotionally: • A wide range of reactions is normal — fear, anger, numbness, confusion, sadness, guilt • Reactions may come and go unpredictably • Sleep disturbances and flashbacks are common • There is no "right" way to feel — whatever you are experiencing is valid

2 weeks: STI testing and pregnancy test with your doctor or clinic 4-6 weeks: Hair specimen collection (if applicable) and HIV test (if PEP started) 3 months: Repeat full STI panel (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, Hepatitis) 6 months: Final HIV test and Hepatitis B vaccine dose 3 (if started) Complete all prescribed medications — finish the full course of doxycycline (7 days) and/or HIV PEP medications (28 days) if prescribed.

• You can file a police report at any time — there is no deadline for reporting • Your evidence specimens are being held safely • You do NOT need to file a police report to have your evidence stored • You can access victim compensation regardless of whether you file a report • You have the right to change your mind about any aspect of your care at any time

Any fever in a patient with recent travel to an endemic area (< 3 months). Consider even if taking prophylaxis. Incubation ranges from 7 days to several months depending on species.

Use the Malaria Severity Calculator to determine if the patient meets WHO 2023 criteria for severe malaria. Any ONE criterion = severe malaria. Severe disease requires IV artesunate and ICU admission.

Thick and thin blood smears (gold standard for species and parasitemia). Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) if available. Repeat smears q12-24h for 48h if initial negative but suspicion high. CBC, CMP, lactate, LFTs, coagulation panel.
Five species infect humans: P. falciparum (most severe), P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi. Species comparison table guides treatment selection. Mixed infections occur.
Chloroquine resistance is widespread in P. falciparum. Artemisinin resistance emerging in Southeast Asia. Resistance patterns by region determine first-line therapy.

Severe malaria: IV {{drug:artesunate}} (preferred) or quinidine + ICU. Uncomplicated malaria: {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}}, {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}}, or {{drug:chloroquine}} (only if chloroquine-sensitive). Start empirically while awaiting smear results if high clinical suspicion.
Pregnancy management requires modified drug selection by trimester. Children receive weight-based dosing. G6PD testing required before primaquine for P. vivax/ovale radical cure.

Severe malaria complications: cerebral malaria (altered mental status, seizures), acute respiratory distress, acute kidney injury, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis. Check glucose frequently.
If patient was on prophylaxis, evaluate for failure causes: non-adherence, resistance, inadequate dosing, drug interactions. Do NOT use same drug for treatment that was used for prophylaxis.

Severe malaria: ICU admission. Uncomplicated malaria: admit for IV therapy if unable to tolerate PO, parasitemia > 5%, comorbidities, or uncertain diagnosis. Low-risk patients may be discharged with close follow-up and daily phone contact. CDC Malaria Hotline available 24/7: 770-488-7788.

Severity: Most severe — causes cerebral malaria, multi-organ failure, death Incubation: 7-14 days (occasionally up to 30) Relapse: No hypnozoite stage — no liver relapse RBC Preference: All ages of RBCs — high parasitemia possible (>10%) Parasitemia: Can exceed 10% — marker of severity Geographic: Sub-Saharan Africa (90% of cases), Southeast Asia, South America Treatment: {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}}, {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}}, IV {{drug:artesunate}} (severe) Resistance: Widespread chloroquine resistance. Emerging artemisinin resistance in Southeast Asia (Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar)

Severity: Usually benign — severe disease rare but reported Incubation: 12-17 days (up to 6-12 months for temperate strains) Relapse: YES — hypnozoites remain dormant in liver. Relapses common without primaquine RBC Preference: Young RBCs (reticulocytes) — limits parasitemia to <2% Parasitemia: Typically <2% Geographic: Central/South America, Asia, Middle East, Pacific islands Treatment: {{drug:chloroquine}} (most regions) + {{drug:primaquine}} 14 days (radical cure). Check G6PD before primaquine Resistance: Chloroquine resistance emerging in Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, parts of Asia. Use {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} or {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} if resistant

Severity: Benign — rarely severe Incubation: 12-20 days (can be months to years) Relapse: YES — hypnozoites in liver. Requires primaquine for radical cure RBC Preference: Young RBCs — low parasitemia Parasitemia: Typically <2% Geographic: West Africa primarily. Rare outside Africa Treatment: {{drug:chloroquine}} + {{drug:primaquine}} 14 days. Check G6PD before primaquine Resistance: No documented chloroquine resistance

Severity: Benign — chronic infection possible Incubation: 18-40 days (longest incubation) Relapse: No hypnozoite stage — but can persist in blood for decades (recrudescence) RBC Preference: Old RBCs — very low parasitemia Parasitemia: Typically <1% Geographic: Sub-Saharan Africa, parts of South America, Southeast Asia (less common than other species) Treatment: {{drug:chloroquine}} alone (no primaquine needed) Resistance: Chloroquine resistance rare

Severity: Can be severe — rapid replication (24h cycle) allows high parasitemia Incubation: 9-12 days Relapse: No hypnozoite stage RBC Preference: All ages — parasitemia can rise rapidly Parasitemia: Can exceed 5% quickly due to 24h cycle Geographic: Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Thailand, Philippines, Indonesia). Zoonotic — natural host is macaque monkeys Treatment: {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} or {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}}. IV {{drug:artesunate}} if severe. Do NOT use chloroquine Resistance: Chloroquine not effective

1. Impaired consciousness — GCS <11, or Blantyre Coma Scale <3 (children) 2. Prostration — generalized weakness, unable to walk/sit without assistance 3. Multiple convulsions — >2 episodes within 24h 4. Acidosis — base deficit >8 mEq/L or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L or venous lactate >5 mmol/L 5. Hypoglycemia — blood glucose <40 mg/dL (<2.2 mmol/L) 6. Severe malarial anemia — Hgb <5 g/dL (children) or <7 g/dL (adults) with parasitemia >10,000/μL 7. Acute kidney injury — Cr >3 mg/dL or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h 8. Acute pulmonary edema / ARDS — radiographically confirmed with SpO2 <92% on room air

1. Hyperparasitemia — >10% parasitized RBCs (or >500,000/μL) 2. Hyperbilirubinemia — bilirubin >3 mg/dL with parasitemia >100,000/μL 3. Hemoglobinuria — macroscopic black/red urine ("blackwater fever") 4. Abnormal bleeding / DIC — spontaneous bleeding from gums, nose, GI tract; prolonged PT/PTT 5. Shock — SBP <80 mmHg (adults) with cool extremities 6. Pulmonary edema — radiographic evidence

Any ONE criterion = Severe Malaria → requires IV {{drug:artesunate}} and ICU admission. Use the Severity Calculator to systematically evaluate all criteria. Do NOT wait for smear confirmation if clinical suspicion is high and patient meets severity criteria. Start IV artesunate empirically. Cerebral malaria is a subset defined by unarousable coma (GCS ≤9) not attributable to another cause, with P. falciparum parasitemia. Mortality 15-20% even with treatment.

Widespread in P. falciparum: • Sub-Saharan Africa — near-universal resistance • Southeast Asia — complete resistance • South America — widespread resistance • Central America, Caribbean, Middle East — variable resistance Still chloroquine-sensitive: • Central America west of Panama Canal (parts of Mexico, Guatemala) • Caribbean (Haiti, Dominican Republic) • Middle East (limited areas) P. vivax chloroquine resistance: • Papua New Guinea, Indonesia — confirmed resistance • Parts of Southeast Asia — emerging resistance • Consider {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} or {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} for P. vivax from these regions

P. falciparum mefloquine resistance: • Thailand-Cambodia-Myanmar border (Golden Triangle) — high-level resistance • Western Cambodia — widespread resistance • Parts of sub-Saharan Africa — sporadic reports Mefloquine is NO LONGER first-line for Southeast Asia. Use artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) instead.

Emerging resistance in P. falciparum (MAJOR CONCERN): • Greater Mekong Subregion (Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam) — confirmed delayed parasite clearance • Eastern India — sporadic reports • Papua New Guinea — under investigation • East Africa (Rwanda, Uganda) — concerning signals in 2021-2023 surveillance Clinical marker: Parasite clearance half-life >5 hours after IV artesunate. Parasites still detectable on Day 3 smear. Treatment adjustment: Extend treatment duration. Consider {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} as alternative. Consult CDC Malaria Hotline (770-488-7788) for resistance patterns.

Widespread P. falciparum resistance: • Southeast Asia — high-level resistance • Parts of South America — common resistance • East Africa — increasing resistance Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is NO LONGER recommended for treatment. Still used in pregnancy for intermittent preventive therapy (IPTp) in some regions despite resistance.

Southeast Asia (artemisinin resistance zone): • {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} (preferred) • {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} (extended 3-day course) • Consult CDC for latest guidance Sub-Saharan Africa: • {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} (first-line) • {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} (alternative) • IV {{drug:artesunate}} (severe malaria) South America: • {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} or {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} Chloroquine-sensitive areas: • {{drug:chloroquine}} (if confirmed sensitive region) Always verify current resistance patterns with CDC (cdc.gov/malaria) before selecting therapy.

Severe malaria: • IV {{drug:artesunate}} (preferred) — benefit outweighs theoretical risk • Quinidine + clindamycin (alternative) • ICU admission Uncomplicated malaria: • Chloroquine-sensitive: {{drug:chloroquine}} (safest in pregnancy) • Chloroquine-resistant: {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} OR quinine + clindamycin × 7 days • Avoid {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} in first trimester (limited safety data) • Avoid {{drug:primaquine}} (hemolytic risk to fetus) • Avoid doxycycline (teratogenic)

Severe malaria: • IV {{drug:artesunate}} (preferred) • Quinidine + clindamycin (alternative) • ICU admission Uncomplicated malaria: • Chloroquine-sensitive: {{drug:chloroquine}} • Chloroquine-resistant: {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} (preferred) OR {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} (limited data but likely safe) OR quinine + clindamycin × 7 days • Avoid {{drug:primaquine}} until after delivery (hemolytic risk) • Avoid doxycycline (tooth/bone effects)

Increased severity risk: • Pregnant women have higher parasitemia, more severe disease, and higher mortality than non-pregnant women • Placental sequestration of parasites occurs even when peripheral smears are negative • First pregnancies carry highest risk Complications: • Severe anemia (Hgb <7 g/dL) • Hypoglycemia (monitor glucose frequently) • Pulmonary edema (avoid fluid overload) • Premature labor • Fetal distress, intrauterine growth restriction, stillbirth Fetal monitoring: • Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring if viable gestational age • Obstetric consultation early Delivery considerations: • Malaria treatment does NOT require immediate delivery unless maternal instability or fet

Radical cure for P. vivax / P. ovale: • Defer {{drug:primaquine}} until after delivery AND after breastfeeding is complete (if infant has not been tested for G6PD deficiency) • Alternative: check infant G6PD, and if normal, mother may take primaquine while breastfeeding Breastfeeding: • Chloroquine, artemether-lumefantrine, atovaquone-proguanil are likely compatible with breastfeeding • Primaquine is contraindicated if infant G6PD status unknown

Non-adherence (most common): • Missed doses or inconsistent timing • Stopped prophylaxis too early after leaving endemic area (must continue 1-4 weeks post-exposure depending on drug) • Did not start prophylaxis before travel (should start 1-2 days to 2 weeks before, depending on drug) Inadequate drug selection: • Wrong drug for region (e.g., chloroquine in chloroquine-resistant area) • Did not consult CDC guidance for destination-specific prophylaxis Drug resistance: • Emerging resistance patterns (e.g., mefloquine resistance in SE Asia) • Artemisinin-resistant P. falciparum in Greater Mekong Subregion Inadequate dosing: • Weight-based dosing not adjusted for obese or pediatric patients • M

History: • Exact prophylaxis drug, dose, duration • Adherence: did patient miss any doses? • When did prophylaxis stop relative to leaving endemic area? • Travel destination (verify resistance patterns) Testing: • Thick and thin smears × 3 (q12-24h for 48h) • Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) • Serum drug levels (rarely available, not practical in ED) Severity assessment: • Use Malaria Severity Calculator • Check CBC, CMP, lactate, LFTs

KEY RULE: Do NOT use the same drug for treatment that was used for prophylaxis. Risk of resistance or subtherapeutic levels. If on atovaquone-proguanil prophylaxis: • Treat with {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} OR quinine + doxycycline/clindamycin If on mefloquine prophylaxis: • Treat with {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} OR {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} If on doxycycline prophylaxis: • Treat with {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} OR {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} If on chloroquine prophylaxis: • Suspect chloroquine resistance → treat with {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} OR {{drug:atovaquone-proguanil}} Severe malaria (regardless of prophylaxis): • IV {{drug:artesunate}} + ICU admission

Key messages for future travel: • No prophylaxis is 100% effective — still use insect repellent, bed nets, protective clothing • Must continue prophylaxis for 1-4 weeks AFTER leaving endemic area (drug-dependent) • Seek medical care immediately for any fever within 1 year of travel • Consult CDC travel website (wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel) for destination-specific prophylaxis recommendations • Consider terminal prophylaxis with primaquine for P. vivax/ovale prevention if prolonged exposure in high-risk area

• Classic triad: Fever, chills, sweats — but only 50% present with classic "paroxysms" every 48-72h. Do not rule out malaria based on fever pattern alone. • Thrombocytopenia is common: Platelet count <150,000 in 60-70% of malaria cases. Helps distinguish from other causes of fever in returning traveler. • Negative smear does NOT rule out malaria: Sensitivity of single smear is only 50-75%. Repeat q12-24h × 3 if clinical suspicion high. • Parasitemia may be low or absent on peripheral smear in severe disease: Placental, cerebral, and splenic sequestration can hide parasites from peripheral circulation. • RDT detects antigen (not live parasites): Can remain positive for weeks after successful

• Start treatment empirically if high suspicion and severe disease: Do NOT wait for smear confirmation. Delay increases mortality in severe malaria. • IV artesunate is superior to IV quinidine: 22.5% relative reduction in mortality with artesunate. Quinidine requires cardiac monitoring and has more side effects. • Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is preferred over monotherapy: Combination reduces resistance emergence. {{drug:artemether-lumefantrine}} is first-line ACT. • Primaquine is NOT needed for P. falciparum: P. falciparum has no hypnozoite liver stage. Only P. vivax and P. ovale require primaquine for radical cure (14-day course). • Hypoglycemia is common: Quinine/quinidine

• Any severe malaria criterion = ICU admission: Use Severity Calculator systematically. Do not miss acidosis, hypoglycemia, or hyperparasitemia. • Parasitemia > 5% = high risk: Admit for IV therapy even if no other severity criteria. • Discharge criteria for uncomplicated malaria: Tolerating PO, parasitemia <5%, reliable for follow-up, able to return immediately if worsening, no comorbidities. • Follow-up smear at 48-72h: Ensure parasitemia is declining. If not, consider resistance or treatment failure. • CDC Malaria Hotline available 24/7: 770-488-7788. Use for treatment guidance, drug procurement (IV artesunate), and resistance patterns. • Exchange transfusion is NO LONGER recommended: His
• Temperature ≥38.3°C (101°F) on multiple occasions • Duration ≥3 weeks • Uncertain diagnosis after 1 week of inpatient investigation This original definition required hospitalization for workup.

Updated criteria for outpatient era: • Temperature ≥38.3°C (101°F) on multiple occasions • Duration ≥3 weeks (outpatient) or ≥3 days (inpatient) • Uncertain diagnosis after: - 3 outpatient visits, OR - 3 days of inpatient investigation Also introduced FUO subclassifications.

1. Classic FUO: Immunocompetent patient, community-acquired 2. Nosocomial FUO: • Hospitalized ≥24h before fever onset • Fever developing after ≥3 days • Common causes: line infection, C. diff, drug fever, surgical site infection 3. Neutropenic FUO: • ANC <500/µL (or expected to fall <500) • Fever ≥3 days despite antibiotics • Broader differential including fungal 4. HIV-associated FUO: • Confirmed HIV infection • Fever ≥4 weeks (outpatient) or ≥3 days (inpatient) • Opportunistic infections dominate differential

Recent expert consensus recommends: • Standardized minimal initial diagnostic tests before applying FUO classification • Qualitative criteria (specific tests completed) rather than time-based only • Earlier use of FDG-PET/CT when initial workup negative • Recognition that ~30% remain undiagnosed despite thorough evaluation

☐ Fever pattern: continuous, intermittent, relapsing, circadian ☐ Duration and maximum temperature ☐ ALL medications (including OTCs, supplements, herbals) ☐ Travel history (past year, endemic exposures) ☐ Occupational exposures (animals, chemicals, healthcare) ☐ Sexual history and HIV risk factors ☐ Animal/pet exposures ☐ Family history (FMF, periodic fever syndromes) ☐ Prior surgeries, implants, devices ☐ Dental work or symptoms ☐ Injection drug use ☐ Sick contacts, TB exposures

☐ Lymph nodes: all regions, especially supraclavicular ☐ Cardiac: new murmurs, splinter hemorrhages ☐ Abdomen: hepatosplenomegaly, masses ☐ Skin: rashes, nodules, embolic phenomena ☐ Eyes: fundoscopic exam (Roth spots, uveitis) ☐ Joints: arthritis, synovitis ☐ Temporal arteries: tenderness, reduced pulse (age >50) ☐ Prostate/rectal exam: prostatitis, abscess ☐ Dental exam: abscess, periodontal disease ☐ Repeat exam daily — new findings may emerge

☐ CBC with differential (anemia, leukocytosis, eosinophilia) ☐ CMP (electrolytes, renal function, glucose) ☐ LFTs (hepatic involvement) ☐ ESR and CRP (inflammatory markers) ☐ LDH (lymphoma, hemolysis) ☐ Ferritin (Still disease, HLH) ☐ Blood cultures x 2-3 (separate venipunctures) ☐ Urinalysis + urine culture ☐ HIV serology (if not recently tested) ☐ ANA, RF (if autoimmune suspected) ☐ Procalcitonin (bacterial vs non-bacterial)

☐ Chest X-ray (pneumonia, masses, adenopathy) ☐ Abdominal ultrasound or CT (abscess, hepatosplenomegaly, masses) Consider early: ☐ FDG-PET/CT — 50-70% diagnostic yield when initial workup negative ☐ Echocardiogram — if any cardiac concern

If travel history: Malaria smears, dengue serology, typhoid cultures If lymphadenopathy: Excisional biopsy, EBV/CMV serology If age >50 + high ESR: Temporal artery biopsy If hepatic abnormalities: Hepatitis panel, liver biopsy If murmur: TTE → TEE If rash: Skin biopsy If TB exposure: Quantiferon, AFB cultures

SHORT (<2 wk): Malaria (P. falciparum), dengue, chikungunya, rickettsial diseases, travelers diarrhea MEDIUM (2-6 wk): Malaria (all species), typhoid, hepatitis A/E, acute HIV, schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) LONG (>6 wk): Tuberculosis, visceral leishmaniasis, brucellosis KEY PATHOGEN: Malaria — #1 cause of fever from Africa. Rule out first.

SHORT (<2 wk): Dengue (#1 from Asia), chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis, scrub typhus, travelers diarrhea MEDIUM (2-6 wk): Typhoid/paratyphoid (South Asia #1), malaria, hepatitis A/E, leptospirosis, melioidosis LONG (>6 wk): Tuberculosis, visceral leishmaniasis (India) KEY PATHOGEN: Dengue most common; Typhoid especially from India/Bangladesh.

SHORT (<2 wk): Dengue, Zika, chikungunya, rickettsial diseases, travelers diarrhea MEDIUM (2-6 wk): Malaria (Amazon basin), typhoid, hepatitis A, leptospirosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis LONG (>6 wk): Tuberculosis, Chagas disease, visceral leishmaniasis, paracoccidioidomycosis KEY PATHOGEN: Dengue most common; Malaria if Amazon basin travel.

SHORT (<2 wk): MERS-CoV, brucellosis, rickettsial diseases MEDIUM (2-6 wk): Typhoid, hepatitis A/E, Q fever, brucellosis LONG (>6 wk): Tuberculosis, visceral leishmaniasis, brucellosis KEY PATHOGENS: Brucellosis (unpasteurized dairy), MERS (Arabian Peninsula).

SHORT (<2 wk): Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, leptospirosis MEDIUM (2-6 wk): Typhoid, hepatitis A, malaria (Haiti/Dominican Republic), ciguatera KEY PATHOGENS: Dengue, chikungunya; Malaria only from Haiti/DR.

<2 weeks: • Dengue, chikungunya, Zika • Rickettsial diseases • Travelers diarrhea • Influenza, COVID-19 2-6 weeks: • Malaria (especially P. vivax/ovale) • Typhoid/paratyphoid • Hepatitis A, E • Acute HIV seroconversion • Leptospirosis >6 weeks (months): • Tuberculosis • Visceral leishmaniasis • Amoebic liver abscess • Chronic fungal infections

Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) — #1 cause Sulfonamides (TMP-SMX) Vancomycin Nitrofurantoin Minocycline Amphotericin B Onset: Usually 7-10 days after starting, but can occur within hours on re-exposure.
Phenytoin — DRESS syndrome Carbamazepine — DRESS syndrome Phenobarbital Lamotrigine May present with rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis (DRESS syndrome).
Procainamide — also drug-induced lupus Quinidine Hydralazine — also drug-induced lupus Methyldopa Nifedipine Diltiazem

Allopurinol — especially with HLA-B*5801 Heparin Bleomycin Interferon-alpha Biological agents (TNF inhibitors, checkpoint inhibitors) H2 blockers (ranitidine, cimetidine) NSAIDs (paradoxically) Barbiturates

Timing: Days to weeks after drug initiation (mean 7-10 days) Appearance: Patient often appears paradoxically well despite fever Relative bradycardia: Pulse inappropriately low for fever degree Rash: Present in ~20% (not required for diagnosis) Eosinophilia: Present in ~20% (not required) Resolution: Fever resolves 48-72 hours after stopping drug (may take up to 5-7 days for some)

Diagnosis of exclusion: 1. Temporal relationship to drug exposure 2. Resolution after drug discontinuation 3. Exclusion of other fever causes Re-challenge: Confirms diagnosis but rarely performed (risk of severe reaction) No specific lab test available

Most Common: • Tuberculosis (most common infectious cause worldwide) • Endocarditis (especially culture-negative) • Intra-abdominal abscess • Osteomyelitis • Prostatitis (elderly men) • Dental abscess Viral: • EBV, CMV (prolonged mononucleosis) • HIV (acute or advanced) Fungal: • Histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis (endemic areas) • Disseminated candidiasis

Hematologic (most common): • Lymphoma (Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin) • Leukemia (especially AML, CLL) • Castleman disease • Myelodysplastic syndrome Solid Tumors: • Renal cell carcinoma (classic FUO cause) • Hepatocellular carcinoma • Ovarian cancer • Atrial myxoma • Colon cancer (with liver metastases)

Vasculitis: • Giant Cell Arteritis (age >50) • Polyarteritis nodosa • ANCA-associated vasculitis Connective Tissue: • Adult Still disease (ferritin >10,000) • Systemic lupus erythematosus • Rheumatoid arthritis • Inflammatory myopathy Granulomatous: • Sarcoidosis Autoinflammatory: • Familial Mediterranean fever • TRAPS

• Drug fever (3-7% of all FUO) • Factitious fever (self-induced) • Habitual hyperthermia • Thyroiditis (subacute) • Pulmonary embolism (recurrent) • Inflammatory bowel disease • Cirrhosis • Hematoma (large, resolving)

Prognosis is generally favorable: • Many resolve spontaneously • ~50% eventually diagnosed on long-term follow-up • 5-year mortality similar to age-matched controls Management: • Close follow-up • Repeat evaluation if new symptoms • Avoid empiric steroids unless infection excluded

Developing countries: • Infections dominate (TB, typhoid, malaria) Developed countries: • Non-infectious inflammatory diseases more common • Malignancy percentage higher • "Undiagnosed" category larger (more thorough workup excludes obvious causes)

ETCO₂ is the most reliable real-time indicator of CPR quality and the earliest detector of ROSC — often minutes before a palpable pulse. • Waveform capnography preferred over colorimetric • Attach immediately after advanced airway secured • Continuous display during resuscitation

• >20 mmHg = adequate CPR quality (EMCrit target) • >10 mmHg = AHA minimum acceptable • <10 mmHg = poor compressions — check technique, depth, rate, recoil • Use feedback to coach compressors in real time • Rotate compressors every 2 minutes (fatigue → declining ETCO₂)

• Sudden rise >10 mmHg from baseline = likely ROSC • Often precedes palpable pulse by 30-60 seconds • Sustained rise to >35-40 mmHg strongly suggests ROSC • Do NOT interrupt CPR to check pulse based on ETCO₂ alone — wait for scheduled rhythm check

• ETCO₂ <10 mmHg after 20 minutes of optimal CPR = very poor prognosis • Combined with no cardiac activity on POCUS = near-zero survival • NOT an absolute criterion — still consider reversible causes • Exception: hypothermia, poisoning (continue resuscitation)

• Sodium bicarbonate causes transient ETCO₂ spike (CO₂ released from buffering) — do not mistake for ROSC • Epinephrine may transiently decrease ETCO₂ (vasoconstriction reduces pulmonary blood flow) • Low ETCO₂ with good compressions → consider massive PE, air trapping, or equipment malfunction • BVM ventilation gives less reliable readings than ETT/SGA

info.h: Obvious Signs of Death (Do NOT Initiate)
info.t: • Decapitation • Hemicorporectomy (transection of the torso) • Dependent lividity (non-blanching discoloration in dependent areas) • Rigor mortis (stiffening of joints and muscles) • Decomposition (tissue breakdown, odor) • Obviously non-survivable traumatic injury (e.g., massive cranial destruction)

• Valid Do Not Attempt Resuscitation order on scene • Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) indicating no CPR • Must be a valid, signed document — verbal reports alone may be insufficient • When in doubt, start CPR — can always stop after verification

• Blunt trauma with CPR >10 minutes and no signs of life = consider futility • Penetrating trauma with CPR >15 minutes and no signs of life • Signs of life: pupillary response, spontaneous movement, organized cardiac rhythm • Exception: penetrating torso trauma → resuscitative thoracotomy may be indicated
When uncertain, always initiate CPR. It is far better to start and then appropriately terminate than to withhold CPR from a potentially salvageable patient.

Consider TOR if ALL of the following: • Arrest not witnessed by EMS • No bystander CPR • No AED shock delivered • No ROSC prior to transport decision Validated in multiple studies — 99.5% specificity for non-survival.

Consider TOR if ALL of the following: • Arrest not witnessed (or witnessed but non-shockable) • No ROSC prior to transport • No shocks delivered during resuscitation Adds ALS-level information to BLS rule.

• ETCO₂ <10 mmHg after 20 minutes of quality CPR • Must ensure adequate CPR technique (not falsely low from poor compressions) • Combined with other criteria, not alone • Exception: hypothermic arrest, poisoning

• No cardiac activity on POCUS after adequate resuscitation duration • Combined with ETCO₂ <10 = strongest futility signal • Cardiac standstill at any point = near-zero survival (but NOT absolute) • Always reassess for reversible causes before calling

• Reversible cause still being treated (hyperK, tension PTX, PE, toxin) • Hypothermic cardiac arrest ("not dead until warm and dead") • Drug overdose (may require prolonged CPR — 60+ min for some toxins) • ECPR in progress or immediately available • Intermittent ROSC • Pediatric arrest (longer resuscitation attempts warranted)

• During scheduled pulse/rhythm checks ONLY (<10 seconds) • Do NOT interrupt CPR for POCUS • Have probe ready and pre-positioned before pausing compressions • Subxiphoid cardiac view is fastest in arrest

Subxiphoid or parasternal long axis: • Cardiac activity present? Organized wall motion vs standstill • RV dilation? RV > LV suggests massive PE • Pericardial effusion? Fluid around heart → tamponade if RV collapse • Global function? Hyperdynamic (hypovolemia) vs poor squeeze (cardiogenic) No cardiac activity = pseudo-PEA / strongest futility signal

IVC (subxiphoid longitudinal): • Collapsed IVC (<1 cm, >50% respiratory variation) = hypovolemia • Plethoric IVC (>2 cm, no variation) = obstructive cause (PE, tamponade) or cardiogenic Lungs (bilateral anterior): • Absent lung sliding = pneumothorax → needle decompression • B-lines = pulmonary edema (cardiogenic, fluid overload) FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma): • Free fluid (Morison, splenorenal, pelvis) = hemorrhage
Abdominal aorta (epigastric): • AAA >3 cm = ruptured aneurysm as cause of arrest (rare but treatable) • Quick sweep from xiphoid to bifurcation

• Wide QRS PEA → look for hyperkalemia signs (clinical), treat empirically • Narrow QRS PEA → RUSH findings direct treatment: - RV dilation → tPA for PE - Pericardial effusion → pericardiocentesis - No lung sliding → needle decompression - Collapsed IVC → volume resuscitation

Think: Sodium channel blockade | Cause | Key Feature | First Treatment | |-------|-------------|------------------| | Hyperkalemia | Peaked T waves, sine wave | CaCl/CaGluc 1g IV, NaHCO₃, insulin+D50 | | TCA overdose | Anticholinergic signs, R in aVR >3mm | NaHCO₃ 1-2 mEq/kg IV push | | Na channel blocker | Drug history | NaHCO₃ + lipid emulsion | | Severe acidosis | pH <7.0 | NaHCO₃ 1 mEq/kg | | Hypermagnesemia | Renal failure + Mg infusion | Calcium 1g IV |

Think: Obstructive or hypovolemic | Cause | POCUS Finding | First Treatment | |-------|---------------|------------------| | Cardiac tamponade | Pericardial effusion + RV collapse | Pericardiocentesis | | Tension pneumothorax | Absent lung sliding | Needle decompression | | Massive PE | RV dilation, McConnell sign | tPA 50mg IV push | | Hypovolemia | Collapsed IVC, empty heart | 1-2L crystalloid rapid bolus | | Auto-PEEP | Ventilated patient | Disconnect ventilator, decompress |

Wide complex PEA has a metabolic/toxic cause until proven otherwise. Narrow complex PEA has a mechanical/obstructive cause until proven otherwise. This distinction guides your first intervention while waiting for definitive diagnosis. Treat empirically — the risk of treating is far less than the risk of delay.

• VF refractory to 3 consecutive standard (anterolateral) shocks with optimal CPR • DSD is applied directly at that point. DOSE-VF did NOT require a vector-change attempt first — vector change was a separate, parallel randomisation arm, not a prior step. Do not delay DSD to trial VC. • Requires two defibrillators and four pads • If a second defibrillator is not available, vector change alone also beat standard care (21.7% vs 13.3%) — it is an evidence-supported option in its own right, not a consolation prize

Defibrillator 1: Standard anterolateral (AL) • Right infraclavicular • Left lateral chest (mid-axillary) Defibrillator 2: Anterior-Posterior (AP) • Left parasternal (anterior) • Left infrascapular (posterior) Pads must not overlap — trim or offset if necessary.

1. Charge both defibrillators to maximum energy 2. Assign one operator per defibrillator 3. Verbal countdown: "Charging... ready... 3-2-1-SHOCK" 4. Deliver shocks <1 second apart (near-simultaneous) 5. Resume CPR immediately after both shocks 6. Continue 2-minute CPR cycle, reassess rhythm

• Address H's and T's at every pulse check — not just once • POCUS is the fastest way to identify tamponade, PE, PTX, hypovolemia • Wide QRS → think hyperK or toxin FIRST • Narrow QRS → think obstructive causes FIRST • Multiple causes may coexist — treat all identified • Empiric calcium + bicarb is reasonable when hyperK/toxin cannot be excluded

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT LP without CT if high-risk criteria present
info.t: CT FIRST if ANY of: Age >60, immunocompromised, CNS disease history, new seizure, altered mental status (GCS <15), focal deficit, papilledema. Risk of herniation. CT criteria.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP in meningitis
info.t: Bacterial meningitis mortality increases with antibiotic delay. Give empiric antibiotics FIRST (ceftriaxone + vancomycin ± ampicillin), then CT, then LP. Meningitis management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT LP through infected skin
info.t: Cellulitis, abscess, or any infection overlying the puncture site is an absolute contraindication. Risk of iatrogenic meningitis or epidural abscess.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT LP with PLT <20,000 without transfusion
info.t: Traditional threshold: PLT >50,000. Evidence-based: PLT >40,000 likely safe. PLT <20,000 = high risk — transfuse first unless emergent meningitis. Coagulation thresholds.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT LP with INR >1.5 (or active anticoagulation)
info.t: Risk of epidural/spinal hematoma. Warfarin: hold 5d, target INR <1.4. DOACs: wait 72h minimum. Heparin: wait 4-6h. Anticoagulant management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT measure opening pressure in sitting position
info.t: Sitting position CANNOT accurately measure OP — falsely elevated. Must use lateral decubitus with legs extended, patient relaxed. OP technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on RBC clearing alone to exclude SAH
info.t: RBC count decrease tube 1→4 is unreliable (25% reduction occurs in SAH too). Xanthochromia with bilirubin (requires >9-10h) is the gold standard. Traumatic tap vs SAH.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use cutting needles if atraumatic available
info.t: Quincke (cutting) needles: 15-30% PDPH. Whitacre/Sprotte (atraumatic): ~4% PDPH. Always use pencil-point needles when available. Needle selection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT remove stylet before withdrawing needle
info.t: Replace stylet before removing needle — reduces PDPH risk. The stylet prevents arachnoid tissue from being pulled through the dura.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore post-LP leg weakness or urinary retention
info.t: Back pain + leg weakness + urinary symptoms = epidural hematoma until proven otherwise. Urgent MRI spine and neurosurgery consult. Complications.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume symptoms are MS relapse without checking for infection
info.t: UTI is the #1 cause of pseudoexacerbation. Check UA, CBC, temp in ALL MS patients with worsening symptoms. Treat infection first, reassess after fever resolves. Assessment

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give oral prednisone ALONE for optic neuritis
info.t: ONTT trial showed oral prednisone monotherapy DOUBLES recurrence risk. Must use IV steroids first, or no steroids at all. Treatment

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give steroids if PML is suspected
info.t: Progressive deficits over weeks (not typical relapse pattern) in patient on natalizumab = PML until proven otherwise. Steroids worsen PML. Get MRI + LP for JCV PCR. PML

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give steroids before ruling out cord compression
info.t: New sensory level, paraparesis, or bladder retention = STAT MRI spine FIRST. Cord compression is a surgical emergency. Transverse Myelitis

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT diagnose MS in the ED
info.t: MS diagnosis requires McDonald criteria with MRI ± LP ± clinical dissemination. Many mimics exist (NMOSD, ADEM, tumors, infections). Refer to neurology. New-Onset

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore baclofen withdrawal — it is LIFE-THREATENING
info.t: Abrupt baclofen discontinuation (oral or pump) causes hyperthermia, rigidity, AMS, seizures, multi-organ failure. Restore baclofen immediately. Baclofen

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start MS DMTs without clarifying NMOSD vs MS
info.t: Some MS DMTs (interferon-beta, fingolimod) WORSEN NMOSD. Check AQP4/MOG antibodies. Document diagnostic uncertainty. NMOSD vs MS

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge severe relapses without safe home/follow-up
info.t: Patients unable to ambulate, with bladder retention, or brainstem involvement need admission. Ensure neurology follow-up within 1-2 weeks for all relapses. Disposition

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget postpartum MS patients are HIGH-RISK
info.t: First 3 months postpartum has highest relapse risk. ~37% relapse within 6 months. Low threshold for evaluation and treatment. Pregnancy

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss respiratory compromise with brainstem/cervical lesions
info.t: High cervical or brainstem lesions can cause respiratory muscle weakness. Accounts for ~47% of MS deaths. Low threshold for intubation. Respiratory
