Use gravity to decompress the cord while maintaining maternal uteroplacental perfusion. Combine with continuous manual elevation of the presenting part and left lateral tilt.

Most gravity assistance — best for stationary OR prep. Technique: • Patient kneels on the bed • Chest and head rest on the mattress (face turned to one side) • Buttocks pointed up toward the ceiling • Knees under hips, arms forward Advantages: maximal gravity decompression Disadvantages: difficult to maintain during transport, awkward for IV and fetal monitoring

Best for transport — maintains IV access and monitoring. Technique: • Bed tilted head-down 15-30° • Hips elevated on pillows or wedge • Left lateral tilt ≥15° to decompress IVC Advantages: easier transport, monitoring, IV access Disadvantages: less gravity assistance than knee-chest

Comfortable for longer waits — good for rural transfer. Technique: • Patient on left side • Hips and pelvis elevated on pillows • Upper leg flexed forward • Head down slightly Advantages: comfortable, sustainable for hours, good for IV and monitoring Disadvantages: intermediate gravity assistance

• ALWAYS left lateral tilt ≥15° in any position — decompresses IVC, maintains uteroplacental perfusion • NEVER supine — aortocaval compression worsens fetal hypoxia AND cord compression • Combine with continuous manual elevation of presenting part • Change position if patient uncomfortable for extended waits — function matters more than position name
Relax the uterus to improve placental perfusion and reduce cord compression during OR prep, transport, or when delivery is delayed. Every 1-minute reduction in cord compression matters.

Terbutaline 0.25 mg SC or IM × 1 dose Onset: 1-5 minutes (SC) Duration: 15-30 minutes May repeat: q15-30 min × 1 if needed Watch for: • Maternal HR — avoid if baseline >120 • Hyperglycemia (~10-15 mg/dL rise) • Hypokalemia • Jitteriness, tremor Contraindications (relative): baseline tachycardia, arrhythmia, active MI, brittle diabetes

Nitroglycerin 50-100 mcg IV push; may repeat q2min up to 400 mcg total Onset: 1-2 minutes (IV) Duration: 2-5 minutes Also available: 0.4 mg SL × 1 (onset 1-2 min, less reliable than IV) Watch for: • Maternal hypotension — main adverse effect • Have phenylephrine 100 mcg IV ready • Have IV crystalloid 500 mL ready • Reflex tachycardia • Headache Contraindications: SBP <90, RV infarction, PDE-5 inhibitor use 24-48h

Mag sulfate onset is 20+ minutes — too slow for acute cord compression. Reserve magnesium sulfate for: • Eclampsia / severe preeclampsia • Fetal neuroprotection in preterm delivery • NOT for acute in-utero resuscitation in cord emergency

Simultaneous with tocolytic: • Oxygen — 10 L/min NRB • IV fluid bolus — 500 mL – 1 L crystalloid • Left lateral tilt ≥15° (IVC decompression) • Stop oxytocin if running (tachysystole is a common reversible cause of fetal compromise)

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt to reduce a prolapsed cord back into the uterus
info.t: Historical teaching now discouraged. It is ineffective, induces cord vasospasm, and delays definitive care. Instead, elevate the presenting part off the cord manually and minimize cord handling.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT leave prolapsed cord exposed to air or handle it repeatedly
info.t: Both cause vasospasm and worsen fetal ischemia. If cord is outside the introitus, cover with warm saline-soaked gauze and minimize contact. Do not clamp the cord. Cord prolapse pathway.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clamp and cut a tight nuchal cord as first-line
info.t: Attempt the somersault maneuver first. Cutting commits you to immediate delivery — if shoulder dystocia follows, the fetus has no placental circulation → acute hypoxia and anemia. Cutting is a last resort after somersault fails.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transport a cord prolapse patient supine
info.t: Supine position compresses IVC AND worsens cord compression. Use knee-chest, Trendelenburg with left tilt, or exaggerated Sims for all transport. Left lateral tilt ≥15° is mandatory in any position.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay C-section for antenatal steroids
info.t: When the fetus is already compromised, deliver now — neonatology manages lung immaturity. Steroids are for planned premature deliveries, not acute emergencies. Cord prolapse result.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rupture membranes if vasa previa is known or suspected
info.t: Amniotomy over unprotected fetal vessels = fetal exsanguination within minutes (fetal blood volume is only 80-100 mL/kg). If pulsating vessels palpable through a dilated cervix, stop the exam and prepare for C-section. Vasa previa pathway.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform digital cervical exam in a third-trimester patient with vaginal bleeding
info.t: Before ruling out placenta previa and vasa previa with ultrasound. Digital exam in these conditions can provoke catastrophic bleeding. Acute vasa previa.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT administer oxytocin during active cord prolapse
info.t: Contractions worsen cord compression. Turn off the pump. Use tocolysis instead — terbutaline 0.25 mg SC or NTG 50-100 mcg IV.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give magnesium sulfate for acute tocolysis in cord emergency
info.t: Mag onset is 20+ minutes — too slow for acute cord compression. Use terbutaline or nitroglycerin. Reserve magnesium for eclampsia or fetal neuroprotection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to drain the bladder before skin incision
info.t: If Vago bladder-fill was used for temporization, uncuff the Foley and drain immediately before cesarean skin incision. A distended bladder is in the surgical field.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the Apt test just because vasa previa seems obvious
info.t: Bedside Apt test (1% KOH — pink = fetal Hgb) distinguishes fetal from maternal blood in ~2 minutes. Confirms diagnosis, documents for medicolegal purposes, guides neonatal resuscitation needs. Do NOT delay C-section for results, but do perform it. Apt test technique.

Standard dose: 1.5 mg PO × 1 High-risk dose (3 mg): Use if: • Weight >165 lbs (75 kg) or BMI >25 • On enzyme-inducing medications How to give 3 mg: Two 1.5 mg tablets at once Timing: Best within 72h; some efficacy to 120h Access: OTC — no prescription, no age limit Cost: ~$40-50
Dose: 30 mg PO × 1 (no dose escalation) Timing: Up to 120h (5 days) — maintains efficacy Access: Prescription required Cost: ~$50 CRITICAL: Wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception

Dose 1: 100 mcg ethinyl estradiol + 0.5 mg levonorgestrel Dose 2: Repeat in 12 hours Using COCs: • Levora/Nordette: 4 pills × 2 (12h apart) • Alesse/Levlite: 5 pills × 2 (12h apart) Timing: Within 72h Side effects: Nausea 54%, vomiting 16% Give antiemetic 1h before: Ondansetron 4 mg or meclizine 25 mg

Most effective EC (>99%) Timing: Within 5 days of intercourse OR within 5 days of ovulation Advantages: • Unaffected by weight • Unaffected by timing • Unaffected by medications • Provides 10 years of contraception

| Method | 0-24h | 24-72h | 72-120h | >120h | |--------|-------|--------|---------|-------| | Cu-IUD | >99% | >99% | >99% | May work* | | Ulipristal | 94% | 95% | 95% | No | | Levonorgestrel | 91% | 87% | 75% | No | | Yuzpe | 86% | 75% | 58% | No | *Cu-IUD may work beyond 5 days if within 5 days of ovulation

Levonorgestrel: • Best within 24 hours (91% efficacy) • Acceptable within 72 hours (87%) • Efficacy drops significantly after 72 hours • UK guidance: consider ineffective after 96 hours Ulipristal: • No efficacy decay from 24-120 hours • 42% better than LNG at 24-72h • 65% better than LNG in first 24h • Maintains efficacy near ovulation (LNG does not)

0-72 hours: Any method works well • LNG acceptable if OTC access critical • UPA slightly better • IUD best if available 72-120 hours: Switch to UPA or IUD • LNG efficacy significantly reduced • UPA maintains ~95% efficacy • IUD unaffected >120 hours: IUD only option • Oral EC not effective • IUD may still work if before ovulation

| Weight | BMI | LNG Efficacy | UPA Efficacy | Best Option | |--------|-----|--------------|--------------|-------------| | <165 lbs | <25 | Full | Full | Any | | 165-195 lbs | 25-30 | Reduced | Slightly reduced | UPA or IUD | | >195 lbs | >30 | Significantly reduced | Reduced | Cu-IUD |

Weight <165 lbs (75 kg): • All methods equally effective • Choose based on access and timing Weight 165-195 lbs (75-89 kg): • LNG efficacy reduced • Prefer ulipristal or copper IUD • If LNG only available: still give (better than nothing) Weight >195 lbs (89 kg): • Both LNG and UPA have reduced efficacy • Copper IUD is best option (unaffected by weight) • If pills only: UPA > LNG

For weight >165 lbs: • Consider 3 mg (double dose) • Mixed evidence — 2024 study showed no clear benefit • Reasonable option when IUD/UPA unavailable For enzyme inducers: • Double dose (3 mg) is recommended • Better evidence than weight-based doubling Important: Do NOT withhold EC based on weight. Any EC is better than no EC.

FDA Classification: • EC is a contraceptive, NOT an abortifacient • December 2022 label update: "does not terminate pregnancy" • Mechanism: prevents ovulation, does NOT disrupt implantation All EC methods are legal in all 50 states.

Plan B (levonorgestrel): • ✅ Legal • ✅ OTC — no prescription needed • ✅ No age restrictions • May be behind counter but no Rx required ella (ulipristal): • ✅ Legal with prescription • Telehealth prescribing available Copper IUD: • ✅ Legal, standard of care • NOT considered abortifacient Minors: • Plan B: OTC, no parental consent needed • Title X clinics: parental consent required (5th Circuit ruling 2024) Pharmacist refusal: • No state law protecting refusal (as of 2026) • SB 1985 (2025) proposes protection — status pending

Idaho: • EC legal; unique: pharmacists can prescribe without age limit • School clinics: EC restricted except for rape Oklahoma: • EC legal, no state bans • Reports of individual pharmacist refusals Louisiana: • EC legal but legal risk from "personhood" language • Reports of pharmacist refusals Arkansas: • EC legal • Some Medicaid access restrictions

States with pharmacist refusal clauses: Arizona, Arkansas, Georgia, Idaho, Mississippi, South Dakota If pharmacist refuses: • Patient can request transfer to another pharmacy • OTC Plan B available at most retailers • Document refusal for risk management Texas: No state refusal law (currently), but pending legislation

Hospital requirements vary by state: Texas: • Must provide information about EC • NOT required to dispense • Patient may go to pharmacy Best practice: • Offer EC to all sexual assault survivors • Document offer and patient decision • If declined, offer to revisit before discharge

info.h: Why Copper IUD is Gold Standard
info.t: Efficacy: >99% (pregnancy rate 0.1%) Advantages over oral EC: • Unaffected by weight — works at any BMI • Unaffected by timing — consistent efficacy within 5-day window • Unaffected by medications — no drug interactions • Long-term contraception — up to 10 years • Immediate protection — no backup method needed

Standard guidance: • Within 5 days of unprotected intercourse Extended guidance: • Within 5 days of ovulation (not intercourse) • If cycle timing known, may extend window • Example: Sex day 7, ovulation day 14 → IUD day 13 still works If timing uncertain: • Can insert any time in cycle if pregnancy test negative • Efficacy less certain beyond 5 days but reasonable option

Absolute contraindications: • Current pregnancy • Active PID or purulent cervicitis • Unexplained vaginal bleeding (until evaluated) • Cervical or endometrial cancer • Uterine cavity distortion (fibroids, anomaly) • Wilson disease (copper overload) NOT contraindications: • Nulliparity (never given birth) • Prior ectopic pregnancy • STI risk factors (test, can insert before results) • Breastfeeding

Can insert in ED if: • Trained provider available • Equipment available • Patient desires IUD for EC + ongoing contraception Pre-procedure: • Pregnancy test (if not done) • Bimanual exam for uterine position • STI testing if high-risk (can insert before results) • NSAIDs for pain (ibuprofen 400-600 mg) If unable to insert: • Give oral EC as bridge • Refer for urgent IUD insertion within 5 days

Expected effects: • Cramping — NSAIDs PRN • Spotting — normal • Heavier, longer periods first 3-6 months Follow-up: • String check in 4-6 weeks • Can remain 10 years Return precautions: • Fever, severe pain, abnormal discharge • String changes (longer, shorter, absent) • Signs of pregnancy

Anticonvulsants: • Phenytoin (Dilantin) • Carbamazepine (Tegretol) • Phenobarbital • Oxcarbazepine • Topiramate (>200 mg/day) • Primidone Antibiotics: • Rifampin (most potent inducer) • Rifabutin Antiretrovirals: • Efavirenz • Nevirapine • Some protease inhibitors Other: • St. John's Wort • Griseofulvin • Bosentan

Ulipristal (ella): • ❌ CONTRAINDICATED with enzyme inducers • Do NOT use — significantly reduced efficacy Levonorgestrel (Plan B): • ⚠️ Reduced efficacy • Double dose to 3 mg (two 1.5 mg tablets) • UK FSRH recommended approach Copper IUD: • ✅ Unaffected by any medications • Best option for patients on enzyme inducers

How long do inducers affect EC? • Effect persists 4 weeks after stopping the medication • If patient stopped inducer within past month, still assume reduced efficacy Practical approach: • Ask about current AND recent (past month) medications • When in doubt, use copper IUD or double LNG dose

Patient on enzyme inducer needs EC: 1️⃣ Best: Copper IUD (unaffected) 2️⃣ If IUD unavailable: Levonorgestrel 3 mg (double dose) 3️⃣ Do NOT use: Ulipristal (contraindicated) Document: Interaction identified, alternative used, rationale

Per Ethical and Religious Directives (ERD) Directive 36: Catholic hospitals use a different EC protocol for sexual assault cases, requiring serum LH testing to determine ovulation status before administering Plan B. Rationale: ERD permits EC only if it prevents fertilization, not implantation. LH testing attempts to identify ovulating patients where fertilization may have already occurred.

• Patient must present within 72 hours of assault • If >72 hours post-assault → EC NOT administered per protocol Note: Standard medical guidance supports EC up to 120 hours. This 72-hour limit is institution-specific.
• Order urine or serum HCG with patient permission • If positive → pregnancy predates assault → NO Plan B • If patient is sterile → no EC needed (may give for psychological benefit if requested)

If conception is possible → order Serum LH | LH Result | Interpretation | Plan B? | |-----------|----------------|---------|| | Outside 19.18-103.03 | Not ovulating OR ovum no longer viable | ✅ YES | | Within 19.18-103.03 | LH surge = likely ovulating | ❌ NO | LH 19.18-103.03 mIU/mL = mid-cycle surge window where fertilization is possible

info.h: If Plan B CAN Be Given
info.t: • Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg PO once (Plan B) • Available from: Inpatient pharmacy OR ED Omnicell • Requires physician order • Counsel: EC is NOT 100% effective

info.h: If Plan B CANNOT Be Given
info.t: • Inform patient why per protocol • Patient may seek treatment elsewhere • Document discussion in chart • Provide information about community resources Patient rights: The patient has the right to seek EC at a non-Catholic facility. Provide this information clearly.

❌ Ella (ulipristal) — post-fertilization mechanism ❌ Mifepristone (RU-486) ❌ Copper IUD for EC ❌ Any agent with post-fertilization mechanism Note: Mirena IUD is also restricted for EC purposes at most Catholic facilities.

Don't forget: • STI/STD prophylaxis discussion with attending • Forensic evidence collection (SANE if available) • Offer Spiritual Care / Social Services • Treat injuries, prophylactic antibiotics as indicated • Document thoroughly • Refer to Sexual Assault Considerations
Dose: 5-10 mL/kg (max 500 mL) Safest option with minimal risk of electrolyte disturbances. May need to repeat 2-3 times for full effect.

Dose: 15-30 mL per year of age (max 240 mL) | Age | Dose | |-----|------| | 2-6 years | ~60 mL (2 oz) | | 6-12 years | ~120 mL (4 oz) | | >12 years | 180-240 mL | Technique: Instill slowly, have child retain for 30-60 minutes. Follow with saline enema 1-3 hours later.

Preparation: Mix 1:1 ratio whole milk and molasses, warm to body temperature. Dose: 5-6 mL/kg (max 135 mL) Efficacy: 88% success rate in ED studies. Comparable to sodium phosphate enemas. ⚠️ Caution: Rare reports of hemodynamic compromise. Use with monitoring in dehydrated patients.

⚠️ Avoid in children <2 years (some recommend <4 years) Risks: Hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia — especially in young children, dehydrated, or renal impairment. | Age | Dose | |-----|------| | 2-4 years | 30 mL (1 oz) — if used | | 5-11 years | 66 mL (2.25 oz) | | ≥12 years | 133 mL (4.5 oz) | Only give single dose. Do not repeat.

Dose: 1-1.5 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day) • Divide into 2-4 doses throughout the day • Mix in 10 mL water per gram of PEG • Continue for 3-6 days until clear watery stools Example (20 kg child): • 20-30 g/day = ~1.5-2 capfuls daily • Divide into morning and evening doses
Alternative for faster clearance: • 6 mL/kg prepared solution (max 135 mL) • May repeat every 12-24 hours × 1-3 doses • Works within 24-48 hours

Start AFTER successful disimpaction. Dose: 0.4-0.8 g/kg/day • Start at 0.4 g/kg, titrate to effect • Goal: 1-2 soft stools daily • Continue minimum 2-3 months • Taper slowly (reduce 25% every 2-4 weeks)
• PEG without electrolytes (MiraLAX) tastes better than PEG-ELS • Mix in juice, Gatorade, or flavored drink • Serve cold • Crystal Light or Kool-Aid powder helps mask taste
Disimpaction phase: • Frequent loose/watery stools within 24-48 hours • Some fecal incontinence expected — warn family • Success rate: 85-95% If no stool output after 3 days → add rectal enema.

🚩 Delayed meconium passage (>48h after birth) 🚩 Onset in first weeks of life 🚩 Failure to thrive 🚩 Explosive stool after rectal exam 🚩 Empty rectum on exam despite constipation 🚩 Severe distention If suspected: Refer for suction rectal biopsy. Do NOT give enemas — risk of enterocolitis.
🚩 Bilious vomiting 🚩 Severe abdominal distention 🚩 Absent bowel sounds 🚩 Complete obstipation (no flatus) Action: Immediate imaging (XR, CT), surgical consult.
🚩 Sacral dimple or tuft of hair 🚩 Asymmetric gluteal cleft 🚩 Abnormal lower extremity reflexes 🚩 Abnormal gait 🚩 Urinary incontinence Action: MRI lumbosacral spine, neurology referral.
🚩 Fever (enterocolitis in Hirschsprung) 🚩 Bloody stool (beyond fissure) 🚩 Significant weight loss 🚩 Thyroid abnormalities (hypothyroidism) 🚩 Abdominal mass (beyond fecal)

95% of pediatric constipation is FUNCTIONAL. Features favoring functional: • Onset at weaning, toilet training, or school entry • Withholding behaviors (tiptoeing, hiding) • Large-diameter stools • Fecal soiling (encopresis) • Otherwise healthy, thriving child

Must include ≥1 month of ≥2 of the following: • ≤2 defecations per week • History of excessive stool retention • History of painful or hard bowel movements • History of large-diameter stools • Presence of a large fecal mass in the rectum In toilet-trained children, also: • ≥1 episode of fecal incontinence per week • History of large-diameter stools that may obstruct toilet

Must include ≥2 criteria for ≥1 month: • ≤2 defecations in the toilet per week • ≥1 episode of fecal incontinence per week • History of retentive posturing or excessive volitional stool retention • History of painful or hard bowel movements • Presence of a large fecal mass in the rectum • History of large-diameter stools that may obstruct toilet With insufficient criteria for IBS.

First-Line Maintenance Dose: 0.4-0.8 g/kg/day • Start low, titrate to 1-2 soft stools/day • Max: 17 g/day (one capful) Duration: • Minimum 2-3 months • Often 6-12 months needed • Taper slowly (25% reduction every 2-4 weeks) Common mistake: Stopping too soon → recurrence.

Toilet Training: • Scheduled sitting 5-10 min after meals (gastrocolic reflex) • Proper positioning: feet flat on stool, knees above hips • Positive reinforcement — sticker charts for sitting (not for stooling) • Never punish accidents Withholding: • Explain holding makes stool bigger/harder • Reassure stool will be soft with laxatives • Never force toilet sitting

Fiber: Age + 5 grams/day • Example: 8-year-old = 13 g/day • Fruits, vegetables, whole grains Fluids: Adequate water throughout day Limit: • Excess cow's milk (>24 oz/day associated with constipation) • Constipating foods: bananas, rice, applesauce, toast (BRAT)
• 2-4 weeks: PCP visit to assess response, adjust dose • 2-3 months: Reassess if ready to taper • 6+ months: GI referral if refractory despite compliance

Before manual disimpaction: 1. Soften stool first: • Mineral oil enema 120-150 mL • Retain 30-60 minutes 2. Pre-medicate: • Acetaminophen 1 g PO/PR or ketorolac 15-30 mg IV • ± Low-dose benzodiazepine for anxiety 3. Position: Left lateral decubitus, knees to chest 4. Supplies: Double gloves, water-soluble lubricant, chux pads, bedpan

1. Lubricate gloved index finger generously 2. Insert finger gently into rectum 3. Break up stool using scissoring motion 4. Hook and extract fragments with flexed finger 5. Move finger in circular motion to loosen stool 6. Remove fragments in small pieces 7. Stop if patient has significant pain or vagal symptoms 8. Repeat until rectum is empty Duration: 15-30 minutes typically required

⚠️ Monitor for: • Bradycardia • Hypotension • Diaphoresis • Nausea/dizziness If symptomatic bradycardia: • Stop immediately • Atropine 0.5 mg IV available Avoid in: Patients with cardiac conduction abnormalities

After disimpaction: 1. Cleansing enema: • Tap water or saline 500-1000 mL • May need to repeat 2-3 times 2. Check: Post-void residual if urinary retention suspected 3. Start maintenance: PEG 17 g daily to prevent recurrence

Dose: 120-150 mL Use: Softening before manual disimpaction Technique: • Instill slowly • Retain 30-60 minutes (up to several hours if possible) • Follow with cleansing enema Safe for: Most patients, including elderly and renal impairment

Dose: 500-1000 mL Use: Cleansing enema after disimpaction Technique: • Warm to body temperature • Limit reservoir height to 3 feet above anus • Instill slowly, guided by patient comfort • Retain 5-15 minutes if possible Safe for: All patients

Dose: 118 mL single dose ⚠️ HIGH-RISK: Use with extreme caution Avoid in: • Age >65 years • Renal impairment (any GFR reduction) • Heart failure • Dehydration • Electrolyte abnormalities • On ACEi, ARB, diuretics, NSAIDs Risks: Fatal hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia — FDA black box warning If used: Single dose ONLY. Never repeat.
⚠️ Generally NOT recommended • Risk of rectal mucosa damage • Chemical colitis reported • If used: mild castile soap only, highly dilute Prefer: Tap water or saline instead
• ACPO refractory to 24-72h conservative management • Cecum ≥12 cm diameter • Duration >4-6 days • No contraindications to neostigmine

❌ Mechanical bowel obstruction (must rule out first!) ❌ Recent MI, severe cardiac disease, bradycardia ❌ Active bronchospasm (asthma/COPD exacerbation) ❌ Pregnancy ❌ Renal failure (relative: Cr >3 mg/dL)
✅ Continuous cardiac monitoring ✅ IV access confirmed ✅ Atropine 0.5 mg at bedside ✅ Foley catheter in place ✅ Rectal tube in place ✅ Patient supine or left lateral

Dose: 2 mg IV over 5 FULL MINUTES ⚠️ Do NOT give as rapid IV push — REAL five minutes on the clock Cautious approach: 1 mg, wait, then another 1 mg Monitoring during administration: • Continuous ECG — watch for bradycardia • BP every 2-3 minutes • Stop immediately if symptomatic bradycardia
Give Atropine 0.5 mg IV if: • HR <60 with symptoms (dizziness, hypotension) • Asymptomatic HR <40

• Passage of flatus/stool within 10-30 minutes • 91% initial response rate (NEJM landmark trial) • X-ray improvement within 4-6 hours If no response in 3 hours: • May repeat 2 mg IV (max 3 doses total) • Half-life ~50 min
🐝 Bradycardia (most common, ~10%) 🐝 Bronchospasm 🐝 Bronchorrhea Also: abdominal cramping, nausea, salivation, vomiting

Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction (ACPO): • Massive colonic dilation (cecum >9 cm) • WITHOUT mechanical obstruction on CT • Often involving cecum to splenic flexure • Decompressed distal colon/rectum • No transition point on imaging

HIGH RISK — urgent intervention needed: 🚨 Cecal diameter >12 cm 🚨 Duration >6 days Cecal perforation mortality: 40-50% | Cecum Diameter | Risk Level | |----------------|------------| | <9 cm | Low | | 9-12 cm | Moderate | | >12 cm | HIGH — act now |

• Recent surgery (orthopedic, cardiac, OB, abdominal) • Critical illness, trauma, sepsis • Electrolyte abnormalities (K+, Mg2+) • Medications (opioids, anticholinergics, CCBs) • Neurologic disease (stroke, Parkinson's, SCI) • Postpartum

| Feature | ACPO | Mechanical Obstruction | |---------|------|------------------------| | CT transition point | No | Yes | | Distention | Cecum to splenic flexure | Proximal to obstruction | | Decompressed bowel | Distal colon/rectum | Distal to obstruction | | Bowel sounds | May be present | High-pitched or absent | | Flatus/stool | May still pass some | Complete obstipation |

PEG 3350 (MiraLAX) ⭐ Strongly recommended • 17 g daily in 8 oz liquid • Safe for long-term use Fiber (Psyllium) — Conditionally recommended • 1-2 tbsp daily with adequate water • May worsen bloating initially Magnesium oxide — Conditionally recommended • 400-800 mg daily • Avoid in renal impairment Senna — Conditionally recommended • 2-4 tablets at bedtime • Safe for short to medium-term use
Lactulose — 15-45 mL daily • Alternative osmotic laxative • More bloating than PEG Bisacodyl — 5-10 mg PO or 10 mg PR • Stimulant, works in 6-12 hours (PO) or 15-60 min (PR) • Good for rapid effect

Linaclotide (Linzess) — 145-290 mcg daily • Secretagogue, also helps abdominal pain • Take on empty stomach Plecanatide (Trulance) — 3 mg daily • Similar to linaclotide Prucalopride (Motegrity) — 2 mg daily • 5-HT4 agonist, prokinetic • Once daily, simple dosing Lubiprostone (Amitiza) — 24 mcg BID • Chloride channel activator • Take with food
❌ Docusate (stool softener) alone — No better than placebo ❌ Mineral oil orally — Aspiration risk, lipoid pneumonia ❌ Repeated phosphate enemas — Fatal electrolyte disturbances

Minimize opioids — #1 modifiable risk factor • Regional anesthesia (epidural, TAP block) • NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors (ketorolac, celecoxib) • Acetaminophen scheduled • Gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) • Lidocaine IV infusion

• Early ambulation — OOB POD0, ambulate TID • Early enteral feeding — clear liquids POD0 • Minimize IV fluids — goal-directed therapy • No routine NG tubes — remove early if placed • Avoid excessive crystalloid
✅ Evidence-based! Sugar-free gum TID starting POD1 • Stimulates cephalic-vagal reflex • Reduces time to flatus by ~12-24 hours • Reduces LOS • Cheap, no side effects

Peripheral mu-opioid antagonist • 12 mg PO 30 min to 5 hours pre-op • Then 12 mg BID (max 15 doses or until discharge) • Reduces time to GI recovery by ~12-24 hours Limitations: • Only via hospital EASE program • Not for chronic opioid users (>7 days) • Only for bowel resection with anastomosis
• Potassium — Keep K+ >4.0 mEq/L • Magnesium — Keep Mg2+ >2.0 mg/dL Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia impair GI motility.

• Classify BP: non-severe (140–159/90–109) vs severe-range (≥160/110) • Screen for severe features: plt<100K, LFTs>2×, Cr>1.1, pulm edema, new HA/visual • Route by presentation: active seizure, severe-range BP, non-severe, postpartum, ASA question

• Treat within 30–60 min — stroke, not seizure, is the leading cause of maternal death • Target 140–150 / 90–100 (not "normal") — do not drop MAP >25% in 1 h • Choose: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or PO nifedipine IR • Labetalol ACOG ladder: 20 → 40 → 80 → 80 mg IV q10min, max 300 mg • Hydralazine ladder: 5–10 → 10 mg IV q20min, max 30 mg • Nifedipine IR: 10 → 20 → 20 mg PO q20min, max 50 mg. NEVER sublingual

• Labs: CBC + smear, Cr, AST/ALT, LDH, uric acid, UA + spot protein/Cr, T&S, coags if HELLP • Fetal: continuous EFM, growth + AFI + UA Doppler US as indicated • Classify: chronic, gestational, preeclampsia ± severe, superimposed, or HELLP

• Admit L&D, control BP, start magnesium prophylaxis • Magnesium: 4–6 g IV load, 1–2 g/hr × 24 h postpartum. DTRs, RR, UOP, Mg level q6h • Antidote for Mg toxicity: calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 3–5 min • Betamethasone 12 mg IM q24h × 2 if 23–34 wk with delivery expected <7 d

• LDH>600, AST/ALT >2× ULN, platelets <100K. 15–20% without HTN/proteinuria • Image if severe RUQ + dropping Hgb — rule out subcapsular hematoma • Mgmt: BP + mag + platelets <20K (or <50K if bleeding/cesarean) + cryo if fibrinogen <100–150 + delivery

• Chronic HTN stable: 38–39 wk. Gestational HTN or PE no-severe: 37 wk • PE with severe features: 34 wk (earlier if unstable) • HELLP: after stabilization — GA irrelevant if maternal deterioration • Vaginal delivery acceptable; cesarean not mandatory

• BP peaks 3–6 d postpartum. 55% postpartum PE has no antepartum PE. Risk to 6 wk • Same acute-BP agents; ACE-i acceptable postpartum + breastfeeding (not in pregnancy) • Every discharge: BP log, recheck 3–7 d, return precautions
• Aspirin 81 mg PO daily 12–28 wk (ideally <16 wk) → cuts preeclampsia ~15% • Indicated: ≥1 high-risk factor or ≥2 moderate-risk factors — counsel every prior-PE patient

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give ACE inhibitors or ARBs in pregnancy
info.t: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and direct renin inhibitors are teratogenic across all trimesters — cause renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull ossification defects, IUGR, and neonatal renal failure. If a patient with chronic HTN conceives on lisinopril/losartan, switch immediately. ACE-i are acceptable postpartum and compatible with breastfeeding (different from pregnancy rule). See chronic HTN node.

Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated — unpredictable absorption produces severe, sudden hypotension with documented strokes and fetal distress. ACOG specifies oral capsules swallowed intact. See nifedipine protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT require proteinuria to diagnose severe preeclampsia
info.t: ~25% of severe preeclampsia presents WITHOUT proteinuria. ACOG 2013 removed proteinuria from severity grading. Diagnose on severe features (BP ≥160/110, platelets <100K, LFTs >2×, Cr >1.1, pulm edema, new HA/visual) regardless of urine protein. Waiting for proteinuria delays magnesium and delivery. See severe features.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay severe-range BP treatment waiting for "definitive" diagnosis
info.t: SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 sustained ≥15 min = treat now. Stroke is the leading cause of maternal death from preeclampsia — not seizure. Treat within 30–60 min even if classification is unclear. BP control is a bridge to delivery, not definitive treatment. See severe-range BP.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT drop MAP >25% in the first hour
info.t: Abrupt BP lowering in preeclampsia causes uteroplacental hypoperfusion → fetal distress, abruption, maternal stroke from relative hypoperfusion. Target 140–150 / 90–100 (not "normal"). If BP drops below 140/90, stop the agent, place left lateral, 250–500 mL NS bolus, continuous fetal monitoring. See BP goals.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give magnesium for mild preeclampsia
info.t: Magnesium is for preeclampsia with SEVERE features (and for active eclamptic seizures). Routine magnesium in preeclampsia without severe features adds toxicity risk without clear benefit. If severe features develop or active labor ensues, start mag then. See mag indication.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore loss of DTRs on magnesium
info.t: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first clinical sign of magnesium toxicity (Mg ~9–12 mg/dL). Next is respiratory depression (12–15), then arrest (>15). Hold the infusion, send a Mg level, support ventilation, and give calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over 3–5 min as antidote. See toxicity ladder.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methylergonovine (Methergine) in HTN/preeclampsia
info.t: Methergine causes severe vasoconstriction and has triggered fatal hypertensive emergencies, MI, and CVA in preeclamptic patients. Absolute contraindication in HTN, preeclampsia, eclampsia, HELLP. Use misoprostol for postpartum atony instead; carboprost is also acceptable if no asthma. See methylergonovine entry.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge postpartum preeclampsia without a 3–7 day BP plan
info.t: Most maternal deaths from preeclampsia occur postpartum. BP peaks at 3–6 days post-delivery. 55% of postpartum preeclampsia occurs in patients who did NOT have antepartum preeclampsia. Every HTN-in-pregnancy discharge needs: BP log, cuff, recheck at 3–7 days, and written return precautions. See postpartum.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss HELLP without hypertension
info.t: 15–20% of HELLP presents without hypertension or proteinuria. Any pregnant patient with RUQ/epigastric pain + N/V + malaise deserves platelets, AST/ALT, and LDH — don't wait for BP to rise. Mortality from missed HELLP (especially hepatic subcapsular hematoma) is catastrophic. See HELLP.

ALL THREE components required for complete HELLP: • Hemolysis — LDH >600 IU/L, schistocytes on peripheral smear, indirect bilirubin elevated • Elevated Liver enzymes — AST or ALT >2× upper limit of normal • Low Platelets — <100,000/µL Partial HELLP = 1 or 2 of the above. Still dangerous — treat as high-risk preeclampsia with severe features.

Class I (most severe) • Platelets <50,000/µL • AST/ALT >70 IU/L • LDH >600 IU/L • Highest maternal morbidity and mortality Class II • Platelets 50,000–100,000/µL • AST/ALT >70 • LDH >600 Class III (least severe) • Platelets 100,000–150,000/µL • AST/ALT >40 • LDH >600

• RUQ or epigastric pain — 65–90% • Nausea and vomiting — 30–80% • Headache — 30–60% • Malaise preceding abdominal symptoms — often the earliest sign • BP may be normal or minimally elevated in 15–20% • Proteinuria may be absent — do not require for diagnosis

• Hepatic subcapsular hematoma / rupture — rare but catastrophic (mortality 60–80%). Consider imaging if severe RUQ pain + dropping Hgb. • DIC — 15–20% • Placental abruption — 15–20% • Acute kidney injury — 5–10% • Pulmonary edema — 5–10% • ARDS, cerebral edema, intracranial hemorrhage — rarer but cause most mortality

Must be distinguished from: • AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy) — glucose <60, ammonia elevated, prolonged PT often out of proportion to platelet drop • TTP/HUS — MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI + neurologic sx + fever; ADAMTS13 <10% in TTP • Viral hepatitis — viral serologies • Cholestasis of pregnancy — pruritus + bile acids, normal platelets/LDH • Lupus flare — ANA/dsDNA, complement

• Same BP control as severe preeclampsia • Magnesium 4–6 g IV load, 1–2 g/hr × 24 h postpartum • Labs q4–6 h in acute phase • Platelets if <20K regardless, or <50K if bleeding/cesarean planned • Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen <100–150 • Delivery is the only definitive treatment (after stabilization) • Labs nadir 24–48 h postpartum — expect platelets to drop further after delivery before recovering • 20–30% of HELLP presents postpartum — maintain suspicion up to 7 days after delivery

• Pre-existing HTN before pregnancy, OR • New HTN <20 weeks, OR • Persists >12 weeks postpartum Management: Target <140/90 (CHAP trial). First-line: labetalol, nifedipine XL, methyldopa. Start aspirin 81 mg 12–28 wk (high-risk indication). Delivery at 38–39 wk if well-controlled.

• New HTN ≥20 weeks • No proteinuria, no end-organ dysfunction • Should resolve by 12 weeks postpartum (otherwise reclassify as chronic HTN) Management: 2×/week BP checks, weekly labs, twice-weekly fetal NSTs. 15–25% progress to preeclampsia. Deliver at 37 wk if stable.

• HTN ≥20 wk PLUS one of: - Proteinuria ≥300 mg/24 h or protein/Cr ≥0.3 or dipstick ≥2+ - End-organ dysfunction below severe thresholds • BP <160/110, platelets ≥100K, LFTs <2× ULN, Cr ≤1.1, no pulm edema, no new CNS sx Management: Admit for initial evaluation. Serial labs and fetal surveillance. Magnesium NOT routine. Deliver at 37 wk.

Any ONE feature defines severe: • BP ≥160 SBP or ≥110 DBP on 2 readings ≥4 h apart • Platelets <100,000/µL • AST or ALT >2× upper limit of normal • Severe persistent RUQ / epigastric pain unresponsive to meds • Serum Cr >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline • Pulmonary edema • New-onset severe headache unresponsive to meds • New visual disturbances (scotomata, photopsia, blurring) Removed as severe features (2013): IUGR, amount of proteinuria. Management: Admit L&D, control BP, magnesium, expedite delivery. Delivery at 34 wk (earlier if unstable).

Chronic HTN PLUS any of: • New proteinuria (or worsening baseline proteinuria) • Sudden BP worsening requiring higher doses • Thrombocytopenia, elevated LFTs, renal insufficiency, pulm edema, new CNS sx (any severe feature) Highest-risk subgroup. Management follows preeclampsia ± severe features rules. Deliver at 37 wk if no severe features, 34 wk if severe features.

See HELLP Criteria — Hemolysis + Elevated LFTs + Low Platelets. 10–20% of preeclampsia; 15–20% present without HTN or proteinuria. Delivery after stabilization regardless of GA if maternal deterioration.

New or persistent HTN up to 6 weeks postpartum. BP peaks 3–6 days post-delivery. 55% of postpartum preeclampsia has no antepartum PE. Same acute treatment; ACE-i acceptable postpartum and in breastfeeding.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure in a preeclampsia patient. Not managed in this tree — see the dedicated Eclampsia consult.
• Aspirin 81 mg PO daily • Start 12–28 weeks gestation — ideally <16 weeks for maximum benefit • Continue until delivery • No loading dose, no higher dose — 81 mg is the evidence-based target

• Reduces preeclampsia by ~15% (RR 0.85) • Reduces preterm birth by ~10% • Reduces IUGR ~10% • No increase in placental abruption, PPH, or fetal bleeding at 81 mg • ASPRE trial (NEJM 2017): 150 mg daily reduced preterm preeclampsia 62% in high-risk screened patients — but 81 mg is the US standard per USPSTF

• History of preeclampsia — especially early-onset (<34 wk) or severe • Multifetal gestation • Chronic hypertension • Type 1 or 2 diabetes mellitus • Chronic kidney disease • Autoimmune disease (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome)

• Nulliparity (first pregnancy) • Obesity (BMI >30) • Family history of preeclampsia (mother, sister) • Sociodemographic — low income, Black race, age ≥35 • Prior poor obstetric outcome — SGA infant, stillbirth, placental abruption • Interpregnancy interval >10 years

Healthy nulliparous or multiparous patients without any high- or moderate-risk factor do NOT need aspirin prophylaxis. Universal prophylaxis has not shown benefit and adds cost/pill burden without evidence.

When you see any patient in the ED or clinic with a history of preeclampsia, HELLP, or eclampsia: > "For your next pregnancy, ask your OB about starting low-dose aspirin at 12 weeks. Research shows it cuts the risk of this happening again by about 15%. It is safe and cheap — just 81 mg, the baby-aspirin dose." Document the recommendation and the OB referral in the discharge summary.

Consider 1–2 g/day calcium in populations with low dietary intake (<600 mg/day). Meta-analyses show modest additional reduction in preeclampsia in low-calcium diets but minimal benefit in replete populations. Not a substitute for aspirin.

• Check your BP at home every day with a properly sized cuff, seated, arm at heart level, after resting 5 minutes. • Log every reading — bring the log to every visit. • Goal: top number (SBP) under 140, bottom number (DBP) under 90. • Follow-up appointment in 3–7 days with your OB — this is critical, not optional. • 6-week postpartum visit — bring your BP log and current meds.

If you were started on a blood pressure medication: • Take it exactly as prescribed — do not skip doses. • Do NOT stop suddenly — even if your BP is normal. Call your OB before any change. • Common pregnancy-safe options: labetalol, nifedipine XL, methyldopa (in pregnancy); labetalol, nifedipine XL, enalapril (after delivery). • If breastfeeding: labetalol, nifedipine, and enalapril are all compatible.

• Blood pressure at home ≥160 systolic (top) OR ≥110 diastolic (bottom) on 2 readings 15 min apart • Severe headache that does not get better with acetaminophen • Vision changes — blurry vision, seeing spots, flashes of light, or loss of vision • Severe pain in the upper-right belly or center chest/upper abdomen — this can signal liver involvement (HELLP) • Shortness of breath, trouble lying flat — possible fluid in the lungs • Seizure — call 911 immediately • Less fetal movement (if still pregnant) • Heavy vaginal bleeding • Swelling in the face or hands with rapid weight gain

Most serious problems from preeclampsia actually happen after delivery, not before. Your BP can peak 3–6 days postpartum — even if it was controlled in the hospital. The risk continues for 6 weeks after delivery. If you feel a severe headache, see spots, have upper-belly pain, or feel short of breath any time in the first 6 weeks, go to the ER — do not wait until your OB visit.

If you had preeclampsia, HELLP, or eclampsia, your next pregnancy has a higher risk of the same problem. Good news: a simple, safe medication can help. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg — baby aspirin) once a day, starting at 12 weeks, reduces your risk by about 15%. Ask your OB about it at your first prenatal visit in any future pregnancy.

Preeclampsia is a marker of elevated lifetime risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, and stroke. Please: • Have your primary care doctor check your BP at least yearly • Maintain a healthy weight, exercise regularly, eat a balanced diet • Do not smoke • Ask your PCP about cardiovascular risk assessment every 5 years

Serious pregnancy complications can be emotionally difficult. If you feel sad, anxious, scared, or overwhelmed, talk to your OB, PCP, or a counselor. Postpartum Support International: 1-800-944-4773. The Preeclampsia Foundation: https://www.preeclampsia.org

GCA can cause permanent bilateral blindness within hours. • Second eye involvement: up to 50% within days if untreated • Early steroids prevent contralateral vision loss • Treatment before biopsy is standard of care

info.h: Lower-Risk BRUE — ALL Must Be Met
info.t: ☐ Age >60 days ☐ If preterm: GA >32 weeks AND corrected age >45 weeks ☐ First BRUE (no prior events, no cluster) ☐ Event duration <1 minute ☐ No CPR required by trained medical provider ☐ Normal physical exam ☐ No concerning historical features If ALL checked → Lower-Risk If ANY unchecked → Higher-Risk

⚠️ Any of these = Higher-Risk: • Age ≤60 days • Preterm <32 weeks OR corrected age <45 weeks • Multiple events or cluster • Event duration ≥1 minute • CPR by trained medical provider • Abnormal exam findings • Concerning history: - Family history of SIDS - Social concerns (NAT) - Prior similar events

Lower-Risk: • Observe 1-4 hours • Consider ECG, pertussis test • Parent education (CPR, safe sleep) • Discharge with 24-48hr follow-up Higher-Risk: • Admit for monitoring • Tiered, hypothesis-driven workup • Prioritize NAT, cardiac, infection • Subspecialty consults as indicated
• >90% of BRUEs classified as higher-risk • ~1% of low-risk have serious underlying condition • ~5% recurrence rate in low-risk • ~5% of high-risk have serious underlying condition

When a cause is identified, the event is no longer a BRUE: | Rank | Cause | Frequency | |------|-------|----------| | 1 | GER with laryngospasm | ~30% | | 2 | Lower respiratory infection | ~15% | | 3 | Seizure | ~10% | | 4 | Child maltreatment | ~5% |
• GER with laryngospasm — event during/after feeding, regurgitation noted • Swallowing dysfunction — coughing/gagging with feeds • Aspiration — recurrent respiratory symptoms with feeding

• Pertussis — paroxysmal cough, apnea, cyanosis (young infants lack classic whoop) • RSV/Bronchiolitis — respiratory symptoms, wheezing • Laryngomalacia — stridor, worse with feeding/crying • Airway obstruction — positional, anatomic
• Seizure — subtle in infants (eye deviation, cycling movements) • Breath-holding spell — triggered by crying, predictable • Apnea of infancy — diagnosis of exclusion
• Long QT syndrome — QTc >460 ms, family history sudden death • WPW — delta wave, short PR • SVT — tachycardia, poor feeding, pallor • Structural heart disease — murmur, failure to thrive

• NAT/Abuse — suffocation, shaking, Munchausen by proxy • Infection — UTI (common in young infants), sepsis, meningitis • Metabolic — hypoglycemia, inborn errors • Medication/Toxin — accidental ingestion

High-Risk Features: • Recurrent events with same caregiver • Inconsistent or changing history • Delay in seeking care • Bruising in non-mobile infant • Unexplained injuries • Prior CPS involvement • Domestic violence in home • Substance abuse • Young, isolated, or stressed caregivers

Bruising in these locations = Highly concerning for abuse: TEN-4: Bruising on... • Torso • Ear • Neck ...in any child <4 years old FACES: Or bruising on... • Face • Arm (any) • Cheek • Eyes • Soft tissue ...in infant <4 months old Sensitivity ~97% for abuse

🚨 "Those who don't cruise, rarely bruise" Bruising in a non-mobile infant (<4 months) is rare and should prompt abuse evaluation. • Accidental bruising uncommon before crawling/walking • Any bruise in non-mobile infant = explain or investigate

Required Evaluation: • Head CT or MRI — subdural hematoma, SAH • Skeletal survey — healing/acute fractures • Dilated fundoscopic exam — retinal hemorrhages • Social work consult — immediate • CPS report — mandated • Admit for safety — do not discharge to suspected abuser Document carefully — detailed quotes, exam findings, timeline
Cardiac arrhythmias can present as: • Apnea • Color change (pallor, cyanosis) • Unresponsiveness • "Seizure-like" episodes ECG recommended for all higher-risk BRUE "May consider" for lower-risk BRUE

ECG Findings: • Short PR interval (<120 ms) • Delta wave (slurred upstroke of QRS) • Wide QRS (>120 ms) Risk: SVT, rarely sudden death If WPW on ECG: Cardiology referral
• SVT — narrow complex tachycardia, rate >220 bpm • Heart block — AV dissociation, bradycardia • Ectopy — frequent PVCs may warrant evaluation Action: Cardiology consult for any abnormal ECG

Ask about family history of: • Sudden death <50 years (especially unexplained) • Syncope with exercise • Drowning (may be arrhythmia-related) • Pacemaker or ICD in young family member • Known Long QT, WPW, Brugada, CPVT • Cardiomyopathy
AAP Strong Recommendations AGAINST: ❌ CBC, BMP, blood gas ❌ Chest X-ray ❌ Echocardiogram ❌ EEG ❌ Neuroimaging ❌ Upper GI series ❌ LP ❌ Empiric acid suppression ❌ Admission solely for monitoring

Weak Recommendations (consider): ✓ 12-lead ECG — screen for Long QT, WPW ✓ Pertussis PCR — if underimmunized or outbreak ✓ Observation 1-4 hours with continuous SpO2 Always provide: • Parent education on infant CPR • Safe sleep counseling • Return precautions
Baseline Testing: • Continuous pulse oximetry (4+ hours) • 12-lead ECG • Blood glucose • VBG or BMP • CBC If respiratory concern: • Respiratory viral panel • Pertussis PCR

⚠️ Key Principle: Testing should be hypothesis-driven, not shotgun. • Low diagnostic yield with broad testing • High false-positive rate creates cascades • Focus on time-sensitive conditions first: 1. Child maltreatment 2. Feeding/aspiration issues 3. Cardiac arrhythmia 4. Serious infection

Required: • High-frequency linear probe (7.5-12 MHz) • Ultrasound gel (generous amount) • Optional: Tegaderm over closed eye Patient Position: • Supine • Eyes closed gently • Looking straight ahead • Avoid excessive eye movement

Remember: 3mm behind, 5mm cutoff 1. Place probe gently on closed eyelid (transverse) 2. Identify the optic nerve as hypoechoic stripe behind globe 3. Measure 3 mm posterior to the posterior globe margin 4. Measure inner edge to inner edge of the nerve sheath 5. Repeat in both eyes 6. Average bilateral measurements

Initial: 500 mg PO BID (1 g/day) Titration Schedule: • Week 1: 500 mg BID (1 g/day) • Week 2: 750 mg BID (1.5 g/day) • Week 3-4: 1000 mg BID (2 g/day) • Beyond: Increase by 250-500 mg/week Target: 2-4 g/day as tolerated Max: 4 g/day
• 89.5% tolerated ≥1 g/day • 44% tolerated maximum (4 g/day) • Mean dose at 6 months: 2.5 g/day Most patients achieve good outcomes on 2-3 g/day.

Expected (warn patients): • Paresthesias (tingling hands/feet) — dose-related • Dysgeusia (metallic taste, carbonation tastes "flat") • Fatigue, malaise • GI upset, anorexia, nausea • Polyuria Monitor for: • Hypokalemia — check BMP at 2-4 weeks • Metabolic acidosis • Renal stones (rare)

❌ Absolute: • Sulfonamide allergy (cross-reactivity possible) • Severe hepatic disease • Severe renal disease (CrCl <10) • Adrenal insufficiency • Hypokalemia (uncorrected) ⚠️ Caution: • Pregnancy (weigh risks/benefits) • Concurrent topiramate (increased acidosis risk)

If acetazolamide not tolerated: • Topiramate 25-100 mg BID - Also causes weight loss (beneficial in IIH) - Similar carbonic anhydrase inhibition • Furosemide 20-40 mg daily - Less effective than acetazolamide - Consider if sulfa allergy

Urgent/Emergent: • Fulminant IIH with rapid vision loss • Severe visual field deficits (PMD <-7 dB) • Visual acuity involvement • High-grade papilledema (Frisén 4-5) Elective: • Failure of medical management • Intolerable medication side effects • Progressive visual loss despite treatment

Indication: Primarily visual symptoms Procedure: • Creates window in optic nerve sheath • Allows CSF egress, decompresses optic nerve • Can be unilateral or bilateral Outcomes: • ~90% visual stabilization or improvement • Headache improvement in ~50% Complications: • Diplopia (usually transient) • Pupil abnormalities • Rare: vision loss

Indication: Primarily headache symptoms Options: • Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt • Lumboperitoneal (LP) shunt Outcomes: • Excellent headache relief initially • Variable long-term success Complications: • Shunt failure/revision (common — ~50% at 2 years) • Infection • Over-drainage (low pressure headache) • Acquired Chiari malformation (LP shunt)

Indication: Transverse sinus stenosis with significant gradient Patient Selection: • Pressure gradient >8 mmHg across stenosis • Failed medical management • Anatomically suitable Procedure: • Endovascular stent placement • Reduces venous outflow resistance Outcomes: • Promising results in selected patients • May reduce need for shunting Note: Still considered investigational at many centers.

✓ Duration >2 minutes ✓ Gradual onset/offset ✓ Preserved awareness during bilateral motor activity ✓ Can follow commands during event ✓ Postictal recall of words spoken during event ✓ Rapid return to baseline ✓ Modulation by bystanders (waxing/waning with attention) ✓ Emotional trigger immediately preceding

⚡ Ictal head version (PLR 5.0 for epilepsy) ⚡ Ictal eye opening (typical in epilepsy) ⚡ Abrupt onset ⚡ Stereotyped pattern (same each time) ⚡ Duration 60-90 seconds (GTC) ⚡ Postictal confusion/drowsiness lasting minutes to hours ⚡ No recall of ictal period

These do NOT distinguish PNES from epilepsy: ❌ Urinary incontinence — occurs in both ❌ Tongue biting — occurs in both (lateral more in epilepsy) ❌ Aura — occurs in both ❌ Falls with injury — occurs in both ❌ Back arching — occurs in both

• 10-30% of PNES patients also have epilepsy — cannot assume all events are functional • Frontal lobe seizures can have bizarre movements mimicking PNES — typically brief (<30 sec), stereotyped, occur from sleep • No single sign is pathognomonic — use overall clinical picture • Video-EEG is gold standard for definitive diagnosis

Functional seizures (also called PNES or dissociative seizures) are real seizures with a different cause than epilepsy. • In epilepsy, seizures are caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain • In functional seizures, the brain's "software" (how it processes information) is affected, not the "hardware" (brain structure) You are NOT faking. These seizures are not under your conscious control. They are a recognized medical condition.

• About 1 in 5 people referred to epilepsy centers have functional seizures • More common in women • Peak age 20-40 years • Often associated with stress, anxiety, depression, or past trauma • Can occur alongside epilepsy (10-30% of patients have both)

Good news: Functional seizures respond to treatment. • Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the most effective treatment • Studies show 50-60% reduction in seizure frequency • Some patients have complete resolution • Anti-seizure medications do NOT help (and can cause side effects) The right treatment is therapy, not pills.

✓ Keep follow-up appointments with neurology and mental health ✓ Be patient — improvement takes time ✓ Learn your triggers — stress, lack of sleep, conflict ✓ Practice coping strategies learned in therapy ✓ Maintain routine — regular sleep, meals, exercise ✓ Connect with support — family, friends, support groups

info.h: When to Return to the ER
info.t: 🚨 Seizure lasting >5 minutes without recovery 🚨 Injury during seizure 🚨 Seizure looks different from your usual events 🚨 High fever with seizure 🚨 Thoughts of hurting yourself 🚨 Unable to return to baseline
• Epilepsy Foundation: epilepsy.org/PNES • FND Hope: fndhope.org • NAMI: nami.org (mental health support)

1. "Your seizures are REAL" • "I can see these events are distressing and real." • "You are not making this up or faking." 2. "This is a recognized medical condition" • "This is called functional seizures." • "It's related to how your brain processes stress." 3. "This is TREATABLE" • "Therapy, particularly CBT, helps most people." • "Many patients have significant improvement." 4. "Epilepsy medications won't help" • "Those medications won't work and can cause side effects."

Use this analogy — it resonates with patients: *"Your brain has two parts — the hardware (the physical brain) and the software (how the brain processes information).* *In your case, the hardware is fine — no tumor, no abnormal electrical activity. But the software has a glitch — your brain is processing stress in a way that causes these episodes."* This validates their experience while explaining the mechanism.

❌ "It's all in your head" ❌ "There's nothing wrong with you" ❌ "It's just stress" ❌ "You're faking" ❌ "Your seizures aren't real" ❌ "You need to stop doing this" ❌ "This is psychological" (without explanation) These statements damage trust and worsen outcomes.

*"I've observed your seizure and reviewed your records. I want to share what I've found.* *First, your seizures are real. You're not faking. This is a recognized condition called functional seizures.* *The best analogy: your brain's hardware is fine — no tumor, no abnormal electrical activity. But the software has a glitch.* *The good news: therapy, especially CBT, helps most people. Some have complete resolution.* *Epilepsy medications won't help here and could cause side effects.* *Do you have any questions?"*

"But I have epilepsy!" → "Some people have both. Video-EEG helps us tell which is which." "This means you think I'm crazy." → "Not at all. This is a neurological condition — your brain is misfiring, just differently than epilepsy." "Why would my brain do this?" → "We're still learning, but it often relates to how the brain handles stress or past experiences."
PNES patients have high rates of: • Depression (very common) • Anxiety disorders (very common) • PTSD (common — 30-40%) • Borderline personality disorder • Suicidal ideation • Self-harm history

Suicidal Ideation: • "Are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself?" • "Have you ever tried to hurt yourself?" Safety: • "Do you feel safe at home?" • "Is anyone hurting you or threatening you?" If SI present: → Psychiatric evaluation before discharge → Safety planning → May need admission for stabilization

info.h: Do NOT Probe Trauma in ED
info.t: ⚠️ 30-40% of PNES patients have trauma history • Do NOT ask directly about trauma details in the ED • This can be retraumatizing • Leave trauma exploration to outpatient therapy • Focus on current safety and immediate needs Instead say: "Many people with this condition have difficult experiences in their past. Your therapist can help explore that when you're ready."

Assess: • Mental health access (do they have a therapist/psychiatrist?) • Insurance/financial barriers • Transportation to appointments • Social support system Connect to: • Social work if barriers identified • Crisis resources if needed • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

26% adverse effect rate in RAMPART/ESETT trials when benzos given to PNES patients • Respiratory depression requiring intervention • 1 in 5 admitted to ICU • Cumulative dosing worsens outcomes If uncertain: Observe and document semiology first.

Deaths reported from attempted intubation for PNES • Prolonged hospitalization • Higher rates of future PNES-related ED visits • Iatrogenic harm far exceeds benefit PNES events resolve spontaneously — usually within 2-15 minutes.
Anti-seizure medications are ineffective for PNES: • Expose patients to unnecessary side effects • Delay appropriate psychiatric treatment • Reinforce incorrect diagnosis

• Ensure patient safety (side rails, remove hazards) • Observe and document semiology (eye position, movements, duration) • Speak calmly: "You are safe, we are here to help" • Time the event • Video record if possible (invaluable for neurology) • Consider verbal reassurance: "I am Dr. [name]. You are in the ER."

Treat as epileptic seizure if: 🚩 Continuous seizure >5 min without recovery 🚩 Lateral tongue bite + prolonged postictal confusion 🚩 This is their FIRST seizure ever 🚩 Clinical uncertainty — when in doubt, treat Remember: 10-30% of PNES patients also have epilepsy. Not all seizures in a PNES patient are functional.
Autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction. Antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors (AChR) or related proteins. Hallmark: Fatigable weakness — worse with use, better with rest.

• Ocular symptoms (ptosis, diplopia) present in 85% at onset • Bulbar involvement: dysarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness • Limb weakness: proximal > distal • Respiratory muscles can be involved — this is the emergency • Diurnal variation — symptoms worsen throughout the day

Myasthenic crisis = respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Red flags: • FVC <15-20 mL/kg • NIF weaker than -20 to -25 cmH₂O • Staccato speech (gasping between words) • Severe bulbar weakness

• Pyridostigmine — symptomatic (does NOT modify disease) • IVIG or PLEX — rapid-acting immunotherapy for crisis • Steroids — can cause initial worsening; give with IVIG/PLEX cover • Rocuronium — use 1/3 to 1/2 dose; MG patients very sensitive

Antibiotics: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides Cardiac: Beta-blockers (including eye drops!), CCBs Other: IV magnesium, full-dose NMBs, botulinum toxin Safe: Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, TMP-SMX, vancomycin
Standardized severity grading for MG. Higher classes correlate with crisis risk and need for aggressive immunotherapy.
• Ptosis, diplopia only • No other muscle involvement • Best prognosis
• IIa: Predominantly limb/axial • IIb: Predominantly bulbar/respiratory Mild weakness affecting muscles other than ocular.
• IIIa: Predominantly limb/axial • IIIb: Predominantly bulbar/respiratory Moderate weakness — may need immunotherapy.
• IVa: Predominantly limb/axial • IVb: Predominantly bulbar/respiratory Severe weakness — high crisis risk.
• Intubation required (with or without mechanical ventilation) • Defines myasthenic crisis • Requires ICU admission, IVIG or PLEX
Respiratory failure in MG can occur rapidly. Serial FVC and NIF measurements detect decline before clinical deterioration.
Normal: >60 mL/kg Concerning: 25-30 mL/kg Critical (intubate): <15-20 mL/kg or <1 L in average adult Measure: Every 2-4 hours in worsening patients
Normal: Stronger than -60 cmH₂O Concerning: -30 to -40 cmH₂O Critical (intubate): Weaker than -20 to -25 cmH₂O Note: NIF is effort-dependent — coach patient to give maximal effort
Consider intubation when: • FVC <20 mL/kg • NIF weaker than -30 cmH₂O • FVC decline >30% from baseline Do NOT wait for hypoxia or hypercapnia — these are late findings.
A declining trend is as important as absolute values. A patient whose FVC drops from 40 to 25 mL/kg in 4 hours is heading toward crisis even if not yet at critical thresholds.
Treatment is OPPOSITE. Getting this wrong can be fatal.

Cause: Worsening MG from disease (underdosed or ineffective treatment) Signs: • DRY — no excessive secretions • Mydriasis (dilated pupils) • No fasciculations • Weakness improves with more anticholinesterase Treatment: IVIG or PLEX, support airway

Cause: EXCESS pyridostigmine (overdose) Signs: • WET — excessive secretions (SLUDGE/BBB) • Miosis (constricted pupils) • Fasciculations present • Weakness WORSENS with more anticholinesterase Treatment: STOP anticholinesterase, atropine for secretions
Salivation Lacrimation Urination Defecation GI cramping Emesis Bradycardia Bronchorrhea Bronchospasm

STOP all anticholinesterase medications — safe for both crisis types. • Support airway • Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV for secretions • Observe 30-60 min • Cholinergic: secretions decrease • Myasthenic: weakness persists without cholinergic signs
Simple, non-invasive bedside test for ocular MG. Cold improves neuromuscular transmission by slowing acetylcholinesterase activity.
1. Measure baseline ptosis (mm of palpebral fissure) 2. Place ice pack or ice-filled glove on closed eyelid 3. Hold for 2 minutes 4. Remove ice, immediately measure ptosis again
Positive: >2 mm improvement in ptosis Sensitivity: ~80% for ocular MG Specificity: ~95% A negative test does not rule out MG. Proceed with antibody testing and EMG if clinical suspicion remains.
Cold temperature: • Slows acetylcholinesterase activity • Prolongs acetylcholine action at NMJ • Temporarily improves transmission This mechanism is specific to NMJ disorders.
• Only works for ocular symptoms (ptosis) • False negatives occur • Does not differentiate MG from Lambert-Eaton • Confirmatory testing still needed

Avoid: • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) • Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin) • Macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin) Safe alternatives: Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, TMP-SMX, vancomycin

Avoid: • Beta-blockers (ALL — including ophthalmic timolol drops!) • Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem especially) • Procainamide, quinidine These drugs impair neuromuscular transmission.

IV Magnesium: Can cause severe weakness — avoid if possible, use with extreme caution if essential. Neuromuscular blockers: • MG patients are VERY sensitive • Rocuronium: Use 1/3 to 1/2 normal dose • Have sugammadex available • Avoid succinylcholine if possible
• Botulinum toxin • D-penicillamine (can induce MG) • Immune checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab) • Interferons • Chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine • Statins (case reports)
Antibiotics: Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, TMP-SMX, vancomycin Pain: Acetaminophen, most opioids (caution with respiratory depression) Other: Most antiemetics, PPIs, H2 blockers
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — increases acetylcholine at NMJ. Symptomatic only — does NOT modify disease course.
Start: 30 mg PO TID (with meals) Titrate: Increase by 30 mg every 3-5 days as tolerated Onset: 30-45 minutes Duration: 3-6 hours
Typical: 60 mg PO q4-6h while awake (4-6 doses/day) Maximum: 120 mg per dose, 480-600 mg/day total Take with food to reduce GI side effects.

Dose: 180 mg at bedtime Purpose: Overnight coverage for morning weakness Important: • Do NOT crush or chew • Absorption less predictable than immediate-release • Not for daytime use — erratic absorption
GI: Cramping, diarrhea, nausea Secretions: Increased salivation, lacrimation Other: Muscle twitching, sweating Watch for cholinergic crisis if excessive dosing — SLUDGE/BBB symptoms.
Both are equally effective for MG crisis and acute exacerbation. Choice depends on availability and patient factors.

Dose: 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days OR 1 g/kg/day × 2 days (total 2 g/kg) Onset: 2-5 days Duration: 3-6 weeks Advantages: • Peripheral IV access only • No specialized equipment • Widely available Risks: Thrombosis, aseptic meningitis, renal toxicity Contraindication: IgA deficiency (anaphylaxis risk)

Protocol: 5 exchanges over 10-14 days (every other day) Onset: 1-2 days (faster than IVIG) Duration: 4-6 weeks Advantages: • Faster onset • Can repeat without cumulative toxicity • No IgA concern Risks: Hypotension, citrate toxicity, line infection Requires: Central venous access, specialized equipment

Prefer IVIG if: • No central access available • Hypercoagulable (PLEX may be safer actually) • Limited apheresis availability Prefer PLEX if: • Need fastest onset • IgA deficiency • IVIG allergy • Renal impairment
Both provide temporary benefit. Must add maintenance immunotherapy (steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate) for long-term control.

info.h: Why This Matters in the ED
info.t: A growing number of MG patients are on newer outpatient maintenance drugs (FcRn inhibitors, complement inhibitors). These are NOT crisis therapies — IVIG, PLEX, and corticosteroids remain first-line for myasthenic crisis. ED relevance: • Recognize what these drugs do, when they were last given, and what side-effect risks they carry • Complement inhibitors carry a CRITICAL meningococcal sepsis risk — must consider in any febrile patient on these agents • FcRn inhibitors transiently lower IgG — patients may be more susceptible to certain infections in the days after infusion • These drugs do NOT replace acute crisis management — escalate as usual

Mechanism: Block the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), which normally recycles IgG. Blocking it accelerates IgG catabolism, lowering circulating IgG — including pathogenic anti-AChR autoantibodies (≈60-70% reduction). Effect is transient and reversible. Typical schedule: • Efgartigimod (Vyvgart): Weekly IV infusion × 4 weeks per cycle, then cycle repeated based on response (typically every 4-8 weeks). SC formulation (efgartigimod alfa/hyaluronidase, "Vyvgart Hytrulo") also available, weekly × 4. • Rozanolixizumab (Rystiggo): Weekly SC × 6 weeks per cycle. ED considerations: • Last infusion timing matters — nadir IgG occurs ~1-2 weeks after start of cycle • Generally lower infection risk than comp

Mechanism: Block terminal complement at C5, preventing C5b-9 membrane attack complex formation at the NMJ. • Eculizumab (Soliris): IV every 2 weeks • Ravulizumab (Ultomiris): IV every 8 weeks (long-acting C5 inhibitor) • Zilucoplan (Zilbrysq): Daily SC (small-molecule C5 inhibitor) ⚠️ CRITICAL ED PEARL — MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS RISK: • Terminal complement is the primary defense against encapsulated organisms, especially Neisseria meningitidis • These drugs carry a black-box warning for meningococcal infection • Patients must be vaccinated against meningococcus (MenACWY + MenB) at least 2 weeks before starting, and many take prophylactic penicillin/macrolide • Any febrile patient on a complement

info.h: What to Ask in the ED
info.t: Quick history checklist for any MG patient on newer therapies: • Which drug, last dose, and date of last cycle? (Efgartigimod cycles, ravulizumab q8w infusion, etc.) • Meningococcal vaccination status? (MenACWY + MenB — both required for complement inhibitors) • On prophylactic antibiotic? (Penicillin VK or macrolide — common with complement inhibitors) • Current signs of infection? Fever, headache, neck stiffness, sore throat, dysuria, rash • Recent infusion reactions or new neurologic symptoms? Bottom line: These are MAINTENANCE drugs. They do not change the acute approach to crisis (IVIG/PLEX/airway/steroids per main consult). They DO change your infection workup and antibiotic threshold

Mitragynine (60-70% of alkaloid content) - Partial mu-opioid receptor agonist - Also binds alpha-adrenergic, serotonin, dopamine receptors 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) (<0.05% of leaf) - 5-10x more potent than mitragynine at mu receptor - More potent than morphine - Key driver of dependence

MGPI (Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl) Formed rapidly in human plasma (54% conversion within 2 hours). Most potent kratom metabolite - mu-opioid binding at 0.087 nM vs mitragynine 7.24 nM. Does NOT form significantly in animal models (only 2-4%). This explains why animal studies underestimate human dependence potential.

Kratom alkaloids exhibit biased agonism at mu-opioid receptors: - Activate G-protein signaling - Do NOT recruit beta-arrestin This may explain: - Reduced respiratory depression vs classical opioids - Reduced constipation - BUT tolerance and withdrawal still develop with chronic high-dose use

Kratom is NOT "just an opioid" - it acts on: - Mu-opioid (partial agonist) - Alpha-2 adrenergic - Serotonin 5-HT2A - Dopamine D2 This multi-receptor profile explains why withdrawal is milder but more protracted than pure opioid withdrawal.

Low doses (2-5g): Stimulant-like - Alertness, energy, mild euphoria High doses (>10g): Opioid-like - Sedation, analgesia, euphoria - Dependence develops here Withdrawal threshold: >3g twice daily for extended period, or any regular use of concentrated 7-OH products.
Onset: 6-12 hours Peak: Day 3-4 (96 hours) Acute phase: 4-7 days PAWS: 2+ weeks Full resolution: Up to 3 months
Onset: 8-24 hours Peak: 36-72 hours Resolution: 5-7 days
Onset: 36-48 hours Peak: 72-96 hours Resolution: 2-3 weeks

| Feature | Kratom | Opioid | |---------|--------|--------| | Intensity | Milder | More intense | | Duration | 1-3 weeks (up to 3 mo) | ~1 week | | Peak | Day 3-4 | Day 1-2 | | Life-threatening | Rare | Uncommon | | Neuropsych | Prominent, protracted | Present but shorter |
Warn patients: symptoms may worsen before improving. Peak is day 3-4, not day 1-2 like opioids. Plan follow-up accordingly - 24-48h check-in recommended to catch peak symptoms.

Mechanism: High-affinity partial mu-agonist displaces kratom alkaloids Advantages: - Best evidence for efficacy (case series) - Rapid symptom control - Can bridge to MOUD if OUD present Concerns: - May create iatrogenic opioid dependence in opioid-naive - Wait for COWS ≥8 to avoid precipitated WD Best for: Prior opioid use, severe symptoms, patient preference

Mechanism: Alpha-2 agonist (clonidine) reduces sympathetic outflow; gabapentin for neuro/muscular symptoms Advantages: - No risk of iatrogenic opioid dependence - No cross-dependence with kratom - Good safety profile Concerns: - May be less effective for severe withdrawal - Hypotension with clonidine Best for: Opioid-naive, mild-moderate symptoms, patient declines opioid therapy

| Factor | Buprenorphine | Non-Opioid | |--------|---------------|------------| | Prior opioid use | Yes | Either | | Opioid-naive | Caution | Preferred | | COWS 5-12 | Either | Good option | | COWS >12 | Preferred | Can try | | Patient preference | Varies | Varies |
Can combine buprenorphine with clonidine for residual adrenergic symptoms. Gabapentin adds value in either pathway for myalgias, restlessness, and sleep.

1. Confirm COWS ≥8 (objective withdrawal present) 2. Document last kratom use (should be >6-12h) 3. Check for contraindications (severe respiratory disease, concurrent full agonist) 4. Obtain baseline vitals

<20g kratom/day: Start 4-8 mg SL (or 4/1 - 8/2 mg buprenorphine-naloxone) >40g kratom/day: Start 12-16 mg SL (or 12/3 - 16/4 mg buprenorphine-naloxone) Unknown/concentrated products: Start 8 mg, titrate based on response

1. Give initial dose 2. Reassess COWS at 60-90 minutes 3. If COWS still elevated (>8), give additional 4 mg 4. Repeat q60-90min as needed 5. Maximum day 1: 16-24 mg total Add clonidine 0.1 mg PRN for residual adrenergic symptoms (sweating, tachycardia)

Short-term (acute withdrawal): Day 1: 8-16 mg Day 2-3: 8 mg Day 4-5: 4 mg Day 6-7: 2 mg then stop Ongoing MOUD: If patient has OUD or prefers maintenance, transition to standard buprenorphine maintenance with addiction medicine follow-up.
If discharging with buprenorphine: - 3-day bridge supply (common) - Arrange follow-up within 72 hours - Provide naloxone kit - Clear instructions on dosing

Documented complications: - Bradycardia at peak (day 3-4) → cardiac arrest (case report) - Tachycardia (early phase) - QTc prolongation (especially 7-OH products) - Brugada exacerbation - Torsades de pointes (rare) Monitor: Continuous telemetry if admitted. ECG on all moderate-severe presentations.

Seizures: Rare, more common in high-dose chronic users Delirium: Hallucinations, confusion documented - May meet CIWA criteria - Treat with dexmedetomidine ± lorazepam Motor symptoms: Tremors, jerky movements, hyperreflexia, coordination issues

Severe dehydration from vomiting/diarrhea - Can cause electrolyte imbalance → arrhythmias - Check BMP, replete aggressively Hepatic injury: - Kratom-induced liver injury (cholestatic/mixed) - Check LFTs if jaundice, RUQ pain, or dark urine - More common with chronic use than acute withdrawal
Depression: Prominent and protracted - May persist weeks (PAWS) - Screen for suicidality Cognitive impairment: "Brain fog" lasting weeks Severe agitation: May require chemical sedation

- HR <50 with symptoms - Arrhythmia on ECG - Hemodynamic instability - Seizure - Altered mental status, hallucinations - Intractable vomiting with severe dehydration - COWS >24 unresponsive to treatment

Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP): • Acquired outside healthcare setting • Most common: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) • IDSA/ATS 2019 guidelines govern treatment Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP): • Develops ≥48 hours after hospital admission • Higher risk of MDR organisms: MRSA, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP): • Develops 48-72 hours after intubation • Highest MDR risk Aspiration Pneumonia: • Often CAP + aspiration event • Modern approach: do NOT routinely cover anaerobes

All patients: • Chest X-ray (or CT if high suspicion with negative CXR) • Pulse oximetry • CBC, BMP, lactate Hospitalized patients: • Blood cultures × 2 (before antibiotics) • Sputum gram stain and culture • Consider procalcitonin (helps guide de-escalation) Severe CAP or specific indications: • Urine pneumococcal antigen • Urine Legionella antigen (severe, outbreak exposure, travel to endemic area) • Influenza testing when flu circulating

1. Where was it acquired? → CAP vs HAP/VAP dictates empiric coverage 2. How severe? → PSI/CURB-65 determines outpatient vs admit vs ICU 3. Risk for resistant organisms? → MRSA and Pseudomonas risk assessment 4. Any complications? → Effusion, empyema, abscess require different approach
• Septic shock requiring vasopressors • Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Either major criterion mandates ICU admission.

• Respiratory rate ≥30 breaths/min • PaO2/FiO2 ratio ≤250 • Multilobar infiltrates • Confusion/disorientation • Uremia (BUN ≥20 mg/dL) • Leukopenia (WBC <4,000 cells/μL) • Thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/μL) • Hypothermia (core temperature <36°C) • Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation 3 or more minor criteria = severe CAP → ICU admission

These criteria identify patients at high risk for: • Intensive respiratory support (BiPAP, mechanical ventilation) • Vasopressor support (ICU-level care) • 30-day mortality >10% Use SMART-COP for objective prediction of IRVS need: • Score ≥5: 33% need intensive support • Score ≥7: 67% need intensive support

• Prior MRSA isolation (any site, especially respiratory) — strongest predictor • IV antibiotics within past 90 days • Hospitalization within past 90 days • Nursing home / long-term care residence • End-stage renal disease (ESRD) • Injection drug use • Lung abscess or empyema • Recent influenza infection • Necrotizing or cavitary pneumonia on imaging
If your facility has MRSA prevalence >10-20% in respiratory cultures, lower your threshold to cover empirically. Check your hospital antibiogram for local resistance patterns.

Excellent negative predictive value (~95%) If nasal MRSA PCR is negative: • Can guide stopping vancomycin at 48h • Reduces unnecessary vancomycin exposure • Cost-effective de-escalation strategy Positive PCR: • Continue MRSA coverage pending cultures • Colonization ≠ infection, but risk is elevated

Vancomycin: • 15-20 mg/kg IV Q8-12h (target trough 15-20) • Loading dose 25-30 mg/kg for severe/ICU Linezolid: • 600mg IV/PO BID • Better lung penetration than vancomycin • Consider for necrotizing pneumonia

• Prior Pseudomonas respiratory isolation — strongest predictor • Bronchiectasis • Severe COPD (FEV1 <25% predicted) • Tracheostomy history • Lung abscess or empyema • Recurrent pneumonia requiring hospitalization • Chronic steroid use (prednisone >10mg/day) • Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics

COPD alone is NOT an indication for Pseudomonas coverage Isolated COPD without additional factors has the same Pseudomonas risk as the general population (~1-2.5% of CAP). Require severe COPD (FEV1 <25%) OR prior Pseudomonas isolation to justify empiric coverage.

Anti-pseudomonal beta-lactams: • Cefepime 2g IV Q8h • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV Q6h • Meropenem 1g IV Q8h (if ESBL concern) Alternative/additional coverage: • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily (also covers Pseudomonas) • Ciprofloxacin 400mg IV Q8h For high MDR risk (HAP/VAP): Use TWO anti-pseudomonal agents from different classes

Stop Pseudomonas coverage at 48-72h if: • Cultures are negative for Pseudomonas • Patient is clinically improving • No risk factors on reassessment Do not maintain broad coverage unnecessarily — promotes resistance

Stage 1 — Simple (Exudative): • Thin, free-flowing fluid • Sterile, low cell count • Usually resolves with antibiotics alone Stage 2 — Fibrinopurulent: • Fibrin deposition, loculations developing • Develops 5-10 days into infection • May progress without drainage Stage 3 — Organizing (Empyema): • Thick pleural peel, trapped lung • Positive culture/gram stain • REQUIRES drainage

Send fluid for: • pH (anaerobic syringe, ice, to lab immediately) • Glucose • LDH • Total protein • Cell count with differential • Gram stain • Culture (aerobic + anaerobic) Also consider: cytology if malignancy concern

Drain if ANY of the following: • pH <7.2 • Glucose <60 mg/dL (or <40 mg/dL = empyema) • LDH >3× upper limit of serum normal (or >1000 IU/L) • Positive gram stain • Positive culture • Frank pus • Loculations on imaging

R — Renal function: Creatinine >141 μmol/L (>1.6 mg/dL) = 1 point A — Age >50 years = 1 point P — Purulence: Frank pus on aspiration = 2 points I — Infection source: Hospital-acquired or immunosuppression = 1 point D — Dietary: Albumin <27 g/L = 1 point Total: 0-7 points

Low risk (0-2 points): • ~2% 3-month mortality • May be candidates for less aggressive drainage Medium risk (3-4 points): • ~10% 3-month mortality • Standard chest tube drainage High risk (5-7 points): • ~25-30% 3-month mortality • Consider early surgical consultation • More aggressive management warranted
RAPID score helps: • Set expectations for outcomes • Guide aggressiveness of intervention • Identify patients needing early surgical input Derived from MIST1/MIST2 trial populations.
• Scene safety, signs of obvious death, valid DNAR/POLST • Confirm arrest in ≤10 sec — unsure = start CPR • Activate team, assign roles, call for defibrillator/AED

• High-quality CPR — 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm, full recoil, rotate q2 min • Airway — BVM with OPA, supraglottic, or ETT after first cycle • IV → IO within 60 sec if no access • Attach pads, defibrillator on, ETCO₂ immediately after airway • First rhythm check at 2 min — minimize interruption <10 sec
