• Shockable: VF, pulseless VT, torsades • VF → defibrillate then resume CPR • Pulseless VT → defibrillate then resume CPR • Torsades → magnesium, overdrive pacing, defibrillate • Non-shockable: PEA or asystole • PEA workflow: POCUS for cardiac activity + reversible causes • Bradycardic arrest / asystole

• Vascular access — IV, then IO if no IV in 60 sec • Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min — non-shockable after 1st cycle, shockable after 2nd shock • ETCO₂ waveform target >20 mmHg = adequate CPR; sudden ↑ = ROSC

• Six H's and six T's — review at every pulse check • POCUS during pulse checks only — RUSH protocol for tamponade, PTX, PE, hypovolemia, contractility • Situation-specific meds: bicarb, calcium, lipid, hypertonic saline, glucose

• ROSC pathway → post-arrest care, target temperature, reperfusion • TOR criteria: ETCO₂ <10 mmHg after 20 min adequate CPR + no reversible cause • No cardiac activity on POCUS = poor prognosis • Code called — TOR documentation, family debrief, organ donation
• Organized rhythm + no palpable pulse = PEA • RUSH exam during pulse check — limit to <10 sec • Cardiac activity on POCUS? — bedside ultrasound divides PEA into pseudo vs true

• Pseudo-PEA: organized contractility on POCUS = profound shock, not arrest • Treat pseudo-PEA as severe shock — fluids, push-dose pressors, address cause • True PEA: cardiac standstill on POCUS — universally poor prognosis

• QRS width drives the "What killed this heart?" question • Wide QRS PEA → metabolic / toxic causes (hyperK, TCA, sodium-channel blockade, acidosis) • Narrow QRS PEA → mechanical / obstructive causes (tamponade, tension PTX, PE, hypovolemia, auto-PEEP)

• Wide-complex differential • Hyperkalemia in arrest — calcium, bicarb, insulin/dextrose • TCA / Na-channel blocker — sodium bicarbonate • Severe acidosis — bicarbonate • Narrow-complex POCUS-directed differential • Mechanical hyperinflation / auto-PEEP — disconnect, prolonged exhalation • Tamponade — pericardiocentesis • Tension pneumothorax — needle decompression / finger thoracostomy • Massive PE — thrombolysis • Hypovolemia — volume resuscitation
• High-quality CPR with ETCO₂ monitoring • Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min from the first cycle in PEA

• Rhythm/pulse check — ROSC achieved? • ROSC → post-arrest care pathway • Continue resuscitation if reversible cause still treatable • Termination criteria — no ROSC + no reversible cause + asystole/standstill • Code called — TOR documentation
• Bradycardia + cardiovascular collapse / arrest • Classify rhythm: asystole, bradycardic PEA, profound bradycardia

• Asystole — confirm in 2 leads, CPR + epi (no pacing benefit in asystole) • Transcutaneous pacing — pads, rate 70-80, current up from 50 mA • Assess electrical AND mechanical capture (palpate femoral pulse)

• Failure to capture — increase current, reposition pads, switch to medications/TVP • Atropine 1 mg IV q3-5 min (max 3 mg) — limited utility in arrest, may try if not asystole • Chronotropic infusions — epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min OR dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min

• Common reversible causes: hyperK, beta-blocker/CCB toxicity, hypoxia, ↑ICP, MI, hypothermia, organophosphate • Identify and treat reversible cause aggressively • Cause-specific therapy: calcium for hyperK/CCB, glucagon/HIET for BB, decompress for ↑ICP

• Transvenous pacing if TCP failing, prolonged need, or unable to tolerate • Post-capture management — confirm pulse with capture, target HR 70-80 • Patient status: ROSC, persistent arrest, or rearrest? • ROSC achieved — post-arrest care pathway • Re-arrest — re-enter pacing/medication algorithm • Termination of resuscitation — no ROSC despite pacing + meds + cause-directed therapy
• Wide-complex tachycardia identified — assume VT until proven otherwise • Pulse check — pulseless = ACLS arrest pathway • QRS morphology: monomorphic vs polymorphic

• Defibrillate immediately — 200J biphasic • CPR 2 min, epinephrine 1 mg q3-5 min, antiarrhythmic (amiodarone 300 mg or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg) • Rhythm check after each 2-min cycle • Refractory pVT — double sequential defibrillation, change pad position, esmolol • Polymorphic in arrest — check QTc; magnesium for torsades • ROSC achieved — post-cardiac arrest care

• Hemodynamic stability assessment — unstable = synchronized cardioversion • Synchronized cardioversion 100J → 200J → 300J → 360J • Post-cardioversion — antiarrhythmic infusion + reversible cause workup

• Stable monomorphic VT — IV antiarrhythmic (procainamide preferred, amiodarone, sotalol) • Response to antiarrhythmic — converted vs persistent • Refractory stable monomorphic VT — synchronized cardioversion under sedation • Polymorphic VT — check baseline QTc to choose pathway • Polymorphic with normal QTc → treat ischemia (cath, beta-blocker) • Polymorphic with prolonged QTc = torsades → magnesium, correct K/Mg, overdrive pacing

• Post-conversion checklist — 12-lead, electrolytes, troponin, echo, structural workup • Recurrent VT management — antiarrhythmic infusion, EP consult, ICD eval • Disposition — ICU vs CCU, EP consult for ablation/ICD
Wide + regular = VT until proven otherwise • Baseline WCT: 80% is VT • Age >35: 85% VT • Prior MI: 98% VT • Hemodynamic stability does NOT differentiate

• Sodium channel blocker OD: Bicarb 1-2 mEq/kg — NOT antiarrhythmics • Hyperkalemia: Calcium first → insulin/glucose • WPW + AFib (irregular WCT): NO AV nodal blockers (adenosine, CCB, BB) — cardiovert or procainamide
• Synchronized cardioversion: 100J → 200J → 360J • Sedate if time permits (midazolam, ketamine, etomidate) • Confirm sync mode enabled • If pulseless → unsync shock 200J

• Brugada: 4-step precordial analysis (98.7% sens, 96.5% spec) • Vereckei aVR: Single lead analysis (faster) • Pathognomonic VT: AV dissociation, fusion beats, capture beats • If uncertain → treat as VT

• Stable monomorphic VT: Procainamide 20-50 mg/min (PROCAMIO > amiodarone) • Torsades (polymorphic + long QT): Magnesium 2g IV then infusion — NOT amiodarone • Polymorphic + normal QT: Treat as ACS, cath lab • If antiarrhythmic fails: Cardioversion
✅ VT treatments SAFE for SVT: Procainamide, cardioversion ❌ SVT treatments may KILL VT: Adenosine, CCB, beta-blockers Bottom line: If any doubt → procainamide or cardioversion

• Secure airway, ETCO₂ 35-45 mmHg, 12-lead ECG immediately • STEMI on ECG — emergent PCI, do not delay • STEMI confirmed — activate cath lab, TTM in lab, no CT head • No STEMI — stabilize hemodynamics first (COACT trial) • Indeterminate ECG or new LBBB — cardiology consult, consider early angio
• MAP ≥65 mmHg, SpO₂ 94-98%, PaCO₂ 35-45 mmHg — titrate FiO₂ down • Norepinephrine first-line, add vasopressin if refractory; dobutamine for low CO
• Assess: patient following commands? • Comatose — prevent fever >37.7°C × 72h, magnesium + meperidine anti-shivering • Following commands — standard care, treat any fever >37.7°C
• Do NOT prognosticate <72h post-rewarming — sedation + hypothermia confound exam • Post-arrest seizures 20-30% — continuous EEG, levetiracetam first-line
• Glucose 140-180 mg/dL, continuous EEG × 24-48h, echo for LV function • ICU admission — document code details, communicate arrest circumstances

• Recognize high-risk features: abrupt pain, pulse deficit, BP differential >20 mmHg • ADD-RS risk stratification to guide imaging approach • Assess for classic AAA triad: hypotension, back pain, pulsatile mass

• ADD-RS ≥2 → immediate CTA; ADD-RS 0-1 + D-dimer <500 → 99% rule-out • Classify: dissection (Type A vs B), IMH, PAU, or ruptured AAA • Unstable + bedside US confirms AAA → straight to OR, skip CT • D-dimer <500 reliable rule-out for ADD-RS 0-1; elevated → proceed to CTA

• Beta-blocker FIRST (HR 60-70, SBP 100-120) — esmolol preferred in unstable • Add vasodilator AFTER beta-blocker if SBP >120 — nicardipine or clevidipine • Hypotensive dissection: check BP all extremities, avoid pure alpha-agonists • Ruptured AAA: permissive hypotension SBP 70-90, 1:1:1 MTP, minimize crystalloid

• Type A dissection → IMMEDIATE surgery; mortality 1-2%/hour untreated • Uncomplicated Type B → medical management, ICU, serial imaging at 24-48h • Complicated Type B (malperfusion, rupture) → TEVAR or open repair • PAU → individualized; TEVAR if symptoms persist or rupture risk • Ruptured AAA → EVAR if anatomy allows, OSR for unsuitable anatomy

• Emergent surgery: Type A, ruptured AAA, complicated Type B • ICU admission: uncomplicated Type B, IMH, PAU; continuous BP monitoring • Urgent admission: symptomatic unruptured aneurysm, rapidly expanding AAA • Malperfusion syndromes: coronary (surgery not PCI), mesenteric (>50% mortality)

• Identify dominant syndrome: ↑ICP, focal deficits, encephalopathy, or seizure • >90% present with headache; seizures 20-40%; focal deficits 20-50% • Acute seizure protocol: lorazepam → levetiracetam; no prophylaxis without prior seizure

• D-dimer BEFORE imaging (NPV 95-99.8%, but 10% CVST normal D-dimer) • MRI + MRV gold standard; CT + CTV acceptable • MRI by phase: acute T1 iso/T2 hypo, subacute T1/T2 hyperintense • Confirm CVST → assess location, parenchymal involvement, ICH presence

• CRITICAL: ICH in CVST is NOT a contraindication — hemorrhage is venous congestion consequence • ISCVT study: no difference in hemorrhage extension with anticoagulation • Proceed immediately to anticoagulation despite ICH

• CVT-GS score: mild 0-2 (1.1% mort), moderate 3-7 (19.6%), severe 8-13 (61.4%) • FIRST-LINE: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h immediately — do NOT delay • Alternative if renal impairment or need rapid reversal: UFH IV (aPTT 1.5-2.5×) • Transition to DOAC after 5-15 days — contraindicated in pregnancy & APS

• Duration: 3 mo (transient), 6-12 mo (idiopathic), indefinite (severe thrombophilia) • Monitor for deterioration despite anticoagulation • Endovascular thrombectomy/thrombolysis for neurologic deterioration • Decompressive craniectomy if herniation or midline shift ≥5 mm

• Pregnancy: LMWH throughout (DOACs teratogenic; warfarin first-tri defects) • Continue LMWH ≥6 weeks postpartum (min 3 months total) • Malignancy: LMWH preferred initial & long-term • OCP users: STOP estrogen-containing — use progestin-only or copper IUD • Admit all CVST: ICU if AMS or high CVT-GS; neuro unit if stable

• Use Broselow tape for weight and equipment sizing • ABCs: airway positioning, assess breathing, check circulation and mental status • Secondary survey: examine head-to-toe, identify primary injury pattern • Tachycardia is early; hypotension is late and ominous
• Direct pressure on external bleeding; 20 mL/kg NS/LR bolus if unstable • Transfuse if Hgb <7-8 or ongoing hemorrhage; 1:1:1 MTP; TXA 15 mg/kg within 3 hr
• Mild TBI (GCS 14-15): use PECARN criteria to decide CT • Moderate TBI (GCS 9-13): CT head + ICU admission • Severe TBI (GCS ≤8): intubate + 3% saline for herniation; CPP >40-50 mmHg

• Compliant chest wall: pulmonary contusion without rib fractures • Stable abdominal trauma: non-operative management for most solid organ injuries • Unstable abdominal trauma: activate MTP, surgical consult, OR • Tension PTX: needle decompression → chest tube; hemothorax >15 mL/kg → thoracotomy

• Physis is weakest point; Salter-Harris classification guides management • Compartment syndrome: clinical dx, pain with passive stretch — emergent fasciotomy • Always consider NAT in non-ambulatory children

• Transfer to peds trauma center if GCS <14, intubated, multisystem, or ICU need • Stabilize before transfer; secure airway if any concern • Admit to appropriate level: ICU if GCS <14, unstable, or major injuries • Discharge: stable, pain controlled, reliable caregiver, follow-up • NAT concern: mandatory CPS reporting; do not discharge to suspected abuser
• What is ECMO? VV vs VA differences; assess failing organ system
• Is cardiac output adequate or failing? • When in doubt — go VA • Hemodynamic assessment + echo findings

• VV indications: P/F ratio <80 despite optimization • Call ECMO center EARLY — mortality doubles if MV >7 days • Circuit basics: femoral drain, IJ return • Initial settings: lung rest, anticoagulation, target flows • Monitor for recirculation

• VA indications: cardiogenic shock, massive PE, arrest • Early initiation improves outcomes — call at SCAI Stage D • Peripheral cannulation: femoral vein drain, femoral artery return • Mandatory right radial arterial line for VA-ECMO • Watch for Harlequin syndrome (differential hypoxemia) • Monitor for LV distension — may need Impella or surgical vent
• Candidates: witnessed arrest, shockable rhythm, <60 min CPR • Target cannulation within 60 minutes of arrest
• Absolute: irreversible disease, severe neuro injury • VV: femorojugular (most common) or dual-lumen • VA: peripheral femoral-femoral with distal perfusion cannula (ESSENTIAL)
• Bleeding 30-50%, thrombosis 10-20%, limb ischemia 10-20% • RESP score (VV) and SAVE score (VA) guide candidacy
• Have P/F ratio, pressor doses, lactate trend, echo findings ready • Proceed with cannulation or transfer to ECMO center

• Classic triad — altered mental status, autonomic dysfunction, neuromuscular excitation • Serotonergic drug exposure required for diagnosis • Onset within 24 hours of drug change; clonus is hallmark • Investigate medication history: SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, MDMA, linezolid

• Hunter Criteria — sensitivity 84%, specificity 97% (better than Sternbach) • Clonus is key — spontaneous, inducible, or ocular • Tremor + hyperreflexia, OR hypertonia + temp >38°C + clonus also meet • Assess if criteria met — positive = SS, negative/equivocal = differentiate

• Consider NMS, anticholinergic, malignant hyperthermia, sympathomimetics, sepsis, thyroid storm • SS vs NMS: SS hyperkinetic with clonus + rapid onset; NMS rigid + slow onset • If NMS likely — stop antipsychotic, dantrolene, bromocriptine, ICU • If other diagnosis — continue workup for alternative etiology

• Mild (tremor, alert), moderate (agitation, T 38.5-40), severe (T>40, rigidity, seizures) • Mild: stop agents, benzos PRN, IV fluids, observe 6-12h • Moderate: benzos, cyproheptadine 12 mg load then 2 mg q2h, cooling, admit • Severe: intubate, aggressive cooling, paralysis if needed, cyproheptadine NG, ICU

• Mild: discharge if resolving after 6-12h, stable vitals, tolerating PO • Moderate: telemetry admit, continue benzos + cyproheptadine 24-48h, tox + psych • Severe: ICU for T>40, intubation, paralysis, instability — MAOI cases longest duration

• Calculate elemental iron dose (20-33% elemental by formulation) • Assess: <20 mg/kg minimal, 20-60 mg/kg moderate, >60 mg/kg severe • Abdominal X-ray — tablets radiopaque, liquids/chewables may not be visible

• Stage 1 (0-6h): GI hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain • Stage 2 (6-24h): deceptive improvement — DO NOT be fooled • Stage 3 (12-48h): shock, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, CV collapse • Stage 4 (2-4 days): hepatotoxicity, hepatic necrosis, hypoglycemia • Stage 5 (2-6 weeks): GI scarring, gastric outlet obstruction, strictures

• Serum iron at 4-6 hours (peak): <350 minimal, 350-500 moderate, >500 severe • Labs: CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags, lactate, ABG — metabolic acidosis = severe • Do NOT rely on TIBC — falsely elevated, does not guide management

• Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron — NOT effective • WBI with GoLYTELY — 500 mL/hr peds, 1-2 L/hr adults via NG • Continue WBI until clear effluent AND no pills on repeat film • Endoscopic removal only for bezoars or failed WBI — rarely needed

• Indication: serum iron >500 mcg/dL OR severe symptoms • Start IV 5 mg/kg/hr, titrate to 15 mg/kg/hr, max 6 g/24h • Do NOT use "vin rosé" urine color to guide therapy — unreliable • Continue until: clinical improvement AND iron <350 AND acidosis resolved
• Refractory shock: exchange transfusion (pediatric) • Hemodialysis removes ferrioxamine — for renal failure or ARDS • Supportive: aggressive IVF for GI losses, blood products, vasopressors
• Low-risk (<20 mg/kg, asymptomatic): observe 6 hr, discharge if well • Moderate (20-60 mg/kg or 350-500 mcg/dL): admit for serial labs • Severe (>60 mg/kg, >500 mcg/dL, or DFO needed): ICU

• Suspect BB toxicity: bradycardia + hypotension + hypoglycemia triad • Identify agent: propranolol (lipophilic, Na⁺ block), sotalol (QT), carvedilol (alpha), atenolol/nadolol (hydrophilic, dialyzable) • ECG: QRS widening (propranolol) or QT prolongation (sotalol) • Severity: mild (alert), moderate (HR<50/SBP<90), severe (seizure, arrest) • Extended-release: 24-48h observation due to delayed toxicity

• ABCs, two large-bore IVs, continuous monitoring • Fingerstick glucose immediately; treat with D50 if needed • Decontamination: charcoal if <2h, WBI for sustained-release • Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV (often ineffective; muscarinic, not beta)

• Glucagon 3-5 mg IV bolus (up to 10 mg total) — bypasses blocked beta receptor • Glucagon 2-10 mg/hr infusion once response achieved • Pretreat with ondansetron — nausea/vomiting common • Calcium gluconate 3 g IV or CaCl 1 g IV over 10-20 min for inotropy

• Cornerstone: regular insulin 1 unit/kg bolus, then 1-10 units/kg/hr infusion • MUST co-administer dextrose — D10/D25 to maintain glucose 150-250 mg/dL • Aggressive K⁺ repletion to 3.5-4.5 (insulin drives K intracellularly) • Monitor glucose q15-30 min, K⁺ q1h — D50 at bedside • Onset 15-60 min — be patient, this is NOT DKA dosing

• HIGH-DOSE norepinephrine 0.1-3 mcg/kg/min — standard doses insufficient • Add epinephrine 0.1-1 mcg/kg/min for cardiogenic component • Vasopressin 0.04 units/min — bypasses adrenergic, add for refractory • AVOID dobutamine and dopamine — use NE + epi • If MAP ≥65 continue; if refractory, escalate to lipid emulsion

• Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min (may repeat ×2 q5 min) • Then 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min infusion ×30-60 min — max 10-12 mL/kg first hour • Best for refractory shock with lipophilic agents (propranolol, metoprolol) • Less evidence for hydrophilic agents (atenolol, nadolol) — dialysis better

• Propranolol + QRS >100 ms: NaHCO₃ 1-2 mEq/kg push (treat like TCA) • Sotalol + QT/Torsades: MgSO₄ 2 g IV + overdrive pacing — AVOID amiodarone • Atenolol/Nadolol: hemodialysis — small Vd, dialyzable, renally cleared • Refractory vasoplegia: methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg over 15-30 min • Refractory shock/arrest: VA-ECMO — toxicity is REVERSIBLE
• Prolonged CPR (30-60+ min) reasonable — toxicological arrest is REVERSIBLE • HIGH-dose epi, glucagon 5-10 mg, CaCl 1-3 g, Intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus
• ICU: any instability, arrhythmia, or on infusions • Monitored bed: stable, normal ECG — min 6h IR, min 24h ER • Discharge: asymptomatic ≥6h, normal vitals/ECG/glucose, IR ONLY, psych clearance

• Identify DHP vs non-DHP agent — determines shock phenotype • Dihydropyridines: vasodilatory shock, reflex tachycardia • Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil/diltiazem): cardiogenic shock, bradycardia • Unknown or mixed ingestion — assess phenotype clinically • Extended-release: delayed toxicity 12-24h, WBI mandatory

• Assess shock phenotype — CRITICAL for treatment routing • Vasodilatory: warm, normal/high CO, low SVR — emphasize vasopressors • Cardiogenic: cool, low CO, bradycardia — emphasize HIET • Mixed: both features — use both HIET AND vasopressors

• ABCs, two large-bore IVs, continuous monitor, 12-lead ECG • CaCl 1-2 g IV q15-20 min or continuous infusion — temporary bridge • Glucagon 3-5 mg bolus then 2-5 mg/hr — less effective than in BB • WBI with GoLYTELY 2 L/hr for extended-release

• HIET is FIRST-LINE for cardiogenic shock phenotype • Regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 1-10 units/kg/hr infusion • Maintain glucose 150-250 mg/dL with D10W; replete K to 4.0-4.5 • Hemodynamic improvement within 15-60 min — do not stop early

• Norepinephrine 0.1-3 mcg/kg/min for vasodilatory shock — HIGH doses needed • Vasopressin 0.04 units/min fixed adjunct for refractory vasoplegia • Escalate aggressively — much higher doses than septic shock

• Intralipid 1.5 mL/kg bolus for refractory toxicity — best evidence for verapamil • Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg for refractory vasoplegia • Temporary pacing for refractory bradycardia • VA-ECMO bridge for arrest or refractory shock — toxicity is REVERSIBLE

• All significant CCB ingestions → ICU • Extended-release: minimum 24-48h regardless of initial presentation • Unstable: ongoing HIET, vasopressors, serial labs q1-2h • Low-risk (small IR DHP, asymptomatic): monitored observation 6h min

• Classic presentation: GI, visual, CNS symptoms • Acute ingestion: high level, low K⁺, deceptively well • Chronic toxicity: insidious, multiple risk factors • Unknown/mixed: treat as chronic if maintenance therapy
• ECG critical — scooped ST, PAT with block, bidirectional VT • Bradyarrhythmias: sinus brady, AV block, junctional rhythm • Tachyarrhythmias: PAT with block, bidirectional VT — AVOID cardioversion
• Assess K⁺ level — hyperkalemia (>5.5) = critical • Hyperkalemia in toxicity: DigiFab indicated, AVOID calcium
• General: decontamination, electrolytes, arrhythmia management • Mild: supportive care, activated charcoal, hold digoxin • AVOID: cardioversion, calcium, pacing, beta-blockers

• Indications: life-threatening arrhythmia, K⁺ >5.5, high level • Dosing methods: known ingestion, serum level, or empiric • Known ingestion formula: vials = (mg × 0.8) / 0.5 • Known level formula: vials = (level × weight) / 100 • Empiric dosing: acute 10-20 vials, chronic 3-6 vials • Post-DigiFab: response 30-60 min, levels meaningless post-Fab
• Disposition: assess for ICU vs telemetry based on severity • ICU: any significant arrhythmia, DigiFab given, K⁺ >5.5 • Telemetry: mild symptoms, stable, normal K⁺, no arrhythmia
• What is lipid emulsion therapy • Mechanism: lipid sink + direct cardiotonic effects

• Select clinical scenario • LAST (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity) — primary indication • CCB overdose with refractory shock • Beta-blocker overdose with refractory hemodynamic collapse • TCA overdose — use AFTER sodium bicarbonate fails • Other lipophilic drug toxicity (diphenhydramine, bupropion)

• Bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 1 min (may repeat ×2 q5 min); infusion 0.25-0.5 mL/kg/min; max 12 mL/kg first 30 min • Administration: IV access, line compatibility • CPR modifications for LAST — epi dosing, what to avoid
• Monitor hemodynamics + response markers • Continue 15-30 min after stability; watch for recrudescence • Lab interference — lipemia affects many assays

• Complications & adverse effects — rare but important • Special populations — peds, pregnancy, obesity dosing • Post-ILE disposition decision • Stable — ICU admission for observation • Vasopressor-dependent — ICU for ongoing support • Refractory arrest — consider VA-ECMO/ECPR

1. Stop vasopressor infusion immediately. 2. Leave catheter in place initially. 3. Disconnect tubing and aspirate residual drug through the catheter. 4. Do not flush. 5. Remove catheter after aspiration unless pharmacy/toxicology directs otherwise. 6. Elevate the extremity and apply dry warm compresses. 7. Mark borders, document neurovascular exam, and photograph per policy. 8. Restart vasopressor through reliable alternate access. 9. If alpha-adrenergic pressor injury: infiltrate phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10 mL NS locally. 10. Escalate early for hand/foot, ischemia, blistering, necrosis, delayed recognition, or neurovascular deficit.

Phentolamine is appropriate for alpha-adrenergic vasopressor injury. Isolated vasopressin injury is not alpha-mediated; use rescue steps, pharmacy/toxicology input, and early specialist escalation if ischemic.
Phentolamine 5-10 mg diluted in 10 mL normal saline, infiltrated locally throughout the affected area using small aliquots.
Norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, dopamine, metaraminol, or unknown/mixed alpha-adrenergic vasopressor extravasation with ischemic risk.

- Use as soon as possible; labeling for norepinephrine specifies treatment within 12 hours. - Infiltrate around the margins and into the ischemic field. - Continue serial neurovascular exams. - Do not delay surgery/plastics/hand consultation for progressive ischemia.

- Terbutaline 1 mg diluted in 10 mL normal saline and infiltrated subcutaneously around the affected area. - Nitroglycerin 2% ointment topically over the ischemic field. - Continue warm compresses, elevation, and serial neurovascular checks.

Evidence is limited and largely case-based. Use local policy and pharmacy/toxicology guidance. Avoid topical nitroglycerin when hypotension, recent PDE-5 inhibitor use, or nitroglycerin contraindication is present.
Vasopressin causes V1-mediated vasoconstriction. Phentolamine is an alpha-blocker, so it is not a direct mechanistic reversal agent for isolated vasopressin extravasation.

- Stop infusion, aspirate, do not flush. - Elevate and apply dry warm compresses. - Restart pressor support through reliable alternate access. - Consult pharmacy/toxicology for local vasodilator strategy if ischemia is present. - Escalate to surgery/plastics/hand surgery for progressive ischemia, high-risk sites, blistering, necrosis, or neurovascular deficit.

info.h: Stop and escalate if any are present
info.t: - Hand, foot, genital/perineal, or large-volume extravasation - Blanching/coolness with poor capillary refill - Numbness, weakness, severe pain, or tense compartments - Blistering, necrosis, or rapidly expanding skin changes - Delayed recognition with ongoing ischemia - Persistent shock requiring ongoing high-dose peripheral vasopressors without reliable access
Call pharmacy/toxicology and surgery/plastics/hand surgery. Continue antidote/local measures when appropriate, but do not rely on antidote alone for progressive ischemia.

1. Call poison center/toxicology and pharmacy. 2. Establish reliable IV access; central access preferred for concentrated dextrose but do not delay insulin in shock. 3. Baseline glucose, potassium, magnesium, phosphate, lactate, VBG/ABG, ECG. 4. If glucose <200 mg/dL: give dextrose 25 g IV. 5. If K <3.0 mEq/L: start potassium replacement immediately. 6. Give regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus. 7. Start regular insulin infusion 1 unit/kg/hr. 8. Start/titrate dextrose infusion to maintain euglycemia. 9. If no hemodynamic improvement, increase insulin by 1 unit/kg/hr q20-30 min, commonly up to 10 units/kg/hr with toxicology guidance. 10. Monitor glucose q15-20 min during initiation/titration an
SBP >90 mmHg or MAP >65 mmHg, HR >50/min when relevant, improving perfusion, lactate, mentation, urine output, and cardiac function.

- Calcium channel blocker toxicity with hypotension, bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, or mixed shock - Beta-blocker toxicity with persistent hypotension/bradycardia or cardiogenic shock - Suspected BB/CCB mixed ingestion with poison-induced cardiogenic shock - Refractory or escalating vasopressor requirement when myocardial dysfunction is present
Failure of prolonged low-yield therapy. Glucagon and calcium may be useful bridges, but HDI should be started early in severe cardiotoxic shock.
Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose Beta-Blocker Overdose
Regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 1 unit/kg/hr continuous infusion.
If no hemodynamic improvement, increase infusion by 1 unit/kg/hr every 20-30 minutes, commonly up to 10 units/kg/hr with poison center/toxicology guidance.
Target SBP >90 mmHg or MAP >65 mmHg, HR >50/min when relevant, improving perfusion, lactate, urine output, mentation, and echo/hemodynamic markers.

- If glucose <200 mg/dL: Dextrose 25 g IV before or with insulin. - Start D10W 1/2NS at 100 mL/hr in adults, then titrate. - Use concentrated dextrose through central access when fluid load becomes excessive. - Target glucose 100-200 mg/dL per Ontario Poison Centre; follow local poison center protocol.

- Check baseline potassium before/at initiation. - If K <3.0 mEq/L, start IV potassium replacement immediately. - Check K at least hourly during titration, then q2h if stable. - Hypokalemia is usually redistribution from insulin; avoid overcorrection and watch for rebound hyperkalemia during wean.

- Insulin concentration and pump programming - Dose entered as units/kg/hr, not DKA rate - Dextrose bolus/infusion plan active - Glucose checks q15-20 min during start/titration - Potassium monitoring and replacement plan active - Poison center/toxicology/pharmacy involved - Escalation plan for refractory shock
Dextrose availability, glucose monitoring, potassium monitoring, telemetry/BP monitoring, and a clear titration endpoint.

1. Confirm current potassium, renal function, and urine output. 2. Identify severity: ECG changes, arrhythmia, paralysis, respiratory weakness, K <=2.5, DKA/HHS. 3. Stop if hyperkalemia, anuria, or indication is unclear. 4. Select access: peripheral usually max 10 mEq/hr per line; central monitored commonly 20 mEq/hr. 5. Use infusion pump and line tracing; never IV push. 6. Correct magnesium if low/unknown with arrhythmia risk or refractory hypokalemia. 7. Recheck K q2-4 hr during aggressive replacement and track total K from all sources.
- Typical max: 10 mEq/hr per peripheral line - Common concentration: 10 mEq/100 mL over 1 hr - Burning/phlebitis: dilute, slow, or split across lines - Use pump; never IV push

- Common severe replacement: 20 mEq/hr - Higher rates require institutional protocol, senior clinician/pharmacy involvement, continuous ECG, and frequent K checks - Use for arrhythmia, paralysis, severe symptoms, or need for rapid replacement

info.h: Do not start routine IV K if
info.t: - Hyperkalemia or rapidly rising K - Anuria or severe renal failure without specialist-directed replacement - No current K/renal function in a high-risk patient - Pump, dose, rate, concentration, or line cannot be verified - Concern for pseudohypokalemia or invalid lab
Life-threatening hypokalemia in renal failure may still require treatment, but it should be managed with senior/pharmacy/nephrology input, small reassessed doses, and continuous ECG monitoring.

- K <3.3 mEq/L: hold insulin; give K 10 mEq/hr until K >=3.3 (10-20 mEq/hr only via central line with cardiac monitoring) - K 3.3-5.2: add 20-30 mEq K per LITRE of IV fluid while insulin runs (concentration, not rate) - K >5.2: hold K initially; recheck q2h and start when K falls - Consider chloride/phosphate/acetate mix based on phosphate and acid-base status
- No pump - No line tracing - IV push order - Rate/concentration cannot be verified - Hyperkalemia or anuria without specialist plan - Insulin in DKA/HHS when K <3.3 before replacement is running

1. Confirm indication: VTE/PE, ACS/STEMI adjunct, procedural bridge, or specialist-directed use. 2. Screen for active bleeding, HIT, platelet collapse, recent surgery/procedure, ICH risk, and duplicate anticoagulants. 3. Decide bolus: standard VTE, ACS capped dose, or no-bolus/high-bleed-risk strategy. 4. Obtain baseline CBC/platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, creatinine, and anti-Xa/aPTT monitoring plan. 5. Start infusion by institutional nomogram. 6. Recheck anti-Xa/aPTT at protocol interval, commonly 6 hr after start/dose change. 7. Handoff target range, current units/hr, next lab time, and bolus/no-bolus rationale.
Unfractionated heparin 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/hr infusion. Titrate by institutional anti-Xa or aPTT nomogram.
Coordinate UFH timing with lytic protocol. Many protocols hold UFH during systemic alteplase and restart without bolus when aPTT/anti-Xa permits.
Unfractionated heparin 60 units/kg IV bolus, max 4,000 units; then 12 units/kg/hr infusion, initial max 1,000 units/hr. Titrate by local nomogram.
Coordinate with antiplatelet plan, cath lab timing, lytic use, and residual LMWH/DOAC effect. Avoid duplicate anticoagulation.

- Anti-Xa or aPTT by institutional nomogram - First level commonly 6 hr after start and 6 hr after dose change - CBC/platelets daily or per protocol - Bleeding exam at every handoff - Consider anti-Xa when aPTT is unreliable or discordant
Stop UFH. Use Protamine Calculator. Typical dose is 1 mg protamine per 100 units UFH received in the prior 2-3 hr, max 50 mg, given slow IV over 10 min.
Avoid excess protamine; it can worsen anticoagulation/bleeding. High aPTT/anti-Xa without bleeding is usually managed by holding/reducing UFH per nomogram.

1. Identify indication: impending herniation/elevated ICP or severe symptomatic hyponatremia. 2. Do not use HTS to correct routine hypernatremia. 3. Herniation: call neurosurgery/neurocritical care; give 3% NaCl 2-5 mL/kg, often 150-250 mL over 10-20 min, or 23.4% NaCl 30 mL central if appropriate. 4. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia: 3% NaCl 100-150 mL over 10-20 min, repeat up to 2 times for persistent severe symptoms. 5. Check sodium q2h during active correction. 6. Prevent overcorrection; consider DDAVP/D5W if sodium is rising too fast.
Hypertonic saline 3% NaCl 2-5 mL/kg IV bolus, often 150-250 mL over 10-20 min. Use HTS Herniation Dose Calculator. 23.4% NaCl 30 mL IV over 10-20 min via central line may be used by protocol.
Avoid hypotension, hypoxia, fever, hypoglycemia. Elevate head, keep neck midline, treat seizures, reverse anticoagulation when indicated, and arrange definitive neurosurgical care.

- Initial severe symptom target: Na rise 4-6 mEq/L - Avoid >10 mEq/L in 24 hr for most patients - Avoid >8 mEq/L in 24 hr in high-risk patients: alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, liver disease, hypokalemia, very low starting Na - Use DDAVP/D5W relowering strategy with nephrology/ICU guidance if overcorrection occurs or is likely
Do not give HTS to correct hypernatremia. Routine hypernatremia is treated with controlled free-water replacement based on chronicity and volume status.

Treat as competing life threats. Call neurocritical care/neurosurgery immediately. Hyperosmolar rescue may still be justified for impending herniation, but sodium/osmolality must be tracked closely and the decision should be specialist-directed when possible.

- Is this herniation/elevated ICP or severe symptomatic hyponatremia? - Is this actually routine hypernatremia correction? If yes, do not give HTS. - Is sodium correction already too rapid? - Is next sodium check ordered? - Is 23.4% NaCl being given via appropriate access/policy?

1. Recognize hypertensive flash pulmonary edema: severe distress, diaphoresis, rales, SBP often >180. 2. Sit upright and apply NIV immediately. 3. Check nitrate contraindications: hypotension, RV infarct, recent PDE-5 inhibitor, severe AS/HOCM. 4. Start high-dose Nitroglycerin: IV push 400-800 mcg q2-5 min by protocol and/or infusion 100-200 mcg/min rapidly titrated. 5. Reassess BP, work of breathing, oxygenation every few minutes. 6. Add diuretics after stabilization when volume overload is likely. 7. Evaluate trigger: ACS, renal failure, valve catastrophe, dysrhythmia, medication nonadherence, severe hypertension.

- SL nitroglycerin 0.4 mg q5 min while IV is prepared if patient can tolerate - IV push by protocol: 400-800 mcg every 2-5 min in severe hypertensive SCAPE - Infusion: start 100-200 mcg/min and rapidly titrate every 3-5 min; severe cases may need 300-800 mcg/min initially - Reduce once work of breathing improves and SBP approaches 140-160

- SBP low or rapidly falling - RV infarct/preload-dependent shock likely - Sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 hr or tadalafil within 48 hr - Severe aortic stenosis or obstructive HCM with instability - Raised ICP concern where nitrate is unsafe

- Apply CPAP/BiPAP immediately with high EPAP/PEEP as tolerated - Improve oxygenation and reduce preload/afterload through positive pressure - Do not delay NIV for IV access, labs, or imaging - Prepare intubation only if NIV/medical therapy fails or airway/mental status deteriorates
Nitroprusside is not the usual ED first-line SCAPE medication. Use NIV plus high-dose nitroglycerin for the classic hypertensive crashing phenotype.

Nitroprusside usually requires ICU-level monitoring and has cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity concerns. Avoid/caution in renal or hepatic failure, raised ICP, pregnancy, and settings without close invasive BP/toxicity monitoring.

1. Choose indication first: stroke, STEMI, massive PE/PE arrest, or specialist-directed reduced-dose/catheter strategy. 2. Screen contraindications using the indication-specific framework. 3. Confirm drug, exact dose, weight, time window, BP target, and antithrombotic plan. 4. Treat BP before stroke lytic if >185/110. 5. Coordinate heparin hold/restart for PE/STEMI protocols. 6. Monitor in ICU/stroke/cath-capable setting. 7. Have bleeding plan: stop lytic/anticoagulants, check fibrinogen, replace fibrinogen, consider antifibrinolytic with specialist input.

- Disabling deficit within treatment window - CT excludes hemorrhage - BP <185/110 before treatment and <180/105 for 24 hr after - No antithrombotics for 24 hr after IV lytic unless specialist-directed
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, max 25 mg, where adopted by protocol. Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV, max 90 mg; 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min.
Eligible STEMI/STEMI-equivalent, symptoms generally <=12 hr, and timely PCI cannot be achieved, commonly FMC-to-device >120 min.
Tenecteplase weight-based IV bolus; reduce by 50% if age >=75 per many protocols. Arrange transfer for rescue PCI if failed reperfusion or pharmaco-invasive PCI even if reperfusion succeeds.
Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hr. Hold/restart UFH per protocol; many protocols restart without bolus when aPTT/anti-Xa permits.
Alteplase 50 mg IV push during arrest; consider repeat 50 mg if no ROSC and PE remains likely per local protocol. Continue prolonged CPR when feasible and activate ECMO/PERT/thrombectomy pathway.

Not automatic systemic lysis. Use anticoagulation unless deterioration or specialist-directed catheter/reduced-dose strategy. Half-Dose Alteplase Calculator supports intentional reduced-dose protocols.

1. Stop thrombolytic and anticoagulants. 2. Activate critical bleeding/MTP if unstable. 3. Check CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, type/cross. 4. Replace fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate per protocol. 5. Consider TXA or aminocaproic acid with specialist input. 6. Repeat neuroimaging for neurologic deterioration after stroke lytic. 7. Involve pharmacy, hematology, and indication-specific team.

1. Confirm the indication and target: pH, potassium, urine pH, QRS width, or bridge to dialysis. 2. Stop if this is routine arrest, primary respiratory acidosis, routine DKA, or unclear lactic acidosis without severe acidemia/AKI. 3. Standard recipe: 150 mEq sodium bicarbonate in 1 L D5W or sterile water per pharmacy policy. 4. Choose rate by indication: 100-250 mL/hr for maintenance/metabolic acidosis, 500-1000 mL/hr if using as resuscitative fluid in acidotic hyperkalemia, 150-250 mL/hr for salicylate/TCA targets. 5. Monitor pH, Na, K, ionized Ca, creatinine, volume status, and ECG when high risk. 6. Ensure ventilation can clear the generated CO2. 7. Stop or slow when target reached, adver

- Severe metabolic acidemia, especially pH <=7.20 with moderate-severe AKI or bicarbonate-loss/NAGMA physiology - Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis when isotonic bicarbonate can be used as resuscitative fluid - Salicylate toxicity requiring serum/urine alkalinization - TCA or sodium-channel blocker toxicity after boluses, when QRS/pH targets need maintenance infusion - Toxic alcohol acidosis as a bridge while antidote and dialysis are arranged

- Routine cardiac arrest/CPR without hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker toxicity - Primary respiratory acidosis; ventilate instead - Routine lactic acidosis without severe acidemia/AKI - Routine DKA; consider only for extreme acidemia per DKA protocol - Metabolic alkalosis, severe hypernatremia, or uncontrolled volume overload
Sodium bicarbonate 150 mEq in 1 L D5W or sterile water per local pharmacy policy. This is typically made from three 50 mEq ampules of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate.

- Severe metabolic acidosis/AKI: 100-250 mL/hr, titrate to pH and sodium/volume status - Acidotic hyperkalemia with hypovolemia: 500-1000 mL/hr as resuscitative fluid when appropriate - Salicylate toxicity: 150-250 mL/hr, titrate to serum and urine pH - TCA/sodium-channel blocker: 150-250 mL/hr after boluses, titrate to QRS and pH

Use a pump, label the line clearly, and track total sodium/bicarbonate delivered. Central access is preferred for repeated hypertonic ampules or concentrated preparations; peripheral isotonic bicarbonate is commonly used when local policy allows.

- Bolus sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg when severe toxicity, acidemia, altered mental status, or before unavoidable intubation - Infusion: 150 mEq in 1 L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr - Add KCl 20-40 mEq/L unless contraindicated - Targets: serum pH 7.45-7.55, urine pH 7.5-8.0, avoid serum pH >7.60 - Failure to alkalinize, severe toxicity, or clinical deterioration should trigger hemodialysis planning

- Bolus sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg first; repeat q3-5 min until QRS narrows or pH target reached - Infusion: 150 mEq in 1 L D5W at 150-250 mL/hr - Targets: QRS <100 ms when feasible and serum pH 7.50-7.55 - Avoid class IA/IC antiarrhythmics; treat seizures with benzodiazepines

- No clear target exists - Routine arrest/CPR without hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker toxicity - Primary respiratory acidosis; ventilation is the treatment - Routine DKA without extreme acidemia - Severe hypernatremia, metabolic alkalosis, uncontrolled pulmonary edema, or symptomatic hypocalcemia - Patient cannot ventilate generated CO2 and ventilation is not being corrected - Dialysis/source control is being delayed because bicarbonate is temporarily improving pH

- Target pH/urine pH/QRS/potassium endpoint is reached - Na is rising too fast or hypernatremia develops - Ionized calcium or potassium falls dangerously - Pulmonary edema or volume overload develops - Definitive therapy such as dialysis has started and specialist team directs transition

1. PPE, expose the access, identify exact bleeding point. 2. Apply one-finger/thumb focal pressure directly over the hole with folded gauze or hemostatic gauze. 3. Hold uninterrupted pressure for 10-20 min; do not repeatedly peek. 4. If brisk bleeding, shock, syncope, or recurrent spontaneous bleed: call vascular surgery/IR, nephrology, and blood bank early. 5. IV/IO access away from fistula/graft arm; type/cross, CBC, BMP/K, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen. 6. Activate MTP if shock or ongoing major hemorrhage. 7. If pressure fails or cannot be maintained: tourniquet/BP cuff bridge to definitive vascular control.

- Confirm thrill/bruit and distal perfusion - Look for scab, ulcer, shiny/non-pinchable skin, aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm, exposed graft, infection, or expanding hematoma - Review last dialysis, dialysis heparin, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, missed dialysis, and hyperkalemia risk - Do not discharge spontaneous, recurrent, aneurysmal, infected, ulcerated, or tourniquet-controlled bleeding without urgent access evaluation

- Use a single finger/thumb, folded gauze, hemostatic gauze, or hard focal pressure device directly over the bleeding hole - Pressure must be narrow and precise; broad bulky wraps often fail by distributing pressure away from the defect - Hold 10-20 min without interruption - Elevate the arm if feasible - Avoid circumferential tight wraps that obscure rebleeding or thrombose the access - Recheck thrill/bruit and hand perfusion after control

- Add chitosan/kaolin/oxidized cellulose/gelatin-thrombin dressing per local stock - Consider topical tranexamic acid 500-1000 mg on gauze with focal pressure - If a single superficial puncture hole persists and vascular support is not immediately available, consider superficial figure-of-eight or purse-string suture around the skin puncture only - Avoid deep bites into the fistula or graft

- Brisk hemorrhage with shock or impending shock - Spurting/pulsatile bleeding not immediately controlled by focal pressure - Bleeding cannot be controlled while moving the patient, placing access, activating MTP, or preparing definitive control - Focal pressure requires hands that must be freed for airway/resuscitation This is a bridge to vascular surgery/IR/OR. Document application time.

- Commercial tourniquet: place proximal enough to stop inflow when bleeding is life-threatening - BP cuff: inflate above systolic pressure and titrate to hemostasis - Reassess every few minutes and transition to focal pressure/vascular control as soon as feasible - If loosened and bleeding remains controlled, check thrill/bruit, distal pulse/capillary refill, motor/sensation Do not use for routine post-dialysis oozing. Risks include access thrombosis/loss, limb ischemia, nerve injury, and rebleeding when released.

- Tranexamic Acid topical 500-1000 mg on gauze/pledget with focal pressure 10-20 min - Hemostatic dressing if available: chitosan, kaolin, oxidized cellulose, gelatin/thrombin, or local protocol product - IV TXA 1 g over 10 min only for major hemorrhage after weighing thrombosis/seizure risk and renal failure dosing issues

- Desmopressin 0.3-0.4 mcg/kg IV over 20-30 min for suspected uremic platelet dysfunction, antiplatelet-associated major bleeding, or refractory diffuse oozing; monitor sodium and restrict free water - Protamine if recent UFH/dialysis heparin is contributing to major bleeding: 1 mg per 100 units UFH in prior 2-3 hr, max 50 mg, slow IV - Warfarin life-threatening bleed: 4F-PCC + Vitamin K - Dabigatran: Idarucizumab; dialysis can remove dabigatran if needed - Xa inhibitors: 4F-PCC per local protocol (andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US)

info.h: Admit, transfer, or urgent vascular/IR evaluation
info.t: - Any spontaneous bleeding between dialysis sessions - Recurrent or prolonged bleeding after dialysis - Tourniquet/BP cuff used - Shock, syncope, transfusion, MTP, significant hemoglobin drop - Scab, ulcer, necrosis, shiny/non-pinchable skin, aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm - Infection, drainage, exposed graft, expanding hematoma - Anticoagulant reversal required or supratherapeutic anticoagulation - No reliable urgent dialysis access follow-up

info.h: Discharge only if all low-risk features are met
info.t: - Simple needle puncture bleed - Hemostasis durable after observation - Stable vitals and acceptable hemoglobin context - Thrill/bruit present, hand perfusion intact - No high-risk skin/access lesion, infection, expanding hematoma, or recurrent bleeding - Dialysis unit/nephrology follow-up arranged and access restrictions communicated

- Do not place broad bulky wraps that hide ongoing hemorrhage - Do not delay vascular/IR activation for spontaneous, recurrent, aneurysmal, infected, or uncontrolled access bleeding - Do not preserve the fistula at the expense of patient survival; use tourniquet/BP cuff for life-threatening uncontrolled bleeding - Do not discharge a scab, ulcer, shiny/non-pinchable skin, exposed graft, or pseudoaneurysm after temporary hemostasis - Do not use the access arm for routine BP, venipuncture, or IV access - Do not deeply suture into the fistula/graft; superficial skin closure only if localized puncture bleeding and access remains patent

1. Identify high-risk substrate: prosthetic valve, prior IE, CIED/VAD, hemodialysis, IVDU, indwelling catheter, congenital heart disease, immunocompromise. 2. Look for IE syndrome: fever/bacteremia, new murmur, heart failure, stroke/ICH, septic pulmonary emboli, splenic/renal infarct, back pain, GN, persistent S. aureus bacteremia. 3. Draw 2-3 blood culture sets before antibiotics if feasible; do not delay antibiotics in shock. 4. Order TTE and plan TEE when high suspicion, prosthetic/device disease, S. aureus bacteremia, poor TTE, or complication concern. 5. Start empiric therapy immediately if unstable; narrow after organism/susceptibility. 6. Call ID + cardiology early; add CT surgery for

Most suspected IE patients require admission. ICU/transfer when shock, acute valve failure, new conduction disease, neuro complication, prosthetic/device infection, persistent bacteremia, dialysis/IVDU with septic emboli, or need for urgent surgery.

- Draw at least 2 sets, preferably 3 sets when IE is suspected - Separate peripheral venipunctures when feasible - Do not wait for fever spikes - Do not underfill bottles; volume is a major yield driver - If unstable, draw cultures immediately but start antibiotics without waiting for ideal timing

- Repeat cultures q24-48h until clearance - Persistent positive cultures should trigger source-control reassessment, TEE/advanced imaging, and CT surgery/device team consideration - S. aureus, enterococcus, Candida, prosthetic/device infection, and dialysis/IVDU presentations deserve a high threshold for persistent-source evaluation

- Large mobile valve-attached mass - New severe regurgitation or gross valve destruction - Tricuspid vegetation with septic pulmonary emboli pattern - Pericardial effusion, RV strain, or heart-failure physiology - Clues to periannular abscess: new conduction abnormality, periannular thickening/cavity/dehiscence on formal imaging

- PLAX and PSAX: aortic and mitral valve assessment - Apical 4/5 chamber: mitral, tricuspid, aortic outflow; add color Doppler - Subxiphoid: alternative window and pericardial effusion - Compare against prior echo when available

POCUS/TTE cannot rule out IE. Small vegetations, prosthetic valves, aortic root abscess, and CIED infection often require TEE and/or cardiac CT/PET. Do not delay cultures, antibiotics for unstable patients, or formal echo because bedside ultrasound is pending.

- Stable suspected IE: cultures first; discuss antibiotic timing with ID when feasible - Unstable/septic or healthcare-associated native-valve concern: Vancomycin + Cefepime pending cultures and local antibiogram - Prosthetic/device disease: broader specialist-driven coverage; involve ID/cardiology early - Adjust for renal function, allergy, local resistance, and previous cultures

- MSSA: Nafcillin or cefazolin when appropriate - MRSA: vancomycin AUC-guided or Daptomycin when appropriate - Viridans strep / HACEK: Ceftriaxone or penicillin-based therapy depending on susceptibility - E. faecalis: Ampicillin + Ceftriaxone when susceptible and appropriate - Culture-negative: ID/microbiology-directed testing before indefinite broadening

- Do not add gentamicin automatically; synergy has nephrotoxicity and narrow indications - Do not start rifampin indiscriminately; in prosthetic staphylococcal IE it is an adjunct after bacteremia is controlled and organism is known - Do not use oral outpatient plans for unstable, complicated, uncontrolled, or early-phase IE without specialist plan

- Acute heart failure from severe valve regurgitation or obstruction - Periannular abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, prosthetic dehiscence, or new AV block - Persistent bacteremia/fever despite appropriate therapy and source control - Fungal IE, Candida IE, resistant organisms, or uncontrolled infection - Recurrent emboli or large mobile vegetation, especially after embolic event - Prosthetic valve IE with complication - CIED endocarditis: device/lead extraction planning is usually required

Consult for persistent bacteremia, large vegetations with recurrent septic pulmonary emboli, severe TR/right-heart failure, fungal infection, or failure of medical therapy. Coordinate catheter/access source control in hemodialysis and IVDU presentations.

- Do not dismiss S. aureus bacteremia as contamination - Do not discharge high-suspicion IE after a negative TTE; obtain TEE/repeat imaging plan - Do not delay antibiotics in shock for ideal culture timing - Do not give thrombolytics for presumed ischemic stroke when IE is suspected - Do not anticoagulate solely for IE; evaluate separate indications and neuro bleeding risk - Do not ignore new AV block/PR prolongation; suspect periannular abscess - Do not treat prosthetic/device IE without source-control planning - Do not use POCUS as a rule-out test

1. Identify instability: altered mental status, Cushing response, irregular respirations, acute neurologic deficit, status epilepticus, severe dehydration from emesis, or unstable vitals. 2. Move unstable patient to resuscitation space, place monitors, obtain IV access, keep NPO, elevate HOB 30 degrees, keep head midline. 3. Call neurosurgery early for suspected malfunction, infection, or high-risk symptoms; do not wait for imaging if herniation physiology is present. 4. Treat impending herniation with airway support and hyperosmolar therapy per local protocol. 5. Obtain focused history: shunt type/date/revisions, last surgery, baseline neuro status, prior malfunction symptoms, fever, abdomi

1. Stable child: rapid/limited brain MRI without sedation if available in a useful time frame. 2. Unstable child or MRI delay: noncontrast head CT now. 3. Compare ventricular size and catheter position with prior imaging whenever possible. 4. Shunt series complements CT/MRI for fracture, disconnection, kinking, migration, and valve setting; it is not a stand-alone rule-out test. 5. Abdominal symptoms or suspected infection: evaluate for distal catheter complication, pseudocyst, loculated CSF, abscess, or peritonitis.

Admission or transfer is typical when malfunction, infection, neurologic abnormality, persistent symptoms, abnormal imaging, concerning caregiver history, or need for neurosurgery evaluation persists. Discharge should be rare and generally requires neurosurgery agreement, reassuring serial exam, clear alternative diagnosis, and reliable return precautions.

- Proximal catheter obstruction: headache, vomiting, lethargy, papilledema, rising ICP; shunt may refill slowly or appear normal. - Distal obstruction: abdominal pain/distension, catheter tip problem, pseudocyst, poor drainage. - Valve failure or programmable valve issue: recurrent underdrainage or overdrainage symptoms; check valve setting on shunt series when relevant. - Fracture/disconnection/kinking/migration: best seen on shunt series, but normal series does not rule out malfunction.

- Highest concern after recent placement or revision, but late infection occurs. - Fever may be absent; infection may present as malfunction alone. - Look for wound erythema, swelling, drainage, CSF leak, skin breakdown, abdominal tenderness, meningismus, or altered mental status. - Workup: CBC, CRP, blood cultures, source search, and neurosurgery discussion of shunt tap/CSF studies and antibiotics.

- Orthostatic headache, nausea, lethargy, slit ventricles, subdural hygroma/hematoma, or cranial nerve symptoms. - CT/MRI may show small ventricles rather than enlarged ventricles. - Requires neurosurgery; avoid assuming small ventricles means "no shunt problem."

- Abdominal pseudocyst, peritonitis, abscess, bowel perforation, catheter migration, hydrocele/scrotal migration, pleural migration/hydrothorax. - Use abdominal ultrasound or CT when abdominal pain, distension, fever, tenderness, or unexplained malfunction is present. - Distal complications can coexist with CNS symptoms from impaired drainage.

- Any exposed tubing, skin erosion, wound breakdown, cellulitis over the tract, or CSF leak is high-risk. - Cover sterile, do not manipulate aggressively, keep NPO, obtain cultures as indicated, and call neurosurgery urgently.

- Stable child: rapid/limited brain MRI without sedation when available promptly. - Unstable child, altered mental status, herniation signs, status epilepticus, or MRI delay: noncontrast head CT. - Always compare to prior imaging if available; baseline ventricular caliber matters. - Do not rule out malfunction solely because ventricles are unchanged.

- Skull/neck/chest/abdomen radiographs can show discontinuity, fracture, disconnection, kinking, migration, and valve setting. - A positive shunt series is highly actionable. - A negative shunt series is not reassuring enough to stop evaluation when symptoms fit malfunction.

- Adjunct for elevated ICP, not a rule-out test for shunt malfunction. - Measure both eyes, 3 mm posterior to the globe, using a high-frequency linear probe. - Interpretation is age/protocol dependent; use local thresholds when available. - Abnormal ONSD should increase urgency, but normal ONSD does not clear the shunt.

- Use when abdominal pain, tenderness, distension, fever, distal catheter concern, or unexplained malfunction is present. - Looks for pseudocyst, loculated CSF, abscess, ascites, catheter tip collection, or other abdominal source. - IDSA recommends abdominal ultrasound or CT for infected VP shunts with abdominal symptoms.

- Fever within months of placement/revision, or fever plus shunt symptoms - Redness, swelling, drainage, CSF leak, skin breakdown, or tenderness over shunt tract - Abdominal pain/tenderness with VP shunt - Meningismus, altered mental status, seizure, or persistent vomiting - Malfunction symptoms without a clear mechanical cause

- CBC, BMP, CRP, blood cultures, and focused source evaluation - UA/urine culture, CXR, viral testing, or other testing only when clinically indicated - Neurosurgery discussion for imaging, shunt tap, and timing of antibiotics - If septic/unstable: draw cultures immediately and start empiric therapy without delay

IDSA empiric regimen for healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis: Vancomycin plus an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: Cefepime, ceftazidime, or Meropenem. Adjust to local antibiogram, renal function, allergy, prior cultures, and severity.

Suspected shunt hardware infection usually requires neurosurgery-directed externalization/removal, temporary CSF diversion, culture-directed antibiotics, and delayed reimplantation after CSF sterilization. Antibiotics alone are often inadequate when biofilm/hardware infection is present.

- Depressed or rapidly declining mental status - Bradycardia + hypertension + irregular respirations - Pupillary asymmetry/dilation, posturing, seizure, or acute focal deficit - Persistent vomiting with severe headache/lethargy in a shunted child - Any concerning trajectory despite unchanged imaging

- Call neurosurgery stat - HOB 30 degrees, head midline, loosen tight collar/tape around neck - Oxygenate; avoid hypoxia and hypotension - Intubate if GCS <8, airway failure, or unsafe transport/imaging - Brief hyperventilation only as a temporizing bridge for active herniation physiology

- Hypertonic saline 3%: 2-5 mL/kg IV bolus over 10-20 min per local neurocritical protocol - 23.4% NaCl: specialist/protocol-directed rescue, typically central line preferred - Mannitol: 0.25-1 g/kg IV when appropriate and hemodynamics/renal status allow - Monitor sodium, osmolality, renal function, hemodynamics, and neuro response
ICP treatment is a bridge. Definitive management is neurosurgery: shunt revision, shunt tap/externalization, EVD, or operative source control depending on malfunction/infection and local capability.

- Suspected infection when CSF is needed and neurosurgery agrees - Suspected obstruction requiring direct pressure assessment - Peri-arrest/impending herniation when neurosurgery is unavailable and ED shunt tap is within local scope/policy - Need for emergent decompression in a crashing shunted patient without immediate operative/EVD access

Prefer neurosurgery. ED clinician-performed shunt tap should be rare, reserved for immediate life threat or institutional protocol, and done with sterile technique after reviewing shunt anatomy/location.

- Sterile prep, mask, sterile gloves, chlorhexidine if appropriate for age/site - Use small-gauge needle into reservoir only; avoid tubing puncture - Do not repeatedly needle or aggressively pump the reservoir - Measure pressure if setup allows, withdraw only needed volume unless decompression is explicitly intended - Stop for resistance, unexpected bleeding, or inability to identify reservoir

- Cell count/differential - Glucose and protein - Gram stain and bacterial culture; hold culture long enough for slow-growing organisms when suspected - Consider PCR/meningitis panel only as adjunct based on local lab and ID/neurosurgery input - Interpret CSF with caution; negative reservoir CSF does not fully exclude hardware infection

- Do not discharge a concerning shunted child solely because CT/MRI/shunt series/ONSD is normal - Do not ignore caregiver report that symptoms match prior malfunction - Do not delay neurosurgery consultation for herniation physiology, persistent vomiting/lethargy, new seizure, focal deficit, or abnormal vital signs - Do not use shunt reservoir pumping as a rule-out test - Do not treat suspected shunt infection with antibiotics alone without source-control discussion - Do not forget abdominal ultrasound/CT when abdominal pain, tenderness, fever, or distal catheter concern is present - Do not perform shunt tap casually; reserve for neurosurgery or true emergency/local protocol - Do not send an

1. Safety: remove hazards, call adequate staff/security, one calm lead communicator. 2. Rapid medical checks: glucose, SpO2, temperature, vitals, obvious trauma/pain, medication exposure. 3. De-escalate/environment: quiet room, family/caregiver, hearing aids/glasses, food/water/toileting. 4. If immediate danger blocks care: use the lowest effective rescue medication and/or restraint per policy. 5. Obtain collateral baseline; acute/fluctuating change is delirium until proven otherwise.

1. Treat reversible drivers: pain, urinary retention, constipation, infection, metabolic disorder, intoxication/withdrawal, trauma/subdural, hypoxia. 2. Assess decision-specific capacity for the current decision. 3. If lacks capacity: use emergency consent for immediate threats or Texas surrogate pathway for ongoing medical care. 4. Use Texas Chapter 573 emergency detention only when qualifying mental illness plus danger criteria are met; dementia alone is excluded from the statutory mental illness definition. 5. Choose disposition based on medical trigger, capacity, surrogate/caregiver reliability, restraint/medication needs, and safe supervision.

- Pain: fall/fracture, wound, dental, arthritis, abdominal pathology, pressure injury - Urinary retention: bladder scan early; decompression can resolve agitation - Constipation/fecal impaction - Hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypoglycemia, fever, dehydration - Infection: pneumonia, UTI with symptoms/systemic illness, cellulitis, sepsis - Metabolic: sodium, calcium, renal/uremic, hepatic, thyroid, glucose - Medication: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, opioids, steroids, fluoroquinolones, dopamine agonists, polypharmacy - Withdrawal: alcohol, benzodiazepines, sedatives - Neurologic: fall/subdural, seizure/NCSE, stroke/ICH, meningitis/encephalitis

- What is baseline cognition, mobility, speech, sleep, and behavior? - When did this start, and is it fluctuating? - What calms the patient normally? - Any new meds, missed meds, alcohol/sedative exposure, missed dialysis, fall, poor intake, urinary symptoms, constipation, or caregiver stress? - Is the home/facility still safe?

- Nonpharmacologic management first when safe - Medication is justified when the patient is dangerous, severely distressed, or agitation blocks urgent evaluation/treatment - Use the lowest effective dose; reassess before repeating - Antipsychotics carry increased mortality warnings in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis - Avoid routine benzodiazepines in dementia/delirium unless withdrawal, seizure, catatonia, severe stimulant toxicity, or a specific severe anxiety indication is present

- Quetiapine: 12.5-25 mg PO; useful when Parkinson/Lewy body concern or mild-moderate agitation and patient can take PO - Risperidone: 0.25-0.5 mg PO/ODT; avoid Parkinson/Lewy body concern - Olanzapine: 2.5-5 mg PO/ODT/IM; do not combine closely with parenteral benzodiazepines - Haloperidol: 0.5-1 mg IM/IV; avoid or use extreme caution with Parkinson/Lewy body dementia, prolonged QTc, severe EPS history

Brexpiprazole and dextromethorphan/bupropion have FDA approvals for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer disease. These are outpatient/chronic-management options, not ED rescue sedatives, and require medication reconciliation, adverse-effect screening, and follow-up planning.

info.pt: Texas Law: Dementia vs Mental Health Detention
info.t: Texas Health & Safety Code Sec. 571.003 defines mental illness as a condition other than epilepsy, dementia, substance abuse, or intellectual disability that substantially impairs thought/perception/emotional process/judgment or grossly impairs behavior. Implication: dementia or neurodegenerative disease alone generally does not satisfy the Texas mental-health emergency detention definition.

info.pt: Texas Law: Dementia vs Mental Health Detention
info.t: A peace officer may apprehend without warrant when there is reason to believe the person has mental illness, because of that mental illness there is substantial risk of serious harm to self or others unless immediately restrained, and there is not sufficient time to obtain a warrant. Use this pathway only when the patient has a qualifying mental illness plus danger because of that illness. Dementia plus separate psychosis/mania/severe depression may qualify if criteria are met; dementia/delirium/medical incapacity alone belongs on the medical pathway.

info.pt: Texas Law: Dementia vs Mental Health Detention
info.t: If the patient lacks capacity for medical decisions and there is no guardian or available medical POA, Texas Chapter 313 allows adult surrogate consent for hospital patients in priority order: spouse, adult children, parents, nearest living relative. If no listed surrogate is reasonably available, another physician not involved in treatment may concur with treatment. Chapter 313 surrogate consent does not authorize voluntary inpatient mental health services or ECT.

- Understanding: can the patient explain condition, recommendation, risks, benefits, alternatives? - Appreciation: can the patient apply consequences to self? - Reasoning: can the patient compare options in a coherent way? - Communication: can the patient state a stable choice? Dementia, agitation, poor judgment, or disagreement with the physician does not automatically remove capacity. Acute delirium, psychosis, intoxication, severe pain, or inability to appreciate consequences may remove capacity for a specific decision.

- Specific decision assessed: leaving, refusing CT/admission, accepting medication, transfer, discharge plan - Patient responses for each ability - Why the deficit is decision-relevant, if capacity is absent - Whether the decision can wait for reversible causes to improve - Surrogate/guardian/POA contacted and their decision - Emergency consent rationale if treatment cannot wait

- Autonomy: respect capable refusal, even if high risk - Beneficence/nonmaleficence: treat reversible suffering and prevent foreseeable harm when capacity is absent - Least restrictive care: family, sitter, environmental control, and redirection before restraint when safe - Proportionality: higher-risk coercion requires higher-risk clinical threat and better documentation - Justice: do not offload medical dementia/delirium patients to psychiatric detention when legal criteria are not met

- No valid decision-maker and patient lacks capacity - Unsafe home/facility, caregiver exhaustion, abandonment, suspected abuse/neglect/exploitation - Recurrent violent/elopement behavior without supervision - Medication/restraint required and needs monitoring - Delirium or medical trigger not resolved Use social work/case management, APS when indicated, ethics consult, legal/risk, and guardianship pathway when ongoing incapacity blocks safe care.

- Do not default dementia agitation to psychiatric detention; Texas mental illness definition excludes dementia - Do not ignore delirium/medical triggers: pain, retention, constipation, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, infection, medication toxicity, withdrawal, trauma/subdural - Do not assume dementia removes capacity; assess the specific decision now - Do not discharge an incapacitated patient to an unsafe environment without surrogate/safe supervision plan - Do not use antipsychotics as convenience sedation; reserve for danger, severe distress, or blocked essential care - Do not use benzodiazepines routinely in dementia/delirium unless withdrawal, seizure, catatonia, stimulant toxicity, or specific

• Diagnose with 2 of 3: epigastric pain, lipase >3× ULN, imaging • Atlanta Classification: mild (no OF), moderate (OF <48h), severe (OF >48h) • BISAP ≥3 within 24h = 12-30% mortality; Modified Marshall for OF

• LR preferred over NS — goal 3-4 L/24h, NOT aggressive • Moderate: 10 mL/kg over 2h if hypovolemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/hr • Monitoring: UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr, decreasing BUN, Hct <44% • Early oral feeding within 24-48h; opioids safe for pain

• All patients: RUQ US, triglycerides, LFTs • Gallstone (40-70%) — assess for cholangitis • Cholangitis → urgent ERCP <24h; no cholangitis → no routine ERCP • Mild AP + gallstones → same-admission cholecystectomy • Alcoholic → thiamine before glucose, watch for withdrawal • HTG (TG >1000) → insulin infusion, target <500, apheresis if >2000

• Image only if no improvement at 48-72h or deterioration • Pseudocyst: observe most — size alone NOT indication for drainage • Sterile necrosis — NO prophylactic antibiotics • Suspect infected necrosis: gas on CT, PCT >3.5, fever, deterioration

• Life-threatening — antibiotics with pancreatic penetration: pip-tazo, carbapenems, FQ+metronidazole • Step-up: delay + abx → drain → minimally invasive → open necrosectomy • If improving on antibiotics: continue, reassess • Stable not improving: PCD or EUS-guided ETD >4 weeks from onset • Urgent drainage if unstable, multiorgan failure, ACS

• Mild: discharge when PO tolerant, pain controlled, labs improving • Gallstone: schedule cholecystectomy same admission or within 2 weeks • Complicated: ICU for persistent OF or infected necrosis; multidisciplinary team

Triad: Severe abdominal pain + Minimal exam findings + Vascular risk factors • Pain out of proportion to exam (visceral innervation only) • Gut emptying (vomiting, diarrhea) — ischemic gut purges • AFib (most common embolic source) • Age >60 with atherosclerosis, CHF, recent MI

• Lactate: Elevated = already necrotic bowel — do not wait for this • CBC: Leukocytosis common, hemoconcentration • BMP: Metabolic acidosis, elevated BUN • D-dimer: Sensitive but nonspecific • LDH/amylase: May be elevated but not diagnostic

• CTA abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast — first-line imaging • Sensitivity >95% for SMA/SMV occlusion • Shows: vessel cutoff, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, portal venous gas • Plain films: Insensitive — only show late findings (thumbprinting, pneumatosis)

• NPO — gut rest • Crystalloid resuscitation — correct hypovolemia before pressors • NG tube if distended • Antibiotics: Pip-tazo 4.5g IV or meropenem 1g IV (translocation risk) • Anticoagulation: Heparin bolus 80 U/kg, drip 18 U/kg/hr (arterial AMI)

• SMA Embolism (40-50%): Heparin + emergent embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis • SMA Thrombosis: Heparin + surgical revascularization (bypass) • MVT: Heparin (may avoid surgery if no peritonitis) • NOMI: Treat underlying cause, optimize CO, papaverine infusion if available

Immediate surgical exploration if: • Peritoneal signs • Pneumatosis or portal venous gas on imaging • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation • Frank bowel necrosis on imaging Time is bowel — every hour of delay = more necrotic bowel = higher mortality

info.h: The 11 A's of Mesenteric Ischemia Risk
info.t: Atrial fibrillation (most common embolic source) Atherosclerosis (aortic, mesenteric vessels) Age >60 Acute MI (recent — source of mural thrombus) Aortic aneurysm/dissection Aortic surgery (recent) Abdominal surgery (recent) Arrhythmias (other than AFib) Angiography (recent — catheter-related embolism) Arterial procedures (recent) Adhesions (postoperative — can cause mechanical obstruction + ischemia)
Patients with 3+ of these factors presenting with acute abdominal pain should be presumed to have mesenteric ischemia until CTA proves otherwise. Do NOT wait for lactate or peritoneal signs.

• SMA occlusion/thrombosis — filling defect or cutoff • SMV thrombosis — filling defect, enlarged vein with rim enhancement • Aortic atherosclerosis — calcified plaques at vessel origins • Mesenteric artery stenosis — narrowing >50% at origin

• Wall thickening (>3mm) — early finding • Hypoenhancement — reduced contrast uptake = ischemia • Hyperenhancement — reperfusion injury or early ischemia • Paper-thin wall — late finding, transmural necrosis • Lack of enhancement — infarcted bowel
• Mesenteric fat stranding — inflammation around vessels • Mesenteric haziness — fluid/edema in mesentery • Engorgement of mesenteric veins — venous congestion

• Pneumatosis intestinalis — gas in bowel wall = necrosis • Portal venous gas — gas in portal system = advanced necrosis • Free air — perforation • Ascites — third-spacing from ischemia ⚠️ Pneumatosis + portal venous gas = near-certain mortality if not immediately explored
Use when the key question is whether the patient understands and appreciates the illness driving the specific decision. Capacity is decision-specific, not a global legal competency ruling.

Illness / problem: "What illness or medical problem do you think you have?" Concern: "What are we worried could happen?" Recommendation: "What treatment or test are we recommending?" Refusal consequence: "What could happen if you decline?" Personal application: "How do those risks apply to you personally?"

• Can repeat the diagnosis but denies it applies to them • Explains risks in general terms but not personal consequences • Decision is driven by delusion, hallucination, or fixed false belief • Reasoning changes dramatically across repeated questioning Example: "I know you say I have sepsis, but I am not sick and nothing bad can happen to me." That may be an appreciation deficit, not just disagreement.

May use MacCAT-T (MacArthur Competence Assessment Tool for Treatment) when the case is borderline, high-stakes, psychiatric, contested, or medicolegally complex. It structures the same core domains: understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expressing a choice. It supports clinical judgment but does not replace the treating physician's capacity determination.
For the full four-abilities framework, use 4 Abilities. For structured questions, use Assessment Questions. For charting language, use Documentation.

• Urea breath test • Stool antigen test • Biopsy-based test if EGD is already being performed Serology is generally a poor ED/outpatient decision test because antibodies may persist after old infection. It also cannot prove eradication.
To reduce false negatives: • Hold PPI or PCAB for 2 weeks • Hold antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks • H2 blockers and antacids can be used as a bridge if symptoms require acid suppression

info.h: When EGD Is the Right Test
info.t: Use an endoscopy lane for GI bleeding, gastric ulcer complication, alarm-feature dyspepsia, malignancy concern, or repeated treatment failure where culture/molecular susceptibility may change the salvage regimen.

Optimized bismuth quadruple therapy x14 days: • PPI standard dose BID • Bismuth subcitrate 120-300 mg QID OR bismuth subsalicylate 300-524 mg QID • Tetracycline 500 mg QID • Metronidazole 500 mg TID or QID Use this when H. pylori is confirmed and susceptibility is unknown, unless contraindications or local GI guidance point elsewhere.

• Vonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1000 mg TID x14 days • Rifabutin 50 mg TID + amoxicillin 1000 mg TID + omeprazole 40 mg TID x14 days • Clarithromycin-containing therapy only when clarithromycin susceptibility is documented • Levofloxacin-containing therapy only when levofloxacin susceptibility is documented

• Adherence matters more than elegance; BQT has a high pill burden • Bismuth can darken stool/tongue • Avoid alcohol with metronidazole • Tetracycline is not appropriate in pregnancy • Always pair treatment with a test-of-cure plan

info.h: First Confirm It Is Real Failure
info.t: • Was the cure test done >=4 weeks after antibiotics? • Was the patient off PPI/PCAB x2 weeks? • Was the patient off bismuth/antibiotics x4 weeks? • Was the test stool antigen, urea breath, or biopsy-based? • Did the patient complete the regimen?

info.h: Do Not Reuse Failed Antibiotics Blindly
info.t: Avoid repeating clarithromycin, levofloxacin, rifabutin, metronidazole, or tetracycline exposure unless susceptibility data or specialist guidance supports it. Clarithromycin and levofloxacin regimens should be susceptibility-guided.

Multiple failures, unclear prior regimen, significant allergy constraints, gastric ulcer complications, or ongoing alarm features should go to GI for culture or molecular susceptibility testing when available.

Erythema and swelling localized to the nail fold, often with fluctuance or visible pus tracking under the cuticle. Most commonly Staph aureus. *Photo displayed inline on the acute paronychia drainage node.*
Multiple digits, absent cuticle, boggy non-tender fold, frequent water exposure. Inflammatory not infectious. *Photo displayed inline on the chronic paronychia node.*
Tense glove-tight pulp, throbbing pain out of proportion, often after minor puncture. Closed septated compartment of the distal pulp. *Photo displayed inline on the felon I&D node.*
Grouped clear vesicles on an erythematous base, burning prodrome, history of orofacial HSV exposure. Do not incise. *Photo displayed inline on the herpetic whitlow node.*
Dark red/blue/black under nail, recent trauma, throbbing pressure. Trephinate based on pain, not percentage. *Photo displayed inline on the trephination node.*
Yellow-white pus under nail, no clear trauma, often associated with paronychia. Drain by lifting fold or partial nail removal. *Photo displayed inline on the subungual abscess node.*

1. Hand surgery consult immediately 2. NPO, mark cellulitis border, serial exams 3. IV vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam (or cefepime) 4. Splint in functional position, elevate 5. Tetanus update if indicated Do NOT attempt bedside drainage of the flexor sheath.

• Seizure + fever ≥38°C, age 6 months to 5 years, without CNS infection or other cause • Brief generalized event in a previously well child is the classic story • Always reconfirm the absence of CNS infection or other identified cause before assigning the diagnosis

• Simple: generalized + <15 min + ONE in 24h + age 6mo-5yr + previously well child • Complex: any focal feature, ≥15 min, recurrent in 24h, post-ictal deficit, or abnormal interictal exam • Febrile status: ≥30 min OR recurrent without recovery between events

• Simple FS: no routine LP, labs, EEG, or imaging (AAP 2011/2025) • LP indicated for: meningeal signs, persistent AMS, petechiae, recent antibiotics, ill appearance, under-vaccinated <12mo • Imaging only for: focal deficit, signs of ↑ICP, suspected NAT, suspected HSV / abscess / bleed • EEG only for: non-convulsive status concern, prolonged AMS in febrile status, recurrent complex events

• Status definition triggering treatment: ≥5 minutes OR recurrent without recovery • First-line benzodiazepine, full weight-based dose, redose once at 5 min if still seizing • Second-line: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg (ESETT 2019) • Refractory ≥40 min: anesthetic infusion + intubation + EEG monitoring

• Simple FS: home with reassurance + return precautions; no labs, LP, EEG, or AED prescription • Complex FS: most go home; admit for febrile status, persistent AMS, recurrent in 24h, no fever source, social barriers, or pending workup • Outpatient neurology referral for any complex febrile seizure
