• Three messages: prognosis is excellent, ~30% recurrence does NOT change long-term outlook, here are return precautions • Antipyretics for COMFORT only — they do NOT prevent recurrence • No routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis • Continue routine vaccinations on schedule — vaccine-triggered FS is benign and timing is reassuring

• Simple febrile seizure with normal exam — NEVER routine • Returns to baseline, no focal deficit, identifiable benign source of fever • AAP 2011 (reaffirmed 2025): no role for routine CT or MRI • Counseling families that imaging is unnecessary is part of good care — imaging exposes the child to radiation, sedation risk, and incidental findings without benefit

• Focal seizure with persistent neurologic deficit (Todd's paralysis lasting >1h) • Signs of increased ICP: papilledema, posturing, Cushing's response • Suspected non-accidental trauma (NAT) — also obtain skeletal survey + retinal exam • Suspected HSV encephalitis with stable child (start acyclovir BEFORE imaging if HSV suspected) • Suspected intracranial bleed, abscess, or mass • Papilledema or other concern for raised ICP requiring confirmation BEFORE LP

• Complex / recurrent febrile seizures with concern for an underlying epileptic syndrome or developmental disorder • Prolonged febrile status epilepticus (FEBSTAT-style) — hippocampal injury risk; MRI sensitivity > CT • Persistent abnormal neurologic exam after recovery • Higher resolution for posterior fossa, brainstem, hippocampi • No radiation — preferred when child is stable • Often arranged outpatient — does not need to happen in the ED in a stable child

info.h: When NOT to Delay LP for Imaging
info.t: • Stable child without focal exam findings does NOT need pre-LP imaging • Routine pre-LP CT delays diagnosis and treatment of bacterial meningitis • Pre-LP imaging is for clinical concerns (papilledema, focal deficit, posturing) — not for "every kid with a seizure" • If empiric antibiotics are warranted, give them BEFORE imaging or LP if there will be any delay

• Reassuring exam + simple FS = no imaging • Concerning focal deficit or ↑ICP = CT now • Stable but recurrent or prolonged complex events = outpatient MRI • Suspected NAT = head CT in the ED + skeletal survey + ophtho consult + child protection workflow • Suspected HSV = empiric acyclovir + LP/CSF studies + MRI when stable

Routine childhood vaccines cause fever in some children, and fever can trigger a febrile seizure. The seizure itself is benign — but parents are scared, and many feel guilty for "making this happen" by vaccinating. Counseling is half the visit.

• Peak window: 8-14 days post-vaccination — corresponds to the peak fever response from live attenuated viral vaccines • Most events are simple febrile seizures with classic features • Same prognosis as any other simple febrile seizure: ≥30% recurrence with future febrile illnesses, ~1-2% lifetime epilepsy risk

• At dose 1 (12-15 months), MMRV combination causes ~1 extra febrile seizure per 2,300 doses compared with MMR + Varicella given separately • No significant difference at dose 2 (4-6 years) • CDC ACIP recommendation: for the first dose at 12-15 months, share the data and let the family decide between MMRV and MMR + V given separately. For subsequent doses, MMRV is preferred for fewer injections. • Reasonable to give MMR + V separately at the first dose if family has strong family history of febrile seizures or prior febrile seizure

• DTaP peak window: 0-2 days post-vaccination • Inactivated vaccines (DTaP, Hib, PCV, hepatitis B, IPV) cause fever quickly when they cause it at all • Live vaccines (MMR, MMRV, rotavirus) cause delayed fever (5-14 days) • Influenza vaccine: rare fever response, can rarely trigger febrile seizure

• Classic timing matching the vaccine fever window • Simple febrile seizure features (generalized, <15 min, single) • Benign post-event course, child returns to baseline • No focal features, no persistent altered mentation, no concerning rash or systemic signs • If all of the above: treat as any other simple febrile seizure — no extra workup, home with reassurance

Prior febrile seizure (vaccine-triggered or otherwise) is NOT a contraindication to any routine vaccine. The diseases prevented — measles encephalitis, Hib meningitis, pertussis, varicella complications — are far worse than another brief, self-limited febrile seizure. Document the event in the immunization record so the next clinician understands the context, but continue the schedule.

"This was a febrile seizure caused by the fever response to the vaccine. The seizure itself looked terrifying, but it was brief, the brain is fine, and your child has the same excellent prognosis as any other child with a febrile seizure. Most kids never have another — those that do still grow out of them by age 5. The diseases the vaccine prevents are much worse than what just happened. We will keep going on schedule, and at the next dose we can talk about giving MMR and varicella separately if that feels safer for your family. For comfort during the next fever, you can use acetaminophen or ibuprofen — not to prevent another seizure, but because it makes them feel better."

- Highest risk age 6 mo – 5 yr - Witnessed choking event = best single feature (95% specific) - Classic triad (cough + wheeze + focal ↓ BS) ~50% sensitive — absence does NOT rule out - Normal CXR does NOT exclude airway FB — most FBs radiolucent - Esophageal: drooling, refusing PO, dysphagia, may be silent

- Effective cough → encourage cough, watch, transport - Ineffective cough <1 yr → 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts - Ineffective cough ≥1 yr → Heimlich (abdominal thrusts) - Unconscious → CPR (compressions first), look + remove visible object, NEVER blind finger sweep

- PA + lateral CXR (insp + exp or decubitus to find air trapping) - High suspicion → ENT/pulm + rigid bronchoscopy (gold standard) regardless of imaging - Mod suspicion + neg imaging → inpatient observation - Post-bronch: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, racemic epi for stridor

- STAT AP + lateral (BB has halo on AP, step-off on lateral) - Button battery → OR <2 hr regardless of symptoms - Multiple magnets or magnet + metal → urgent removal or surgery - Sx coin/sharp → <2 hr; asx → <24 hr (or 16-24 hr trial for distal coin in older child)

- Honey 10 mL PO q10min × up to 6 doses - Eligibility: age ≥12 mo, awake, <12 hr since ingestion, no perforation - NEVER honey <12 mo (infant botulism) — use Sucralfate instead - NEVER delay OR for mitigation

- Admit any post-procedure × 24 hr - BB → ICU; esophagram at 4 wk if circumferential injury; 28-day AEF vigilance - Discharge requires asymptomatic + normal exam + clear return precautions - Counsel: food cutoffs <4 yr, household BB/magnet safety, Reese's Law compliance

| Location | Timing | |---|---| | Esophagus (any size, any age, sx or asx) | OR within 2 hours | | Stomach, ≥20 mm, age <5 yr | Within 24-48 hr (NASPGHAN); some recommend <24 hr | | Stomach, <20 mm, asx, age ≥5 yr, <2 hr ingestion | Observation acceptable | | Beyond stomach, asymptomatic | Serial X-rays; observe for passage |

| Scenario | Timing | |---|---| | Esophageal, symptomatic | Endoscopic removal <2 hours | | Esophageal, asymptomatic | <24 hours, OR observation trial with repeat XR at 16-24 hr (Waltzman 2005) | | Stomach | Discharge, expectant passage, repeat XR in 2-4 wk if no documented passage |

| Scenario | Timing | |---|---| | Single, esophageal, sx | <2 hr | | Single, esophageal, asx | <24 hr | | Single, beyond esophagus, asx | Observe + serial XR + magnet/metal isolation | | Multiple OR magnet + metallic co-ingestion (any location) | Urgent removal; surgical consult if beyond stomach |

| Scenario | Timing | |---|---| | Esophageal, symptomatic | <2 hours | | Esophageal, asymptomatic | <24 hours | | Gastric | Endoscopic removal if feasible (point-trailing) | | Long object >5 cm (<1 yr) or >6 cm (older) | Endoscopic removal — won't round duodenal sweep | | Beyond duodenum | Serial daily XR; surgical consult if no progression × 3 days |

| Scenario | Timing | |---|---| | Cannot handle secretions | Endoscopic removal <2 hours | | Handling secretions | Endoscopic removal <24 hours | | Trial of Glucagon | Modest data; ALL peds food bolus → GI for EoE workup |

Lithium coin batteries lodged in the esophagus generate hydroxide at the negative pole within minutes. Local tissue pH exceeds 12, causing liquefactive necrosis. Viscous, mildly acidic / pH-neutralizing fluids form a protective coating and slow injury.

Eligibility (ALL must be true): - Age ≥12 months (NEVER under 12 mo — infant botulism risk) - Awake and able to swallow safely - <12 hours since ingestion - No signs of perforation, mediastinitis, hematemesis - Battery confirmed in esophagus on imaging Dose: 10 mL PO every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses. Continue while mobilizing ENT/GI/anesthesia/OR. Do NOT delay OR for honey administration.

Use when honey unavailable, or in infants <12 months (honey contraindicated). Dose: 10 mL of 1 g / 10 mL oral suspension PO every 10 minutes, up to 3 doses. May be given in addition to honey if both available.
- Suspected esophageal perforation or mediastinitis - Hematemesis - Inability to swallow safely / depressed consciousness - Honey only: age <12 months - Honey only: >12 hours since ingestion

Record each dose time and volume — hand-off to OR / endoscopy team. The time the battery was ingested, time of imaging, and time of each mitigation dose all matter for prognosis and post-op surveillance planning.
Honey and sucralfate are bridge therapy. They reduce injury severity but do not replace emergent endoscopic removal. The goal is OR within 2 hours of presentation.
- Effective cough (can cry/speak, color normal): Watch, do NOT intervene. Encourage cough. Position for comfort. Transport. - Ineffective cough (no sound, cyanotic, decreasing LOC): Act now (Step 2).

1. Position infant face-down on forearm, head lower than trunk, supporting head with hand 2. 5 back blows with heel of hand between scapulae 3. Turn infant face-up, supporting head 4. 5 chest thrusts (2 fingers on lower sternum, same location as CPR — depth ~1/3 chest diameter) 5. Repeat sequence until object out OR infant becomes unresponsive

1. Stand or kneel behind child 2. Fist above umbilicus, below xiphoid (thumb side against abdomen) 3. 5 quick abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) — inward and upward 4. Repeat until object out OR child becomes unresponsive

1. Start CPR — chest compressions first (may dislodge FB) 2. Open airway: look in mouth before each breath cycle 3. Remove only visible objects — no blind finger sweeps (risk of pushing FB deeper) 4. Continue cycles; activate EMS / code 5. If still cannot ventilate: prepare for direct laryngoscopy + Magill forceps, then advanced airway interventions (push FB distal, surgical airway)

MOCHI registry (Norii 2024) demonstrated that early effective bystander relief before EMS arrival is associated with better neurological outcomes. Community education in CPR + choking maneuvers matters.
- Blind finger sweeps in any patient - Abdominal thrusts in infants <1 yr (liver injury risk) - Delay CPR for futile back-blow / Heimlich attempts in an unresponsive child

1. Red flags? — fever/IVDU/immunocomp, cancer hx, sudden posterior HA, RA, progressive deficit 2. Myelopathy? — Hoffman, Lhermitte, hyperreflexia, gait, hand clumsiness 3. Radiculopathy? — dermatomal arm pain, myotome weakness, reflex change 4. Mechanical / myofascial? — axial pain only, normal exam 5. Mixed? — treat as the highest-acuity component

• MRI emergent: myelopathy, infection (with contrast), MSCC (whole spine + contrast), progressive deficit • MRI urgent: refractory radiculopathy >6 weeks, pre-op planning • CTA / MRA neck: suspected vertebral artery dissection • CT cervical: if MRI contraindicated, bony pathology, RA AAS workup paired with XR • Flex/ext XR: RA atlantoaxial subluxation screen • No imaging: mechanical pain <6 weeks with no red flags

Mechanical / myofascial: • NSAID (naproxen 500 BID or ibuprofen 600 TID) + APAP 1 g q6h • Short muscle relaxant if spasm (tizanidine 2-4 mg TID × 5-7 d) • No collar past 1-2 weeks. No opioids unless severe + brief Radiculopathy: • Above + consider gabapentin 300 mg TID titrated for neuropathic • Short PO steroid (prednisone 60 mg × 5d taper) for severe acute • PT referral 1-2 weeks Myelopathy / cord syndrome: • MRI now, spine surgery consult, MAP >85 if cord injury • Falls precautions, avoid manipulation Infection: • Vanc + ceftriaxone or cefepime, blood cx × 2, ESR/CRP, MRI w/ contrast MSCC: • Dex 10 mg IV NOW, MRI whole spine, neurosurg + rad onc

Return immediately for: • New weakness in any arm or leg • Loss of bowel or bladder control • Numbness in groin or saddle area • Worsening gait, balance, or falls • Hand clumsiness or dropping things bilaterally • Fever or new severe pain • Severe posterior headache

| Root | Dermatome | Myotome | Reflex | Tip | |------|-----------|---------|--------|-----| | C5 | Lateral upper arm, deltoid | Shoulder abduction | Biceps | Pain to lateral arm | | C6 | Lateral forearm, thumb + index | Wrist extension | Brachioradialis | Thumb tingling | | C7 | Middle finger, post forearm | Wrist flexion, triceps | Triceps | Most common — triceps weak | | C8 | Medial forearm, ring + little finger | Finger flexion | Finger flexor | Numb pinky | | T1 | Medial upper arm, axilla | Hand intrinsics | None | Hand wasting; Horner = T1 |

• Fingers: Thumb = C6 · Middle = C7 · Pinky = C8 • Reflexes — count to 8: Biceps = C5-6 · Brachioradialis = C6 · Triceps = C7 · Finger flexor = C8 • C7 dominates — accounts for ~60% of cervical radiculopathy presentations

• T1 with Horner → think Pancoast tumor (apical lung) • Bilateral C8/T1 hand wasting → think cord pathology (syringomyelia, ALS, central cord) — image the cord, not just the foramen • C5 weakness with fasciculations → anterior horn pathology (consider EMG / neurology)

Extend neck → side-bend toward symptomatic side → apply downward axial pressure. • Positive: reproduction of radicular arm pain (not just local neck pain) • Sensitivity 30-60% / Specificity 92-100% • Use only if no instability or cord compression concern
Patient places palm of affected arm on top of head. Reduces nerve root tension. • Decreases pain = positive • Specificity ~80%
Gentle axial traction on the head while seated. • Relieves radicular pain = positive • Specificity ~90%

info.h: Upper Limb Tension Test (ULTT, neural Spurling)
info.t: Sequential shoulder abduction, elbow extension, wrist + finger extension, contralateral neck side-bend. • Reproduces symptoms = positive • Sensitivity 75-95% / Specificity 22-50% — good for ruling OUT
Neck flexion → electric shock down spine or limbs. • Suggests CORD pathology (myelopathy, MS, B12, central disc) • If positive — escalate to myelopathy workup with MRI
3 of 4 positive = high likelihood: 1. Spurling positive 2. Distraction positive 3. ULTT positive 4. Ipsilateral cervical rotation <60°

• Myelopathy (any UMN signs) • Progressive motor deficit • Suspected spinal infection — with contrast • Suspected MSCC — with contrast, image whole spine • Severe acute radiculopathy with significant motor weakness

info.h: URGENT MRI (within 1-2 weeks, arrange from ED)
info.t: • Radicular symptoms >6 weeks despite conservative care • Progressive sensory symptoms • Pre-operative planning by spine surgery

Suspected vertebral artery dissection: • Sudden severe posterior HA, post-manipulation, posterior circ symptoms • Age <50 with new severe posterior HA + neck pain Use CTA in ED (faster, more available).

Limited role in non-traumatic neck pain: • MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, cochlear implant) • RA atlantoaxial concern (paired with flex/ext XR) • Suspected fused-spine fracture (ank spond) after minor trauma
• Flex/ext views — RA atlantoaxial subluxation (ADI, PADI) • Generally NOT routine for mechanical neck pain
• Mechanical/myofascial pain <6 weeks • No red flags, normal neuro exam • Imaging would not change management — counsel patient explicitly

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the APAP level on any altered + jaundiced patient
info.t: APAP is the most common cause of acute liver failure in the US. Patients deny exposure, forget chronic dosing, or present after the level has fallen. Send APAP level on every "altered + jaundiced" or "encephalopathic + INR climbing" case — even when the patient denies APAP. Delayed-presentation APAP can show a negative or low level with skyrocketing AST/ALT. NAC is still indicated. Acetaminophen consult

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT correct INR with FFP in ALF unless actively bleeding
info.t: INR is the prognostic marker that drives King's College Criteria and transplant center decisions. Correcting it with FFP / PCC erases the signal and the receiving center loses the data they need. Give Vit K 10 mg IV (corrects nutritional component) but reserve FFP / PCC for active bleeding or pre-procedure. Kings College

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics for the ERCP slot in cholangitis
info.t: Charcot triad → blood cultures × 2 → antibiotics within 1 hour. ERCP source control comes later. Reynolds pentad (Charcot + hypotension + AMS) = Tokyo Grade III = emergent ERCP / PTBD within 24 h, ICU level care, vasopressors, lactate-guided resuscitation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT mistake Reynolds pentad for ALF encephalopathy
info.t: Septic shock from cholangitis presents with AMS + jaundice + hypotension + fever. Looks like ALF on first glance but the source is biliary, not hepatocellular. Source control via ERCP / PTBD changes the trajectory. Differential is driven by RUQ US showing dilation + recent fever pattern.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge "painless jaundice in age ≥50" as viral hepatitis
info.t: Painless jaundice + weight loss + age ≥50 + cholestatic LFT pattern (alk phos / GGT out of proportion) = malignant biliary obstruction until proven otherwise. Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common culprit. RUQ US → CT pancreatic protocol → GI for ERCP with brushings → oncology. Outpatient discharge is rarely appropriate at first presentation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss Wilson disease in the young ALF patient
info.t: Young patient + ALF + LOW alk phos + alk-phos-to-bili ratio <4 + Coombs-negative hemolysis = Wilson disease. Wilsonian ALF has the worst transplant-free survival of any ALF subtype (<10%). Order ceruloplasmin + 24-h urine copper + slit-lamp from the ED. Chelation does NOT rescue fulminant Wilsonian ALF — transplant is the definitive therapy.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget glucose monitoring q1h in ALF
info.t: Hepatocyte gluconeogenesis failure causes hypoglycemia that is silent in the encephalopathic patient. Glucose q1h, D10W infusion if any hypoglycemia, treat as aggressively as you would in DKA-style monitoring frequency.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give platelets in suspected TTP
info.t: TTP pentad (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + fever + AMS + renal failure) — platelets fuel microthrombi and worsen end-organ ischemia. Reserve for catastrophic bleeding. Emergency plasma exchange is the therapy; steroids while waiting.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the hub as a treatment playbook
info.t: The hub is a triage map. Once you commit to a phenotype (APAP, cholangitis, ALF, hemolysis), leave the hub and work the deep-dive consult — that consult holds the dosing, monitoring, and disposition criteria specific to the diagnosis.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without written return precautions and a booked 48-72 h recheck
info.t: Even benign-pattern jaundice (Gilbert, stable cirrhosis at baseline, very mild non-progressive viral hepatitis) requires hepatology or PCP follow-up within 48-72 hours. Written return precautions cover: worsening yellowing, confusion / drowsiness, new RUQ pain or fever, persistent vomiting, dark urine + light stool worsening, bleeding, intractable pruritus. Patients must abstain from acetaminophen, NSAIDs, alcohol, and untested supplements.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the pre-oxygenation step
info.t: Skipping preoxygenation dramatically shortens your safe apnea time. Spend 3–5 min on NRB or flush-rate O2 and use apneic oxygenation (15 L/min NC) during laryngoscopy. See pre-assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT paralyze without backup equipment at bedside
info.t: Once you paralyze, the patient cannot protect their airway. Have the surgical airway kit open and the SGA within arm's reach before you push any paralytic. See backup assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT preload the bougie through the ETT
info.t: Preloading locks the bougie in a fixed curve and destroys maneuverability. Hold the bougie separately, railroad the ETT over it only after tracheal placement is confirmed. See equipment setup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on tracheal clicks alone for confirmation
info.t: Clicks are felt in only ~90% of correct placements and are absent in obese patients. Use the hold-up sign AND waveform capnography — clicks alone are insufficient. See bougie technique node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT remove the laryngoscope before the ETT clears the cords
info.t: Losing your view during ETT advancement over the bougie is a common cause of failed railroad. Maintain laryngoscopy until the tube has clearly passed through the cords. See bougie technique node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT accept anything less than sustained waveform capnography
info.t: Transient CO2 (2–3 breaths then fade) indicates esophageal placement — the stomach holds some CO2. Insist on a sustained 4-phase waveform over 5–6 ventilations before securing. See confirmation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt more than 3 laryngoscopies
info.t: Each attempt causes edema, bleeding, and secretions that worsen the next view. After 3 failed attempts declare a failed airway and move to rescue — more attempts are not rescue. See max attempts node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgical airway once CICV is declared
info.t: Cannot-Intubate/Cannot-Ventilate is a surgical emergency. Hesitating on the scalpel while the patient desaturates is the proximate cause of death. Cut early, cut confidently. See surgical airway node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget ETT rotation on arytenoid hang-up
info.t: If the ETT catches after passing the cords, rotate it 90° counterclockwise — the bevel will clear the arytenoid. Forcing the tube without rotation can traumatize the supraglottis. See bougie technique node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay epinephrine for antihistamines or steroids
info.t: Antihistamines and steroids do not treat the life-threatening components of anaphylaxis. Epinephrine IM is the only first-line treatment — every minute of delay increases mortality. See source control node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT inject epinephrine subcutaneously in anaphylaxis
info.t: Subcutaneous injection is slower and less reliable than the anterolateral thigh IM route. The thigh achieves peak plasma levels significantly faster. See epinephrine node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give cardiac arrest dose (1 mg IV push) to a patient with a pulse
info.t: This is a 61-fold overdose compared to IM dosing and causes hypertensive crisis, arrhythmias, and death. In non-arrest patients requiring IV epinephrine, use a weight-based infusion starting at 10 mcg/min. See IV access node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold epinephrine for cardiovascular disease
info.t: There are NO absolute contraindications to epinephrine in anaphylaxis — the risk of untreated anaphylaxis always exceeds the risk of the drug. Coronary disease, hypertension, and pregnancy are not contraindications. See start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge after epinephrine without adequate observation
info.t: Biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of patients 1–72 hours after the initial event. Observe a minimum of 4–6 hours; admit patients with severe reactions, asthma, or unreliable access to care. See diagnosis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat angioedema without urticaria as routine anaphylaxis
info.t: ACE-inhibitor angioedema (bradykinin-mediated) and hereditary angioedema do not respond to epinephrine. Identify the mechanism before treating. See airway node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT sit or stand a hypotensive anaphylaxis patient upright
info.t: Up to 35% of intravascular volume extravasates within minutes during anaphylaxis. Lay the patient flat and elevate legs — positional change from supine to standing can be immediately fatal. See peri-arrest node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay intubation for worsening airway edema
info.t: Airway edema from anaphylaxis can close completely within minutes. Call anesthesia and ENT early, use a smaller ETT, and have a surgical airway kit open. Waiting for "further deterioration" is too late. See critical airway node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antibiotics if STEC (E. coli O157) is suspected
info.t: Antibiotics in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli increase bacterial lysis and toxin release, raising the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) by up to 17-fold. Suspect STEC with bloody diarrhea, afebrile patient, and history of undercooked beef. See bloody diarrhea node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antimotility agents in bloody or febrile diarrhea
info.t: Loperamide and bismuth delay pathogen clearance in inflammatory diarrhea and increase the risk of systemic spread and HUS in STEC. Reserve antimotility agents for watery, afebrile traveler's diarrhea. See bloody diarrhea node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss C. difficile in patients on recent antibiotics
info.t: Any antibiotic in the past 3 months warrants C. diff testing, not just the stereotypical clindamycin. C. diff can present without pseudomembranes and with near-normal WBC in early disease. See C. diff node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use metronidazole alone for severe C. difficile
info.t: Metronidazole monotherapy has inferior outcomes for severe C. diff (WBC >15K, Cr >1.5). Oral vancomycin 125 mg QID is first-line for all severities; add IV metronidazole only in fulminant disease. See C. diff treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on gastroenteritis in a patient with severe abdominal pain
info.t: Diarrhea is a common early symptom of appendicitis — especially in pediatric patients (27% misdiagnosed). In gastroenteritis, vomiting precedes pain; in appendicitis, pain precedes vomiting. See surgical differential node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fluoroquinolones for traveler's diarrhea from Southeast Asia
info.t: Campylobacter resistance to fluoroquinolones exceeds 80% in Southeast Asia. Use azithromycin as first-line for all moderate-severe traveler's diarrhea from that region. See traveler's diarrhea node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget HUS screening in bloody diarrhea
info.t: Get a CBC with platelets and creatinine in every patient with bloody diarrhea — thrombocytopenia and rising creatinine may be the first sign of HUS before oliguria or neurologic findings develop. See bloody diarrhea node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop HAART without HIV specialist guidance
info.t: Abruptly discontinuing antiretrovirals causes viral rebound, resistance selection, and immune reconstitution complications. If a drug must be held (e.g., surgery, GI intolerance), consult HIV specialist — all drugs should be stopped simultaneously. See immunocompromised disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop tenofovir/emtricitabine/lamivudine in HBV co-infection
info.t: These NRTIs are active against HBV. Stopping them in a co-infected patient can trigger severe HBV reactivation hepatitis. Screen for HBV co-infection before any ARV changes. See HBV caution node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss ectopic/radiolucent kidney stones in PI-treated patients
info.t: Atazanavir and indinavir form radiolucent stones invisible on noncontrast CT. If a PI patient has flank pain and CT shows only secondary signs (hydroureter, stranding), do not discharge as "no stone" — urology consult is warranted. See renal node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on COPD when an HIV patient has pleuritic chest pain
info.t: HIV patients have a 2.5× higher VTE risk from chronic inflammation. Pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea warrants PE evaluation even when COPD is a known diagnosis. PERC criteria were not validated in HIV patients. See respiratory node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use 3rd-generation (antibody-only) test to rule out acute HIV
info.t: 3rd-gen tests cannot detect acute infection during the p24 antigen window (days 5–20 post-exposure). Use a 4th-gen (Ab + p24 Ag) test, and add HIV viral load if acute seroconversion is suspected despite a negative 4th-gen result. See seroconversion testing node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume diarrhea in HIV is always medication-related
info.t: C. difficile is significantly more common in HIV patients than the general population. Obtain careful antibiotic and hospitalization history before attributing diarrhea to ARVs. See GI node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss ACS in a young HIV patient based on age alone
info.t: HIV independently increases cardiovascular risk independent of traditional risk factors. Abacavir has been associated with increased MI risk. Apply standard ACS evaluation regardless of the patient's age. See cardiovascular node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay PEP past 72 hours post-exposure
info.t: Post-exposure prophylaxis must start within 72 hours — efficacy drops sharply after this window. Time from exposure is the single most critical variable. See prevention node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order head CT without applying a validated decision rule
info.t: The Canadian CT Head Rule and PECARN are prospectively validated tools with near-100% sensitivity for significant injury. Reflexive CT without applying these rules exposes patients to unnecessary radiation and may paradoxically reduce diagnostic quality. See CT start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply CCHR to patients on anticoagulation
info.t: The Canadian CT Head Rule excludes patients on anticoagulants — even trivial head trauma warrants CT in anticoagulated patients due to the high risk of intracranial hemorrhage. See CCHR clinical judgment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the PECARN intermediate-risk shared decision step
info.t: PECARN intermediate-risk children (0.8–0.9% ciTBI) have a viable observation alternative. Immediately scanning every child with a single intermediate criterion bypasses a legitimate radiation-sparing option. See PECARN observe node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use NEXUS instead of Canadian C-Spine Rule when both apply
info.t: The Canadian C-Spine Rule has 100% sensitivity for C-spine injury vs 99.6% for NEXUS and is significantly more specific (42.5% vs 12.9%), reducing unnecessary imaging. Prefer CCR in alert, stable trauma patients. See C-spine alert node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order CT-PE without pre-test probability (Wells or PERC)
info.t: Low pre-test probability patients who are PERC-negative have a <2% PE prevalence — CT-PE in this population creates false positives, unnecessary anticoagulation, and incidentaloma cascades. See PE pre-test node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order CT-PE as the first test in a low-probability patient
info.t: D-dimer is the appropriate first test in low-to-moderate pre-test probability. A negative age-adjusted D-dimer rules out PE without radiation exposure or contrast risk. See PE pre-test node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip documentation of the clinical decision rule result
info.t: Documenting which rule was applied, what criteria were met, and the result protects the patient, guides follow-up providers, and is required by Choosing Wisely and ACR appropriateness criteria. See CT start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT fail to page OB and Pediatrics immediately
info.t: Even if delivery looks minutes away, page OB and Pediatrics the moment you recognize active labor — they need maximum lead time. "She just walked in" is not a reason to wait. See call for help node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust a multiparous patient to have "time left"
info.t: Multiparous patients can progress from 4 cm to delivery in minutes. The classic teaching: "Never trust a multip." Assume delivery is more imminent than the patient thinks. See history node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT pull on the fetal head to speed delivery
info.t: Traction on the head during crowning risks brachial plexus injury and perineal tears. Let the uterus do the work — apply only gentle counter-pressure to control the speed of head delivery. See head delivery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT routinely suction the airway after delivery
info.t: Routine nasopharyngeal suctioning is no longer recommended per NRP 8th edition. Suction only if the airway is visibly obstructed. Vigorous suctioning causes vagal bradycardia. See head delivery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clamp the cord immediately in a vigorous term infant
info.t: Delayed cord clamping (30–60 seconds) improves iron stores, hemoglobin, and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Only clamp immediately if the infant requires resuscitation or the cord is too tight to reduce. See cord clamping node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply traction in the wrong axis during shoulder delivery
info.t: Traction must be along the long axis of the fetal neck — lateral bending causes brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy). If the head retracts ("turtle sign"), stop and proceed to the Shoulder Dystocia protocol. See shoulder delivery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give oxytocin before the placenta delivers
info.t: Oxytocin given before placenta delivery can trap the placenta if there is an undiagnosed second twin. Confirm single fetus before administering uterotonic agents. See oxytocin node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt transfer when delivery is imminent
info.t: EMTALA requires stabilization before transfer — and an imminent delivery is not a stable condition. Delivering in an ambulance is significantly more dangerous than delivering in the ED with a team. See transfer node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT pull laterally or twist the fetal head
info.t: Lateral traction or twisting the neck while pulling is the primary mechanism of brachial plexus stretch injury (Erb's palsy). All traction must be in the long axis of the fetal neck — axial, not lateral. See traction node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT panic — call out "shoulder dystocia" and start the clock
info.t: The most dangerous response is uncoordinated frantic pulling. Announce shoulder dystocia calmly, designate a timekeeper, and systematically move through your maneuvers. You have 4–5 minutes. See initial response node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply fundal pressure during shoulder dystocia
info.t: Fundal pressure drives the impacted shoulder further into the pelvis and worsens the dystocia. Suprapubic pressure (pushing the shoulder to an oblique position) is the correct adjunct maneuver. See McRoberts node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip McRoberts + suprapubic as the first-line combination
info.t: Together they resolve 50–60% of all shoulder dystocias with minimal risk. Jumping directly to internal maneuvers without first attempting McRoberts + suprapubic wastes time and increases maternal and fetal injury risk. See McRoberts node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to try both rotational directions
info.t: Wood's screw can be rotated clockwise or counterclockwise. One direction often succeeds where the other fails because shoulder anatomy varies. Try both before moving to posterior arm delivery. See rotational maneuver node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay attempting posterior arm delivery if rotation fails
info.t: Posterior arm delivery has the highest success rate of all second-line maneuvers per Hoffman 2011 data. Humeral fracture risk (~12%) is an acceptable trade-off in a life-threatening situation — these fractures heal. See posterior arm node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform Zavanelli without setting up for C-section simultaneously
info.t: Zavanelli (cephalic replacement) is only viable if an emergency cesarean section is immediately available. Attempting cephalic replacement without surgical backup ready is not a rescue maneuver. See last resort node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT fail to document timing and maneuver sequence after delivery
info.t: The head-to-body interval and the specific sequence and timing of all maneuvers is medicolegally critical. Designate a note-taker in the room and document immediately after delivery. See resolved node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss ectopic in an unstable patient by waiting for labs
info.t: A hemodynamically unstable pregnant patient is a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. Free fluid on FAST + no IUP on bedside US = emergent OB surgical consult. Do not wait for a quantitative beta-hCG. See unstable ectopic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a rising beta-hCG to rule out ectopic
info.t: One-third of ectopics show a ≥53% rise in 48h, and 20% decline like a completed miscarriage. Beta-hCG trends are insufficient to exclude ectopic — serial US and OB follow-up are mandatory. See PUL node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give hormonal therapy without ruling out pregnancy
info.t: All hormonal AUB treatments (estrogen, progestins, OCPs) are contraindicated in pregnancy. An hCG must be confirmed negative before any hormonal therapy is initiated. See AUB pregnancy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold Rh immune globulin from an Rh-negative patient with first-trimester bleeding
info.t: Any vaginal bleeding or uterine instrumentation in an Rh-negative patient requires RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin) to prevent Rh sensitization that could affect future pregnancies. See miscarriage complete node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methotrexate if fetal cardiac activity is present
info.t: Fetal cardiac activity on ultrasound carries an OR of 9.1 for methotrexate failure and indicates a higher-volume ectopic at greater rupture risk. These patients need surgical management, not medical therapy. See ectopic medical node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume a confirmed IUP rules out ectopic in ART patients
info.t: In patients who used assisted reproductive technology, heterotopic pregnancy (simultaneous IUP and ectopic) occurs in 1 in 100 — 30× higher than the general population. Maintain suspicion for ectopic even with a confirmed IUP. See IUP confirmed node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fluoroquinolones for UTI in first-trimester pregnancy
info.t: Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal cartilage toxicity. Use amoxicillin, nitrofurantoin, or cephalexin — and avoid nitrofurantoin at term due to hemolytic anemia risk. See UTI eval node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give NSAIDs for pain in the first trimester
info.t: NSAIDs are associated with early miscarriage and cardiac defects in the first trimester. Use acetaminophen for analgesia. See NVP assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start hormonal therapy without ruling out pregnancy
info.t: Estrogen and progestins are contraindicated in pregnancy. Obtain a urine hCG before initiating any hormonal treatment regardless of the patient's reported menstrual history. See pregnancy exclusion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give IV conjugated estrogen without planning a progestin follow-up
info.t: IV estrogen (Premarin 25 mg IV) effectively stops bleeding but causes endometrial proliferation. It must be followed within 24 hours by a progestin (e.g., MPA 10 mg PO daily × 10 days) to prevent rebound hemorrhage. See estrogen treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use NSAIDs if coagulopathy is suspected
info.t: NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and can significantly worsen bleeding in a patient with von Willebrand disease or thrombocytopenia — the two most common coagulopathic causes of heavy menstrual bleeding. See coagulopathy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip endometrial biopsy criteria in older or obese patients
info.t: Endometrial biopsy is mandatory for women ≥45 with AUB, and for women <45 with obesity, PCOS, or unopposed estrogen exposure — endometrial cancer is the diagnosis you cannot afford to miss. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT overlook coagulopathy as a cause of heavy menstrual bleeding
info.t: Up to 20% of women with heavy menstrual bleeding have an underlying coagulopathy — von Willebrand disease accounts for up to 13%. Screen with structured history questions before assuming a hormonal cause. See coagulopathy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give DDAVP to a massively hemorrhaging patient receiving IV fluids
info.t: Desmopressin causes fluid retention and hyponatremia — combining it with aggressive IV resuscitation can precipitate dangerous dilutional hyponatremia. Use tranexamic acid as first-line in the unstable patient. See coagulopathy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay GYN consult in unstable AUB
info.t: Hemodynamically unstable AUB requires emergent GYN consultation for potential procedural intervention (curettage, embolization). ED medications are temporizing — they buy time, not definitive control. See unstable AUB node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt reduction without adequate analgesia
info.t: Pain and muscle spasm prevent successful reduction. A hematoma block (5–10 mL 1% lidocaine, wait 5–10 min) takes less than 15 minutes and dramatically improves success rate without requiring procedural sedation resources. See analgesia node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip traction (disimpaction) before reducing
info.t: Impacted distal radius fragments are locked together — you cannot reduce what you cannot separate. Apply longitudinal traction first to recreate length, then reduce. Reduction without prior traction almost always fails. See traction node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT inject hematoma block without aspirating first
info.t: Aspirating dark blood confirms you are in the fracture hematoma, not a vessel or the wrong compartment. Injecting without confirmation risks systemic local anesthetic toxicity. See hematoma block node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fiberglass for an unstable distal radius fracture
info.t: Fiberglass cannot be molded adequately to maintain reduction. Unstable fractures require plaster (10 layers, minimal padding at fracture site) shaped with flat palms to create a three-point bending force. See splint application node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT mold the cast with fingertips
info.t: Fingertip molding creates focal pressure points that cause pressure sores and compartment syndrome. Mold only with flat palms to distribute pressure evenly and achieve an oval cross-section. See mold node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT immobilize the wrist in too much flexion
info.t: Extreme wrist flexion increases carpal tunnel pressure and risks median nerve compression. Target 10° of flexion with ulnar deviation — not the historically taught "Cotton-Loder" position of maximum flexion. See position node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT block elbow, MCP joints, or thumb in the cast
info.t: The cast should end at the proximal palmar crease (full MCP flexion) and leave the thumb and elbow free. Immobilizing these joints causes stiffness that can be permanent. See position node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without ortho follow-up and repeat x-rays at 5–7 days
info.t: Reduced distal radius fractures re-displace in 15–50% of cases as swelling resolves. Repeat films at the first ortho visit are mandatory to catch loss of reduction before the window for re-reduction closes. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT splint without a pre-splint neurovascular exam
info.t: Document neurovascular status (pulses, capillary refill, 2-point discrimination, nerve function) before applying any splint. If a deficit develops after splinting, you need a pre-splint baseline to determine causation. See splint start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use hot water to dip plaster
info.t: Hot water accelerates the setting reaction and generates excess exothermic heat — second-degree burns from plaster casts are a real and preventable complication. Always use lukewarm water. See general principles node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply a circumferential cast over acute swelling
info.t: Circumferential casts over acutely injured extremities cause compartment syndrome as swelling peaks at 24–72 hours. Use a splint (3-sided) that allows expansion until swelling resolves. See splint start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT mold the splint with fingertips
info.t: Focal pressure from fingertips creates pressure points that cause skin ulceration. Use flat palms for molding to distribute force evenly across the splint surface. See splint start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT extend the splint past the proximal palmar crease
info.t: A splint that blocks the metacarpophalangeal joints prevents finger flexion and causes rapid intrinsic muscle contracture. Ensure full MCP flexion is maintained in every upper extremity splint. See wrist/hand node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wrap elastic bandage too tightly over a fresh splint
info.t: Tight elastic wrap over a fresh plaster splint (which continues to stiffen and contract as it sets) is a common cause of iatrogenic compartment syndrome. Wrap snugly but loosely — the patient should be able to insert a finger. See splint start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send a patient home without written return precautions
info.t: Compartment syndrome can develop hours after splinting. Every patient needs written instructions to return immediately for increasing pain despite elevation, numbness/tingling, inability to move fingers/toes, or skin discoloration. See splint start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold dexamethasone in mild croup
info.t: Dexamethasone reduces return visits by ~50% (NNT = 7) even in mild croup. There is no severity threshold below which steroids should be withheld — all children with croup benefit from a single dose. See mild treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT agitate the child with croup
info.t: Crying and agitation significantly worsen dynamic subglottic obstruction. Minimize procedures, keep parents at bedside, avoid IV attempts until clinically necessary, and let the child sit in the position of comfort. See severe treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge early after epinephrine — observe 2 hours minimum
info.t: Nebulized epinephrine has a duration of action of only 1–2 hours. Patients must be observed for a minimum of 2 hours after the last dose to detect rebound stridor before discharge. See post-epi observation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT limit epinephrine to a single dose in severe croup
info.t: Repeated doses of nebulized epinephrine can prevent intubation in many patients with severe croup. There is no evidence-based maximum dose limit — clinical response guides repeat dosing. See repeat epinephrine node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a standard-size ETT when intubating a croup patient
info.t: Subglottic narrowing is the pathological lesion of croup — the standard age-predicted tube will not fit. Use an ETT 0.5–1.0 mm smaller than predicted, and have progressively smaller tubes immediately available. See respiratory failure node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reassure parents that humidified air or cool mist helps
info.t: Multiple RCTs have found no benefit from mist therapy or humidified air in croup. Counseling parents to run the shower at home may delay return to care when symptoms are worsening. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on croup when alternative diagnoses are possible
info.t: Failure to improve with dexamethasone + epinephrine should trigger consideration of bacterial tracheitis (toxic-appearing, subglottic pseudomembrane), epiglottitis (tripod posture, drooling), or foreign body aspiration (sudden onset without prodrome). See respiratory failure node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay PPV to suction a meconium-stained non-vigorous infant
info.t: Per 2025 NRP guidelines, ventilation is the priority over suctioning in non-vigorous meconium-stained infants. Delaying PPV to perform routine tracheal suctioning worsens acidosis and hypoxia. Suction only if the airway is visibly obstructed. See meconium node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start 100% oxygen for term or near-term infants
info.t: Hyperoxia is toxic to the neonatal brain and retina. Start PPV at 21% FiO2 for term (≥35 wk) infants and titrate to preductal SpO2 targets — saturations of 60–65% at 1 minute are normal and expected. See SpO2 targets node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT monitor SpO2 on the left hand or feet
info.t: Postductal SpO2 (left hand, feet) is normally 2–3% lower than preductal values in newborns and does not represent cerebral or coronary oxygenation. Always place the pulse oximeter on the right hand or wrist. See breathing support node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clamp the cord immediately in a vigorous term infant
info.t: Delayed cord clamping (30–60 seconds) improves iron stores, hemoglobin, and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Immediate clamping in vigorous infants deprives the neonate of 30–40 mL/kg of placental blood. See cord management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT place infant cord milking in infants <28 weeks
info.t: Intact cord milking in very premature infants (<28 weeks) is associated with intraventricular hemorrhage risk. This technique is contraindicated — use delayed cord clamping when feasible. See cord management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip PPV corrective steps (MR SOPA) before escalating
info.t: Most PPV failure is from a poor mask seal or poor airway position — not from the infant needing chest compressions. Work through Mask adjustment, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase, and Alternative airway before starting CPR. See corrective steps node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give endotracheal epinephrine if IV/IO access is available
info.t: ET epinephrine has unpredictable absorption and requires a 10× higher dose. Umbilical venous catheter (UVC) should be established first — it is the preferred access route for all neonatal resuscitation medications. See UVC node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT allow hyperthermia in a resuscitated neonate
info.t: Both hypothermia AND hyperthermia worsen neonatal outcomes. Target normothermia (36.5–37.5°C) strictly. Overheating under the radiant warmer or with excessive blankets is a preventable harm. See post-resuscitation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT omit LP in neonates 0–21 days with fever
info.t: All neonates 0–21 days with fever require a full sepsis workup including lumbar puncture regardless of how well-appearing they seem. Neonatal meningitis can present subtly and is fatal without treatment. See neonatal labs node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss HSV in a febrile neonate <21 days
info.t: Neonatal HSV encephalitis has 70% mortality without acyclovir. Skin vesicles, seizures, CSF pleocytosis, transaminitis, or maternal HSV history mandate acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h while awaiting PCR results. See HSV workup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ceftriaxone in infants 0–7 days old
info.t: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin binding sites and can cause bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) in neonates. Use ampicillin + gentamicin in the first week of life. See neonatal age node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply a well-appearing infant "pass" to a febrile neonate
info.t: Neonates have limited immune and physiologic reserve — they can appear well and rapidly deteriorate. Well-appearing does not alter the workup or admission decision for infants 0–21 days. See neonatal screening node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anchor on a viral source without completing the age-appropriate workup
info.t: A concomitant URI or RSV bronchiolitis does not exclude bacteremia or meningitis in young infants — especially those <60 days. Age-stratified inflammatory markers still guide LP and admission decisions. See start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip vancomycin in febrile infants 29–60 days with CSF pleocytosis
info.t: S. pneumoniae meningitis in this age group increasingly involves penicillin-resistant strains. Add vancomycin to ceftriaxone whenever meningitis is possible, until culture and sensitivity are available. See toxic infant node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT accept a bag urine specimen for culture
info.t: Bag specimens have a false-positive rate of 85% for UTI diagnosis. Culture results from bag specimens are uninterpretable. Catheterized or suprapubic aspirate specimens are mandatory for any culture-based diagnosis. See UTI risk node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send a bag urine specimen for culture
info.t: Bag specimens have a contamination rate so high that culture results are diagnostically meaningless. Any UTI diagnosis that will drive antibiotic therapy requires a catheter or suprapubic aspirate specimen for culture. See catheter UA node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip UTI screening in uncircumcised febrile males
info.t: Uncircumcised males are at 5–20× higher UTI risk than circumcised males. Screen ALL febrile uncircumcised males in the 2–24 month age group regardless of number of risk factors present. See infant screening node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat a neonatal UTI with oral antibiotics alone
info.t: Neonates with UTI have a high rate of concurrent bacteremia. Neonatal UTI requires IV antibiotics: ceftazidime + ampicillin for Pseudomonas and Enterococcus coverage until culture and sensitivity are available. See neonatal antibiotic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use TMP-SMX empirically for pediatric UTI
info.t: E. coli susceptibility to TMP-SMX is only 71% in many regions — empiric use has an unacceptably high treatment failure rate. Use cephalexin or ceftriaxone as empiric first-line until culture-directed therapy is possible. See ED antibiotic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT repeat a urine culture for test of cure in standard UTI
info.t: Test-of-cure cultures are not indicated for standard E. coli UTI — they add cost and parental anxiety without clinical benefit. Reserve test-of-cure for Candida UTI or ESBL-producing organisms only. See neonatal diagnosis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order VCUG after every first febrile UTI
info.t: VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) is indicated after a first febrile UTI only if the renal ultrasound shows abnormalities. Routine VCUG in all first febrile UTI patients is no longer recommended. See imaging results node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT routinely prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis post-UTI
info.t: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis after a first febrile UTI is no longer routinely recommended due to lack of benefit and increased antimicrobial resistance. Reserve for recurrent UTI or confirmed high-grade VUR. See prophylaxis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip inhalation injury screening
info.t: Inhalation injury can be present with a normal initial exam — stridor, singed nasal hairs, carbonaceous sputum, and a closed-space history are the key flags. Missed inhalation injury leads to fatal airway loss hours later. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay intubation in airway burns
info.t: Airway edema progresses rapidly over 12–24 hours. If you see oropharyngeal burns, stridor, or hoarseness, intubate early while anatomy is still recognizable — a delayed airway in a swollen face is a surgical emergency. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget CO poisoning in house fires
info.t: CO is colorless and odorless — pulse oximetry is falsely normal because carboxyhemoglobin reads as oxyhemoglobin. Co-oximetry or ABG is required. Treat with 100% O₂ regardless of SpO₂ reading. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss cyanide toxicity in structure fires
info.t: Burning synthetic materials (plastics, upholstery) releases hydrogen cyanide. Patients with altered mental status or refractory lactic acidosis out of proportion to CO level should receive empiric hydroxocobalamin — do not wait for confirmatory testing. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ice water on burns
info.t: Ice or cold water causes vasoconstriction, worsens tissue injury, and can induce hypothermia in large burns. Cool (not cold) tap water for 20 minutes is the correct first-aid intervention. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT over-resuscitate with IV fluids
info.t: "Fluid creep" — exceeding Parkland formula volumes — causes abdominal compartment syndrome, pulmonary edema, and increased mortality. Target UOP 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hr and titrate down if exceeding formula. See this node.

Children have higher body surface area to mass ratio and limited glycogen stores. Use the pediatric Parkland formula and add maintenance fluids with dextrose — dehydration and hypoglycemia develop faster than in adults. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss circumferential burns needing escharotomy
info.t: Circumferential full-thickness burns of extremities or the chest can cause compartment syndrome and respiratory failure within hours. Check pulses, assess chest excursion, and act early — escharotomy is a time-critical procedure. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay burn center transfer for appropriate patients
info.t: Major burns (TBSA ≥20%, full-thickness, hands/face/genitalia, inhalation, chemical, electrical) require burn center expertise. Stabilize the airway and vascular access, then transfer — do not attempt definitive wound management in the ED. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat chemical burns without continuous irrigation
info.t: Chemical burns require prolonged irrigation (30–60 min for acids, longer for alkalis) — a brief rinse is inadequate. Alkali burns continue to penetrate tissue well after exposure ends. Check pH of runoff to confirm adequacy. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the last known well time
info.t: IV tPA eligibility is based on time from last known well (LKW), NOT time of symptom discovery. Wake-up strokes and unwitnessed events still qualify for imaging-based protocols if the DWI/FLAIR mismatch or CT perfusion shows viable tissue. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give tPA with BP ≥185/110
info.t: Uncontrolled hypertension before tPA dramatically increases hemorrhagic transformation risk. Bring BP to <185/110 before bolusing — if it cannot be maintained there, do not give tPA. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT aggressively lower BP in untreated ischemic stroke
info.t: Penumbral tissue depends on collateral flow driven by elevated BP. Unless BP >220/120 (or >185/110 if tPA eligible), do not lower pressure — you will extend the infarct. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold large vessel occlusion workup
info.t: Patients with NIHSS ≥6 and proximal deficits should receive CTA head and neck immediately. Missing a large vessel occlusion means missing a thrombectomy candidate — the intervention with the strongest mortality and functional outcome data in all of medicine. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give aspirin or anticoagulants before hemorrhage is excluded
info.t: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in hemorrhagic stroke is catastrophic. Always obtain non-contrast CT before any antithrombotic treatment. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start anticoagulation for AF stroke in the first 24 hours
info.t: Immediate anticoagulation after a large cardioembolic stroke converts ischemic infarct to hemorrhagic infarct. The standard approach delays anticoagulation 4–14 days based on infarct size (the 1-3-6-12 rule). See this node.

After IV alteplase, patients require q15-min neuro checks and blood pressure monitoring for 2 hours, then q30-min for 6 hours. New headache, vomiting, or acute neurological deterioration after tPA = hemorrhagic transformation until proven otherwise — stop the infusion and get a stat CT. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give tPA for NIHSS 0–5 minor strokes without shared decision
info.t: Minor disabling strokes may still warrant tPA, but NIHSS ≤5 non-disabling strokes have a favorable natural history. For minor non-disabling strokes, DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days) is the evidence-based alternative. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for labs before reversing anticoagulation
info.t: In ICH on anticoagulation, empiric reversal should begin as soon as the agent is identified — do not wait for INR, anti-Xa level, or anti-IIa level to return. Hematoma expansion risk is highest in the first 3 hours. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use platelet transfusion for ICH on antiplatelets
info.t: The PATCH trial showed platelet transfusion in ICH patients on antiplatelets leads to significantly WORSE outcomes. Do not reflexively transfuse platelets — it is contraindicated. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT lower BP below SBP 130 in ICH
info.t: Dropping SBP below 130 is potentially harmful in ICH. Target SBP 130–150 for presenting SBP of 150–220. Avoid drops >70 mmHg in the first hour regardless of starting pressure. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use nitroprusside or nitroglycerin for BP control
info.t: These agents are vasodilators that increase cerebral blood volume and raise ICP — the opposite of what is needed in ICH. Use clevidipine, nicardipine, or labetalol instead. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prophylactically prescribe antiseizure medications
info.t: Seizure prophylaxis is NOT recommended in ICH — phenytoin was shown to have no benefit and may worsen outcomes. Treat only witnessed convulsive seizures or EEG-confirmed seizure activity with levetiracetam. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use dabigatran reversal agents for Xa inhibitors
info.t: Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran. For rivaroxaban and apixaban, use 4-factor PCC (andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US) — giving the wrong reversal agent wastes time and money. Confirm the specific agent before ordering reversal. See this node.

Cerebellar hemorrhage >15 mL with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus requires immediate neurosurgical evacuation. EVD alone without posterior fossa decompression risks upward herniation. Rapid deterioration is the rule — act before herniation occurs. See this node.

Even mild coagulopathy (INR >1.3) can drive hematoma expansion. Correct all abnormal coagulation including elevated INR, thrombocytopenia, and uremic platelet dysfunction. Check a full coagulation panel including the specific anticoagulant level. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore ICP crisis signs
info.t: Perihematomal edema peaks at 5–6 days post-ICH — anticipate delayed deterioration. Rising ICP requires osmotic therapy bridge (hypertonic saline bolus), urgent neurosurgical consultation, and consideration of EVD. See this node.

Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (up to 4 mg) or diazepam 0.2 mg/kg IV are the evidence-based doses. Subtherapeutic dosing (e.g., "2 mg of Ativan") is the most common error in SE — inadequate dosing fails to terminate seizures and delays the treatment ladder. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay second-line ASM after BZD failure
info.t: If the seizure persists 5 minutes after adequate BZD, administer a second-line agent (levetiracetam, valproate, or fosphenytoin) within 5–10 minutes. The ESETT trial showed all three have equivalent efficacy — just choose one and give it at full dose. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use phenytoin as first choice in SE
info.t: The ESETT trial demonstrated phenytoin (as fosphenytoin) is equivalent to levetiracetam and valproate but has more adverse effects, drug interactions, and a slower infusion rate. Levetiracetam or valproate are generally preferred first unless specific contraindications exist. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use long-acting paralytics in refractory SE
info.t: Vecuronium and rocuronium abolish motor activity but do not stop electrical seizures — the brain continues to seize even with no visible movement. If you must intubate, use succinylcholine (short-acting) and immediately start continuous EEG monitoring. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start RSE infusions without continuous EEG
info.t: Refractory SE infusions (propofol, midazolam, ketamine) cannot be titrated without continuous EEG — you have no way to confirm seizure suppression or detect breakthrough seizures in a paralyzed/sedated patient. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss metabolic causes before escalating therapy
info.t: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia all cause SE and will not respond to antiseizure medications until corrected. Check a bedside glucose immediately and send full electrolytes and calcium with initial labs. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss eclampsia in a seizing pregnant patient
info.t: Seizure in a pregnant patient should be treated as eclampsia first — magnesium sulfate is the definitive treatment and benzodiazepines are adjunctive. Using BZDs alone without magnesium fails to prevent recurrence. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give valproate in pregnancy or suspected mitochondrial disease
info.t: Valproate is teratogenic (Class X/D) and is contraindicated in pregnancy. It also precipitates acute liver failure in POLG1 mitochondrial disease — use levetiracetam or fosphenytoin in these patients. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge first-time SE without identifying the underlying cause
info.t: New-onset SE mandates an urgent workup: LP (if no mass lesion), MRI brain, metabolic panel, toxicology, and neurology consultation. Discharging without a cause identified exposes the patient to recurrent life-threatening events. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge thunderclap headache without SAH workup
info.t: Up to 5% of SAH patients are missed on initial ED visit — the misdiagnosis rate is highest when the headache is the only symptom (sentinel bleed). Any sudden, severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds requires CT and LP or CTA workup. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on CT alone if it is performed >6 hours after onset
info.t: CT sensitivity for SAH drops significantly after 6 hours as blood breaks down. A negative CT >6 hours after onset requires LP (xanthochromia) or CT angiography to exclude SAH. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT allow BP to spike before aneurysm is secured
info.t: Rebleeding from an unsecured aneurysm is catastrophic, with mortality approaching 70%. Target SBP <160 mmHg from time of diagnosis until the aneurysm is secured surgically or endovascularly. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give NSAIDs for SAH headache
info.t: NSAIDs impair platelet function, which can worsen bleeding in a patient with an unsecured aneurysm. Use acetaminophen and opioids cautiously (impair neuro exam) for pain. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start nimodipine before confirming no hemorrhagic contraindication
info.t: Nimodipine prevents vasospasm and improves outcomes in SAH — but it is a potent vasodilator that can cause dangerous hypotension, especially in already hypotensive patients. Confirm hemodynamic stability and avoid co-administration with other antihypertensives. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antifibrinolytics beyond 72 hours
info.t: Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid reduce rebleeding risk in the very early period but increase the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia and hydrocephalus if continued beyond 72 hours. Definitive aneurysm treatment takes priority over antifibrinolytics. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip ECG and troponin in SAH
info.t: SAH causes ECG changes in 50–100% of patients (QT prolongation, T-wave inversions, ST changes) and neurogenic myocardial injury with elevated troponin. These are neurogenic, not ischemic — do not take the patient to the cath lab. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform aggressive seizure prophylaxis
info.t: Routine prolonged antiseizure prophylaxis in SAH is not recommended — evidence supports short-term use (≤3 days) at most. Phenytoin in particular is associated with worse cognitive outcomes. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT manage SAH at a non-specialized center without transfer
info.t: Outcomes in SAH are significantly better at high-volume centers with dedicated neurovascular teams. Stabilize and transfer — do not attempt definitive aneurysm treatment or complex ICP management at a facility without neurosurgical capability. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay anticoagulation while awaiting cardiology
info.t: Anticoagulation with heparin or a factor Xa inhibitor should begin in the ED as soon as NSTEMI is confirmed. Waiting for cardiology sign-off or cath lab scheduling before starting anticoagulation leaves the culprit lesion unprotected. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat all NSTEMIs the same — emergent PCI is sometimes needed
info.t: Ongoing chest pain, hemodynamic instability, signs of heart failure, malignant arrhythmia, or EF ≤35% are indications for emergent (within 2 hours) invasive strategy. These patients should go to the cath lab immediately, not wait for morning rounds. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give morphine routinely for chest pain
info.t: Morphine delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption by slowing gastric motility and is associated with increased mortality in ACS. Reserve opioids for truly refractory pain and rely on nitrates and oxygen first. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give routine oxygen if SpO₂ ≥90%
info.t: Supplemental oxygen in normoxic ACS patients may increase infarct size through coronary vasoconstriction. Apply O₂ only if SpO₂ <90% or the patient is dyspneic. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give prasugrel to patients with prior stroke or TIA
info.t: Prasugrel is absolutely contraindicated in patients with prior stroke or TIA — the TRITON trial showed a significant net harm in this population due to ICH risk. Use ticagrelor or clopidogrel instead. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use clopidogrel if the anatomy is unknown and CABG is possible
info.t: Clopidogrel requires a 5-day washout before CABG. In patients going to early invasive strategy where anatomy is unknown, ticagrelor (3-day washout) or withholding P2Y12 until anatomy is known are preferred strategies to avoid surgical delay. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss MINOCA as a NSTEMI mimic
info.t: Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries (MINOCA) causes troponin elevation with a culprit mechanism other than plaque rupture (spasm, dissection, embolism, myocarditis). Standard ACS anticoagulation and P2Y12 therapy may not be appropriate — workup determines treatment. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prescribe triple therapy without explicit indication
info.t: Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor + oral anticoagulant (triple therapy) dramatically increases bleeding risk. It is only indicated in very specific scenarios (AF + recent PCI + high thrombotic risk). Most patients require dual therapy or anticoagulant alone. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss posterior STEMI in anterior ST depression
info.t: ST depression in V1–V3 with upright T waves and a prominent R wave is posterior STEMI until proven otherwise. Obtain posterior leads V7–V9 immediately — these patients need emergent reperfusion, not medical management. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss new LBBB without Sgarbossa criteria evaluation
info.t: New LBBB with ongoing ischemic symptoms should be managed as STEMI regardless of whether the LBBB is "new" or "old." Apply Sgarbossa criteria and activate the cath lab when clinical suspicion is high. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give nitroglycerin in suspected RV infarct
info.t: Right ventricular infarct (inferior STEMI with right-sided lead STE) depends on preload to maintain output. Nitroglycerin causes catastrophic hypotension in this setting. Obtain right-sided leads in all inferior STEMIs before giving nitrates. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give oxygen if SpO₂ ≥90%
info.t: Routine supplemental oxygen in normoxic STEMI patients may increase infarct size through coronary vasoconstriction and generation of reactive oxygen species. Apply O₂ only if SpO₂ <90%. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use prasugrel in prior stroke/TIA patients
info.t: Prasugrel is absolutely contraindicated in patients with prior stroke or TIA due to excess ICH risk. Use ticagrelor (180 mg) or clopidogrel (600 mg) instead. Verify this contraindication before loading. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give fibrinolytics without checking contraindications
info.t: Absolute contraindications to lytics include prior ICH, ischemic stroke within 3 months, known intracranial malignancy, aortic dissection, and significant closed head trauma. Giving fibrinolytics in these patients causes catastrophic hemorrhage. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT take STEMI patients to the cath lab within 2–3 hours of fibrinolytics
info.t: Post-lytic angiography should be performed 3–24 hours after fibrinolysis, not within the first 2–3 hours. Early post-lytic intervention is associated with higher rates of bleeding and reocclusion. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold vasopressors in cardiogenic shock out of fear of worsening ischemia
info.t: In cardiogenic shock, coronary perfusion pressure is dependent on MAP. Withholding vasopressors allows hypotension to worsen ischemia. Norepinephrine to maintain coronary perfusion is mandatory while the patient is being prepared for emergent PCI. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay transfer for non-PCI center STEMI patients
info.t: Door-to-balloon time is the most modifiable mortality predictor. If primary PCI is not available at your facility, the correct move is immediate transfer — not fibrinolytics as a substitute for a PCI-capable center with short transfer times. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assess suicide risk in an intoxicated patient
info.t: An intoxicated patient cannot reliably report suicidal ideation or engage in safety planning. Observe until clinically sober, then re-administer the C-SSRS. Documenting "patient denies SI" in an intoxicated patient is medically and legally inadequate. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without a written safety plan
info.t: A verbal safety conversation is insufficient — the patient must leave with a written, personalized safety plan that includes warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts, and 988/crisis line information. The safety plan must be in the chart. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip lethal means counseling
info.t: Means restriction is the single most evidence-based intervention for suicide prevention. Firearms account for 50% of suicides. Ask specifically about firearms, medications, and other means, and create a specific plan for restriction before discharge. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without confirmed outpatient follow-up
info.t: The period immediately following ED discharge is highest risk. A specific appointment — not just a referral — within 24–72 hours must be confirmed before discharge. Patients without confirmed follow-up should be reconsidered for hospitalization. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT leave a high-risk patient unmonitored
info.t: High-risk patients require 1:1 observation, removal of all ligature risks, sharps, and medications from the room, and continuous monitoring. A chart note is not a safety measure. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss suicidal ideation as "attention seeking"
info.t: All expressed suicidal ideation requires structured risk assessment. Prior attempts are the strongest predictor of future attempts — patients with prior high-lethality attempts are at extremely high risk regardless of stated intent at the current visit. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without completing documentation
info.t: Joint Commission NPSG 15.01.01 requires specific documentation elements including validated screening tool used, risk and protective factors identified, lethal means counseling provided, safety plan in chart, and specific follow-up plan. Suicide within 7 days of ED discharge is now a sentinel event. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply adult criteria to adolescent or geriatric patients
info.t: Adolescents and elderly patients have distinct risk profiles and social circumstances that require tailored assessment. Elderly men are at particularly high suicide risk but often underreport ideation. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat severe hyperkalemia before getting an ECG
info.t: The ECG confirms clinical significance — a K+ of 7.5 with a normal ECG likely represents pseudohyperkalemia and should be repeated before treating. A normal ECG in the face of a critical lab value should trigger a repeat specimen. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give temporizing therapy without definitive elimination
info.t: Calcium, insulin, and albuterol shift potassium into cells temporarily — K+ rebounds in 2–4 hours. These measures must always be paired with definitive elimination therapy (diuretics, kayexalate/patiromer, or dialysis). See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give hypertonic bicarbonate (ampules alone) for hyperkalemia
info.t: IV bicarbonate ampules alone are ineffective for hyperkalemia per multiple RCTs — osmotic shifts counteract the K-lowering effect. Use isotonic bicarbonate (3 ampules in 1L D5W) as the resuscitative fluid if alkalinization is desired. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to check and correct magnesium in hypokalemia
info.t: Up to 50% of hypokalemic patients have concurrent hypomagnesemia, which renders potassium repletion refractory. Check and correct Mg before assuming K+ replacement is failing. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use glucose-containing fluids for IV potassium replacement
info.t: Dextrose-containing IV fluids stimulate insulin release, which drives K+ further into cells and worsens hypokalemia. Use glucose-free normal saline for IV potassium administration. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT aggressively replace K+ in hypokalemic periodic paralysis
info.t: In hypokalemic periodic paralysis, the hypokalemia is transcellular redistribution — NOT true depletion. Aggressive K+ replacement causes dangerous rebound hyperkalemia as the attack resolves. Small, carefully titrated doses with close monitoring are required. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss pseudohyperkalemia before escalating treatment
info.t: In vitro hemolysis (most common), prolonged tourniquet time, and extreme leukocytosis or thrombocytosis can all falsely elevate K+. A critical K+ with a normal ECG is pseudohyperkalemia until proven otherwise — repeat the specimen. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give calcium gluconate via peripheral IV at rapid rates without monitoring
info.t: Calcium gluconate in hyperkalemia (3 g IV) should be given over 10 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring. Too-rapid infusion causes bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Calcium chloride requires a large-bore or central line due to high risk of tissue necrosis with extravasation. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT correct hyponatremia faster than 10 mEq/L in 24 hours
info.t: Overcorrection of chronic hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) — an irreversible pontine injury causing locked-in syndrome, quadriplegia, or death. In high-risk patients (Na ≤105, alcohol use disorder, liver disease, malnutrition), limit to ≤8 mEq/L per 24 hours. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay hypertonic saline for severely symptomatic hyponatremia
info.t: Seizures, coma, and respiratory distress from cerebral edema are life-threatening. Give 100 mL of 3% NaCl IV over 10–20 minutes immediately — do not delay for central line placement. Peripheral access is acceptable for boluses. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give normal saline to patients with SIAD
info.t: In SIAD, normal saline is excreted as concentrated urine while the free water is retained — it paradoxically worsens hyponatremia. Fluid restriction, oral urea, or salt tabs with furosemide are the appropriate therapies. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use vaptans (tolvaptan) in hyponatremia
info.t: Vaptans cause unpredictable and rapid sodium correction with a high risk of ODS, carry risk of serious hepatotoxicity, and have no mortality benefit. European guidelines and IBCC explicitly recommend against their use. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT correct hypernatremia faster than 10–12 mEq/L per 24 hours
info.t: Rapid correction of chronic hypernatremia causes cerebral edema, seizures, and herniation as osmoles that accumulated to protect neurons are now washed out. Correct chronic hypernatremia over 48–72 hours. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget potassium correction counts toward sodium correction
info.t: Potassium replacement raises serum sodium — K+ enters cells, displacing Na+ into extracellular fluid. If you give 40 mEq KCl, expect Na+ to rise ~1 mEq/L. Concurrent K+ repletion must be factored into your correction trajectory. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss non-hypotonic causes of hyponatremia
