info.t: Deep neck infections are polymicrobial with obligate anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium). Ampicillin-sulbactam or piperacillin-tazobactam are first-line — monotherapy with a cephalosporin alone is inadequate. See antibiotics node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume cellulitis means no abscess
info.t: Ludwig angina is predominantly cellulitis, but CT often underestimates abscess in DNIs (sensitivity 100%, specificity only 45%). Clinical deterioration after 48–72h of antibiotics mandates surgical reassessment regardless of imaging. See surgical node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay CT for "watchful waiting"
info.t: CT neck with IV contrast is required urgently to delineate the infected space, identify drainable collections, and evaluate for mediastinal extension. Clinical exam alone cannot exclude the "danger space" or carotid sheath involvement. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT extubate early in Ludwig angina
info.t: Swelling resolves over days. Extubating before the cuff leak test is positive risks immediate re-obstruction. Plan for prolonged intubation and ICU airway monitoring. See ICU disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to screen for mediastinitis
info.t: Descending necrotizing mediastinitis carries 40–60% mortality. Any chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema below the clavicles, or rapid sepsis worsening requires CT chest with contrast immediately. See mediastinitis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT anticoagulate Lemierre syndrome routinely
info.t: There is no consensus that anticoagulation improves outcomes in IJV thrombosis from Lemierre syndrome. Reserve it for cavernous sinus extension, progressive thrombosis, or no improvement at 72h on antibiotics. See Lemierre treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT combine IV/IM olanzapine with benzodiazepines
info.t: Parenteral olanzapine plus parenteral benzodiazepines carries a risk of fatal respiratory depression and cardiovascular collapse. Use one or the other — not both parenterally. See young adult agitation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give benzodiazepines to elderly delirium patients
info.t: Benzodiazepines are an independent risk factor for delirium in older adults, cause paradoxical agitation, increase fall risk, and cause respiratory depression. Use low-dose haloperidol or olanzapine instead. See elderly node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give haloperidol or droperidol to Parkinson/Lewy Body patients
info.t: High-D2 receptor blockade from typical antipsychotics can trigger severe, potentially fatal neuroleptic sensitivity reactions and dramatically worsen motor symptoms. Use quetiapine (lowest D2 affinity) instead. See Parkinson's node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antipsychotics for stimulant-induced agitation
info.t: In cocaine or methamphetamine intoxication, antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold, impair thermoregulation, and worsen hyperthermia. Benzodiazepines are the drug of choice. See intox/withdrawal node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prone-restrain a delirious patient
info.t: Prone restraint causes positional asphyxia and has been associated with patient deaths. Always restrain supine with head of bed elevated. Minimum 5-person team is required. See restraints node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip the search for reversible causes
info.t: Delirium is always secondary to an underlying medical problem. Skipping glucose check, hypoxia assessment, and medication review misses life-threatening and easily reversible causes. See rapid reversible node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip QTc monitoring with antipsychotics
info.t: Haloperidol and droperidol prolong QTc. A QTc >500 ms is a contraindication to typical antipsychotics — use olanzapine or benzodiazepines instead. See monitoring node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use physical restraints as first-line management
info.t: Restraints paradoxically worsen agitation and increase injury risk. Verbal de-escalation, environmental modifications, and a show of force (security presence) should precede physical restraint. See safety node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reimplant a primary (baby) tooth
info.t: Reimplanting a primary tooth risks permanent damage to the underlying adult tooth bud, ankylosis, and infection. Always confirm tooth type before any intervention. See primary tooth node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT touch or scrub the root
info.t: The periodontal ligament cells on the root surface are the key to successful reimplantation. Touching, scraping, or drying the root kills these cells and dramatically worsens prognosis. Handle by crown only. See storage node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT store the tooth in water
info.t: Water is hypotonic and rapidly destroys PDL cells. Cold milk (up to 6h), saline (up to 2h), or HBSS (up to 24h) are acceptable media. Dry storage is the worst option. See storage node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for dentist availability if >15–30 min away
info.t: Every minute of dry extraoral time halves reimplantation success. If a dentist is more than 15–30 minutes away, reimplant in the ED immediately. See reimplantation decision node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a rigid splint
info.t: Rigid splinting causes ankylosis of the reimplanted tooth to the alveolar bone. A flexible splint for 2 weeks is the standard of care — it preserves physiologic micromovement that supports healing. See splint node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip CXR if the tooth cannot be found
info.t: A missing tooth can be aspirated into the bronchus, requiring urgent removal. Always obtain CXR (PA and lateral) when the tooth is unaccounted for, especially with any respiratory symptoms. See missing tooth node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip antibiotics after reimplantation
info.t: Doxycycline 100 mg BID × 7 days (adults/children >12y) is first-line. It has anti-resorptive properties beyond just antimicrobial coverage. Amoxicillin is the alternative for younger children. See medications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without a 24–48h dental follow-up
info.t: Even optimal ED management is a bridge — permanent splinting, root canal planning, and monitoring for resorption all require same-week dental evaluation. Failure to arrange follow-up leaves patients at high risk for tooth loss. See follow-up node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reimplant avulsed primary teeth
info.t: Reimplanting a baby tooth risks damaging the underlying permanent tooth bud (20–30% risk with severe trauma) and causing ankylosis. Confirm primary vs. permanent before any reimplantation. See primary avulsion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt to manually pull out an intruded tooth
info.t: Intruded teeth are locked in alveolar bone; forced extraction causes additional trauma and fracture. Management depends on depth — teeth <3 mm are allowed to erupt spontaneously over 4–6 weeks. See intrusion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss an Ellis III fracture as minor dental pain
info.t: Pulp exposure is a dental emergency — the pulp is viable for only 3–6 hours. Apply calcium hydroxide paste immediately and arrange same-day dental referral. Delay results in pulp necrosis and mandatory root canal. See Ellis III node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip CXR when a tooth fragment cannot be located
info.t: An unaccounted tooth or fragment can be aspirated into the bronchus, especially in children and unconscious patients. Obtain CXR (PA and lateral) before discharge in any trauma with a missing dental fragment. See start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a rigid splint for luxation injuries
info.t: Rigid splinting causes ankylosis. Flexible wire-composite or resin-bonded splints for 2 weeks are standard for subluxation and extrusive luxation. Alveolar fractures require 3–4 weeks of semi-rigid splinting by the consulting oral surgeon. See splinting node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore malocclusion after dental trauma
info.t: A bite that "feels off" suggests alveolar fracture, lateral luxation, or significant displacement requiring repositioning. Multiple teeth moving as a unit confirms alveolar fracture — needs same-day oral surgery referral. See alveolar node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge lateral luxation without repositioning
info.t: Lateral luxation has a 77% pulp necrosis rate and the tooth is locked in displaced bone. Firm digital pressure is needed to disengage the bony lock before splinting, or same-day dental referral. See lateral luxation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use phenytoin as first-line seizure prophylaxis
info.t: Magnesium sulfate is far superior to phenytoin for eclampsia seizure prevention — it reduces recurrence by 50% (MAGPIE trial). Phenytoin is reserved only for true magnesium allergy or severe toxicity. See prophylaxis node.

Sublingual nifedipine has unpredictable absorption and can cause precipitous hypotension with uteroplacental insufficiency. Use oral immediate-release nifedipine, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine instead. See nifedipine node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT overlook absent warning signs
info.t: 20% of eclampsia has NO prodromal symptoms, and 16–38% have minimal or no hypertension at seizure onset. Never use the absence of headache or visual changes to exclude eclampsia risk. See warning signs node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give labetalol in asthma or heart block
info.t: Labetalol is first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy but is contraindicated in severe reactive airway disease, 2nd/3rd degree heart block, decompensated heart failure, and bradycardia <60. Use hydralazine as an alternative. See labetalol node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT aggressively fluid-resuscitate eclamptic patients
info.t: Eclampsia patients are at high risk for pulmonary edema. Limit resuscitation to 1–2L max unless there is hemorrhage. POCUS-guided fluid management is strongly preferred. See stabilization node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay delivery for seizure control alone
info.t: Definitive treatment of eclampsia is delivery. Seizure control and BP management are bridges — once the patient is stabilized, delivery planning must begin immediately with OB. See delivery decision node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop magnesium at 24h postpartum
info.t: Eclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum, and the risk of recurrent seizure is highest in the first 48h after delivery. Continue magnesium infusion 24–48h postpartum per protocol. See postpartum node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methadone without verifying OTP enrollment
info.t: Federal law (21 CFR §1306.07) limits ED methadone administration to a one-time dose while arranging OTP referral. Always verify enrollment before giving more than one dose — guest dosing at an unverified clinic dose risks overdose. See guest verify node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methadone with QTc ≥500 ms
info.t: Methadone prolongs QTc in a dose-dependent manner. A QTc ≥500 ms is a high-risk threshold — avoid methadone if possible and obtain cardiology consultation. Always get an ECG when dose >100 mg/day or combining with other QT-prolonging drugs. See QTc risk node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT combine methadone with benzodiazepines
info.t: The combination carries an FDA black box warning for additive respiratory depression and death. If the patient is on benzodiazepines, reassess whether methadone is the right MOUD choice or reduce other CNS depressants first. See monitoring node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume the stated home dose is accurate
info.t: Patients may overreport their dose, OTP records may be unavailable after hours, and tolerance drops during missed doses. If dose is unverified, start at 20–30 mg max (never exceed 40 mg first dose). See unclear dose node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without observing for ≥2–4h after dosing
info.t: Methadone has delayed peak respiratory depression at 2–4h post-dose (much later than other opioids) and a long half-life. Discharging immediately after the dose misses the period of highest overdose risk. See resp depression node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use methadone as first-line if buprenorphine is an option
info.t: Buprenorphine is safer (partial agonist ceiling effect), has no QTc risk, and can be prescribed by ED providers without OTP linkage. Reserve methadone for patients already enrolled in an OTP program. See buprenorphine redirect node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without prescribing naloxone
info.t: Methadone tolerance is dose-dependent and drops rapidly during any missed doses. All patients receiving ED methadone must leave with naloxone and overdose risk counseling — a single adult dose can be fatal to a child. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methadone to actively intoxicated patients
info.t: Active opioid or CNS depressant intoxication is a contraindication to methadone initiation — there is no reliable baseline to judge tolerance. Observe until AMS clears, then reassess MOUD options. See alt approach node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT tilt the head back during active bleeding
info.t: Head tilt causes blood to run posteriorly into the pharynx, increasing swallowing and aspiration risk. The correct position is sitting upright, leaning slightly forward. See initial measures node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip assessment for hemodynamic instability
info.t: Posterior epistaxis can cause significant blood loss that is underestimated because blood is swallowed. Always check vital signs, assess for tachycardia and hypotension, and get a CBC if bleeding is heavy or prolonged. See stability node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT immediately hold anticoagulation for nosebleed
info.t: Antiplatelet agents should generally NOT be held unless there is severe hemorrhage and no recent coronary stent. For warfarin, hold if INR is supratherapeutic. Reversing anticoagulation has serious thrombotic risks. See antiplatelet node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge anterior-packing patients without antibiotics
info.t: Nasal packing creates an anaerobic environment that risks toxic shock syndrome (Staphylococcal). Prescribe cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate for the duration of packing and ensure mandatory ENT follow-up at 24–48h. See discharge with pack node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge posterior-packing patients from the ED
info.t: Posterior nasal packs cause hypoxia, and patients can desaturate rapidly — especially in those with underlying cardiopulmonary disease. Admission for monitoring is mandatory. See posterior disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT cauterize both sides of the septum simultaneously
info.t: Bilateral chemical cauterization of the nasal septum can cause septal perforation. If bilateral cauterization is needed, perform one side and allow healing before treating the other. See anterior cautery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss hypertension as a contributing factor
info.t: Severe hypertension does not cause epistaxis but worsens it significantly. Treat BP >180/110 acutely to reduce rebleeding risk, using short-acting agents. Do not miss hypertensive emergency as a comorbidity. See HTN management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT test extensor function with the wrist flexed
info.t: Wrist flexion passively extends the fingers, masking a complete extensor tendon laceration. Always test with the wrist in neutral or slight extension and compare to the contralateral side. See exam node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss a partial tendon laceration
info.t: A patient with >50% tendon laceration may retain near-normal active extension and appear intact on exam. Direct wound exploration with the finger in flexion is required to exclude partial injury. See exam pearls node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT repair Zone I–II injuries in the ED
info.t: Zones I and II (distal phalanx/mallet finger area) are managed with static extension splinting or surgical repair — not primary ED tendon repair. Acute primary repair in this zone has high complication rates and is deferred to hand surgery. See Zone 1 node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a cutting needle for tendon repair
info.t: Cutting needles traumatize tendon fibers and increase adhesion risk. Use a tapered needle with braided non-absorbable suture (3-0 to 5-0 depending on zone) for all extensor tendon repairs. See repair overview node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT immobilize in finger flexion after repair
info.t: Post-repair immobilization requires the wrist extended and the MCP joint in slight extension — splinting in flexion gaps the repair. The exact position varies by zone; consult the zone-specific splint protocol. See splint types node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay repair beyond 5–7 days
info.t: Optimal outcomes occur with repair within 5 days (97.8% ROM vs. 89.5% if >5 days). If there is a delay, keep the wound clean with loose skin closure, splint, and ensure urgent hand surgery follow-up. See repair overview node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT refer without a splint in place
info.t: All extensor tendon injuries being referred to hand surgery must leave the ED splinted in the appropriate position. An unsplinted injury allows the tendon ends to retract, increasing surgical complexity. See refer node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT draw blood from or put a BP cuff on an AV fistula/graft arm
info.t: Venipuncture and BP cuffs can thrombose a fistula or graft — the patient's lifeline. Always use the contralateral arm. Protecting access is a non-negotiable priority in every ESRD patient. See access main node.

Uremic pericarditis creates hemorrhagic pericardial effusions. Anticoagulation risks hemopericardium and tamponade. Dialyze WITHOUT heparin and consult cardiology for tamponade assessment. NSAIDs are also contraindicated in ESRD. See uremic pericarditis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat hyperkalemia in HD patients without cardiac monitoring
info.t: Severe hyperkalemia in ESRD can cause immediate fatal arrhythmias. Get an ECG at first evaluation to identify peaked T waves, widened QRS, or sine wave patterns — findings that mandate emergent treatment before labs return. See hyperkalemia ECG node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use NSAIDs for pain in ESRD patients
info.t: NSAIDs worsen residual renal function, increase fluid retention, and raise potassium. They are contraindicated in virtually all dialysis-dependent patients, including for uremic pleuritis and pericarditis. See uremia main node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore a clotted or poorly functioning access as "outpatient only"
info.t: A clotted fistula or graft that cannot be salvaged leaves the patient without vascular access for dialysis — an immediate emergency. Contact nephrology urgently; time to intervention determines whether the access can be rescued. See access clotted node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
info.t: Rapid fluid removal and osmolar shifts during first dialysis sessions can cause cerebral edema — headache, nausea, seizures, and coma. Prevent with slow, conservative first sessions and consider mannitol. See uremic encephalopathy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics for suspected catheter sepsis
info.t: Bacteremia in HD patients with tunneled catheters carries high mortality and can cause endocarditis. Start empiric vancomycin (MRSA coverage) plus gram-negative coverage before cultures result. See infection main node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge hyperkalemia in HD patients without dialysis scheduled
info.t: Medical treatment of hyperkalemia in ESRD (insulin/glucose, kayexalate) is a bridge — potassium will rebound because there is no renal excretion. Dialysis must be arranged before discharge or the patient requires admission. See electrolyte disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antipyretics (aspirin or acetaminophen)
info.t: Heat stroke hyperthermia is caused by failed thermoregulation, not fever. Antipyretics are ineffective and aspirin may worsen coagulopathy and DIC — a common fatal complication. Active cooling is the only effective treatment. See recognition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay cooling to complete workup
info.t: Target core temperature <39°C as rapidly as possible — every degree-minute of hyperthermia above 40°C increases neurological injury. Start ice water immersion or evaporative cooling immediately upon recognition, before labs or CT. See cooling start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use succinylcholine for intubation
info.t: Rhabdomyolysis causes hyperkalemia in heat stroke patients. Succinylcholine-induced potassium efflux can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Use rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg instead. See intubation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop cooling at the target temperature
info.t: Stop active cooling at 39°C (102.2°F) — not lower. Core temperature continues to drift down after immersion ends ("afterdrop"). Overcooling to <38°C can cause rebound hypothermia. See cooling endpoint node.

Rhabdomyolysis occurs in virtually all exertional heat stroke cases and is the primary driver of acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia. Check CK every 6–12h; if CK >5,000, target urine output 200–300 mL/hr with aggressive IV fluids. See rhabdo node.

Heat stroke directly activates the clotting cascade and destroys platelets. Check PT/INR, fibrinogen, and platelets early — DIC is a common cause of death. Treat the underlying hyperthermia; DIC typically resolves with cooling. See coags node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge heat exhaustion without reassessment
info.t: Heat exhaustion can rapidly progress to heat stroke with continued exertion or inadequate cooling. Monitor temperature trends, mental status, and ensure it is normal before discharge. See heat exhaustion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use oral, axillary, or tympanic thermometry
info.t: Peripheral thermometers are unreliable in hypothermia and may be falsely normal or falsely low. A rectal or esophageal core temperature probe is mandatory to guide all decisions. See temperature measurement node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT declare death before rewarming to ≥32°C
info.t: "No one is dead until they are warm and dead." Fixed/dilated pupils, muscular rigidity, and prolonged down time are NOT contraindications to resuscitation in hypothermia. Continue CPR until core temp ≥32°C. See arrest termination node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT resuscitate if K+ >12 mEq/L (confirmed)
info.t: A serum potassium >12 mEq/L in a hypothermic arrest patient represents a hard contraindication to resuscitation — there are no documented survivors. Rule out hemolysis artifact before using K+ for termination. See arrest decision node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rewarm the extremities before the trunk
info.t: Warming extremities first mobilizes cold peripheral blood back to the core, causing "afterdrop" — a paradoxical drop in core temperature that can trigger fatal arrhythmias. Always apply warming to the trunk only. See transport details node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT handle hypothermic patients roughly
info.t: Physical agitation of a hypothermic patient — including rough movement during transport — can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Always move patients horizontally, gently, and use mechanical CPR during transport. See CPR node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT defibrillate more than once if core temp <30°C
info.t: The hypothermic heart is refractory to defibrillation below 30°C. Attempt defibrillation once — if unsuccessful, defer repeat attempts until temperature reaches 30°C. Continue CPR and active rewarming. See defib node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give repeated doses of ACLS drugs while severely hypothermic
info.t: Drug metabolism is severely impaired below 30°C and medications accumulate to toxic levels. Standard ACLS drug intervals are inappropriate — withhold or give at extended intervals per hypothermia protocols. See ACLS drugs node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transport to the nearest hospital if ECMO is needed
info.t: Hypothermic cardiac arrest with K+ <12 requires ECMO rewarming for best outcomes. Activate the ECMO team and transport to an ECMO-capable center, even if a closer hospital exists. Continuous mechanical CPR during transport is mandatory. See ECMO transport node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform RSI without a surgical airway backup plan
info.t: When awake intubation is indicated, RSI is contraindicated — paralysis in a patient with structural obstruction risks a cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate emergency. Mark the cricothyroid membrane and have a surgical airway tray open before every attempt. See indications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT lay the epiglottitis patient flat
info.t: Supine positioning in epiglottitis or supraglottitis worsens edema-related obstruction and can trigger complete obstruction. Keep the patient sitting upright and do not use a tongue depressor. See epiglottitis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt awake intubation in an uncooperative patient without DSI
info.t: An agitated, combative patient cannot cooperate with topicalization or scope guidance. Dissociative sedation with ketamine (DSI — Delayed Sequence Intubation) maintains airway reflexes while enabling cooperation. See DSI node.

Excessive secretions coat topical anesthetic and prevent adequate mucosal anesthesia, making the procedure fail. Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg IV (preferred — no CNS penetration) or atropine should be given 10–20 min before topicalization. See antisialagogue node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT pass the scope through active blood or thick secretions
info.t: Active airway bleeding is a relative contraindication to nasal fiberoptic intubation — blood obscures the scope and can be aspirated. In severe epistaxis or airway hemorrhage, use video laryngoscopy or consider surgical airway first. See epistaxis complication node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT advance the ETT without seeing the cords
info.t: "See cords, go" — never advance the endotracheal tube over the scope without directly visualizing the vocal cords and confirming the tip is in the trachea. Esophageal intubation with a nasal approach is catastrophic. See nasal technique node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT over-sedate during awake intubation
info.t: The goal is a cooperative, spontaneously breathing patient — not a sedated one. Too much ketamine or dexmedetomidine eliminates the protective airway reflexes that make awake intubation safe. Titrate to light dissociation only. See sedation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt awake intubation in severe metabolic acidosis without preparation
info.t: A patient compensating severe acidosis with a high respiratory rate may fatally decompensate during even brief apnea. Plan for apneic oxygenation and have a ventilator ready to match the pre-intubation minute ventilation immediately post-intubation. See acidosis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use HFNC as first-line for pure hypercarbic failure
info.t: HFNC provides minimal CO2 clearance and is ineffective for COPD exacerbation or obesity hypoventilation with CO2 retention (pH <7.35, PaCO2 rising). Use NIV (BiPAP) instead. See COPD node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay intubation for a prolonged HFNC trial
info.t: Clinically deteriorating patients on HFNC who are not improving within 1–2h should be intubated early, while still compensating. Delaying for an extended "trial" leads to crash intubation in extremis with higher mortality. See intubation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore the ROX Index
info.t: ROX Index (SpO2/FiO2 ÷ RR) <3.85 at 2–6h predicts HFNC failure with high accuracy. Monitor every 2h and escalate to NIV or intubation when trending downward, not when the patient crashes. See ROX monitoring node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT target SpO2 >96% on HFNC
info.t: Hyperoxia worsens outcomes in ARDS, stroke, and post-cardiac arrest. Target SpO2 92–96% and titrate FiO2 to the minimum needed. Starting FiO2 should be 50–60% for moderate hypoxemia, not 100% for all patients. See titration node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip airborne precautions for COVID or TB patients on HFNC
info.t: HFNC generates aerosols and significantly increases infectious particle dispersion. Use airborne precautions (N95 minimum) for all suspected or confirmed COVID, TB, or other airborne pathogens. See setup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transition directly from HFNC to standard nasal cannula
info.t: Wean HFNC by decreasing FiO2 first, then flow rate. Only transition to standard nasal cannula when tolerating ≤20–30 L/min and FiO2 ≤50%. Abrupt discontinuation risks acute decompensation. See titration node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt intubation without pre-oxygenating on HFNC
info.t: Leave HFNC running at maximum settings during RSI preparation and laryngoscopy. HFNC during apnea provides significant apneic oxygenation, extending the safe apnea window beyond standard pre-oxygenation. See intubation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interview a trafficking patient in front of their companion
info.t: Traffickers frequently accompany victims to the ED and answer on their behalf to prevent disclosure. Always separate the patient from any companion before asking sensitive questions — a companion's refusal to leave is itself a red flag. See separate node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ask accusatory or leading questions
info.t: "Are you being trafficked?" is rarely effective — victims rarely self-identify with that label. Use open-ended, trauma-informed screening questions that build trust without presupposing or labeling their situation. See screening node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT force intervention on an adult who declines help
info.t: Autonomy must be respected — except for minors. Forced intervention on a competent adult who is not ready to leave can increase danger and permanently destroy trust. Provide resources, leave the door open, and document. See not ready node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT release a minor identified as a trafficking victim
info.t: Minors who screen positive for trafficking require mandatory CPS notification and cannot be discharged to an unverified guardian or companion. Consider admission for safety while child protective services are engaged. See minor node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document trafficking details in chart where companion can access
info.t: Documentation should protect the patient — never include details that could identify them to their trafficker if the companion were to view the chart. Use safe language and consult social work on documentation strategy. See documentation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss multiple ED visits as drug-seeking or noncompliance
info.t: Trafficking victims often present repeatedly with injuries, STIs, or "frequent flyer" patterns that get labeled as non-compliance. Multiple visits by young patients with vague complaints or inconsistent histories should trigger a trafficking screen. See red flags node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip universal screening to "preserve the relationship"
info.t: Universal screening for all patients — not just those who fit a stereotype — is the standard. Trafficking victims are of all genders, ages, and demographics. Offering resources universally removes stigma and normalizes the conversation. See universal node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for cardiac arrest to give ILE in LAST
info.t: ILE should be given at the first signs of severe local anesthetic systemic toxicity — seizures refractory to benzodiazepines, significant hemodynamic instability, or any arrhythmia. Waiting for arrest dramatically worsens outcomes. See LAST node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use standard ACLS epinephrine doses in LAST arrest
info.t: High-dose epinephrine (1 mg IV) may worsen arrhythmias and reduce ILE efficacy in local anesthetic toxicity. Start at 10–100 mcg and titrate slowly — ASRA recommends avoiding doses >1 mcg/kg. See CPR modifications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give vasopressin, CCBs, or beta-blockers in LAST arrest
info.t: Vasopressin has been shown to worsen outcomes in local anesthetic toxicity. Calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers are contraindicated — both compound the cardiac depression already caused by the local anesthetic. See CPR modifications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use propofol as the initial treatment for LAST seizures
info.t: Propofol is itself a lipid vehicle and carries cardiac depressant properties. Use benzodiazepines (midazolam) for seizures in LAST. Propofol should be a last resort if benzodiazepines fail and only in hemodynamically stable patients. See CCB/LAST node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT terminate resuscitation early in LAST arrest
info.t: LAST patients have recovered neurologically after >60 minutes of CPR as ILE progressively sequesters the drug. Continue CPR far longer than standard protocols before considering termination. See CPR modifications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay ILE because of egg or soy allergy
info.t: In life-threatening LAST, an egg or soy allergy is NOT a contraindication to ILE. The theoretical anaphylaxis risk is far outweighed by the risk of untreated local anesthetic cardiovascular collapse. See complications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust labs drawn after ILE administration
info.t: ILE causes significant lipemia that interferes with electrolytes, troponin, liver enzymes, and drug levels. Draw critical labs before giving ILE when possible, and note lipemia on all orders. Labs normalize 12–24h after stopping infusion. See lab interference node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge after ILE without monitoring for recrudescence
info.t: As ILE is metabolized over 4–6h, drug levels in tissues can re-equilibrate and toxicity may recur. All patients receiving ILE for LAST require ICU admission for at minimum 12–24h of cardiac monitoring after stabilization. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT perform RSI in suspected laryngeal trauma
info.t: Paralysis removes the patient's spontaneous ventilation and backup airway. If intubation fails after RSI, you face a CICO catastrophe with an injured, distorted airway. Awake tracheostomy is the preferred approach. See airway decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt cricothyrotomy if laryngeal fracture or tracheal separation is suspected
info.t: Cricothyrotomy is contraindicated in laryngeal fracture or cricotracheal separation — it can enter a false passage. Proceed directly to tracheostomy below the level of injury. See cricothyrotomy decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip CT imaging in stable patients
info.t: CT neck with IV contrast is the gold standard and only performed once the airway is secured or confirmed stable. Subtle CT findings can indicate significant occult injury. Do not rely on clinical exam alone. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge asymptomatic patients too early
info.t: Edema and hematoma can progress over hours to days. Even asymptomatic patients with a concerning mechanism need flexible laryngoscopy and at minimum 6-12 hours of observation. See observation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgical repair beyond 48 hours for Grade III-IV
info.t: Early repair (within 24-48 hours) yields 58% good voice outcomes vs 22% when delayed beyond 48 hours. Waiting significantly worsens long-term voice and airway function. See management by grade.
8% of laryngeal trauma patients have associated cervical spine fractures. Maintain c-spine immobilization until imaging clears the cervical spine. See associated injuries.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget esophageal evaluation in penetrating trauma
info.t: Esophageal or pharyngeal injury occurs in 3% of cases and is easily missed. In the OR, perform direct laryngoscopy AND esophagoscopy. A missed esophageal injury can result in mediastinitis. See consults and disposition.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use cricothyrotomy alone for Grade V laryngotracheal separation
info.t: Grade V injuries require emergent tracheostomy BELOW the level of injury. The distal tracheal segment may retract into the mediastinum and must be retrieved. See Grade V management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use vinegar for bluebottle / Portuguese Man-of-War stings
info.t: Vinegar causes nematocyst discharge in Physalia (bluebottle/man-of-war) stings and will worsen envenomation. Use seawater rinse and hot water immersion instead. Vinegar is only appropriate for box jellyfish. See bluebottle management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give 1 mg IV epinephrine for box jellyfish cardiac arrest without antivenom attempt first
info.t: Box jellyfish cardiac arrest requires up to 6 ampoules of CSL box jellyfish antivenom given rapidly IV. Standard ACLS dosing applies, but antivenom is the targeted treatment — administer it early in the resuscitation. See box jellyfish management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss Irukandji syndrome as anxiety
info.t: Irukandji presents with severe hypertension, intense back/limb pain, and the pathognomonic "sense of impending doom" 30-120 minutes after a nearly unnoticed sting. Untreated HTN can cause intracerebral hemorrhage and cardiomyopathy. See Irukandji management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge blue-ringed octopus or cone snail patients prematurely
info.t: Both cause progressive ascending paralysis with intact consciousness. There is no antivenom — treatment is intubation and mechanical ventilation for days. Even a stable-appearing patient can deteriorate rapidly. See octopus management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use freshwater to rinse jellyfish stings
info.t: Freshwater rinses cause osmotic discharge of undischarged nematocysts, worsening envenomation. Always rinse with seawater. See minor jellyfish management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip imaging for stingray wounds near joints or neurovascular structures
info.t: Stingray barbs are retroserrated and may fragment. They are radioopaque on X-ray. Retained barb near a joint or vessel requires imaging (MRI or US for cartilage fragments) and likely surgical removal. See stingray management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use polyvalent snake antivenom for sea snake envenomation
info.t: Polyvalent terrestrial snake antivenom does NOT provide coverage for sea snake myotoxin. CSL sea snake antivenom must be used. Contact poison control early for rare envenomations. See sea snake management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip tetanus and antibiotic prophylaxis for deep stingray wounds
info.t: Stingray wounds carry Vibrio vulnificus risk from marine water contamination. Antibiotics with Vibrio coverage (ciprofloxacin or doxycycline) are recommended for all stingray injuries. See stingray management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rub marine stings with sand or a towel
info.t: Rubbing activates and discharges any remaining attached nematocysts, significantly increasing venom load. Remove tentacles by careful picking after appropriate deactivation (vinegar or seawater). See minor jellyfish management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate with a small ETT
info.t: Massive hemoptysis requires at least an 8.5mm ETT (9.0mm for larger men). A small tube prevents bronchoscopy, endobronchial blocker placement, and adequate suctioning — turning a survivable emergency into a fatal one. See ETT selection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a double-lumen ETT as first-line in the ED
info.t: Double-lumen tubes are difficult to place emergently, have narrow lumens that clog with blood, and cannot accommodate a therapeutic bronchoscope. Only 7% of physicians advocate for initial DLT use. Use a large single-lumen ETT first. See ETT selection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT position the patient bleeding-side UP
info.t: Place the patient in lateral decubitus with the BLEEDING lung DOWN. Gravity prevents blood from flooding the good lung. Getting this backwards can rapidly cause bilateral aspiration and death. See positioning.

Cough is the primary mechanism for clearing blood from the airway. Suppressing it leads to retained blood, airway obstruction, and asphyxiation — death from drowning in the patient's own blood. See recognition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to reverse anticoagulation immediately
info.t: Anticoagulated patients need urgent reversal: warfarin → 4F-PCC + Vitamin K; dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → 4F-PCC (andexanet alfa is no longer marketed in the US). Vitamin K alone is insufficient — it takes 6-12 hours and must be paired with PCC. See coagulopathy assessment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip bronchial artery embolization for definitive control
info.t: BAE has 92-97% technical success and is first-line definitive therapy. Consult IR early — before the patient deteriorates. CT before bronchoscopy improves yield (~75% vs ~50%). See BAE node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use epinephrine bronchoscopic lavage without caution
info.t: Topical epinephrine (1:10,000) instilled bronchoscopically can cause fatal arrhythmia. Use cold saline lavage first; consider vasoconstrictors only when less risky alternatives fail. See cold lavage node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transfer without stabilizing the airway first
info.t: Transferring a patient with massive hemoptysis without a large ETT in place, with the bleeding side unknown, or without TXA started risks airway loss in transit. Stabilize first — intubate, position, start TXA, then transfer. See transfer node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip airborne isolation for any suspected measles case
info.t: Measles has an R0 of 12-18 — it is the most contagious respiratory pathogen known. An exposed, unmasked patient in a waiting room can infect 90% of susceptible contacts. Place the patient in a negative-pressure AIIR immediately, before any workup. See isolation protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for lab confirmation before reporting to public health
info.t: Measles is a nationally notifiable disease requiring SAME-DAY reporting on clinical suspicion alone. Waiting for IgM or PCR results before reporting delays contact tracing and risks outbreak propagation. See public health reporting.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antibiotics or steroids prophylactically
info.t: Prophylactic antibiotics have no benefit and can mask superinfection signs. Steroids may prolong viral shedding. Antibiotics are only appropriate for documented secondary bacterial infection. See supportive care.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT omit Vitamin A for hospitalized or high-risk patients
info.t: Vitamin A reduces measles mortality by 64% overall and 87% in children under 2. It is mandatory for all hospitalized patients and should be given immediately on diagnosis — not after labs return. See Vitamin A dosing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give MMR vaccine as PEP beyond 72 hours after exposure
info.t: MMR PEP is only effective within 72 hours of exposure. After that window (up to 6 days), immune globulin (IGIM or IVIG) is required. Beyond 6 days, no prophylaxis prevents infection. See PEP timing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give MMR to pregnant women or severely immunocompromised patients
info.t: MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression. These patients require immune globulin for PEP. Giving MMR instead can cause serious harm. See MMR PEP eligibility.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without strict home isolation instructions
info.t: Patients are contagious for 4 days before AND 4 days after rash onset. Discharge without explicit 4-day home isolation instructions, including a ban on healthcare facility visits without calling ahead, perpetuates outbreak spread. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the neurologic complication of acute encephalitis
info.t: Measles encephalitis occurs in 1:1,000 cases, carries 25% mortality, and presents 3-10 days after rash onset with fever recrudescence, altered mental status, and seizures. Any encephalopathy in a measles patient is encephalitis until proven otherwise. See encephalitis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT trust pulse oximetry readings in suspected MetHb
info.t: Standard pulse oximetry plateaus at 82-86% regardless of true oxygenation because MetHb absorbs light at both oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin wavelengths. A normal SpO2 does NOT exclude methemoglobinemia — only co-oximetry confirms the diagnosis. See diagnostic workup.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ABG-calculated oxygen saturation to rule out MetHb
info.t: The ABG calculates oxygen saturation from PaO2 using a standard formula, not by measuring MetHb directly. PaO2 is NORMAL in methemoglobinemia, creating a false "saturation gap." Only co-oximetry (venous or arterial) measures MetHb directly. See workup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methylene blue to patients with G6PD deficiency
info.t: Methylene blue requires G6PD-generated NADPH to function. In G6PD deficiency, it not only fails but can paradoxically worsen methemoglobinemia and cause severe hemolytic anemia. Use alternative therapies (exchange transfusion, hyperbaric oxygen). See G6PD alternatives.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT exceed 7 mg/kg total methylene blue dose
info.t: At high doses (>7 mg/kg cumulative), methylene blue itself acts as a methemoglobin-forming oxidant and paradoxically worsens the condition. Limit total dose and space repeat doses by 30-60 minutes. See methylene blue protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give methylene blue too fast
info.t: Infusing methylene blue faster than over 5 minutes causes chest pain. Administer the 1-2 mg/kg dose over at least 5 minutes. Do not push it undiluted as a rapid bolus. See methylene blue protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold methylene blue in a critically ill patient while waiting for G6PD results
info.t: In a critically ill patient with MetHb >30%, the risk of untreated methemoglobinemia far outweighs the risk of proceeding without G6PD status. Treat empirically and monitor for hemolysis. G6PD testing should not delay life-saving therapy. See treatment decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT fail to remove the causative agent
info.t: Methylene blue treats the acute crisis but does not prevent rebound if the offending agent (dapsone, benzocaine, phenazopyridine) is still present or being absorbed. Remove topicals, discontinue medications, and decontaminate as appropriate. See causes node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without confirming declining MetHb on serial co-oximetry
info.t: Dapsone has a very long half-life and can cause rebound methemoglobinemia 4-12 hours after initial treatment. Serial co-oximetry every 2-4 hours is mandatory before safe discharge, especially for dapsone toxicity. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT routinely remove the nail for large subungual hematomas
info.t: Modern evidence shows trephination alone yields equivalent cosmetic outcomes to nail removal and repair, even for hematomas >50% of the nail surface. Remove the nail only if the plate is avulsed, margins are non-adherent, or hematoma cannot be decompressed. See hematoma management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip X-ray for nail bed injuries
info.t: Approximately 50% of nail bed injuries have an associated distal phalanx fracture. A nail bed laceration with an underlying fracture is an open fracture requiring antibiotics and potentially orthopedic involvement. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discard the avulsed nail plate
info.t: The original nail plate is the best biologic splint after repair. Clean it with saline, trim sharp edges, and replace it under the nail fold secured with a mattress suture. Losing it forces use of a substitute stent. See nail fold stenting.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT leave the nail fold unstented after repair
info.t: If the nail fold is not stented after repair, the eponychium adheres to the nail bed (synechiae) and the new nail cannot grow out properly, resulting in a permanently split or absent nail. Always stent with the original nail plate, foil, or silicone sheet. See stenting node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss a Seymour fracture in a child with apparent mallet finger
info.t: A Seymour fracture (physeal fracture of the distal phalanx in a child with the nail plate lying superficial to the eponychium) looks like a mallet finger but is an open fracture requiring nail removal, formal I&D, reduction, and antibiotics. Missing it leads to osteomyelitis. See fracture management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT repair nail bed without magnification if available
info.t: The germinal matrix produces 90% of the nail plate. Imprecise germinal matrix repair under poor visualization leads to permanent split nail, ridging, or absent nail growth. Use loupes or loupe-equivalent magnification whenever available. See repair technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT place amputated fingertip tissue directly on ice
info.t: Direct ice contact causes tissue frostbite, further destroying already compromised tissue. Wrap the amputated part in saline-moistened gauze, place in a sealed plastic bag, then set the bag on ice. Maximize ischemia time with proper technique. See complex injuries.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attribute bruising in a non-mobile infant to accidental trauma
info.t: Bruising in infants who cannot yet roll over is rare (<0.6% accidental). Any bruise in a pre-mobile infant warrants full abuse evaluation. "Those who don't cruise, don't bruise." See recognition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use PECARN rules when abuse is suspected
info.t: PECARN head trauma rules were validated for accidental trauma only. Applying them to suspected abuse cases will result in missed intracranial injuries. All children under 1 year with suspected abuse require head CT regardless of PECARN score. See imaging summary.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip skeletal survey in children under 2 with suspected abuse
info.t: Skeletal survey is mandatory for all children <2 years with suspected abuse. Occult fractures — especially rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions — are highly specific for abuse and will be missed without dedicated imaging. See skeletal survey node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt to "date" subdural hematomas on imaging
info.t: Imaging cannot reliably date subdural hematomas. Attempting to do so in the context of abuse creates false certainty that can be exploited in legal proceedings or lead to diagnostic error. Document what is seen, not when it occurred. See AHT imaging protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without CPS involvement if abuse is suspected
info.t: You are legally required in all 50 states to report reasonable suspicion of abuse to CPS — a diagnosis is NOT required. Discharging a child to an unsafe environment before CPS assessment can result in the child's death. See mandatory reporting.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interview caregivers together or conduct an investigative interview
info.t: Interview caregivers separately and document their accounts using direct quotations. Do NOT conduct an investigative interview — that is CPS's role. Your role is medical evaluation and documentation. See documentation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip labs for bleeding disorders in cases with bruising or ICH
info.t: Coagulopathies (hemophilia, VWD, ITP) can mimic abuse. Always send CBC, PT, aPTT, Factor VIII/IX, and fibrinogen for any unexplained bruising or intracranial hemorrhage. Negative labs do not exclude abuse, but they must be checked. See laboratory evaluation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip a repeat skeletal survey if the initial is negative but suspicion remains high
info.t: Some fractures — especially healing rib fractures and metaphyseal lesions — only become visible during the healing phase 10-14 days after injury. A normal initial skeletal survey does not exclude abuse when suspicion is high. See skeletal survey node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold diagnostic imaging out of fear of fetal radiation
info.t: The teratogenic radiation threshold is 50-100 mGy. Fetal dose from CTPA is approximately 0.1 mGy — 500-1000x below the threshold. Missing PE is far more dangerous than diagnostic radiation. Do not defer imaging in a pregnant patient with concerning symptoms. See diagnostic approach.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use DOACs or warfarin to anticoagulate in pregnancy
info.t: DOACs cross the placenta and are teratogenic. Warfarin in the first trimester causes warfarin embryopathy. LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BID) is the only safe anticoagulant throughout pregnancy — it does not cross the placenta. See anticoagulation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use standard D-dimer cutoffs in pregnancy
info.t: D-dimer rises physiologically throughout pregnancy, making standard cutoffs unreliable. Use the YEARS algorithm with pregnancy-adapted thresholds: 0 criteria + D-dimer <1000 pg/mL excludes PE; otherwise imaging is required. See clinical probability node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold thrombolysis for massive PE with cardiac arrest
info.t: Thrombolysis is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy when maternal life is at stake. Maternal mortality from untreated massive PE approaches 25-65%. tPA does not cross the placenta. The fetus survives only if the mother does. See thrombolysis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use UFH as standard anticoagulation for stable PE in pregnancy
info.t: UFH is reserved for massive PE (where reversibility is needed) and peripartum management. For stable diagnosed PE throughout pregnancy, LMWH is preferred due to predictable pharmacokinetics and no required routine monitoring beyond monthly anti-Xa levels. See LMWH dosing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss dyspnea and tachycardia as "normal pregnancy"
info.t: While dyspnea and tachycardia do occur in normal pregnancy, PE is the leading cause of maternal mortality and must be on the differential for any pregnant patient with these symptoms. Pleuritic chest pain or hemoptysis are highly specific red flags. See presentation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give LMWH within 24 hours of planned delivery or neuraxial anesthesia
info.t: LMWH must be held 24 hours before planned delivery to allow safe neuraxial anesthesia and to prevent peripartum hemorrhage. Regional anesthesia is safe 12-24 hours after the last LMWH dose. See LMWH dosing.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics to wait for cultures or imaging
info.t: In an ill-appearing child with suspected osteomyelitis, empiric antibiotics should start within 1 hour of suspicion. Blood cultures should be drawn first but must not delay treatment — septic hematogenous spread can progress rapidly. See clinical recognition.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss concurrent septic arthritis
info.t: Osteomyelitis and septic arthritis coexist — especially in infants where transphyseal vessels allow spread. A joint effusion adjacent to bone infection requires emergent arthrocentesis. Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency that requires surgical drainage. See septic arthritis assessment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use plain X-rays as the primary tool to rule out osteomyelitis
info.t: X-rays are normal in early acute osteomyelitis — bone destruction only becomes visible 10-21 days after infection onset. MRI is the gold-standard imaging modality with >90% sensitivity and should be ordered when clinical suspicion is moderate to high. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use MSSA-only coverage in sickle cell patients
info.t: Sickle cell osteomyelitis is caused by Salmonella in 50-80% of cases due to functional asplenia and bowel ischemia. Empiric coverage MUST include both S. aureus and Salmonella — typically cefazolin plus a third-generation cephalosporin or a fluoroquinolone. See sickle cell node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss Kingella kingae in children under 5
info.t: Kingella kingae is the predominant cause of osteomyelitis in toddlers and preschoolers. Standard cultures are insensitive. Send synovial fluid and bone aspirate for Kingella PCR in children <5 years — a negative culture does not exclude the diagnosis. See young child antibiotics.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss puncture-wound Pseudomonas osteomyelitis
info.t: A puncture wound through a sneaker carries specific risk for Pseudomonas aeruginosa osteomyelitis of the foot. Standard MSSA coverage will fail. Empiric anti-pseudomonal therapy is required. See special populations.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transition to oral antibiotics before confirming clinical and lab response
info.t: IV-to-oral transition is appropriate only after the patient is afebrile, has clinically improved, and CRP is trending down. Premature oral transition risks treatment failure and progression to chronic osteomyelitis. See oral transition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay orthopedic consultation for multifocal or subacute presentations
info.t: Multifocal osteomyelitis, subperiosteal abscess, or failure to improve in 48-72 hours all require orthopedic consultation. Surgical debridement significantly improves outcomes for aggressive MRSA or subacute/chronic presentations. See surgical consultation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antibiotics for suspected STEC infection
info.t: Antibiotics are contraindicated for suspected STEC — they induce bacterial lysis, releasing massive amounts of Shiga toxin and significantly increasing the risk of HUS. Hold antibiotics unless the child is septic-appearing or stool Shiga toxin is confirmed negative. See antibiotic controversy.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give antimotility agents for bloody diarrhea
info.t: Loperamide and diphenoxylate are absolutely contraindicated in bloody diarrhea. They delay toxin clearance, increase systemic toxin absorption, prolong illness, and are associated with toxic megacolon and increased HUS risk. See antibiotic controversy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on stool culture alone to confirm STEC
info.t: Culture on sorbitol-MacConkey agar detects O157:H7 but misses up to 50% of STEC cases from non-O157 strains. Always order Shiga toxin EIA (or PCR) in addition to culture for any child with bloody diarrhea. See diagnostic workup.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transfuse platelets in HUS without a compelling indication
info.t: Platelet transfusions in typical STEC-HUS can worsen microvascular thrombosis and worsen organ injury. Platelet transfusion is reserved only for life-threatening hemorrhage, CNS hemorrhage, or invasive procedures with platelets <50,000. See transfusion guidelines.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give FFP for typical STEC-HUS
info.t: FFP is not indicated and may be harmful in typical STEC-HUS — it provides additional substrate for microangiopathic thrombosis. FFP is only appropriate for atypical HUS (aHUS) or TTP. See transfusion guidelines.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give NSAIDs for abdominal pain in STEC
info.t: NSAIDs carry renal risk and increase bleeding risk in a patient already at risk for AKI. Use acetaminophen for pain management and avoid opioids where possible (ileus risk). See STEC management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a high-risk child without ensuring daily lab follow-up
info.t: HUS typically develops on days 5-10 of illness. Any STEC-positive child under 5 with bloody diarrhea requires daily CBC, BMP, and LDH through the risk window even if labs are initially normal. A single ED visit is not sufficient follow-up. See monitoring protocol.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ACE inhibitors or ARBs acutely in HUS with AKI
info.t: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in the acute phase of HUS with AKI due to the risk of severe hyperkalemia. Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nicardipine) are preferred for hypertension management. See hypertension management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start chest compressions before rescue breaths in drowning
info.t: Drowning cardiac arrest is a RESPIRATORY emergency — the primary mechanism is hypoxic arrest, not VF. ILCOR guidelines require 5 rescue breaths BEFORE starting compressions. Skipping rescue breaths for a "hands-only CPR" approach will fail this patient. See cardiac arrest node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt Heimlich maneuver to remove water
info.t: Aspirated water cannot be expelled with abdominal thrusts and attempting Heimlich wastes critical time, risks vomiting and aspiration, and delays CPR. Clear visible airway obstruction if present, then proceed with rescue breaths and CPR. See cardiac arrest node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT declare death without fully rewarming a hypothermic drowning victim
info.t: "Not dead until warm and dead." Core temperatures below 28°C cause refractory VF that responds only after rewarming. Withhold medications below 30°C, limit defibrillation to 3 shocks, and arrange ECMO transfer if available. See severe hypothermia node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a truly asymptomatic patient in under 4 hours
info.t: Delayed pulmonary deterioration in drowning typically manifests within 4-8 hours of a symptomatic presentation. True "secondary drowning" does not exist in asymptomatic patients — but ensure the patient is genuinely asymptomatic (SpO2 ≥95% RA) throughout a full 4-hour observation. See ED observation criteria.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give diuretics for drowning pulmonary edema
info.t: Post-submersion pulmonary edema is NOT fluid overload — it results from surfactant washout and alveolar injury. Diuretics will cause hypovolemia without improving the underlying lung injury. See respiratory treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give empiric antibiotics unless sewage water exposure occurred
info.t: Aspiration pneumonitis from drowning is not bacterial and does not require prophylactic antibiotics. Empiric antibiotics are only indicated for confirmed sewage or grossly contaminated water exposure. See ICU monitoring node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attribute altered mental status solely to drowning without ruling out other causes
info.t: AMS following submersion may be due to pre-event seizure, hypoglycemia, head trauma, or toxic ingestion that caused the drowning event. Check glucose immediately and obtain CT head if any concern for trauma or focal neurologic findings. See AMS node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT allow hyperthermia after cardiac arrest resuscitation
info.t: Post-resuscitation hyperthermia significantly worsens anoxic brain injury. Target temperature management (32-34°C) or strict normothermia (36-37.5°C) must be maintained. Fever must be treated aggressively in the ICU post-arrest period. See post-arrest care.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT confuse MSE with MMSE
info.t: The Mental Status Examination (MSE) is a comprehensive 10-component evaluation of psychological state. The MMSE (Mini-Mental State Exam) is a brief cognitive screening tool only. Documenting MMSE score does not fulfill psychiatric assessment documentation requirements. See MSE overview.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document mood as your observation — quote the patient's exact words
info.t: Mood is the patient's SUBJECTIVE description — always document in quotes (e.g., "I feel empty"). Affect is your OBJECTIVE observation of emotional expression. Confusing the two produces a legally and clinically inaccurate assessment. See mood documentation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip asking directly about suicidal ideation
info.t: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea. Ask every patient directly: "Have you had thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?" and "Do you have a plan? Do you have access to the means?" Passive screening only misses high-risk patients. See safety assessment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a patient with active SI and a plan without psychiatric consultation
info.t: Active suicidal ideation with a specific plan and means requires immediate 1:1 observation, means removal, and psychiatric consultation for inpatient risk assessment. Discharging such a patient with only a phone number is medically and legally indefensible. See active SI node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attribute psychiatric symptoms to mental illness without ruling out organic causes
info.t: New-onset psychosis, altered mental status, and behavioral changes can be caused by thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, hepatic encephalopathy, neurosyphilis, CNS infection, or medication toxicity. Always consider labs and CT before attributing to primary psychiatric illness. See laboratory considerations.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document vague affect descriptions — be specific
info.t: Phrases like "patient seems sad" are legally inadequate. Document affect using specific dimensions: intensity (flat/blunted/normal/exaggerated), range (restricted/broad), congruence (mood-congruent/incongruent), and appropriateness to content. See affect documentation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interview a patient with homicidal ideation alone
info.t: Always ensure staff safety first. For patients endorsing homicidal ideation, have security at bedside, do not interview alone, and perform a weapon search per hospital protocol. Assess for identifiable targets — Tarasoff duty may apply. See homicidal ideation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT copy-paste MSE templates without individualizing to the patient
info.t: Template-cloning psychiatric documentation is a major medicolegal risk. Each MSE must reflect the actual encounter — use standardized terminology as a reference guide, but every entry must specifically describe THIS patient at THIS visit. See MSE overview.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document "passive suicidal ideation" without further characterization
info.t: Passive SI ("I wish I was dead") and active SI with plan ("I want to overdose on my pills tonight") have very different risk implications. Always specify: passive, active without plan, active with plan, or active with plan AND intent. See thought process and content.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss command auditory hallucinations
info.t: Command hallucinations directing violence toward self or others represent an immediate safety concern requiring 1:1 observation and psychiatric consultation. Always ask specifically: "Are the voices telling you to do anything?" See perceptions and cognition.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document flat and blunted affect interchangeably
info.t: Flat affect means ABSENT emotional expression. Blunted affect means significantly DIMINISHED but not absent. These terms carry different diagnostic weight — flat affect is more associated with schizophrenia; blunted with depression and antipsychotic effects. See appearance and behavior.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT conflate poor insight with lack of capacity
info.t: A patient with poor insight into their psychiatric illness (anosognosia) may still retain decision-making capacity. Capacity requires the ability to express a choice, understand information, appreciate its application, and reason — not simply agreeing with the treatment plan. See insight, judgment and risk.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT document circumstantial and tangential thought process as equivalent
info.t: Circumstantial thought eventually reaches the point but with excessive detail. Tangential thought never reaches the point — it derails to unrelated topics. These reflect different degrees of disorganization and different diagnostic implications. See thought process content.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT classify mood-incongruent affect without clinical significance
info.t: Mood-incongruent affect (laughing while describing loss, smiling while recounting a suicide plan) is a red flag for psychosis or significant dissociation. It must be specifically documented and flagged in the risk formulation — it is not simply unusual demeanor. See speech and mood documentation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give 1 mg IV epinephrine to a patient with a pulse
info.t: The standard cardiac arrest epi dose (1 mg IV) is 100x the push-dose pressor dose (10 mcg). Giving 1 mg to a patient with a pulse causes severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, and myocardial ischemia. This is a 61-fold dosing error compared to IM dosing. See indications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use push-dose pressors as definitive treatment
info.t: Push-dose pressors are a bridge — they buy time while a continuous vasopressor infusion is prepared or a central line is placed. They must be transitioned to a continuous drip within 10-15 minutes. Using repeated push doses indefinitely instead of starting an infusion delays definitive care. See transition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use phenylephrine for bradycardic hypotension
info.t: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 vasoconstrictor that can reflexively worsen bradycardia. It is contraindicated when bradycardia is contributing to hypotension. Use push-dose epinephrine (combined alpha/beta) for bradycardic hypotension. See agent selection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip labeling all push-dose syringes clearly
info.t: Epinephrine (10 mcg/mL) and phenylephrine (100 mcg/mL) are prepared in identical-looking syringes and administered during resuscitation under high stress. An unlabeled or mislabeled syringe can result in a 10x dosing error. Label every syringe before use. See safety node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use phenylephrine in patients with low cardiac output
info.t: Phenylephrine causes pure vasoconstriction and increases afterload, which decreases cardiac output. In cardiogenic shock, septic shock with impaired contractility, or post-intubation hypotension, push-dose epinephrine (with beta-1 inotropic effects) is strongly preferred. See phenylephrine indications.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat peri-intubation hypotension with fluids alone
info.t: Fluid boluses take 5-10 minutes to circulate and may be insufficient for hypotension from vasoplegia induced by induction agents. Have push-dose epinephrine drawn and ready BEFORE initiating RSI so treatment can begin within seconds of hypotension onset. See peri-intubation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give push-dose norepinephrine via peripheral IV without confirming patency
info.t: Peripheral extravasation of norepinephrine causes severe tissue necrosis. Confirm IV patency before administration and monitor the site closely. Peripheral administration is acceptable as a bridge but requires a fast-flowing, recently placed line. See norepinephrine peripheral node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT repeat push-dose pressors without addressing the underlying cause
info.t: If two doses of push-dose pressor provide only transient response, aggressively reassess: Is there hypovolemia? Obstructive cause? Cardiogenic component? Simply repeating doses without identifying and treating the cause delays definitive management. See troubleshooting node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT insert the needle deeper than 8-10 mm
info.t: The carotid artery lies 2.5-4 cm posterior and lateral to the tonsil. Inserting the needle beyond 10 mm risks catastrophic carotid artery injury. Mark the syringe or use a commercial depth limiter before every aspiration attempt. See aspiration technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT drain a PTA without first using Color Doppler to identify the carotid
info.t: In rare cases the carotid artery is displaced medially (medially displaced carotid). Always activate Color Doppler on POCUS before any drainage to confirm the location of the pulsatile vessel before committing to a drainage site. See POCUS technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt drainage without confirming abscess on ultrasound
info.t: Clinical exam alone has only ~75% sensitivity for PTA vs cellulitis. Draining peritonsillar cellulitis is unnecessary trauma with no benefit. Intraoral POCUS has 91% sensitivity for confirming a drainable collection before any procedure. See ultrasound node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT suture the incision after I&D
info.t: The PTA cavity must be left OPEN after incision and drainage for continued dependent drainage — the abscess heals from the inside out over 3-5 days. Suturing the incision traps residual pus and guarantees recurrence. See I&D technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give penicillin alone for PTA antibiotics
info.t: PTA is polymicrobial, including anaerobes that are frequently penicillin-resistant. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (875 mg BID x 10-14 days) is first-line for adequate anaerobic coverage. Penicillin or amoxicillin alone is inadequate. See antibiotic selection.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip dexamethasone — give it before or during the procedure
info.t: Single-dose dexamethasone (10 mg IV/IM) significantly reduces pain, trismus, and recovery time. It is most effective when given before the procedure. There is no increased infection risk from a single steroid dose. See corticosteroids node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without mandatory ENT follow-up within 24-36 hours
info.t: Reaccumulation occurs in 2-15% of PTAs. ENT or PCP follow-up within 24-36 hours is mandatory to confirm adequate drainage and healing. Failure to arrange this follow-up means a recurrent abscess may not be caught before it causes airway compromise. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss signs of deep neck space extension requiring CT
info.t: Parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal extension can cause descending mediastinitis — a life-threatening complication. Signs include severe trismus, inability to extend the neck, sepsis, or a bulge below the angle of the jaw. These patients need CT, not needle aspiration. See disposition decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip vector change after 3 failed shocks
info.t: Standard anterolateral pad position may deliver insufficient energy through scar or obesity. Switch to AP position (left parasternal + left infrascapular) before escalating to a second defibrillator — it's faster and may be sufficient alone. See vector change node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use high-dose epinephrine routinely
info.t: High-dose epinephrine in VF/VT is Class 3: No Benefit per 2025 AHA. Excessive catecholamines actually impair defibrillation and worsen post-ROSC myocardial dysfunction. Stick to 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 min. See epinephrine timing node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay searching for reversible causes
info.t: Hyperkalemia, toxins, PE, and tension pneumothorax are all correctable causes of refractory VF. Treating the underlying cause is what allows defibrillation to succeed — VF caused by hyperK will not respond to shocks alone. See H's and T's node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give amiodarone in magnesium-responsive VF
info.t: If TdP or hypomagnesemia is suspected, give magnesium sulfate 2 g IV first, followed by a continuous magnesium infusion. Amiodarone is appropriate for VF/pVT but is contraindicated in TdP — always verify QTc and exclude torsades before choosing amiodarone. See antiarrhythmic selection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold esmolol out of fear of bradycardia
info.t: After 3 shocks + 3 mg epinephrine + 300 mg amiodarone, esmolol may dramatically improve ROSC rates by reducing catecholamine-driven VF threshold elevation. Its very short half-life (~9 min) makes it safe to trial. See esmolol protocol node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT activate ECPR too late
info.t: The window for ECPR closes fast — collapse to ECMO flow must occur within 60 minutes. Waiting to see if "one more round of ACLS works" before calling the ECMO team is a common fatal delay. Activate simultaneously with ongoing resuscitation if criteria are met. See ECPR assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt DSD without two operators
info.t: Double sequential defibrillation requires two defibrillators and two operators delivering near-simultaneous shocks (<1 second apart). One operator attempting both machines in sequence negates the benefit and risks equipment damage. See DSD setup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use pure beta-blockers in cocaine-associated VF
info.t: Cocaine causes unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction when beta receptors are blocked, precipitating severe hypertension, coronary spasm, and worsening VF. Avoid pure beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, esmolol). Mixed alpha/beta agents (labetalol, carvedilol) have conflicting evidence and are not first line. Benzodiazepine comes first, then sodium bicarbonate. See toxin-induced VF node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT call no pulse "cardiac arrest" without Doppler
info.t: Continuous-flow LVADs produce minimal or zero pulsatility — absence of a palpable pulse is NORMAL. Checking for pulse with a standard technique will falsely trigger a cardiac arrest response. Always use Doppler to measure MAP in LVAD patients. See VAD start node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT manage any VAD visit without calling the VAD coordinator
info.t: VAD coordinators know the patient's baseline parameters, anticoagulation targets, and device history. Missing this call leads to treating numbers out of context — what looks like "high flow" may be normal for that patient. Call immediately, every visit, no exceptions. See VAD coordinator node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore absence of pump hum
info.t: A missing pump hum means the pump is not running — this is a critical emergency. The patient now depends only on severely impaired native cardiac function. Immediately troubleshoot connections and power before reaching for vasopressors. See no-hum node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT clamp the outflow graft
info.t: Clamping the LVAD outflow graft causes acute, severe aortic regurgitation and immediate cardiogenic shock. This is never an appropriate intervention regardless of circumstances. Emergent transfer to the VAD center is the correct action. See no-hum node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT allow MAP to exceed 90 mmHg
info.t: Hypertension in LVAD patients dramatically increases hemorrhagic stroke risk and reduces pump efficiency by increasing afterload. Target MAP is 70–80 mmHg. Do not use standard automated BP cuffs — use Doppler. See MAP check node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transfuse non-irradiated blood products
info.t: VAD patients require ONLY leukoreduced, irradiated blood products. Using standard blood products causes HLA allosensitization that may permanently disqualify the patient from future heart transplantation. See active bleeding node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order MRI for a VAD patient with stroke
info.t: MRI is absolutely contraindicated in all current LVAD patients. The magnetic field will damage the pump electronics and is immediately life-threatening. For stroke workup use CT head and CTA head/neck only. See VAD stroke node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT increase pump speed during a suction event
info.t: When the LV is too empty and a suction event occurs, increasing pump speed worsens the problem by pulling the septum harder against the inflow cannula. Give a 250–500 mL volume challenge first and assess with bedside echo. See suction event node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use IV beta-blockers for VAD hypertension
info.t: Beta-blockers reduce native cardiac contractility in patients whose hearts are already severely impaired. For acute VAD hypertension, use hydralazine PO or IV nicardipine/clevidipine. See VAD hypertension node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use normal saline without watching for acidosis
info.t: Large volumes of NS cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) which counteracts urine alkalinization goals and worsens tubular myoglobin precipitation. Lactated Ringers is preferred for rhabdomyolysis — the 4 mEq/L potassium does NOT clinically worsen hyperkalemia, contrary to common belief. See fluid choice node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT target urine output less than 1 mL/kg/hr
info.t: Inadequate fluid resuscitation is the most common cause of AKI in rhabdomyolysis. The target is 1–3 mL/kg/hr (200–300 mL/hr) — not "adequate urine." Patients require a Foley catheter and aggressive rate adjustments. CK >15,000 carries a 5–14% dialysis rate. See fluid resus node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT aggressively replace asymptomatic hypocalcemia
info.t: Early hypocalcemia in rhabdomyolysis is caused by calcium depositing into injured muscle — it is protective, not dangerous. Aggressive IV calcium replacement worsens heterotopic calcification and may not even raise serum levels. Only treat symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, QT changes). See hypocalcemia node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay fasciotomy when compartment syndrome is present
info.t: Crush injury patients with pain disproportionate to exam, paresthesias, and compartment pressure >30 mmHg (or delta pressure <30 mmHg) require urgent fasciotomy. A 6-hour delay leads to irreversible muscle necrosis. Do not wait for complete pressure measurements if clinical suspicion is high. See compartment eval node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on bicarbonate for urine alkalinization
info.t: Multiple RCTs and a 2025 meta-analysis show urine alkalinization with bicarbonate does NOT significantly prevent AKI or reduce dialysis rates compared to fluids alone. Aggressive LR resuscitation is the evidence-based priority — bicarbonate is only for severe acidosis (pH <7.1). See bicarbonate evidence node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore the statin medication list
info.t: Statin-induced rhabdomyolysis is severely worsened by fibrate combinations, CYP3A4 inhibitors (cyclosporine, macrolides, azoles), and high-intensity formulations. Stop the statin immediately and screen for drug interactions. See drug-induced node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give pure beta-blockers in cocaine-induced rhabdomyolysis
info.t: Cocaine-associated sympathomimetic excess causes rhabdomyolysis through hyperthermia and vasoconstriction. Pure beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, esmolol) cause unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, worsening both the cocaine toxidrome and muscle ischemia. Mixed alpha/beta agents (labetalol, carvedilol) have conflicting evidence and are not first line. Benzodiazepines and aggressive cooling are the correct approach. See drug-induced node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay joint aspiration to start antibiotics
info.t: Joint fluid Gram stain and culture are essential for guiding therapy — they cannot be interpreted after antibiotic administration.
