Aspiration must precede antibiotics unless the patient is septic and critically unstable. Diagnosis without synovial fluid analysis leads to empiric therapy that may miss atypical organisms. See workup overview node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on synovial WBC alone to exclude septic arthritis
info.t: Synovial WBC >50,000 is classically cited, but septic joints can have lower counts — particularly in immunocompromised patients, early infection, and gonococcal arthritis (which can have WBC <20,000). Clinical suspicion and culture results drive the diagnosis. See synovial fluid node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss gonococcal arthritis in sexually active patients
info.t: Gonococcal arthritis is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active adults under 40. It presents with a migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and sometimes a characteristic rash — not always a monoarthritis. Culture yield is low; treat empirically if suspected. See gonococcal node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget prosthetic joint criteria
info.t: Prosthetic joint infections require different empiric antibiotics and different surgical management than native joints. Never treat a prosthetic joint infection the same as a native one without orthopedic consultation. See prosthetic joint node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prescribe oral antibiotics without drainage for purulent joints
info.t: Purulent septic arthritis requires mechanical drainage — either serial aspiration or surgical washout — in addition to antibiotics. Antibiotics alone are insufficient; pus under pressure causes cartilage destruction within hours. See drainage node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the diagnosis after prior antibiotic treatment
info.t: Patients who received partial antibiotic courses before presentation will have falsely reassuring synovial cultures. Clinical features still indicate septic arthritis — do not let a negative culture talk you out of the diagnosis when WBC and clinical features are compelling. See prior antibiotics node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without orthopedics consultation
info.t: All confirmed or strongly suspected septic arthritis requires orthopedics consultation and admission for surgical assessment and IV antibiotics. Outpatient management is not appropriate for purulent native joint infections. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt reduction without a pre-reduction X-ray
info.t: Fracture-dislocations (humeral neck fracture, Hill-Sachs lesion, bankart fracture) require modified technique or orthopedic consultation before manipulation. Reducing a shoulder with an unrecognized proximal humerus fracture can convert a stable fracture into a displaced one or cause neurovascular injury. See imaging decision node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip a neurovascular exam before AND after reduction
info.t: Axillary nerve injury (C5-C6 dermatome — lateral deltoid numbness) occurs in up to 42% of anterior dislocations. Documenting neurovascular status before reduction establishes baseline and ensures post-reduction deficits are recognized and not missed. See neurovascular exam node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use procedural sedation unnecessarily for first-time dislocations
info.t: Scapular manipulation and the Cunningham technique achieve >80% success rates without any analgesia or sedation when performed correctly. Intra-articular lidocaine injection is an effective alternative to procedural sedation. Reserve PSA for failed attempts or extremely anxious patients. See analgesia choice node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt reduction of a fracture-dislocation without consultation
info.t: Greater tuberosity fractures, surgical neck fractures, and Bankart lesions found on imaging change the management plan entirely. Forced reduction can displace fragments into the joint, damage the rotator cuff insertion, or injure the axillary artery. Get orthopedics on the phone first. See fracture-dislocation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT immobilize in internal rotation for first-time dislocators
info.t: Traditional slings in internal rotation do NOT reduce recurrence risk and may worsen outcome. Evidence supports external rotation bracing (arm at side, palm forward) for 3 weeks to reduce recurrence, particularly in young patients. Counsel on recurrence rates at the time of discharge. See immobilization node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without post-reduction X-ray
info.t: Post-reduction imaging confirms concentric reduction and identifies occult fractures only visible once the humeral head is back in position. Sending a patient home without post-reduction films misses this safety check entirely. See post-reduction node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss a posterior dislocation
info.t: Posterior dislocations are commonly missed on AP X-ray — the "light bulb sign" (symmetric humeral head) is subtle and often overlooked. Posterior dislocations cause an arm fixed in internal rotation and are associated with seizures and electrocution. When in doubt, obtain an axillary view. See X-ray findings node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT catheterize urethral trauma without a retrograde urethrogram
info.t: Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal ecchymosis, high-riding prostate, or a pelvic fracture mechanism all indicate possible urethral injury. Blind Foley catheterization through a urethral disruption converts a partial tear into a complete one. Get a retrograde urethrogram first; call urology for suprapubic catheter if disrupted. See urethral trauma node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss cauda equina syndrome as the cause of retention
info.t: New urinary retention in a patient with back pain, saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, or fecal incontinence is a surgical emergency — not a BPH problem. Emergent MRI spine and neurosurgery consult are required. Time to decompression determines neurologic recovery. See neuro emergency node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT drain more than 1000 mL immediately in chronic retention
info.t: Rapid decompression of a chronically overdistended bladder (>800–1000 mL) can cause hematuria, reflex hypotension, and post-obstructive diuresis. Drain to 500–1000 mL, clamp 15–30 minutes, then continue. Place a Foley for ongoing monitoring in high-volume retention. See high-volume node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip tamsulosin at the time of catheterization
info.t: Alpha-blockers started at the time of catheter placement significantly improve the trial-without-catheter (TWOC) success rate. Discharging a BPH patient with a catheter and no alpha-blocker leads to a failed TWOC and unnecessary return visits. See BPH medications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss post-obstructive diuresis in high-volume retention
info.t: Post-obstructive diuresis (>200 mL/hr urine output after decompression) is a medical emergency that requires IV fluid replacement at 50–75% of hourly output. Patients can become severely volume-depleted, hyponatremic, and hypotensive if sent home or watched passively. See POD management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to review the medication list
info.t: Anticholinergics, opioids, antihistamines, alpha-agonists (decongestants), TCAs, and antipsychotics are all common causes of medication-induced urinary retention. Discharging a patient without identifying and stopping the offending agent guarantees recurrence. See causes node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give NSAIDs for pain in viral myositis
info.t: NSAIDs are contraindicated in viral myositis because they reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis and impair the renal blood flow needed to safely clear myoglobin. In a patient already at risk for AKI, NSAIDs can precipitate acute tubular necrosis. Use acetaminophen for analgesia instead. See pain management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a child with BACM without checking CK
info.t: Most children with BACM resolve without complication, but CK >10,000 or myoglobinuria flags a subset at risk for AKI who need admission and IV fluids. Never diagnose "benign" myositis without verifying CK level. See pediatric high risk node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use diuretics to increase urine output in rhabdomyolysis
info.t: Diuretics worsen hemoconcentration, increase myoglobin concentration in tubules, and raise VTE risk in an already immobilized patient. Urine output goals are achieved through aggressive IV fluid resuscitation alone. See rhabdo treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss Guillain-Barré syndrome masquerading as myositis
info.t: GBS can present with leg weakness following a viral illness — exactly the same context as BACM. Ascending weakness (proximal > distal, then spreading up), areflexia, and cranial nerve involvement are the key differentiators. Missing GBS and discharging the patient is a catastrophic error. See peds exclusion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold oseltamivir in confirmed influenza myositis
info.t: Influenza is the most common cause of viral myositis. Oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptom onset reduces viral replication, shortens illness duration, and may reduce the severity of the myositic process. It should not be withheld in admitted patients with influenza-associated myositis regardless of timing. See influenza node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reassure parents based on CK level alone in BACM
info.t: Pediatric BACM can have markedly elevated CK (sometimes >50,000) with an excellent prognosis, while adults with similar CK levels have much higher AKI risk. The pediatric rhabdomyolysis threshold is less aggressive — but only for classic BACM presentations, not for ill-appearing children. See rhabdo threshold node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rule out shunt malfunction based on normal imaging
info.t: Chronically shunted ventricles may have lost compliance and will NOT dilate despite rising ICP. Normal CT and normal shunt series do not exclude malfunction. If clinical suspicion is high — headache, vomiting, lethargy, altered mental status — neurosurgery consultation is mandatory. See imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt a shunt tap without neurosurgery
info.t: Shunt taps are a neurosurgical procedure with specific sterile technique requirements and risks of introducing infection or causing hardware damage. An emergency physician should never attempt to tap a shunt. Get neurosurgery to the bedside. See shunt tap indications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss the parent or caregiver who says "this feels like a malfunction"
info.t: Caregivers of shunted patients are highly accurate at identifying malfunctions — they have seen it before. Caregiver report of "acting like the last malfunction" should significantly raise clinical suspicion and lower your threshold for neurosurgery consultation, even with initially reassuring imaging. See presentation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay ICP reduction when herniation signs are present
info.t: Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations), pupil dilation, or posturing indicate impending herniation. Immediate ICP reduction with mannitol or hypertonic saline is indicated while neurosurgery is activated — do not wait for imaging to return first. See emergent ICP node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on shunt pumping to assess function
info.t: Manually compressing and releasing the shunt reservoir (pump test) has poor sensitivity and specificity. A "normal" pumping shunt does not exclude malfunction. This exam can be misleading in both directions and should never be the primary basis for clearing a patient with symptoms. See physical exam node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start antibiotics before blood cultures in suspected shunt infection
info.t: Shunt infections require identification of the causative organism to guide prolonged antibiotic therapy and hardware revision decisions. Starting empiric antibiotics before blood cultures renders culture results uninterpretable and complicates management. See infection workup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT overlook abdominal symptoms in VP shunt patients
info.t: The distal peritoneal catheter can cause abdominal pseudocysts, ascites, bowel obstruction, peritoneal irritation, and catheter migration into abdominal viscera. Abdominal pain in a shunted patient is a VP shunt problem until proven otherwise. See imaging strategy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold naloxone in xylazine overdose
info.t: Xylazine itself is not reversed by naloxone, but 95% of xylazine exposures involve fentanyl co-ingestion. Withholding naloxone because "it won't work" will miss the fentanyl component and allow the patient to die from opioid-induced respiratory arrest. Always give naloxone. See naloxone node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT titrate naloxone to wakefulness in xylazine OD
info.t: Unlike pure opioid overdose, xylazine causes persistent sedation that does NOT resolve with naloxone — titrating to wakefulness will require dangerous naloxone doses that precipitate acute withdrawal and aspiration risk. Titrate to respiratory rate >12 and adequate airway protection, then stop. See naloxone node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use atropine for xylazine-induced bradycardia
info.t: Xylazine causes central alpha-2 agonist bradycardia + peripheral vasoconstriction. Atropine blocks the bradycardia but not the vasoconstriction, resulting in a hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Use IV fluids and supportive care; only treat hemodynamically significant bradycardia with caution. See bradycardia node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT aggressively debride xylazine wounds
info.t: Xylazine-associated wounds (XAW) contain islands of viable tissue within necrotic-appearing areas. Aggressive debridement destroys this healing potential and worsens outcomes. These wounds are NOT necrotizing fasciitis. Staged wound care with TMP-SMX for MRSA coverage is the standard approach. See stage 1 wound node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send standard hospital tox screen and call it done
info.t: Xylazine is NOT detected on standard urine immunoassay drug screens. A negative urine drug screen does not exclude xylazine. Forensic GC-MS/LC-MS confirmation is required for definitive detection. Treat clinically based on the OA2A toxidrome. See OA2A toxidrome node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore xylazine withdrawal as a distinct syndrome
info.t: Xylazine withdrawal includes severe anxiety, agitation, tachycardia, and diaphoresis that is distinct from — and additive to — opioid withdrawal. Standard MOUD protocols alone will not control xylazine withdrawal. Clonidine 0.1–0.3 mg PO q4–6h is first-line; hold if SBP <90 or HR <50. See withdrawal treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss xylazine wounds remote from injection sites
info.t: Unlike typical injection site wounds, xylazine wounds can appear anywhere on the body — even in patients who smoke or snort the drug rather than inject it. Mechanism is systemic vasoconstriction and direct tissue cytotoxicity, not local injection injury. Full skin inspection is mandatory. See wound assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use VV-ECMO for cardiogenic shock
info.t: VV-ECMO provides oxygenation and CO₂ removal only — it provides zero hemodynamic support. A patient with cardiogenic shock placed on VV-ECMO will continue to deteriorate hemodynamically despite excellent oxygenation. If there is any doubt about cardiac function, choose VA-ECMO. See ECMO selection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay ECPR activation in refractory arrest
info.t: For ECPR to be successful, CPR time to ECMO flow must be under 60 minutes and no-flow time under 5 minutes. Waiting to see if ACLS resolves the arrest before calling the ECMO team is a fatal delay. Activate the team simultaneously with ongoing resuscitation. See ECPR node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT initiate VA-ECMO in severe aortic regurgitation
info.t: VA-ECMO generates retrograde aortic blood flow. In the setting of severe AR, this retrograde flow dramatically increases left ventricular diastolic volume and pressure, causing acute LV distension and pulmonary edema — the exact opposite of the intended support. This is an absolute contraindication. See contraindications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss Harlequin syndrome in VA-ECMO patients
info.t: Harlequin (differential hypoxia) syndrome occurs when the ECMO provides oxygenated blood to the lower body via the femoral artery, but native cardiac function is pumping deoxygenated blood to the coronary arteries and brain. Upper body cyanosis with lower body pink = LV failure on VA-ECMO requiring urgent intervention. See Harlequin node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT put a patient on ECMO without prognostic scoring
info.t: RESP score >3 predicts 75% VV-ECMO survival; RESP score <-2 predicts only 18% survival. Initiating ECMO in patients with non-reversible underlying disease (metastatic cancer, severe chronic organ failure, septic shock without reversible cause) leads to futile care and iatrogenic suffering. Use prognostic tools to guide candidacy decisions. See scores node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT increase recirculation by raising VV-ECMO flow without repositioning cannulas
info.t: In VV-ECMO, recirculation (oxygenated blood returning directly to the drainage cannula without passing through the patient) significantly reduces effective oxygenation. Simply increasing pump flow worsens recirculation. Reposition cannulas to increase the distance between drainage and return ports. See VV recirculation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget LV venting in VA-ECMO with poor LV ejection
info.t: VA-ECMO increases afterload, which can lead to LV distension if native cardiac function is severely impaired. An overdistended LV causes pulmonary edema and myocardial injury. LV venting (via Impella or IABP) may be required — evaluate with bedside echo. See LV distension node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give amiodarone for TdP
info.t: Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and will worsen torsades de pointes. This is a fundamental error — TdP is polymorphic VT in the context of QT prolongation, and adding a QT-prolonging drug can precipitate fatal ventricular fibrillation. Magnesium is the correct first-line drug. See pulseless TdP node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give procainamide for TdP
info.t: Procainamide also prolongs the QT interval and is contraindicated in TdP just like amiodarone. This mistake is common because procainamide is a standard antiarrhythmic for polymorphic VT without QT prolongation — always check the baseline QTc before choosing an antiarrhythmic. See drugs to avoid node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use synchronized cardioversion for pulseless TdP
info.t: Pulseless TdP is a cardiac arrest — it requires unsynchronized defibrillation, not synchronized cardioversion. Attempting synchronization on a chaotic polymorphic rhythm will fail to detect the R-wave and result in dangerous delays and potential arrhythmia triggering. See pulseless TdP node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT correct potassium to normal — target K >4.5 mEq/L
info.t: Hypokalemia dramatically increases TdP risk by reducing the repolarization reserve. The target is not just "normal" (3.5–5.0) — you must replace to >4.5 mEq/L to provide adequate protection against recurrence. The same principle applies to magnesium (target Mg >2.0 mg/dL). See electrolytes node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss QT-prolonging drugs as the causative agent
info.t: Acquired QT prolongation from drugs is the most common cause of TdP in the ED. Antibiotics (macrolides, fluoroquinolones), antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide), and antiarrhythmics must all be reviewed and stopped. Continuing the offending drug guarantees recurrence. See drug cessation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge recurrent TdP without monitored admission
info.t: Recurrent TdP — even if self-terminating — indicates high risk of degeneration to VF and sudden cardiac death. All patients with documented TdP require admission for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction, QT-prolonging drug review, and electrophysiology consultation. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT confuse TdP with regular polymorphic VT
info.t: Polymorphic VT without QT prolongation (e.g., in acute MI or catecholaminergic VT) requires completely different treatment — including amiodarone and beta-blockers, which are contraindicated in TdP. Always obtain and interpret the baseline QTc before treating any polymorphic VT. See etiology node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send standard hospital tox screen and consider it done
info.t: Standard hospital urine immunoassay drug screens miss most DFSA agents — GHB, benzodiazepines (especially non-prescribed), ketamine, scopolamine, and most sedative-hypnotics require forensic GC-MS/LC-MS confirmation. Send specimens directly to the state crime lab or forensic reference lab. See panel selection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay GHB collection beyond 6 hours from the assault
info.t: GHB has an extremely short detection window — undetectable in blood after 6 hours and in urine after 12 hours. Delaying specimen collection while waiting for social work, SANE, or consent resolution will permanently lose the most time-sensitive forensic evidence. Collect urgently, consent discussions can continue simultaneously. See urgent collection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT store clothing in plastic bags
info.t: Plastic bags create a humid environment that degrades DNA evidence and promotes bacterial growth. All clothing must be placed in paper bags to preserve biological material. This is a chain-of-custody standard that affects prosecutorial outcomes. See clothing collection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a grey-top tube for standard labs — use it for GHB
info.t: Standard red-top or gold-top serum tubes allow in-vitro production of GHB by bacteria, creating false positives and degrading true samples. GHB specimens require grey-top tubes (sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate) which inhibit microbial production and preserve the sample. See urgent collection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT require a police report before providing STI prophylaxis
info.t: Consent to exam, consent to specimen collection, and consent to prophylaxis are each independent decisions. A patient who declines to involve law enforcement still deserves full STI prophylaxis, emergency contraception, and HIV PEP assessment. Never withhold medical care on the basis of reporting decisions. See consent introduction node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip HIV PEP assessment
info.t: Sexual assault carries HIV transmission risk that must be assessed within 72 hours for PEP eligibility. Failing to offer HIV PEP counseling and initiation to eligible patients who were assaulted within 72 hours is a missed preventive opportunity with lifelong consequences. See HIV PEP node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT break chain of custody for forensic specimens
info.t: Forensic specimens are only legally admissible if chain of custody is maintained from collection through transport. Every specimen must be labeled, sealed in tamper-evident packaging, and all transfers documented with signature and time. A single undocumented handoff can render the entire specimen set inadmissible. See urgent collection node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT replace electrolytes aggressively without monitoring for refeeding
info.t: Aggressive refeeding in severely malnourished patients causes refeeding syndrome — rapid intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Start feeds slowly, replete electrolytes first, and check levels every 6 hours when initiating refeeding. See refeeding protocol node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge bradycardia below 40 bpm from the ED
info.t: Sinus bradycardia <40 bpm (or <50 bpm with QTc >450 ms) in anorexia nervosa is a MARSIPAN high-risk threshold that mandates inpatient admission for cardiac monitoring. The arrhythmia is a direct consequence of malnutrition-driven electrolyte disturbance and autonomic dysfunction. See cardiac monitoring node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give ipecac or allow the patient to vomit post-ingestion
info.t: Ipecac contains emetine, which causes irreversible cardiomyopathy in patients with eating disorders who use it chronically. Even a single dose in a patient with pre-existing myocardial damage from malnutrition can be fatal. Never use ipecac in eating disorder patients under any circumstance. See BN assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat the psychiatric disorder before stabilizing the medical one
info.t: Psychiatric disposition decisions cannot be made until the patient is medically stable. A patient with HR <40, SBP <90, or QTc >450 ms needs inpatient medical admission before any psychiatric evaluation. Medical instability takes absolute precedence. See acute management node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT normalize a low BMI without addressing the refeeding risk
info.t: BMI <15 kg/m² is a high-risk threshold — BMI <13 is extreme risk with ICU-level physiologic vulnerability. These patients cannot simply be fed normally; caloric increases must be gradual (starting 20–30 kcal/kg/day) with electrolyte monitoring. Aggressive normalization causes preventable death. See BMI classification node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss potassium <3.0 mEq/L as a QT risk in bulimia
info.t: Chronic purging causes severe hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypochloremic alkalosis. Hypokalemia with QTc >470 ms in a bulimic patient is a setup for Torsades de Pointes. Aggressively replace K and Mg, obtain ECG, and reassess QTc before discharge. See electrolytes node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without a psychiatric safety assessment
info.t: Eating disorders carry the highest mortality of any psychiatric illness — partly from medical complications but also from suicide. Every eating disorder patient requires a structured suicide risk assessment and safety plan before discharge. A "medically stable" patient with active suicidal ideation requires psychiatric admission. See psychiatric assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use adult vital sign norms to assess pediatric hemodynamic status
info.t: Children maintain blood pressure until 25–30% blood volume is lost — by the time hypotension appears, the child is in late decompensated shock. Tachycardia is the EARLY sign. Using adult BP thresholds as reassurance in a tachycardic child will cause you to miss hemorrhagic shock. See primary survey node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give a 1 mg/kg epinephrine dose without weight
info.t: All pediatric resuscitation is weight-based — a dose error in a 10 kg child versus a 30 kg child is a 3-fold difference. Use Broselow tape immediately for all pediatric trauma activations. Guessing weight causes preventable medication errors. See weight estimation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss a history inconsistent with the injury pattern
info.t: Non-accidental trauma (NAT/child abuse) must be considered in ALL pediatric trauma patients, especially injuries that do not match developmental stage, multiple injuries at different healing stages, or delay in presentation. Mandatory reporting to CPS is required when NAT is suspected. See NAT report node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT apply adult fluid resuscitation principles to pediatric shock
info.t: The pediatric massive transfusion trigger is different from adults — activate MTP early based on clinical assessment of shock, not just vital signs. TXA must be given within 3 hours of injury at 15 mg/kg IV. The damage control resuscitation principle (1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets) applies. See transfusion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order CT head without using the PECARN rule for mild TBI
info.t: CT radiation in children carries meaningful lifetime cancer risk. The PECARN decision rule identifies children with <1% risk of clinically important TBI who can safely be observed without CT. Over-imaging children with mild TBI exposes them to unnecessary radiation. See PECARN node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT elevate a limb with suspected compartment syndrome
info.t: Elevation reduces perfusion pressure in an already-ischemic compartment and worsens compartment syndrome. Keep the limb at heart level. Remove constrictive dressings. Measure compartment pressure and contact orthopedics immediately if delta pressure <30 mmHg. See compartment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT manage significant solid organ injuries without pediatric surgery consultation
info.t: Children with solid organ injuries (liver, spleen, kidney) that are hemodynamically stable are managed non-operatively — but this requires pediatric surgery oversight, serial exams, and specific activity restrictions. An emergency physician alone cannot safely discharge or determine disposition for these injuries. See solid organ node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat new bladder dysfunction without ruling out cauda equina syndrome
info.t: New urinary retention or incontinence + back pain + any leg weakness or saddle anesthesia = cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. This is a surgical emergency requiring emergent MRI and neurosurgery consult. Missing this diagnosis and attributing symptoms to BPH or UTI causes permanent neurologic injury. See cauda equina node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT catheterize without checking for urethral trauma signs
info.t: Blood at the meatus, perineal hematoma, high-riding prostate, or pelvic fracture mechanism all indicate possible urethral disruption. Blind Foley insertion through a urethral tear completes the disruption and makes definitive repair far more complex. Assess for these signs before any catheter attempt. See retention neuro node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT leave high-volume retention without monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis
info.t: Patients with chronic high-volume retention (>800–1000 mL) are at risk for post-obstructive diuresis after catheter drainage, losing >200 mL/hr and developing severe volume depletion, electrolyte disturbances, and hemodynamic instability. They cannot be safely discharged without a period of monitored urine output. See high-volume node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip spinal cord compression in patients with acute paraparesis and retention
info.t: Spinal cord compression from epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, or malignant cord compression causes urinary retention with ascending sensory and motor deficits. This is a distinct emergency from cauda equina — management and prognosis differ. Emergent MRI and neurosurgery are required immediately. See cord compression node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss new incontinence as "stress incontinence" in the ED
info.t: New-onset incontinence in the ED deserves investigation. Overflow incontinence from high PVR, neurogenic incontinence from spinal pathology, and urge incontinence from UTI or detrusor instability are the ED-relevant diagnoses. Stress incontinence is a chronic outpatient diagnosis that should not be made in the acute setting. See incontinence type node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT initiate alpha-blockers without ruling out neurogenic retention
info.t: Alpha-blockers are effective for BPH-related retention but are ineffective and potentially harmful in neurogenic retention from cord injury or cauda equina syndrome. Starting tamsulosin without first characterizing the etiology delays appropriate imaging and surgical intervention for neurogenic causes. See alpha blocker node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge a post-op urinary retention patient without evaluating for surgical complications
info.t: Post-operative urinary retention can be caused by epidural hematoma, spinal cord injury, or procedural complications in addition to common benign causes. Retention following spinal, pelvic, or perineal surgery warrants a focused neurologic exam and low threshold for imaging before discharge. See postop node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat GC without covering Chlamydia
info.t: Always co-treat: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days. Failing to cover both leads to persistent infection and resistance. See treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use doxycycline in pregnancy
info.t: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy — use azithromycin instead for chlamydia. This is one of the most common STI prescribing errors in pregnant patients. See pregnancy modifications.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use penicillin alternatives for syphilis in pregnancy
info.t: Benzathine penicillin G is the ONLY proven treatment for syphilis in pregnancy. Doxycycline, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone are not reliable alternatives — they do not prevent congenital syphilis. See syphilis treatment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss PID in sexually active women with pelvic pain
info.t: PID is a clinical diagnosis — empirically treat if cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness is present in a sexually active woman. Waiting for positive cultures delays treatment and risks tubo-ovarian abscess. See PID severity.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge PID without inpatient criteria assessment
info.t: Admit for IV antibiotics if: TOA present, pregnancy, failed outpatient therapy, severe illness, surgical emergency cannot be excluded. Outpatient treatment is only appropriate for mild PID. See PID severity.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip 3-site testing in MSM patients
info.t: Testing only urethra misses up to 70% of GC/CT infections in MSM. Always test all three sites: urethral, pharyngeal, and rectal. Untreated pharyngeal GC is a reservoir for transmission. See MSM-specific protocols.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT mistake LGV proctitis for hemorrhoids or IBD
info.t: LGV (Chlamydia L1-L3) causes severe proctitis with tenesmus, bloody discharge, and rectal pain — often misdiagnosed. Treat with doxycycline 100 mg BID × 21 days (not the standard 7-day CT regimen). See LGV treatment.

Treating the patient without addressing partners guarantees reinfection. Expedited partner therapy (EPT) is legal in most states — provide prescriptions or referrals. Reinfection, not treatment failure, is the most common cause of repeat STI. See partner management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip Test of Cure for pharyngeal GC
info.t: Pharyngeal gonorrhea is harder to eradicate than urogenital GC. Test of cure at 1–2 weeks is recommended for pharyngeal infection, not just for treatment failures. See TOC indications.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fluoroquinolones for gonorrhea
info.t: Fluoroquinolone-resistant GC is widespread globally. Ceftriaxone remains the only reliable first-line agent. Avoid ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin for GC regardless of local resistance patterns. See urethritis treatment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give diuretics for OHSS ascites
info.t: Diuretics worsen hemoconcentration in OHSS — the problem is third-spacing, not fluid overload. IV albumin and cautious crystalloids are the appropriate fluid strategy. Diuretics can precipitate renal failure and thromboembolic events. See why no diuretics.

In OHSS the ovaries can be 10+ cm and are easily injured with a blind approach. Always use ultrasound guidance and approach midline or laterally — away from massively enlarged ovaries. Ovarian puncture causes hemorrhage. See paracentesis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss VTE in OHSS
info.t: OHSS dramatically increases clotting risk — DVT, PE, and cerebral venous thrombosis all occur at elevated rates. Hemoconcentration (Hct >45%) and immobility are key drivers. Anticoagulation should be considered early. See VTE prophylaxis.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss ovarian torsion in OHSS
info.t: Enlarged OHSS ovaries are at high risk for torsion. Sudden worsening pain, especially unilateral, with nausea should prompt emergent US with Doppler. Absent flow is not required to diagnose torsion — intermittent torsion occurs. See torsion node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge moderate or severe OHSS
info.t: Moderate OHSS (symptomatic ascites, Hct >41%) and all severe/critical cases require admission. OHSS can progress rapidly — a patient who looks OK in the ED may decompensate within 24 hours. See disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget pregnancy status changes management
info.t: A concurrent intrauterine pregnancy worsens and prolongs OHSS (hCG drives it further). This changes counseling, disposition, and follow-up intensity. Always obtain a beta-hCG. See OHSS history node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT neglect albumin replacement after large-volume paracentesis
info.t: Removing >2 L of ascites without albumin replacement accelerates fluid re-accumulation and worsens circulatory dysfunction. Give 25% albumin 6–8 g per liter removed. See paracentesis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip Rh(D) typing in early pregnancy bleeding
info.t: Every pregnant woman with vaginal bleeding must have Rh(D) status confirmed before determining RhoGAM need. A missed Rh-negative patient who sensitizes loses future pregnancy options. See Rh check node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold RhoGAM for molar pregnancy
info.t: Gestational trophoblastic disease requires RhoGAM regardless of gestational age — the hydatidiform mole contains fetal red cell antigens. This is a mandatory indication at any gestational age. See molar pregnancy node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip RhoGAM after ectopic pregnancy
info.t: Ectopic pregnancy — whether treated medically (methotrexate) or surgically — is a sensitizing event. All Rh-negative patients with ectopic pregnancy must receive RhoGAM. See ectopic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold RhoGAM after invasive procedures
info.t: CVS, amniocentesis, and cordocentesis all cause feto-maternal hemorrhage. Rh-negative patients require RhoGAM after any invasive obstetric procedure regardless of gestational age. See procedure node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume Rh-positive means no action needed
info.t: Confirm the blood type result — never assume based on prior history or patient report. Also check for already-sensitized (antibody-positive) patients, who need MFM follow-up, not RhoGAM. See sensitized node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget the Kleihauer-Betke test for large bleeds
info.t: In cases of significant trauma or heavy hemorrhage, a standard 300 mcg dose may be insufficient. The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies feto-maternal hemorrhage and determines if additional RhoGAM is needed. See massive FMH node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat Weak D as Rh-negative without checking
info.t: Weak D status is complex — most Weak D types (1, 2, 3) do not require RhoGAM as they cannot be sensitized. But some Weak D types do. Molecular typing should guide management; default is to treat as Rh-negative if uncertain. See Weak D detail.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume gout without ruling out septic arthritis
info.t: Acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — gout and septic arthritis look identical clinically. Crystals do NOT exclude infection; 1–2% of cases have both simultaneously. Tap the joint. See monoarthritis overview.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for culture results
info.t: If septic arthritis is suspected, start empiric antibiotics immediately after aspiration. Cartilage destruction begins within 8 hours of bacterial infection. Do not wait for Gram stain or culture results to initiate treatment. See empiric antibiotics.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a single NSAID for all crystal arthritis
info.t: Gout treatment requires choosing between NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids based on contraindications. NSAIDs are contraindicated with CKD, CHF, GI bleeds, and anticoagulation — using them blindly causes serious harm. See gout treatment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop DMARDs in RA patients during an ED visit
info.t: Abruptly stopping methotrexate, biologics, or other DMARDs can precipitate a severe RA flare. Continue current disease-modifying medications unless there is a specific acute contraindication and rheumatology has been consulted. See RA overview.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss cervical spine instability in RA patients
info.t: Atlantoaxial subluxation (C1-C2 instability) occurs in up to 25% of RA patients. Any RA patient with neck pain and neurological symptoms needs urgent cervical spine imaging before manipulation or airway procedures. See RA overview.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use a dry tap to exclude septic arthritis
info.t: A failed arthrocentesis does not rule out septic arthritis — especially in small joints or early in the course. If clinical suspicion remains high after a failed tap, arrange urgent orthopedic consultation and consider imaging-guided aspiration. See tap decision.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the prosthetic joint infection threshold
info.t: Prosthetic joint infections use a much lower synovial WBC cutoff — >3,000/µL (not the 50,000 used for native joints). Applying native joint criteria to a patient with a joint replacement will falsely reassure you. See PJI node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ABI alone to assess perfusion in diabetics
info.t: ABI >1.4 indicates calcified non-compressible vessels — a false normal — which is extremely common in diabetics and ESRD. Use the toe-brachial index (TBI) or TcPO2 instead. Trusting ABI in a diabetic can lead to missing critical limb ischemia. See vascular intro.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat uninfected ulcers with antibiotics
info.t: Even if osteomyelitis is present on imaging, antibiotics are not indicated unless there are clinical signs of infection (≥2 of: purulence, erythema, warmth, tenderness, induration). Antibiotic overuse drives resistance. See infection grading.

25% of acute Charcot foot is misdiagnosed as cellulitis, gout, or DVT — average delay to correct diagnosis is 7 months. A red, hot, swollen foot WITHOUT an open wound in a neuropathic diabetic should trigger Charcot workup. Early immobilization prevents irreversible deformity. See Charcot intro.

Pain out of proportion to exam (early) or complete absence of pain (late, due to nerve destruction) with systemic toxicity, crepitus, or rapidly spreading erythema demands emergent surgical consultation. Do not wait for imaging to consult surgery. See necrotizing fasciitis node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without an offloading plan
info.t: Offloading is the single most important intervention for neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer healing. A patient sent home without a cast walker, TCC, or half-shoe will continue pressure injury and the wound will not heal. See offloading node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT confuse wet and dry gangrene disposition
info.t: Dry gangrene can be observed; wet gangrene is a surgical emergency requiring broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergent amputation consultation. Sending a patient with wet gangrene home is a sentinel error. See wet gangrene node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT order X-ray alone for osteomyelitis workup
info.t: Plain X-ray is insensitive for early osteomyelitis — bone changes lag clinical infection by 10–21 days. MRI is the gold standard. A normal X-ray does not exclude osteomyelitis in a chronic wound with bone probe-positivity. See osteomyelitis imaging.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start steroids before ruling out malignancy
info.t: Corticosteroids can mask leukemia and other malignancies presenting as joint pain in children. Do not initiate steroids in new pediatric arthritis without specialist input — always obtain CBC with differential first. See JIA management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss septic arthritis of the hip
info.t: Hip septic arthritis in children is an orthopedic emergency — delayed treatment causes avascular necrosis and permanent joint damage. Apply Kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, elevated ESR, elevated WBC) and proceed to OR if high risk. See Kocher evaluation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt to reduce a SCFE
info.t: Attempting to reduce a slipped capital femoral epiphysis dramatically increases the risk of avascular necrosis. Immediately make the patient non-weight-bearing and call orthopedics. In-situ fixation is the treatment, not reduction. See SCFE management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT dismiss growing pains without a proper exam
info.t: True growing pains are bilateral, nocturnal, and absent during activities. Any limp, morning stiffness, unilateral pain, fever, weight loss, or swelling is NOT growing pains and requires workup. Never label pain "growing pains" without a normal joint exam. See growing pains node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss uveitis in JIA patients
info.t: Uveitis in JIA is often silent — no redness, no pain, no photophobia — and can cause permanent vision loss. ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA carries the highest risk. Urgent ophthalmology referral for screening is mandatory, even in asymptomatic patients. See JIA management.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss acute rheumatic fever
info.t: Migratory polyarthritis with dramatic NSAID response plus recent streptococcal infection is ARF until proven otherwise. Missing ARF and failing to start penicillin prophylaxis risks recurrent carditis and valvular damage. Apply revised Jones criteria. See ARF workup.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use adult synovial fluid thresholds in children
info.t: The WBC cutoff for septic arthritis is the same in children (>50,000/µL with >90% PMNs), but the Kocher clinical criteria should be applied first. A low-risk Kocher score with low synovial WBC supports transient synovitis, but high-risk clinical features override lab results. See synovial interpretation.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume crystals exclude septic arthritis
info.t: Crystals in synovial fluid do NOT rule out concurrent septic arthritis. Gout and pseudogout joints are at INCREASED risk for bacterial superinfection. If there is any clinical suspicion, send cultures even when crystals are identified. See septic concern node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use NSAIDs when CrCl <60 mL/min
info.t: NSAIDs in renal insufficiency worsen kidney function and can precipitate acute kidney injury. Use colchicine (dose-adjusted) or oral corticosteroids in any patient with CKD or impaired renal function. See NSAID treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give colchicine with clarithromycin or cyclosporine
info.t: Clarithromycin, ketoconazole, ritonavir, and cyclosporine are strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors that raise colchicine levels to toxic concentrations. Fatal colchicine toxicity has been reported with these combinations. See contraindication screen.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT start allopurinol during an acute gout flare
info.t: Initiating or changing urate-lowering therapy (ULT) during a flare prolongs the attack by causing urate crystal mobilization. Continue existing ULT but never start new ULT during an acute attack without concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis. See gout summary.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use low-dose aspirin to treat gout
info.t: Low-dose aspirin (81–325 mg) interferes with uric acid excretion and worsens hyperuricemia. It should not be used as an anti-inflammatory for gout. Use indomethacin, naproxen, or colchicine instead. See treatment assessment.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give sub-therapeutic NSAID doses
info.t: Full anti-inflammatory NSAID doses are required for gout — analgesic doses are insufficient. Indomethacin 50 mg TID, naproxen 500 mg BID, or ibuprofen 800 mg TID are the correct doses. Under-dosing leads to treatment failure and re-presentation. See NSAID treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss systemic illness driving the flare
info.t: Acute gout can be triggered by infection, surgery, dehydration, or starting diuretics. Always look for a precipitating cause — missing an occult infection while treating only the gout leads to a dangerous delay in diagnosis. See septic concern node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate before screening for HOp killers
info.t: Hypotension, hypoxia, acidosis, RV failure, hyperkalemia, and elevated ICP are the six pre-intubation killers. Missing any one of them and proceeding with standard RSI causes peri-intubation cardiac arrest. Screen every high-risk patient systematically. See screening node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate a hypotensive patient without push-dose pressors ready
info.t: RSI induction agents cause vasodilation and myocardial depression — a patient with SBP <100 will crash on propofol or even etomidate. Have push-dose epinephrine (10–20 mcg IV) and a norepinephrine infusion running or ready before laryngoscopy. See hypotension prep node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate a DKA patient without matching their minute ventilation
info.t: Patients with severe metabolic acidosis breathe fast to compensate (Kussmaul respirations). Standard vent settings (RR 12, TV 500) will allow CO2 to rise, pH to crash, and cardiac arrest to follow. Pre-oxygenate with BVM matching their RR, then set vent to match. See acidosis ventilator node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use high PEEP or large tidal volumes in RV failure
info.t: High intrathoracic pressure from aggressive ventilation in RV failure worsens preload, increases RV afterload, and causes circulatory collapse. Use low PEEP (≤5 cm H2O) and accept mild hypoxia rather than risking RV catastrophe. See RV vent settings.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT reflexively avoid ketamine in TBI
info.t: The old teaching that ketamine raises ICP has been refuted by multiple studies. In a hypotensive TBI patient, ketamine is the preferred induction agent — it maintains BP, preserves cerebral perfusion pressure, and may be neuroprotective. See ketamine ICP node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip apneic oxygenation in the hypoxic patient
info.t: Patients with shunt physiology (ARDS, pneumonia, severe pulmonary edema) desaturate to critical levels in seconds once apneic. High-flow nasal cannula at 15 L/min during laryngoscopy extends the safe apnea window significantly. See hypoxia nodesat node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate a hyperkalemic patient without treating K+ first
info.t: Succinylcholine is absolutely contraindicated when K+ >5.5 mEq/L — it raises potassium by 0.5–1.0 mEq/L and can precipitate VF arrest. Use rocuronium. Also treat the hyperkalemia before induction when possible. See metabolic treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ABCD2 score alone to discharge TIA patients
info.t: ACEP 2016 explicitly states the ABCD2 score should NOT be used alone to determine safe discharge. Low scores still miss high-risk patients. Use the Canadian TIA score and always identify high-risk features independently. See risk stratification intro.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without vascular imaging
info.t: CTA head and neck is the preferred workup — ~50% of TIA patients have abnormal cerebrovascular imaging. Symptomatic carotid stenosis ≥50% requires urgent intervention. Missing this delays a potentially stroke-preventing carotid endarterectomy. See vascular imaging node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use antiplatelet therapy for AFib-related TIA
info.t: When the TIA source is atrial fibrillation, DAPT is insufficient — anticoagulation is required. Using aspirin + clopidogrel instead of a DOAC fails to protect against the embolic mechanism and risks recurrent stroke. See cardioembolic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait to start high-intensity statin therapy
info.t: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg reduces stroke recurrence by 16% (SPARCL). Do not wait for lipid results before prescribing — start immediately in the ED. Every day of delay is lost stroke prevention. See statin treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss DWI-positive stroke masquerading as TIA
info.t: If the MRI DWI sequence shows an acute infarct, this is a stroke — not a TIA — even if symptoms have resolved. Stroke patients have higher early recurrence risk and require different admission pathways and more urgent neurology involvement. See DWI positive node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT allow TIA discharge without a rapid follow-up plan
info.t: The EXPRESS trial showed 80% reduction in 90-day stroke risk with same-day versus delayed assessment. If a rapid TIA clinic within 24–48 hours is not confirmed, the patient should be admitted. Speed matters more than setting. See discharge criteria.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget to load antiplatelet therapy before discharge
info.t: Clopidogrel requires a loading dose (300–600 mg) to achieve rapid platelet effect. Sending a patient home on 75 mg/day without loading provides no protection for the first 5–7 days — the period of highest stroke risk. See discharge orders.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop antiplatelet DAPT therapy before 21 days
info.t: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days post-TIA significantly reduces early stroke recurrence. Stopping early — or prescribing aspirin alone — misses this critical prevention window. After 21 days, transition to aspirin monotherapy. See discharge orders.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attribute dyspnea to normal pregnancy without echo
info.t: Orthopnea, PND, and dyspnea at rest in a pregnant or postpartum woman must be evaluated with echocardiography. PPCM is diagnosed when LVEF <45% — a finding that is completely missed if you assume dyspnea is physiologic pregnancy adaptation. See workup node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ACE inhibitors or ARBs during pregnancy
info.t: ACEi/ARBs are teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. For peripartum patients still pregnant, use hydralazine plus nitrates as a safe vasodilator alternative. Reserve ACEi/ARBs until after delivery. See vasodilators node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give bromocriptine without anticoagulation
info.t: Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin and improves LV recovery, but increases thrombotic risk (MI, stroke, VTE). It MUST be co-administered with at least prophylactic-dose LMWH. Bromocriptine monotherapy without anticoagulation is dangerous. See bromocriptine node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT withhold anticoagulation for LVEF <30%
info.t: PPCM with LVEF <30% or an identified LV thrombus has a high stroke and embolic risk. Anticoagulation is indicated in these patients — fear of anticoagulating a pregnant woman should not override this. See anticoagulation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give milrinone as first-line in hypotensive cardiogenic shock
info.t: Milrinone causes significant vasodilation and can worsen hypotension in cardiogenic shock. Dobutamine is preferred as the first-line inotrope; add norepinephrine if MAP <65. Reserve milrinone for patients not tolerating dobutamine. See shock medications node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT prematurely withdraw support in PPCM
info.t: PPCM has uniquely high recovery potential — up to 50% of patients recover normal EF within 6 months. Young, previously healthy patients with no CAD who appear critically ill can achieve full recovery. Do not counsel futility prematurely. See ICU disposition node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay perimortem C-section in cardiac arrest
info.t: In cardiac arrest at ≥20 weeks gestation, delivery within 4–5 minutes improves maternal resuscitation (relieves aortocaval compression) and improves neonatal survival after 24 weeks. Do not wait to call OB — this decision belongs to the ED team. See urgent delivery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay button battery removal
info.t: Button batteries cause liquefaction necrosis of the ear canal within 1–2 hours via an electrical current. This is a time-critical emergency requiring immediate removal — do not irrigate or delay for any reason. See battery node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT irrigate organic or soft foreign bodies
info.t: Cotton, foam, seeds, beans, and other organic material absorb water and swell dramatically when irrigated. Irrigation converts a removable foreign body into one that is tightly impacted and requires ENT. See organic material technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use alligator forceps on round hard objects
info.t: Alligator forceps have no grip on smooth spherical objects (beads, pebbles) and reliably push them deeper. Use a right-angle hook or curette passed behind the object instead. Pushing deeper risks TM perforation or object entry into the middle ear. See sphere technique.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt removal with TM perforation signs
info.t: Vertigo, nystagmus, sudden hearing loss, or severe pain at FB insertion are red flags for TM perforation or impaction. Stop all attempts and refer urgently to ENT. Continued attempts risk ossicular chain damage and permanent hearing loss. See TM perforation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt repeated extractions on an uncooperative child without sedation
info.t: Each failed attempt increases canal trauma, edema, and the risk of pushing the object deeper. After one failed attempt on an uncooperative child, proceed to procedural sedation or ENT referral rather than repeated blind attempts. See intolerance node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT neglect to kill a live insect before removal
info.t: A live insect in the ear canal causes severe pain, moves unpredictably, and can damage the TM during attempted removal. Instill mineral oil, lidocaine, or 2% lidocaine gel to immobilize it before any extraction attempt. See insect kill node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use ototoxic drops with TM perforation
info.t: Neomycin and polymyxin B are ototoxic and absolutely contraindicated when TM integrity is uncertain. If antibiotic drops are needed after a complicated removal, use ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone — both are safe with perforated TMs. See TM perforation node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the hot-cold reversal sign
info.t: Paradoxical dysesthesia — cold objects feeling burning hot, hot objects feeling cold — is pathognomonic for ciguatera. This symptom is often not volunteered by patients unless specifically asked. Always ask about temperature sensations in suspected fish poisoning. See symptoms node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge cardiac involvement without monitoring
info.t: Ciguatera can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and conduction abnormalities. Any patient with cardiac symptoms (chest pain, palpitations, bradycardia) requires ECG monitoring, not discharge. See cardiac assessment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give opioids for ciguatera pain
info.t: Opioids can worsen the dysesthesia and neurological symptoms in ciguatera toxicity. They are relatively contraindicated. Amitriptyline and gabapentin are more appropriate for the painful peripheral neurological symptoms. See treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give mannitol beyond 72 hours of symptom onset
info.t: Mannitol (1 g/kg IV over 45 minutes) may reduce neurological severity but only if given within the first 72 hours. After this window, mannitol provides no benefit and adds risk (dehydration, renal injury). See mannitol node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give alcohol to patients with ciguatera
info.t: Alcohol dramatically worsens ciguatera symptoms and can trigger severe recurrence of neurological and GI symptoms. Patients must be counseled to strictly avoid alcohol for at least 6 months after the acute illness. See chronic node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the differential with other fish toxidromes
info.t: Scombroid fish poisoning mimics ciguatera with flushing, GI symptoms, and headache but responds to antihistamines, not mannitol. Distinguish by: scombroid onset within 30 minutes, flushing rash, and warm/improperly stored fish (tuna, mahi-mahi). See differential node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay malaria testing in any febrile returning traveler
info.t: P. falciparum can progress from uncomplicated to severe malaria and death in 24–48 hours. STAT thick and thin blood smears plus rapid diagnostic test (RDT) are mandatory for any febrile traveler from an endemic region, regardless of prophylaxis use. See malaria screen node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fluoroquinolones empirically for typhoid fever
info.t: Fluoroquinolone-resistant Salmonella Typhi is now widespread in South Asia and Southeast Asia. Empiric fluoroquinolone monotherapy for suspected typhoid can fail, allowing disease to progress to perforation and death. Use azithromycin or ceftriaxone. See typhoid node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for rickettsial serology before treating
info.t: Doxycycline must be started immediately on clinical suspicion of rickettsial infection (fever + eschar, or fever + rash + travel to endemic area). Serology lags by 7–14 days. Delayed treatment of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever or African tick bite fever causes preventable death. See rickettsial node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss dengue hemorrhagic warning signs
info.t: Dengue warning signs (persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, mucosal bleeding, rapid deterioration, platelet <100K) indicate impending dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome. These patients must be admitted and monitored — not discharged with symptomatic care. See dengue node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT fail to isolate possible viral hemorrhagic fever
info.t: Any traveler with fever plus hemorrhagic findings (bleeding, petechiae, ecchymosis) from West/Central Africa or other endemic regions must be immediately isolated with droplet/contact precautions pending evaluation. Missed VHF isolation has caused index case clusters. See fever initial node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay post-exposure rabies prophylaxis
info.t: Rabies PEP must begin immediately after any animal bite or scratch in an endemic region — do not wait for animal observation or testing. Once clinical rabies develops, it is nearly universally fatal. There is no time to wait. See rabies node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attribute diarrhea to diet when Giardia or parasites are possible
info.t: Persistent diarrhea (>2 weeks) returning from travel requires stool ova and parasite examination, Giardia antigen, and Cryptosporidium antigen. Empiric treatment without diagnosis delays appropriate targeted therapy. See persistent diarrhea node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume prophylaxis use rules out malaria
info.t: Prophylaxis failure occurs due to non-adherence, drug-resistant parasites, or stopping too early. Malaria can and does occur in patients on chemoprophylaxis. Always test febrile travelers regardless of reported prophylaxis use. See prophylaxis failure node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use the same drug for treatment that failed as prophylaxis
info.t: If malaria develops despite atovaquone-proguanil prophylaxis, resistance is likely — do not use it for treatment. Switch to artemether-lumefantrine or quinine + doxycycline. Same-class drug re-exposure fails and delays cure. See prophylaxis failure node.

Species identification drives everything: P. falciparum requires urgent treatment and hospitalization; P. vivax and P. ovale require primaquine for radical cure of liver stages; P. malariae can cause nephrotic syndrome. A "malaria positive" result without speciation is incomplete. See species node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat severe malaria with oral therapy
info.t: Severe malaria (altered consciousness, respiratory distress, renal failure, hyperparasitemia >5%) requires IV artesunate — the only appropriate treatment. IV artesunate must be obtained through the CDC IND protocol (CDC Malaria Hotline: 770-488-7788). See severe treatment node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget primaquine for P. vivax and P. ovale
info.t: P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) that cause relapses weeks to months later. Standard chloroquine or artemether-lumefantrine treats the blood-stage but NOT liver stages. Primaquine is mandatory for radical cure — check G6PD first. See vivax/ovale node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give primaquine without checking G6PD status
info.t: Primaquine causes severe hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient patients. G6PD deficiency is common in populations from malaria-endemic regions. Always check G6PD before prescribing primaquine. See primaquine node.

Mixed malaria infections (5–10% of cases) must be treated for the most dangerous species present. If P. falciparum is identified alongside any other species, treat with a falciparum-active regimen. See species node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interpret a silent chest as improvement
info.t: A silent chest — no wheezing on auscultation — indicates critically severe obstruction with near-zero air movement. It is a sign of impending respiratory arrest, not improvement. Call for anesthesia, ICU, and RT immediately. See severity node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use intermittent instead of continuous nebulization in severe asthma
info.t: Continuous albuterol nebulization is far more effective than intermittent q20-minute dosing in severe exacerbations. The dose-response curve in acute asthma strongly favors continuous delivery — use it for all severe presentations. See continuous nebs node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT omit magnesium sulfate in severe asthma
info.t: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is underutilized despite strong evidence. It causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation independent of beta-agonist receptors. Give it early in severe asthma — there is no reason to wait for SABA failure. See magnesium node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT set standard vent parameters in intubated asthmatic
info.t: Normal vent settings (RR 12, TV 500) in severe asthma cause dynamic hyperinflation, breath stacking, and tension physiology. Use low respiratory rate (6–10), large tidal volume to allow full exhalation, and accept permissive hypercapnia (pCO2 60–80 mmHg). See vent settings node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT try to correct the CO2 level by increasing vent rate
info.t: Increasing the respiratory rate in a mechanically ventilated asthmatic prevents complete exhalation, worsens air trapping, and can cause fatal breath-stacking. The correct response to high CO2 is to accept it — permissive hypercapnia with pH >7.15 is the target. See permissive hypercapnia node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT intubate before maximizing non-invasive options
info.t: "Intubation is often the beginning of the end in severe asthma." Maximize medical therapy (continuous nebs, magnesium, epinephrine IM) and BiPAP with ketamine sedation before proceeding to RSI. Intubation dramatically increases mortality in status asthmaticus. See critical decision node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT discharge without steroids and action plan
info.t: Systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 40–60 mg or equivalent) must be prescribed at discharge to prevent relapse. A written asthma action plan and inhaler technique review are equally critical. Discharging with SABA alone leads to rapid return visits. See discharge node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT forget IM epinephrine in severe beta-agonist-refractory asthma
info.t: IM epinephrine (0.3–0.5 mg of 1:1000 q20 min × 3) is safe, fast, and dramatically underutilized in severe asthma unresponsive to continuous nebulization. It bypasses receptor downregulation from excessive prior SABA use. See epinephrine node.

Positive UA or culture without urinary symptoms is NOT a UTI in the vast majority of patients. Treating ASB increases C. diff risk, adverse effects, and antibiotic resistance without improving outcomes. The only exceptions are pregnancy and pre-urologic procedures. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT diagnose UTI from UA alone in the elderly
info.t: Bacteriuria is present in up to 50% of elderly nursing home residents and does NOT indicate infection. Confusion or "change in mental status" alone is not a UTI — always look for other causes first. UTI should be a diagnosis of exclusion in the elderly. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis
info.t: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal tissue concentrations and is ineffective for upper urinary tract infection. It is only appropriate for uncomplicated lower UTI. Use a fluoroquinolone or ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated cystitis
info.t: FDA black box warnings (tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects) and rising resistance rates (15-25% E. coli) make fluoroquinolones inappropriate first-line therapy for uncomplicated UTI. Reserve them for complicated UTI and pyelonephritis where alternatives fail. See this node.

Absence of pyuria (negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite) has a >95% NPV for UTI. Treating without pyuria targets colonization, not infection. Always seek alternative diagnoses (vaginitis, cervicitis, urethritis, kidney stone). See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use TMP-SMX if local resistance >20%
info.t: TMP-SMX resistance among E. coli varies widely (10-30% in many regions). Prescribing it empirically in a high-resistance area risks treatment failure. Always check your local antibiogram before using TMP-SMX as first-line therapy. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT admit all pyelonephritis without assessment
info.t: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant patient who can tolerate PO and has reliable follow-up can be safely treated as outpatient with oral fluoroquinolones. Reflexive admission wastes resources and increases hospital-acquired infection risk. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip culture in complicated or male UTI
info.t: All UTIs in men, pregnant patients, catheterized patients, those with recent antibiotics, and pyelonephritis require urine culture. Without culture, treatment failure from a resistant organism cannot be recognized or corrected. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT use TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolones in pregnancy
info.t: TMP-SMX causes neural tube defects in the first trimester and kernicterus at term. Fluoroquinolones cause fetal cartilage damage. Safe options are nitrofurantoin (avoid at term), cephalexin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pyelo in pregnancy always requires admission for IV antibiotics. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT remove and replace a CAUTI catheter before culturing
info.t: In catheter-associated UTI, always change or remove the catheter before obtaining the culture sample. Old catheters harbor biofilm with resistant organisms that do not reflect the true infecting pathogen. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT transfuse platelets in TTP
info.t: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP — it adds fuel to the microvascular thrombotic fire. Historical reports document sudden death, MI, and stroke after platelet transfusion. The only exception is life-threatening CNS hemorrhage, and even then requires hematology discussion first. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT wait for ADAMTS13 results to start TPE
info.t: ADAMTS13 is a send-out test with a 2-7 day turnaround. If the PLASMIC score is ≥6 or the patient is critically ill, initiate plasma exchange immediately. Waiting for lab confirmation delays life-saving treatment — mortality without TPE exceeds 90%. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT draw ADAMTS13 after plasma exposure
info.t: FFP and plasma exchange fluid both contain ADAMTS13 and will falsely normalize levels, rendering the test uninterpretable. Draw ADAMTS13 samples BEFORE any plasma exposure and document the time drawn. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay TPE beyond 4-8 hours
info.t: TPE is the cornerstone of TTP treatment and must be initiated within 4-8 hours of suspicion. If TPE is not immediately available, start FFP infusion (30 mL/kg) as a bridge and arrange emergent transfer to a TPE-capable facility. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT mistake HELLP for TTP postpartum
info.t: HELLP resolves within 48-72 hours of delivery. TTP continues to deteriorate postpartum without TPE. If a postpartum patient with MAHA is not improving by 72 hours after delivery, suspect TTP, expedite ADAMTS13, and initiate TPE. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT treat DIC with plasma exchange
info.t: DIC is characterized by abnormal coagulation studies (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer) — features that are NORMAL in TTP. TPE is not the treatment for DIC. Address the underlying trigger and provide supportive transfusion as needed. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT combine amiodarone + procainamide in TTP antiarrhythmic decisions
info.t: In low-PLASMIC patients, consider alternative TMA diagnoses before committing to TTP treatment. A PLASMIC score of 0-4 has a 98% NPV — a low score should prompt consideration of HUS, drug-induced TMA, malignant hypertension, or DIC. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop TPE when platelets normalize without monitoring
info.t: Remission requires platelet count >150 × 10⁹/L for 2 consecutive days AND LDH trending toward normal. Stopping TPE too early risks relapse. Continue caplacizumab 30 days after the last TPE session if ADAMTS13 remains <10%. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT miss the early signs of TTP relapse
info.t: Up to 50% of patients relapse, most within the first 2 years. Early relapse symptoms are nonspecific: lethargy, fatigue, headache, dark urine. Monitor ADAMTS13 every 3-6 months in remission and educate patients to present early. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT blindly reinsert a fresh trach (<7 days)
info.t: The tract is not epithelialized in the first 7 days — blind reinsertion creates a devastating false passage into the pretracheal space, causing subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and complete loss of airway. For fresh trach dislodgement, oxygenate via face and call the surgeon immediately. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt oral intubation in a laryngectomy patient
info.t: In a total laryngectomy, there is NO connection between the oropharynx and the lungs. The stoma is the only airway. Oral or nasal intubation attempts waste precious time and fail. Always check the bedside sign (red = laryngectomy, green = tracheostomy) and treat accordingly. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT skip inner cannula removal first in obstruction
info.t: The NTSP algorithm starts with inner cannula removal — the most common fix for tracheostomy obstruction. Mucus plugging of the inner cannula is the most frequent cause of trach distress. Remove it first, reassess before escalating. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT rely on misting in the tube to confirm placement
info.t: Misting (condensation) can occur in a false passage or the pretracheal space — it is NOT a reliable sign of correct tracheal placement. Always confirm with waveform capnography (gold standard), suction catheter passage, bilateral breath sounds, and chest rise. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ignore late trach bleeding as minor
info.t: Any bleeding occurring 7-21 days after tracheostomy must be treated as a potential tracheo-innominate fistula (TIF) sentinel bleed until proven otherwise. A small self-limited bleed may precede catastrophic arterial hemorrhage within 24-48 hours. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT force a trach tube into a difficult stoma
info.t: Forcing a tube when reinsertion is difficult creates false passages and can result in complete airway loss. Use tracheal dilators, try one size smaller, use a bougie or fiberoptic guidance, and maintain a low threshold for oral intubation as backup. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT attempt interventional radiology for TIF hemorrhage
info.t: Tracheo-innominate fistula with massive hemorrhage requires emergency median sternotomy. Delay for IR stent-graft placement in an unstable patient is lethal. The priority is cuff hyperinflation → finger tamponade → direct transport to the OR. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT keep cuff pressure above 25 cmH₂O chronically
info.t: Chronic high cuff pressure is the leading cause of tracheal stenosis (3-12% of trach patients) and a risk factor for TIF. Always target cuff pressure 20-25 cmH₂O. Excessive pressure causes mucosal ischemia and eventual cartilage erosion. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT remove the tracheostomy tube during hemorrhage
info.t: The tracheostomy tube provides both airway control and tamponade against the innominate artery during active TIF hemorrhage. Removing it before airway backup is secured and finger tamponade is ready will cause uncontrolled exsanguination. The tube is your friend until the moment of Utley maneuver. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT send patient for CT or imaging if clinical suspicion is high
info.t: CTA, bronchoscopy, and angiography combined have only 20-30% sensitivity for TIF. The diagnosis is clinical. Delaying hemorrhage control for imaging in an unstable patient is lethal. Once TIF is suspected, activate surgery and proceed to hemorrhage control immediately. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay surgical notification for the sentinel bleed
info.t: A sentinel bleed — a small self-limited hemorrhage — precedes massive arterial hemorrhage by only 24-48 hours in 50% of TIF patients. This is a narrow window to prepare the OR, blood products, and team. Call surgery immediately, not after "watching" the patient. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT release finger tamponade before the surgeon takes over
info.t: Once you begin the Utley maneuver (finger compression of innominate artery through stoma), you are physically committed to that patient until you are in the OR under surgical supervision. Releasing pressure even briefly during transport can result in uncontrolled hemorrhage. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT ligate the innominate artery without dividing it
info.t: Innominate artery ligation without division allows re-fistulization. The surgical standard is ligation AND division proximal and distal to the fistula, plus tracheal defect coverage with a muscle flap. Surgeons performing TIF repair must be aware of this requirement. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT assume early bleeding (<72h) cannot be TIF
info.t: While TIF classically occurs at 7-14 days, it can develop as early as 48 hours post-procedure. Any arterial-appearing, pulsatile, or large-volume bleeding regardless of timing requires urgent evaluation for vascular injury. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT suction aggressively through the trach during active bleeding
info.t: Aggressive suctioning through the trach during active TIF hemorrhage may dislodge clot and worsen bleeding. While gentle suction to maintain the airway may be necessary, the priority is tamponade via cuff hyperinflation, not clearing the airway of blood. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT move a patient with a cuff tamponade to imaging
info.t: A successfully tamponaded TIF can re-bleed fatally with any tube movement. Once cuff hyperinflation achieves hemorrhage control, the only acceptable movement is direct transport to the OR. No imaging, no repositioning, no unnecessary procedures. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT give amiodarone for Torsades de Pointes
info.t: Polymorphic VT with prolonged QTc is Torsades — and amiodarone prolongs the QT interval, making it directly contraindicated. The correct treatment is magnesium sulfate 2g IV, repeated at 5-15 minutes if it persists, then a continuous infusion. Confusing TdP with standard VF/VT and giving amiodarone can be fatal. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT interrupt CPR for >10 seconds
info.t: Every second of interrupted compressions degrades coronary perfusion pressure. All pauses — for rhythm checks, shocks, intubation — must be <10 seconds. Shock immediately after charging; do not wait. Use continuous compressions once an advanced airway is in place. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT delay IV/IO access to attempt central line
info.t: IO drug delivery is equivalent to IV in cardiac arrest and is achievable in seconds. Never delay epinephrine or other resuscitation medications to place a central venous catheter. IO within 60 seconds if peripheral IV fails. See this node.

High-dose epinephrine (doses above 1 mg) is a Class 3 intervention (No Benefit) per AHA guidelines — it does not improve survival and may worsen neurological outcomes. Standard dosing is 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes throughout the resuscitation. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT stop POCUS during compressions
info.t: POCUS assessments must occur during scheduled pulse/rhythm checks only — never during active compressions. Prolonged ultrasound evaluation that delays CPR resumption worsens outcome. The entire POCUS assessment must fit within the <10 second pause window. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT routinely give sodium bicarb or calcium
info.t: NaHCO3 and calcium have no benefit in undifferentiated cardiac arrest and both have potential harms. Reserve sodium bicarb for wide QRS/TCA toxicity, known hyperkalemia, or prolonged arrest. Reserve calcium for hyperkalemia, calcium channel blocker OD, or hypermagnesemia only. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT declare futility without checking for reversible causes
info.t: All 5 Hs (Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, H+, Hypo/HyperK, Hypothermia) and 5 Ts (Tension PTX, Tamponade, Thrombosis-PE, Thrombosis-MI, Toxins) must be actively excluded before any termination discussion. Hypothermia and toxicologic arrests particularly warrant prolonged resuscitation. See this node.

info.h: 🛑 Do NOT hyperventilate the intubated arrest patient
info.t: Hyperventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return, and decreases cardiac output — directly harming CPR effectiveness. Target 10 breaths/min (one breath every 6 seconds) with continuous compressions. Avoid the reflex to ventilate rapidly. See this node.
