The carotid artery lies 2.5-4 cm posterior and lateral to the tonsil. Inserting the needle beyond 10 mm risks catastrophic carotid artery injury. Mark the syringe or use a commercial depth limiter before every aspiration attempt. See aspiration technique.

Standard anterolateral pad position may deliver insufficient energy through scar or obesity. Switch to AP position (left parasternal + left infrascapular) before escalating to a second defibrillator — it's faster and may be sufficient alone. See vector change node.

Continuous-flow LVADs produce minimal or zero pulsatility — absence of a palpable pulse is NORMAL. Checking for pulse with a standard technique will falsely trigger a cardiac arrest response. Always use Doppler to measure MAP in LVAD patients. See VAD start node.

Large volumes of NS cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) which counteracts urine alkalinization goals and worsens tubular myoglobin precipitation. Lactated Ringers is preferred for rhabdomyolysis — the 4 mEq/L potassium does NOT clinically worsen hyperkalemia, contrary to common belief. S

Joint fluid Gram stain and culture are essential for guiding therapy — they cannot be interpreted after antibiotic administration. Aspiration must precede antibiotics unless the patient is septic and critically unstable. Diagnosis without synovial fluid analysis leads to empiric therapy that may mis

Fracture-dislocations (humeral neck fracture, Hill-Sachs lesion, bankart fracture) require modified technique or orthopedic consultation before manipulation. Reducing a shoulder with an unrecognized proximal humerus fracture can convert a stable fracture into a displaced one or cause neurovascular i

Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal ecchymosis, high-riding prostate, or a pelvic fracture mechanism all indicate possible urethral injury. Blind Foley catheterization through a urethral disruption converts a partial tear into a complete one. Get a retrograde urethrogram first; call urology for s

NSAIDs are contraindicated in viral myositis because they reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis and impair the renal blood flow needed to safely clear myoglobin. In a patient already at risk for AKI, NSAIDs can precipitate acute tubular necrosis. Use acetaminophen for analgesia instead. See pain mana

Chronically shunted ventricles may have lost compliance and will NOT dilate despite rising ICP. Normal CT and normal shunt series do not exclude malfunction. If clinical suspicion is high — headache, vomiting, lethargy, altered mental status — neurosurgery consultation is mandatory. See imaging node

Xylazine itself is not reversed by naloxone, but 95% of xylazine exposures involve fentanyl co-ingestion. Withholding naloxone because "it won't work" will miss the fentanyl component and allow the patient to die from opioid-induced respiratory arrest. Always give naloxone. See naloxone node.

VV-ECMO provides oxygenation and CO₂ removal only — it provides zero hemodynamic support. A patient with cardiogenic shock placed on VV-ECMO will continue to deteriorate hemodynamically despite excellent oxygenation. If there is any doubt about cardiac function, choose VA-ECMO. See ECMO selection no

Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and will worsen torsades de pointes. This is a fundamental error — TdP is polymorphic VT in the context of QT prolongation, and adding a QT-prolonging drug can precipitate fatal ventricular fibrillation. Magnesium is the correct first-line drug. See pulseless TdP

Standard hospital urine immunoassay drug screens miss most DFSA agents — GHB, benzodiazepines (especially non-prescribed), ketamine, scopolamine, and most sedative-hypnotics require forensic GC-MS/LC-MS confirmation. Send specimens directly to the state crime lab or forensic reference lab. See panel

Aggressive refeeding in severely malnourished patients causes refeeding syndrome — rapid intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium leading to fatal cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Start feeds slowly, replete electrolytes first, and check levels every 6

Children maintain blood pressure until 25–30% blood volume is lost — by the time hypotension appears, the child is in late decompensated shock. Tachycardia is the EARLY sign. Using adult BP thresholds as reassurance in a tachycardic child will cause you to miss hemorrhagic shock. See primary survey

New urinary retention or incontinence + back pain + any leg weakness or saddle anesthesia = cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise. This is a surgical emergency requiring emergent MRI and neurosurgery consult. Missing this diagnosis and attributing symptoms to BPH or UTI causes permanent neuro
Always co-treat: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days. Failing to cover both leads to persistent infection and resistance. See treatment node.

Diuretics worsen hemoconcentration in OHSS — the problem is third-spacing, not fluid overload. IV albumin and cautious crystalloids are the appropriate fluid strategy. Diuretics can precipitate renal failure and thromboembolic events. See why no diuretics.

Every pregnant woman with vaginal bleeding must have Rh(D) status confirmed before determining RhoGAM need. A missed Rh-negative patient who sensitizes loses future pregnancy options. See Rh check node.

Acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — gout and septic arthritis look identical clinically. Crystals do NOT exclude infection; 1–2% of cases have both simultaneously. Tap the joint. See monoarthritis overview.

ABI >1.4 indicates calcified non-compressible vessels — a false normal — which is extremely common in diabetics and ESRD. Use the toe-brachial index (TBI) or TcPO2 instead. Trusting ABI in a diabetic can lead to missing critical limb ischemia. See vascular intro.

Corticosteroids can mask leukemia and other malignancies presenting as joint pain in children. Do not initiate steroids in new pediatric arthritis without specialist input — always obtain CBC with differential first. See JIA management.

Crystals in synovial fluid do NOT rule out concurrent septic arthritis. Gout and pseudogout joints are at INCREASED risk for bacterial superinfection. If there is any clinical suspicion, send cultures even when crystals are identified. See septic concern node.

Hypotension, hypoxia, acidosis, RV failure, hyperkalemia, and elevated ICP are the six pre-intubation killers. Missing any one of them and proceeding with standard RSI causes peri-intubation cardiac arrest. Screen every high-risk patient systematically. See screening node.

ACEP 2016 explicitly states the ABCD2 score should NOT be used alone to determine safe discharge. Low scores still miss high-risk patients. Use the Canadian TIA score and always identify high-risk features independently. See risk stratification intro.

Orthopnea, PND, and dyspnea at rest in a pregnant or postpartum woman must be evaluated with echocardiography. PPCM is diagnosed when LVEF <45% — a finding that is completely missed if you assume dyspnea is physiologic pregnancy adaptation. See workup node.

Button batteries cause liquefaction necrosis of the ear canal within 1–2 hours via an electrical current. This is a time-critical emergency requiring immediate removal — do not irrigate or delay for any reason. See battery node.

Paradoxical dysesthesia — cold objects feeling burning hot, hot objects feeling cold — is pathognomonic for ciguatera. This symptom is often not volunteered by patients unless specifically asked. Always ask about temperature sensations in suspected fish poisoning. See symptoms node.

P. falciparum can progress from uncomplicated to severe malaria and death in 24–48 hours. STAT thick and thin blood smears plus rapid diagnostic test (RDT) are mandatory for any febrile traveler from an endemic region, regardless of prophylaxis use. See malaria screen node.

Prophylaxis failure occurs due to non-adherence, drug-resistant parasites, or stopping too early. Malaria can and does occur in patients on chemoprophylaxis. Always test febrile travelers regardless of reported prophylaxis use. See prophylaxis failure node.

A silent chest — no wheezing on auscultation — indicates critically severe obstruction with near-zero air movement. It is a sign of impending respiratory arrest, not improvement. Call for anesthesia, ICU, and RT immediately. See severity node.

Positive UA or culture without urinary symptoms is NOT a UTI in the vast majority of patients. Treating ASB increases C. diff risk, adverse effects, and antibiotic resistance without improving outcomes. The only exceptions are pregnancy and pre-urologic procedures. See this node.

Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP — it adds fuel to the microvascular thrombotic fire. Historical reports document sudden death, MI, and stroke after platelet transfusion. The only exception is life-threatening CNS hemorrhage, and even then requires hematology discussion first. See this

The tract is not epithelialized in the first 7 days — blind reinsertion creates a devastating false passage into the pretracheal space, causing subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and complete loss of airway. For fresh trach dislodgement, oxygenate via face and call the surgeon immediately. S

The tracheostomy tube provides both airway control and tamponade against the innominate artery during active TIF hemorrhage. Removing it before airway backup is secured and finger tamponade is ready will cause uncontrolled exsanguination. The tube is your friend until the moment of Utley maneuver. S

Polymorphic VT with prolonged QTc is Torsades — and amiodarone prolongs the QT interval, making it directly contraindicated. The correct treatment is magnesium sulfate 2g IV, repeated at 5-15 minutes if it persists, then a continuous infusion. Confusing TdP with standard VF/VT and giving amiodarone

Pseudo-PEA (PREM — cardiac motion present on POCUS) is profound shock, NOT true cardiac arrest. Standard 1mg epinephrine causes tachycardia and increased myocardial oxygen demand in a heart that is already contracting. Use titratable vasopressors: norepinephrine infusion, push-dose epinephrine 5-20

Asystole is a non-shockable rhythm. Defibrillation of a flatline is ineffective and wastes precious time. Always confirm asystole in 2 leads and check lead connections — fine VF can mimic asystole at low gain settings. True asystole requires CPR + epinephrine + aggressive cause search. See this node

Torsades de Pointes (polymorphic VT with prolonged QTc) is treated with magnesium, overdrive pacing, and stopping QT-prolonging drugs. Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval further and will worsen or perpetuate the arrhythmia. Always check baseline QTc before choosing an antiarrhythmic for polymorphic

Hyperoxia (PaO₂ >300 mmHg) causes oxidative injury to post-ischemic brain tissue and is independently associated with worse neurological outcomes. Immediately titrate FiO₂ down to target SpO₂ 94-98%. Most post-ROSC patients do not require 100% oxygen once circulation is restored. See this node.

HINTS is only valid in patients with continuous vertigo AND spontaneous nystagmus (true AVS). In a BPPV patient who has no spontaneous nystagmus at rest, the Head Impulse Test will appear "normal" — which HINTS interprets as worrisome for stroke. This leads to unnecessary imaging and false alarm. Se

Both methanol and EG have biphasic toxicity — patients may appear clinically improved as intoxication wanes, only to deteriorate hours later as toxic metabolites accumulate. Formate (methanol) and glycolate/oxalate (EG) cause the organ damage, not the parent compounds. All suspected methanol/EG inge

Irregular wide complex tachycardia may be AFib with WPW. Adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, beta-blockers, and digoxin are ALL contraindicated — they block the AV node, forcing all conduction down the accessory pathway → VF. If irregular WCT + rate >200 → assume WPW until proven otherwise.

Lactate is a LATE finding in mesenteric ischemia. By the time lactate is elevated, bowel may already be necrotic. Suspect AMI based on clinical presentation (pain out of proportion, gut emptying, vascular risk factors) — do not wait for confirmatory labs. Early CTA and surgery consult save bowel.

Extubation is elective unless it is part of a documented goals-of-care plan. If the patient still needs invasive ventilation for hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shock, airway protection, procedure safety, or incomplete diagnostic workup, keep the tube and reassess later. See this node.

Up to 20% of patients labeled "psychiatric" have an underlying organic cause — hypoglycemia, hypoxia, infection, electrolyte derangement, intoxication/withdrawal, intracranial pathology. Vital signs, glucose, and a focused neuro exam are mandatory before any psych disposition. "Frequent flyer" statu

Primary psychiatric psychosis almost always presents before age 40. New psychosis after 45 = medical cause until proven otherwise — stroke, tumor, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosyphilis, dementia with psychosis, metabolic, drug-induced. Get CT head, full labs, urine tox, and consider LP. See this no

Capacity is clinical (assessed by physicians, decision-specific, can fluctuate). Competency is legal (determined by a court, global). Any physician can — and must — assess capacity in real time. Do not defer routine medical decisions to a court hearing. See this node.

First- and second-generation antipsychotics can convert simple catatonia into malignant catatonia or NMS — autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity, death. Hold all dopamine blockers until catatonia is resolved. Treat with benzodiazepines first. See this node.

Stop ALL antipsychotics, antiemetics with dopamine antagonism (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine), and lithium immediately. Restart the dopamine agonist if NMS occurred from withdrawal of Parkinson medication. The first treatment is removal of the trigger. See this node.

Grouped clear vesicles on an erythematous base = HSV until proven otherwise. Incision spreads virus, causes bacterial superinfection, and slows healing. Treat with antivirals when indicated, analgesia, and a dry occlusive dressing. See this node.
An SGA can ventilate but does not seal the trachea like a cuffed ETT. If aspiration risk or prolonged ventilation matters, use it as a bridge while preparing the definitive airway. See this node.

Confirm mechanism, signs of life, CPR duration, rhythm, and cardiac motion when available. Avoid nonbeneficial thoracotomy when there is no realistic path to reversible physiology or definitive source control. See indications.

Current ACG guidance recommends against empiric clarithromycin-containing therapy unless susceptibility is documented. Clarithromycin resistance can make the classic PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin regimen fail. See regimen node.

extraNodes.title: Asystole: act while confirming the rhythm
extraNodes.summary: CPR now; epinephrine promptly for nonshockable arrest; confirm the monitor signal.
extraNodes.body: Adult pulseless arrest: activate the team, start CPR and attach defibrillation pads. If pulse assessment is uncertain, limit it to 10 seconds and start CPR. True asystole is nonshockable; promptly check whether apparent asystole is fine VF. Do not delay CPR, ventilation or early epinephrine to troubleshoot the monitor. Steps · Fine VF checklist · LIFEPAK 15 controls Use the bottom tools for immediate access. This adult pathway does not replace special-circumstance protocols.

extraNodes.title: Confirm asystole, not fine VF
extraNodes.body: Check the patient and the signal while CPR continues. Confirm cable connections, pads/electrode adhesion, and absence of a lead-off message. A disconnected lead is not asystole. At the scheduled brief rhythm check: inspect a second available ECG vector and increase display gain/size if the trace is very small. Keep interruption under 10 seconds; resume compressions promptly. Prepare settings during CPR. Fine VF: irregular, chaotic electrical activity without organized QRS complexes. Confirmed VF is shockable even when low amplitude. True asystole: no ventricular electrical activity after check

extraNodes.title: What rhythm is present?
extraNodes.body: Assess during a brief scheduled rhythm check. Resume compressions promptly; do not wait for a long diagnostic pause.

extraNodes.title: Nonshockable arrest: CPR + epinephrine
extraNodes.body: CPR: 100–120 compressions/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil, rotate compressor every 2 minutes. Minimize pauses. Bag-mask with oxygen; 30:2 without an advanced airway. With an advanced airway, continuous compressions and 1 breath every 6 seconds; avoid hyperventilation. Epinephrine: 1 mg IV/IO as soon as feasible, then every 3–5 minutes. Prefer IV; use IO if IV is not feasible or delayed. Do not wait for a completed CPR cycle to give the first dose. Use waveform capnography after advanced airway placement. Do not interrupt compressions for airway placement when ventilation is effective. No routin

extraNodes.title: VF / pulseless VT: defibrillate
extraNodes.body: Deliver an unsynchronized shock using the manufacturer/local biphasic energy protocol. Resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes. Do not delay confirmed fine-VF defibrillation to make VF coarser. Open cardiac arrest pathway for ongoing shockable-arrest management.
extraNodes.recommendation: Defibrillate VF/pVT; immediately resume CPR.

extraNodes.title: Organized rhythm without pulse: PEA
extraNodes.body: Continue CPR, give early epinephrine and treat reversible causes. Do not shock an organized pulseless rhythm. Open PEA consult.
extraNodes.recommendation: Treat PEA; continue CPR and search for reversible causes.

extraNodes.title: P waves without QRS: ventricular standstill
extraNodes.body: This is not complete electrical silence. Continue the pulseless-arrest bundle and seek expert rhythm review. ERC 2025 selected pacing consideration for P-wave ventricular standstill is distinct from routine pacing of true asystole and must not delay CPR or epinephrine. If pacing is attempted, confirm immediate electrical AND mechanical capture; if absent, immediately resume CPR.

extraNodes.title: Uncertain fine VF vs asystole
extraNodes.body: Check the patient and the signal while CPR continues. Confirm cable connections, pads/electrode adhesion, and absence of a lead-off message. A disconnected lead is not asystole. At the scheduled brief rhythm check: inspect a second available ECG vector and increase display gain/size if the trace is very small. Keep interruption under 10 seconds; resume compressions promptly. Prepare settings during CPR. Fine VF: irregular, chaotic electrical activity without organized QRS complexes. Confirmed VF is shockable even when low amplitude. True asystole: no ventricular electrical activity after check

extraNodes.title: Find and treat a reversible cause
extraNodes.body: Hypoxia: verify ventilation, airway position and oxygen supply. Hypovolemia: control hemorrhage; blood/fluids as indicated. Hydrogen ion / metabolic disturbance: treat the underlying cause; avoid routine bicarbonate. Hypo-/hyperkalemia: review context, point-of-care electrolytes and ECG; use cause-specific treatment. Hypothermia: temperature and rewarming pathway. Tension pneumothorax: decompress when clinically suspected. Tamponade: selected expert ultrasound and drainage pathway. Toxins: exposure-directed resuscitation / toxicology support. Thrombosis: consider PE and coronary causes. POCUS

extraNodes.title: Reassess every 2 minutes
extraNodes.body: Brief rhythm assessment every 2 minutes; check pulse only with an organized rhythm or signs of ROSC. Continue epinephrine every 3–5 minutes while pulseless. Reassess CPR quality and reversible causes each cycle.

extraNodes.title: ROSC: stabilize and hand over
extraNodes.body: Confirm a sustained pulse, support oxygenation and ventilation, avoid hypotension, obtain 12-lead ECG and treat the cause. Open post-ROSC care.
extraNodes.recommendation: Begin post-cardiac-arrest care.

extraNodes.title: Termination requires the whole clinical picture
extraNodes.body: Senior team decision using circumstances, resuscitation quality/duration, reversible causes, patient wishes and local policy. Consider special circumstances such as hypothermia or poisoning before stopping. Do not apply prehospital termination rules automatically to ED patients. ETCO2 or ultrasound standstill alone is insufficient. Document the decision and support family.
extraNodes.recommendation: Individualized team decision; no single-test stopping rule.

extraNodes.title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
extraNodes.summary: Spontaneous SAH: 85% aneurysmal, 40% mortality at 1 week, 5% misdiagnosis rate on initial ED visit — delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes
extraNodes.body: SAH Steps Summary — quick reference. Spontaneous SAH (sSAH) results from extravasation of blood into the CSF. 85% are caused by aneurysm rupture. 10% are nonaneurysmal perimesencephalic hemorrhage (better prognosis). • Incidence: ~10 per 100,000/year in the US • Mortality: ~40% at 1 week; 10-15% die prehospital • Misdiagnosis rate: up to 5% on initial ED visit • Delayed or missed diagnosis → significantly worse outcomes Risk factors: Hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol use, cocaine, family history of aSAH, polycystic kidney disease, connective tissue disorders, female sex.

extraNodes.title: Clinical Presentation
extraNodes.summary: Thunderclap headache in 10-16% is SAH, 70% present with headache alone, normal neuro exam in 75% — pain responding to analgesics does NOT exclude SAH
extraNodes.body: Classic: Sudden-onset severe headache ("worst headache of my life") peaking within seconds — thunderclap headache. Neither sensitive nor specific for SAH. • 10-16% of thunderclap headaches are SAH • 70% present with headache alone, no focal symptoms • Normal neurologic exam in 75% of aSAH patients • Transient LOC in ~25% • Vomiting in ~70%; neck stiffness in ~60% • Seizures or cranial nerve palsies suggest serious pathology Atypical presentations: • Isolated neck/back pain (8% have no headache) • General malaise without typical headache • Sentinel/warning headache (10-43%) days to weeks before

extraNodes.title: Ottawa SAH Rule
extraNodes.summary: Ottawa SAH Rule (100% sensitivity): age >=40, neck pain/stiffness, LOC, exertional onset, thunderclap, limited neck flexion — any present needs workup
extraNodes.body: For patients with acute nontraumatic headache reaching maximal intensity within 1 hour and a normal neurologic examination, apply the Ottawa SAH Rule. Further workup required if ANY present: • Age ≥40 years • Neck pain or stiffness • Witnessed loss of consciousness • Onset during exertion • Thunderclap headache (peaks within 1 minute) • Limited neck flexion on examination Sensitivity 100% (validation studies). Specificity 27.5%. 2019 ACEP Clinical Policy supports using this rule to identify patients who may not require imaging.

extraNodes.title: Ottawa Rule Negative — Low Risk
extraNodes.body: Patient meets no Ottawa SAH Rule criteria (age <40, no neck pain/stiffness, no LOC, no exertional onset, no thunderclap, normal neck flexion). 2019 ACEP Clinical Policy supports that these patients may not require imaging for SAH. However, if clinical suspicion remains high based on overall presentation, proceeding with CT is still appropriate. The rule is designed to identify the lowest-risk cohort, not to replace clinical judgment. Discharge instructions: • Return immediately for worsening headache, new neurologic symptoms, or altered consciousness • Follow up with primary care within 1-2 we
extraNodes.recommendation: Low-risk per Ottawa SAH Rule — may discharge with return precautions if clinical suspicion is low

extraNodes.title: Noncontrast CT Head
extraNodes.summary: CT sensitivity: 98.7% within 6h, 86% at day 1, 58% at day 5 — requires 3rd-gen scanner and attending radiologist read for highest sensitivity
extraNodes.body: The initial test for suspected sSAH is noncontrast head CT. CT sensitivity is time-dependent — blood is degraded and diluted by CSF circulation over time. CT sensitivity by timing: • Within 6 hours: 98.7% (meta-analysis of 8,907 patients) • Day 0: 92-100% • Day 1: 86% • Day 2: 76% • Day 5: 58% Conditions for highest sensitivity (≤6h): • Third-generation or newer scanner • Interpreted by attending radiologist • Normal neurologic examination • Normal hematocrit (anemia may make blood isodense with CSF) Key pearl: A negative CT does not rule out SAH, especially with later presentations.

extraNodes.title: CT Result
extraNodes.summary: Interpret CT in context of time from onset — positive = confirmed SAH, negative <=6h may rule out, negative >6h needs LP
extraNodes.body: Interpret the noncontrast head CT result in the context of time from symptom onset. CT positive: Hyperdensity in the basal cisterns (typical aneurysmal pattern) or cerebral convexities (consider traumatic or convexal SAH). CT negative ≤6h: In a prospective study of 3,132 patients, CT within 6 hours had 100% sensitivity. A meta-analysis reports 98.7% sensitivity with appropriate conditions. CT negative >6h: Sensitivity decreases progressively — additional testing is needed.

extraNodes.title: CT Negative Within 6 Hours
extraNodes.summary: ACEP 2019 Level B: negative CT within 6h on 3rd-gen scanner + attending read + normal neuro + no anemia may rule out SAH without LP
extraNodes.body: A negative CT within 6 hours of symptom onset has very high sensitivity for SAH, but may not be 100% depending on scanner generation and interpretation. ACEP 2019 Level B recommendation: In patients presenting within 6 hours with a negative CT on a third-generation or newer scanner read by an attending radiologist, a normal neurologic exam, and no anemia, sSAH may be ruled out without LP. Consider proceeding to LP if: • High clinical suspicion despite negative CT • Uncertain scanner generation • CT read by non-radiologist • Patient has anemia (Hct <30%) • Symptom onset time uncertain

extraNodes.title: Lumbar Puncture
extraNodes.summary: LP technique: lateral recumbent, opening pressure, 4 serial tubes, last tube for xanthochromia — xanthochromia takes up to 12h to develop
extraNodes.body: LP Interpretation Guide — detailed reference. For patients with negative CT and ongoing suspicion for SAH, LP is the next diagnostic step. Technique: • Patient in lateral recumbent position • Measure opening pressure (elevated >20 cm H₂O in 60% of sSAH) • Collect 4 serial tubes of CSF • Send last tube for cell count AND xanthochromia Key considerations: • Traumatic tap occurs in 10-15% of patients • Xanthochromia takes up to 12 hours to develop • If LP performed <12h after onset, accept either RBCs or xanthochromia as positive • Finding normal CSF at any time point excludes SAH Opening pressur

extraNodes.title: LP Interpretation
extraNodes.summary: Xanthochromia or persistent RBCs = SAH, partial clearing = equivocal (get CTA), normal CSF = SAH excluded — visual xanthochromia 93% sens/95% spec
extraNodes.body: Assess the CSF results: Positive for SAH: • Xanthochromia (yellow color from hemoglobin breakdown) — highly suggestive, unlikely with traumatic tap • Persistent RBCs constant across all 4 tubes (usually in thousands) Equivocal: • Partial clearing of RBCs (e.g., 3,000 in tube 1, 400 in tube 4) — may be traumatic tap OR SAH • >10,000 RBCs in final tube = 6x more likely SAH Negative: • Zero RBCs in final tube = traumatic tap • Normal CSF (no RBCs, no xanthochromia) = SAH excluded Visual xanthochromia: Centrifuge last tube, compare against water on white background. Sensitivity 93%, specificity 95

extraNodes.title: Equivocal CSF Results
extraNodes.summary: Equivocal CSF: get CTA (97-99% sensitivity for aneurysm) — negative CTA with bloody CSF = low risk, consult neurosurgery for shared decision-making
extraNodes.body: With partial clearing of RBCs, the distinction between traumatic tap and true SAH can be difficult. Obtain CTA to evaluate for aneurysm. CTA sensitivity for aneurysms is 97-99% compared to digital subtraction angiography. Key findings: • Patients with bloody CSF and negative cerebrovascular imaging are at low risk for subsequent SAH • CTA may identify incidental aneurysms (2% of population) — require neurosurgical consultation • Aneurysm detection decreases for aneurysms <4 mm Consult neurosurgery for shared decision-making regarding further workup or observation.

extraNodes.title: SAH Excluded
extraNodes.body: SAH has been excluded by the diagnostic workup. Negative CT + negative LP = SAH confidently ruled out, supported by multiple prospective studies with long-term follow-up (no subsequent SAH over 3+ years). Negative CT within 6h (with appropriate conditions) = SAH ruled out per ACEP 2019 Level B recommendation. Consider alternative diagnoses: • Migraine or other primary headache syndrome • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension • Spontaneous intracranial hypotension • Meningitis • Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) Discharge safely with outpatie
extraNodes.recommendation: SAH excluded — safe discharge with outpatient follow-up and clear return precautions

extraNodes.title: SAH Confirmed
extraNodes.summary: SAH confirmed: immediate neurosurgery consult + CTA for aneurysm — 85% aneurysmal (70% in ACA/PCA/MCA), 10% perimesencephalic (excellent prognosis)
extraNodes.body: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is confirmed. Immediately: • Obtain neurosurgical consultation — arrange definitive therapy • Order CTA (if not already done) to identify the aneurysm • Begin ED management and monitoring CT hemorrhage patterns: • Basal cisterns — typical aneurysmal SAH • Cerebral convexities — traumatic SAH, or convexal SAH (RCVS if <60y, cerebral amyloid angiopathy if >60y) • Perimesencephalic — blood around midbrain with normal angiogram; 10% of sSAH, excellent prognosis (98% survive without deficits) Aneurysm locations (85% of sSAH): • 70% in anterior communicating, posterior commun

extraNodes.title: Clinical Severity Grading
extraNodes.summary: Hunt & Hess (clinical) and Modified Fisher (CT/vasospasm risk) — grades 4-5 historically 70-90% mortality, improved with modern care
extraNodes.body: Grade severity to guide management and predict outcomes. Hunt & Hess Scale — most widely used clinically: • Grade 1: Asymptomatic or mild headache • Grade 2: Severe headache, stiff neck, no focal deficits • Grade 3: Drowsy, mild focal deficit • Grade 4: Stupor, moderate-severe hemiparesis • Grade 5: Coma, decerebrate posturing Higher grade = higher mortality. Grades 4-5 historically 70-90% mortality, improved with modern care. Modified Fisher Scale — predicts vasospasm risk from CT: • Grade 0-1: Low vasospasm risk • Grade 2-3: Moderate-high risk • Grade 4: Thick SAH with IVH → highest vasospas

extraNodes.title: Vasospasm Risk Assessment
extraNodes.summary: Vasospasm peaks days 7-10 — all SAH patients get nimodipine, high Fisher = closer monitoring, VASOGRADE further stratifies risk
extraNodes.body: Cerebral vasospasm is a delayed complication developing days to 2 weeks post-SAH, with peak incidence at 7-10 days. Risk prediction (Modified Fisher Scale): • Thick clot and intraventricular hemorrhage → highest risk • Thin SAH without IVH → lowest risk Vasospasm may be: • Asymptomatic — detected only on imaging • Symptomatic — delayed neurologic deterioration causing significant morbidity Key management implications: • All confirmed SAH patients should receive Nimodipine for vasospasm prevention • High-grade Fisher patients need closer monitoring and earlier neurosurgical intervention • The V

extraNodes.title: Initial ED Management
extraNodes.summary: HOB 30 degrees, NPO, continuous cardiac monitoring, acetaminophen for pain — avoid NSAIDs, use opioids cautiously (interfere with neuro exam)
extraNodes.body: Prioritize: Airway management, hemodynamic monitoring, supportive care, and prevention of complications. General measures: • Bed rest with head of bed at 30° (facilitates venous drainage) • NPO until surgical/endovascular treatment plan is decided • Continuous cardiac monitoring — ECG changes in 50-100% of patients • Serial neurologic examinations — monitor for deterioration • Adequate analgesia — Acetaminophen 1 g PO/IV q6h. Avoid NSAIDs (platelet dysfunction). Use opioids cautiously (interfere with neuro exam). • Antiemetics as needed for comfort Outcomes are best when care is provided by mu

extraNodes.title: Blood Pressure Management
extraNodes.summary: Target SBP <160 until aneurysm secured — labetalol or nicardipine IV, avoid nitroprusside (increases ICP), arterial line recommended
extraNodes.body: Target: SBP <160 mmHg until aneurysm is secured (AHA/ASA 2023 — no precise numeric target mandated, but avoiding hypertension minimizes rebleeding). Higher pressures may increase rebleeding risk, but aggressive lowering may compromise cerebral perfusion. Titratable IV agents: • Labetalol — 10-20 mg IV bolus over 1-2 min. Repeat or start infusion 2-8 mg/min. Max 300 mg/24h. • Nicardipine — 5 mg/hr IV, titrate by 2.5 mg/hr q5-15 min. Max 15 mg/hr. • Clevidipine — 1-2 mg/hr IV, double q90 sec to target. Ultra-short t½ (~1 min). Avoid nitroprusside — increases intracranial pressure and risk of tox

extraNodes.title: Vasospasm Prevention — Nimodipine
extraNodes.summary: Nimodipine 60mg PO q4h x21 days — only proven intervention for vasospasm, oral route only, IV magnesium and statins NOT effective
extraNodes.body: Nimodipine is the only proven pharmacologic intervention to reduce morbidity from vasospasm-related ischemia. Dosing: 60 mg PO every 4 hours × 21 days • Start within 96 hours of ictus — the initiation window used in the landmark trial (Pickard 1989); earlier is better • If unable to swallow: crush and administer via nasogastric tube • No evidence for IV nimodipine — oral route only • Give to hemodynamically stable patients • Part of comprehensive stroke center measures Evidence: Cochrane review of 16 trials — risk ratio 0.67 (95% CI 0.55-0.81) for secondary ischemia. Landmark RCT (554 patients

extraNodes.title: Seizure Management
extraNodes.summary: Seizures in up to 20% — levetiracetam preferred over phenytoin (worse outcomes), short course <3 days if prophylaxis used
extraNodes.body: Up to 20% of patients have a seizure during or soon after aSAH. Seizures can cause rebleeding from an unsecured aneurysm. Key points: • No RCTs on prophylactic antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) in SAH • Phenytoin should be avoided — associated with worse outcomes, functional decline, and cognitive disability • If prophylaxis is used, prefer a short course (<3 days) — same benefit as longer courses without cumulative adverse effects If prophylaxis is initiated: • Levetiracetam 500 mg PO/IV BID — preferred due to better side-effect profile • No hepatic metabolism, no drug interactions, no cardiac effec

extraNodes.title: Rebleeding Prevention
extraNodes.summary: Rebleeding 8-23% in first 72h (50-90% within 6h) — highest mortality of any SAH complication, early repair is primary prevention. TXA NOT recommended per 2023 AHA/ASA (ULTRA trial negative).
extraNodes.body: Rebleeding is one of the most devastating complications after aSAH, with the highest mortality of any complication. • Cumulative incidence: 8-23% in first 72 hours • 50-90% of episodes occur within first 6 hours after primary bleed • Clinical signs: acute/worsening headache, decreased consciousness, loss of brainstem reflexes, posturing, respiratory arrest, seizures Risk factors for rebleeding: • High-grade SAH (Hunt & Hess 4-5) • Larger aneurysms • Prolonged time to surgery • Sentinel/warning bleeds • Catheter angiography Prevention strategies: • Early definitive repair — primary strategy (wi

extraNodes.title: Cardiac Complications
extraNodes.summary: ECG changes in 50-100%, troponin elevated in 20-40% — neurogenic stunned myocardium (Takotsubo), SAH contraindicates thrombolytics/anticoagulants
extraNodes.body: SAH ECG Changes — detailed reference. Cardiac abnormalities are common following acute sSAH due to catecholamine surge and autonomic stimulation. ECG changes (50-100% of patients): • Nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave changes • Prolonged QRS, U waves, prolonged QT interval • ST elevations mimicking MI — coronary angiography typically normal • Serious arrhythmias in <5% (associated with worse outcomes) Troponin: Elevated in 20-40% of acute cases. Indicates cardiopulmonary complications and worse outcomes. Neurogenic stunned myocardium (Takotsubo): • Acutely depressed EF (can be as low as 20%) •

extraNodes.title: Definitive Aneurysm Repair
extraNodes.summary: Endovascular coiling (ISAT: improved outcomes) vs microvascular clipping — early treatment within 72h, choice depends on anatomy and expertise
extraNodes.body: Vascular imaging: Cerebral angiography (DSA) is the gold standard for preoperative planning. CTA has 97-99% sensitivity. Angiography may be negative in 10-20% (perimesencephalic hemorrhage, vasospasm, thrombosed aneurysm). Two approaches to aneurysm repair: Endovascular coiling: • ISAT trial (2,143 patients) — improved outcomes vs clipping • Slightly higher rebleeding risk • Increasing use as first-line approach Microvascular clipping: • Higher seizure risk • May be necessary for certain aneurysm anatomies Timing: Early treatment within 72 hours is the common approach. The choice depends on an

extraNodes.title: Special Populations
extraNodes.summary: Pregnant/postpartum: same principles, also consider CVT/RCVS/preeclampsia — anticoagulated: reverse, but do NOT reverse antiplatelets without surgical plan
extraNodes.body: Pregnant/Postpartum Women: • Pregnancy and postpartum are hypercoagulable states • Also consider: ischemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, RCVS, pre-eclampsia, PRES • Management principles are the same Anticoagulated Patients: • Reverse therapeutic anticoagulation in the acute setting • Do NOT reverse antiplatelet agents unless neurosurgical procedure is planned — transfusion without benefit increases mortality Perimesencephalic Hemorrhage: • 10% of sSAH; blood confined around midbrain on CT • Normal angiogram required (DSA is test of choice) • Excellent prognosis — 98% survive without def

extraNodes.title: Disposition
extraNodes.summary: All confirmed SAH require ICU admission — better outcomes at high-volume centers (OR 0.77 mortality), 90% arrive without GCS deterioration
extraNodes.body: All patients with confirmed SAH require ICU admission, preferably a neurointensive care unit, for continuous monitoring until definitive aneurysm repair. Better outcomes at high-volume centers — meta-analysis of 36,000+ patients: reduction in mortality (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.60-0.97). Transfer considerations: • Average 5.2 hours from diagnosis to arrival at neurosurgical center • 90% arrive without significant GCS deterioration • Air transport is safe and effective • Prearranged interfacility agreements facilitate efficient transfer

extraNodes.title: Transfer to High-Volume Center
extraNodes.body: Arrange emergent transfer to a center with: • Neurosurgical ICU • Both surgical (clipping) and endovascular (coiling) capabilities • Multidisciplinary neurovascular team Pre-transfer management: • Secure airway if GCS ≤8 • Continuous cardiac monitoring and BP management (SBP <160) • Start Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h if hemodynamically stable • Communicate Hunt & Hess grade, Fisher grade, and CT findings to receiving team • NPO for potential procedural intervention • Bring all imaging on disc or ensure electronic transfer Transfer is generally safe — 90% of patients arrive without significant clini
extraNodes.recommendation: Emergent transfer to high-volume neurosurgical center for definitive aneurysm repair and neurointensive care

extraNodes.title: Neuro ICU Admission
extraNodes.body: Admit to neurointensive care unit for: • Continuous hemodynamic and neuro monitoring • Definitive aneurysm repair (within 72 hours) • Vasospasm surveillance (peak risk days 7-10) • Management of secondary complications Ongoing ED management until bed available: • BP target SBP <160 with titratable IV agents • Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h • Serial neuro checks q1h • NPO status maintained • Adequate analgesia and antiemetics • Watch for clinical deterioration — repeat CT immediately if decline Prognosis: In-hospital mortality >30% even at high-volume centers. Aggressive approaches may still be warran
extraNodes.recommendation: Neurointensive care admission with definitive aneurysm repair within 72 hours and vasospasm monitoring for 14 days

extraNodes.title: Wrist Injury Assessment
extraNodes.summary: Mechanism-based triage: FOOSH, dorsal fall, direct blow, high-energy; assess neurovascular status first
extraNodes.body: Wrist injuries account for ~15% of ED orthopedic visits. Recognition of fracture patterns, associated dislocations, and neurovascular compromise is critical. Mechanism guides injury pattern: • FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand) → distal radius, scaphoid, perilunate dislocation • Fall on dorsum of hand → Smith fracture, triquetral fracture • Direct blow to hypothenar → hamate hook fracture • High-energy hyperextension → perilunate/lunate dislocation • Forced rotation → DRUJ dislocation, TFCC tear Red flags requiring emergent management: • Neurovascular compromise (absent pulses, motor deficit, m

extraNodes.title: Distal Radius Fracture Types
extraNodes.summary: Colles (dorsal), Smith (volar), Barton (intra-articular rim) — always check median nerve and DRUJ stability
extraNodes.body: Three main patterns: 1. Colles Fracture (Most Common) • Dorsal angulation + displacement • "Dinner fork" deformity • FOOSH with wrist dorsiflexion • Often with ulnar styloid fracture 2. Smith Fracture (Reverse Colles) • Volar displacement/angulation • "Garden spade" deformity • Fall on dorsum of hand • More unstable — often requires surgery 3. Barton Fracture • Intra-articular rim fracture (dorsal or volar) • Carpal bones dislocate with rim fragment • Inherently unstable • High likelihood of operative fixation 🚨 ALWAYS assess for: • Neurovascular status (median nerve most at risk) • Ulnar sty

extraNodes.title: Distal Radius Fracture Classification
extraNodes.summary: Classify by radiograph: Colles (dorsal angulation), Smith (volar), or Barton (rim + carpal dislocation)
extraNodes.body: Based on radiographs, what type of distal radius fracture?

extraNodes.title: Colles Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Classic Charnley Reduction Technique: Pre-Reduction: • Procedural sedation • Consider hematoma block (10-15 mL lidocaine into fracture site) • Finger traps × 10 minutes (optional) Reduction Steps: 1. Apply continuous longitudinal traction 2. Disimpact fracture: exaggerate dorsal angulation (increase deformity) 3. Robert-Jones maneuver: While maintaining traction, force distal fragment volarly (push volar with thumbs on dorsal fragment) 4. Return wrist to neutral to slight extension (10-20°) 5. Maintain traction while applying splint Post-Reduction: • Sugar tong splint (limits forearm rotation)
extraNodes.recommendation: Reduce with Charnley technique. Sugar tong splint. Ortho follow-up 3-5 days if stable, urgent if intra-articular or unable to maintain reduction.

extraNodes.title: Smith Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Smith Fracture = Reverse Colles Key Point: More difficult to maintain closed reduction than Colles. High rate of operative intervention. Reduction Technique: 1. Procedural sedation 2. Apply longitudinal traction 3. Force distal fragment dorsally (opposite of Colles) 4. Return to neutral position Immobilization: • Volar splint if attempting closed management • BUT: inherently unstable, often loses reduction 📞 URGENT Orthopedic Referral: • Most Smith fractures require surgical fixation • Low threshold for urgent consultation (within 24-48h) Pitfall: Attempting prolonged conservative management
extraNodes.recommendation: Urgent orthopedic consultation (24-48h). If attempting ED reduction, use volar splint, but expect surgical referral. Smith fractures are inherently unstable.

extraNodes.title: Barton Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Barton Fracture = Intra-Articular Rim + Carpal Dislocation Definition: • Fracture of dorsal or volar articular rim of distal radius • Carpal bones sublux/dislocate WITH the rim fragment • Dorsal rim more common (forced dorsiflexion + pronation) Why It Matters: • Inherently unstable • Intra-articular involvement • High likelihood of operative fixation • Cannot be adequately treated with closed reduction ED Management: 1. Neurovascular assessment 2. Splint for comfort (sugar tong) 3. URGENT orthopedic consultation 📞 Call Orthopedics NOW: • All Barton fractures require urgent surgical evaluation
extraNodes.recommendation: Urgent orthopedic consultation. Sugar tong splint. Do NOT attempt closed reduction in ED. Barton fractures require surgical fixation.

extraNodes.title: Carpal Bone Fracture Identification
extraNodes.summary: Scaphoid 60-70% of carpal fractures; scaphoid and lunate at high AVN risk due to retrograde blood supply
extraNodes.body: Carpal bone fracture frequency: 1. Scaphoid — 60-70% (most common) 2. Triquetrum — 15% (second most common) 3. Lunate — 0.5-4% 4. Hamate — 2-4% 5. Others — trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, pisiform (rare) Clinical exam guides diagnosis: • Snuffbox tenderness → scaphoid • Dorsal ulnar tenderness → triquetrum • Central dorsal wrist pain → lunate • Hypothenar pain → hamate ⚠️ High-risk fractures for AVN: • Scaphoid (proximal pole) • Lunate (Kienböck disease) Both have retrograde blood supply → immobilize aggressively

extraNodes.title: Scaphoid Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Most commonly fractured carpal bone (60-70%) Clinical Diagnosis (even if X-rays negative): • Snuffbox tenderness (dorsal) • Scaphoid tubercle tenderness (volar) • Pain with axial thumb loading • Decreased grip strength Imaging: • Initial: PA, lateral, oblique, scaphoid view (PA with ulnar deviation) • Plain X-rays only 70% sensitive — negative films do NOT exclude fracture • If clinical suspicion + negative X-rays → immobilize and arrange MRI/CT in 3-5 days • MRI preferred (detects bone marrow edema) • CT: alternative for immediate triage Immobilization: • Thumb spica splint (includes thumb IP
extraNodes.recommendation: Thumb spica splint for all clinically suspected scaphoid fractures, even if X-rays negative. Arrange MRI/CT in 3-5 days if initial films negative. Urgent ortho for proximal pole or displaced fractures.

extraNodes.title: Triquetral Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Second most common carpal fracture (15%) Two Types: 1. Dorsal chip fracture (most common) — FOOSH mechanism, visible on lateral view 2. Body fracture — less common, requires CT for diagnosis Imaging: • Standard wrist series • 18.9% require CT for accurate diagnosis • Dorsal chip: look on lateral radiograph Clinical Presentation: • Tenderness over dorsal triquetrum (between pisiform and ulnar head) • Pain with ulnar deviation Management: • Dorsal chip (FOOSH mechanism): - Removable splint × 3-4 weeks - Early mobilization acceptable - Very low complication rate • Body fracture: - Plaster/fibergl
extraNodes.recommendation: Dorsal chip: removable splint × 3-4 weeks. Body fracture: short arm cast × 6 weeks. Routine ortho follow-up. Excellent prognosis.

extraNodes.title: Lunate Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Rare (0.5-4% of carpal fractures) but HIGH RISK Mechanism: High-energy trauma, axial loading Clinical Presentation: • Central wrist pain • Tenderness over lunate (dorsal and volar) • Reduced grip strength Imaging: • Standard wrist radiographs • MRI for suspected occult fracture (preferred) • Look for: - Lunate fracture line - Increased density (suggests AVN/Kienböck disease) - Collapse (late finding) ⚠️ HIGH RISK FOR AVN (Kienböck Disease): • Tenuous retrograde blood supply (like scaphoid) • Can progress to collapse, fragmentation, carpal instability • Early immobilization critical Immobilizat
extraNodes.recommendation: Long arm thumb spica × 10-12 weeks. URGENT orthopedic referral (24-48h) for all lunate fractures due to high AVN risk. Consider MRI if clinical suspicion despite negative X-rays.

extraNodes.title: Hamate Fracture Management
extraNodes.body: Hook of Hamate Fracture (Most Common Hamate Injury) Mechanism: • Direct blow to hypothenar eminence • Common in racquet sports, baseball, golf ("grip injuries") Clinical Presentation: • Hypothenar pain and tenderness • Pain with resisted finger flexion (FDP to ring/small fingers) • May have ulnar nerve symptoms (paresthesias in ring/small fingers) Imaging Challenge: • Standard wrist views often MISS hook fractures • Carpal tunnel view (skyline view) — hand supinated, wrist hyperextended • CT scan for confirmation (gold standard) Complications if Missed: • Non-union → chronic pain, weak grip •
extraNodes.recommendation: High clinical suspicion in athletes with hypothenar pain. Carpal tunnel view or CT for diagnosis (standard X-rays miss it). Short arm cast × 6 weeks for non-displaced. Routine ortho referral; surgical excision often needed.

extraNodes.title: Perilunate vs Lunate Dislocation
extraNodes.summary: Perilunate: capitate dorsal; lunate dislocation: lunate volar into carpal tunnel; 15-50% acute CTS — reduce emergently
extraNodes.body: Two stages of the same injury spectrum: 1. Perilunate Dislocation: • Carpus (capitate + distal row) dislocates dorsally • Lunate maintains normal relationship with radius • Lateral X-ray: Lunate aligned with radius, capitate displaced dorsally 2. Lunate Dislocation (More Severe): • Lunate dislocates volarly (rotates into carpal tunnel) • "Spilled teacup" sign on lateral view • Lateral X-ray: Lunate tilted volar, loss of relationship with radius Mechanism: • High-energy hyperextension injury (FOOSH with ulnar deviation) • MVA, fall from height • Progressive perilunate instability (Mayfield clas

extraNodes.title: Perilunate/Lunate Reduction Technique
extraNodes.body: Tavernier Method for ED Reduction: Pre-Reduction: • Procedural sedation (required) • Neurovascular documentation (especially median nerve) • Assistant for countertraction Reduction Steps: 1. Finger trap traction × 10 minutes with elbow flexed 90° 2. After distraction, release traction 3. Extend wrist while stabilizing lunate on volar aspect with thumb 4. Gradually flex wrist to allow capitate to reduce into lunate concavity 5. Push lunate dorsally while flexing wrist 6. Return to neutral position 7. Maintain reduction while applying splint Alternative Technique (if finger traps unavailable): •
extraNodes.recommendation: REDUCE EMERGENTLY using Tavernier method (finger traps × 10min, extend then flex wrist, push lunate dorsally). Thumb spica after reduction. Call ortho immediately — most require surgery.

extraNodes.title: DRUJ (Distal Radioulnar Joint) Dislocation
extraNodes.body: DRUJ Dislocation — Easily Missed! Types: • Dorsal (more common) — forced pronation + hyperextension • Volar — forced supination injury Clinical Presentation: • Ulnar-sided wrist pain • Dorsal dislocation: Prominent ulnar head dorsally • Volar dislocation: Absent ulnar head prominence • Limited/painful forearm rotation (pronation/supination) • Often subtle → frequently missed Imaging: • True lateral wrist radiograph essential • Compare DRUJ relationship bilaterally • CT for subtle cases 🚨 ASSOCIATED WITH: • Distal radius fractures (Galeazzi fracture-dislocation) • Ulnar styloid base fractures
extraNodes.recommendation: Reduce with longitudinal traction + forced supination (dorsal) or pronation (volar). Above-elbow cast in position of stability × 4-6 weeks. URGENT ortho referral, especially if unstable. Always check DRUJ with distal radius fractures.

extraNodes.title: Wrist Ligament Injury Type
extraNodes.summary: Scapholunate: radial pain, Terry Thomas sign >5mm gap; TFCC: ulnar pain, clicking with rotation
extraNodes.body: Two major ligamentous injuries: 1. Scapholunate Dissociation • Disruption of scapholunate interosseous ligament • Radial-sided wrist pain • "Terry Thomas sign" (gap >5mm on PA X-ray) • Progressive SLAC wrist if untreated 2. TFCC (Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex) Tear • Ulnar-sided wrist pain • Clicking with forearm rotation • Associated with DRUJ instability • Often requires MRI or arthroscopy for diagnosis Both can be occult on plain films. Clinical suspicion guides management

extraNodes.title: Scapholunate Dissociation Management
extraNodes.body: Scapholunate Dissociation = Disruption of SL Interosseous Ligament Mechanism: Forceful wrist hyperextension in ulnar deviation (FOOSH) Clinical Presentation: • Radial-sided wrist pain • Tenderness over scapholunate interval (1cm distal to Lister tubercle) • Watson test (scaphoid shift test): Clunk/pain with scaphoid displacement • Weakened grip strength Imaging: • PA radiograph: - Scapholunate gap ≥5mm ("Terry Thomas sign" or "David Letterman sign") - Normal gap: ≤2mm - Clenched fist PA view accentuates gap • Lateral radiograph: - Scapholunate angle >70° (normal: 30-60°) - DISI pattern (dorsal
extraNodes.recommendation: Thumb spica splint. URGENT hand specialist referral (24-48h). Surgical repair within 6 weeks for best outcomes. Do not dismiss as simple sprain — risk of SLAC wrist.

extraNodes.title: TFCC Tear Management
extraNodes.body: Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex (TFCC) Tear Anatomy: TFCC = fibrocartilaginous disc + ulnar collateral ligament + ECU subsheath + radioulnar ligaments Mechanism: • Acute: FOOSH, axial loading with pronation/ulnar deviation • Degenerative: Chronic overload, positive ulnar variance Classification: • Class 1: Traumatic (1A-D) • Class 2: Degenerative (2A-E) Clinical Presentation: • Ulnar-sided wrist pain • Clicking/popping with forearm rotation • Point tenderness between pisiform and ulnar head • TFCC compression test: Pain with ulnar deviation + axial loading • Ulnar grind test: Pain with passi
extraNodes.recommendation: Ulnar gutter splint. Trial of conservative treatment × 3-6 weeks (splint, NSAIDs, rest). URGENT ortho if DRUJ unstable. Routine ortho if failed conservative treatment or mechanical symptoms. Many improve without surgery.

extraNodes.title: Wrist Imaging Approach
extraNodes.summary: PA + lateral + oblique standard; scaphoid view with ulnar deviation; always check DRUJ on lateral and carpal arcs on PA
extraNodes.body: Standard Wrist Series: • PA (posteroanterior) • Lateral (true lateral, not oblique) • Oblique Special Views: • Scaphoid view: PA with ulnar deviation + slight supination (for suspected scaphoid fracture) • Carpal tunnel view: Wrist hyperextended, hand supinated (for hook of hamate) • Clenched fist PA: Accentuates scapholunate dissociation Systematic Review: PA View: 1. Carpal arcs: Three smooth curves (proximal carpal row, distal carpal row, distal carpal articular surfaces) - Disruption suggests dislocation 2. Scapholunate gap: Normal ≤2mm; ≥5mm = dissociation 3. Carpal alignment: Lunate shou

extraNodes.title: Wrist Splinting Techniques
extraNodes.summary: Sugar tong for distal radius; thumb spica for scaphoid (even if XR negative); ulnar gutter for 4th/5th MC
extraNodes.body: Four Main Splint Types: 1. Volar Splint • Indications: Carpal fractures (except scaphoid), soft tissue injuries, stable distal radius • Position: Wrist 20° extension • Coverage: Volar forearm from proximal forearm to just proximal to MCP joints • Advantage: Allows thumb motion 2. Sugar Tong Splint • Indications: Acute distal radius fractures, distal ulna fractures • Position: Forearm neutral rotation, wrist neutral to 10-20° extension, elbow 90° • Coverage: U-shaped from dorsal MCPs, along dorsal forearm, around elbow, along volar forearm to volar MCPs • Advantage: Limits forearm rotation (pro

extraNodes.title: Wrist Injury Complications
extraNodes.summary: Acute CTS up to 20% of wrist fractures; AVN risk for scaphoid/lunate; always check DRUJ with radius fractures
extraNodes.body: 1. Acute Carpal Tunnel Syndrome • Incidence: Up to 20% of wrist fractures; 15-50% of perilunate dislocations • Pathophysiology: Hematoma, fracture displacement, soft tissue swelling compress median nerve • Presentation: Median nerve paresthesias (thumb, index, middle, radial half ring finger), thenar weakness (late) • Management: Urgent carpal tunnel decompression + fracture fixation • Best outcomes: Decompression within 40 hours of symptom onset 2. Avascular Necrosis (AVN) • High-risk fractures: - Scaphoid (especially proximal pole) — retrograde blood supply - Lunate (Kienböck disease) — tenu

extraNodes.title: Orthopedic Referral Guidelines
extraNodes.body: 🚨 EMERGENT Referral (Immediate ED Consultation): • Open fractures • Neurovascular compromise (absent pulses, motor deficit, acute carpal tunnel syndrome) • Compartment syndrome • Tense compartments, severe skin tenting • All perilunate/lunate dislocations (after ED reduction attempt) • Joint dislocation with neurovascular compromise • Irreducible dislocations ⚠️ URGENT Referral (24-48 Hours): • Intra-articular fractures with displacement • Unstable fractures (Barton, Smith, most DRUJ dislocations) • Scapholunate dissociation • TFCC injury with DRUJ instability • Fractures that lose reduction
extraNodes.recommendation: Refer emergently for open fractures, neurovascular compromise, compartment syndrome, or irreducible dislocations. Urgent referral (24-48h) for unstable fractures, intra-articular displacement, scapholunate dissociation, proximal scaphoid/lu
